Uniform Title: Merutantra Main Title: Merutantra with Ṭippanī Commentator: Raghunāthaśāstrī
Notes: Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S.G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0: October 21, 2009.
Revision 1: February 11, 2010 – chapters 21–23 added.
Revision 2: April 5, 2010 – Chapters 24 to the end added.
Publisher: Śrī Venkateśvara.
Year of Publication: 1908.
Place of publication: Bombay.
Country of publication: India.
Composed as a dialogue between Śrī Śiva and Śivā.
The Merutantra,
edited by the scholar Ojhopakhya Paṇḍita Raghunātha Śāstrī and refined with commentaries and other annotations.
Khemarāja Śrīkṛṣṇadāsa Prakāśana, Bombay edition, 1935.
Om.
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Salutations to the illustrious Gaurī and Śaṅkara.

Now the Meru Tantra begins: Salutations again and again to Her, by whom the non-existent appears as if existent, yet the existent never truly appears; and when She is known, that [appearance] no longer shines. || 1 ||
When the entire world of gods, asuras, and humans had been conquered by Jalandhara, they all sought refuge with Maheśa in a subtle form. || 2 ||
Having beheld him established in samādhi for thousands of divine years,
she was entreated and honored by those who follow the left-hand and right-hand paths.
Then Ambā, endowed with awakening, bowed to him and addressed him:
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others meditate upon you; whom, in turn, do you meditate upon? (4)
They call me the Supreme Śakti, and they call you the Supreme Śiva; out of compassion for me, tell me what the reality to be meditated upon by both of us is.
Having heard these words of theirs, Maheśvara smiled slightly and, having seated Brahmā,
Indra, and the others, spoke this speech.
Sadāśiva said: One hundred years is the maximum lifespan for humans; that constitutes one year for those of divine origin, and their lifespan is one hundred such years.
In that Kali Yuga, his supreme honor increases; according to the authority of the Dharmaśāstras, half of Dharma, three-quarters, and the whole shall prevail.
But this [period] is distinct from the Śaiva, Aindra, Āyuṣka, and Mānava; it is a year measured by human action, and time is that which fills the body.
A single day of Brahmā is said to consist of fourteen Indras; that Mahāmāyā who is meditated upon by me is the exhalation of his breath. (10)
The day of Brahmā is the *prapañca*, while his night is the *kumbhaka*; thus, by one of his *ghaṭikās*, a single year of the Creator is said to be measured.
Brahmā lives for one hundred ghaṭīs like a worm within her;
Satī [lives] for one fortnight, Śukla for a white fortnight, and Pārvatī for a black fortnight.
Hari lives for only a single season, while I, Śiva, live for only a year;
yet she is indeed the wife of Mahākāla for a full hundred years.
Like a snake casting its skin, having repeatedly abandoned the body, Mahākāla remains eternally young when he is brought under control by the *samaya*.
Having heard these words of his, the Goddess, Brahmā, Hari, and the gods, having brought about the dissolution of their ego, were terrified and bowed down once more. (15)
The gods said:
"Save us, save us, O Mahādeva, you who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge! We were all possessed by egoism, speaking thus: 'We are lords. (16)
"O Lord, though we are shameless and have been utterly defeated, we are but mosquitoes seeking the death of Jalandhara;
yet you do not act like a mosquito. (17)
O Sadāśiva, tell us: how is that Mahākāla to be known, before whom even he whom you and we regard as equal is not our equal by even half a quarter-part? 18.
"O God, how many kinds of liberation are there, and what is the supreme means for each? Tell us, if you have compassion for the Goddess, for Viṣṇu, and for the gods. (19)
Īśvara said:
By its power, everything is known through the words of the Vedas; moreover, the world created by his Māyā experiences joy and growth.
The number of tantras composed by me is one hundred and eight;
for whatever [purpose] I was requested, O Goddess, I was entreated by you. (21)
By means of the goddesses, the Pramathas, and the gods, that liberation is fourfold; whatever path leads to it, each such path has been revealed. || 22 ||
Therefore, O Goddess of the gods, those gods were deluded by egoism.
Constantly devoted to the six duties, they revile other gods.
Deprived of their good fortune by Kali, they become addicted to food, drink, and sexual intercourse; consequently, they are born poor and take on the form of hungry ghosts (pretas). || 24 ||
Indeed, the gods are seen by you exactly as you have correctly described; [you have spoken] the essence of the Vedas, the essence of Dharma, and the supreme heart of the Tantras. (25)
That which was proclaimed by Mahākāla as the means for liberation on the fifth [tithi], that tantra known as Meru becomes the Meru (the central peak) for all. || 26 ||
Let them listen to that which is being seen, which brings delight to the mind; and let those who are hesitant remove their own doubts by means of inquiry. (27)
Just as the clouds, having taken water from the ocean, rain it down by their own power, and the wind then reduces that water to the form of droplets. || 28 ||
In the same way, Mahāmāyā draws forth the portions of Great Time (Mahākāla); and those [portions], divided by actions, become millions of gods.
Just as drops attain the state of being raised through the quality of proximity, even so do the qualities of the path of worship attain the state of the deity. (30)
Just as water fallen from rivers into a pit might reach a lake, yet that lake would be far away from the surface, even so is the Lord deluded. || 31 ||
Again he becomes a man, again an animal, and the remainder is like a reservoir; again placed in the rays of the sun, again rain, and again water. (32)
In the same way, through evil karma, the living being decays within various wombs; just as a flood of water flows from a stream on the right path into a great river. || 33 ||
Having entered the ocean, he afterwards goes to the state of those who are not subject to rebirth.
Just as [the fire] from entering the belly of Vāḍava, so too does the individual soul [attain] divinity.
Having attained the state of Viṣṇu and the state of Śiva, he is born as Mahākāla.
Someone was brought from the ocean, but by fate he was abandoned there.
Just as it is with the ocean, so it is with the sons of Brahmā.
They are completely liberated through the knowledge of Brahman, having abandoned the sequence of ritual worship. || 36 ||
Śrī Devī said:
Through the distinction between the left and the right, and by the sequence of five and five, the worship of the Left and the Right is praised in various places. (37)
Therein, the activity of enjoyment, the activity of liberation, and even the dual activity are obtained; and what deity is there that is the most excellent of all? || 38 ||
Śiva said:
In ancient times, during the Kalpa when the great ocean was being churned by the gods and asuras, the goddess Śyāmā emerged there, holding a vessel of wine.
The goddess, fair-limbed and clad in reddish garments with a shimmering green bodice and a white upper covering, is the enchantress even of the three worlds. || 40 ||
Seeing those gods superior to the preceptor Śukra, all the Dānavas conquered them, seized her, and drank the liquor from that jar. || 41 ||
Seeing that the gods had fled, the Śaktis who were stationed there also drank that meritorious liquor, the mother of the deities. 42.
The mothers of the gods would grant even many boons;
those men who satisfy us with this [liquor] and take what remains are beyond doubt our very forms, the sole recipients of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 43 ||
Surā is the Gaṅgā, Surā is the Sindhu, Surā is the goddess Sarasvatī; Surā is the Godāvarī and the Revā—Surā alone is the supreme state. || 44 ||
Those fools who revile liquor are fools in birth after birth; those Śaktis are praised by Gandharvas, as are those Dānavas.
Furthermore, together with the gods who were lacking in strength, they churned the ocean once again.
He held a jar of nectar in his hand as he arrived from the intermediate region.
But they, intoxicated by wine, said, "What is this that has been brought by a man? Viṣṇu spoke sweetly, consoling them and deceiving them. (47)
"By drinking this liquor of mine, may you all become the gods of the past.
That which was produced at the very beginning is celebrated as *pīyūṣa* (nectar). Even though it was extracted by the Puruṣa for the sake of the gods, it has now become essence-less. || 48 ||
Then Hari, assuming the form of Mohinī, caused her to drink [the nectar] with her left hand while [he himself] caused the former gods,
Śaktis, and all the red ones such as Bhairava and others to drink it; he uttered these mantras while raining [nectar],
and with his right hand, causing the gods to drink the nectar, those respective mantras were recited.
He oppressed the former gods; Śukrācārya understood all of that which had occurred in the battle. || 50 ||
Then, his eyes copper-red with rage, he took water in his hand and uttered a curse.
"Fie, fie upon the knowledge of the enemies of the gods! It has been stolen away by this liquor. || 51 ||
Therefore, all those who drink this [liquor] are indeed sinners; let them go to a terrible hell and remain here like Piśācas. || 52 ||
Having heard that terrible curse, the gods then blazed with anger.
As if burning away the three worlds, the gods and asuras trembled. || 53 ||
Then I praised the Goddess with the most excellent hymns containing the seed-syllables (bīja-garbha), and Śukra was cast at her feet: "O Mother, let this son be united with me. (54)
"Either through illusion or through pleasure, let those who have been awakened for three years release the curse of Śukra once more, and let them regain their original complexion and luster."
The mantra of whichever [deity] one worships is encased by its seed-syllable.
The hymn known as the Ṣoḍaśārṇa is declared to consist of one hundred and eight mantra-words.
"He renders the target free from curses, making him a single vessel for both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O Goddess, this is the sequence of initiation that has come down in their lineage. (57)
O Goddess, that Kaula is difficult to find; he is the giver, the enjoyer, and the purifier. That path in which he is the primary authority is known as the Vāmapatha. || 58 ||
Liquor, meat, fish, parched grain, and sexual intercourse.
One who has entered the path of the family should always practice this with great joy. || 59 ||
The Kaulika [mudrā] reaches the thumb; the Vāma [mudrā] is equal to the index finger; the Madhyama [mudrā] is the Cīna-krama;
and that which is the lowest is the Siddhāntin. || 60 ||
The Śābara path is the youngest; thus, the left [path] is fivefold. Those by whom the nectar was drunk are the Soma-drinkers, arrogant with power.
Together with Lakṣmī, they were born, as were the Śatayatnas and the Somapas.
The worship of them has been declared by the twice-born to be performed according to the path of Dakṣa.
The Vedic rite is the most excellent; the Smārta rite is middling and superior.
The ancient [tradition] is known as the middle one, while the Tantric is remembered as the inferior.
The worship of Kālī, which belongs to the lineage of the Goddess (Daiśī) and is the youngest, is the best when the Vāmamārga enters the Dakṣa [path]. // 64 //
He is also afflicted by obstacles and does not attain success. O gods, when the path of the right enters the left, then [this occurs]. || 65 ||
They cause that speaker of falsehood to fall into both worlds and swallow him up.
Therefore, having understood one's own family lineage, one should perform worship.
When both the disciple and the preceptor are endowed with devotion and faith and possess all the required characteristics,
then every path bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation at that very moment.
In the Kali age, however, gurus seek wealth while disciples seek supernatural powers; therefore, there is no accomplishment for either, and it is merely a mockery of the deities.
(5) For the twice-born who have not undergone initiation, there is no entitlement here to their own duties such as Vedic study and the like, nor to rites such as the *upanayana*. (69)
And likewise, for those who are uninitiated, [there is no entitlement] to the worship of Manu, the gods, and so forth.
Therefore, one has no authority [to perform it]; hence, one should first consecrate oneself with mantras.
Knowledge and discernment are bestowed, and heaps of sins are destroyed; therefore, when this is received from the mouth of a true guru, it is called *dīkṣā*. || 71 ||
How can one who is himself lost, being a false teacher, deliver another?
He who is endowed with twenty-one qualities shall be a guru.
He who is most excellent, possessing the aforementioned limbs, pure in appearance, and captivating to the mind.
He knows the reality of all paths and limbs, and he is conversant with the ritual procedures of all mantras.
One who has distanced himself from the wicked by observing their hints, facial expressions, and gestures.
Inward-turned, with vision not directed outward, he is omniscient and knows both place and time.

Accomplished through his master’s command, endowed with compassion, peaceful, and a knower of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, he was devoted to blameless rites—whether obligatory, occasional, or performed for specific desires. (75)
A teacher who is free from greed, non-violent, and impartial is considered a true guru. A mantra from such an unworthy teacher causes the suffering of death and exhaustion.
A Brahmin should be made our teacher of such a kind; if not, then one who is like this.
One born of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes should not initiate [a disciple] in the reverse order.
On the path of the right-hand way (dakṣamārga), he is devoid of power over his father and maternal grandfather;
on the left-hand way (vāmamārga), however, he is exceedingly powerful over his uterine brother who lives as a householder.
The teacher should examine the disciple, who is endowed with the characteristics recognized by the learned.
One should initiate him for twelve years, or half of that, or even half of that again.
One who knows the authority of the Guru’s words and is devoted to service of the Guru.
Free from shame, pride, arrogance, and the like, he is the leader of his lineage. || 80 ||
He was indifferent toward the teacher's property and longed for his favor.
Devoted to recitation and meditation, he was one who had set out upon the path to liberation. || 81 ||
One who is endowed with the practice of meditative concentration, possesses a pure body, is righteous, firm in his vows, of good conduct, and is filled with faith and devotion. || 82 ||
He spoke words that were humble, truthful, immeasurable, and affectionate, and was esteemed by the virtuous.
It is consistent, endowed with what is dear, steadfast, and beneficial to all. || 83 ||
One should always maintain a pleasant countenance toward the disciple for the sake of pleasing the deity;
however, by bestowing initiation out of greed or other such motives, one incurs the curse of the deity.

Initiation is indeed fruitless for one who is a disciple of another, for one of a low lineage, for a rogue, for one who fancies himself a scholar, for one who hates women, for one bound by worldly conventions, for one who is terrified, or for one who is physically impaired. || 85 ||
A mantra arising from the Veda does not exist apart from the Praṇava; therefore, a mantra is considered supreme to the Veda, and the Āgama is remembered as a limb (aṅga) of the Veda. || 86 ||
Rites such as subjugation and attraction, which bestow both visible and invisible fruits, as well as all [rites] such as the sacrifice to the planets, are indeed accomplished through the Veda. (87)

There are no sacrifices without the Veda, nor are there Vedas devoid of sacrifice. Therefore, a mantra is said to be supreme when based on the Veda; a mantra not rooted in the Veda is not considered a mantra at all. 88.
There is no entitlement for Śūdras to the mantras beyond the [prescribed] rules. (p.
6) As many syllables as one might impart to a Śūdra of the mantras, [for that many years he must undergo penance]. 89.

"There would be as many killings of a Brahmin as there were [omissions]; therefore, one should perform his consecration. One should give him what is appropriate for his own caste, devoid of the [specific] syllable 'svāhā', and afterwards, that which is Tantric. (90)

Even by women and Śūdras, worship should be performed according to the path taught in their own scriptures; and by those [others], it should be performed with Sanskrit according to the way taught in their own scriptures.
A widow may be initiated at the command of her son, and a maiden by the order of her father;
for it is the husband alone who always remains the spiritual preceptor (guru) of his wife.

He should be worshipped by her as well with all ritual means, according to the understanding of the Lord; whether he be a Śaiva or a Vaiṣṇava, for women and Śūdras, his name should end with "namaḥ" (salutation). || 93 ||
Knowing this to be the name-mantra, one should initiate even outcastes (cāṇḍālas). || 94 ||
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those born of the Paulastya lineage.
The five types of men are well known, and they are to be given [in marriage] according to the natural order. || 95 ||
The syllable *māyā* is the seed-syllable of a Brāhmaṇa, while *śrī* is recorded as the seed-syllable of a Kṣatriya.
The seed-syllable of desire (Kāma) is for the Vaiśya, while Vāgbhava is said to be for the Śūdra.
The mantra known as Paulastya consists of four seed-syllables. One should not bestow a mantra of a higher caste upon one of a lower caste. || 97 ||
The *anuṣṭubh* mantras of Śakti, Nīlasarasvatī, and Vindhyavāsinī as declared in the *Kalpa*, should be given by Brahmins according to the Vedic tradition. (98)
The [mantra] named Pāśupata should be given by Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas as well; the Saudarśanī, the Nārasiṃhī, and that of Kārtavīrya are not from any other source. 99.
The Aghora-mantra of Dakṣiṇāmūrti should also be imparted to those of the three castes.
The eight-syllable Hayagrīva mantra, as well as the Umā-Māheśvara mantra.
[Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa], [Vāsudeva], and Varāhaka. || 101 ||
Agni, Sūrya, Ghṛṇi, Tāra, and the others who are the lords of Aruṇa;
Kālikā as well as Śyāmalā should be bestowed upon all castes.
Chinnamastā, Mātaṅgī, Bagalā, and Ugratārā; the Yoginīs, the wives of the Yakṣas, the Traipuras, Baṭuka, and the others. || 103 ||
The Śābaras and Pulastyas do not perform recitation for the sake of being born as twice-born. Worship is said to be threefold, and among them, the Sāttvika is the most excellent. (104)
Among these, mental worship is considered the most excellent form of worship. The southern path is characterized by passion (rājasa), as is worship performed before an image. || 105 ||

It is distinguished by all the formal verbal expressions at its beginning and end; the Tāmasa form of worship is said to consist of the offering of oblations (bali) upon the pedestal and other such items. || 106 ||
Therefore, having abandoned the first letter, the left path is praised;
this is declared to be the supreme path among both the left and the right. || 107 ||
It is concealed in all tantras; what else do you wish to hear? || 108 ||
Thus ends the first chapter, the Illumination of the System of Rules as Proclaimed by Śiva, in the Merutantra, authorized by the illustrious Mahāmāyā and Mahākāla. 1.
The Goddess said:
O Lord, hundreds of people here are established on the path of Tantra, yet nowhere is success (siddhi) seen; will it perhaps come about in the next world? || 1 ||
If karma is the primary factor, what is the use of propitiating the deities? If propitiating the deities were truly effective, why would practitioners be suffering? (2)
Cut through this doubt of mine: what is the purpose of these wheels and mantras?
And tell me how the ritual procedures (saṃskāra) of the Tantrikas are to be performed. || 3 ||
The Lord said:
One should perform three rites while [the child] is in the womb, and likewise ten while being born;
then three more rites—thus the sacraments (saṃskāras) are traditionally recorded as sixteen.
The preceptor should perform the three rites with mantras for the twice-born; then he should initiate ten disciples, and once the mantra is mastered, he should perform the three rites again.
Six birth-sacraments are prescribed even for women and Śūdras;
likewise, six mantra-sacraments alone are proclaimed for them as well.
Indeed, those same four [mantras] prescribed for the Cāṇḍālas and others are mentioned in the Mantra-kalpa;
and the three mentioned in the Yavana-kalpa are likewise present in those mantras.

Listen to how they should be arranged according to the distinction between left and right: one should prepare liquor in the place of clarified butter on the left for the purpose of the fire-oblation and other rites.
And meat may be used in cooking and other such acts; however, specific rules are prescribed regarding mountains and similar locations.
Sexual union, celibacy, and likewise the mudrās pertaining to those actions.
First, the rite of conception (garbhādhāna) should be performed according to the procedure prescribed in one's own ritual manual.
Then, one should perform the second limb on the right and the left [sides]. || 10 ||
One should satisfy the deity of the limbs with mantras, and the womb from the sacred sites (tīrtha). One should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) upon the limbs of this goddess.
One should contemplate all the nyāsas within one's own body and that [form] as Bhairavī; having oneself become Bhairava, one should perform the act of union.
Seated on a comfortable seat and forming the *bhaga* and the *dhvaja*, one should recite this mantra five thousand times; thus one obtains a son according to one's desire. || 13 ||
"Lakṣmī, Prāṇeśvarī, and Ceti—protect me; this is the nine-syllable mantra."
Soma was her womb, and Sūrya remained within her as the embryo upon the surface of the earth.
Now, the second sacrament called Puṃsavana should be performed; the wise man should perform the Puṃsavana in the third month. (15)

On the day prescribed by the Vedas and proclaimed [by tradition], according to the method stated in one's own ritual manual (kalpa), there [in that place], at the site of the Vedic primary fire-sacrifice (homa), one's own deities [should be worshipped]. || 16 ||
One should offer oblations by means of the causal [mantra] exactly four times; for the deities of those enclosures, two oblations each for the male deities. || 17 ||
One woman [is required] in the Vāmamārga; the rest has been declared as before. One should offer a sacrifice to Bhairava at night, together with a sacred site and an animal. 18.
Furthermore, the third sacrament is proclaimed as that called Sīmantonnayana (the parting of the hair).
In the fourth, sixth, and eighth months, [the results are] good, middling, and inferior, respectively. || 19 ||

On a day prescribed by the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra), according to the method taught in her own Kalpa, Vāmī should inscribe the deity-mantra on the parting of the hair (sīmanta) with beautiful lines.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of that disease-removing mantra upon her limbs; thereafter, out of fear of the deity’s curse, one should not approach that wife. (21)

Whether through desire, or delusion, or at an improper time, or by some other unlawful means, a union that is performed in such a manner is called *sīmanta*, and it leads downward from there. || 22 ||
Then, however, one should perform the fourth consecration (turya-saṃskāra) even for women and Śūdras.
The Brahmin should perform the rite called Jātakarman according to the procedure prescribed in his own Kalpa.
Upon the birth of a daughter for Brahmins, or the birth of a son for a Śūdra, one should perform the rite silently,
preceded by the remembrance of Viṣṇu.
One who follows the left-hand path (vāmamārgī) should not perform the rite for generating intelligence; rather, he should write with a golden stylus at the tip of his hand. 25.

One should satisfy the root seed-syllable in the region of the palate, as well as the mantra in the tongue; thereafter, one should satisfy the deity, and the remaining ritual action is to be performed as on the right side.
Now, the fifth sacrament, called the naming ceremony (nāmakarma), is indeed fixed [for the day of birth].
Thus it has been prescribed for all that, at the end of the period of impurity (sūtaka), on an auspicious day, [the rite should be performed]. || 27 ||

One should perform the naming ceremony according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Kalpa. Furthermore, those sixteen wheels of measures (mātrācakras) which are mentioned in the Tantras [should be employed]. (28)

Having deliberated upon them, one should perform that naming ceremony which will be fruitful. If such a name has not been performed here, and if the Guru is of such a nature, then [the following should be done]. || 29 ||
One should perform the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka); that is now described along with its seed-syllables (sabīja).
For it is by means of the qualities of the senses that the success of the Brahmins is fully accomplished. || 30 ||
I shall now proclaim the Tārā-cakra for the sake of the mantra-attainment of beginners: A Ā Haye Iryame Ca, and likewise Ī U Ū Vahnibhe. (31)
The vowels ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, and ḹ are in Rohiṇī; e is in Mṛgaśiras and Śivabha (Ārdrā); ai is in Punarvasu; o and au are in Puṣya;
the letter ka is in Āśleṣā; and kha and ga are in Maghā.
In the Pitṛ (Maghā) asterism, *gha* and *ṅa* are prescribed; in Bhaga (Pūrvaphalgunī) and Āryama (Uttaraphalgunī), *cha* and *ja* are considered [the lords]; in Hasta, *jha* and *ña*;
in Tvaṣṭṛ (Citrā), *ṭa* and *ṭha*; in Svāti, *ḍa*; and in Viśākha, *ḍha* and *ṇa*. (33)
Likewise, when it is in Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, or Mūla, [the letter] *dha*; in Pūrvāṣāḍhā, the letters *na*, *pa*, and *pha*;
and in Viśvabha (Uttarāṣāḍhā), the letter *bha*.
Ma and ka are in Dhaniṣṭhā; ra and la are in Śatatārakā;
va and śa are in Pūrvabhādrapadā; and ṣa, sa, and ha should be in the penultimate [asterism, i.e., Uttarabhādrapadā]. (35)
Laṃ, kṣaṃ, aṃ, and aḥ are to be counted among the Revatī asterism according to the syllables of the mantra.
The results, however, are determined by repeating three times the letters of the name of the person for whom the rite is intended, as well as their corresponding asterisms. || 36 ||
Loss of position, association with the wicked, excessive friendship, and death—these, or mental anguish or physical disease, the practitioner encounters for the sake of accomplishing his task. (37)
The onset of many enemies, calamity, and the loss of prosperity—having understood these fruits of the circle of stars (tārācakra), one should act accordingly. || 38 ||
Having understood the division [of letters] through the Mātṛkās spoken by Tārā for both the practitioner and the object of practice, [one should proceed].
One should consider the *gaṇacakra* for both a woman and a man, or even for each of them individually.
Firm, with fierce waves and currents, this is known as the Raudra Naraka.
The lion, the enemy (the tiger), the sun, the moon, the wind, the fire, the elephant, and the horse [are the eight guardians]. || 40 ||
The remaining [planets] are deities and Rākṣasas; this is the result for the practitioner and the one being practiced.
The fruit for both humans and gods is swift; for those who are separated, the fruit comes through hardship.
From the separation of the human and the Daitya through the favor of Manu, death shall occur.
A battle between a god and a dānava would be fruitless if they were separated. || 42 ||
One should examine the Moon-wheel among the mantras of the planets and their satellites;
they say it consists of four, three, two, two, two, and six [squares]. || 43 ||
Then, from the six groups [of letters], one should take the six syllables of the name from the positions of the mantra.
Wherever the first letter occurs, there this result shall be. || 44 ||
A beloved servant and a nourisher is auspicious, as is one who causes freedom from disease and bestows sons.
It brings happiness from women, produces wind, bestows good fortune, and accomplishes one's undertakings. || 45 ||
The Mātṛkās in the yantras are said to be both profit-giving and loss-causing.
For women, Śūdras, and those born of inverse castes (pratiloma), worship is performed with name-mantras.

The previously mentioned zodiac signs are to be known as beginning with Pisces (Mīna), and the castes as beginning with the twice-born (Brāhmaṇa). Among these, the Manu of the highest caste, specifically the Vedic one, is to be accepted here. || 47 ||
Now I shall describe the five-elemental [mantra], which brings about accomplishment on the Kaulika path.
One should place the five elements—wind, fire, earth, water, and space. || 48 ||
Two vowels each should be written on the base (tale), and thereafter, the letters beginning with 'ya' [should be written].
The six groups beginning with *ka* as well, and *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, *ha*, and likewise *kṣa*.
The mantra should be written repeatedly, with its name equal in number to the syllables of the mantra.
Therefore, Manu should be written again so that the completion may occur simultaneously. 50.

Having first written down [the mantra] as many times as necessary, one should then investigate the reality of the phonemes (varṇatattva). The form (rūpa) should be established within the single reality and within the reality of friendship; such is its power.

One quarter [of the strength] is assigned to a neutral planet; its conjunction, divided by five, becomes the desired [strength]. However, the enemy's strength is one unit, while for an equal [planet], it is half. || 52 ||
Likewise, if it is in a friend [house], it is a quarter; that [result] would be as difficult [to endure] as a sixteenth part. || 53 ||

But when the desired [result] is predominant and the difficulty is slight, one should perform the practice for mantra-siddhi; otherwise, ghosts, vetālas, and piśācas cause obstacles to the mantra. (54)
There is friendship between earth and water, and also between fire and wind; likewise, there is a commonality between fire and earth, as well as between water and wind.
The wheel of the enemy is composed of the five elements and functions in the opposite manner.
I shall now describe the wheel of the Siddhas and others, knowing which one should perform the naming ceremony.
On the path of southern worship, one should [place] one's own mantra and one's own deity in the twelve-spoked wheel,
excluding the *kūṭas* and *ṣaṇḍhas*.
One should inscribe the letters from 'a' to 'kṣa' starting from the east and extending as far as the northeast (Īśvara).
Starting from the syllable of one's own name, it should be known to extend up to the final syllable of the mantra. || 58 ||
The *siddha*, the *sādhya*, the *susiddha*, and the *ari* are to be understood again and again.
The *siddha* succeeds in due time; the *sādhya* may succeed or it may not. (59)
By the very act of grasping [the mantra] well-perfected, one cuts down the root of the enemy. Now I shall describe the *Siddhimātṛkā* for the accomplishment of the Great Vidyā. (60)
In that [mandala], sixteen squares should be known according to the root sequence;
one should properly arrange the letters of the Mātṛkā in these squares in their respective order. (61)
The bulls [of the zodiac] are located at six, three, one, four, five, twelve, ten, and sixteen [degrees].
In that [diagram], squares for the five limbs, the lunar days (tithi), and the Viśvedevas are proclaimed.
First, the Siddhas and others are to be known in the four squares and in the intermediate directions.
Then, according to the instructions of the Guru, one should [count] from the square reached by each respective position using the previous finger. || 63 ||

A *siddha* mantra becomes effective through recitation; a *siddhasādhya* mantra becomes effective with double that number. A *siddhasusiddha* mantra brings about great success, while a *siddhāri* mantra destroys one's kinsmen.

A *sādhya* [disposition] that is unestablished causes extreme affliction; a *sādhya* that is difficult to establish produces great suffering. A *sādhya* that is easily established [arises] from devotion; a *sādhya* that is an enemy destroys its own support. (65)
From Susiddhasiddha, Urdhvajapa, and Bahurūpa, one proceeds to Tatpara; then Atidruta, Dvija, Susiddha, Susiddhāri, and Kulāpaha. || 66 ||

An *ari* [planet] in the *siddha* state kills the son; an *ari* in the *sādhya* state kills the daughter. An *ari* in the *susiddha* state kills the wife; likewise, an *ari* in the *ari* state destroys the practitioner (*sādhaka*). (67)
In this context, there may be a well-known name by which one should be awakened;
however, as for the mantra consisting of seed-syllables, the six-petalled [lotus] therein contains the Mātṛkās.
In that regard, one should fashion an auspicious six-petalled lotus;
there, one should place the letters of the Mātṛkā, excluding the *kūṭas* and the neuter (*ṣaṇḍha*) vowels. (69)
One should investigate, beginning from that point where the first syllable of one's own name occurs.
Generosity, poverty, fortitude, and the danger of conflict with kinsmen. || 70 ||
The total destruction [of the mantra] occurs gradually through the letters beginning with 'ka' starting from the grid;
for the sake of explaining how the success of the mantra may be achieved, I shall speak of this. || 71 ||
The matrices of wealth and debt are multiplied by zero, five, six, three, two, four, six, and eight.
I shall now explain here how the eleven vowels are to be written as numerical figures.
On that level, the letters should be written on glass or mica, numbering thirty-three.
Below that are [the distances] of two, seven, four, three, seven, five, and four [yojanas]. (73)
The six and five figures of the practitioner and the figures of the mantra have been previously described.
Of the mantra-syllables, distinguished by vowels and consonants, [one should recite] each one separately. || 74 ||
Furthermore, the application of the marks should be performed according to the name of the practitioner.
Both remaining portions should be set aside until the name-number of the Manu is reached. (75)
If there is an excess, that mantra should be given to the practitioner; it is thereby accomplished.
One should accomplish that same number of unions, even those that are difficult to achieve. || 76 ||

And if [the practitioner] is deficient due to the conjunction of planets as well as the birth in an inauspicious lunar mansion (ṛkṣa), he should perform the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) once again for the sake of rekindling the power of the mantra. || 77 ||
But the practitioner is to be known as a debtor when the mark of the practitioner is greater.
As long as there may be a remainder, for that long one should perform the counting of the numerical units.
When his state becomes equal to that which is known as *puraścaraṇa*, then, having performed the *puraścaryā* once more, he shall become an accomplisher of all tasks. || 79 ||

Once a single task has been accomplished, that [mantra] again becomes blunt; only by performing the recitation (japa) once more does it become capable of accomplishing another task. This truth, which is hidden in all the Tantras, has been revealed here. 80.

(11) However, for the sake of victory when two [fighters] are contending, I shall incidentally describe the *mallamātṛkā* (the Mother of Wrestlers). One should indeed construct its wheel in this very manner. 81.

The syllables *pa*, *ñca*, *pañ*, *ca*, *gni*, *rā*, *mā*, *gni*, *ra*, *sa*, *rtū*, *gra*, *mu*, *khā*, *ni*, *kha*, *bhu*, and *śca* should be written; below these, the five [vowels] excluding the neuter ones (*e*, *ai*, *o*, *au*, *am*) should be placed. (82)
The eleven vowels, excluding the final one (ḥ), should be written beneath that.
One should write the letters beginning with ka, ca, and ṭa, excluding the characters ṅa, ña, and ṇa.
The conjunction of the names and syllables is determined by the remainder of the sum of the two; when the two are equal, their sum should be divided by eight and the remainder taken. || 84 ||

One who possesses [the required number of] letters in one's own Veda, Ṛtu, Śara, Agni, Bhū, and Śeṣa is victorious over the opponent. In this case, when both are equal, Kali prevails in the absence of Mantra and Yantra. 85.
I shall now describe the measure of a thief, which is to be understood in relation to both the deposit and the thief.
Six, two, three, five, seven, four, seven, six, and one thousand [years]. || 86 ||

The upper digits are as before; the remainder is the sum of the digits reduced by eight. In case of a deficit, there is a loss; in case of a surplus, there is victory. This must be kept secret, O Bharas. (87)
I shall now describe the Rājamātrā, which bestows victory upon two kings.
The numbers of the eight classes are fire, water, six, Vedas, moon, and fires. || 88 ||

One should divide the two by seven; if the remainder is greater [than zero], there is victory. If the remainders are equal, [victory is determined] by the strength of the varga, or by the vital force (prāṇavīrya) of the sum of the vargas. || 89 ||
I shall now declare the Mātṛkā-kalaha, which bestows victory in conflict.
One should write the five vowels, which are [represented by] the numbers three, one, four, two, and one.
Below that, the number of letters in the name [of the practitioner] starting from 'ka' is the same for both.
If the remainder is greater than five, there is victory; if it is less, there is defeat. || 91 ||
Listen to the Mātṛkā, which grants victory to men and women in love or in battle.
In the [years] fifty-six, three, four, three, two, one, and zero, the arrows (five) were placed. || 92 ||

One should write the letters beginning with 'ka' as they are declared by the Sun, distributed three and two times below; having gathered the numerical values of the letters of the name according to the sequence of the divisions of the mātrās. || 93 ||

If the remainder after division by seven is greater [in one's own number], there is victory; if less, there is defeat. But if the remainder is equal, one should make a distinction based on the vital breaths (prāṇa) and the classes (varga). || 94 ||
May the deities listen to this measure for the sake of the general’s victory.
Six flavors, three fires, two eyes, eight serpents, six limbs, four oceans, and three fires. || 95 ||
The sky and the earth, along with what lies beneath them, are to be written here; the vowels previously mentioned are to be placed within these.
In this case, the sum of the first two figures is subtracted from eight; if the result is less than eight, it is a loss, but if it is greater, there is victory. (96)
One should write the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ha*, excluding the neuter letters *ṅa*, *ña*, and *ṣa*.
The sequence is six, three, four, two, six, seven, three, one, zero, and earth (one). || 97 ||
Having drawn the figures beneath the messenger and the mace, the measurement of the figures is established.
If there are eight plus six [i.e., fourteen] dots, it shall be the life of a swordsman. || 98 ||

"In the case of equality, it is as stated before"; thus these sixteen Mātṛkās have been declared. One should learn this from the mouth of the Guru and perform the rites of naming and action accordingly. 99.
The sixth sacrament, the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana), is common to all people.
For Śūdras and others, [the rite] is performed without mantras, according to the procedure prescribed for their own class. || 100 ||
There, the Pitṛs are joined with the Bhairavas on the left-hand path; these eight deities of the wheel are to be offered at the conclusion of the worship. (101)
Reciting the root mantra, one should bestow the fruit together with the sacred water (satīrtha); for one who has performed the ritual in this manner, no misfortune from hunger shall arise. (102)
Now, O Pārvatī, hear about the seventh sacrament called Cauḍa.
Thus has been taught for all the destruction of the sins committed in childhood.
Neither for the Buddhists nor for the Yavanas is the topknot established here.
And this should also be performed by women for the increase of their good fortune and health. || 104 ||

A crest should be fashioned on the left, and the hair should be equal to the seed-syllables of the mantra; having cast it into a sacred ford, one should bury it in the earth—this is the special rule for those of the Left-hand path (Vāmīs). || 105 ||
Now I shall describe the eighth sacrament, the binding of the girdle of muñja grass; leading [the boy] into the presence of the preceptor is known as the initiation (upanayana). || 106 ||

One should perform that for the sake of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Tantra. First, the initiation into the family lineage (*kuladīkṣaṇa*) must be performed by twice-born practitioners of the Left-hand Path (*vāmācāra*). (107)

If the initiation with the Sāvitrī mantra is performed later [than the initiation with the deity], one becomes fallen due to this transposition. The initiation with the minor deity should come first, and likewise that with the great deity should follow. || 108 ||
When the Bṛhaddaivata mantra has been mastered, the minor [mantras] become self-subdued;
one should receive their mantra-initiation and then commence the preparatory rite (puraścaryā). || 109 ||
One should never perform ritual applications (prayoga) for anyone other than one's own beloved; nor should one cause a worthy disciple or a good son to be initiated by another. 110.
If one should give a perfected mantra to another out of greed or fear, the disciple attains success, but a curse arises for the guru. || 111 ||
Whichever deity one is devoted to and in whatever path that devotion lies, that very personal knowledge (svavidyā) shall become sovereign, like a king, within that particular path. 112.
O Pārvatī, one hundred and eight tantras have been proclaimed by me; whichever [tantra] was asked about by anyone, that has been described in detail.
I shall speak without partiality, according to the truth, as it is in the Merutantra:
"The Vedic is superior to all, and the Smārta is even more excellent than that. (114)
Then there is the Tantra, and even there, the oceans are joined together.
Yāmalā, from her union with him, as well as Mantrīśānī and Tāṇḍava. (115)
The Indrajāla, the Kakṣapuṭī, the Buddhist, the Jain, and the Śabara [traditions].
It should be understood that [the status] diminishes in sequence, with primacy according to what is appropriate. 116.

If one worships that which is base, one will surely fall; for that which is base inevitably falls from the high. And he shall grant knowledge to everyone who performs their duty according to his own conduct.

One should know the tenth sacrament as that called the Prājāpatya-vrata; it may be performed either according to the Vedic path or, alternatively, according to the Tantric path as taught in one's own ritual manual. || 118 ||
In the consecration of this vow, the mantra of Gāṇapati is prescribed.
Vakratuṇḍa and the others are on the right, while Ucchiṣṭa and the others are on the left.

One should perform the tenth rite, the Saumya-saṃskāra, according to the Vedic vow; however, a follower of Tantra should perform it in that same place according to the path prescribed in his own ritual manual.
One should receive the Bhairava mantra or that known as Baṭuka from the Vāmaka tradition.
To the south of whichever [liṅga] there may be, belonging to the division of Kālabhairava.
Since Bhairava is the destroyer of those who merely perform the preliminary rites (puraścaryā) as worshippers, the Svarṇākarṣaṇa-Bhairava should be adopted by practitioners who are poor. 122.
The twice-born should perform the eleventh sacrament, known as the Āgneya vow.
In that place, however, the practitioner of Tantra should perform [the rite] according to the path prescribed in the Gṛhya texts.
At the outset, one should receive the mantras of the deities of the limbs from the mouth of the guru.
The mantras for worship and so forth, their instructions, and likewise the rules regarding the ritual substances.
And the twelfth sacrament is called the Vaiśvadeva-vrata;
in that place, there should be initiation (dīkṣā) into one's own chosen Tantric mantra.
The thirteenth sacrament is proclaimed as the Godāna;
in its place, the Tantrika should perform the Sarvapāpavimokṣaṇa.
Seated in a pure place, having placed a mirror or water in a vessel before him, he should then make this request with truthful speech: || 127 ||
Desiring to perform the *puraścaraṇa* rite, I am intent on destroying my sin; I shall perform my recitation until the afternoon—may the deities be my witnesses. (128)
O deities, as long as sins remain within my body, so do earth, water, fire, ether, wind, sun, moon, and the stars. || 129 ||
And let my reflection appear as if mingled with sins;
let it be seen just as one sees [the image] when mercury has been stilled. || 130 ||
Having become pure and consisting of existence and consciousness, one should contemplate the personification of sin.
It is black, situated in the right side of the abdomen, and the size of a thumb.
It has a head joined with the murder of a Brahmin, arms from the theft of gold, a heart from the drinking of liquor, and a waist associated with violating the teacher's bed. (132)
It was a pair of humps joined by evil, with hair like minor sins;
it bore ringworm and leprosy, being wicked, face-downward, and most unbearable. || 133 ||

Having reflected thus, one should then perform the recitation (japa) while contemplating; at the conclusion of the recitation, one should again visualize the personification of sin as being consumed away. || 134 ||
When a mirror or similar object is clear and all reflections are seen therein, then one's sin has departed and one is fit for the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa). || 135 ||
The fourteenth sacrament is called *samāvartana* (the return home); in its place, the Tantric practitioners should perform the *puraścaryā*. 136.
Having first performed the abbreviated worship on the day, the Kaulika should perform the recitation until evening,
and likewise the worship of the circle at night.
Accompanied by the Śaktis and endowed with the five M-s (pañcamakāra) and so forth, one thus attains success; not otherwise, even through ten million recitations. || 138 ||
Marriage is ordained as the fifteenth [sacrament] for all;
however, the marriage of a widow should be performed with a pippala tree alone. (139)
Freed from all sins, she shall indeed go to the abode of Viṣṇu; but if she be a non-Brāhmaṇa woman, she may likewise take another man as her husband.
The sixteenth [book], known as the Pitṛmedha, is according to the path prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra.
There, in that place of the deity, the one following the Vedic tradition [should worship] his own deity according to the Tantric system.

Having set them aside, one should perform the śrāddha for those Brāhmaṇas who have died while on a journey; or else, in their absence, for those who were on the road at the time of the sacrificer's death. 142.

One should perform the *āmaśrāddha* (the raw-food ancestral rite) for one's mother, while the *palapaitṛka* (the meat-based ancestral rite) is for the father. Brāhmaṇas endowed with power (*śakti*) are considered followers of the Kaula path in the worship of the *cakra*. 143.
One should avoid *tulasī* there and worship with *bhṛṅgarāja*; the cooked offerings of the Kaula substances and the ritual cakes (*piṇḍas*) should be sprinkled with blood. || 144 ||
The supreme practitioner, consecrated by these sixteen purificatory rites, [is perfected].
Then he should be known as one liberated while living; in his capacity, he is equal to a deity. || 145 ||
Now, I shall here describe the sixteen consecrations established by mantra.
By performing these mantras created by the gods, one is liberated from curses.
Now, first of all, I shall describe the awakening of all mantras; it must be performed by the guru for the sake of the disciple's accomplishment. (147)

One should recite the seed-syllable of Tārā and Agni when it belongs to the Āgneyaka [day]; the other, belonging to Soma, is the time for sleep during the flow of the Iḍā [nāḍī] for one whose form is that of Agni.
The *saumya* [mantra] should reside in the *piṅgalā*; elsewhere, those two remain in a state of wakefulness. At the time of awakening, the mantra, having been incited, becomes awakened. (149)

Alternatively, having encased the letters beginning with 'la' and ending with 'na', together with the bindu and then with the visarga, one should recite them alone at the three periods of the day. 150.
When recited in this manner, it is beloved and, once awakened, bestows swift accomplishment. Now, O Pārvatī, hear the awakening of the Śabara mantras. (151)
Having brought a bell-metal vessel that has been purified with ashes and other such means.
One should mutter [the mantra] eight hundred times during each watch of the day and night.
One should strike a bell-metal vessel with a staff made of Khadira wood and say:
"O Mantra, wake up! Speak now in the fourth [age]. || 153 ||
During the watch (yāma), one should offer an oblation (bali) in a bronze vessel for Bhairava, consisting of an egg-born creature—that is, a cock;
for other deities, one should crack open a coconut.
When the ancient gods were utterly deluded by wine and nectar, then the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana spoke. || 155 ||
"Who among you is worthy of worship, and who is the most excellent? Let that be told."
Then the gods, becoming intoxicated, said, "I am the best! || 156 ||
Smiling slightly, the Blessed One, deluding them by means of his own māyā, spoke these words which were capable of both cursing and bestowing grace. || 157 ||
"Whether he be the foremost deity here previously or even subsequently," having heard these words of Viṣṇu, they indeed reviled one another. (158)
Therefore, O Goddess, the forms of the mantras [are purified] by means of consecratory rites;
for without the release from the curse, what person could attain perfection? || 159 ||
The Goddess said:
By whom and how was the curse given? And what is the fruit when it is uttered and when it is recited?
Tell me how there can be success regarding them, since they are free from curses. || 160 ||
Īśvara said:
He in whose beginning, middle, and end the wind is established.
The first four and the single seed-syllable, having been deposited together in one place, constitute the union. || 161 ||
Furthermore, if he has been overcome by someone who has indeed recited a mantra, his desires will be shattered by the curse of Kārttikeya. || 162 ||

The pair of earth-seeds (la-lā) may occur at the beginning, the middle, or the end; or else, the Vajrinī [syllables] may be twofold at the beginning, threefold in the middle, and twofold [at the end]. 163.
Obstructed by the curse of Śukra and deprived of both enjoyment and liberation, these two mantras became renowned on the paths of the Left (Vāma) and the Right (Dakṣa). || 164 ||
Hrīṃ sauṃ preṃ śrīṃ; whichever [of these] seed-syllables is not seen therein.
Or that mantra was "Huṃ," which was rendered powerless by the gods. || 165 ||
And such a mantra, when recited, destroys the power of the practitioner.
For one who is devoid of power and is perverse, death occurs; of this there is no doubt. || 166 ||
The syllable *hrīṃ* is not seen at the beginning, nor *klīṃ* in the middle, nor *kro* at the end;
this mantra has become turned away due to the curse of the Sun. || 167 ||
If one recites the mantra with one's face turned away, the deity will likewise turn her face away.
Even when a task is accomplished through fate, the world may turn its back on you.
"Neither at the beginning, nor at the end, nor likewise in the middle is 'haṃ' or 'saṃ' seen; these mantras have been rendered deaf by the Preceptor of the Gods through his curse. (169)
"If one recites a mantra while deaf, forgetfulness of it arises; he certainly becomes deaf—thus was it spoken by Mahākāla. (170)
The letter *ha* is the seed-syllable of the sun, while *sa* is remembered as the seed-syllable of the moon.
The letter *ra* is declared to be the seed-syllable of fire; *me*, *e*, and *na* are my three eyes.
If even a single [syllable] is missing from this five-syllabled mantra, then by my curse he shall be deprived of sight and shall experience suffering, grief, and disease. (172)
Neither at the beginning, nor in the middle, nor at the end, there is *hsauṃ*, or *haṃsa*, or *hauṃ*;
or *eṃ*, or *śrūṃ*, or *hrūṃ*, or *namaḥ*, or *hrīṃ*—that indeed is the mantra. (173)
O Pārvatī, a mantra that has been pinned down by a curse from the King of the Gods, even when recited, does not attain success. (174)
If there is a single *ra* in the middle, or two *la*s at the end of the *phaṭ*, or two *phaṭ*s, or three *la*s, then the mantra is not paralyzed. || 175 ||
(16) By the curse of Bhairava, our accomplishment (siddhi) becomes auspicious; never indeed will there be suffering, though for the most part it will be abundant. (176)
If, however, at the beginning of a mantra there are seven syllables in sequence, joined with either the letter *ra* or the letter *ya*, that mantra is indeed [efficacious]. (177)
Scorched by the curse of Vāyu and Agni, he shall torment the practitioner.
Therefore, O Goddess, the best of practitioners should perform consecration for the sake of accomplishment. || 178 ||
It is perceived through two, three, six, or eight [factors].
That which has the syllable *phaṭ* separated by other letters is called *nigadyate*.
Terrified by the curse of Nārasiṃha, he shall always cause [others] to tremble; the practitioner is never seen as one who has attained perfection, even in dreams and the like. || 180 ||
Oṃ, vā, haṃ, vā, or the letter sa—this is the mantra, which is to be meditated upon at the navel.
Due to the curse of a Brahmin, one's spiritual accomplishments (siddhi) shall be lost, resulting in extreme suffering.
When combined at the beginning, middle, and end, it forms a set of four seats; that mantra is impure, causing impurity through the curse of Māyā. (182)
If the pair of *phaṭ* mantras occurs at the beginning, in the middle, or at the end of the mantra, it neutralizes the curse of Rudra and accomplishes the task that has been frustrated. (183)
O fair-faced one, if [the mantra] has two *tāra*s at the beginning and *vaṣaṭ* at the end, it causes family quarrels, as it is divided by the curse of Bālā. (184)
That three-syllabled mantra which is devoid of the letters 'ha' and 'sa' is said to be in a state of deep sleep due to the curse of Siṃha; it destroys the desired fruit. || 185 ||
In this [mantra], there are eighteen syllables preceded by five *phaṭ* sounds.
Born from the curse of Cāmuṇḍā, he became intoxicated with pride and was no longer auspicious. || 186 ||
If there are five *phaṭ* syllables in the middle due to the curse of Kālikā, he will cause fainting; he especially causes the left-hand practitioner (*vāmī*) to faint. (187)
Thus, in the mantra, there are five *phaṭ* syllables at the end; that [mantra] was [revealed] by Rambhā.
But his vigor having been destroyed by the curse, he was rendered one whose skin was withered.
In which there are four utterances of "phaṭ," occurring at the beginning, the middle, and the end.
If it lacks eighteen syllables, there is loss due to the curse of Bhairava. || 189 ||

If it consists of nineteen syllables and is joined with *krīṃ*, *krom*, and the syllable *oṃ*, it destroys [the foe] who has been ruined by the curse of Kāma, and it brings about the destruction for the sake of Kāma. || 190 ||
The seven-syllable mantra is known as Manu, and the eight-syllable mantra is remembered as Kumāra.
The sixteen-syllable mantra is the youth, while the forty-syllable mantra is the mature one. || 191 ||

Thirty kalās make one kṣaṇa, and where there are a hundred vedas (four thousand) kṣaṇas, that is a kāṣṭhā; and where there are varṇas (sixteen thousand) kāṣṭhās, these, when cursed by Time even once, bring about sufferings. || 192 ||
The nine-syllable mantra joined with the syllable Oṃ was cursed by Cāmuṇḍā; thus declared seedless (nirbīja), it constantly brings about hopelessness.
A sword may cut the practitioner by means of a sword; of this there is no doubt.
Whether it ends with "namaḥ" or "svāhā," or whether its middle portion is absent— (194)
The mantras beginning with *vaṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, *hum*, and *phaṭ* have been declared; such a mantra as that does not exist at all.
While performing service, he shall receive the teaching on the divisions [of the path] after three years from the beginning. || 195 ||
But he in whose [mantra] there are *phaṭ* syllables at the beginning, middle, and end, is deprived of success by the curse of Kaumārī; he does not achieve accomplishment. || 196 ||
As for that ten-syllabled mantra of Gaṇeśa, due to a curse it becomes ineffective when recited;
it causes ignorance in birth after birth. || 197 ||

If, at the beginning, there is a conjunction of consonants followed by only a single vowel, that is known as a *kūṭa*; from such a *kūṭa*, a loss [of the syllable] occurs due to the curse of Mātaṅgī. || 198 ||
He shall become two-colored and devoid of strength due to the curse of the son of Āśvinī.
It destroys the power of the practitioner and annihilates the king's army. || 199 ||
Born with four colors, he became squint-eyed due to the curse of the enemy of serpents; having muttered the Kekara mantra, he no longer sees with his eyes. || 200 ||
The six-syllable mantra became deprived of its seed-syllable due to the curse of Rāvaṇa.
From the recitation of that [mantra], the lineage increases; otherwise, there is no happiness from women.
Due to the curse of Dhūmāvatī, for twenty-one suns (three times seven), the mind of the practitioner becomes agitated during the recitation of that [mantra]. || 202 ||
Twenty, twenty-one, and thirty syllables belong to Tārā; by reciting this [mantra] embraced by the seven [syllables], death occurs swiftly for one who is intent on its practice. (203)
The twenty-two-syllable mantra of Sarasvatī, when affected by a curse, may cause the practitioner to become deluded and addicted to vices such as drinking. || 204 ||
This mantra of twenty-four syllables belongs to Varānanī; however, due to the curse of Rājamātaṅgī, it causes poverty for one who is afflicted by hunger. || 205 ||
The mantra consisting of twenty-three syllables is of the color of Rudra; due to the curse of the Kaulikas, that mantra becomes arrogant, and by that very arrogance, dullness arises in men. (206)
Consisting of twenty-six, twenty-nine, thirty, and twenty-six syllables, he was deprived of his limbs due to the curse of Pūṣan; thus, he could not fulfill desires. || 207 ||
If a mantra consists of twenty-eight or thirty-one syllables due to the curse of Nandīśa, it will be extremely cruel;
having brought about the destruction of the target, the practitioner himself shall perish. || 208 ||
The mantra consists of thirty-eight syllables due to the curse of the Mātṛkās.
If one is excessively angry while reciting that [mantra], there will be destruction for oneself by one's own hand. || 209 ||
Starting from forty up to sixty-three syllables.
Due to the curse of their mothers, who were filled with shame, his practitioners became ashamed. || 210 ||
Those mantras which consist of sixty-five syllables lead to a tranquil mind.
Due to the curse of Kāma, there is no fruit from the exertion of reciting that mantra.
Wherein three hundred syllables are sworn by Chinnamasta: five, one, two, two, one, one, two, one, and two, with eight at the end. || 211 ||
May you be devoid of affection and terrifying to practitioners.
Recited by those free from desire and endowed with vigor, these [mantras] destroy attachment to worldly existence.
Starting from four hundred [syllables] up to a thousand syllables, those that exceed this limit are excluded from rites such as *pauṣṭika* due to the curse of the sacrifice. (213)
Mantras exceeding one thousand syllables result in punishment for the reciter due to a curse.
Those known as the Daṇḍakas, when oppressed by that [mantra], shall suffer misfortune through its recitation. || 214 ||
However, due to the curse of Bhārgava, there are more than two thousand mantras.
Divided into seven parts, they are known as the "Siddhi-khaṇḍakas" (the makers of the section on spiritual accomplishments). || 215 ||
O gods, listen to another thing: when no success was attained by the chanting sages, then a most terrible curse was pronounced. (216)
Reassurance for the deities arises from the absence of obstacles to success; therefore, the Guru should perform that purification of the mantra during the instruction. || 217 ||
I shall explain that method; let all the gods listen. The Guru is seated in Siddhāsana (its definition is given in the Śivasaṃhitā:
"The practitioner, having firmly pressed the perineum with the root of the foot, places the root of the other foot upon the penis...").

The knower of yoga should always place [the mind] thus: looking upward at the space between the eyebrows, motionless, with senses restrained, the body perfectly straight, and free from agitation in solitude.
This is to be known as Siddhāsana, which bestows success upon the perfected ones;
it is the firm joining of the anus and the genitals. 218.
Having pressed [the left foot] with the heel of the left foot, one should place the right foot upon it, pressing the two ankle-joints against each other. || 219 ||
It should be performed in such a way that [the breath] flows; then, having firmly pressed the base of the *liṅga* with the right heel, one should sit with the body steady. || 220 ||
Then the Guru, contracting the anus and properly restraining the downward-moving breath known as apāna, should cause the vital breath (prāṇa) and the wind to rise upward. || 221 ||
With one-pointed mind, one should effect the union of the apāna and prāṇa breaths within the mūlādhāra,
which is the nature of consciousness, in the kuṇḍalinī, the Supreme Self.
The true guru should contemplate his own mantra which has become defective;
then, he should contemplate the syllables of that mantra one by one in their proper sequence. (223)
One should cause it to enter through the path of the Suṣumṇā into the Mūlādhāra, and then into the Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūra, and Anāhata cakras. || 224 ||

One should cause [the breath] to enter the pure *ājñācakra*, piercing it again and again; having thus led it to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), [one should take] from the nectar of the lunar orb (*somamaṇḍala*). || 225 ||
The wise one should then clearly visualize the mantra-syllables as being sprinkled with nectar.
Then, one should recite that mantra, preceded by the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the ṛṣi and other components.
By reciting it one thousand and eight times, the mantra becomes purified.
After he has been liberated from the aforementioned curse, one should then instruct him.

The fruit of a blessing is meager, whereas the fruit arising from prior sins and the like is great; therefore, the means for the destruction of verbal curses and so forth are now being explained. (228)
Or on a seat made of śrīparṇī, sandalwood, or mango wood and the like.
And with musk, saffron, and other substances, one should draw the diagram representing the five elements.
One should invoke there the wheel, which is Sarasvatī known as Mātṛkā.
Having performed the worship according to the prescribed rule, one hundred and eight [times].
Having recited the Mātṛkā, [one should extract] from its midst the mantra desired by oneself.
And the vowels, consonants, and bindus, as well as the syllables suitable for creation. || 231 ||

Having extracted [the parts] individually and then unified them according to the instructions of the Guru, one should grasp the mantra; this is declared to be "sañjanana" (the act of generating). || 232 ||
Having placed the *praṇava* at the beginning and end, one should recite [the mantra] with the *praṇava* interspersed between them.
These one hundred and eight syllables of the mantra constitute this very life.
One should write the mantra on birch bark with yellow pigment (rocanā) and saffron; then, for each syllable, one should strike it one hundred times with sandalwood water.
Uttering this seed-syllable of Vāyu is called "striking. Mantras that have become blunted are made effective when struck. || 235 ||
Having written [the name] upon the previously mentioned pedestal according to the number of syllables of that mantra, one should then take karavīra flowers and recite [the mantra]. || 236 ||
And one should strike each syllable with those flowers one hundred times.
And pronouncing the seed-syllable of fire (RAṂ)—this is called "awakening. || 237 ||
And as before, upon the pedestal, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus with those same materials.
Upon its pericarp, one should draw a single bud of the mālatī flower. || 238 ||
Each individual syllable of the mantra [should be worshipped] according to the number of syllables in that mantra.
And having taken the sprouts of the Bodhi tree, one should recite the mantra. || 239 ||
"I consecrate this mantra with 'Namaḥ'; thus one should perform the consecration.
Adorned with sprouts endowed with various fragrances, as far as the syllable [is concerned]. (240)
This consecration (abhiṣeka) is considered to consist of one hundred and eight [repetitions];
just as water purifies men, so does this consecration bring about the purification of mantras. || 241 ||
The light-mantra (jyotirmantra) should be meditated upon within the solar orb at the mūlādhāra; one should contemplate that the mind of that mantra is to be purified and thus consumed by fire. 242.

That which is called "face" (ānana) is known as innate (sāhajika), adventitious (āgantu), and karmic (kārmaṇa); that which is called "yoga" is said to be illusory (māyika). These three impurities reside within that mantra. || 243 ||
One should contemplate each [syllable] as being individually consumed by the fire of the Jyotir-mantra; thus, one should think, "My own mantra has become pure. || 244 ||

The *jyotirmantra*, beginning with the Veda as "Oṃ" (which is said to be the beginning of the Vedas), is considered to consist of two syllables. This is the purification (*vimalīkaraṇa*); one should also perform its application. || 245 ||
As before, one should inscribe the mantra upon the pedestal using substances such as saffron.
And with water scented with camphor in a vessel made of copper or other such metal. || 246 ||
Having filled [the vessel] with pure [water], one should write [the mantra] one hundred and eight times;
then, having consecrated the water with that same mantra, one should sprinkle it with drops from *kuśa* grass.
One should sprinkle water over each syllable three times; this is known as the rite of nourishment (āpyāyana).
For those distressed by the hardships of *puraścaryā*, this [rite] is like a formal graduation ceremony.
p. 20) One should inscribe the mantra in the center of a copper vessel using musk and other [fragrant substances].
And in another vessel, water scented with camphor pills. || 249 ||

Having taken [the water] with the *arghya* vessel while reciting this mantra, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) by saying, "I offer libations; *namaḥ*" at the end. Thus is the libation. (250)
One should recite the aforementioned mantra one hundred and eight times.
One should recite this; it serves as an illuminator and is desired for all mantras. || 251 ||
The concealment of the mantra being recited—that is, its non-disclosure—is the tenth consecration; these ten consecrations are proclaimed in all tantras as being kept secret. || 252 ||
Thus, the sixteen purificatory rites (saṃskāras) have been declared;
for each mantra, there shall be recitation (japa), fire-oblation (homa), and libation (tarpaṇa), as will be described hereafter. || 253 ||
Washing and feeding the twice-born—these are the sixteen consecrations of the mantra that have been declared. What else do you wish to hear? || 254 ||
Thus ends the second chapter, the Illumination of Consecrations (*saṃskāraprakāśa*), in the *Merutantra* composed by Śiva with the approval of the illustrious Mahāmāyā and Mahākāla. || 2 ||
The Goddess said:
How does initiation occur on the left path, and how does it occur on the right? What is the necessary ritual action therein? Tell me your definitive conclusion on this. || 1 ||
The Lord said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the fivefold procedure for initiation, which is concealed in all tantras and is the most excellent among those intended for kings. (2)
The highest [degree] belongs to the [qualities] beginning with Mahat; however, the middling degree belongs to the common [qualities].
That which has been spoken by the Brāhmaṇas is little, and that which has been spoken by the ascetics (yatis) is also little.
Therefore, I shall first explain to you that which is the most supreme among the supreme; by knowing which, the scope of the various categories beginning with the "supreme" becomes understood.
In that regard, first one should construct a pavilion for the most excellent of rites.
The ground for the pavilion is said to be twelve finger-breadths in height from the level surface.
The ground, however, is to be purified by digging down from one's desired sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or similar site.
Free from bones, insects, husks, charcoal, and impurities, it brings about auspiciousness. || 6 ||
Otherwise, having discarded that clay, one should fill it with auspicious clay.
By one staying outside the village there, along with Brahmins and others of their own respective castes.
Having made that [surface] perfectly level there, one should fill a wide vessel with water, divide it into eight parts with fine lines,
and then stir it.
That vessel in which the water from the writing has risen up, he should fill;
or that place where it has sunk, the wise man should lower.
When the ground has been leveled in this manner, one should perform the determination of the directions.
Having taken the thread, the hook, and the pegs within the night.
A tube joined at its beginning and end with apertures is for piercing the pole star;
one should draw a circle from the center between the southern and northern directions. || 11 ||
Then, with that same compass, one should draw a circle in the middle of the line;
from there, one should draw a bow, and from there again, one should draw another bow. (12)
In this manner, there are six bows there, and a six-petalled lotus is formed; having placed three [lines] each in the north and south, from the middle of the petals. (13)
That long line, however, should be divided into three parts from east to west.
In the south-western and north-eastern [corners], and in the two upper [corners]. (14)
The thread extending halfway between the two bows would be the Īśānī and the Rākṣasī [lines].
And for the other two bows, in this same way, the southern one would be the northern one. || 15 ||
The lines situated in the intermediate directions must indeed be equal in length to those of the circle; having brought them out as desired, one should drive stakes into the ground there.
A firm thread is tied at the top of four stakes.
With equal ears reaching to the ends of the quarters, that pure [space] shall be square.
Having first worshipped Gaṇeśa, the wise man should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited;
thereafter, he should construct an auspicious pavilion accompanied by the five musical sounds.
For the family initiation (kuladīkṣā), one should construct a pavilion measuring twenty cubits.
Just as there may be a coming together of liquor, meat, and women. || 19 ||
In the Siddhānta and in the Vāmamārga, the pavilion (maṇḍapa) is eighteen cubits; because of the smallness of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) there, even though they are five more in number.
In the Vedic rite with many ritual materials, there are sixteen fire-pits;
however, when the number of pits is small and the materials are few, there shall be one pit measuring four cubits.
In the south, when there is an abundance of materials, the pavilion should be ten cubits; when materials are few, it should be nine cubits for all directions.
For Śūdras it should be seven cubits, and for those of mixed castes (saṅkara), five; this measurement of pavilions (maṇḍapa), hidden in all Tantras, has been declared. || 23 ||
Various types of hand gestures (*hasta*) have been described; now hear their determination, as well as the place and time in which the barley grains (*yava*) originated and how they were formed. (24)

For those twice-born ones with eight cubits, that [unit] shall be one finger-breadth (aṅgula); for Śūdras with seven cubits, and likewise for those of mixed castes and others, it shall be by six [finger-breadths].
In a case where a non-Vedic person, such as a Brahmin and others, is himself the performer, this [measurement] applies there with those possessing half of this number; otherwise, it is different.
[He should place it] upon the middle finger of the teacher's right hand.
The interval between two joints is declared to be one long measure (dīrghamātrā) of a finger. || 27 ||
The height of the image and of the temple or other structure has been determined.
This applies by the same measure to altars, seats, palanquins, chariots, and so forth. || 28 ||
A fist is formed by the remaining fingers with the thumb excluded; one should divide that into four parts, and that single part is a finger-breadth (muṣṭyaṅgula). || 29 ||
The implements for the oblation, such as the *sruva* ladle and others, as well as the sacrificial pit, the leveled ground, and the altar.
One should make the sacrificial thread (yajñopavīta) from muñja grass and other materials, measuring it with the fist and fingers.

Having divided any given human cubit (*pauruṣāyāma*) into ten parts, and having further divided one of those parts into twelve, one of those [twelfth] parts constitutes one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*). || 31 ||
One should know that, furthermore, it is called the "finger-measure obtained from the body" (dehalabdha-aṅgula).
By these twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas), one hand (hasta) is formed. || 32 ||
By this [treatise], one should perform the measurement of the limbs of the images, as well as their proportions; this, which was previously kept secret, is now made public for both men and women.
In a koṭihoma accompanied by prosperity, the [fire-pit] should be fourteen cubits; otherwise, for lakṣahomas, it should be twelve cubits or ten cubits.
Having divided the pavilion into nine parts, there shall be an altar in its central portion;
the pillars at the corners of the altar are raised outside to half the height of the pavilion.
One should place a fifth part on the ground according to the thread of the portion for nourishment;
one should fashion the shape of a water-pot at the top with a tenth part of that.
The altar should be made of nine pieces of wood joined together;
one should well-arrange pillars for the pavilion that are one-third as long [as the structure]. || 37 ||
Thus, on the fifth part of the ground, there are twelve [units], and the pinnacle is ten parts.
One should fashion a pinnacle situated upon the central pillar, resembling the shape of a mṛdaṅga drum.
Indeed, twelve offerings should be presented at the midpoint of each of the outer pillars.
In the ritual procedure for Dakṣa’s initiation, one should have a lotus-like peak constructed.
In the initiation of the left-hand path, it has three streams; in the Vaiṣṇava mouth, it is indeed conch-white.
A four-cornered altar, being square, bestows all fruits. || 40 ||
Likewise, for the consecration of limbs and so forth, the *padminī* pattern, resembling a lotus, is used; for kings, the *sarvatobhadra* is used during the consecration of the four auspicious ones.
In marriage, the altar of Śrīdhara is provided with twenty corners; however, in initiation according to the Vāmamārga, the altar is triangular and kept secret.
One should place unblemished vessels filled with ghee upon the pillars; having tied leaves of a single species together, one should set them at the necks of the pillars.
One should cover it on all sides with coconut leaves and bamboo.
In such a way that there shall be no fear of storms, rain, and the like. || 44 ||
One should construct four doors for the pavilion in the directions previously established;
the threshold (dehalī) shall measure five parts, and there the two door-panels (kapāṭa) and their frames (śākha) shall be twice as high.
This door is on the left path, while in the southern excellent pavilion, [there is another].
One should construct a beautiful threshold, measuring two cubits and eight finger-breadths. || 46 ||
In the central pavilion, one should construct [a space] measuring two and a half finger-breadths.
In the lowest [type], its height is considered to be two cubits, and twice that for the others.
Having left a space of one cubit outside the eastern door of the dwelling, however, || 48 ||

For the best, middle, and lowest [sizes], one should make the raised plank seven, six, and five cubits long respectively; its width should be three times that [length] in finger-breadths (aṅgulas). || 49 ||
Likewise, on both sides of the door, there should be [ornaments] five fingers thick, uneven, square, one span high, and with raised crests. || 50 ||
One should place two planks in the best, middle, and lowest [mandapas];
in length, those two in the pavilion should be respectively two and a half cubits. (p. 23) 51.
Two and a quarter cubits in height, with two hands joined, it has five limbs upon the ground.
One should bury the fire with the verse "agnim īḷe" in the two side positions while reciting the Gāyatrī.
One should drive stakes upon two [sides] of a square that is uneven, having a width and depth made of wood of the same species as that [wood used for the main structure]. || 53 ||
And one should tie a garland of darbha grass at the eastern gate; this is the prescribed ritual. Likewise, at the southern gate, that gate should be made of *plakṣa* wood.
With the mantra "iṣe tvā," one should place the garland and then bind it as before; this [image] made of udumbara wood should be placed from the western door.
In a Vedic sacrifice, one should fashion an image from the Plakṣa tree using the mantra "O Agni, come hither" (agna āyāhi), just as previously described;
likewise, one should do so with an image made from the Vaṭa tree.
One should place [the vessel] from the door in the northern direction with the mantra "śanno devī". Above those, in the middle of the horizontal wooden beams, there is a cavity. || 57 ||
Having prepared it, one should fashion a beautiful structure using wood of the *toraṇa* species.
In the Śaiva sacrifice, the trident is [placed] among the superior, middling, and inferior [vessels]. (58)
The length of Viśveśa’s limb is one finger-breadth, and its width is one-fourth of that.
In the Vaiṣṇava [mandala], one should draw the conch, discus, mace, and lotus using one-twelfth of the [total] measure.
