Even a Vaiṣṇava should likewise perform the placement (nyāsa) according to the sequence beginning with the east; the central prong should be straight, while those on the two sides are slightly curved.
In this manner, Śūla, Gaṇapati, Śiva, and the others are considered to be like Śiva himself. Then, in front of the pavilion, there should be a space measuring ten cubits from the ground upwards.
On the ground, with both hands, one should place a bamboo staff covered with a clean cloth.
The banner is one cubit wide and five cubits long.
One should draw the deity of the mantra there, together with its weapons and its vehicle.
It is equipped with bells and chowries, and possesses the colors and appearance of the deity. || 63 ||
Having first erected the banner, one should subsequently arrange them in the ten directions; the flags for the lords of the directions should be half the size of the banner.
There, one should place those respective letters in their corresponding directions using mantras declared in the Vedas.
And [the mantra] "trātāram indram" [is for the goddess] of yellow complexion in the direction of Hari (the southeast).
In the southeast is Piṅgalā from the mantra "tvanno agne," and Kṛṣṇavarṇā is remembered as being in the south from the mantra "suganno panthām. || 66 ||
With the mantra *asunvantam*, she is smoke-colored in the southwest;
with *tattvāyāmi brahmaṇe*, she is white-colored in the west. || 67 ||
And with the mantra "ā noniyudbhiḥ," she should be green in the northwest; with "vayaṃ somavrata," she is moon-colored in the north. (68)
To the northeast of that Īśāna, there is an exceedingly white banner dedicated to Īśānī.
Between the northeast and the east is Śeṣa, who has a red banner. || 69 ||

Between the directions of water (west) and nairṛta (southwest), one should place Vidhi, who has a red banner; on the left path, he is remembered as being equal to the fall of a thunderbolt through the Vedic mantra.
For Brahmins, the left-hand path leads only to hell. In the absence of mantras, one should recite name-mantras preceded by the *praṇava* (Om) and ending with the *hṛdaya* (heart-mantra). || 71 ||
One should recite [the mantras] on the right path, but on the left, excluding the *praṇava*.
One should fasten an exceedingly white canopy over the pavilion.
One should thus adorn it with flower garlands and the like, and encircle it in this manner.
With a long rosary fashioned from the leaves of the mango and the holy fig tree. || 73 ||
Having wrapped the pillars with fine silk cloths, one should construct a pedestal in their center.
With unburnt bricks, [he should construct] a pedestal one cubit in width. || 74 ||

Or it may be raised by parts equal to the number of the pavilion's pillars, the Rudras (eleven), the Aṃśas (twelve), the Navas (nine), the Saptas (seven), the Iṣus (five), or the Rāmas (three), having observed the relative proportions. || 75 ||
The pavilion is [constructed] so that the assembly of all necessary components may take place.
An oblation of ten thousand burnt offerings (ayutāhuti) should be performed upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit is prescribed for up to one million recitations;
for every ten million recitations, one should increase the size by one cubit.

It is declared that for Vedic rites, a fire-pit ten crores of cubits in size is prescribed; however, the offering of liquor, meat, and so forth is ordained specifically within the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
When fifty oblations have been offered, the measurement of the pit is one fore-arm with the fist clenched;
when one hundred [oblations] have been offered, it shall be equal to a full cubit.
At one thousand [cubits], it should be one cubit; at ten thousand, it is considered to be two cubits; at one hundred thousand, it measures four cubits;
and at ten million, it is six cubits.
And for a ten-million-fold oblation (koṭihoma), an eight-cubit sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is prescribed on the left.
In the ritual procedure for a single pit, however, a square shape is prescribed. || 81 ||
It is especially for the immobilization of Brahmins, and it is the foremost among such rites.
In the ritual procedure for the nine pits, however, the portion belonging to Agni is shaped like a vulva.
For the sake of enjoyment or for the sake of sons, it is like a square for those who possess it.
For Vaiśyas, in all rites, it should resemble a half-moon in the south.
For the killing of others, it is taught that [the rite] is also desired in four sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
A triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the southwest is known to cause the destruction of enemies. || 84 ||
This [practice] causes enmity and is especially forbidden for Śūdras; however, it is the primary conduct for all Kṣatriyas in the performance of their duties. || 85 ||
In the west, however, that same rite bestows success upon Buddhists and others as well.
A hexagon is raised up, and it is distinguished by its cuts. || 86 ||

One should cause that [pit] to be made in the northwest; it is especially recommended for those of mixed caste. In the north, the pit for rites of nourishment (pauṣṭika) bestows both livelihood and satisfaction. || 87 ||
In all ritual applications, this is remembered as that which brings joy to others; an eight-cornered [diagram] is prescribed in the northeast for the sake of granting liberation. || 88 ||
Likewise, one shall obtain liberation from prison, from disease, from anxiety, and so forth.
This sequence applies to the rite of nine sacrificial pits (navakuṇḍaka), whereas the procedure for eight sacrificial pits (aṣṭakuṇḍīvidhāna) is as follows.

The ninth [fire-pit] should be square, located in the intermediate direction between the east and the northeast; according to the ritual procedure for the five fire-pits, the fifth one shall be in the northeast.
In the procedure for constructing a square pit, however, there is no excavation outside in the Vedic manner; another [pit], pentagonal, is for the destruction of malevolent magic. 91.
Likewise, there is another seven-cornered sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) which destroys the hosts of spirits. Now, first, the procedure for the square sacrificial pit is described. (92)
The excellent sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), joined with the navel and the source (yonisamāyukta), should have three girdles (mekhalā).
The Śūdras have two girdles, while those of mixed caste have a single girdle.
The depth of the excavation should indeed be exactly equal to the width of the pit.
When the directional wealth has been calculated, it should be as much as the desired pit (kuṇḍa) here.
The expert artisan should make it square and equal, with equal sides; for that which has one cubit as its diagonal, its two arms (sides) are each two cubits.
For Karṇa, who was two cubits tall, the measurement of his arms was three cubits.
In this same manner, even for sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) measuring four cubits and so forth, they should be level with the ground in all cases.
Its external girdles (mekhalās) should be made equal to one part of the Jina.
It is twelve finger-breadths in width and four finger-breadths in height. || 97 ||
Above that, it is eight finger-breadths wide and eight finger-breadths high.
It should be four finger-breadths in length, as high [as that], and half of that in width.
The yoni is twelve finger-breadths in length according to the solar measurement, but it is reduced by one-third in width.
It is one finger-breadth high, and likewise enters into the interior by that same measure.
It is considered to be joined with two jars and resembling the leaves of the Aśvattha tree.
It is joined with a girdle of big toes; in the middle and on the outside, it is steadfastness and forbearance. 100.
To the west of the *yoni*, outside the three *mekhalās*, there should be a square pedestal (*pīṭha*), and the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) should be one-eighth as wide [as that pedestal]. || 101 ||
The stalk in the middle of that should be as long and as high; in the center of the *yoni*, it should be circular with a measurement equal to one-sixth of the *kuṇḍa*.
The yoni of the fire-pits (kuṇḍas) located in the east, south-east, and south is said to face north; the yonis of the remaining [pits] face east.
One should avoid a yoni that is itself shaped like a fire-pit.
Then, from the center situated in the middle of the *kuṇḍa*, one should draw [a circle] with a compass extended to a length equal to twelve parts of the diameter. || 104 ||
The circle should be made with one-sixth [of the diameter], while the previous circle is the pericarp (karṇikā).
At the tip of the pericarp, within the outer circle, are eight petals.
Thus, the navel should be six finger-breadths high; it is said to be four-cornered (quadrangular). A portion of the desired square is called a *jina* (one-eighth) part. 106.
One should extend the central line by five and a quarter parts; then, one should divide the eastern side into four squares. || 107 ||
One should rotate the karkaṭaka from the middle between the two situated in the west.
One should cast a thread in the shape of a half-arch from the outer directions of Rudra toward their tips, ending at Agni; then, for both [the inner and outer squares], it shall be so formed.

The Yoni-kunda, resembling an Ashvattha leaf, is located facing north; here, the measurements should be understood as having the form of a yoni with beautiful girdles. A wise man should divide the square field into ten parts. (109)

The knower of the tantra should discard one part each from below and above; he should then drop the chord-line at the front and rotate it according to that measurement. This pit, resembling a half-moon, will thus become beautiful. 110.
In this case, that [point] would indeed be the back of Yama; thus it is for the purpose of slaying him.
Then, having shifted the gentle back, the yoni is directed toward the western direction.
First, an equilateral triangle should be constructed with three equal perpendiculars; while in all other systems it is said to have an interval, here it is without an interval. (112)
In the case of one cubit, the height of the arms shall be twelve cubits; for two cubits and so forth, it shall be three and five [respectively]; and for three cubits, it shall be twelve cubits. (113)
In a four-cubit [measurement], there are three and one; in a five-cubit [measurement], there are those with three ranges; in a six-cubit [measurement], there are three, three, and three;
and in a seven-cubit [measurement], there are three, twenty-seven, and four. (114)
In a space of eight cubits, the deities of the earth, Viśvakarman, Viśvāmitra, and Agni are established.
The Vedas, the fires, and the pairs [of hands] are remembered as the ten arms. || 116 ||
The half-diameter of the square is increased by its own eighteenth part.
A circle drawn from that very point [of the center] to the crab-sign (Karkaṭaka) is here called the circular kuṇḍa. || 116 ||
One should construct the half-diameter of the square, increased by one-sixteenth part.
To that extent, one should also fashion a charming circle with a compass.
Having marked six points according to that same *karkaṭa*-measure as before,
and having drawn three sides [of a hexagon], one should thus construct the wall so that it possesses six corners.
Having divided the desired square into twenty-four parts, one should then mark the solar portion from the center using a compass. 119.
One should again construct a circle with divisions corresponding to the number of solar lunar days (tithis) for the second [circle].
And one should cast eight threads in the intermediate directions between the cardinal points.
Then, from the tip of the thread at the northeast (Īśa) of the inner circle, one should lead a line to the top of the eastern thread of the outer circle. || 121 ||
Then, on the southern line at the top of the inner circle, one should draw a petal;
from that, one should likewise draw the eight petals.
The circle drawn with half the diagonal of the petals is the pericarp (karṇikā); from that, the circle with half the diagonal of six parts constitutes the filaments (keśarāṇi). 123.
The pericarp and the filaments are raised to a height measuring one-sixth of the width.
One should dig according to the method taught by the guru so that it takes the form of a lotus.
One should fashion the shape of a lotus together with the neck and the girdle;
likewise, it should be made square and even by means of sand.
The diameter of that desired square, increased by one-twelfth, is used to describe a circle;
one should then mark points there at the eight directions.
One should place [the measurements] in sequence upon that and provide equal arms; thus the pit (kuṇḍa) becomes eight-cornered, and likewise its neck and girdles (mekhalā). || 127 ||
The half-diameter of the desired square, increased by one-seventh of itself.
A circle should be drawn with that as its radius; therein, there shall be five marks.
One should cause the lines to be laid out upon them with equal proportions;
by omitting the bow-shape of the string, the pit (kuṇḍa) becomes five-cornered.
The half-diameter of the desired square is increased by one-fifth.
One should rotate that entire circle there seven times.
Other types of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) are prescribed for Tantric and Smārta rituals.
Vessels without handles are called "viyoni" in the Śruti. || 131 ||

The ninth pit for the preceptor (ācāryakuṇḍa) should be square according to the Vedic tradition; however, in the Tantric system, if one is unable [to construct nine], there should be four pits in the cardinal directions.
If one is unable to do that, one should fashion a single square; or, according to one's capacity for worship, a Yoni-shaped pit with its path on the left.
Indeed, if the measurement is excessive, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) bestows many defects.
Therefore, one who desires what is auspicious should perform this after having investigated it thoroughly. || 134 ||
If the pit is too deep, there will be illness; if it is too shallow, there is loss of cattle and wealth. In a curved pit, there is suffering; in one with a broken rim, death occurs. (135)
If it is devoid of a girdle, there is grief; if it is excessive, there is loss of wealth.
A *kuṇḍa* that is fashioned without a *yoni* is declared to be the destroyer of one's wife. (136)
A *kuṇḍa* that is devoid of a neck is declared to be a destroyer of one's offspring.
And that sacrificial pit which is devoid of beauty and has a worn-out girdle. || 137 ||
If the cord snaps, it leads to the destruction of the patron;
if there is an excess of cord, it causes hatred toward friends; if the cord is deficient, it results in poverty. || 138 ||
In a stomach that does not digest, there is disease; in a jar with a hole, there is only reproach.
Even in a fire-pit as described above, when such portents arise, the result is as follows: || 139 ||

There should be five girdles, measured by six, six, six, four, and two [units] respectively. This applies when there is a difference in dharma or a difference in caste between the preceptor (ācārya) and the sacrificer (yajamāna). || 140 ||
The two girdles are considered to be one-sixth and one-eighth [of the width] respectively, in the Kaulika, Vāmamārga, Bauddha, Jaina, and Śābara traditions. (141)

When the pavilion has been thus prepared, one should commence the worship of Vāstu; however, in the case of a new house, one should do so otherwise, for otherwise there will be great calamity. || 142 ||
That worship is said to be twofold: Smārta and Tāntrika. Formerly, there was a certain supreme Asura named Vāstu. (143)
By him the three worlds were conquered, as were the fifty-three deities; those who came before him in battle were utterly crushed by him. || 144 ||
He who was repeatedly victorious in battle was indeed that very Prajāpati.
At the end of a thousand divine years, the gods came for refuge. || 145 ||
That was heard by Viṣṇu, by me, by Pārvatī, and even by the lord of the Daityas;
urged on by Nārada, he rushed forward, desiring to fight. (146)
A battle was waged by us with him for five years;
thereafter, the Daitya became intoxicated with pride, deluded by the Māyā of Viṣṇu. || 147 ||
Being pleased, he spoke these words: "Choose, choose! (148)
"Indra and Kubera have brought me satisfaction;
yet that battle was fought even by you, though you were matted-haired and accompanied by an army. (149)
This was accomplished by him who has Viṣṇu as his helper and who bears Pārvatī as half of his body; therefore, I, the supreme lord of the three worlds, have attained satisfaction. (150)
"There is nothing whatsoever that cannot be given by me; let even all three of you ask. Having heard these words of his, [Brahmā] was impelled by the eyebrows of Śiva and Śivā. (151)
Hari said: "O Lord of Daityas, you are most blessed by my word. Make the truth three times; then a boon shall be granted by me. Even by Śiva and Pārvatī, there is indeed no other god. (152)
The Daitya spoke thus, and then Viṣṇu made his request:
"Let that means be shown by which your death may be hastened. Knowing this to be a deception on the part of Viṣṇu, the lord of the Daityas addressed him: (153)
All must inevitably go into the mouth of Death;
nevertheless, he who goes for the sake of his own vow lives. (154)
However, there is only one person in my lineage who has performed service to me;
having shown him the way, let this body be cast down. || 155 ||
And at that time, O gods, an incorporeal voice spoke: "O Lord of the Daityas, do not grieve; your birth upon the earth has come to pass. (156)
Go to dissolution right there; O Pārtha, hear from me the boon [concerning] those castes who shall build a new house for their own enjoyment. || 157 ||
There, however, apart from your festival, the female servants beginning with Kālakarṇī and those headed by Vināyaka are afflicted by various miseries. (158)
"The servants shall cause him suffering"—this is the command of the Supreme Lord. Having heard these words, he too dug a pit, a great chasm. (159)
Then he entered [the city] which had been filled with gods, earth, and stones by those gods whom he had previously conquered, out of fear that they might emerge again. 160.
Above that, fifty-three [deities] established their residence with great effort;
therefore, they must certainly be worshipped by those who desire the happiness of domestic life. || 161 ||
Let the gods who know that procedure listen from the left and right paths;
O Vāstoṣpati, one should likewise perform [the rite] upon a stone or in an image. || 162 ||

One should perform the invocation and worship of that [deity] with the *pratijānīti* mantra; having performed the worship of the others with their respective name-mantras, one should fulfill [the rite]. || 163 ||

In the south-western corner of the house, having prepared a ground that is auspicious and square in shape, one should construct an altar (vedikā) with a level surface and a height of one span. || 164 ||
There, the wise one should draw [the design] measuring one cubit in both width and length.
The wheel consists of eighty-one squares; the Vedic deities reside therein.
One should first worship Brahmā in the nine central compartments.
One should place Āpavatsanta in the northeast (Īśāna) and Aryaman in the eastern (Prāc) section consisting of three squares.
In the southeast, one should worship Savitṛ and Vivasvat; in the three [locations] of the waters, Indra in the southwestern quarter, and Mitra in the three locations situated in the west. 167.
In the northwest [one should worship] Rājayakṣman; in the three northern [cells], Sumeru;
in the Veda-cells (the intermediate corners), Īśa in the northeast; and from the corner, the two [deities] Dava and Taro. || 168 ||
Śikhin, Parjanya, and Āpas are declared as Diti in two pairs.
These five deities are to be known in succession from the left-hand path. || 169 ||
Jayanta and Indra, Sūrya, Satya, and Vṛṣa are in the south-eastern corner; likewise Antarikṣa, Vāta, Pūṣan, and Savitṛ [are located there]. (170)
In the northeast are the four gods; then, in the southern pentad, Vitatha, Gṛhakṣata, and Yama appear in order within the pair [of directions]. (171)
The Gandharvas and Bhṛṅgarāja are situated in the four-cornered space located in the southwest (Nairṛtī). Likewise, from the northeast (Īśānī), there are Jaya, Mṛga, Pitṛ, and Dauvārika. (172)
Thereafter, in the second pair, there are five: Sugrīva and Puṣpadantaka.
Varuṇa, Asura, and Śeṣa are in the northwest, while Āhi is outside of Īśa.
Rudra, Pāpayakṣa, and Roga are in the five northern [directions]; likewise, Mukhya, Bhallāṭa, Soma, Bhujaṅga, and Aditi. || 174 ||
These forty-five deities are to be worshipped with devotion;
furthermore, according to the Tantric path, they likewise reside within the sixty-four squares.
One should worship Brahmā in the center after drawing two threads across the two corners; then, in the four squares starting from that eastern one, in each pair of squares [one should worship].
Āryaka, Vivasvat, Mitra, and another Mahīdhara; Sāvitra, Savitṛ, Śakra, Indrajit, Rudra, and his conqueror. || 177 ||
According to the followers of Śaunaka, one should place Āpavatsura and Kaurava in the half-cells at the corners; [and likewise] Śarva, Guha, Aryaman, Jambhaka, and Pilipicchaka. (178)
One should worship Carakī, Vidārī, and Pūtanā in the east; then Īśāna, Parjanya, Jayanta, Śakra, and Bhāskara.
Satya, Vṛṣa, and Antaka are located in the eastern quarter-cells in sequence; then Agni, Pūṣan, Vitatha, Yama, and Gṛharakṣaka [are in the south]. (180)
The Gandharvas, the Bhṛṅgarājas, and the Mṛgas are situated in the southern direction.
And then Nirṛti, Dauvārika, and likewise Sugrīvaka. || 181 ||
Varuṇa, Puṣpadanta, and the one called Suraśeṣa are the presiding deities of the diseases; then, in the west and subsequently in the north, are Vāyu and the chief Nāgas. || 182 ||

To the north are those known as Soma, Bhallāṭa, and Argala, along with Aditi and Diti. The station of Brahmā is red in color, and the directions are marked by yellow [lines] intersecting at the intermediate points.
Then, the cardinal directions should be marked with green and the intermediate directions with black; a reddish halo should be made so that the mandala becomes beautiful. || 184 ||
With rice, mung beans, and barley, sequentially soaked in honey, ghee, and milk.
One hundred and eight, and likewise twenty and eight.

One should offer oblations with each of those substances and worship according to the prescribed rite; one should also present a bali-offering to them consisting of milk-rice accompanied by side dishes.

Thus, when the sun has entered Leo, on the full moon day of every year, one should perform the Vāstu-pūjā in one's own home or in pavilions. There shall be no untimely death, no disease, and no fear of spirits, ghosts, and the like. 187.
There shall be no affliction from serpents, nor any inauspicious events such as mutual quarrels and the like.
He becomes a possessor of sons, grandsons, wealth, health, cattle, and female slaves; free from disease and victorious, he lives long and renowned in his home. (188)
Everywhere in the royal palaces, as well as in the quarters of the queens.
In the houses of the ministers, counselors, and generals, as well as in the city, the excellent preceptor should perform this annually for the sake of the success described. || 189 ||
If it were not as described, then suffering would arise together with its fruits.
Especially for the Bhairavas, the Kṣetrapālas, and the Yoginīs. || 190 ||
An offering should be made by those of left-hand conduct using buffaloes or even cocks; for when propitiated through the left-hand path, they become exceedingly hungry [for the sacrifice]. || 191 ||
The deities desire an offering; if that is deficient, they destroy the practitioner.
Intoxicated by liquor and meat, they were impelled by their past karma. || 192 ||
Since they sometimes desire auspiciousness, the virtuous do not perform worship of them from the left;
rather, it is done in their presence in the morning.

Whether it be auspicious or not is as it is in the scriptures and among the people. As long as a person does not eat meat or drink intoxicants, they remain free from greed; but when they consume them, their mind becomes fixed upon that—where then is the recitation of mantras, and where are the deities? (194)
He who, through the renunciation of liquor, meat, and the like, and through the constant practice of that [discipline], appears identical in form [to the perfected ones], is a *siddha*;
any other, however, is a sinner. || 195 ||

Having examined them in this manner, one should cultivate association even with those who have attained perfection. What need is there for much speaking on this point? For from the contrary course follows total ruin. (196)

Having reflected thus, O gods, [he said]: "One's own duty leads to the highest good. Having thus performed the rite for the pacification of the site (vāstu-śānti) for the sake of discerning between the real and the unreal, || 197 ||
Within seven or even nine days prior to the day of initiation.
This rite of sowing the seed must be performed; it grants all desires.
In another well-enclosed area to the north of the pavilion,
the skillful practitioner should construct a pavilion facing east or west.
In the initiation of the left-hand path (vāmamārga), a [mandala] extending from south to north is highly recommended.
On ground smeared with cow dung, either on the right or on the left.
With rice mixed with oil and with the juice of Vijayā mixed with oil, five long lines measuring five cubits each should be drawn there.
Lines for Rudra should be drawn, separated by a span (vitasti) and of equal length.
There should be forty squares [formed] by twenty-four squares. || 202 ||
There, a pathway should be made with the limbs of Vāyu and filled with red powders.
The four compartments that follow are declared to be the station of Brahmā.
Beginning from the southeast cell and proceeding up to the northeast, one should fill [the grid] with yellow, red,
and black powders, following the path of emanation.
Then one should fill two squares and the pathway with red [pigment]. That area of four squares in front should be known as the station of Viṣṇu. || 205 ||
Having filled it with dust as before, one should also construct four paths in front of that, shaped like hand-drums (ḍamaruka), which have Viṣṇu as their presiding deity. (206)
Adorned with dūrvā grass, mango sprouts, and leaves of the aśvattha tree, and wrapped with thread,
one should place them in the four squares of the station of Viṣṇu.
The five principal Vairiñcya [vessels] are made of wood and measure sixteen finger-breadths.
One should subsequently establish them as endowed with what are called length, height, and breadth. || 208 ||
In the station of Brahmā, four earthen bowls belonging to Śiva, twelve aṅgulas in height, are joined with threads made of sprouts and other materials as before. || 209 ||
Having washed it and wrapped it with threads, one should place it in the directions starting from the east, as before, beginning with the fire.
And upon heaps of śāli rice, and upon mats made of darbha grass and other fragrant materials. || 210 ||
One should fill those vessels with sand, clay, and cow-dung, accompanied by the sound of conch shells,
the five musical notes, and the blessings of the Brahmins.
Then, one should sow ten seeds in a vessel made of gold or other materials; the practitioner of mantra should recite the *vaṃ* seed-syllable and wash them again with milk. || 212 ||
These are the priyaṅgu, śyāmāka, sesame, mustard, and rice.
Mudga, āḍhakī, tuvarī, niṣpāva, khalva, and māṣa are proclaimed [as the legumes]. || 213 ||

One should first scatter [the offerings] upon the vessel of Brahmā, then upon that of Viṣṇu, and then upon that of Śiva, preceded by the five musical instruments and the chanting of the Veda. || 214 ||
Then, having sprinkled it with turmeric and other substances, one should cover it with cloths.
One should offer the bali-oblation during both twilights and also at night.
Following the path instructed by the guru, one should properly offer the bali for nine days before the three vessels, dedicating each to its respective deity. || 216 ||
On the first day, there shall be boiled rice, sesame seeds, parched grain, and barley meal.
Combined with turmeric powder, this is considered an offering (bali) for the spirits (bhūtas). || 217 ||
Thus, on the second day, [offerings] with sesame circles are for the ancestors;
on the third, groats mixed with curd are for the yakṣas.
Those parched grains which have been soaked in coconut water are [known as] *nāgebhyaḥ-saktavaḥ*.
One should joyfully offer a bali-offering of lotuses and unbroken rice grains to Brahmā on the fifth day.
On the sixth day, rice mixed with cakes is recommended for Śiva; on that occasion, one should offer cooked rice to Viṣṇu on the seventh day.
O gods, at the station of Brahmā there is Vetāla, and a ram is his sacrificial offering; at the station of Viṣṇu there is Bhairavī, and a goat is considered her offering. || 221 ||
Bhairava, however, desires a buffalo as an offering in the place of Śiva; there, liquor made from molasses, honey, and flour is considered appropriate in that order. || 222 ||
An offering of fish-meat combined with liquor is prescribed for the spirits (bhūtas); hare-meat for the ancestors (pitṛs), and cock-meat with honey for the yakṣas.
This is the bali offering for the frogs, the bali for the snakes, and this is the bali for those on the left-hand path; one should observe these when nine days have thus passed. || 224 ||
Has its arising occurred correctly? And what has been lost in the middle?
When there is a correct emergence, success is achieved; when it is blunted, one encounters obstacles. || 225 ||
If it is eaten by insects and the fruit cracks open, there is total ruin. Success is to be known through *priyaṅgu* seeds; with *śyāmāka* grains, there will be happiness from women. (226)

With sesame seeds there is delight for those worthy of worship; with mustard seeds, there is no malevolent magic. With rice, there is universal honor; with mung beans, there shall be the grace of the gods. (227)

Likewise, with *aḍhakī* beans one obtains four-footed animals; with *niṣpāva* beans in the field or house; with *khalva* beans there is success in virtuous deeds; and with *māṣa* beans there shall be peace in battle. (228)
If all [the breaths] rise on the left, there is accomplishment; otherwise, there is a fall.
From Caitra, the fruit of initiation is suffering for the sake of the accomplishment of the jewel of consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
Inferiority, death, loss of kinsmen, and suffering follow in succession; then joy, growth, sorrow, exhaustion, and censure follow in order. (230)
Poverty and omniscience; excellence in virtue and happiness; the destruction of wisdom and the loss of intelligence; the acquisition of gold and the increase of knowledge. || 231 ||
One should abandon prosperity, success, excellence, and the intercalary month (malamāsa) and the waning moon (kṣaya).
Mental anguish is the prosperity of the wealthy; the success of a mantra is its true happiness. || 232 ||
The accomplishment of minor deities, swift success, and auspicious intelligence.
Friendship with gods leads to total ruin, as does quarreling, which brings great fear. || 233 ||

From the recitation [of mantras] on the right or on the left, the results for the planets are, respectively: the attainment of all goals, fever, success, affliction, heat, lordship, and the fruit of universal accomplishment. (234)
The fruit of the tenth part is the destruction of intellect; the excellent accomplishments are to be known in their successive order.
Those who do not honor Gaurī, those who have fallen from their mantras, and those who do not honor Gaṇeśa are miserable. || 235 ||
All mantras will be accomplished, and they shall never fail to be accomplished.
Prosperity, the attainment of suffering, foolishness, and the destruction of one's teacher. || 236 ||
There is the destruction of the ill-fortune of dullness, and every fruit shall become complete. For Hari, the white [conch] is excellent, never the black; the bright one is most auspicious. || 237 ||
Success shall come from all mantras, and even great danger has been declared [to be overcome].
Success comes specifically from the element, while the loss of sons occurs apart from the ancestors.
The results for each door in sequence are said to be: intelligence, dullness, death, lack of authority, sons, acquisition of wealth, and death. (239)
The results of the yogas beginning with Viṣkumbha shall correspond to their respective names.
The fruit of the yogas beginning with Ānanda is complete in every respect.
Having abandoned the *viṣṭi* yoga, one should practice during the [other] *karaṇas*; success will then be swift.
All success is achieved during the tail of Viṣṭi; during a fixed (sthira) yoga, however, there shall be stability. || 241 ||
Now, the results of the ascendant (lagna): wealth, grain, prosperity, sovereignty, or the attainment of divine powers; [otherwise] loss or the destruction of intelligence. || 242 ||
There is the attainment of prosperity such as jewels, as well as wealth, grain, and supernatural powers.
Full accomplishment and majesty, as well as loss and the destruction of higher knowledge. || 243 ||

There will be the attainment of former goals, success in mantras, cattle, and abundant wealth; yet there will always be suffering as well as loss, though the union of couples shall be auspicious. (244)
In many ways, it is auspicious, yet contrary to the interests of the Vāmins and the Yavanas.
Malefic planets situated in the three *ṣaḍāya* houses, and benefics situated in the quadrants (*kendras*) and trines (*trikoṇas*). || 245 ||
If all planets are in the eighth house, they bestow death; if a planet is in the twelfth or the sixth house, there is illness.
A mantra should be received when the moon is strong; otherwise, there will be the occurrence of evil. || 246 ||

The grace of the deity arises in accordance with the strength of one's stars; [the deity] bestows dharma, bestows sovereignty, and bestows accomplishment, while the middle one brings about destruction. (247)
In the morning, the forenoon, midday, the afternoon, and likewise at evening; during a lunar eclipse there is poverty, but during a solar eclipse there is all prosperity.

When the Guru is aspected by malefic planets, yet a most auspicious *siddhakṣetra* (place of accomplishment) is available—if by chance the Guru arrives there, then the initiation (*dīkṣā*) should take place. On the day prior to the day of initiation, having performed the morning rites, [one should proceed]. || 249 ||
Having adorned his own body, he should perform worship in his own home according to the ritual for Gaṇeśa, and thereafter have the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) recited. || 250 ||
Having offered libations to the Nāndīmukha ancestors, accompanied by the five musical instruments;
Having gathered the necessary provisions as prescribed, one should proceed toward the teacher’s residence.
The requisites for the selection of the preceptor and the officiating priests are considered to be tenfold. || 251 ||
The seats made from Śrīparṇī wood should be one cubit in measurement according to the prescribed dimensions.
They are equal in size and possess a height of eight finger-breadths. || 252 ||
Twenty-seven blades of darbha grass, adorned with knots at their tips, form the braid.
These are the seats prescribed as the defining characteristics for all sacrifices. || 253 ||

There were copper basins filled with pleasantly warm water for the purpose of washing the feet; conch shells containing fragrant flowers and water for the offering of the *arghya*; and water-pots of fine copper filled with sweetmeats for rinsing the mouth.
Those two were made of bell-metal, filled with curd and other ingredients for the sake of the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
Very costly garments and excellent ornaments such as signet rings and the like.
One should provide parasols made of Madhūka leaves along with turbans. || 255 ||
And one should bring sandals there, adorned with armor and ornaments.
Having performed this, one obtains a fruit comparable to the honor bestowed at a great sacrifice. || 256 ||
Honoring other Brahmins with the madhuparka offering is prescribed; however, one who possesses true devotion should give double that amount to the Ācārya with sincere devotion. || 257 ||
Wherein the worship of the preceptor is performed together with other twice-born ones.
In that [state], the fruit of sacrifice is meager, like that of the earth during a drought. || 258 ||
Having thus gone to the teacher’s house and bowed to the teacher’s sandals,
and having presented the materials for the formal request and made the ritual resolve (saṅkalpa), he should choose the teacher.
"O best of the twice-born, having spoken thus regarding the non-acceptance of the mantra once uttered and recited, and regarding the status of a guru, I therefore choose you. (260)

Having spoken thus, the disciple should choose [the teacher], saying, "I am chosen. Then the teacher should say, "Perform the duties toward the teacher as is appropriate," and the disciple should reply. (261)
And then, by the command of the Guru alone, the Preceptor says, "I shall do so."
He should choose eight Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
When those who worship that deity are [appointed] as officiating priests (ṛtvij), or alternatively, when there are four sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa), then four officiating priests are prescribed. (263)
Then the Guru, accompanied by his disciple, should go to the sacrificial hall; having sat down at its door, he should then begin the examination.
One should give the disciple a tooth-stick consecrated with the root-mantra. Having cleansed his teeth, [the disciple] stands before a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) measuring one cubit. || 265 ||
One should bring four [lines] and then the Guru should examine them; whatever direction that tip points toward, there this result is from the east. || 266 ||
Prosperity, mental anguish, loss of kinsmen, as well as intelligence, sorrow, agitation, happiness, and the attainment of knowledge—these are the results in successive order. || 267 ||
One should perform an expiation for traveling in an inauspicious vehicle:
either one thousand and eight, or one hundred, or even twenty [repetitions of the mantra]. || 268 ||
And with their names enclosed by the weapon-mantra (astra) and followed by "svāhā."
One should utter the mantra "doṣāñjahi jahī" (destroy the defects, destroy them), followed by the word "namaḥ" at the end. || 269 ||
One should likewise offer oblations with clarified butter alone in the case of a bad dream; furthermore, a tooth-stick should be used again if the result is still unfavorable.
If even a third [time] she is found to be corrupt, that deity must not be accepted; for on the Vāmamārga, a disciple may destroy his guru even with a single [instance of such corruption]. || 271 ||
Then one should perform the examination of dreams; the procedure for that is now described. It applies to those who follow the Vedas, the Dakṣiṇas, the Vaiṣṇavas, and the Vāmas. || 272 ||
That divine power which, while one is awake, goes far away, having enveloped the three gods with restrained mantras.
"Eating sacrificial food and lying on his right side, he should examine the dream according to the instruction:
'O Blessed One, Lord of the gods, wielder of the trident, whose vehicle is the bull! Tell me of the desired and the undesired; what is the fruit for one who has fallen asleep in a dream? (274)
Thus, while sleeping on a bed strewn with kusha grass with a mind intent on eating only once a day, he sees at the end of the night a dream, whether auspicious or inauspicious. || 275 ||

Oṃ [Namaḥ || Arthāt || Oṃ namaḥ sakalalokāya viṣṇave prabhaviṣṇave viśveśaviśvarūpāya svapnādhipataye namaḥ; one should recite this, "May Viṣṇu bring the dream," from the heart. To Viṣṇu, the lord of all worlds.
Salutation to the powerful one, the Lord of the universe, whose form is the universe, the sovereign of dreams.
"Bring this mantra for obtaining dreams; one who has fasted and conquered his senses, lying upon a bed of *darbha* grass at night, shall see a dream just as it is. (277)
Having eaten, he should sleep on a very clean bed or upon the surface of the earth; then, having risen at midnight and performed the cleansing of his feet, [he should proceed]. || 278 ||
Having sipped water, worshipped the deity, and meditated upon Him on one's own head (the meaning is:
at the crown of the head), one should contemplate the identity of Śiva and the deity and recite this: || 279 ||
Salutation to the unborn, the three-eyed, the tawny-hued, the Great Soul;
salutation to the Auspicious One, whose form is the universe, the Lord of Dreams. || 280 ||
"O Maheśvara, tell me daily in my dreams everything regarding all matters without exception;
by your grace, O Great Lord, I shall bring about the accomplishment of these tasks. (281)
Just as one who is initiated among those who are initiated is born according to his own dream, so let all you gods listen with full attention to that procedure. 282.
At the conclusion of the worship of the Lord of the Earth, one should mutter the mantra which has the color of the sun.
One should perform oblations with a tenth part of that amount, using bilva leaves soaked in clarified butter.

Having performed the libation and the ritual sprinkling, one should provide a meal for Brahmins; thus his mantra becomes perfected, and that which resides in the heart speaks to him in a dream. || 284 ||
*Tāra* (Oṃ), *hali* twice, followed by *śūlapāṇaye* and *dviṭha* (svāhā) is declared; this twelve-syllable mantra is said to summon dreams. || 285 ||
If, however, [the dream occurs] in the first watch of the night, its fruit will manifest within a year.
In a two-watch [day], [it is accomplished] in six months; in a three-watch [day], in three months. || 286 ||
In the fourth month, during the early morning hours, sleep quickly becomes fruitless; the dream should not be interpreted otherwise. || 287 ||
Whatever thought dwells in his heart, its fruit is not found at all.
Due to a predominance of wind (vāta), there occurs a dream preceded by a sudden upward flight. || 288 ||

From pitta arise fire, light, yellow, and so forth, as well as blood, anger, and the like; from phlegm (śleṣman) arise white, cold, and so forth, as well as lying down, sitting, and strength. || 289 ||
From the Vātas there is body ache in the morning, while from the Pittas there is burning in the eyes.
From phlegm (kapha), there is constant trembling; in the pair [of humors], there is pain in the heart; and in all three, all three symptoms occur. || 290 ||
Or one may worship a perfected being (siddha), one’s own guru, the deity, a pleased maiden, Gaṅgā Bhāgīrathī, the Sun, a bearer of the sectarian mark (liṅgin), or the Liṅga of Īśvara. || 291 ||
A young boy, an umbrella, a chariot, a lamp, a palace, a lotus, and a river.
An elephant, a bull, a garland, the ocean, and a tree bearing fruit. || 292 ||
A mountain of blazing fire, raw meat, and liquor; the planets, the stars, the moon, and the sun; and jewels and ornaments. || 293 ||
The lion throne, the celestial chariot, the banner, the musical instruments, and the consecration.
White sandalwood, garments, śāli rice, saffron, and honey. || 294 ||
The king [bestowed] Siddhārthaka, women, new vessels, milk-rice, a horse, fruits, prepared food, curd, a child, and a gallant man. || 295 ||
Milk, musical instruments, a blue jay, a peacock, a mongoose, and a deer—
A single well-composed verse is like a bound flower; it is a true word that serves as collyrium for the eyes.
A full water-pot, a mirror, a pair of fish, wine, food, a corpse devoid of weeping, sectarian marks (puṇḍra), and small flags. || 297 ||
He saw the Vedic chants of the Bharadvāja kings, the singing of bards, the whip, auspicious songs, and the beloved goad that bestows victory in battle. || 298 ||
Having seen these in a dream, the practitioner shall attain success.
For one afflicted by disease and the like, there is no suffering; he shall attain common happiness. || 299 ||
When, during rites performed for the sake of desired objects, one sees in dreams a woman who is full of desire, or a river, or the ocean, or a twice-born man clad in white garments; || 300 ||
And likewise, at the rising of the sun, as well as during the eclipses of the moon and the sun.
Climbing onto a palace, a mansion, an elephant, a horse, a bull, a mountain, or fire. || 301 ||
The food consists of curd-rice and the eating of cooked meat.
Anointing with worms and excrement, and sprinkling with blood. || 302 ||
Chewing betel, drinking liquor, and bowing down to curd.
Seeing the moon's rays in a dream is a favorable omen for the successful accomplishment of one's purpose.
If a woman wearing black garments, anointed with black perfumes and ointments,
embraces one in a dream, that night is his last.
Thus, with a red [line], there is disease; with one resembling the dawn (aruna), grief; with a blue one, quarrel;
with a yellow one, there shall be the giving of tribute (karada). || 305 ||
The woman who, wearing white garments and adorned with white garlands and unguents, embraces a man in a dream, for him prosperity is manifest in every direction. || 306 ||
Whether while eating, sleeping, drinking, or regarding his body, vehicle, or house, if he awakens as if they were ablaze, his prosperity shall be all-encompassing. || 307 ||
If a bite from a white snake occurs on the right hand, he shall become a possessor of enjoyments after ten days;
if he is afflicted by disease, he is liberated from that disease.
He may be bound by shackles or many snares, or he may be joined with them; yet his status increases, and there is an end to the drinking of milk and the loss of wealth. || 309 ||
A Brahmin drinking red wine shall obtain knowledge and supreme wealth. If curd is seen, there will be joy; and from wheat, the arrival of riches. (310)
Through success one should know the arrival of knowledge; likewise, gain is indicated by *siddhārthaka* seeds.
The acquisition of curd brings wealth; from the acquisition of ghee, certain victory follows.
From eating ghee comes affliction regarding wealth, but from consuming curd comes victory.
Having observed the worship of the lingas, worldly convention arises here.
But he who, in the middle of a pond or similar body of water, should eat ghee and milk-rice upon a steady lotus leaf—one should know him to be a lord of the earth. || 313 ||
Deities, ascetics, cows, ancestors, Brahmins, and kings—whatever they tell a man in a dream, that shall indeed come to pass. || 314 ||
He who encircles a village or likewise a city with rice-husks shall obtain a kingdom within a circle in that village, or become a sovereign in that city. || 315 ||
The eclipses of the moon, stars, and sun, as well as their search [for one another], the swallowing of the earth and the oceans, or the act of slaying enemies; || 316 ||
There is victory in disputes and in gambling, as well as victory over enemies.
The milking of mares, buffaloes, lionesses, cows, female elephants, and so forth. || 317 ||
Faith toward gurus and Brahmins brings auspiciousness from gods, Siddhas, and others; bathing, royal consecration, the severing of one's own head, and death [are likewise indicated]. || 318 ||
Likewise, crossing over sacred waters and leaping over uneven ground [are prohibited].
The birth of cows, elephants, and mares, as well as the acquisition of fire, and likewise the birth of a mare; |||
Embracing another's wife, obtaining her, and weeping; || 319 ||
(37) The sight of excrement, smears, and of jasmine, Arabian jasmine, and *bakula* flowers.
In the conflicts of battle and gambling, victory results in the bondage of fetters.

The acquisition of livestock, mortals, and wild animals, as well as the act of sitting upon them; the appearance of a crest [the obtaining of a peacock]; white clothing; and the wearing of flowers and sandalwood paste. (321)
Silver [is forbidden] in vessels made of gems, pearls, gold, and so forth, as well as in those used for eating.
Then one should observe; from this [observation], the success of the practitioner is to be known here and there. || 322 ||
For those distressed by their undertakings, there shall be the accomplishment of their tasks; for others, there shall be the arrival of wealth.
The hide of a barren woman, chaff, fire, and so forth; salt, charcoal, and fuel. || 323 ||

A man who is a libertine, impotent, insane, or smeared with oil and the like; one whose hair is matted; a sick person; a renunciant among men; one who is naked; one who has been abandoned; or one afflicted by hunger—[these are not to be served]. (324)
One with disheveled hair, one who has fallen, one wounded by an arrow or smeared with oil, a cat, a fight, cotton, and a pregnant woman in her courses—[these are inauspicious]. || 325 ||

Molasses, buttermilk, and mud in the house of one wearing saffron robes; the stumbling of a thunderbolt-wielder (or similar powerful being); liquor and the impurity of animals; blindness, hunchbackedness, foul speech, deafness, and being both lame and hunchbacked—[these are the results]. 326.
Vomiting, an empty jar, and a washerman with soiled garments—when these are seen, no purpose will be achieved;
the sick man shall meet his death. || 327 ||
Having seen even in a dream an Aśoka tree, a Karavīra, or a Palāśa in flower, as well as water, a man shall encounter sorrow. || 328 ||
Entering another form, likewise going toward the southern direction, sinking into mud, bathing, and the destruction of one's son and wife. || 329 ||
It is auspicious when a cow, an elephant, a twice-born man, a brahmin, or the color black is seen.
Clad in red garments and perfumes, wearing a garland, he should be black in color or face the south.
One who mounts a donkey, a camel, or a buffalo does not live for three months; likewise, he whose door is closed in a dream, or in a monastery or his own home, [does not survive]. || 331 ||
And he does not rise again; indeed, his life lasts only until the end of that month.
He who, in a dream, sees vomiting, urine, feces, the birth of offspring, or the emission of semen, has a lifespan of ten months. || 332 ||
He is oppressed by black, deformed men with uplifted weapons.
Or if he is struck with stones, his death will occur without a doubt. || 333 ||
Mounted upon a buffalo, a camel, or a donkey, smeared with oil, and shaven-headed.
For one who has set out toward the southern direction, death is certain; of this there is no doubt.
One may see the collapse of a palace, or the falling of the planets, the moon, and the sun; there shall also be a fall from one's position for mountains and trees. || 335 ||
There is indeed the wasting away of one's own limbs, as well as being overcome by disease.
The sweeping of the house and its smearing with cow-dung or even with clay. || 336 ||
Having crossed the river, he arrived at the bank where another garment was worn; the sick man would be freed from his disease, while for one who is healthy, a loss occurs. || 337 ||
Herds of deer with male names, the *potakī* bird (a specific type of bird), the sow, the *piṅgalā* (a courtesan), the *chucchukā* (a bat), the *pallī* (a lizard),
and auspicious *kokilā* birds on the left side [are favorable]. (338)

The groups of deer named after women, Śrīkaṇṭha, the monkey, and the ruru (a species of deer); the chikara, the priyaka (a type of antelope), the bhāsa, the crow, the hyena, and the dog are on the right. || 339 ||

If sick persons are seen, there will be the destruction of disease; for the success of the practitioner, there will be the acquisition of wealth and so forth for one who is healthy, as well as the excellence of many undertakings. (340)
Having fasted for three nights and subsisted on sacrificial food (haviṣya), the domestic priest should offer one hundred fuel-sticks soaked in milk and anointed with ghee.
A Śūdra, having bathed with palāśa leaves while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra, shall eat sacrificial food (haviṣya).
One should offer lamps in the house of a Brahmin, in the temple of Viṣṇu, and in the shrine of Śiva.

Having seen such an auspicious dream, one should take up the mantra; otherwise, if it is taken up [at the wrong time], there will surely be loss. One should contemplate this matter further in the following way. || 343 ||
Having reflected thus, one should constantly undertake the worship of the guru.
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) there, and having prepared the general offering (sāmānyārghya), || 344 ||

Having sprinkled [the area] with water for the guest-offering (arghyodaka), one should perform the worship of the door; thereafter, the preceptor [should dispel] divine obstacles by means of a forceful strike.
One should gradually expel those situated in the intermediate space with the subsequent mantras.
Then, one should drive away the earthly spirits with three blows of the heel.
Having slightly contracted the limb, one should touch the branch extending to the left.
One should clear away obstacles, making way for them on the right side.
Then, one should enter the yoga-maṇḍapa with the right foot;
or, in the Śākta path, preceded by the left foot.
One should worship Brahmā and Vāstvadhiśa in the south-western direction.
And one should well sprinkle the place of sacrifice with water for the guest-offering (arghya) and with cow-products (gavya). || 349 ||
Then, one should perform purification in four ways, beginning with the gazing [upon the disciple].
Having inspected it with the root mantra, one should then sprinkle it with the Astra mantra.
One should perform the striking with the Astra-mantra and sprinkle [the victim] with the Kavaca-mantra.
And having fumigated it seven times with incense made of śrīkhaṇḍa, aguru, and mantras.
Victory, sandalwood, white mustard seeds, dūrvā grass, ashes, unbroken rice grains, and kuśa grass.
The practitioner should scatter parched rice mixed with sesame seeds within the pavilion, for these indeed destroy obstacles.
One should purify them with the Astra-mantra using a handful of darbha grass; then, for the sake of providing a seat, one should place them in the northeast with the Vardhanī vessel.
Then, having caused the Brahmins to recite the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) formula and having diligently gratified them,
one should subsequently draw the Sarvatobhadra mandala upon the altar.
Listen to the procedure for that which is desired as auspicious in both the Śrauta and Smārta rites.
Quadrangular enclosures should be constructed, equal in size to the section for the Dhṛti verses. || 355 ||
One should fill the corner with the color white using three parts of a broken moon;
the chain formed by the five squares situated in the corners shall be black in color. || 356 ||
The chain on both sides is blue; the creeper is the Śaṅkarakoṣṭhaka.
The Śṛṅkhala-bhadra consists of nine syllables on both sides and is reddish in color. || 357 ||
The pond for the Jina’s feet should be white, with a yellow inner perimeter; in the center, one should encircle a beautiful sixteen-petaled lotus on the outside. || 358 ||
In this manner, the Sarvatobhadra mandala is formed using white, reddish-brown, and black [colors].
Now I shall further explain another [matter] which one should perform in Tantric ritual action. || 359 ||

One should construct square compartments equal in number to the groups of letters (the six vargas). In the center, one should erase six of those compartments and there inscribe [the following]. || 360 ||
Then, having excluded one-twelfth of the length on the outside from the center,
one should duly fashion three equal circles in the middle according to the prescribed rule.
With the second circle, one should draw the filaments in the middle of the pericarp; with the innermost circle, the petals;
and the tips of the petals from the portion left over.
Having placed [the lotuses] on the tips of the filaments, one should place half-moons at the sides; then, in front of those, one should arrange the feet in the corners using three squares.

The remaining [sections] have yellow bodies; beyond that, one should form two rows. Having cleared away the ground, one should create a pathway (vīthī) in the four directions and in the center. || 364 ||
The Sarvatobhadra-cakra:

(40) By these [letters] in sequence, four doorways are formed by four squares each.
And with one [unit] of three cells each on both sides of the door. || 365 ||
From this point, let there be the *śobhās* with three squares on one side;
then, one should fashion the *upaśobhās* with six squares and the *kośas*. || 366 ||
The white powder of rice should be equal in height and length;
the boundary lines and the petals should be made with a measure of one finger-breadth.
One should worship the pillars, the body-parts, and the fourfold group at the door with that [substance]; the petals should also be filled with blood by those who are not Brahmins. || 368 ||
The door-decorations (dvāraśobhās) should be filled with safflower powder (kusumbhacūrṇa) made reddish;
their bases (pādas) are yellow, as determined by all the colors.
Turmeric powder should be yellow, and the pericarp should be within the pedestal.
And the ornaments were yellowish in the center and black at the edges by the Brahmin.
One should fill it with that green powder produced from the grinding of bilva leaves.
Adorned with the forms of leaves, roots, and fruits, they are heart-pleasing. || 371 ||
In the middle of the fourfold street, one should fill in the *kalpavallī* creepers; the junctions and the *kalpavallī*s with yellow-red, and the filaments with red.
The skillful preceptor should fill them with powders of various colors; the corners [should be filled] with black color, and then three lines should be drawn outside. || 373 ||
One should adorn [the mandala] in sequence with powders known as white, reddish-brown, and black.
This Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala is proclaimed in all tantras. || 374 ||
"You shall describe the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala for the divine classes; search there in the south for the nine-square sections. (375)

Just as before, however, in the middle of that [space], there should be an auspicious lotus made of six squares; the pedestal (pīṭha) should consist of a single row, while the door-ornaments (dvāraśobhā) are as previously described. || 376 ||
The sheaths should be colored with six compartments, as before.
The pedestal-feet, the enclosures, and the lotus and other elements are considered to be as described previously. || 377 ||
In the left-hand path (vāmamārga), the mandala should consist of eight groups of squares; a lotus should be in the center with four [squares], and there may be a pathway outside of it. || 378 ||
That lotus is indeed always joined with a wish-fulfilling creeper (kalpavallī). One should proceed with four lotuses in the four directions using four squares. || 379 ||
In the intermediate directions, there should be four groups of four, numbering according to the Vedas.
In the center of the four-cornered lotus-paths, it resembles a svastika.
It is produced by means of four quadrants in all four intermediate directions;
one should fill them with powders that are white, yellow, red, and blue. || 381 ||
Another [diagram] consisting of one hundred svastikas is proclaimed as being like the previous one; this is indeed declared to be the very beautiful Mandala of the Nine Nāgas (Navanāga). || 382 ||
This very [point] has been stated by the following method: the central door is that which abandons the intermediate directions.
I shall now describe the five-petalled lotus, beginning with the single-square fourfold [arrangement]. || 383 ||

The lotus is first fashioned with its doors and the four squares marked with svastikas; the pathways are to be filled with colors, and on the pedestal, within the divine wombs (surayoni), [the deities are placed]. || 384 ||
(p. 41) Now, for the purpose of consecrating the mantra, I shall describe the Vāruṇa maṇḍala.
Whoever should construct a square [mandala] consisting of sixty-four compartments; || 385 ||
One should sweep the corners of the squares in the directions starting from the southwest (antya) and ending with the northwest (antima).
The four squares situated in the middle are called the "doorkeepers" (dvāssthā), starting from the east. || 386 ||
One should fill them with yellow and dark dust made from turmeric.
Excluding one corner cell, those five are designated as "feet. || 387 ||
It should be yellow, pale white, and red; one should fill it with yellow and black [pigments].
From the southeast corner, the square compartments are colored red, green, and black. || 388 ||
Then one should fill half of that [space] and fasten a canopy as is appropriate; with white color, one should have four circles made in the center. || 389 ||
First, from the pedestal, there is a circle with a diameter of six [units] plus half the [distance to the] northeast (Īśa) and other directions;
that is yellow, shaped like a lotus pericarp, and surrounded by a white line. || 390 ||
The second [lotus] is joined with filaments whose width is double [that of the first].
Its filaments are yellow, red, and white in color at the base, middle, and tip respectively.
In front of that, he makes a white [square] measuring seventy-two parts;
the third [element] is circular, with a width equal to one-third [of the total]. || 392 ||
Therein, [draw] a white eight-petalled lotus with red tips on its petals and a white base; outside that, it should be black in color;
as before, draw a white line.
Outside of that, one should fashion sixteen-sided figures joined to the circular perimeters.
Within that, on the exterior of the stūpa, [the colors] are dark blue, yellow, reddish, and white. || 394 ||
Five lines—white, yellow, reddish, dark blue, and green—should be made very beautiful;

thus one should fill the interior of the pedestal. One should draw a thunderbolt (vajra), a spear (śakti), a staff (daṇḍa), a sword (khaḍga), a noose (pāśa), a goad (aṅkuśa), and a mace (gadā). || 395 ||
Likewise, in the east and the northeast, there is a trident accompanied by a wheel and a lotus.
Then, one should sit upon a seat on the altar facing the east; having assumed the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), remaining silent, with the body straight, and the senses subdued. || 396 ||
The supreme preceptor, having arranged the articles for worship, should place an auspicious water-pot on his right side and on his left side. || 397 ||
Having placed a fragrant vessel filled with water for washing the hands, he should then set down another vessel and light auspicious lamps. || 398 ||
The knower of mantras [should place] a fan, a mirror, an umbrella, and a chowrie in the various directions.
One should consecrate all of them according to the procedure that will be described hereafter. || 399 ||
Having performed the purification of the hands, one should then utter three *tāras*—the *tāra* being the *praṇava*, and the *śara* being *huṃ phaṭ*;
having recited "Oṃ Oṃ Oṃ Huṃ Phaṭ," the practitioner, being composed, should perform the binding of the directions (*digbandha*) with the *śara* mantra. (400)
I shall now describe that which has arisen from the Mahat in every respect.
Then, having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should practice the stabilization of the vital breath (prāṇasthāpana).
Then the preceptor, with a restrained mind, should perform the nyāsa and other rites; he should place the Ṛṣi upon his head and place the Chandas within his mouth. (402)

Having placed the deity in the heart, the preceptor, as a reciter of mantras, should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the six limbs or the five limbs of the root mantra according to the prescribed rule. (403)
The eye is prescribed as the fifth limb of whichever mantra it may be.
For one who is deprived of limbs, one should restore the limb of the mind by means of that very same [mind]. || 404 ||
Then, according to the path taught in the mantra, the knower of mantras should perform other ritual placements (nyāsa) upon his own body and fashion the yoga-pīṭha.

Then, one should meditate upon the deity of the mantra within the seat (pīṭha) whose nature is the body; having displayed the mudrās, one should then establish the excellent arghya offering. || 406 ||
Then, one should place the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, filled with water, on the right side.
There, one should place a very small amount of water from a conch shell, dedicated to each respective deity.

The knower of mantras, being composed, should then offer water for the feet, water for sipping, and the honey-mixture (madhuparka), sprinkling them with the root-mantra and the water from the consecrated vessel.
One's own self, the mandala, and other requisites for worship and so forth.
The best of preceptors should sprinkle that place with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Having worshipped the Yoga-pīṭha according to the path of ritual placement (nyāsa), the knower of mantras should then worship his chosen deity there within the pīṭha. || 410 ||
Then, identifying oneself with the deity, one should offer five beautiful handfuls of flowers: upon the head, the heart, the base (the navel), the feet, and all the limbs. || 411 ||
And one should worship with offerings and prepared substances such as sandalwood and the like.
That [deity] is to be worshipped with all ritual services according to the path instructed by the Guru. || 412 ||
One should complete all of this and perform the rites with the water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel.
Having set aside the water contained in the *prokṣaṇī* vessel and having sprinkled [the area] as before, || 413 ||
The Guru should worship the maṇḍala with offerings such as sandalwood paste and other services;
first, he should fill the pericarp with *śāli* rice grains. || 414 ||
One should place darbha grass upon these, and then place that [vessel] which was previously mentioned directly on top.
The long kuśa grass blades, twenty-seven in number, have their roots severed. || 415 ||
That which is joined with the Brahma-knot at its tip is here called the *kūrca*.
One should worship [the deities] beginning with Ādhāraśakti and ending with the mantra of the pedestal (pīṭha). || 416 ||
There, one should place a pitcher made of gold or other materials, free from any cracks or holes.
It is encircled on all sides on the outside by a thread consisting of the three qualities (guṇas). || 417 ||
The best of teachers should certainly place [the vessel] here, filled perfectly in the middle with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor, even without the recitation of mantras (japa). || 418 ||
Having placed the nine gems into the pitcher, one should then place a tuft of grass (kūrca) upon it.
One should place [the offering] combined with dūrvā grass and sandalwood, accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Blue flowers, lapis lazuli, coral, and likewise pearls.
Reciting the root mantra at the end, he should contemplate the oneness of his own self.
And the most excellent practitioner should contemplate the non-difference between the jar and its pedestal.
Immediately thereafter, one should fill it with the decoction of fifty medicinal herbs.
Together with one [other], these are the medicinal plants of the [respective] castes:
red sandalwood, white sandalwood, and likewise agallochum (aguru). (422)
Camphor, uśīra, kuṣṭha, bālaka, and keśara; kaṅkolaka, nutmeg, jaṭāmāṃsī, and likewise murā. (423)
Granthika, rocanā, jātipatra, pippalī, bilvaka, pṛṣṭhiparṇī, citraka, mudgaparṇī, and again kuśa. || 424 ||
Kaṭphala, guñjā, udumbaraka, kāśmarī, padmakoṣā, śaṅkhapuṣpī, and likewise the crest of a peacock (mayūraśikhā). || 425 ||
Furthermore, there are the Plakṣa, the Agnimantha, as well as the Śālaparṇī and the Kuśa grasses.
Pāṣāṇabhedaka, kṛṣṇā, śaśipuṣpī, and rohiṇī. || 426 ||
Syonā, chinnaruhā, pāṭalī, mukhakarṇikā, tulasī, śikharī, indravallī, and bhṛṅgī—these are the plants that are most pleasing to the king. || 427 ||
Then Rājitapātālamūlī, with palms joined in reverence, offered the herb known as Śrīdevakanyā, as well as Bhadra and Mustaka. || 428 ||
And these, together with the cloves, are fifty in number.
With decoctions of the bark of milk-exuding trees and that produced from the bark of the Brahmabhūru tree.
Or with auspicious waters perfumed with fragrant paste, flowers, and the like.
Having filled the conch with water such as decoctions and the like, one should stir [the contents] within it.
Now, the eight fragrances for each respective deity are proclaimed.
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, gorocana, saffron, and musk. || 431 ||
Water produced from red sandalwood is declared to belong to Gaṇapati.
Hrīvera, candana, kuṣṭha, aguru, kuṅkuma, murā, sihlaka, and jaṭāmāṃsī—this is declared to be the Vaiṣṇava [incense]. || 432 ||
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, chora, saffron, gorocana, jaṭāmāṃsī, and kapi—these they know as the eight fragrances of Śakti. || 433 ||
And with water, saffron, kuṣṭha, red sandalwood, and sandalwood.
The eight-fold fragrance for Śambhu consists of tagara, aguru, and karpūra. || 434 ||
With water, saffron, kuṣṭha, red sandalwood, and sandalwood;
They know the eight fragrances of the sun to consist of tagara, aguru, and karpūra. || 435 ||
Gorocanā, bell-metal, camphor, agallochum, saffron, sandalwood, the two intoxicants (madayantikā and mādhavī), and the leaf-born [betel] with water; || 436 ||
Through the combination of the eight fragrances and by the power of the instructor, [the result is achieved].
The wise know that in this manner there shall be soot together with the *śakti* in the jar. || 437 ||
First, one should worship the ten digits associated with Agni: Dhūmrārcis, Ūṣmā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, Visphuliṅginī, Suśrī, Surūpā, Kapilā, and both Havyavahā and Kavyavahā. (438)
Immediately after that, one should worship the twelve solar *kalās*: Tapinī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvālinī, and Ruci. (439)
Suṣumṇā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Bodhinī, Dhāriṇī, and Kṣamā.
Afterwards, the most excellent guru should worship the sixteen digits (kalās) of the moon.
Amṛtā, Mānadā, Puṣṭā, Puṣṭi, Tuṣṭi, Rati, and Dhṛti.
Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, and Aṅgadā. || 441 ||
Pūrṇā, Pūrṇāmṛtā, Kānti, Dīpinī, and Aśvarajā are the Kalās.
The fifty digits (kalās) produced from the divisions of the Vedas and so forth are joined with the Bindu.
Having brought them near and established them, one should worship them in due order: Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, Ṛddhi, and Dīpikā. || 443 ||
Recikā, Mocikā, Pārā, Sūkṣmā, Asūkṣmā, and likewise Amṛtā.
She is the one who nourishes with the nectar of knowledge, the all-pervasive, and whose form is like space.
Infinite creation, prosperity, memory, intelligence, and radiance.
Lakṣmī, Dyuti, Sthira, Acchitti, Siddhi, and Pālinī are the Jarās. || 445 ||
Kṣānti, Īśvarī, Rati, Kāmā, Varadā, and Ahlādinī; likewise Dīrghā, Tīkṣṇā, Raudrī, Bhayā, Nidrā, and Tandrīkā. || 446 ||
One should worship Kṣutkrodhinī, Kriyotkārī, Mṛtyu, Pītā, Sitāruṇā, Asitā,
and likewise Anantā, one after another in the middle.
"Hamsaḥ śuciṣad" and so forth, as well as "Pratadviṣṇustave," the "Tryambaka" mantra, the Gāyatrī, and likewise the "Viṣṇoryoni. || 448 ||
The wise one [should perform] the worship of the digits arising from the fivefold divisions of Tāra.
Having invoked the ten Kalās beginning with Sṛṣṭi and having caused them to become present, || 449 ||
Having recited the verse beginning with "haṃsaḥ śuciṣat," one should perform worship.
Having performed the stabilization of the vital breaths (prāṇa), one should worship those digits (kalās).
In this manner, one who knows the ritual procedures [should employ] those [substances] such as old age, sharpness, and yellow.
The wise practitioner should also worship Nivṛtti and the others according to the method already described. || 451 ||

The letter *a* is said to be *ākāra*, and *ukāra* is *makāra*; *bindu* and *nāda* are likewise [the letters *śa* and *ha*]. These seven are proclaimed as the divisions of Śakti and Śānti, which are indeed eternal. (452)
These last two varieties have been described separately. Now, [one should take] the firm sprouts of the Aśvattha, Panasa, and Cūta trees. (453)
One should tie an *indravāruṇī* creeper around the mouth of the jar, and one should meditate upon that [creeper] above the jar as being the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*). || 454 ||
A bowl filled with rice and accompanied by a coconut fruit.
For this is indeed the fruit of the wish-fulfilling tree; one should establish it with this understanding. || 455 ||
Then, one should wrap the flask with a pair of fine cotton cloths.
This is proclaimed to be the installation of the primary pitcher (pradhānakumbha). || 456 ||
Then, in the directions beginning with the east, near the archways, one should fashion mandalas and eight-petaled lotuses according to one's desire.
Above that, one should place a heap of rice at each door;
above that, one should place a full water-pot and worship these [deities] therein. || 458 ||
One should place Budha in the east, Varuṇa in the south, Vākpati in the west, and Vighneśa in the north;
then, one should arrange the water-pots (kumbhas) in the cardinal directions, beginning with the southeast.

One should worship Amṛta, Durjaya, Siddhārthaka, and Maṅgala. Then, starting from the direction of Rudra (the north-east) and proceeding in order through the cardinal directions, one should worship the [deities] beginning with Rudra. (460)
Likewise, the world-protectors [should be placed] upon the jars in the mandalas; [and the elephants]: Airāvata, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Kumuda, and Añjana. || 461 ||
[He should worship] Puṣpadanta, Sārvabhauma, and Supratīka in front of them; then the Guru, having gone to his own altar, shall sit upon his own seat. || 462 ||
Having intentionally [visualized] the form with the root mantra, the supreme guru, having invoked the chosen deity into that form, should worship it. || 463 ||
Then, having recalled the root mantra within the Mātṛkās, the practitioner of mantra should cause the consciousness to emerge,
exiting through the tip of the nose.
The Guru, having raised the lotus of the Mātṛkās within his joined palms—which is filled with great flowers—up to the top of his head, should then invoke [the deity] into it. || 465 ||
Then one should practice the stabilization, the bringing near, and the complete cessation.
Then there is the direct radiation and the fragmentation [of the rays]. || 566 ||

Then the veiling (avaguṇṭhana) should be performed, and after that the immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa). One should perform the supreme transformation (paramīkaraṇa), and [apply] its mudrās in due order.
And one should perform those respective services in due order, arranging them accordingly.
And having performed the ritual services beginning with the seat and ending with the flowers. || 468 ||

Then, within the ritual procedures of the mantras, there is also the worship of the limbs and the enclosures as prescribed, followed at the very end by the worship of the world-protectors and their weapons.
Having thus performed the worship with incense, lamps, and food offerings, and having presented the offering,
one should then [draw] the mandala around it in due order.
The officiating priest, having prepared an excellent sacrificial mound on the southern side of the altar, should place sprouts and leaves of coral there.
Having established the fire and performed the consecration rites, one should commence the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.
Then, according to the prescribed rule, one should worship the deity there with perfumes and other offerings.
There, having first offered oblations with the *praṇava* and then sequentially with the *vyāhṛtis*,
one should offer milk-rice and clarified butter with the root mantra.

Afterwards, having offered oblations with the twenty-five *vyāhṛtis* in sequence, and having worshipped it with sandalwood paste and other offerings, one should place it upon the pedestal-image (*pīṭhamūrti*). || 474 ||
Having dismissed the fire, one should offer the oblation with the desired milk-rice.
To the attendants [he offers] sandalwood paste along with flowers and unbroken grains of rice. || 475 ||
Then, having removed that food offering, the wise one should cleanse that place.
One should again worship with the five services and then demonstrate [the ritual]. || 476 ||
The practitioner, with a concentrated mind, should recite the root mantra one thousand times while holding a mirror, a fan, an umbrella, a chowrie, and mouth-perfume. (477)

Then, having offered that recitation (japa) to the deity for the sake of prosperity, one should also offer the scattered oblation (vikira) here in the northeast direction where it was previously placed.
One should place here a water-pot (karaka) joined with golden cloth and filled with water mixed with añjali-measurements [of offerings],
and one should worship the weapon-deity (astra-devatā) of terrible form.
From the western end to the beginning, she holds a bow and is seated upon a lion.
Then, having stood there and performed worship, he took it and circumambulated it.

At the end of this, one should utter "rakṣa" (protect) and "lokeśāni" (O Queen of the World); then, by means of water consecrated with the Tāra mantra, one should cause the deity to cross over. || 481 ||

One should establish it in its own place with the *phaṭ* mantra and then worship it; thereafter, the best of preceptors, having sat down again, [should worship] it with perfumes and other offerings. (482)
Then, having properly consecrated the fire, one should offer the sacrificial porridge (caru) mixed with cow's milk.
The vessel for the deities and the iṣṭādi offerings should be washed with the śara-mantra. || 483 ||
Then, having consecrated with the root-mantra, [he should take] rice grains produced from the *śāli* paddy.
One should cook the *śara* atoms by means of a measure equal to the *prasṛti* of lunar days and then cast them [into the crucible].
Then, with the vessel washed, the best of preceptors, having covered the mouth [of the disciple] with it, [should perform the rite] with the *huṃ* mantra and then with the root mantra. || 485 ||
The preceptor, facing eastward, should cause the disciple to grasp the Siddhānta;
then, with the root mantra, he should cause it to descend by means of the clarified butter situated in the *sruva* ladle.

Having consecrated the kuśa grass with the *astra-mantra* (HUM) and spread it out, one should divide that [offering] into three parts for a single deity and offer the supreme portion into the fire. || 487 ||
The preceptor, who knows the mantras, should eat the remainder together with his disciple.
The tooth-stick, as previously described, should be one span in length and used after reciting the mantra over the heart. || 488 ||
He should give it to the disciple after purifying it; he should discard what has been washed. || 489 ||

Having performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth with the mantra according to the rules, and having tied that [mantra] upon his crest-lock by means of his own crest-lock, the practitioner should lie down upon the sacrificial altar on a bed of kusha grass during the night together with this disciple; this is declared to be the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa).
