Having risen at dawn, one should again perform the ritual bath, the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), and other duties; then the preceptor, the disciple, and the officiating priests should proceed toward the sacrificial hall.

All of them should offer oblations of sesame seeds mixed with ghee into their respective fire-pits; furthermore, they should perform one thousand and eight oblations with the mantra of the person to be accomplished (sādhya).

Or he should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the substances prescribed by the ritual rules. Then, the best of mantra-knowers should make the bathed disciple drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having brought him near the sacrificial pit, one should observe him with divine vision.
One should unite the consciousness of the heart-lotus of the disciple with one's own self.
The teacher, however, should gradually purify the sixfold path therein;
those [paths] consist of kalās, tattvas, worlds (bhuvanas), phonemes (varṇas), and words (padas), preceded by mantras.
The teacher should contemplate these kalās upon the feet of the disciple:
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti. || 496 ||

(47) Then, the fivefold sequence of purification is taught as follows: beginning with that which transcends peace (śāntyatīta). While touching the disciple with the *kūrca* [broom] brush, the Guru should offer oblations into his own fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*). || 497 ||
With sesame seeds smeared with ghee, the Tāra-mantra is used; here, "you" (tvam) is the path for [the deceased].
One should offer eight oblations with the mantra ending in *dviṭha* (svāhā) for the purpose of purification.
One should contemplate the path of the *kalās* as dissolved into the path of the *tattvas*; then, one should contemplate the path of the *tattvas* in the region of its *liṅga*. 499.
Therein are these Gāṇeśa and Śaiva [mantras], numbering sixty-three (rasāgnayaḥ);
namely, Śiva and Śakti, as well as Sadāśiva and Maheśvara. || 500 ||
Vidyā consists of the five pure [tattvas] and the seven that are both pure and impure: Māyā, Vidyā, Kalā, Rāga, Kāla, and Niyati. || 501 ||
Furthermore, the Puruṣa, as well as the pure [elements], Prakṛti, the intellect (buddhi), and the ego-sense (ahaṃkṛti).
The mind, the ten sense organs, the five subtle elements, and the five gross elements. || 502 ||

Now, the Vaiṣṇava principles (tattvas) are indeed numbered at twenty-two: the individual soul (jīva), vital breath (prāṇa), mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), the subtle elements (tanmātras), and the five gross elements (bhūta-pañcaka). || 503 ||
The ten sense organs, the heart-lotus, as well as the sun, moon, and fire; Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha. || 504 ||
The solar [elements], the subtle elements of the beings, and the organs of cognition and action.
And "nature" (prakṛti) and "intellect" (buddhi)—these constitute the twenty-four principles. || 505 ||
There are exactly ten Śakti-tattvas: Ātman, Vidyā, and Śivā; then Śivā, Vidyā, and likewise Ātman; and again Ātman, Vidyā, and Śivā. (506)
And having performed the oblation with the body as before, one should again contemplate the path of the principles (tattvādhvan) as dissolved into the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan). || 507 ||
The fourteen worlds are to be meditated upon at the disciple’s navel; these, in order, are Pātāla, Rasātala, and Mahātala. (508)

Talātala, Sutala, Vitala, and Atala are the [lower] worlds; then Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, Mahaḥ, Janaḥ, Tapaḥ, and Satyaḥ are the worlds in order. The arrangement of the oblations (homavyūha), however, is as before. || 509 ||
One should contemplate the path of the worlds as dissolved into the path of the phonemes.
One should contemplate the letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa' within the heart.

One should contemplate the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) dissolving into the path of words (padādhvan). Here, the flood of oblations (homaugha) is as before; thereafter, one should contemplate [it] in the forehead.
The path of the feet consists of the syllables of the root mantra in their essential form.
One should perform the journey, the mounting of the vehicle, the oblation, and so forth, exactly as before. || 512 ||

One should contemplate the path of words (padādhvan) dissolving into the path of mantras (mantrādhvan). The complete mantra, as the path of mantras, one should contemplate upon the head of the disciple. || 513 ||

The offering of the *homoha* is as before; it dissolves here into the supreme Śiva. One should meditate on this as situated in the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*); this constitutes the purification of the paths (*adhva-śodhana*). || 514 ||
The supreme guru should emanate those [beings] who were dissolved in Śiva through that very emanation.
And the lord of teachers, having beheld that disciple with his divine vision,
should unite that very consciousness which was abiding within himself back into him.
Then, with the *hunem* and the great *vyāhṛtis*, the most excellent of teachers [performs the rite].
One should indeed offer oblations repeatedly with clarified butter for the functions associated with the limbs of the ritual.
With the mantra known as *brahmārpaṇa*, the wise one [performs] the severing of all karma. || 517 ||

The knower of mantras should offer eight oblations of pure clarified butter; having offered the final full oblation and praised [the deity] with the root mantra, the practitioner of mantras should then proceed.

Having invoked Agni with the mantra pertaining to Agni and his limbs, one should offer a single oblation. Having filled the *sruva* ladle with clarified butter, placing a flower above it with its face downward, and having placed the *sruva* over [the flower], one should cause the flower to fall therein. (519)
With the right and left hands joined together like a conch shell,
one should perform the oblation with meat and mung beans, and bring it to completion with the two sacred waters (tīrtha).
A follower of the Vedic path should perform [the rite] with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, but with the fruit-mantra (*phala-mantra*) for others.
Placing his right foot forward, Dakṣa should perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).

In the Śakti-homa, the practitioner of the Vāmamārga should place his left foot on all sides; then, the knower of mantras, having worshipped again with perfumes and other offerings using the root mantra, [proceeds]. || 522 ||

Having raised the deity from the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the preceptor (ācārya) should place it in the water-pot (kalaśa); there he should worship it, together with its limbs and its retinue, according to the prescribed rite.

Then, having performed the unification of the seven *vyāhṛtis*, the tongues of fire (*agni-jihvās*), the limbs (*aṅgas*), and the forms (*mūrtis*), the preceptor should sprinkle the fire with milk and offer this prayer: || 524 ||
O Agni, O you of great power, O bestower of all desires! Even when another ritual act has arrived, grant your presence with respect. || 525 ||
Having thus offered this prayer with the mantra, one should also dismiss the fire;
then, having dismissed Brahmā, one should present [the offerings] to the Brāhmaṇa.
A copper vessel fashioned from exactly thirty-two palas [of copper].
Having filled it with rice, together with gold and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), [he should offer it]. || 527 ||

One should give that full vessel to a Brahmin for his satisfaction; this is what is called the "full vessel" (pūrṇapātra). Thereafter, one should place the enclosing sticks (paridhi) around the fire, but not the spreading grass (paristaraṇa). || 528 ||
The best of preceptors should cast those [flowers] during both the regular and occasional rites;
the disciple's eyes are then bound with a cloth while reciting the Netra-mantra. || 529 ||
Having taken a cubit from the pit, he should lead him into the vicinity of the maṇḍala;
having filled his hands with flowers, O Hara, he should cause him to cast them as añjalis.
Preceded by the recitation of the root mantra, the Guru [performs this] for the sake of pleasing the deity.
Having removed the blindfold, one should cause him to sit upon a bed of kuśa grass.
Then the best of gurus should cause the disciple to recite this mantra; the disciple, intent on devotion to the guru, should indeed recite the verse therein. || 532 ||
Salutation to that illustrious Guru, by whom the eye of one blinded by the darkness of ignorance has been opened with the collyrium-stick of knowledge. || 533 ||
By means of the preceding ritual of worship, one should remove that [impurity] and generate it; then the disciple should perform the ritual placements (nyāsa) of that mantra upon his body. || 534 ||
Having worshipped one's own chosen deity in the water-pot with the five types of offerings, (p. 49).
There, one should perform the ritual of the complete form according to the path taught in the Tantras.
Then, one should cause the disciple, who has been adorned, to sit within the mandala.
The preceptor [should place] the celestial trees located on the pitcher-mouths upon the head of the child.
Then, accompanied by the five musical sounds and the benedictions of the Brahmins, one should sprinkle the well-established and self-restrained person with water from the ritual pitchers and flowers.
In whatever manner the gods were joined with those consisting of nectar.
With jars filled with water joined by syllables, one should proceed by that very same path. || 538 ||
Then, one should quickly consecrate the disciple for the attainment of perfect accomplishment.
Having first taken up the consecrated water-pot, which is the very embodiment of the mantra.
The most excellent preceptor should then sprinkle that good disciple with those waters;
thereafter, the guru should cause the disciple to rinse his mouth with the remaining water.
And having donned two pure and beautiful garments by the command of the Guru, one should perform the sakalīkaraṇa rite, manifesting the essential nature of that deity.
Having sipped water (ācamana), he should then go near her;
thereafter, the learned man should properly utter the mantra preceded by the syllable Oṃ into the right ear of the Brahmin woman.
The wise preceptor should likewise speak the mantra to others; he himself should meditate upon the Vidyā as consisting of light, proceeding toward its own limbs. || 543 ||
The disciple, having arrived, should especially contemplate, "I am the deity"; the disciple should then mutter one hundred and eight times what has been instructed by the Guru.
One should recite it twenty-eight times, or else eight times.
The disciple should contemplate the identity of the Guru, the Deity, and his own mantra. || 545 ||
The devoted practitioner should repeatedly offer salutation to the Guru.
Furthermore, the eight-limbed and the five-limbed [prostrations] are approved for acts of worship. || 546 ||
Prostration with the two hands, the two knees, the chest, the head, the gaze, and likewise the mind is declared to be the eight-limbed (aṣṭāṅga) salutation. || 547 ||
The hands, knees, head, speech, and gaze are declared to be the five limbs.
The disciple, having reflected, should always carry out the command of the teacher. (548)
And one should respectfully give ornaments and garments to the officiating priests.
And he was gladdened by the thought of offering [the fruit] to the Lord and by the blessings of the twice-born.
The disciple should give half of his own wealth to the guru, or half of that amount; or he may give a tenth part, provided he is free from stinginess regarding his possessions. || 550 ||
Furthermore, one should give cows, land, gold, forests, houses, fields, and so forth, as well as food, clothing, and other necessities without hardship, according to one's wealth. || 551 ||
Adopting another method, one should diligently please the Guru; with a mind perpetually dependent on him, one should be devoted to constant contemplation of him. || 552 ||
Adorned with the dust from the lotus-feet of that [deity], he becomes the best of practitioners (sādhaka).
Then, with various kinds of foods—those to be chewed, those to be licked, those to be sucked, and others as well—[he should offer]. 553.

One should properly feed the Brāhmaṇas and bestow abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). Thus has been described the initiation consisting of ritual action (kriyāmaya-dīkṣā), which bestows prosperity. || 554 ||

(50) This sequence of initiation, which is endowed with enjoyment, has been proclaimed for kings, wealthy Vaiśyas, Brahmins, and those engaged in worldly occupations who desire spiritual perfection. 555.
Then, performing the initiation consisting of the phonemes (varṇamayī-dīkṣā), which bestows the permission for the [higher] teachings, |||
And that which has been proclaimed as the essential nature of the phonemes is the reality of the self.
Such a reality exists within this body, as has been declared by the teachers;
therefore, the best of teachers should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the phonemes upon the child's body. || 557 ||
The preeminent teacher, by his own power, should withdraw the phonemes situated in their respective places in reverse order and cause them to attain the nature of the deity. || 558 ||

Then the disciple shall become one with the deity through the complete absorption of his true nature. Now I shall describe the initiation into the Kalās (kalādīkṣā), which bestows the eight supernatural powers beginning with atomization (aṇimā). || 559 ||
In the Veda, initiation is considered to consist of five kalās; among the Dakṣas, it is held to consist of three kalās.
The fifty bad *kalās* are on the left; that [series] belongs to the perfected mantra-teacher.
The one to be grasped quickly brings about accomplishment, while the contrary leads to the opposite result. The five kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti, are said to belong to living beings. || 561 ||
The wise one should pierce those [energies] sequentially within the body of the disciple, which is composed of the elements.
The kalā Nivṛtti is established from the feet up to the knees.
The portion extending from the knees up to the navel is known as the kalā called Pratiṣṭhā.
From the navel up to the throat, the digit known as Vidyā is situated.
Indeed, the digit known as Śānti is situated from the throat up to the forehead.
Likewise, the kalā Śāntyatītā is said to extend from the forehead up to the head. || 564 ||
Through the process of withdrawal, the wise one should pierce [the disciple] from one place to another;
by his own command at that very place, initiation is said to consist of five parts.
O deities, listen to the method for the initiation consisting of thirty-eight parts (kalās): therein, the twelve letters beginning with 'ka' are established in their proper sequence. (566)
Wherever the digits (kalās) beginning with Bhā are in reverse order, there the sixteen digits of the Sun and likewise those of the Moon should be meditated upon in two places. || 567 ||

In the section beginning with the letter *ya*, the ten digits (*kalā*) of Fire are to be meditated upon. Then follows the withdrawal of the digits of the letters from their respective locations. (568)
Furthermore, the disciple should generate [the deity]; this is the procedure for the initiation into the *kalās*. In the Kaulika and Vāma paths, this initiation bestows its fruit.

Those [other paths] are on the southern path, but one who follows otherwise would fall; I shall now describe the initiation consisting of the Vedas, which, once obtained, bestows happiness upon people. (570)
At that very moment, one becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta) within saṃsāra. One should meditate upon the four-petalled lotus at the disciple’s mūlādhāra. || 571 ||
In its center is a triangle, and within that, too, is Kuṇḍalinī.
The Goddess, composed of the three letters, whose form is like a mass of lightning.
She is the very embodiment of Mahādeva, manifest in form through mere consciousness alone.
The Goddess, subtler than the subtlest, who pierces through the six wheels.
Traveling by way of the Suṣumṇā path toward the divine abode of Śiva.
One should collect the syllables situated in the group of peaceful deities and place them in the position of the lotus.
In the region of the *liṅga*, there is a six-petaled lotus; that is called the *svādhiṣṭhāna*.
On its petals are (*baṃ bhaṃ maṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ*). Furthermore, at the navel, there is a ten-petaled lotus; therein are (*ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ paṃ*).

*Phaṃ*: At the heart is a twelve-petaled lotus; on its petals are [the syllables] *kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ*. Again, at the throat is a sixteen-petaled lotus; on its petals are *aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ*.

Ḷaṃ, ḹṃ, eṃ, aiṃ, oṃ, auṃ, aṃ, aḥ. Furthermore, there is a two-petaled lotus between the eyebrows; one should sequentially assign *laṃ* and *kṣaṃ* to its two petals. Having properly joined the syllable *taṃ* and the pair of letters beginning with *la* to the petals of that lotus in the Svādhiṣṭhāna, the Guru [should proceed].
But one should pierce it. || 575 ||
One should bring those vowels into the bindu, and that bindu into the navel-lotus.
One should oneself pierce the petals of the directions joined with the phonemes beginning with *pha* and *ṭa*.
One should join those phonemes with Rudra, and that Rudra within the lotus of the heart.
One should oneself pierce the lotus of the letters beginning with *ṭha* and ending with *ka* within the Lord.

One should bring those phonemes (varṇas) into that [lotus], and likewise that [seed-syllable] into the lotus of the throat; having diligently joined the vowels to the lotus consisting of petals of kalās. || 578 ||
Then, having joined him with Sadāśiva in the lotus between the eyebrows, which has two petals and is endowed with the *lakṣa*, the preceptor pierces it. || 579 ||
Thus, by means of his power, he should lead the self up to the level of Paraśiva; then, under the command of the Guru, the disciple, with his ignorance burnt away, [remains] upon the earth.
Therefore, one who has attained this realization becomes omniscient; he himself shall become Sadāśiva—this is the truth, there is no doubt. || 581 ||
This auspicious initiation, which consists of the Vedas, is said to bestow knowledge. The Guru himself should meditate upon the Guru in his own hand as having the form of Śiva. (582)
One should recite the root-vidyā, the six limbs, the Mātṛkā-mantra, and so forth; then, out of compassion, placing the right hand upon the head of the disciple—583.

Afterwards, he should instruct [the disciple]; this aforementioned initiation by touch bestows supreme accomplishment. The Guru should cause the mind to rest within Sadāśiva, whose nature is consciousness. (584)
One should meditate upon all the mantras born from that [reality] as being identical with it, thinking:
"By the grace of the Guru, I am born as the absolute Sadāśiva alone. (585)
Meditating thus, one should instruct; this is declared to be the "vow of speech" (vāgdīkṣā). Having closed the eyes and meditated upon the deity within the Supreme Self, || 586 ||
With eyes filled with the bliss of seeing that, the Guru, being of serene mind, should show [it] to the disciple and subsequently instruct him. || 587 ||
For one who has already attained mantra-perfection, this initiation shall be the bestower of further success.
Merely by the sight of the Guru, or even by his speech or touch, [the disciple attains realization]. || 588 ||
Knowledge arises immediately; that is remembered as the Śāmbhavī initiation.
Having examined [the disciple] according to the prescribed rule for the sake of attaining worldly enjoyment and liberation, the Guru— || 589 ||
One should teach the mantra afterwards; otherwise, it becomes fruitless. He who gives [the mantra] by an improper method, and he who receives it by an improper method, [both fail]. (590)
Whether giving or receiving, there will be a curse upon the family.
Both the teacher and the disciple, out of delusion, having failed to examine one another, [proceed]. || 591 ||
One who gives instruction or receives it [in such a manner] shall both incur the state of a piśāca.
But he who receives instruction that is contrary to the scriptures, and he who gives it— || 592 ||
Both of them experience twenty-one terrible hells.
But he who, being of deluded intellect, gives instruction without performing the preparatory rites, || 593 ||
And those mantras perish like rice seeds sown in sand;
the knowledge of mantras never remains in one who is unworthy. (594)
Therefore, an action should be performed after careful examination; otherwise, it will be fruitless.
Knowledge is imparted to a true disciple who possesses supreme devotion.
I tell you that one attains that [state], just as one finds clarified butter at the end of cow's milk.
If one should initiate an unworthy person due to desire for wealth, fear, or attachment and the like, [the following occurs]. || 596 ||
One incurs the curse of the deities, and what has been performed becomes distorted. Having thus bestowed the initiation, the Guru should perform the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣecana). || 597 ||
Without the Vinaya-abhiseka, the practitioner does not attain full enlightenment, the status of an Ācārya, or the desired higher rebirth. (598)
Therefore, having instructed his beloved disciple, the Guru should consecrate him after having fashioned extensive wheels within a beautiful pavilion. || 599 ||
One should place a jar filled with alkaline water in the center of the circle,
and other jars there, provided with cloth and gold.

Various [deities] should be placed upon the petals; there, one should indeed worship one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) in the center, and the deities of the limbs and the surrounding retinue at the ends [of the petals]. 601.
And touching the central jar, the preceptor should recite the four Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs; then, with that water, [he should sprinkle].
"The Guru should consecrate the disciple"—this is the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣecana). From the gods [came] all the tantras, and likewise from the tantras, the sages [received them]. (603)
From whomsoever one is born, that disciple is the unique vessel for all tantras.
He may bear the name of an Ācārya, and the Guru may give him another name.
Whoever should receive initiation from such a person as this shall indeed possess spiritual accomplishment.
He becomes capable among all the foremost mantras. || 605 ||

All the gods are under his control; let the path in the Veda be that which is characterized by goodness (sāttvika). This alone is his rule; his path shall be known as the Southern (dakṣiṇā). || 606 ||
In that regard, the wise man should fetch the waters of various sacred fords (tīrthas): from the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, the Sarasvatī, and the great ocean. || 607 ||
From the Sindhu, Godāvarī, Revā, and Kāverī; from Pṛthūdaka; from the wife of Mahendra (Gaṅgā), the Sarayū, and the Carmaṇvatī; and from Puṣkara. || 608 ||
The waters of the Kṣiprā and the Vetravatī [flow] from the altar of the great river.
Of Kurukṣetra, of the Gaṇḍakī, of the Pūrṇā, and of Mānasa. || 609 ||
Having placed [the substances] in a jar, one should recite the mantras belonging even to various tantras;
indeed, a human being who is consecrated here by those waters becomes a perfected one (siddha). (610)
For the sake of ritual practice, or for the sake of giving to another, or for the sake of the left [side], one should place the pitcher of the sacred ford (tīrtha-ghaṭa) in the middle;
the remaining pitchers are considered to be water-pitchers.
May those very deities who were invoked by the preceptor into the auspicious jar manifest their presence through his mouth in the form of mantras. 612.
For one who has attained self-perfection should never bow his head to anyone;
there is no doubt that death awaits him for whose sake he has bowed his head. (613)
If one has such a guru on the left-hand path who has attained siddhi, and if the disciple is free from ego and always devoted to the deity; || 614 ||
He whose mind is not fixed on the three enjoyments for the sake of the deity, he alone shall be a perfected one in the Vāmā;
any other is a vessel for hell. 615.
He is poor, miserable, and foolish, both in this world and in the next.
One should perform the ritual procedure for the initiation of action according to one's capacity, following the instructions of the Guru.
This reality has been fully explained; what else do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the third chapter, the Illumination of Initiation (*Dīkṣāprakāśa*), in the *Merutantra* composed by Śiva with the approval of the illustrious Mahāmāyā and Mahākāla. || 3 ||
The goddess was requested by name by the sages who were desirous of hearing her.
Then, for the sake of attaining her desired goal, she addressed the God there in this manner: || 1 ||
The Goddess said:
O Śiva, these sages devoted to the Śrauta and Smārta rites ask this;
dispel their doubt, for there is no other person besides you who can do so.
The Lord said:
Let the sages and even the gods ask whatever is on their minds, until the time for the slaying of Jalandhara arrives.
The sages said:
Where is Agni, and where are the gods? How do the deities receive the offerings made into the fire?
Tell us, why are they distinct from it, even though they are its very constituents? (4)
The Lord said:
Neither in heaven, nor in sacred fords, nor in herbs, nor in medicines do the Ṛṣis or deities reside;
rather, the mantras alone are the deities.
The gods assumed those various forms in order to bestow the fruit of their practice upon the practitioners.
But their primary essential nature consists of the mantras alone, and nothing else.
Sanskrit mantras characterized by sattva bestow happiness both in this world and the next.
And they would undoubtedly exist in the form of seeds in another birth. || 7 ||
Even there, the Vedic mantras are proclaimed to be golden;
by serving them, a person does not fall into an evil state.
Having attained the status of the twice-born in this world, those of evil intellect who, like common folk, abandon gold and instead follow the mantras of the Tantrikas, wander about as outcasts.
The Mantras are of the nature of stars because they deliver [one across], and the Tantric practitioners as well grant fruits both in this world and the next,
provided their seeds are not corrupt, even in another birth.
Those beings who possess a certain portion of rajas, however, after the end of their torments, become givers of fruit, just like the vaṭa, udumbara, and pippala trees. || 11 ||

In this world, the mantras belonging to the tamasic and material nature yield great fruits; however, they do not bear fruit in the next world, just as grapes, dates, jackfruit, and the like [do not ripen on trees in the afterlife]. || 12 ||

When that which has been offered into the fire with those mantras is consumed by the purifier, how does the digestive fire (pāvaka) digest it? Just as the planetary deity (graha) gathers that excellence, so too [the fire] draws up the essence produced from the channels (nāḍī).
When the channel flows without defect and carries the light essence of food, then the deity,
like a vessel fit for the gods, conveys prosperity.
In the three signs starting from the sign occupied by the Sun, at the solar hour (arka-nāḍī), prosperity increases.
One should nourish the divine mantras; otherwise, one destroys them like a libertine.

Then, in three [periods] of Saturn, the nāḍī brings about the play of intelligence; from that, in three [periods] of Venus as well, it bestows nourishment even upon those who are left-handed (vāmāḥ). 16.
Then, one should have no doubt regarding the mantra of Saturn during the three [periods]; and likewise, the mantra of the Moon brings nourishment to all mantras during those same three. (17)
Therefore, the guru’s nāḍī in the three [periods] causes the destruction of fruits; conversely, the guru’s nāḍī in those same three [periods] swiftly bestows the accomplishment of mantras. 18.

Then, in the three [fingers] from there, the Rāhu-nāḍī is not present in the true hand of the man; thereafter, in the three [fingers], the Ketu-nāḍī is established by the deity of the mantra in the true element. 19.

In the conjunction of the lunar day (tithi) and the day of the week (vāsara), when the remainder is three (guṇa-śeṣe), he is the consumer of oblations (hutāśana). In the Kau, Svarga, and Kutala systems, he possesses the manifest form of fire.
It kills the practitioner in heaven and takes away his wealth on earth; manifest as fire, it bestows fruit, for on earth it indeed possesses a universal form. || 21 ||

The follower of the Vedic path should perform the installation of the fire according to the Vedic ritual procedure; the follower of the Tantric path should perform the eighteen purificatory rites of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
One should visualize with the root mantra and sprinkle with the weapon mantra.
Reciting the Astra-mantra three times, he should strike the sacrificial pit with Kuśa grass.
Then, sprinkling the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with the armor-mantra (kavaca-mantra) is prescribed; digging the pit to a depth of one finger-breadth with the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra). || 24 ||
One should extract that clay with the thumb and ring finger while reciting the Astra-mantra;
then, one should fill it again with pure clay while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra.
Then one should level it with the Astra-mantra and sprinkle it with the Kavaca-mantra; one should crush it with wood or other materials while reciting that mantra, so that it becomes firm.
One should sweep the sacrificial pit with kuśa grass using the armor-mantra (kavacāṇu); then, one should perform the smearing with cow-dung and water using the same armor-mantra.
In the kavaca [mantra], one should contemplate the digits of fire, the sun, and the moon within the vessel (kuṇḍa).
One should wrap it with a triple-stranded cord around each girdle.
One should perform the worship of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) three times with the armor-mantra (*varma-mantra*). [The mantra is:
"Oṃ, obeisance to the seat for such-and-such a pit. (29)
One should perform the entire worship with modifications such as "eṣorghyaḥ" (this is the water-offering) and so forth;
one should likewise perform the worship of the navel and the girdles.
Then, one should contemplate that sacrificial pit as being as firm as a vajra by means of the weapon-mantra.
Then, with kuśa grass and the heart-mantra, one should extinguish the flames of the fire.
One should construct four paths on the four sides of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa),
using uncut-pointed kuśa grass consecrated with the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra) along the walls of the pit.

One should perform [the rites] for those who have visions of spirits, ghosts, and the like, as well as for weapons and so forth. These consecrations (saṃskāras), equal in number to the Dhṛti verses, are declared to be "High-Faced" (uccānanas). || 33 ||

By this procedure, the removal of the impurities of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is accomplished; however, in the case of the left-hand homa, only the first four purificatory rites (saṃskāras) are indeed performed. 34.

The lines should be triangular and non-triangular, extending toward the east and north, while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*. Viṣṇu, Īśa, and Vāsava are traditionally assigned to the tips of the lines facing the east.
For the lines with their tips facing north, Brahmā, the Sun, and the Moon are situated in sequence.
One should draw [the lines] with a blade of darbha grass on the left path, using the Astra-mantra.
Within the triangle, there is a hexagon, which belongs to the pair of triangles.
There, however, is the worship of six deities, beginning with Viṣṇu, Īśa, and Vāsava.
On the left-hand path, however, the worship of the chosen deity (iṣṭadevī) takes place within a triangle;
having sprinkled it with the Praṇava, one should then worship the Yoga-pīṭha. || 38 ||
I shall now fully explain that procedure: one should visualize the maṇḍala upon its surface; above that, one should contemplate Kālāgnirudra joined with Śakti.
Above that, one should contemplate the Tortoise, and upon its back, the Earth.
There, Śvetadvīpa is to be meditated upon, beautifully surrounded by an ocean of nectar.
Mandāra, pārijāta, santāna, and haricandana trees.
One should likewise contemplate and worship the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas) in that very place. || 41 ||
Within such a house, one should contemplate a beautiful mansion made of jewels; in its center is a golden throne, and one should meditate upon its feet. (42)
The goals of human life, beginning with dharma, consist of dharma, knowledge, and dispassion.
Furthermore, sovereignty and the limbs [of the deity] are said therein to be the seat (pīṭha). || 43 ||
In the center, one should contemplate a lotus whose bulb consists of bliss; its stalk is said to be consciousness, and its filaments consist of the transformations [of the elements]. || 44 ||
The petals consist of the primordial nature (prakṛti), and the pericarp consists of the fifty letters; thereafter follows the triad of mandalas of the sun, the moon, and the fire.
Then, in the directions starting from the east, [he places] Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas.
The self is endowed with the inner self, and beyond that is the supreme self.
Here, the essence of knowledge (jñānātman) resides within the principle of Māyā and is established in the principle of Kalā.
The reality of knowledge (vidyātattva) is the supreme reality; it is declared to be the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha). || 47 ||
On the filaments of that lotus, one should worship these goddesses— Jayā and Vijayā as well— from the center outward, in a clockwise direction starting from the eastern petal. (48)
And another named Ajitā, as well as Jitā, Nityā, and Vilāsinī.
And there, moreover, [he established] Dogdhrī, Aghorā, and likewise Maṅgalā.
"Hrīṃ, obeisance to the lotus-seat of all powers" is what is recited. Having offered a handful of flowers into the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should worship Bhuvaneśvarī. || 50 ||

One should perform the worship beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) and ending with the supreme transformation (paramīkaraṇa); there, one should likewise worship the Goddess Śivā, who is intoxicated with desire and in her menses.
In the systems of Gāṇeśa, Śaiva, and Śākta, one should meditate and worship [the deity]; likewise, in the Vaiṣṇava and Saura systems, one should remember Lakṣmī as being in her menses.
One should contemplate the fire born from the union with Nārāyaṇa; the young girl should provide the fire either from the forest or from the house of a Brahmin. || 53 ||
A married woman who has performed her purificatory rites should collect [the offerings] from the left hand into another auspicious vessel, such as one made of copper, which has been covered.
One should perform the bringing forth of the fire using a new earthen bowl;
having established the fire in the vessel with the *kavaca* mantra, one should offer it with the *astra* mantra.
One should not bring forth the fire from a worn-out bowl, a skull, a broken vessel, or likewise from a firebrand;
doing so brings about the fear of disease and loss.

The wise practitioner should discard the portion for the flesh-eaters toward the southwest with the Astra-mantra from the southeast; he should then establish the portion for the gods in front of him with the root mantra.
Afterwards, one should consecrate that fire with the purificatory rites, such as inspection and the rest.
Then, one should invoke the fire in the form of a lamp-flame.
And then, there is the unification of the earthen element with one's chosen deity and the fire.
Then, having recollected the seed-syllable of fire, one should subsequently unite it with consciousness.
Then, having consecrated it with the syllable Oṃ and rendered it nectar through the Dhenu-mudrā, one should protect it with the Śara-mantra and veil it with the Kavaca-mantra.

Then, having performed worship, one should circumambulate the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) three times clockwise; thereafter, with the syllable Om (praṇava), one should bring one's own two earrings into alignment facing oneself.
There, at the womb of the Goddess, the preceptor, knowing that the ground has been touched, should recognize it as the seed of Śiva and quickly cast the fire there. || 62 ||
One should mentally perform the *ācamana* (sipping of water) for the God and Goddess at the conclusion of sexual union. "Cit piṅgala, slay, slay! Cook, cook! Burn, burn! Make everything known, svāhā!
This is the twenty-four-syllable fire-mantra (*agnimantra*). There is also a reading: "nāla-mekhalayoḥ" (of the stalk and the girdle).
Hana hana! Paca paca! Daha daha! || 63 ||
"Reveal everything, svāhā"—this is the mantra of the excellent Jina beginning with the syllable TĀRĀ.
Having recited this mantra, one should then kindle the fire. || 64 ||
I pay homage to Agni, the blazing one, the knower of all beings, the consumer of oblations.
Golden-hued, stainless, blazing, and facing in all directions. || 65 ||
With this mantra, one should attend upon the blazing fire;
one should blow upon the fire with the mouth alone, for it was born from the mouth.
Not with kuśa grass, nor with leaves such as those of the palāśa tree, nor with any other non-purificatory substance;
thereafter, one should well-place the tongue upon the body with the mantras of Vibhāvasu (Fire). || 67 ||
On the forehead, the mark (liṅga), the thighs, the head, the mouth, the nose, and the eyes, as well as on all the limbs and the tongue—these will be described as being of threefold nature. || 68 ||
Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, Suprabhā, Bahurūpā, and Atiraktā—these seven tongues are of the nature of sattva. || 69 ||
The practitioner should again duly place the limbs of Fire (Agni), endowed with the syllables beginning with 'a' and ending with 'sa', along with the bindu, in their proper sequence.
Sahasrārcis, Svastipūrṇa, Uttiṣṭhapuruṣa, Dhūmavyāpin, Saptajihva, and Dhanurdhara—these are the ones thus proclaimed. || 71 ||
One should place the eight forms of Fire in sequence upon the body, proceeding from left to right.
And upon the head, the face, the sides, the waist, the feet, the hips, the flanks, and the shoulders. || 72 ||
Beginning with the syllable Om and ending with "namas," preceded by the word "agnaye" (to Agni), [the names are]: Jātavedas, Saptajihva, and Havyavāha as the third. || 73 ||
Aśvodaraja, Vaiśvānara, Kumāratejas, Viśvamukha, and Devamukha—these are proclaimed as the eight forms. (74)
Having meditated upon it in a clockwise sequence, one should then [purify] with water.
Furthermore, with four blades of darbha grass purified above the girdle. || 75 ||
Having left a space, one should spread [the grass] with its tips pointing east and north;
in a pit that has only a single girdle, one should spread it below the girdle. (76)
On a sacrificial mound with two, two middle, or three ridges,
one should spread sand on the outer ground.
The wise man should likewise make an opening between the waistband and the self-band, as well as for the placement of the girdle,
above the middle waistband.
[One should use] those produced from the palāśa, kāśmari, bilva, and vikaṅkata [trees].
The enclosing sticks, made from a single tree, should be unmoistened and as long as an arm. || 79 ||
Having restrained the vital breaths according to the rule, and having strewn around [the fire] with other kuśa grasses;
Or, according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra, [he should do so] to the east of the place dedicated to Vāyu. || 80 ||
The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the *praṇītā* vessel, and the pair of *prokṣaṇī* vessels.
And likewise the vessel for clarified butter, the enclosing sticks, and handfuls of kuśa grass. || 81 ||
The vessels, the sacrificial materials for the fire-oblation, and likewise the offering (bali) should be turned face downwards.
Then, one should set out all the items, beginning with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata).
Having sprinkled those seats with water using the purifier (pavitra) and having arranged them, |||
Having filled the pair of *prokṣaṇī* vessels with auspicious water.
Having offered the purifiers (pavitra) there and having filled them completely, one should set them down; that vessel in the northern direction is called *praṇītā* by the wise. || 84 ||
Then, having placed some purified water in the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, with those waters—
One should sprinkle the materials required for the sacrificial rites with the root mantra. || 85 ||
One should choose a Brāhmaṇa who is empowered by the Śakti and initiated into the deity-mantra;
one should seat him on a seat of Kuśa grass to the south of the sacrificial pit.
I, belonging to such-and-such a lineage, [address] him who belongs to such-and-such a lineage.
"In this oblation which is an auxiliary part of the initiation (dīkṣā), I choose you as the Brāhmaṇa priest. || 87 ||
Having clothed him with garments, ornaments, and so forth, one should worship him; one should also prepare a seat of kuśa grass if a Brahmin cannot be found. || 88 ||
In the center of the pit, within a hexagon, there is a golden pericarp as described.
It was endowed with various filaments and surrounded by four gates. || 89 ||
One should meditate upon an eight-petalled lotus surrounded by a square; that is the seat of worship for the Fire-god, [adorned] there with mandalas and so forth.
Having worshipped the seat of yoga, whose essence is knowledge, one should also worship [the deities] upon the eight petals.
Moving clockwise to the middle and the end, [one should visualize them] as yellow, white, and likewise red.
One should worship Kṛṣṇā, Dhūmrā, Tīvrā, and Visphuliṅginī.
One should worship Rucirā and Jvālinī, as well as all the pīṭhas. || 92 ||
The twelve-syllable heart-mantra is for the one who possesses all powers and whose seat is the lotus.
In the worship of all the pīṭhas, the fire-mantra has been proclaimed. || 93 ||

Then one should meditate upon the Fire-god (Hutāśana), who is perfectly resplendent with arms joined by the boon-granting gesture (vara), the auspicious sign (svastika), the spear (śakti), and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya). || 94 ||
(59) [He is] the color of vermilion, seated upon a lotus, and adorned with golden ornaments.
Three-eyed, with matted hair upon his crown, and wearing dark blue garments and a reddish garland. || 95 ||

Having meditated thus, one should worship with the ritual offerings using this mantra. Furthermore, since a triangular fire-diagram (*vahni-yantra*) has been drawn within the circle, one should also perform the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) at the time of the fire-worship as follows:
*oṃ sahasrārciṣe aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*. *Oṃ*...
To Svastipūrṇa, salutation with the two index fingers. Oṃ, to Uttiṣṭhapuruṣa, salutation with the two middle fingers. Oṃ, to Dhūmavyāpin, salutation with the two ring fingers.

Oṃ, salutation to Saptajihva with the two little fingers. Oṃ, salutation to Dhanurdhara with the palms and backs of the hands. Thus is the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa). Oṃ, salutation to Sahasrārcis at the heart. Oṃ, svāhā to Svastipūrṇa at the head.

Oṃ, to the one who has risen, for the *śikhā*, vaṣaṭ! Oṃ, to the one who pervades with smoke, for the *kavaca*, hūṃ! Oṃ, to the wielder of the bow, for the *astra*, phaṭ! Thus is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the heart and other limbs. Following the performance of these two types of *nyāsa*, there is the worship of the *yantra*.
O Vaiśvānara, O Jātavedas, O red-eyed one, bring [the gods] here in a wondrous manner! (96)
Accomplish all rites, beginning with the *praṇava* and ending with *svāhā*.
This mantra, consisting of twenty-seven syllables, is for the worship of Agni.
Then, in the center of the hexagon, one should perform the meditation on the tongue and its worship.
All of them possess the luster of flames from their tongues, and likewise hold the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
In the northeast is Hiraṇyā, golden-hued, for rites of pacification and nourishment.
The golden Vaiḍūryavarṇā river flows in the east, engaged in the act of immobilization.
In the case of enmity, she resembles the rising sun and is red in the southeast corner.
Resembling a mass of black collyrium, she is capable of killing when situated in the southwest.

Suprabhā, possessing the luster of a ruby and bestowing wealth, is located in the western direction; Atiraktā, with the brilliance of victory, is situated in the northern direction for the purpose of subjugation. || 101 ||
Bahurūpā, however, is in the center of the hexagon, joined with six syllables.
It is considered to be the accomplisher of many tasks and the destroyer as well. || 102 ||
If the tongue is seen directed toward its own quarter in accordance with the intended action, it appears in the form of a flame;
likewise, success is achieved, whereas in the opposite case, the result is the reverse.
Prabhā, Dīpti, Prakāśā, Marīci, Tāpinī, Karālā, and Lelihā—these are indeed the tongues in the ritual of Viṣṇu. || 104 ||
The tongues are situated in the east, southeast, southwest, west, northwest, and the center; they are all complete, bestowing boons and the gesture of fearlessness with their hands. || 105 ||
Having thus quickly performed worship before the deity and in the cardinal directions,
one should also worship the six limbs upon the petals and the deities of the surrounding retinue.
Thereafter, one should again worship Indra and the others, equipped with their weapons, and finally, the complete Fire.
Then, having turned the *sruc* and *sruva* ladles face downwards, one should heat them. || 107 ||
One should cleanse the tip of those two with the tips of *kuśa* grass, the middle with the middles,
and having cleansed the base with the bases in three ways, one should heat them.
Holding those two with his left hand, he should sprinkle them with the water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel;
then, with the tip of his right hand, he should heat them again.

Having scattered kuśa grass into the fire, and having placed the sruk and sruva ladles upon a bed of kuśa grass to his right, he should thereafter perform the consecration of the clarified butter (ghṛta).
Then, having taken up the vessel of ghee, one should sprinkle it with the mantra; having filled it there with ghee that has been well-consecrated by the rites of inspection and so forth. || 111 ||

Having placed embers outside in the northwest direction, one should deposit them upon them with the Heart mantra; this is designated as "heating," and then one should cast two blades of Kuśa grass there. || 112 ||
This shall be the illumination; then the "kindling" is described. Having fanned the blazing *kuśa* grass, one should show it and cast it [into the fire] with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*). || 113 ||
Having removed the ghee from the fire, one who knows the mantras should cast it into the embers; then, without touching it, he should perform the leaping over.
The practitioner of mantra should recite the weapon-mantra while holding two blades of kusha grass, each a span in length.
And having taken [the vessel] with the thumb and the ring finger, one should cause the clarified butter to overflow.
Then, one should firmly immerse [the vessel] facing oneself with two blades of kuśa grass; that immersion shall be with clarified butter.
These are declared to be the six purificatory rites (saṃskāras). || 116 ||
Cow's ghee is declared to be the best; that produced from a buffalo is middling.
The birth from a goat is the lowest; however, that which is born from a sheep and so forth is forbidden.
When clarified butter purchased in the marketplace is both sweet and of bovine origin, one should place two blades of *kuśa* grass,
measuring a span in length, into that ghee.
Having formed a knot with the tips of two kuśa blades, one should contemplate the white and black wings;
then, the iḍā on the left, the piṅgalā on the right, and [the central channel] in the middle. || 119 ||
The practitioner of mantra should contemplate the Suṣumṇā and then perform the fire oblation (homa).
One should take up the clarified butter from the right side with the sruva ladle while reciting the hṛdaya-mantra.

One should offer oblations into the right eye of the sacrificial fire with the mantra "agnaye svāhā"; likewise, taking clarified butter from the left side, one should offer it into the left eye of the fire.
"Omnipresent One, my offering is for Hunetsoma, svāhā!"—with this, one should take the clarified butter from the center with the Heart-mantra, O Madhyalocanā. (122)
And he should offer a third oblation with the formula: "To Agni and Soma, svāhā! for the sake of his hunger.
Then, one should again take clarified butter from the right side with the Hṛdaya-mantra.
In the fire-mouthed [vessel], one should offer the oblation with the mantra: "To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, svāhā!"
One should again offer oblations of clarified butter with the *vyāhṛtis* accompanied by the stars.
The most excellent preceptor should offer oblations three times with the Agni-mantra.
The rites beginning with the impregnation (garbhādhāna) and ending with the marriage of the fire (vahni-samudvāha).
In auspicious rites, the beloved [deities] should be worshipped with eight oblations of clarified butter; having first uttered the Praṇava, one should pronounce the name of the rite. 126.

"I accomplish [this], svāhā!"—this is the procedure for all rites. [These include] the impregnation ceremony (garbhādhāna), the rite for a male child (puṃsavana), the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana), and the birth ceremony (jātakarman). || 127 ||
And the expulsion as well as the consumption have been described by the wise in that same manner.
The caulopanayana, the initiation of the sacred fire, and likewise the mahānāmavrata; || 128 ||
The Mahāvrata, the Upaniṣad-vrata, and the Godāna; likewise, the Samāvartana and the Udvāha—these belong to the Śākta [tradition] and are preceded by the Vāgbhava [syllable]. || 129 ||
Then, having likewise worshipped the parents of the fire— namely the God and Goddess—
and having dismissed them, [one should offer oblations] soaked in ghee at the root and the tip.
Then, as before, one should cast five fuel-sticks into the fire.
One should indeed offer each individual oblation with its own seed-syllable and name. || 131 ||
Then the limbs: [Oṃ sahasrārciṣe svāhā, Oṃ svastipūrṇāya svāhā,
Oṃ uttiṣṭhapuruṣāya svāhā, Oṃ dhūmavyāpine svāhā, Oṃ saptajihvāya svāhā, Oṃ dhanurdharāya svāhā, Oṃ agnaye jātavedase].
Svāhā! Oṃ, to Agni Saptajihva, svāhā! Oṃ, to Agni Havyavāha, svāhā!
Oṃ, to Agni Aśvodaraja, svāhā! Oṃ, to Agni Vaiśvānara, svāhā! Oṃ, to Agni Kaumāratejas, svāhā! Oṃ, to Agni Viśvamukha, svāhā! Oṃ, to Agni...
"Devamukhāya svāhā. In this manner, one should likewise offer oblations to the eight forms of Agni.
Then, the world-protectors beginning with Indra, as well as their weapons, are written;
the mantras are inscribed within the wheel of the city-fortress, and the weapons follow thereafter.
Then, indeed, with the previously mentioned fire-mantra ending in "vauṣaṭ," (he should perform the rite). || 133 ||
p. 62) With the ten variations beginning with Tārā: [1. oṃ oṃ svāhā; 2. oṃ śrīṃ svāhā; 3.
oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ svāhā; 4. oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ svāhā; 5. oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ svāhā; 6. oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ]
Svāhā. 6. Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ gaṇapataye svāhā. 7.
Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ gaṇapataye varavarada. 8. Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ gaṇapataye varavarada sarvajanaṃ me.
*Vaśaṃ svāhā* (9). *Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ, to Gaṇapati, O bestower of boons, bring all people under my control, svāhā* (10).
One should first perform the oblation with this mantra of Gaṇapati, preceded by each of the preceding [syllables].
Ten oblations. || 134 ||
And one should offer oblations; furthermore, one should offer four times with the entire Gaṇeśa mantra.

Having worshipped four times with that very [mantra] in its entirety, and having understood the deity in the fire to be in the form of fire through the mental visualization of the divine pedestal within the fire—
The Guru should then properly perform the worship of the deity's seat within the fire.

There, one should worship one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) assuming the form of fire. With clarified butter (ājya), one should offer twenty-five oblations to the fire using the fire-mantra previously mentioned [beginning with *oṃ viśvānara jātaveda ihāvaha*]. 136.
The mantra of the oblation is this unification of the mouth within the mouth of the Fire.
The knower of the Self, contemplating the identity of the self, the fire, and the deity, [remains thus]. (137)
Then, one should offer eleven oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra.
This is indeed called the "joining of the channels" (nāḍī-sandhāna) by the most excellent teachers.
One should offer one oblation for each of the rites beginning with the limbs (aṅga) and so forth, according to the prescribed rule, in all the fire-pits starting from the eastern direction.
The Guru should enter the consecrated fire according to the path previously described.
Having worshipped all the officiating priests with sandalwood paste and other offerings, [he should worship] the aforementioned deity.
Then, they should offer oblations twenty-five times with the root mantra, using beloved food mixed with ghee, for the sake of [removing] all obscurations. || 141 ||

One should offer clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle, the fuel sticks with the hand holding the *sruc* ladle, and the remainder with the hand; in that case, it should likewise be offered in a divine or a ṛṣi-designated sacred spot (*tīrtha*). || 142 ||
That man who does not offer oblations into the flame of the fire, nor indeed into a fire with defective limbs.
He is born afflicted with the disease of weak digestion and is also impoverished. || 143 ||
One should respectfully offer the bali-oblation, preceded by perfumes, flowers, and incense, separately for each of the lunar mansions, the days of the week, and the zodiac signs. || 144 ||
The word for the deities is said to be *devatābhyaṃ*; after that, one should say "by day and by night" (*divā naktaṃ*).
Then one should utter "namas" to all the days of the week and to all living beings. || 145 ||
Thus, O gods, this tantric procedure for the fire-oblation has been proclaimed by me. Let them ask about anything else;
even that which is secret, I shall speak to you who have come for refuge. 146.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Illumination of the Ritual of Fire-offerings (*homavidhiprakāśa*), in the *Merutanttra* composed by Śiva, with the approval of the illustrious Mahāmāyā and Mahākāla.
The illustrious goddess said:
[This applies] to the wealthy, the middling, the poor, and those who laugh.
And for those residing in foreign lands, as well as those dwelling in prisons and similar places. || 1 ||
And for those [mantras] uttered regarding the body and so forth, which are joined with birth-impurities (sūtaka) and the like;
Or, O treasure-house of compassion, when the objects that are parts of the ritual action are absent, for those who follow the left-hand path (vāmikas). || 2 ||

O Lord, tell me how the daily rite (*nityāhnika*) may be performed according to the secret of the six traditions (*ṣaḍāmnāya*), and also describe the daily conduct for those who possess a sense of worldly shame.
The Lord said:
That which was spoken by Mahākāla, that which was heard by Mahāmāyā— the secret,
most secret [teaching] hidden within all tantras.
O gods, listen all of you to this secret of the sacred traditions which I proclaim as the daily ritual that grants success to practitioners. || 5 ||
In that regard, the eternal is said to be threefold, according to the distinction of the three qualities (guṇas).
Furthermore, that [initiation] may also be of three kinds, according to the distinction of the qualified recipients.
Whether pure, mixed, or dissolved, it yields fruit in exactly that same manner. There is no transgression in not performing [the rite], but for people, there is fruit when it is dissolved.
If it is devoid of egoism, preceded by right knowledge, and performed with a tranquil mind by an ascetic, that [action] is considered pure. || 8 ||
If such [a rite] is performed by a householder, or by one who is destitute of wealth, or even by one who is ill, a traveler, or one who has been cast into prison; || 9 ||
Or even out of devotion mixed with that [material], due to the requirement for external worship; or out of fear of cold and the like, from the depletion of wealth, or due to other duties. || 10 ||

The mind of the householder is considered to have fallen away from the observance of the *tri-saṃdhyā* and other duties; likewise, external worship and the like performed with fixed rules in solitude [are also lost]. (11)
That which is performed by a householder with devotion is pure and approved by the King; having recited it for the sake of worship, one should cultivate faith and devotion. || 12 ||
Out of fear of the world and fear of the gods, that which was mixed with exertion was requested from the gods for the sake of deceiving the people. || 13 ||

That which was prepared as a material offering has dissolved; that indeed belongs to the King (Rājasika). Having resorted to the Left-hand path (Vāmamārga) and having reflected upon the Kaula doctrine, [one should proceed]. 14.

Furthermore, an action performed out of non-aversion toward other dharmas is pure, whereas that which is performed out of desire—whether it pertains to this world or the next—is characterized by tamas. (15)

Resorting to the left-hand path (vāmamārga), that is indeed mixed and characterized by darkness (tāmasa); it consists of drinking out of greed for the tongue, eating out of desire, and sexual union according to one's whim. || 16 ||
Alternatively, that which is performed for the purpose of killing and so forth is tamasic; through pure sattva there is liberation, and through mixed sattva there is heaven. (17)
Success comes from one whose essence has dissolved; and from the *oha* [state], human status. From the pure *rājasa* [nature] there would be heaven; from the mixed *rājasa*, desire would arise. (18)
Even for one who has fallen from the state of royalty into the womb of an animal, there may be happiness.
From a sattvic or a tāmasa [state], a man may attain birth among the gods.

From the *tāmasa* [nature] one becomes non-existent, from the *duḥkhī-tāmasa* one becomes a hell-being, and from the *antyatāmasa* [one attains the lowest state]. Karma is said to be fivefold, bestowing liberation in five ways. (20)
Prasarpaṇa, upādāna, ityādi, adhyāya, and likewise dyuti.
In the temple of the deity, there are purificatory rites such as sweeping and smearing with cow dung.
Devotion, straightforwardness, and compliance will thus bring about health.
The gathering of the requisites for worship and the service of the devotees. || 22 ||
That joy shall be the material cause that bestows the form of the deity.
And preceded by the worship of the seat and its preliminary rites, with the sixteen and other such offerings. || 23 ||
Worship performed upon an image or a yantra is the adoration that accomplishes one's desired aim.
Having properly studied that scripture, one becomes a vessel for the meaning of the mantras.
Having performed this, let the student recite it; it brings about union with the deity.
The perfect contemplation of the essential identity of the Guru, the Deity, and one's own Self. || 25 ||
The conjunction [of breaths] brought about by the sacrifice of time is the destroyer of the subtle body (liṅgadeha). During the final watch of the night, one should meditate upon the beloved deity.
Having risen, one should place the left foot on the ground with the right side [of the body]. Then, having gone outside the house, one should carefully perform the necessary bodily functions.
Having discarded his night-garment and having put on two garments (or alternatively, having wrapped them around himself).
Having sipped water, one should become pure of body in the temple of the yoga of the deity.

Then, having removed the withered offerings (nirmālya), one should likewise offer a handful of flowers; having presented them in the vessel for the guest-offering (arghyapātra), one should indeed give the tooth-stick.
Having performed the washing of the face, one should offer water for sipping (ācamanīya). Then, for the purpose of wiping the hands, one should give a pure and auspicious garment.
Then, one should contemplate a thousand-petaled lotus upon the crown of the head; there, one should remember the venerable Guru in his own form, radiant as camphor.
Extremely serene, adorned with shimmering ornaments, and anointed with white sandalwood paste.
With hands displayed holding the gestures of granting boons, fearlessness, and knowledge, as well as a book. || 32 ||
Clad in white garments, peaceful, and adorned with white flowers.
He is embraced by Śakti, who rests upon his left lap and is red in color. || 33 ||
With garments and ornaments of red, and with a garland of red sandalwood.
Embraced by her with her left hand, which held a playful lotus, and with her right [hand].
One should meditate upon the yogin who is inward-turned, empowered by Śakti, and whose form is Śiva.
By the stream of nectar falling from his pair of lotus feet. || 35 ||
The disciple should thus contemplate his own body as being consecrated.
One should worship with external offerings such as perfumes and flowers, or else with mental ones.
Having bowed thus with various names and perfected praises of the Guru, one should meditate on its dissolution within the heart by means of the heart-mantra (hṛnmanu). || 37 ||
Then, [he should contemplate] the column of light rising from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *brahmarandhra*,
reaching as far as the *suṣumnā* and resembling a thousand-fold lightning flash.

Then, having meditated upon the root mantra as being of that same nature and enveloped by its splendor, one should contemplate one's own body as thus permeated and then perform breath control (prāṇāyāma). || 39 ||

One should perform the ritual assignment (*nyāsa*) of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other elements of the mantra using the root-mantra. Then, having performed the assignment of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), one should meditate upon the deity in the heart. (40)
O primordial God Śrī Śaṅkara, who consists of the consciousness of the three worlds, by the command of your feet—
Rising early in the morning for the sake of your pleasure, O Śaṅkara, God of gods, I shall follow the course of worldly existence according to your command as I traverse that journey.

Having prayed to the Lord of Gods, "O Master, may rivalry, contempt, strife, negligence, and fear not overcome me," and having obtained his permission, one should request the Earth and place the foot accompanied by the *śvāsa* mantra. (43)
O Goddess whose girdle is the ocean, whose breasts are the mountain ranges, O Consort of Viṣṇu, salutations to you;
forgive this touch of my feet. || 44 ||

Then, from the house, he should go toward the southern or the south-western direction; remembering the weapon-mantra (*astra*) at every step—[the mantra being *phaṭ*]—he should proceed from the brahmin’s dwelling to a distance.
Having passed a distance of one bow-length from the village and having looked around the ground, [he should perform the purification].
One should recite this at a place of purification that is free from insects, women, and the like. || 46 ||
Let the sages, gods, gandharvas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas arise!
"Please move aside from this spot; it is for my discharge of excrement and urine. (47)
Having removed the deities from the clod of earth with blades of grass while reciting this mantra, one should perform the discharge of the impurity there;
then, having entered the water, one should [wash] with a cloth. 48.

One should not look toward that direction; having performed the purification with water, [one should apply] one application [of earth] to the penis, seven to the anus, and likewise ten to the left hand. (49)
Seven applications of clay should be given to both hands, and three each to the two feet.

During the voiding of urine, five applications of clay are for the left hand and five for the penis; or alternatively, one may perform the rite with three applications to both hands and one to the feet.
One should perform twelve mouthfuls of gargling, which removes odors and stains and is supremely beneficial for clearing mental fatigue,
following the evacuation of feces.
Having first washed his feet, he should thereafter perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) three times.

[The wood] produced from mango, banyan, khadira, karañja, [or vaṭa], or from kakubha and other such trees— such as the arjuna tree— measured twelve finger-breadths in length and as thick as the tip of the little finger.
The experts in the Tantras have declared that the tooth-stick (dantadhāvana) is indeed [the means for purification]. || 53 ||

Having uttered "Kṛm" [namely, "Kṛṃ kāmadevāya sarvapriyāya namaḥ"], this mantra—ending with "namaḥ," consisting of fifteen syllables, and addressed to Kāmadeva, the beloved of all people—is for cleansing the teeth. After rinsing the tooth-stick, one should discard it in front toward the upper part of the head. To speak...
One should constantly observe the root [mantra] for the sake of attaining success. || 55 ||

Now, the ritual bathing for the successful accomplishment of the acts of worship and fire-oblation is described. Having taken earth from a pure place with a wooden probe (śaṅku) consecrated by the Astra-mantra, and having sprinkled it with water using the Astra-mantra, one should proceed to the water-retreat.
Therein, first there should be a water-bank; the wise one should wash it with the water of the *astra* [mantra], having made the slope smooth, and then, in one part thereof— (57)
Having placed cow dung, darbha grass, and consecrated sesame seeds [therein].
And one should perform a bath up to the waist using clay and cow dung. || 58 ||
Then, having gone outside, one should perform the impurity-bathing with water;
thereafter, one should perform the Vedic bathing, as well as its ancillary rites and the libation (tarpaṇa). || 59 ||
Then, according to the ritual for the tantric bath, one should [take] earth with the Astra-mantra.
Having taken up grass and other materials, he should consecrate them with the weapon-mantra.
Having removed it with the *śikhā* mantra, one should consecrate it with the three-rooted (*trimūla*) mantra.
Having smeared [the body] from the head down to the feet, one should prostrate oneself in the water.
They are the support of all beings and of Viṣṇu of incomparable splendor; they have arisen from Him and possess His very form—to those waters I bow. || 62 ||
Having formed the *sammukhīkaraṇī* mudrā and restrained his vital breaths (*prāṇa*), a man should submerge himself silently and then rise in water reaching up to his navel. (63)

Having performed the ritual resolve (*saṅkalpa*) for the Tantric bath, preceded by the mention of the month and other details, one should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). (64)
Having performed the assignment of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), one should fashion a sacred site (tīrtha) in front; that water should be prepared within a square space measuring one cubit. || 65 ||
O Sun, the sacred fords within the belly of the cosmic egg have been touched by your rays; by that truth, O Lord of Gods, O Maker of Day, grant me a sacred ford.
Having thus supplicated the Sun, [one should say] "Krom" with the goad mudrā.
Having pierced through the solar disc, one should therefore invoke the sacred fords here.
O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī—be present in these waters! 68.

Having spoken thus, one should unite the sacred fords (tīrthas) with that water; then, with the root mantra, one should invoke the power of the sacred ford (tīrtha-śakti) therein. Having meditated upon the orb of the sun, one should worship it with its specific mantra. (69)
Consisting entirely of bliss, destroying all misfortunes, radiant as the moon,
and three-eyed; holding in her two upper hands a noose and a goad (aṅkuśa) on the left,
and internally possessing a hand-held jar filled with nectar and a rosary of pearls.
I worship the power of the sacred fords (tīrtha-śakti), accompanied by the Gaṅgā, Sindhu, Saridvarā, and other rivers. || 70 ||

Then: *Hrāṃ [hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hraiṃ hrauṃ hraḥ, O Tīrtha-śakti consisting of all-bliss, hili hili svāhā |]*; *hrīṃ hrūṃ hraiṃ hrauṃ hraḥ*, the word *sarvānandamaye* (consisting of all-bliss); the *tīrtha-śakti*; likewise, the pair *hili*.
The wife of Agni. || 71 ||
The great mantra of Tīrthaśakti is said to consist of twenty-two syllables. One should consecrate that water eight times with the Gāṅga mantra.

*Tāra* [Oṃ namo bhagavati ambe ambike ambālike mahāmālini ehyehi bhagavati aśeṣatīrthālavāle hrīṃ śrīṃ śivajaṭādhirūḍhe gaṅge gaṅgāmbike svāhā]. One should say "namo bhagavati," then "ambe," and then "ambike."
O Ambālikā, O Mahāmālinī, come, come, O Blessed One! || 73 ||

One should utter the seed-syllable of Māyāśrī at the basin of all holy fords without exception; then [one says] "O Gaṅgā, who has ascended the matted locks of Śiva, O Mother Gaṅgā," ending with the Dviṭha (svāhā). || 74 ||

This is declared to be the Gaṅgā-mantra consisting of fifty-three syllables. Having stirred [the water] with the mantras of Bhuvaneśī (beginning with *oṃ vaṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ*, etc. and with the *hrīṃ* mantra, one should render it nectar-like using the *sudhāṇu* and the *vaṃ* seed-syllable.

Then, having veiled [the deity] with the Kavaca mantra and protected it with the Astra mantra, the knower of mantras should [worship] the deity there with the root mantra, together with the limbs (aṅga) and the enclosures (āvaraṇa).
Having invoked [the deity] into the water and meditated upon it, one should visualize the sacred ford (tīrtha) as emerging from its two feet;
then, recollecting the root mantra, one should bathe in the water three times.
Afterwards, one should remember the deity in the heart and sprinkle [it] with the *kumbha-mudrā* [the formation of which with both hands in the shape of a jar is called the *kumbha-mudrā*].
The *tāraka* [mantra] is preceded by the seed-syllables and the three root-mantras of the three worlds. || 78 ||
As he desires to emit the entire universe, the pure seed is produced again and again. May the divine Waters, the mothers of all beings, purify me. (79)
May the divine Waters, who are misfortune in the form of impurity residing within all beings, wash me clean by their very touch and purify me. 80.
Whatever ill fortune is in my hair, at the parting of my hair, or on my head; whatever is in my forehead, my ears, or my eyes—may your waters destroy that. Homage to you! 81.

One should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) three times with the root mantra ending in "namaḥ" and "svāhā. Having thus satisfied the deity thrice, one should proceed from the middle of the water to the bank.
Having put on a pair of washed garments and likewise having washed his hands.
Then, having performed the ritual sipping (ācamana) with earth and water, the procedure for the bathing of the deity is prescribed.
The mantra-bath should be performed during cool places and times;
when water is unavailable, in difficult terrain, when the body is unwell, or in old age. || 84 ||
Having washed his feet and sipped water with water drawn up [from a vessel], he should then purify his place and the ten directions as before and sit down. || 85 ||
Having placed the water upon the palm of the hand, one should then perform the ritual placements (nyāsa) of the pitchers.
Likewise, [he should perform] the nyāsa of the Mātṛkā and so forth, as well as the root mantras, in their entirety. || 86 ||
At the conclusion of the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should touch water; this is the excellent mantra-bath.
Merely from bathing in water that is devoid of purificatory rites.
One should meditate upon the Lord, the lotus-eyed one, who is well-established and whose form is the mantra.
The stream of water from his feet falling upon one's own head.
One should contemplate her entering the body of one's beloved through a subtle aperture.
Therefore, one should wash away all this impurity residing within the body.
At that very moment, the practitioner becomes free from passion (viraja) and resembles a crystal.
This supreme bath is considered eight times more efficacious than the mantra-bath.
He whose mind is always pure is pure in all his actions. Now follows the mental bath, performed mentally with the root mantra. (91)
Having restrained the breaths, one should perform [the rite] with devotion at visible sacred sites;
or else, having made the sacred site identical with Śiva by means of mantras whose essence is Śiva. (92)
The purification with the Saṃhitā mantras is declared to be the "bath of Śiva. All ritual acts preceded by this bath become pure and attain perfection. || 93 ||

Therefore, one should first perform a bath from among these according to one's physical capacity; thereafter, one should apply a sectarian mark (tilaka) belonging either to one's caste or to one's tutelary deity. 94.
Whatever brings auspicious fruit, whether through sacred fords or with earth, arises from devotion.
The vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) belongs to the Brāhmaṇa, while the triple horizontal mark (tripuṇḍraka) belongs to the Kṣatriya.
The half-moon shape is for the Vaiśya, while that of the Śūdras is circular in form.
One should apply the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) with clay and the triple horizontal mark (tripuṇḍra) with sacred ash.
With saffron and musk, the remainder should be prepared as desired, keeping it cool.
The vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) belongs to a Vaiṣṇava, while the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is for the service of Śiva.
The mark of Gaṇeśa is a half-moon; for a devotee of the Goddess, it is circular. For one who is devoted to Nārāyaṇa, his mark is a crescent moon, and his [the Goddess's] is a trident.
He who wears sacred ash on his forehead is of the nature of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
for the ash (vibhūti) is indeed the bestower of prosperity (bhūti) when it is worn according to the prescribed rite. || 99 ||
If held in any manner whatsoever, it reduces a person to ashes; the ash of Śiva’s fire is to be accepted, whether it originates from Agni or Soma. 100.
Or else, food cooked on the nuptial fire, which is pure and fragrant; or cow-dung from a tawny cow caught in a cloth as it falls from the sky—[these are used for purification]. 101.
Neither moist, nor boiled, neither foul-smelling nor stale; having discarded what is above and below, one should take with the heart what has fallen, using the mantra "Namaḥ."
Having formed it into a single mass, one should cast it into the Śiva-fire while reciting the root mantra.
Having discarded both the uncooked and the overcooked portions, one should take the white ash, stir it with a cloth, and deposit it into the receptacle for ashes. || 103 ||
One should collect the ashes when the deity has been dismissed; for once the dismissal has been performed, the ash becomes "Caṇḍa-ash. (104)

Alternatively, having thus brought the ashes of a twice-born man with the *sadyojāta* mantra: [Oṃ, I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutations indeed to Sadyojāta! In every existence, beyond existence, and even further than existence—be gracious to me;
salutations to Bhavodbhava! and the cow dung with the *vāmadeva* mantra: [Oṃ, salutations to Vāmadeva].

Salutation to the Eldest, salutation to the Most Excellent, salutation to Rudra, salutation to Time, salutation to the Dissolver of Time, salutation to the Dissolver of Strength, salutation to Strength,
salutation to the Destroyer of Strength, salutation, salutation to the Subduer of all Beings, salutation to the Churner of the Mind.
Having joined it to the vessel with the Aghora mantra— [Oṃ aghorebhyaḥ athaghorebhyaḥ ghora-ghoratarebhyaḥ sarvataḥ sarva-sarvebhyaḥ namaḥ astu rudra-rūpebhyaḥ ||]— one should burn it away. 105.

Having lifted it up with the *Puruṣa* mantra: *Oṃ tatpuruṣāya vidmahe mahādevāya dhīmahi tanno rudraḥ pracodayāt*, [one should place it] with the *Īśāna* mantra: *Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām īśvaraḥ sarvabhūtānām*.
"May the Lord of Brahmā, the Sovereign of Brahmā, the auspicious Brahmā, be ever propitious to me—Sadāśiva.
Thus one should purify the consecrated ashes with the mantra beginning with "Agni...
[1. *Oṃ agniriti bhasma*, 2. *Oṃ jalamiti bhasma*, 3. *Oṃ sthalamiti bhasma*, 4. *Oṃ...*].
"Vāyu" is ash; 4. "Oṃ Vyoma" is ash; 5. "Oṃ, all this indeed is ash. 6. || 106 ||

p. 69) One should recite the mantra with the Yajus formula beginning with *yā te rudra* [Oṃ, that auspicious form of yours, O Rudra, which is not terrible and does not cause suffering—by means of that most peaceful form, O Giriśanta, look upon us with favor]. One should address him by the name "Rudra."

With the names beginning with *praṇava* (Oṃ), ending in the dative case and the word *namaḥ*, and consisting of the [eight] parts: [Oṃ bhavāya namaḥ, Oṃ śarvāya namaḥ, Oṃ paśupataye namaḥ, Oṃ ugrāya namaḥ,
Oṃ mahādevāya namaḥ, Oṃ bhīmāya namaḥ, Oṃ īśānāya namaḥ].

One should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on the head with the five-syllable mantra, using portions of the garland consisting of the letters beginning with the five colors and joined with the heart of Hara [i.e., the mantras beginning with "Oṃ namaḥ śivāya"]. || 108 ||
Furthermore, the twice-born should maintain these names for the sacred ash:
Brahmā is to be known on the forehead, and Havyavāhana (the Fire) at the heart. (109)
Skanda is at the navel, Pūṣan at the throat, and the Rudras in the right arm;
Āditya is in the middle of the arm, and the Moon at the wrist.
Vāmadeva is on the left arm, Prabhañjana is in the middle of the arm, the Vasus are at the wrist, and Hari is remembered to be in the region of the back. || 111 ||
Śambhu is proclaimed as the summit; Śiva is remembered as the Supreme Self (Paramātman).
One should wear that ash which has been mixed with musk and other such substances.
With the root mantra or the five-syllabled mantra of Śiva,
one should apply the Tripuṇḍra on the forehead, which consists of the essence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
Having taken it with the three middle fingers consecrated by the root mantra.
Alternatively, the triple mark (tripuṇḍraka) may be made with the ring finger, the middle finger, and the thumb.

One should perform the Tantric twilight rite (sandhyā) with the root mantra, followed by three sips of water (ācamana). Having tied the topknot (śikhā) with the root mantra, one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma). || 115 ||

One should perform the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) upon the body, preceded by the placement of the hands (karanyāsa). Having consecrated the water in front with the Dhenu-mudrā [reciting: aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ...].

After that, [it should be done] seven times at most. || 116 ||
[With the letters of the alphabet] beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa', together with the nasal bindu—[Kaṃ means water].
One should sprinkle water three times on the head with kuśa grass and the root-mantra, syllable by syllable.
