Having meditated upon the deity established within the circle of knowledge (jñānamaṇḍala) by means of the mantra, one should take up water while reciting the seed-syllables (bīja) that consist of the elements (bhūtātman). || 118 ||
Having consecrated the water seven times with those mantras— laṃ, vaṃ, raṃ, and haṃ—
one should then consecrate it again seven times with the root mantra.
Holding that water with the left hand, one should sprinkle it with droplets splashed from it using the right hand, and then recite the root mantra while shaking [the vessel]. || 120 ||
By reversing the hands, one should perform the sprinkling with the left hand; then, relying upon the nose, one should do so with that remaining [liquid] which has the form of radiant energy.
Having entered, the deity went inside, purified the impurity, and emerged.
Having remembered this through the right nostril, one should [use] the right hand.

Having meditated upon a diamond-stone (vajraśilā) on his left side, he should cast it away with the Astra-mantra; then, having washed his hands and sipped water, the knower of mantras [should proceed] with the root-mantra. || 123 ||
Or else, one should finally offer three *arghya* oblations with either the *gāyatrī* or the root mantra.
One should offer libations to one's chosen deity (iṣṭadeva) who is situated within the solar disc.
Having said, "With water, by means of the root mantra, I satisfy [the name] so-and-so," one should perform the libation three times using the left hand for that reason.
One should recite the Gāyatrī of one's chosen deity twenty-eight times; however, in its absence, one who adheres to the Vedic tradition should recite the Brāhmī Gāyatrī. 126.

The Tantrika should mutter the Śivagāyatrī; that is now described: "Oṃ, may we know that Maheśa; let us meditate upon Him whose speech is pure; may that Śiva impel us. (127) Then, with a purified mind and observing silence, having muttered the root mantra one hundred and eight times,
Having thus praised his chosen deity, he should indeed offer [the oblation] after bowing down.
One should place the deity from the solar disc within one's own heart; then one should prostrate to the gurus—this is the Tantric Sandhyā. 129.

In this manner, the twilight devotion (saṃdhyā) must be performed at all three times; there is no fruit from its omission. If an omission occurs due to a divine cause, then one should recite the root mantra a hundred times.
For the sake of expiation, one should recite that root mantra for the expiation of failing to perform the twilight rites (*saṃdhyā*).
Having performed that, one should carry out the observances (*samaya*) as they arise. Having performed the Vedic libation (*tarpaṇa*), one should then perform the Tantric one. (131)
Having performed the threefold breath-retention (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the root mantra.
Then, in front of the triad beginning with the Ṛṣi, [he should perform the rite] with the Dhenu-mudrā. || 132 ||
Chanting "Vaṃ," having rendered the water immortal, one should meditate upon the deity together with the wheel, along with the limbs and the enclosures, and recite the root mantra. || 133 ||
Having said, "I satiate such-and-such a person," one should perform this one hundred and eight times,
or for that purpose twenty-eight times, into the lotus of the mouth.
One should satisfy the deity with the waters of those sacred fords, perceiving them as nectar.
And likewise, one should worship the deities of those obstructions one by one. || 135 ||

Having satisfied the deity within his own heart, he should dismiss the Sun at the sacred bathing place; then, bowing to the Guru, the lords of the directions, and the birds, he should hold the vessel in his hand.
He should go to a secluded, uninhabited place that is pleasing and free from defects; he should not look toward other directions until he has reached his home. || 137 ||
Having performed a circumambulation of the sacrificial enclosure, as well as his feet and hands;
Having washed and sipped water for purification, he stands at the entrance of the house for worship. || 138 ||
And standing at the doorway of the house, he should bow mentally to his guru.
One should mentally prostrate to one's own chosen deity as well as to the guardians of the directions.
Whatever sin was previously accumulated, whether on that very day or on another day, one should recite these two mantras for the purpose of removing that sin. (140)
O God, this mind of mine is an ordinary mind overcome by evil; therefore, expel that evil from my consciousness—phaṭ huṃ, and salutations to you! || 141 ||
The Sun, the Moon, Yama, Time, and the five great elements—these are the witnesses among men of the auspicious and inauspicious actions performed here. || 142 ||
One should utter "huṃ phaṭ" and look toward both sides with a wrathful gaze.
When this has been done, first of all, in the rite for the eradication of evil. || 143 ||
Whatever sin may be most grave, let it remain far away; let its place of worship in the past depart once more to its own abode. (144)
Whatever sin may be even very slight, let it go to destruction. By abandoning the worship of this sinner, one’s desired object shall be attained in an instant. (145)
Then, having washed his feet and hands and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with care, he should offer the arghya to the Lord of Day; the method for that is described here. || 146 ||
Having prepared a mandala on ground smeared with cow dung, one should then sit upon one's own seat using vermilion. 147.
Facing the east, one should bow down to the chosen deity with devoted intent.
Having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas) with the Sūrya mantra, the knower of mantras [should proceed].

"Hrīṃ hrīṃ saḥ" is declared to be the three-syllabled mantra of the Sun. Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) and meditated upon Indra and the other deities in that manner, one should contemplate the Sun with undistracted mind. || 149 ||
Holding a pair of lotuses, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons with his lotus-like hands, he wears a crown of rubies, possesses a reddish bodily luster, and has three eyes.
I worship the Sun, who sits upon a seat of red lotuses, the unique ocean of all virtues, and the sovereign of the entire world. || 150 ||
One should worship with ritual offerings according to the procedure prescribed in that very tantra; having fashioned a square mandala with water in front of oneself. || 151 ||
Having placed there a copper vessel containing water along with its base,
[He should offer] scents, flowers, unbroken rice grains, *darbha* grass, *dūrvā* grass, and mustard seeds combined together. || 152 ||
One should also place sesame seeds, flowers as prescribed, and barley; while touching that vessel with the mantra dedicated to the Sun, one should recite it one hundred and eight times. || 153 ||
Having consecrated that vessel and risen from his seat with both hands, the wise practitioner should offer the *arghya* up to the head with the Sūrya mantra. || 154 ||

Hrīṃ [Hrīṃ Hrīṃ Saḥ, to the venerable Sūrya, seated upon a throne surrounded by the planets, zodiac signs, lunar mansions, yogas, and karaṇas; this is the arghya for you, Svāhā]. Hrīṃ Saḥ—one should utter the words "along with the planets, zodiac signs, and lunar mansions."
Then, in the practice of yoga, there is also the "reversal of the seat" (parivṛttāsana). || 155 ||
This arghya is offered to the illustrious Sūrya; it is remembered as "svāhā" by men.
This [mantra] consisting of thirty-four syllables is for the offering of arghya to the Sun. || 156 ||

One should recite the Sūrya mantra according to one's capacity with undistracted mind; the best of teachers should then meditate upon that Sūrya while holding the water of the arghya offering. || 157 ||
Having praised and bowed down, he should dismiss that Sun from the maṇḍala; then, having risen, he should duly perform the worship of the door. 158.
Having sprinkled the door with water for the guest-offering (arghya), one should worship the Lord of Obstacles (Vighnapa) in its center.
To her right [he should place] Mahālakṣmī, and to her left, Sarasvatī. || 159 ||
And one should place the Goddess of the Door’s Splendor (Dvāraśrī) in the middle of that, on the right and left branches.
From the upper portion upwards, up to the fivefold division of five [parts]. || 160 ||

Furthermore, the first syllable of a name—among the initial syllables of names that include the *anusvāra*, end in the dative case, and conclude with *namaḥ*—shall be the mantra for the worship of that respective deity. For example:
*gaṃ gaṇapataye namaḥ*; *kṣeṃ kṣetrapālāya namaḥ*.
Salutation to the one joined with the Earth, the treasure of the conch and the lotus.

Salutation to Pañcapadmanidhi, who is united with Vasumatī. Salutation to Māyāśakti, the power of illusion. Hṛṃ, salutation to Hṛcchakti, the power of the heart. Gaṃ, salutation to Gaṅgā. Yaṃ, salutation to Yamunā. Dhāṃ, salutation to Dhātṛ, the Creator. Viṃ, salutation to Vidhātṛ, the Ordainer.
Having uttered the syllable ending in *ṅ* joined with the *bindu*, and ending with the heart-mantra (*hṛd*), one should worship these deities. (161)
Then, with a stream of wealth, [he should worship] Gaṇapati and Kṣetrapāla;
and the Śaṅkha-nidhi joined by Vasudhārā on the right, and [the Padma-nidhi] joined by Vasumatī on the left.
Having worshipped Padmanidhi, one should likewise worship Māyāśakti and Hṛcchakti to his right and left, as well as Gaṅgā and Yamunā below him. || 163 ||
Salutations again and again to the threshold (Daihali), who is the sustainer and the ordainer. Thus, this worship of the western door has first been revealed. || 164 ||
And Nandin and Mahākāla are also at the right and left doors.
Having worshipped in this manner, one should worship the northern gate, as well as those in the eastern and southern directions.
In those [positions], the doorkeepers are, in order, Gaṇeśa and Vṛṣabha, as well as Bhṛṅgirīṭi, Skanda, Umā, and Caṇḍeśvara. (166)
Of Viṣṇu there are Nanda and Sunanda, as well as Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍaka; also Bala and Prabala, and Bhadra and Subhadraka. || 167 ||
Vakratuṇḍa, Ekadanta, Mahodara, Gajanana, Lambodara, and Vikaṭa— these are the Gaṇeśas who serve as the gatekeepers; their names are clearly stated in the root text.
Vighnarāja, smoke-colored, [is located] in order from the western door; and these eight Yoginīs of the Goddess are the guardians of the gates. 169.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, as well as Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Śrī. || 170 ||
Now I shall describe the meditation on the deities of the door, which is concealed in the tantras—that divine gateway which the door-deities themselves open. (171)
I salute the heroic Vighneśvara, who has the face of an elephant and three eyes, whose hands hold a noose, a goad, a fruit, and a lotus leaf, and who is pot-bellied. || 172 ||
She has four hands, shining with two lotuses and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
[He saw] Mahālakṣmī, whose limbs were as fair as burnt gold, and who possessed three eyes.

Sarasvatī has three eyes; her hands hold a rosary, a book, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons; she is white, seated upon a white lotus, and clad in white garments. || 174 ||
I meditate upon the fierce leader of this sacred field (kṣetranāyaka), who has a black body, three eyes, and brandishes a skull-bowl, a trident, and a flashing sword. (175)
I worship the Śaṅkhanidhi, who resembles a pearl, embracing Vasundharā with his right arm while holding a conch in his left, and who possesses beautiful ornaments. 176.
I eternally worship Padmanidhi, who embraces the Earth, whose forehead is marked with the lotus sign, and who holds a blue lotus in his left hand. || 177 ||
I worship Māyā, who is dark-complexioned, with three eyes, whose hands hold a boon-granting gesture, a goad, and a noose, and who is the root of saṃsāra. || 178 ||
Holding a noose, a goad, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, she possesses a reddish glow.
I salute Gaṅgā, the best of all rivers, who has mounted upon a crocodile. || 179 ||
Mounted upon a black tortoise, with a garland of blue lotuses around her neck.
I bow to Kālindī, who has a dark form and whose hands grant boons and fearlessness. || 180 ||
I bow to the creator of the worlds, who bears the conch, discus, mace, and lotus;
who is mounted upon Garuḍa, the sustainer, whose form is Kṛṣṇa. 181.

I bow to the Creator, who is red in hue, whose eyes are like red lotuses, who holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness along with a water-pot, who is mounted upon a swan, and who is endowed with three eyes. || 182 ||
Mounted upon a lion, dark-complexioned, and bearing a sword and a shield.
I salute the southern-faced Sudakṣiṇā, who resides below at the threshold.
Having reached the western door and performed three *tāla* hand-claps, he should open the door with the *astra-mantra*, scattering consecrated mustard seeds and unbroken grains of rice.

The wise preceptor should scatter flowers joined together within the pavilion, having correctly [warded off obstacles] with the Astra-mantra using the Nārāca-mudrā (the arrow-mudrā)— the Nārāca-mudrā being formed by the index finger extended from the right fist. || 185 ||
May the spirits and piśācas depart in every direction!
And whatever other deities dwell here, established upon the earth, [should be honored]. || 186 ||
May those beings depart who dwell upon the earth;
may those beings who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva. || 187 ||
And at the end of the two verses, reciting the Astra-mantra with the Nārāca-mudrā.
Then, one should drive away those obstacles that have emerged from within the pavilion.
By contracting his own left side, he should clear a path and remove [the obstacles], while recollecting the Astra-mantra and striking with the left heel three times. || 189 ||
One should dispel terrestrial obstacles with three claps of the hands, and those belonging to the intermediate space likewise.
With a sidelong glance, one should ward off divine obstacles.
One should enter the temple of the deity placing the right foot forward; however, a Śākta should cover the door with his left foot and a cloth. || 191 ||
Sprinkling the interior of the pavilion with the five products of the cow and with water for the guest-offering (arghya).
By means of sweeping, smearing with cow dung, and other such acts, it has been made like the surface of a mirror. (192)
It was stainless, adorned with incense, lamps, and garlands of flowers.
The painting with five-colored powders is considered this purification of the site. || 193 ||

In the southwest (nairṛtya), one should worship the Vāstupuruṣa with sandalwood and other offerings; in that very place, one should also worship the Lord of the Site (Vāstvadhīśa) with the mantra "Obeisance to Brahmā. (194)
Having worshipped Dīpanātha Bhairava, who is red in color and joined by twelve red-colored Śaktis, one should pray as follows: || 195 ||
O you of exceedingly sharp fangs and massive body, resembling the fire at the end of an aeon; salutations to you, Bhairava! You should grant me your permission.
Then, with the mantra "Oṃ Phaṭ," one should enter the altar of worship.
One should consecrate the place of the seat with the four [rites], beginning with the gazing.
There, during the ritual of consecration (saṃskāra), the deities of the seat (pīṭhadevatāḥ) ending with Vedyantā should be fully worshipped.
Beginning with the foundational power (ādhāraśakti), one should place one's own seat there. || 198 ||
Then, having sat upon one's own seat for worship— which is covered with cloth, a deerskin, and kuśa grass in that order— one should duly meditate upon Viṣṇu as well as the Guru.
Merupṛṣṭha is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi), Sāvitrī is said to be the meter (chandas), and Pṛthivī is declared to be the deity; its application (viniyoga) is for one's own seat. || 200 ||
O Earth, by you the worlds are supported; O Goddess, you are supported by Viṣṇu.
Therefore, O Goddess, support me and make this seat pure.

In the four corners of the seat, one should worship Gaṇeśa and Sarasvatī, as well as Durgā and Kṣetrapati, starting from the southeast (and proceeding clockwise): in the southeast, "Gaṃ, obeisance to Gaṇeśa";
in the southwest corner, "Saṃ, obeisance to Sarasvatī"; in the northwest, "Duṃ, obeisance to Durgā."
In the northeast, one should worship with "kṣaṃ, obeisance to Kṣetrapati. || 202 ||

Facing either north or east, seated in the *svastika* posture— having properly placed both soles of the feet between the knees and the thighs, with the body held straight and sitting comfortably— that is called the *svastika*. Or, having assumed the *padmāsana* (lotus posture), [placing the right foot] upon the left thigh...
Having placed the left foot upon the right thigh and firmly grasping it with both hands according to the prescribed method, one should place the thumbs at the heart and the chin against the chest,
then gaze at the tip of the nose; this is called Padmāsana, which destroys the entire multitude of diseases.
Or else, with the body straight and the mind steady. || 203 ||
One should place one's own materials for worship on the right side.
On the left, a beautiful jar filled with well-perfumed water. || 204 ||
For the purpose of washing the hands, one should place them upon the back of the vessel.
One should place auspicious lamps, ignited with ghee and other substances, all around.
Having placed the mirror, the chowrie, the umbrella, the fan, and the sandals in their proper positions, the self-possessed one should consecrate them accordingly. || 206 ||
One should offer flowers, food offerings, perfumes, and so forth with the mantra "hrīṃ hrūṃ phaṭ."
Having gazed with the Nārāca-mudrā and observing the pledges (samayas), || 207 ||
The defilement of flowers and other such items has been correctly observed and understood by me through speech.
Or even the touching of that which is untouchable, or whatever has been acquired through unjust means. || 208 ||
Likewise, that which has been touched by flower-offerings (nirmālya) or upon which insects and the like have ascended;
That [sin] goes to destruction beforehand by the mere sight of the food offering (naivedya) and other such items. || 209 ||
Then, with the mantra *raṃ*, one should touch the crest of the lamp;
that lamp shall be auspicious, free from the smell of raw flesh, and bestow happiness. (210)
From the burning of insects such as moths and hair, it is designated as *kravyāda* (the flesh-eater).
It is employed with substances such as clarified butter, which are produced from fat, marrow, and so forth. || 211 ||
All that defect, which consists of ignorance, perishes through contact with it.

The mantra practitioner should utter the seed-syllable *kṣauṃ* using the *daivī-tīrtha* (the divine sacred space). Regarding the sacred spaces: the tip of the finger is the *daiva* (divine) space; the base of the little finger is the *ārṣa* (sage) space; the middle of the thumb and finger is the *paitra* (ancestral) space;
and the base of the thumb is the *brāhma* (brahmic) space. The *bāṇamudrā* (arrow-gesture) is formed by the index finger of the right fist.
It should be long; it should touch. 212.
Having clearly seen the water situated within the jar, the practitioner, holding the jar located at his left side with his left hand, [should proceed]. || 213 ||
One should place [the vessel] upon the base; whatever is deficient here due to ignorance, [that too should be corrected].
Water that has come into contact with a corpse in a reservoir, as well as water collected in its natural place [is defiled]. || 214 ||
Thus, such defects as these are destroyed when one is devoted to the worship of the deity;
thereafter, purified and with palms joined in reverence, [one should stand] on the left and right sides. (215)
Having bowed to the Guru, Gaṇapati, and one's own chosen deity before them;
Having taken fragrant flowers smeared with sandalwood paste, the knower of mantras [should proceed].
Then, one should rub [the hands] with the *hauṃ* mantra and the *astra* mantra; having taken that flower with the left hand, one should place it upon the head. || 217 ||
One should cause it to revolve—[whirling it all around above the head of that person]—while reciting the *tāra* [the *oṃ* mantra].
Having smelled it again, one should recite the verse: "Hauṃ Oṃ, may they all go to dissolution," while reciting the *phaṭ* mantra everywhere.
Having formed the arrow-mudrā, the best of practitioners should cast that flower toward the northeast corner and recite this verse: || 218 ||
May all those who harm me, the injurers, go to dissolution everywhere.
May the fears and afflictions of death and disease fall upon the head of the enemy! (219)

With the weapon-mantra, one should perform the fire-enclosure mudrā: both hands, with their tips like tridents, crossed and positioned on both sides of the fire, constitute that which is called the weapon-mudrā.

By raising the three finger-joints of both hands and rotating them in opposite directions, the Vahni-prākāra mudrā (Fire-Wall Seal) is formed; this very same seal is also known as the Astra mudrā (Weapon Seal).

The mudrā known as the Trident (triśūla) is formed by joining the thumb with the little finger and then extending the remaining three fingers. Having pressed the two little fingers with the two thumbs,
the three remaining fingers are held straight.

From that, one should extend [the fingers], whereby it becomes the Triśūla-mudrā. One should cast the Nārāca-mudrā toward the eastern direction. Then, one should perform the purification of the hands with the Astra-mantra, and thereafter perform the three claps (tālatraya). || 220 ||

With the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra), one should perform the binding of the directions (digbandha) by ascending higher and higher; with that same mantra, one should [ward off] the falling splendor by means of the fire-enclosure mudrā (vahniprākāra-mudrā). || 221 ||

One should protect oneself with the *śūla* mantra and perform three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). Then one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*); I shall now describe its procedure. || 222 ||
From the feet to the knees, it is square, equipped with wheels, marked with the syllable *laṃ*, yellow in color, the locus of the earth, and has Brahmā as its presiding deity. || 223 ||
The place presided over by the power known as Nivṛtti is thus described;
one should contemplate this form as the source from which living beings arise. || 224 ||
From the knees up to the navel is the locus of water, which has a white luster.
The two peaks resemble a half-moon and are marked with that lotus.
A hexagon joined with six dots and endowed with the seed-syllable *vaṃ*.
One should meditate upon that which has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity, conjoined with the digit of installation (pratiṣṭhā-kalā).
From the navel up to the throat, it is reddish in color, has Rudra as its presiding deity, is joined with the seed-syllable "Raṃ," and is likewise endowed with the digit known as Vidyā. || 227 ||
Endowed with a radiant svastika, it has assumed the form of a triangle.
One should contemplate the fire element as being situated like that of the great dissolution. || 228 ||
From the throat up to the space between the eyebrows, it assumes the form of a hexagon.
A black-colored circle marked with six dots. || 229 ||
The station of Vāyu is presided over by the Śāntika-kalā and has Śiva as its deity.
Having thus meditated upon the form of the seed-syllable, one should contemplate the form of the vital breath (prāṇa).
The space between the eyebrows and the aperture of Brahmā is called the station of space.
Circular in shape, smoke-colored, and marked with a very tall banner.

Having meditated thus upon that which is presided over by the kalā called Śāntyatītā, has Śiva as its deity, and is joined with the seed-syllable *haṃ*, one should place the elements within the body. (232)
Having fashioned [the heart] arising from the stalks of Dharma, beautifully adorned with the stalk of knowledge, situated within its pericarp like the flame of a lamp. || 233 ||

The practitioner, by means of the method joined with yoga and using the "so'ham" mantra, should unite the individual soul (jīva) with the Supreme Self (paramātman) through the path of the suṣumṇā. || 234 ||

By that very [light], one should contemplate all beings as dissolved; then, one should contemplate the Person of Sin (pāpapūruṣa) within the body, specifically in the left side of the belly. || 235 ||
The personification of evil (pāpapūruṣa), with the luster of lampblack, is situated in the left side of the belly.
He has the murder of a Brahmin upon his head and shoulders, and the theft of gold upon his two arms.
The heart is joined with the drinking of liquor, and the two hips with violating the teacher's bed.
The pair of words "association with that" is a sin for every limb and member of the body. || 237 ||
One should contemplate the wicked one as having body hair like that of a minor offender, with red beard and eyes, holding a sword and a shield, cruel, enraged, and sinful. || 238 ||
In that manner, one should indeed completely dry it up through the sequence of *pūraka* and the rest;
having restrained the vital breath (*prāṇa*) by means of the wind-seed syllable (*vāyubīja*), one should act with the wind. || 239 ||
One should burn that [impurity] with the very fire arisen from the *mūlādhāra*; having thus burned it all around for thirty-two measures (*mātrā*), one should then [proceed]. (240)
The practitioner of mantra should again exhale it through the iḍā [nāḍī] together with the ashes;
in the left channel is the seed-syllable of the Moon, possessing a radiance equal to the kunda flower and the moon. || 241 ||

Then, having joined [the breath] with the moon of the forehead (bhāla-indu) by means of sixteen mātrās, one should [place] the water-seed (toyabīja) into the suṣumṇā by means of sixty-four mātrās. || 242 ||
Having meditated upon the creation consisting of nectar, which takes the form of the fifty phonemes,
one should thus contemplate the body with the mind through the path of Piṅgalā.
The practitioner should firmly lead [the vital energy] with the seed-syllable *laṃ* for thirty-two measures.
When the entire body has become capable of the worship of the deity, [it is accomplished]. (244)

Then, one should cause the principles (tattvas) dissolved in the Self to return to their own respective places; thereafter, one should lead the Self from the lotus of the heart back to the Supreme Self.
One should contemplate that, through the *haṃsa* mantra according to the prescribed rite, a body in the form of radiant energy has arisen, fit for the propitiation of the deity. (246)
A worship performed by one devoid of the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) is like malevolent magic (abhicāra); it yields a contrary result, just as worship performed without devotion does.
Having thus performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should practice the installation of the vital breath (prāṇasthāpana).

Regarding the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra: "Oṃ! Of this glorious *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are the seers (*ṛṣi*); the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas are the meters (*chandas*); the deity (*devatā*) is the power of life (*prāṇaśakti*) whose form is consciousness; its application (*viniyoga*) is in the installation of the vital breaths."

Salutation to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara, and to the sages, upon the head; salutation to the meters of the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāma Vedas, upon the face; salutation to the deity Prāṇa-śakti, upon the heart;
salutation to the seed-syllable *Āṃ*, upon the secret place; salutation to the power (*Śakti*), *Hrīṃ*.

*Kroṃ* to the *kīlaka* on the two feet; *namaḥ* to all limbs. (251) Now, the placement (*nyāsa*) of the heart and other parts: *Āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ*, to the self consisting of ether, air, fire, water, and earth; *āṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*. *Oṃ āṃ*.
Hrīṃ kroṃ īṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ,
to the Self of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, īṃ, svāhā to the head. Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ uṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ.

Oṃ, *vaṣaṭ* to the tuft (*śikhā*) for the self consisting of ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose. Oṃ Āṃ Hrīṃ Kroṃ Eṃ Taṃ Thaṃ Daṃ Dhaṃ Naṃ; *huṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*) for the self consisting of speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals. Oṃ Āṃ Hrīṃ...
Kroṃ Voṃ Paṃ Phaṃ Baṃ Bhaṃ Maṃ;
to the self consisting of speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and pleasure, Oṃ, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes.

Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ aṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ kṣaṃ, to the self consisting of mind, intellect, ego, and consciousness: aḥ, to the weapon, phaṭ. Now, the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa): Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ aṃ, to kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ.

To the one whose self consists of ether, air, fire, water, and earth: *āṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*. *Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ iṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ*, to the one whose self consists of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell: *āṃ* to the two index fingers, *svāhā*. *Oṃ*.
Āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ uṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ;
to the self of the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose, ūṃ, [I offer] with the two middle fingers, vaṣaṭ.
Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ eṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ, to the self of speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals; aiṃ, to the two ring fingers, huṃ. Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ oṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ.

To the self consisting of speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and bliss: *oṃ* to the two little fingers, *vauṣaṭ*. *Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ aṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ kṣaṃ*, to the self consisting of mind, intellect, ego, and consciousness: *aḥ*.
*Phaṭ* with both palms and backs of the hands. (257) *Āṃ namaḥ*, starting from the navel down to the feet;

*hrīṃ namaḥ*, from the navel up to the heart; *kroṃ namaḥ*, from the heart up to the crown of the head. (258) Now, the procedure for the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) is [to be learned] from another source.
Having taken [the mantras], it is said: "Just as: *yaṃ* to the self of skin, *namaḥ* to the heart;
*raṃ* to the self of blood, *namaḥ* to the right shoulder; *laṃ* to the self of flesh, *namaḥ* to the nape of the neck;
*vaṃ* to the self of fat, *namaḥ* to the left shoulder; *śaṃ* to the self of bone, *namaḥ*..."
From the heart to the tip of the right arm: *ṣaṃ* salutation to the self of marrow (*majjātman*).
From the heart to the tip of the left arm: *saṃ* salutation to the self of semen (*śukrātman*).
From the heart to the tip of the right foot: *hauṃ* salutation to the self of vigor (*ojātman*).

From the heart to the tips of the left foot: *haṃ* to the self of breath (*prāṇātman*), salutation from the heart to the navel; *saṃ* to the self of vitalization (*sañjīvātman*), salutation from the heart to the crown of the head.

Having thus performed the aforementioned nyāsa, one should place these syllables— laṃ, raṃ, haṃ, ṣaṃ, vaṃ, saṃ, śaṃ, chaṃ, kṣaṃ— in the eight petals and the pericarp of the heart-lotus in the order starting from the east; thereafter, one should perform the meditation.
The sages are those born from the lotus of the Lord. || 248 ||
The meters are the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, while the deity is the power of breath (prāṇa-śakti). One should place the sages on the head, the meters in the mouth, and the deity in the heart. (249)

"Oṃ āṃ, salutation to the Seed-syllable in the secret place; Hrīṃ, salutation to Śakti in the feet; Namaḥ Kroṃ, salutation to the Kīla in the navel—this is the application for the firm establishment [of the deity]. (250)
Oṃ āṃ hlīṃ kroṃ, [I bow] to the group of consonants together with the anusvāra; homage to the heart.
Having recited the five principles (pañcatattva) and likewise the long vowel 'Ā', || 251 ||

The letter *i* along with the *ca*-group, the letter *śa* and so forth, the head (*śiras*), and the wife of fire (*vahnigehinī*, the letter *ra*)—these are the seed-syllables. Similarly, the *uṃ* [syllable], the *ṭa*-group, and the ear (*śrotra*) and so forth. (252)

Having spoken those [syllables] to that very self, one should say "vaṣaṭ" for the crest-lock (śikhā). Those seed-syllables are *eṃ* and *tuṃ*, pertaining to speech and the other faculties, as well as to that self.
Having uttered "aimuktvā kavāya," one should say "huṃ" immediately thereafter; then the four seed-syllables previously mentioned, and likewise the pavarga group. || 254 ||

One should likewise utter "Oṃ netrāya vauṣaṭ" for the self consisting of speech and so forth; then the four seed-syllables, the Ṛgveda at the end, the *ya*-group of consonants, and the mind (*manas*) and so forth. (255)

One should utter "tadātmane" followed by the final vowel, "astrāya phaṭ," and indeed perform the placement (nyāsa) in this very manner, beginning from the thumb and ending at the palms of the hands. || 256 ||

Having sequentially assigned [the syllables] ĀṂ, HRĪṂ, and KROṂ below the navel, below the throat, and below the head— ending there— one should also assign them to the eight petals of the heart-lotus.

From the east, one should sequentially place the syllables ending with the heart-mantra (namaḥ) upon the pericarp, according to their groups: Laṃ, Raṃ, Haṃ, Ṣaṃ, Yaṃ, Vaṃ, Saṃ, Śaṃ, and Kṣaṃ. || 258 ||

Then one should assign [the syllables] to the directions and meditate upon the power of breath (prāṇaśakti) residing in the heart. O beloved, listen as I describe here the very meditation upon her. || 259 ||

I bow to the Goddess who is red in hue, three-eyed, seated upon a lotus as crimson as the sun over a sea of blood, holding in her lotus-hands a noose, a goad, a bow, an excellent sword, an arrow, a trident, and a skull-cup.
Thus ends the meditation on the power of the vital breath (prāṇa-śakti).

Placing the hand upon the heart, one recites the primordial seed-syllables: *āṃ krīṃ kroṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ haṃ haṃsaḥ sohaṃ mama prāṇā iha prāṇā mama jīva iha sthitaḥ mama vāṅmanaścakṣuḥ śrotraṃ ghrāṇaḥ*.
"Oṃ! May the vital breaths (prāṇas) come here and remain happily for a long time, svāhā!
This mantra is extracted from three verses spoken by Mūla; however, the Prāṇapratiṣṭhā mantra as stated in the *Mantramahodadhi* is superior to this one.

It should be known as follows: having uttered the *pāśa* (the noose), *māyā* (the illusion-seed), and *śṛṇi* (the goad), one should join them with the seven [vowels] ending in the Moon (*i*) and the Sky (*ha*) conjoined with *tārā* (the *praṇava*). Then, while reciting the seven-syllable mantra: "My vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are here; my life-force (*jīva*) is stationed here; my..."

Having addressed all the sense organs, one should utter: "My speech and mind! Then, having invoked the eyes, ears, the locus of the nose, and the vital breaths here, and having uttered "Come! Be well! one should recite this seven-syllable mantra ending with the wife of fire (svāhā): "May these remain for a long time. One should recite this.
One might further say: this is remembered as the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra for the installation of the vital breaths. With the *bindu*, it is:
*meru-haṃsa-ākāśa-sargī-bhṛgu-māyā*.
Enclosed by the *tāra*, this mantra is considered to consist of seven syllables. Thus.
Having established the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), one should perform the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*.
As extracted from these verses: *āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ hoṃ oṃ kṣaṃ saṃ haṃ saḥ hrīṃ oṃ sohaṃ mama*.

The vital breaths are here; my life-force is established here. All my senses—speech, mind, sight, hearing, smell, and breath—having come here, may they remain happily for a long time. Svāhā! Oṃ kṣaṃ saṃ haṃ saḥ hrīṃ oṃ.
The eight [syllables] beginning with *yādi* are: "Haṃsaḥ so'haṃ, my vital breaths (prāṇāḥ), [state] here" by repeating [the phrase] twice;
and having spoken likewise, "O Father, my life (jīva) is established here."
Having spoken that again, let my speech, mind, and sight proceed upward.
Having come here, may the ear, the nose, and the vital breath abide happily for a long time.
Having uttered [the mantra] ending with the wife of Vahni (svāhā), one should then recite the Tāra (oṃ). || 264 ||
"One should meditate on the body as consisting of light"—thus should be the stabilization of the vital breath.
Having performed three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma), he performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Mātṛkās.

Prāṇāyāmas are said to be of three kinds: Tantric, Vedic, and Yuktita (logical/rational). Their results are, respectively, the attainment of perfection for the destruction of sins and the attainment of yoga-siddhi. || 266 ||

The Tantric [mantra] is considered to be of two kinds: that called *mātṛkā* and that called *mantra*. If the one called *mātṛkā* is performed at the beginning of the recitation and at the end of the recitation, [it brings success]. || 267 ||

Listen to that which destroys all defects, such as the transposition of syllables, without exception: one should fill the breath with the vowels and the consonants beginning with *ka* during the *kumbhaka* (retention) by means of Vāmā; then one should exhale through the right nostril with the letters of the Mātṛkā alphabet beginning with *ya*.
Restraining the vital breath as much as possible, one should mutter the mantra with the mind alone. || 269 ||
The practitioner of mantras, having held the nose with the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb, [should proceed].
Three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) have been prescribed; whatever else is performed mentally [is also included]. || 270 ||
Recitation, worship, and other such acts remove his fault. [One should recite] the Gāyatrī together with its head (śiras) and preceded by the seven Vyāhṛtis. || 271 ||
One who recites this three times, joined with each *praṇava*, is the most excellent here.
The area from the middle of the base up to the tip is pressed with the thumb.
That is called a "mātrā" by the wise; it bestows the desired goal through yogic practice.
One should perform circumambulations by kneeling for as long as it takes for Hastaka.
The measure (mātrā) is equal to the duration of one's own breath; the lowest is the length of a cock's crow, while the middle is the length of a lion's roar. || 274 ||
The best [practitioner] should consist of only the six-fold group, being well-versed in the three yogas;
when Kumbhaka alone is mastered, the perfection born of Rājayoga shall be attained. || 275 ||
There is firmness of vigor, long life, and the destruction of wrinkles and graying hair; when pūraka and kumbhaka are mastered, the perfections of kriyā-yoga are attained. || 276 ||

And for those previously mentioned, there is no longer affliction by cold or heat, nor hunger or thirst; when inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka) become equalized, [this state arises]. || 277 ||

Then Haṭhayoga is indeed perfected for the sake of the eight Siddhis beginning with aṇimā; however, the inferior [practice] yields only slight fruit, the middling [yields] middling [fruit], and the superior [yields] everything else.
Through practice for three uninterrupted years, the entire fruit shall be attained.
The procedure for breath control (prāṇāyāma) has been declared by me to you, O fair-faced one. (279)
The seer (ṛṣi) is on the head because of his gravity; the meter (chandas) is in the mouth because it consists of phonemes (varṇa).
But the retention [of the seed-syllable] in the heart of the deity who is the knower of the mind is prescribed. || 280 ||

The verbal root *ṛ* in the sense of "going" is considered to be that which brings about the attainment [of the goal]; whereas *ṣi*, in the sense of "desiring," is understood as knowledge, and thus it is that which brings about the attainment of that [knowledge]. (281)
Because the desire "let there be a covering" (chadiḥ) arises here, the face (mukha) is called *chanda* as it bestows that desire;
or else, it is *chanda* because it covers the meaning of the mantra. || 282 ||
The root *div* signifies play; thus, the word *devatā* is fully derived from it.
She is proclaimed as the deity because she bestows what is desired by the practitioner. || 283 ||
When one protects that which is of the nature of consciousness (cidātmaka) within one's own heart, therefore one should bow to it and touch it with the primary thumb (mukhyāṅguṣṭha). || 284 ||
For by means of the Svāhā, the removal of the world is properly accomplished.
And that [mudrā] is intended here when the ring finger and the index finger are drawn together. || 285 ||
The *śikhā* is the word *vaṣaṭ*, and by means of the *śikhā*, the planet is the body of the Self.
Therefore, for that reason, the syllable "vaṣaṭ" is uttered with the middle finger.
The kavaca-element is for the purpose of grasping; it is grasped with the *huṃ*-hand. However, the kavaca from the body is [grasped] with the index finger and the ring finger. || 287 ||
"Vauṣaṭ, which produces knowledge according to reality, is born from those two eyes."
Therefore, that which was spoken there is known as *vauṣaṭ* when performed with the index finger and the other fingers. || 288 ||
Because he possesses only one eye, one should utter that [name] ending in "bhyaḥ" among the gods such as Kubera;
however, for Viṣṇu and others, it should end in "bhyām," while for Rudra and others, it consists of three eyes. (289)
Whatever form, internal and so forth, is disciplined by the practitioner—that weapon born of ignorance—is manifested from the two hands with the syllable *phaṭ*. (290)

Having performed the breath control (prāṇāyāma) of the Mātṛkā, one should perform the ritual placements (nyāsas). These are said to be twenty-one, according to the different types of desires as well. || 291 ||
That secret is explained according to the distinction of qualified practitioners, by its eternality as well, or even by the distinction of deities. || 292 ||
In the Puruṣa deity, the Svara-mātṛkā alone is eternally present.
Through the performance of nyāsa and other such rites, the various dharmas are established for the practitioner who seeks the ultimate goal.

The Seer is Brahmā; [Oṃ, for this venerable Mātṛkā-nyāsa, Brahmā is the seer, Gāyatrī is the meter, the deity is Sarasvatī known as Mātṛkā, the consonants are the seeds, the vowels are the powers, the unmanifest is the pin; the application is for the attainment of one's desired goal].
Salutation to the Brahman-sage at the head; salutation to the Gāyatrī metre at the mouth;

salutation to the goddess Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī at the heart; salutation to the consonants, the seed-syllables, at the private parts; salutation to the vowels, the powers, at the feet; salutation to the unmanifested pillar.
Salutation at the navel. The deity is Sarasvatī, known as Mātṛkā; the consonants are the seeds, Gāyatrī is the meter, and the vowels are remembered as the power (śakti). || 294 ||

The unmanifest (*avyakta*) is designated as *kali*; its application is for the attainment of desired goals. Regarding *dakṣe* [the palm and back of the right hand]: furthermore, *karabha* refers to the outer part of the hand, from the wrist (*maṇibandha*) to the base of the little finger (*kaniṣṭhikā*).

Furthermore, one should place these eight Mātṛkās— *aṃ*, *āṃ*, *iṃ*, *īṃ*, *uṃ*, *ūṃ*, *ṛṃ*, *ṝṃ*— upon the fingers beginning with the thumb; then, one should again place them upon the little finger, ring finger, middle finger, index finger, thumb, the palm, and the back of the left hand.

Ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ—one should place these eight Mātṛkās in sequence. Aṃ namaḥ on the palm of the right hand; Āṃ namaḥ on the back of the right hand; Iṃ namaḥ on the fingers of the right hand; Īṃ namaḥ...
Uṃ namaḥ on the right thumb; Ūṃ namaḥ on the right index finger;
Ṛṃ namaḥ on the right middle finger; Ṝṃ namaḥ on the right ring finger; Ḷṃ namaḥ on the right little finger; Ḹṃ namaḥ on the left hand.
On the left little finger: *ḷṃ* namaḥ; on the left ring finger:
*eṃ* namaḥ; on the left middle finger: *aiṃ* namaḥ; on the left thumb: *oṃ* namaḥ;
on the palm of the left hand: *oṃ* namaḥ; on the back of the left hand: *aṃ* namaḥ.
"Aḥ! Homage to the palm of the left hand. Thus is the placement for stability (sthitinyāsa). [It is likewise performed] on the back of that hand and on the wrist. || 295 ||
Then one should place [the syllables] on the left hand, starting from the thumb, in reverse order.
This is the first nyāsa, consisting of the vowels joined with the bindu in their proper sequence.

Furthermore, they call this the performance of the placement in reverse order the *saṃhāranyāsa* (dissolution placement). Again, that placement which is performed by combining the *visarga* with the sequence of the *mātṛkās* in the very same *sthitinyāsa* (static placement) is called the *sṛṣṭinyāsa* (creation placement). For example: *aḥ*.

*Namo* on the palm of the right hand; *Āḥ* on the back of the right hand; *Iḥ* on the fingers of the right hand—it should be understood in this manner. Alternatively, when performed from the left, it is called the *saṃhāra-nyāsa*. For the purpose of destroying sins, enemies, and so forth, one should first perform it in the proper sequence.
One should practice [this]. || 297 ||

One should place fifteen syllables, from *ka* with its *visarga* up to *ṇa*, on the fifteen joints of the right hand; then, one should place those same syllables, from *ta* up to *śa*, on the joints of the left hand. For example: *kaṃ namaḥ*.
At the base of the right thumb: *khaṃ* namaḥ; in the middle of the right thumb: *gaṃ* namaḥ; at the tip of the right thumb: *ghaṃ* namaḥ; at the base of the index finger: *ṅaṃ* namaḥ;
in the middle of the index finger: *caṃ* namaḥ; at the tip of the index finger: *chaṃ* namaḥ; at the base of the middle finger: *jaṃ* namaḥ.

Jaṃ namaḥ to the middle of the middle finger; jhaṃ namaḥ to the tip of the middle finger; ñaṃ namaḥ to the base of the ring finger; ṭaṃ namaḥ to the middle of the ring finger; ṭhaṃ namaḥ to the tip of the ring finger; ḍaṃ namaḥ to the base of the little finger; ḍhaṃ namaḥ...

*Ṇaṃ namaḥ* on the middle of the little finger; *ṇaṃ namaḥ* on the tip of the little finger. In this very same manner, one should place the corresponding syllables on the joints of the left hand: *taṃ namaḥ* at the base of the left thumb; *thaṃ namaḥ* on the middle of the left thumb; *ḍhaṃ namaḥ*...

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) beginning with "at the tip of the left thumb" and so forth—this being the *sṛṣṭinyāsa* (emission-placement) consisting solely of the vowels performed like a standard *nyāsa*—it should be performed at the beginning of the practice for its successful accomplishment. One should place [the syllables] starting from the palm of the left hand up to the little finger; these are eight.
Likewise, he should [place] the vowels beginning with *a* and *u* upon the palms of his right hands. || 299 ||

This placement (nyāsa) is said to consist of the letters beginning with 'a', joined with the bindu and the visarga; it is performed at the beginning of the maintenance [of the ritual] and so forth, as before, for the sages, deities, and others while they abide in the body. 300.
Indeed, there are exactly fifteen letters, beginning with 'ka' and ending with 'ṇa'.
The joints of the right hand, from the thumb to the little finger. (301)
One should assign all [the syllables] joined with the *bindu* on the left as well, starting from *tā*.

From the thumb to the little finger, [one should assign them]; furthermore, [the mantra] "ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ namaḥ" on the right hand and "ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ namaḥ" on the left hand—thus also on both hands.
One should place [them]. || 302 ||
One should utter the five syllables ending with "namaḥ" simultaneously while placing the hand on each respective location;
this is the purification of the hands.
Between *aṃ* and *āṃ* [as follows: *aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ* to the two thumbs (*aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*); *īṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ īṃ* to the two index fingers (*tarjanībhyāṃ namaḥ*);
*uṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ ūṃ*].
*Madhyamābhyāṃ namaḥ*, *eṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ aiṃ* to the two middle fingers; *oṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ auṃ* to the two ring fingers (*anāmikābhyāṃ namaḥ*);
*aṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ* to the two little fingers (*kaniṣṭhikābhyāṃ namaḥ*).

*Haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ aḥ*, salutation to both palms and backs of the hands. In this very same manner, the performance of the *nyāsa*s for the heart and other limbs is likewise appropriate. The *ka*-group (*kavarga*) should be placed between *i* and *ī*; the *ca*-group (*cavarga*) between *u* and *ū*; the *ṭa*-group (*ṭavarga*) between *e* and *ai*; and the *ta*-group (*tavarga*) between *o* and *au*.

Oṃ Auṃ. In the middle [of the syllables] should be the labial class (pavarga), and in the middle of Aṃ and Aḥ should be the semi-vowels (yādi). With these [syllables], accompanied by the bindu, one performs the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the fingers and so forth, as well as on the heart and other [limbs]. 305.

This must also be performed for the sake of accomplishing the application (*viniyoga*) of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and other elements. For example, as has already been written at the very beginning: "For this venerable *mātṛkā-nyāsa*, Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the *gāyatrī* is the meter (*chandaḥ*), the goddess Sarasvatī named *mātṛkā* is the deity (*devatā*), and the consonants are the seed-syllables (*bīja*)," and so forth.
The placement (nyāsa) should be performed in that very manner for the purification of the six limbs and for the cessation of the sins born from anger and other [defilements]. || 306 ||

One should perform the binding of the directions with the weapon-mantra (astramantra) and three claps of the hands. Then, one should meditate upon the white lotus-colored [deity] situated upon the head. || 307 ||

Furthermore, regarding the pericarp (*karṇikā*): having first performed the recollection of the placement of the *ṛṣis* and so forth, it is appropriate to perform another placement. Having performed the meditation on an eight-petaled lotus upon the head, one should again [place] the *haṃsa* within that fruit which exists in the center of its pericarp.
Beyond the first petal, which contains the meaning starting from *keśara*, there is a second [petal];

between these two are the double vowels. Furthermore, on the seventh petal are the seven groups of consonants beginning with *ka*, and on the eighth petal is (*laṃ kṣaṃ*), which belongs to this mantra.

Meditation should be performed; its wheel is drawn as follows: one should recollect one's own mantra upon the eight filaments, likewise a pair of vowels on the seven petals, and the consonants beginning with *ka* [on the remaining petals]. (308)
One should thus contemplate the syllable "Laṃ" in the eighth of the seven groups; for one who contemplates in this way, disease and untimely death are destroyed. || 309 ||

Now, the internal nyāsa of the Mātṛkās: "Next, I shall describe the internal nyāsa of the Mātṛkās, which brings about internal accomplishment. Although this has been stated, however, the specific method for this Mātṛkā-nyāsa has not been revealed.

The procedure for that is written here, having been extracted from another tantra: *aṃ iṃ uṃ ṛṃ ḷṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ namaḥ*—thus [one worships] at the Viśuddhi-cakra, located in the region of the throat, which has sixteen petals and is smoke-colored. *kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ*... [and so forth].

*Ñaṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ namaḥ*— thus, at the heart, in the future wheel (*anāgata-cakra*) with twelve petals, which is coral-colored. *Ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ paṃ phaṃ namaḥ*— thus, above the navel, in the [present] wheel with ten petals, which is blue-colored.
At the Maṇipūraka-cakra: *baṃ bhaṃ maṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ namaḥ*.
At the Svādhiṣṭhāna-cakra, located six finger-breadths below the navel, which is six-petaled and the color of lightning:
*vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ namaḥ*. At the Mūlādhāra-cakra, which has four petals and the luster of gold.

"Haṃ kṣaṃ namaḥ"—thus [one should worship] in the Ājñā-cakra, located between the eyebrows, resembling the moon and possessing two petals; and in the thousand-spoked [cakra], white as snow and adorned with all colors.
[On the lines not chewed by the teeth, adorned with three marks: "Salutation to the Supreme Bindus.
I shall describe that which brings about internal accomplishment; having performed which, the mind of yogis does not engage in sin. (310)
Having heard the sound in the *mūlādhāra*, the *kuṇḍalinī* power is awakened.
In some places she resembles fire, having the nature of subtle radiance. || 311 ||

Now I shall describe the external placement (bahirnyāsa) in the previously mentioned aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra); one should meditate upon Sarasvatī, known as Mātṛkā, within the lotus of letters (varṇāravinda). || 312 ||
Her own face, arms, feet, belly, and chest are adorned with the fifty distinct letters;
she possesses a radiant matted lock from which a digit of the moon emerges, and she is as white as the moon or jasmine.

I bow to that Bhāratī, who holds a rosary, a water-pot, and a book written with excellent characters in her hands, who has three eyes, is seated upon a lotus, possesses a rosary and ornaments, and bears the weight of full breasts and hips. || 313 ||
From the verse numbered one hundred and ten among the verses totaling one thousand and eight,

up to the final letter of the alphabet, one should meditate upon the Bindu, whose nature is consciousness, from the base (mūlādhāra) to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). Then, with the streams of nectar flowing from it, one should satisfy the Mātṛkā letters.

In other tantras, one should write "hasa" in place of this mantra "haṃsa. On the perimeter of the earth [mandala], there is the worship of the previously mentioned guardians of the directions and their weapons; it should be visualized in this manner.
The illustration on page 84 [shows] the forehead,
up to the eighteen verses that complete the three hundred verses of the *Bhūtapariccheda*.
The procedure for the placement (*nyāsa*) of its *mātṛkā* resides within the root mantra. For example: *aṃ* on the forehead;

*āṃ* salutation on the mouth; *iṃ* salutation on the right eye; *īṃ* salutation on the left eye; *uṃ* salutation on the right ear; *ūṃ* salutation on the left ear; *ṛṃ* salutation on the right nostril; *ṝ*...
Namo to the left nostril; ḷṃ namo to the right cheek;

ḹṃ namo to the left cheek; eṃ namaḥ to the upper lip; aiṃ namaḥ to the lower lip; oṃ namaḥ to the upper row of teeth; auṃ namaḥ to the lower row of teeth; aṃ namaḥ to the crown of the head; aḥ namo to the mouth; aṃ.

Furthermore, in this text, the two locations for the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *mātṛkā* "Aḥ" are stated to be the head and the mouth; however, in other tantras such as the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*, the placement of "Aḥ" is seen on the tip of the tongue with the mantra "namaḥ," which is also appropriate. [The placement of] "Kaṃ" is with "namaḥ" [on the heart].
At the base of the right arm: *khaṃ* *namaḥ* at the elbow; *gaṃ* *namaḥ* at the wrist;
*ghaṃ* *namaḥ* at the base of the fingers; *ṅaṃ* *namaḥ* at the tips of the fingers; *caṃ* *namaḥ* at the base of the left arm; *chaṃ* *namaḥ* at the elbow; *jaṃ* *namaḥ* at the wrist; *jhaṃ*.

Namaḥ to the base of the fingers; ñaṃ namaḥ to the tips of the fingers; ṭaṃ namaḥ to the base of the right foot; ṭhaṃ namaḥ to the knee; ḍaṃ namaḥ to the ankle; ḍhaṃ namaḥ to the base of the toes of the right foot;
ṇaṃ namaḥ to the tips of the toes; taṃ namaḥ.
At the base of the left foot, *thaṃ namaḥ*; at the knee, *daṃ namaḥ*; at the ankle, *dhaṃ namaḥ*;
at the base of the toes of the left foot, *naṃ namaḥ*; at the tips of the toes of the left foot, *paṃ namaḥ*;
on the right side, *phaṃ namaḥ*; on the left side, *baṃ namaḥ*; on the back, *bhaṃ*.

Namo at the navel; maṃ namo at the abdomen; yaṃ to the self of the skin, namo at the heart; raṃ to the self of the blood, namo at the right shoulder; laṃ to the self of the flesh, namo at the back of the neck; vaṃ to the self of the fat, namo at the left shoulder; śaṃ to the self of the bone, namo.
From the heart to the tip of the right arm: *ṣaṃ* salutation to the self of marrow (*majjātman*). From the heart to the tip of the left arm: *saṃ* salutation to the self of semen (*śukrātman*).
From the heart to the tip of the right foot: *haṃ* salutation to the self (*ātman*).

From the heart to the tips of the left foot: *laṃ* to the Inner Self (*antarātman*), from the heart to the crown of the head. Furthermore, it is seen elsewhere in another text as *laṃ* *namaḥ* from the heart to the belly; this is the Mātṛkā-nyāsa according to the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*).

*Kṣaṃ* to the Supreme Self, salutation from the heart to the mouth. By means of these very letters of the Mātṛkā, devoid of the *bindu* but accompanied by the *visarga*, the Mātṛkā-nyāsa is performed in the aforementioned locations.
For example: *Aḥ* namaḥ on the forehead; *Āḥ* namaḥ on the mouth; *Iḥ* namaḥ... [and so forth].

"Oṃ *īḥ* namas* to the right eye; *it* [namas*] to the left eye," and so forth. Furthermore, this very same assignment (nyāsa), when applied with the nasal bindu (*m*) in reverse order, is called the Saṃhāra-nyāsa (dissolution assignment). This begins with the letter *kṣa* and ends with the letter *a*, becoming complete as follows: *kṣaṃ*.

*Paramātmane namaḥ* (Salutation to the Supreme Self) from the heart to the mouth; *laṃ Antarātmane namaḥ* (Salutation to the Inner Self) from the heart to the abdomen; *haṃ Ātmane namaḥ* (Salutation to the Self) from the heart to the left foot; *saṃ Śukrātmane namaḥ* (Salutation to the Self of Semen) from the heart to the right foot; *ṣaṃ Majjātmane* (Salutation to the Self of Marrow).

*Namaḥ* from the heart to the left arm; *śaṃ* to the self of bone, *namaḥ* from the heart to the right arm; *vaṃ* to the self of fat, *namaḥ* on the left shoulder; *laṃ* to the self of flesh, *namaḥ* on the crown of the head; *raṃ* to the self of blood, *namaḥ* on the right shoulder; *yaṃ*.

*Tvagātmane namaḥ* in the heart; *maṃ namaḥ* in the abdomen; *bhaṃ namaḥ* in the navel; *baṃ namaḥ* in the back; *phaṃ namaḥ* in the left foot; *paṃ namaḥ* in the right foot; *naṃ namaḥ* on the tips of the toes of the left foot; *dhaṃ namaḥ* at the base of the toes of the left foot; *daṃ*...

*Namaḥ* to the left ankle; *thaṃ namaḥ* to the left knee; *taṃ namaḥ* to the root of the left foot; *ṇaṃ namaḥ* to the tips of the right toes; *ḍhaṃ namaḥ* to the base of the right toes; *ḍaṃ namaḥ* to the right ankle; *ṭhaṃ namaḥ* to...
*Ṭaṃ namaḥ* at the right knee; *ñaṃ namaḥ* at the base of the right foot;
*jhaṃ namaḥ* at the tips of the fingers of the left hand; *jaṃ namaḥ* at the base of the fingers of the left hand;
*chaṃ namaḥ* at the wrist of the left hand; *caṃ namaḥ* at the elbow of the left arm.
Ṅaṃ, homage to the root of the left arm; Ghaṃ, homage to the tip of the right hand finger;

Gaṃ, homage to the base of the right hand finger; Khaṃ, homage to the wrist of the right hand; Khaṃ, homage to the elbow of the right arm; Kaṃ, homage to the root of the right arm; Aḥ, homage to the mouth; Aṃ.

*Namaḥ* on the crown of the head; *oṃ namaḥ* on the lower row of teeth; *oṃ namaḥ* on the upper row of teeth; *aiṃ namaḥ* on the lower lip; *eṃ namaḥ* on the upper lip; *ḷṃ namaḥ* on the left cheek; *ḷṃ namaḥ* on the right cheek; *ṝṃ namaḥ*... [on the nose].
*Ūṃ* namaḥ to the left nostril; *Uṃ* namaḥ to the left ear; *Īṃ* namaḥ to the right ear; *Īṃ* namaḥ to the left eye; *Iṃ* namaḥ to the right eye; *Āṃ* namaḥ to the face-circle;
*Aṃ* namaḥ to the forehead. This is the Saṃhāra-mātṛkā-nyāsa.

Furthermore, it is appropriate to perform the placement of the *mātṛkā* (the alphabet) starting from the letter *ḍa* and ending with the letter *ṭha*. Thus: *ḍaṃ namaḥ* on the right ankle; *ḍhaṃ namaḥ* at the base of the toes of the right foot; *ṇaṃ namaḥ* at the tips of the toes of the right foot; *taṃ*...
*Namaḥ* at the base of the left foot; *thaṃ namaḥ* at the knee; *daṃ namaḥ* at the ankle;
*dhaṃ namaḥ* at the base of the toes of the left foot; *naṃ namaḥ* at the tips of the toes of the left foot; *paṃ namaḥ* on the right side; *phaṃ namaḥ* on the left side; *vaṃ namaḥ*.
On the back: *bhaṃ* namaḥ; at the navel: *maṃ* namaḥ; in the abdomen:

*yaṃ* svagātmane namaḥ; in the heart: *raṃ* asṛgātmane namaḥ; on the right shoulder: *laṃ* māṃsātmane namaḥ; at the crown of the head: *vaṃ* medātmane namaḥ; on the left shoulder: *śaṃ* asthyātmane namaḥ.
*Namaḥ* from the heart to the right arm: *ṣaṃ*, salutation to the self of marrow. *Namaḥ* from the heart to the left arm: *saṃ*, salutation to the self of semen.
*Namaḥ* from the heart to the right foot: *haṃ*, salutation to the self.
From the heart to the left foot: *laṃ* to the Inner Self (*antarātman*), obeisance.
From the heart to the belly: *jñaṃ* to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), obeisance. From the heart to the mouth: *aṃ*, obeisance to the head; *āṃ*, obeisance to the perimeter of the face; *iṃ*.
Salutation to the right eye: *īṃ*; salutation to the left eye: *uṃ*; salutation to the right ear: *ṛ*; salutation to the right nostril:
*ṝṃ*; salutation to the left nostril: *ḷṃ*; salutation to the right cheek:
*ḹṃ*; salutation to the left cheek: *eṃ*; salutation to the upper lip: *aiṃ*.

*Namaḥ* to the lower lip; *oṃ namaḥ* to the upper row of teeth; *auṃ namaḥ* to the lower row of teeth; *aṃ namaḥ* to the crown of the head; *aḥ namaḥ* to the mouth; *kaiṃ namaḥ* to the root of the right arm; *khaṃ namaḥ* to the elbow; *gaṃ namaḥ* to the wrist; *ghaṃ* [to the fingers].

*Namaḥ* to the base of the fingers, *ḍaṃ*; *namaḥ* to the tips of the fingers, *ṛṃ*; *namaḥ* to the base of the left arm, *chaṃ*; *namaḥ* to the elbow, *jaṃ*; *namaḥ* to the wrist, *jhaṃ*; *namaḥ* to the tips of the fingers; *ṭaṃ* *namaḥ* to the base of the right foot; *ṭaṃ* *namaḥ* to the knee of the right foot. Thus.

The placement for maintenance (sthitinyāsa). It should be understood that the placements for emanation (sṛṣṭi) and maintenance (sthiti) arise from the letters of the Mātṛkā together with the vowels ending in *u* (sendu) and those with the visarga (visarga), whereas the placement for withdrawal (saṃhāra) occurs solely through the letters of the Mātṛkā joined with the nasal bindu.
One should place the vowels upon the face, the forehead, the eyes, the ears, the nose, the two cheeks, the two lips, the two rows of teeth, the head, and the mouth. (314)
The wise practitioner should place the *ka* and *ca* groups at the joints of the upper arms;
likewise, the *ṭa* and *ta* groups on the two sides of the feet, and [the *pa* group] from the region of the back. (315)
Having placed the *pavarga* at the navel and the abdomen, and then the letter *ka* with its *kaku* (anusvāra) at the heart,
one should then place the four letters beginning with *ya* and the six [letters] beginning with *cha*.
This assignment (nyāsa) is performed in the heart and other [limbs], in the two hands, in the two feet, in the belly, and likewise in the mouth;
it fulfills the recitation that was deficient in syllables and measures.
If the ritual placement (nyāsa) is performed beginning with "Kṣamā" and ending with the letter "a," then:
This [method] consisting of the nyāsa of withdrawal is called the nyāsa of the bindu. || 318 ||
For those who have entered the left-hand path and practice the service of the Śakti,
After the internal placement (antarnyāsa), there should be the retention of semen during the placement of the Bindu.
As long as the power remains moist, so long is enjoyment prescribed.
The visualization of the deity by way of the left and right channels is now described. || 320 ||

Bow down to the Mistress of Colors (Varṇeśvarī), who holds in her hands a rosary of beads, a young deer, a lofty book, and sacred knowledge; who has three eyes, wears the crescent moon upon her crest, is ruddy-hued, dwells within the lotus, and is bent by the weight of her breasts.
When the Śākta desire is fulfilled, one should perform the placement of the Visarga (visarganyāsa). From that, the Bindu falls;
therefore, there are both the Bindu and the Visarga.
When these two depositions are proclaimed for a Śākta-vāmin or a Kaulika, (p. 86) ...
Without satisfaction through the Śaktis, everything is liberated even by means of ritual placement (nyāsa). || 323 ||
Then he goes to hell for as long as the moon and sun endure;
even in this world, he shall be without lineage, deprived of the splendor of Brahman.
Those who strive to fall into the left path with the hope of attaining enjoyment or liberation are like those striving to seize a snake's jewel without the use of a mantra. || 325 ||

The nyāsa of the mātṛkā with the visarga should be performed exactly like the simple mātṛkā; however, the specific distinction is that the pronunciation of the letters should end with the visarga. || 326 ||

One should place the letters from *ṭha* to *na*, joined with the *bindu* (nasal dot) and the *sarga* (visarga), within the Egg and so forth during the stage of maintenance (*sthiti*). It is said that the visualization of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) consists of the same mantras and so forth as previously mentioned.

One should meditate upon the Goddess who stands by his side, possessing the luster of saffron, adorned with ornaments of immeasurable splendor, and three-eyed; she holds a book, a rosary, a deer-calf, and a water-pot in her hands, has a golden radiance, and wears a garland of letters.
The students should perform the ritual placements (nyāsa) according to the sequences of maintenance, withdrawal, and emanation.
The processes of withdrawal, emanation, and maintenance are projected by those who dwell in the house.
And the forest-dwellers and ascetics [attain liberation] through the internalization of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.

"Thus it is said that one should perform the nyāsas; this is the detailed exposition of the Mātṛkā-nyāsa. I shall now describe the nyāsa of the Kalāmātṛkā; its seer (ṛṣi) is traditionally remembered as [the following]. || 331 ||
Prajāpati is the deity here, and Gāyatrī is the metre; Sarasvatī, known as Mātṛkā, is the presiding power for the attainment of one's desired goal. || 332 ||
With the long vowels: *aṃ oṃ āṃ* to the two thumbs (*aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*),
*iṃ oṃ īṃ* to the two index fingers (*tarjanībhyāṃ namaḥ*), *uṃ oṃ ūṃ* to the two middle fingers (*madhyamābhyāṃ namaḥ*),
*eṃ oṃ aiṃ* to the two ring fingers (*anāmikābhyāṃ namaḥ*), *oṃ oṃ auṃ* to the two little fingers (*kaniṣṭhikābhyāṃ namaḥ*), and *aṃ oṃ*.

"Aḥ! *Namaḥ* to both palms and backs of the hands—thus is the *karanyāsa*. Likewise, the *hṛdayādinyāsa* (the ritual placement on the heart and other limbs) should be performed according to the stated method.
One should perform the six-limbed rite (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with [the syllables] situated between the short and long vowels. [This is] the visualization (*dhyāna*)."
I shall now describe the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Kalāmātṛkā; listen, O beloved.
Holding in her hands a lotus, a discus, a bow, a deer, a book, a rosary, a chisel, a bright skull-cup,
and a golden jar overflowing with nectar— [the goddess] Muktā...

I bow to that Śāradā, who resembles the full moon, who is bent by her breasts, and who possesses five faces with three eyes each, beautiful as lightning, clouds, crystal, and a rosary of beads. || 334 ||
Having meditated thus, one should [recite] the mantra beginning with *Tāra* (Oṃ) and ending with the vowels starting from *a*,
together with the syllables of the Mātṛkā alphabet (*oṃ* and the *bindu*), followed by the names of the *kalās* such as *Nivṛtti* and so forth in the dative case, ending with the word *namaḥ*.
Having joined [the syllables], the placement (nyāsa) should be performed in the previously mentioned locations such as the forehead, as follows:
*oṃ aṃ* to Nivṛtti, salutation to the forehead; *oṃ āṃ* to Pratiṣṭhā, salutation to the perimeter of the face;
*oṃ iṃ* to Vidyā, salutation to the right eye; *oṃ īṃ* to Śānti, salutation to...
In the left eye: *oṃ uṃ ṛddhikāyai namaḥ*; in the right ear: *oṃ ūṃ dīpikāyai namaḥ*;

in the left ear, and so forth. And [one should worship] the Mātṛkā, joined with the nasal dot (*bindu*), enriched by the names of the phonemes ending in *ṅ*, and accompanied by the word *namaḥ*. (335)
One should place the previously mentioned pure measures (mātrās) in the locations for the ritual placement (nyāsa): Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and likewise Ṛddhikā. || 336 ||
Dīpikā, Recikā, and Mocikā as another name; then Sūkṣmā, Sūkṣmāmṛtā, Jñānāmṛtā, and Āpyāyinī. (337)
Pervasive, of the nature of space, infinite, and the source of prosperity is Sṛṣṭi; then Smṛti, Medhā, Kānti, Dyuti, Lakṣmī, Sthirā, and Sthiti. || 338 ||
Siddhi, Jarā, Pālinī, Kṣānti, Īśvarikā, Rati, Kāmikā, Varadā, and another, Hlādinī, who is endowed with affection (prīti). || 339 ||
Dīrghā, Tīkṣṇā, as well as Raudrī, Māyā [an alternative reading is *mayā*], Nidrā, and Tandrikā; Kṣudhā, Krodhinī, followed by Kriyā, Utkārī, and Samṛtyukā. (340)
Yellow, white, reddish, and finally black, endowed with a downward curve—this is said to be the Kalāmātṛkā;
one should place it in the positions beginning with the letter 'A'. || 341 ||
Among those, the notes born of *nāda* arise from Sadāśiva.
A rosary, a book, a noose, a bow, and a skull-bowl. || 342 ||
They should be meditated upon as holding [these] in their hands and being anointed with yellow fragrant unguents.
The ten digits of the *ka*-group were born from the syllable *u* of Viṣṇu.
Likewise, the excellent ones are red in color, holding lotuses in their hands and bearing rosaries.
From the *ukāra* of Viṣṇu, the ten digits (*kalā*) of the *ṭa*-group [of consonants] are born. (344)

The nine digits of the *pa*-group are said to be dark-complexioned, with their hands holding the gestures of granting fearlessness (*abhaya*), a conch, and a lotus; they are born from the letter *ma* and originate from Rudra. || 345 ||
Resembling the autumnal moon, they should be visualized by the practitioners as holding in their hands the gesture of fearlessness, a trident, a skull-cup, and the boon-granting mudrā. || 346 ||
The Lord of the five letters beginning with Śa arises from the Bindu; he holds the gesture of fearlessness, a deer, a battle-axe, and a boon-granting mudrā in his sprout-like hands. || 347 ||
And they should be meditated upon as being red in color during the ritual placement (nyāsa) consisting of the kalās.
The sage Nārāyaṇa is the one to be realized through the Mātṛkā beginning with Keśava. || 348 ||
The Gāyatrī meter is Amṛtā and others; the Goddess Lakṣmī is the deity Hari. With the doubled [syllables]:
*hrīṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *śrīṃ* to the head, *svāhā*; *klīṃ* to the crest-lock, *vaṣaṭ*; *hrīṃ* to the armor, *huṃ*; *śrīṃ* to the two eyes, *vauṣaṭ*; *klīṃ*.
"Astrāya Phaṭ!"—one should perform the six-limbed ritual with power, fortune, and desire. || 349 ||
I worship Lakṣmī-Hari, who bears the conch, discus, mace, lotus, water-pot, mirror, lotus, and book, and whose complexion is as swift and dark as a rain-cloud. || 350 ||

The Śaktis, seated upon the laps of their beloveds with smiling faces, should be meditated upon in this manner; then one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the syllables encased within the *Śrī*, *Kāma*, and *Śakti* mantras. [Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ aṃ klīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Keśava and Kīrti.]

On the forehead: *oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ āṃ klīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ nārāyaṇakāntibhyāṃ namaḥ*. On the perimeter of the face: *oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ iṃ klīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ mādhavatuṣṭhibhyāṃ namaḥ*. On the right eye: *oṃ*... [The text continues].
*Hrīṃ śrīṃ īṃ klīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ*, salutation to Govinda and Puṣṭi at the left eye. (p.
88) The powers beginning with Keśava and ending with Bhyānta, starting from *Tārā* (Oṃ) and ending with the *hṛdaya* (namaḥ).
One should utter the *namonta* [mantras] and place them in their respective positions beginning with the letter 'a'.
But for the Śāktas, this service to Viṣṇu is eternal, being merely a fraction [of their devotion]. Keśava is endowed with fame, and Nārāyaṇa is endowed with splendor. || 353 ||
Mādhava is endowed with contentment, Govinda is endowed with nourishment, Viṣṇu is endowed with fortitude, and Madhusūdana is joined with peace. || 354 ||
Trivikrama is endowed with action; Vāmana is possessed of compassion; Śrīdhara is joined with wisdom;
and Hṛṣīkeśa is filled with joy. || 355 ||
Śraddhā is united with Padmanābha; Lajjā is accompanied by Dāmodara; Vāsudeva is joined with Lakṣmī; and Madhusūdana is conjoined with Sarasvatī. || 356 ||
Pradyumna is joined with Prīti, and Aniruddha is joined with Rati; Cakrī is with Jayā, Gadī is with Durgā, and Śārṅgī is endowed with Prabhā. || 357 ||
The wielder of the sword (Khaḍgī) is joined with Samayā; the wielder of the conch (Saṅkhī) is accompanied by Caṇḍā;
the wielder of the plow (Halī) is united with Vāṇī; and the wielder of the mace (Muśalī) is with Vilāsinī. || 358 ||
Śūlin is joined with Vijayā (an alternative reading is Vinodā); Pāśin is accompanied by Virajā; Aṅkuśin is joined with Viśvā; and Mukunda is accompanied by Vinayā.
Born of Nanda, joined with Sunandā, Nandin is endowed with Satī; Nara is possessed of supernatural power (ṛddhi), Naraka-jit is joined with Samat, and Hari is united with Śuddhi. || 360 ||
Kṛṣṇa is known as the Sātvata because he is endowed with intelligence, prosperity, truth, and wisdom.
Bhūdhara is joined with Kledinī, and Viśvamūrti with Klinnā.
Vaikuṇṭha is joined with Vasudhā; Vasudā and Puruṣottama [are joined] with Bali, who is endowed with supreme [power], and [he is] devoted to Balānuja.
In Bāla-sūkṣma, Vṛṣaghna is joined with Sandhyā, while Vṛṣa is joined with Prajñā; Haṃsa is joined with Prabhā, and Varāha is accompanied by Niśā. (363)

Vimala is endowed with intelligence, and Nṛsiṃha is accompanied by lightning. Keśava and the others are declared according to the [Mātṛkā] sequence; the application of the vowels and so forth is as before. || 364 ||
One should state that for the devotees of Śiva, the Mātṛkā begins with Śrīkaṇṭha; Dakṣiṇāmūrti is said to be the sage, and Gāyatrī is declared to be the metre. (365)

Lord Hara, born from half the mountain, is the injunction for the attainment of all perfections. One should place the consonants (hal) as the seeds in the secret place, and the vowels (svara) as the powers (śakti) on the feet. || 366 ||
Having placed the short and long vowels in between, one should likewise place the groups (vargas) as before, starting with the short *a*.
Having joined them with the six long vowels, one should perform the placement of the six limbs upon the body.

We perpetually take refuge in that body which resembles the Bandhūka flower and gold, which holds a rosary of blood-red beads, a noose, a goad, and the gesture of granting boons in its own staff-like arms; which wears the crescent moon as an ornament, possesses three eyes, and has the Goddess Ambikā as half of its head. 368.
Having uttered "Hrasauṃ" followed by the Mātṛkā, one should then recite it at the end of the word "deva."
One should place the power that pierces and shatters [all things], ending with "namaḥ," in the location of the Mātṛkās. || 369 ||

One should state the vital breaths (*asūn*) as skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen; likewise, one should state the powers (*śakti*), anger, and the self (*ātman*) ending in the suffix *-ṅ*, across all ten [categories]. (370)
Śrīkaṇṭha with Pūrṇodarī, Ananta accompanied by Virajā, Sūkṣmeśa joined by Śālmallī, and Trimūrtika joined by Lolākṣī. || 371 ||
Amareśa is with Vartulākṣī, and Varṣīśa is with Dīrghagoṇā.
Bhārabhūti, Dīrghamukhya, Tithīśa, and Gomukhīya. || 372 ||
Sthāṇvīśa, who is joined by Dīrghajihvā and Kuṇḍodarī, is the destroyer of the pair.
Jhiṇṭīśa and Ūrdhvakeśin, along with Bhautika and Vikṛtāsyā. (373)
Sadyojāta is accompanied by Jvālāmukhī, and Aghora by Ulkāmukhī;
Akrūra is Śrīmukhī, and Mahāsena is joined with Vidyāmukhī. || 374 ||
Krodhana with Mahākālī, Caṇḍeśa with Sarasvatī, and Pañcāntaka joined with Sarvasiddhigaurī are thus proclaimed. || 375 ||
Śivottameśa is to be placed, joined with Trailokyavidyā; Ekarudra with Mantraśakti, and Kūrmeśa joined with Aṣṭaśakti.
Ekanetra is joined with Bhūtamātrā, and Caturānana is likewise joined [with her]. Ajeśa is said to be joined with Lambodarī, and [he is] joined with Drāviṇī. || 377 ||
Sarveśa is joined with Nāgarī; Someśa is joined with Khecarī; Lāṅgalīśa is joined with Mañjarī;
and Dārukeśa is joined with Rūpiṇī. || 378 ||
Ārdhanārīśa is joined with Vāriṇī, while Umākānta is again joined [with Umā]. Likewise, Āṣāḍhī is said to be joined with Kākodaryā, and Pūtanā is joined [with her consort]. || 379 ||
Caṇḍīśa is joined with Bhadrakālī, and Trīśa is joined with Yoginī;
Mīneśa is joined with Śaṅkhinī, and Meṣeśa is joined with Tarjanī. || 380 ||
Lohita is united with Kālarātri, and Śikhīśa with Kubjinī; Chagalaṇḍa is joined with Kapardinī, and Dvidaṇḍīśa with Vajrā.
Mahākāla joined with Jayā, Bālīśa with Sumukheśvarī; Bhujaṅga joined with Recanī, and Pinākī with Mādhavī. || 382 ||
Khaḍgīśa is joined with Vāruṇī; Bakeśa is joined with Vāyavī; Śveta is joined with Rakṣovidāriṇī; and Bhagu is joined with Sahajā. || 383 ||
Nakulīśa conjoined with Lakṣmī, Śiveśa conjoined with Vyapinī, and Saṃvartaka conjoined with Mahāmāyā—these indeed are the Mātṛkās. || 384 ||
One should employ the term beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha and ending with Ādimaheśa, in the nominative singular (ending in -ṅ).
All these Rudras are remembered as being red in color and holding tridents and skull-bowls. || 385 ||
The Śaktis, residing in the Rudra-pīṭhas, possess bodies as red as vermilion.
Their lotus-like hands are adorned with a red utpala lotus and a skull-cup.
O gods, he who worships the ten Mahāvidyās possesses authority over them; first, one should perform the nyāsa of the Mātṛkā with the Bīja of Bhuvaneśī. || 387 ||
The seer is Śakti, and the meter is Gāyatrī, consisting of the Mātṛkās.
The deity is Bhuvaneśī, and the application [of this mantra] is for the attainment of one's desired goal. || 388 ||
By means of the six groups [of consonants] situated between the short and long vowels, conjoined with the long vowels.
As before, there should be the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) for Hari, beginning with the thumbs, in that very same manner. || 389 ||
May she—who possesses lofty, full, and fleshy breasts resembling ten million rising suns;
who is adorned with a crown, necklaces, a girdle, and anklets shaped like crescent moons;
and who holds a rosary, a noose, a goad, and a book in her lotus-like hands—grant us [her blessings].
The mistress of the world, three-eyed, sits comfortably upon a lotus. || 390 ||
Having first uttered the seed-syllable of modesty (Lajjābīja), this indeed is the Mātṛkā-nyāsa; the Nyāsa of the Mātṛkās of Bhuvaneśī is for the accomplishment of the Nārpatya [mantra]. || 391 ||
Those householders who desire prosperity should perform [this rite] preceded by the seed-syllable Śrī.
The seer is Bhṛgu, and Gāyatrī is the meter, who is the very embodiment of the Mother. || 392 ||

Lakṣmī is declared to be the deity; place the two arrows in the position of Hara. For the purpose of the ritual placement (nyāsa), perform the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) and so forth, preceded by the Śrī-bīja. || 393 ||
She possesses a radiance equal to a flash of lightning and is being sprinkled by four arms, which resemble the snowy mountains and hold jars of nectar uplifted by their trunk-like stalks.
