One should meditate upon the Mistress of the World, who holds a rosary of *japā* seeds, a pair of lotuses, and a book in her lotus-like hands; she is radiant with shining jewels and possesses the beauty of budding breasts.

For the sake of attaining merely the company of a beloved woman, the sage should perform the Mātṛkā-nyāsa preceded by the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja); this is known as the Sammohana [nyāsa]. || 395 ||

The Gāyatrī is declared to be the meter, and the deity is composed of the Mother-letters (Mātṛkā). The Great Goddess Sammohanī [is worshipped], and the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) is performed according to the previously mentioned method. || 396 ||

One should meditate upon the Mother of all beings, who has a crescent moon as her crest-jewel, three eyes, and holds in her lotus-like hands a rosary of crystal radiant as ten million rising suns, a bow made of sugarcane, and the five arrows, as well as the Vidyā-mantra. (397)
For men who perform the nyāsa of the Mātṛkā upon the seed-syllables of Śakti, Śrī, and Kāma, the many-described defects of mantra, such as enmity and the like, are destroyed. || 398 ||
The sage is Mahāsammohana, the meter is said to be Gāyatrī, and the goddess is named Sammohanī;
the ritual placement (nyāsa) is the same as that of the Mātṛkā. || 399 ||
One should meditate upon her who holds in her nine hands the rosary, the noose, the bow of sugarcane, two lotuses, the goad,
the boon-granting gesture, and a book; she is reddish-brown with nine folds, distressed by her full breasts, the enchantress, three-eyed, and mounted upon the crescent moon.
For the purpose of dispelling all obstacles, one must certainly perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).
For the Gaṇeśamātṛkā, the sage is said to be Gaṇaka. || 401 ||

With the Gāyatrī as the meter for the withdrawal (nivṛt), and Śakti-Vināyaka as the deity, one should perform the ritual assignment of the limbs (aṅga-nyāsa) using the mantra beginning with "dīrgha" and so forth, and then meditate upon the elephant-faced god. || 402 ||

I worship Gaṇeśa, who is red in complexion, has three eyes, and holds a spear, a goad, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in his hands; he is embraced by his beloved, whose hand rests upon his red lotus. || 403 ||
Vighneśa is joined with Hrī; Vighnarāja is endowed with Śrī. Vināyaka is joined with Puṣṭi; Śivottama is joined with Śānti. (404)
Vighnakṛt is joined with Svasti, Vighnahartā with Sarasvatī; Gaṇa is joined with Svāhā, and Ekadanta with Sumedhā. || 405 ||
Dvidanta is joined with Kānti, and Gajavaktra is joined with Kāminī; Nirañjana is joined with Mohinī, while Kapardin is joined with Naṭī. || 405 ||
Dīrghajihva, Pārvatīyuk, Kukarṇa, Jvālinī, Vṛṣadhvaja, Nandāyuk, Suyaśas, and Gaṇanāyaka—these are the Sureśas. 407.
Gajendra was with Kāmarūpiṇī, and likewise Śūrpakarṇa was with Umā.
Trilocana [was united] with Tejovatī, while Lambodara [was united] with Satyā.
Mahānanda is with Vighneśī, who is his own form in four manifestations; Sadāśiva is with Kāmadā, Yugāmoda is with Madajihvā. (409)
Durmukha is joined with Bhūti; Sumukha is joined with Bhautika; Pramoda is joined with Sitā;
and Ekapāda is joined with Ramā. || 410 ||
Dvijihva is joined with Mahiṣī, and Śūra with Jambhinī; Vīra is joined with Vikarṇā, and Ṣaṇmukha with Bhrukuṭī. || 411 ||
Varada is with Lajjā; Vāmadeva is with Dīrghaghoṇā; Dhanurdhara is with Vakratuṇḍa; and Dvirada is with Yāminī. || 412 ||
Sinīśa is conjoined with Rātri; Kāmāndha is joined with Grāmaṇī; Matta is joined with Śaśiprabhā; and Vimatta is joined with Lolalocanā. || 413 ||
Unsteady on his intoxicated mount, wearing matted locks and endowed with radiance; shaven-headed and joined with Subhagā, and likewise bearing a sword and joined with Durbhagā. || 414 ||
Vareṇya is joined with Śivā; Bhagāyu is joined with Vṛṣaketana; Bhaktapriya is joined with Bhaginī;
and Gaṇeśa is joined with Bhoginī. || 415 ||
Pervaded by the beauty of Meghanāda, he may be joined with Kālarātri; Gaṇeśvara is called Kālikā, the mother of Vighneśa.
The association of the skin and other [elements] with the letters *ya* and so forth has been proclaimed as before.
This ritual placement of the sacrifice of proliferation (prapañcayāga-nyāsa), which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, shall now be described.

One should perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the mantra of Mahāgaṇeśa. Gaṇaka is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi) of the Prapañcayāga, and its meter (chandas) has been proclaimed. || 418 ||
One should place the Gāyatrī preceded by Nivṛtti, the deity Mahāgaṇapati, and those [mantras] upon the head and other parts, as well as the seed-syllable *gaṃ* in the secret part.
"Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ"—this pair of six long vowels joined with the preceding [syllables] is for the application of the Svāhā-śakti at the feet for the attainment of one's desired goal. (420)

Having uttered [the seed-syllables], one should perform the limb-assignments: [Oṃ gāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ, śrīṃ gīṃ śirase svāhā, hrīṃ gūṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ, klīṃ gaiṃ kavacāya huṃ, glauṃ gauṃ netratrayāya vauṣaṭ, gaṃ gaḥ astrāya].
With "phaṭ," one should likewise perform the ritual placements (nyāsa) beginning with the thumbs;

thus, one should place [the mantras] on the thumbs and so forth. Having likewise performed the protection of the two palms with the Astra-mantra, one should carry out the binding of the directions (digbandha). (421)

Then, by means of the sound made with the index finger and thumb, one should contemplate [the ten directions]; thereafter, one should perform meditation for the sake of attaining the desired success of Gaṇeśa. 422.

[I bow to Him] whose face is like that of the lordly elephant, who has the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, who possesses a ruddy luster and three eyes, and who is passionately embraced by His beloved, who rests upon His own lap with her lotus-hand placed against Him.
I worship Him who holds a citron, a mace, a trident, a discus, a lotus, a noose, a blue lotus, the tip of a grain of rice, His own tusk, and a jewel-filled jar in His hands. || 423 ||
Then one should recite the mantra of Mahāgaṇapati eight times; "Gam" is its single-syllable seed-mantra (bīja), and Gaṇaka is considered its sage (muni). || 426 ||
The deity is Vighneśvara, and the metre is called Nivṛt-Gāyatrī; this is for the sake of accomplishing the perfection of the limbs of the sacrifice known as Prapañca. || 425 ||
This is the application for the purpose of reciting forty-four times. Then, one should perform the limb-assignments (*aṅga*) with [the mantra] joined with the six long vowels. || 426 ||
Holding a mace, a noose, and a goad in his hands, he has three eyes, is pot-bellied, and is most excellent.
Having the luster of vermilion, with the moon upon his crest, adorned with serpents, and with ichor trickling down.
One should recite it once, followed by the Vedic mantra "gaṇānāṃ tvā."
For the Gaṇeśamālā-mantra, the sage is remembered as Gaṇaka; the meter is Mita, and Gaṇapati is proclaimed as the deity. || 428 ||
Hrīṃ kroṃ tāro namaḥ; thereafter, [one should utter] "sarva" ending in the letter ṅa, followed by "vidyādhipa".
"Bestower of the accomplishment of all aims" and "Pacifier of all sufferings. || 429 ||
Then: "O Manāyā, come, come! O Blessed One, cause [the drum] to sound! And: "Paralyze the two! Hrīṃ Gaṃ Gāṃ! Salutation to the one whose abode is fire. (430)

"Kroṃ hī m itthaṃ"—this mantra of fifty-five syllables is thus declared. One should recite this four times and perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) together with the sages and other deities. || 431 ||
Having first performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should recite [the mantra] three times while preceded by meditation on the Mātṛkā.
One should duly place the seven planets using the seven groups beginning with the vowels.
In the mouth, the two arms, the two feet, the belly, and the heart, respectively, [one should place] the Tāra (Om), Māyā (Hrīṃ), Haṃsa, So'haṃ, and Svāhā once again. || 433 ||
This eight-syllable mantra of the Prapañcayāga has been proclaimed.
The sage Brahmā is proclaimed to be the mantra for the sacrifice of conceptual proliferation (prapañca). || 434 ||
The supreme primordial one is declared to be Gāyatrī, the most excellent meter; the Great is declared to be the supreme deity, whose nature consists of pure consciousness. || 435 ||

[They] protect that which is uncontradicted, eternal, all-pervading, and stainless, by means of the five syllables arranged in reverse order and established within the phenomenal world (prapañca). || 436 ||
By means of the short, long, and internal [vowels], and the classes of consonants beginning with ka, preceded by their respective counterparts.
By means of these syllables of Hari and Hara, joined with *tāra*, *māyā*, and so forth; || 437 ||
The preceptor should perform the six ancillary rites, conjoined with their respective mantras.

Having set aside that which is perceived through the five means of knowledge beginning with the Vedas, O sages, worship that supreme light— the sole root of the universe, which is existence, consciousness, all-pervading, imperishable, infallible,
and an ocean of perfect compassion. (438)
At the end of the Veda and the Māyā [syllables], [there are]: oṃ hrīṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ.

Having pronounced separately the letters from *dha* to *kṣa*, each with its nasal bindu— namely: *dhaṃ naṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ*— and then reciting *haṃsaḥ sohaṃ svāhā*.
Speaking thus in his heart. || 439 ||

"One should visualize these phonemes and offer them as oblations into the fire of the Self; having thus offered those ending with the letter *kṣa*, one should again offer those ending with the letter *a*. (440)

Placing [the letters] ending with *kṣa* along with the *visarga* in the locations of the Mātṛkā, thus is declared the placement of the Mātṛkā known as the Sacrifice of the Universe (*prapañcayāga*). || 441 ||

Then one should perform the placement known as the twenty-one-fold Yoga-pīṭha; having first performed that which was previously mentioned, one should thereafter proceed with the mantra of one's own chosen deity. 442.
Thereafter, one should display the respective mudrās prescribed for each kalpa. He who daily performs the ritual placements (nyāsa) according to the path taught in the Āgamas— || 443 ||
One attains the state of a deity and the perfection of mantra arises for him who is clothed in the armor of ritual placement (nyāsa) and is devoted to the recitation of mantras. 444.
Upon seeing him, the obstacles flee, just as elephants do upon seeing a lion.
That fool who performs japa without first performing the network of nyāsas, [attains no fruit]. || 445 ||
He will surely be afflicted by obstacles, like a young deer by tigers.
Because the nyāsas are widely practiced, their fruits are likewise abundant.

The previously mentioned nyāsa must certainly not be abandoned; however, one may perform additional rites according to one's desire. One should perform the binding of the mudrā with the two seed-syllables *oṃ* and *klīm*. One should display [the mudrā] with the root mantra and perform the placement (*nyāsa*) with the seed-syllable *hasauṃ*. || 447 ||
Then the mantra-practitioner should perform meditation according to the methods prescribed in the respective ritual manuals (kalpas).
That [meditation] is said to be of two kinds: with attributes (saguṇa) and likewise without attributes (nirguṇa). || 448 ||
Within the lotus of one's own heart, radiant with its pericarp and filaments, fully blossomed and resplendent with the orbs of the Moon, Sun, and Fire— 449.
There, one should worship one's own chosen deity as revealed by the Āgamas;
such knowledge is indeed declared to be meditation with attributes (saguṇa-dhyāna). || 450 ||
The realization that "I am He," which is the oneness of the individual soul and Brahman—that indeed the knowers of the Veda understand to be meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa). || 451 ||

Now I shall describe the internal restraint (antaryatana); listen attentively as it truly is. Having drawn up the left channel (nāḍī), one should slightly contract the anus; one should exhale through the central path and cause the tongue to reach the palate.
Having joined the *śakti* with the supreme *Śiva*, one should slightly contract [the breath] downwards.
Having done this, the knower of mantras should worship on the pedestal (*pīṭha*) according to the path of ritual placement (*nyāsa*). (453)

Having meditated upon one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) seated upon that pedestal in embodied form, one should worship her with sandalwood paste and other offerings, mentally, ending with the offering of food. || 454 ||
At the time of eating, however, one should perform the internal Vaiśvadeva rite; one should remember the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) at the Mūlādhāra, blazing with the fire of Kuṇḍalinī. || 455 ||

In the fourfold [mandala] consisting of the Self, the Inner Self, the Supreme Self, and the Knowledge-Self, one should place the root mantra at the forefront within the triangle endowed with dharma and adharma. || 456 ||
Then, one should offer oblations individually, saying "I sacrifice, svāhā! for each.
The oblation consists of egoism, untruth, backbiting, lust, anger, and so forth. || 457 ||

The mind alone is declared to be the sacrificial ladle (sruva), and Suṣumṇā and the others are said to be the channels (gudī). Having become absorbed in that at its end, one should mutter [the mantra] one hundred and eight times. || 458 ||
One should offer that root to the deity for the sake of all prosperity; then, having prostrated before the Guru, one should withdraw the circle of worship.
Kings become submissive when [the deity is placed] on a seat fashioned of gold; a machine adorned with silver is considered to bestow all forms of sovereignty. || 460 ||
The crystal yantra, being transparent, bestows whatever is desired by the mind.
And this [liṅga], fashioned from rubies, bestows sovereignty as well as worldly enjoyment and liberation. (461)
A yantra fashioned from emeralds brings about the destruction of all enemies; a yantra produced from the three metals is considered to bestow all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis). || 462 ||
Śrīkhaṇḍa (sandalwood) should be known as bestowing power, while red sandalwood is nourishing.
The Śrīparṇī pedestal is prescribed for the purpose of worship; it bestows wealth and sovereignty. (463)
Four-footed animals are [indicated] by an abundance of *bailvaka* wood and birch bark.
On the stones originating from the Gaṇḍakī, enjoyment and liberation are not far off. || 464 ||
A yantra fashioned from lead or bell-metal, even if drawn on the ground with vermilion powder as a granter of all desires, will instead destroy one's wealth and progeny. || 465 ||
One should never place [the image] upon a wooden plank or on another friend; if, out of delusion, it is so placed, it will destroy that person's entire lineage. || 466 ||
The beautiful pedestal for the image should be made with a width of two *aratni* fingers from east to west and from south to north, and it should measure one *pala* in weight. || 467 ||
One should make the eastern half high and square on all sides; upon that pedestal, one should cause the construction of the worship-circle (pūjācakra) to be made. || 468 ||
On pedestals made of rubies and other gems, a smaller measurement does not constitute a fault.
If there is an excess of śrīparṇī, sandalwood, and so forth, it does not cause any fault.

When the hosts of auspicious planets are in the ascendant and possess favorable qualities, one should have a new image fashioned, provided that the lunar day and other astrological factors are observed to be favorable. || 470 ||
Having first consecrated [the image] with honey, clarified butter, and milk, and then with coconut water, one should subsequently bathe it with water boiled with excellent medicinal herbs. (471)
Having invoked and worshipped [the deity], one should establish it upon that [auspicious] moment (lagna) in the wheel and perform worship.
With perfumes, flowers, fresh incense, lamps, and offerings of food, as well as a mirror; || 472 ||
O Goddess, one should worship for three nights at the three junctions of the day, and then at night; those who practice the worship of Vāminī should do so while joined with the five "M" syllables.
And on the second day, the Kaulika should perform the worship of Śakti at night; having performed this for three days, he should thereafter follow the daily ritual sequence.
Thus, in the consecration of a goddess, this is the sequence that brings about her presence.
This is the rule for women, Śūdras, Vāmins, and Kaulikas. || 475 ||

They do not commit great sins, following the path of the Vedas like cattle. Regarding the term *ākhyānada* (givers of names): since it is through the commission of sins that birth occurs, and since living beings receive their names by virtue of that birth, they are therefore called *ākhyānadas*.
[This is] a qualification of evil: [by the Raghus, whose sins were destroyed by the performance of the twilight devotions. 476.
They are not defiled by mortal sins; therefore, they are remembered as being beyond the state of ordinary animals.
The yantra worshipped by Vāminī came within the range of their vision.
Causing agitation to that deity, the practitioner becomes distracted.
The yantra worshipped with sacrificial fees possesses a splendor equal to that of the sun and fire.
Sinners do not see it at all, just as owls do not see the darkness; just as the rising of the sun is desired here by all men. (479)
The machine established by Dakṣa is likewise approved by those of meritorious soul.
For all living beings alike, both suffering and happiness are equal.
The left and right paths are likewise the paths of the celestial dwellers; however, the preeminence belongs to the women on the left side and the men on the right side. (481)

In the same way, the path for men is also divided according to what should and should not be done. Furthermore, *kuṇḍas* are so called because they lead living beings from one world to another; thus, they possess the quality of *raghu* (swift-moving). [A *kuṇḍa* is one born of adultery while the husband is alive; a *golaka* is one born of adultery after the husband has died. *Golakas*.
Those who have fallen away from their caste, such as the twice-born and others. || 482 ||
And those Brahmins who are unrefined (asaṃskṛta) are proclaimed to be vrātyas.

Because they have lost their Brahminhood, those base and fallen individuals engage in the left-hand path (*vāmamārga*). Even though they consume liquor, meat, and the like, by performing the worship of the deities, recitation of mantras (*japa*), and so forth, after experiencing the fruits of their own karma over many days, they are eventually liberated.
Because they lack the qualification for the Vedas, they are swiftly liberated from saṃsāra by way of the southern path. [482] Alcohol, meat,
and sexual intercourse— [483]

Those who are not Brahmins have entered upon the left-hand path (vāmamārga), and by them it has been practiced; whether through the Kaula or the Vāma [path], one certainly attains perfection—of this there is no doubt. (484)
Success arises for others [only] through this; otherwise, it leads solely to hell.
First, the Brahmin should perform the rite of fire-ascension (*agnyuttāraṇa*) with mantras proclaimed in the Vedas. || 485 ||

p. 96) Agni [Now the Agnisūkta]. Agni bestows a swift steed; Agni bestows a hero renowned for his deeds and steadfast in action. Agni moves between the two worlds, uniting them; Agni [bestows] a woman who is a mother of heroes and a mistress of the household. 1. O Agni...
The auspicious Agni has entered the two great worlds, heaven and earth, as he sits among the people like a bee.
Agni alone impels [the warrior] in battles; Agni shatters many Vṛtras. 2.
Agni drove away the slayer from Karṇa; Agni burned Jarūtha out from the waters.
May Agni protect Atri within the law; may Agni endow Nṛmedha with progeny.
Agni, through his wondrous power, bestows wealth; Agni is the seer who wins thousands.
Agni has extended the oblation to heaven; Agni’s many stations are maintained throughout the worlds.
The seers honor Agni with hymns; men, free from distress, urge Agni forward on his course.
Agni flies through the mid-air as the best of the host; Agni goes around thousands of cattle.
Human clans worship Agni, those many men born of various lineages who serve him.
Agni, the Gāndharvī, the path of the nectar of immortality; Agni’s movement and impulse are in the clarified butter; he is seated in Agni.
For Agni, the Ṛbhus fashioned a prayer; we have proclaimed a great hymn for you, O Agni.
O Agni, most powerful one, further the singer; O Agni, win for us great wealth through sacrifice. || 7 ||
One should place the palm of the left hand upon the back of the right hand and move both thumbs properly; this mudrā is called Matsyarūpiṇī. One should then form a square with the fingers.
The hymn beginning with "saptiṃ vājam" is said to consist of seven verses (ṛcas). The sage is [Garga], and Triṣṭubh is the meter (chandas).
It has been said that the deity is proclaimed to be the fire. || 486 ||
One should recite this hymn, together with the word "Agni," one hundred times.
Then one should consecrate [the image] with fragrant waters accompanied by the complete Sūktas.
One should perform the consecration one hundred times; this is known as the "Fire-Crossing" (agnyuttāraṇa).
One should always wash a machine made of metal with earth and water.
Just as wood and gems are polished by means of flour-paste and water respectively, so too should the cleansed yantra be adorned with sandalwood paste and other such substances. (489)
One should place [the image] on the pedestal in front and then offer a handful of flowers.
Then, by means of the root mantra, one should proceed toward those deities as one's own.
The triangle should be properly encircled with a border and smeared with sandalwood water.
And outside of that, one should fashion a square using the fish-seal gesture (matsyamudrā). || 491 ||

Having worshipped with perfumes using the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to the maṇḍala of the gods and others," the limbs [of the deity] were established in the four corners starting from the southeast and in front. || 492 ||
While reciting the mantra, having sprinkled [the vessel] with water, one should place the support for the conch;
then, having uttered the mantra for the conch and the support, one should establish them within the maṇḍala.
Having said "Maṃ Raṃ Dharmaprada," one should utter that which consists of ten kalās ending in the dative case (Ṅe), as well as the mandala of fire and the name of the deity. (494)
Then, [one should worship] the conch with its own mantra, saying: "Obeisance to the support of the arghya vessel."
Having washed the arghya vessel for such-and-such deity, I now establish it. || 495 ||

Having spoken thus, and having established it there upon that support, one should pronounce "Aṃ" for the solar orb and the name of the deity ending in "Ṅe", and worship the vessel of *arghya* with this mantra: "Obeisance to the *arghya* vessel. (496)
One should likewise visualize that vessel as the circle of the earth; there, one should worship the six limbs as before. (497)

The twelve digits (kalās) of the Sun are said to be there; one should circumambulate them. Then, with waters consisting of nectar, one should recite the Mātṛkā at the end of the root mantra. || 498 ||
The worshipper should fill that [vessel] in reverse order with this mantra: "Oṃ, to the lunar maṇḍala, to the sixteenfold self of the kalās. (499)
Obeisance to Amukārghyāmṛtāya for the filling of the conch.
Fragrant substances, flowers, unbroken rice grains, barley, tips of kuśa grass, sesame seeds, and mustard seeds.
O gods, the eight substances for the arghya vessel are said to be dūrvā grass and the rest.
Then, having honored it with water, incense, flowers, and so forth, one should worship it thoroughly. || 501 ||
And thereafter, the sixteen digits of the moon are present within all the digits.
Then, at the conclusion of the worship, the practitioner should perform the rite of vitalization (prāṇapratiṣṭhā). || 502 ||
Having invoked the sacred site (tīrtha) as before, one should unite it there with the root mantra;
then, having placed a flower with the root mantra, one should apply it with the arrow-mantra (śarāṇu).
Having displayed the Gālinī mudrā, [he should seal it] with the mudrā known as Dhenusañjñā.
Having consecrated [the offering] with the seed-syllable *svadhā* according to the prescribed rule, the practitioner [should offer it]. || 504 ||

Having meditated upon one's chosen deity there, one should perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa; and by means of the assignment of limbs (aṅganyāsa) and the weapon-mantra (astra), one should demarcate the ten directions.
There, having gazed with the mantra and with the mudrā known as the conch;
Then, having firmly grasped [it], one should blaze with the mudrā in the form of the womb.
There, one should worship the chosen deity with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings; having fully worshipped the six limbs, one should recite [the mantra] with the root mantra. || 507 ||
Then, one should cause the arghya offering to be presented eight times with the matsya-mudrā.
One should pour a little of that water from the conch into the water in the pitcher. || 508 ||
Having placed the water for the feet (pādya) and the water for sipping (ācamanīya), as well as the honey-mixture (madhuparka), in the northern part of the arghya vessel,
one should arrange them in the three corners in due order.
One should consecrate each individual vessel eight times with the root mantra. As for the *madhuparka*, it consists of honey and curd;
however, curd is not available there. (510)
Curd, milk, molasses, honey, and ghee—there is no substitute for these; that supreme state, O Goddess, which is called "Madhu," is indeed such. (511)

That rite which is for the purpose of nourishment is called the *madhuparka*. For Śiva, it is an excellent conch-shell made of either bell-metal or silver; for Hari, it is likewise [an excellent conch]. (512)
The great conch shell is on the left path, and the crystal is for the leader of the planets;
having placed the *prokṣaṇī* vessel on the right, one should fill it with water.
Having taken a little water for the arghya offering, one should add it to the water in the sprinkling vessel.
Then, one should place a vessel for the purpose of water for sipping (ācamana).
The water for washing the feet (pādya) is said to consist of śyāmāka grain, dūrvā grass, lotus, and viṣṇukrāntā.
The water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) is considered to consist of nutmeg, cloves, and kaṅkola.
One should drop kuśa grass, flowers, barley, rice, bahumūla, tamālaka, uśīra, and sandalwood into the prokṣaṇī vessel in a graceful manner, accompanied by the syllable Om. || 516 ||
The water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) should be prepared with pure water; in the absence of such materials, auspicious washed rice grains should be offered. || 517 ||
(p. 98) Now, I shall describe the auspicious and inauspicious results of the vessels for the *arghya* and other offerings.
A golden one grants all desires; a silver one bestows long life and sons.
Good fortune is attained through a copper vessel, while the increase of dharma occurs with an earthen one;
likewise, satisfaction of the gods arises from a coconut vessel.

The attainment of fortune comes from a vessel made of bilva wood; Brahminhood is attained from one born of the Brahma-tree (palāśa). For killing and driving away, an iron vessel should be used; for paralyzing, it should be made of stone. || 520 ||
For the propitiation of the mantra, the wood is that of the *taumbika* tree on the left-hand path.
Furthermore, vessels made of precious gems and other materials should be marked with auspicious lines.

One should worship by offering water for the guest (arghya), food offerings (naivedya), and the gesture of joined palms (añjali); one must show reverence toward the vessels, for the vessels themselves are indeed supreme. || 522 ||
Furthermore, rites such as the bali offering and the homa will not succeed without a worthy recipient.
A bowl measuring thirty-six finger-breadths is proclaimed to be the best.
The middle [size] is that minus one-third, and the smallest is twelve finger-breadths.
One should never have a bowl made that is deficient by eight finger-breadths. (524)

One should imagine vessels shaped like the forms of the openings of the navel, having the appearance of white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*), and possessing the luster of conch shells and blue water-lilies (*nīlotpala*). 525.
White and other such colors are highly praised for the Brahmins and the other classes, respectively.
One should sprinkle [the area] with the water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel while reciting the root mantra.
One's own self, the sacrificial materials, the articles of worship, and so forth, as well as the maṇḍala.

One should display the *dhenumudrā*—[the little fingers and ring fingers joined facing each other, and likewise the index and middle fingers; this is proclaimed as the *dhenumudrā*]. And this is considered to be the purification of substances. 527.

One should worship the deities of the nyāsa on the yoga-pīṭha in their respective locations; thereafter, one's own deity is to be worshipped through meditative visualization upon the maṇi-pīṭha. || 528 ||
One should meditate on oneself as having the form of the deity five times with the root mantra.
Handfuls of flowers should be offered upon the head, the heart, and the anus.
One should worship the feet and all the limbs with sandalwood paste and other offerings.
And one should present the food offering with the four types of services.

One should complete the remainder according to the procedure taught by the Guru; with a concentrated mind, one should employ all of this using the water from the sprinkling-vessel (prokṣaṇī). || 531 ||

Thereafter, the offering of the *arghya* should be performed; now the ritual of sacrifice (*yajña*) is described. One should visualize a four-cornered fire-pit (*agni-kuṇḍa*) at the *mūlādhāra*. (532)
There, while reciting the root mantra, one should meditate upon the fire in the form of Kuṇḍalinī.
Indeed, with the mind, one should offer the oblation of dharma and adharma into the fire of the Self, which is kindled by them.
"By means of the path of the Suṣumṇā, I constantly offer these eight oblations. I offer merit; Svāhā!"—thus one should further utter at the end of each verse. (534)
Again the root, again the verse, and again I offer the evil; "what is to be done and what is not to be done"—this resolve, this conceptualization, and even this dharma. (534)
Having spoken [the previous mantras] individually, each ending with *svāhā*, one should again recite this verse:
And having grasped [the state] within the Unmanī [consciousness] with the hands of Light (prakāśa) and Reflection (amarśa).
I offer [this] into the fire filled with the oil of the particles of merit and demerit; having offered the oblation ending with "svāhā," [I do so] through the restraint of prāṇāyāma. || 537 ||
One should meditate upon the Self as consisting of pure consciousness, from which all adventitious limitations have been cast away.
Having performed three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seers and other elements.
Having fashioned the seat of worship, one should worship the deities of the seat.
The lineage of gurus is to be worshipped facing north, while Mahāgaṇapati is worshipped facing downward.
One should worship the seven [deities] beginning with Anala beneath the God; above him are Maṇḍūka, Rudra, and likewise Kālānala. (540)
One should again worship Mūlaprakṛti, Ādhāraśakti, Kūrma, and Antaka, and then the Earth upon the tip of the tusk of Varāha. || 541 ||
In that [ocean] is the ocean of nectar, and in it is the island of the nine jewels; in its center is the mountain of gold, and above that is the Nandana grove.
In the midst of that [he saw] wish-fulfilling trees, and in the midst of those, a ground of jewels.
At its edge is a golden wall, and in its center is a pavilion of jewels.

Within that, one should likewise visualize a golden altar and a jeweled lion-throne; situated in the middle of the altar, one should worship [the deity] with sandalwood paste and other offerings. || 544 ||

One should visualize the pedestal as the support for the wheel of worship and as a lion-throne; upon its legs, one should properly worship [the deities] starting from the southeast (āgneya) and ending with the northeast (śiva).
Dharma has the body of a bull, Jñāna is variegated, and Kṛṣṇa is like a lion.
Dispassion is like water that has been drunk; sovereignty is like a black snake held in the hand. || 456 ||

One should worship Adharma and the others, in their various colors, beneath the pedestal; and in the center of that, one should worship Māyā and Vidyā, as well as Ananta, who has the form of the Tattva.
Upon its summit, one should worship a lotus with eight petals representing the eight primordial natures (prakṛtis), having bliss as its bulbous root, consciousness as its stalk,
and the transformations (vikāras) as its filaments.
One should worship the eight supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇimā*, in sequence upon its petals, together with the *mātṛkā* in the pericarp;
I shall now state their names.
Aṇimā, mahimā, garimā, and likewise laghimā; prāpti, prākāmya, īśitva, and vaśitva—these are the eight siddhis. || 550 ||
Beneath the pericarp, however, are the Sun, the Moon, and likewise Fire.
In that same manner, one should likewise worship the three qualities, beginning with sattva, there at the front.
Then [he should place] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa in the cardinal directions and in the center; likewise, the principles (tattvas) beginning with Jñāna, Māyā, Kalā, Vidyā, and Parā. || 552 ||
Likewise, in the filaments and in the center, starting from the east and so forth, in due order.
One should worship the nine Śaktis of the Pīṭha mentioned in that respective Mātra. || 553 ||
One should worship the seat on all sides with perfumes and other offerings using the seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra).
With the fourth case-ending joined with the word "namaḥ" and the names of their respective deities. || 554 ||
In the center, the practitioner should offer a handful of flowers with the seat-mantra (pīṭhamaṃtra), having uttered the root-mantra followed by the name of the seat in the genitive case. (555)
Thinking, "I shall fashion the image," one should place it within the center of the mold; then, having again uttered the root mantra, followed by the name of the deity, [one should proceed]. (556)
Thinking, "I worship the form," one should honor it with a flower.
He who performs another worship on the same seat without [first completing] the yantra; || 557 ||
One incurs the curse of the deity and shall go to the Raurava hell;
if one worships the yantra according to the tantric method, one will incur the curse of the deity. || 558 ||
Having invoked one deity, one should worship another deity; or if one performs the worship of one deity with the yantra of another, that deity will bestow a curse. || 559 ||
If the worship of many forms should take place upon a single pedestal, [the following applies].
One should offer sandalwood, flowers, incense, lamps, and so forth separately, accompanied by mantras. || 560 ||
When it is broken, cracked, burnt, fallen, or devoid of the proper measurements.
When touched by a limb-deficient person, an Arhat, or an animal, or when fallen upon impure grounds; || 561 ||
Furthermore, in places where another mantra has been worshipped, or which have been defiled by the touch of a fallen person, the gods do not grant their presence in such locations. (262)
The worship of Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, Viṣṇu, Īśa, and Devī is performed in sequence.
And ten locations have been prescribed for the worship of the gods. || 563 ||
The presence of all the gods will necessarily arise through the mantra; for the mantra is said to be like the soul, while the image and so forth are like the body. (564)

Even when the collection of causal conditions is complete, there is indeed no fruit without the mantra. [This applies regardless of whether the object of worship is] a Śiva-liṅga, a gem, a yantra, a śālagrāma, a water-pot, or the sun. (565)

One should perform worship in these locations: on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), in the fire, on the head, and in the heart. Worship performed upon the bare ground destroys one's sons, longevity, and wealth. || 566 ||
Measuring ten fingers or again measured at fifteen fingers, this is the first image of Viṣṇu to be worshipped by householders in their homes. || 567 ||
One should worship the Śiva-liṅga endowed with the five threads; for householders, it bestows enjoyment, liberation, wealth, and health. || 568 ||
Then, the width and height of the top of the liṅga, as well as the liṅga-śālākī and the jalāhārī of the liṅga [should be measured]. || 569 ||
The equality of the five [aspects] of the Liṅga-pīṭha is the fivefold thread.
Listen to the most wonderful account of the origin of the Śālagrāma.
"O deities, let all of you become my sons so as to bestow happiness upon people; thus [I have performed] penance on the Gaṇḍakī in the past. Thus those gods [spoke]. || 571 ||
Delighted by her ascetic penance, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara prepared to grant her a boon;
she chose the status of being their son, but as they were unable to grant that boon, they were then cursed by her in anger. || 572 ||
"O gods, because you have repeatedly practiced deception against me, enter the wombs of insects! Thus they were cursed by her in her anger. (573)
"Since we have been cursed by you, who are arrogant because of your asceticism, without due deliberation, by the ripening of that karma,
you shall indeed become the river Kṛṣṇā."
Having heard this mutual curse, a great clamor arose.
Trembling, the gods went to Brahmā and informed him [of what had occurred].
"O Brahmā, save us from this great curse, for we have fallen upon one another out of wrath! Having heard these words of the gods, Brahmā spoke to Śaṅkara: || 576 ||
Śiva said to the Creator: "I am the agent of dissolution;
you are the creator of the universe, while Viṣṇu is the protector and the most highly intelligent. || 577 ||
"He should be questioned so that [the truth] may arise for both of us in due order.
Having heard those words of Maheśvara, Viṣṇu spoke: || 578 ||
Listen, O Brahmā; listen, O Mahādeva; listen, O goddess Gajānana! When my two attendants, the Brāhmaṇas Grāha and Mātaṅga, [fell] due to a curse... 579.
I shall bring about the liberation of those two when their bodies have become decayed;
then that which is produced from their fat and marrow [shall perish]. (580)
"Insects dwelling within stones shall become known as 'Vajras' (diamonds). This very day, the Gaṇḍakī, a great and meritorious river equal to the Gaṅgā, [shall flow]. || 581 ||
To the south of the king of mountains, extending ten yojanas along the Gaṇḍakī, is that Manu-kṣetra, a meritorious field upon the surface of the earth. || 582 ||
This Cakratīrtha is renowned and celebrated throughout the three worlds.
Wherever there is a Śālagrāma stone, there also is a stone from Dvāravatī.
Where there is a union of both, there is liberation; of this there is no doubt.
She who brings delight to all the gods and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 584 ||
O gods, those stones which were within that river—
"May all [others] become diamond-insects (vajrakīṭa), except for the portion belonging to the earthly king. || 585 ||
By this very [act], even you shall attain the status of sons to the Gaṇḍakī; the gods are pleased not merely by the worship of an image nor even of a tree. (586)
"Contentment arises for them just as it does from worshipping the stones of the Gaṇḍakī.
Having heard these words of Viṣṇu, Brahmā spoke these words. (587)
O Viṣṇu, what kind of stone is worthy of worship? To whom is it dear? What is its fruit, who is its officiant, and by what path is it attained? Please tell me that. (588)
Having heard these words of Brahmā, Viṣṇu spoke these words: "The stone of one's own caste is to be worshipped by Brāhmaṇas and the others for the attainment of happiness. (589)
A smooth stone brings about the perfection of mantras, while a rough one does not; a pale stone pacifies sins, whereas a dark one produces sinful thoughts.
Yellow [smoke] bestows the fruit of sons; the color of a mango tree brings forth daughters; blue indicates prosperity;
and smoke-colored [smoke] destroys the intellect.
Bestowing disease, red in color, with the luster of vermilion, she brings about great strife.
Crooked, she causes poverty; straight, she accomplishes all goals. || 592 ||
A [line] that is too thick destroys longevity; one that is too thin takes away intelligence. (p.
102) The fruit of worship is obtained through a marked [line]; without the mark, it is fruitless. 593.

A tawny cow causes mental derangement, and a brindled one causes eye disease; one that is stuck [in the mud] brings about ruin and strife, while one with many circles on her body bestows preeminence. (594)
If it lacks other characteristics, such as the absence of wheels, it leads to various calamities.
And with a navel that has deformed whorls, one acquires abundant wealth and food. || 595 ||
The extinction of the lineage of householders occurs through Nārasiṃhī; Rekhāvartā bestows suffering, while Amṛtā is as [beneficial] as nectar. || 596 ||
As is her affection, so is her fortune; hear now of its various distinctions.
He is to be known as Lakṣmī-Hari where there is a lotus together with a discus. || 597 ||
Or, a mere garland of forest flowers that grants the desires of householders—He should be known as Vāsudeva at whose gate there is a pair of discs. (598)
That white [linga], which is continuous and even, is the destroyer of sins; it is to be known as Saṃkarṣaṇa, with a pair of discs before and behind. || 599 ||
One should contemplate a large, beautifully adorned gem situated on the front part; in Pradyumna, there should be a subtle wheel, and one should visualize a long cavity.
One that is hollow within with many holes and yellow in color bestows desired objects. Aniruddha, however, is blue-hued, circular, and exceedingly beautiful. || 601 ||
At its entrance, there are two lines, and the back is marked with a lotus; that should be known as Keśava, whether it has one or two [lines]. || 602 ||
If the cakra is situated both before and after [the house], it is quadrangular and brings good fortune.
Nārāyaṇa is dark-complexioned, and likewise, he has a prominent wheel on his navel.
That stone which is joined with long lines, broad on the right side, and has its face turned upwards, is of the form of Hari. || 604 ||
The door is seen as Hari; it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. He who is endowed with the lotus and the discus is to be known as Parameṣṭhin. (605)
One shaped like a bilva fruit and white in luster, with a large cavity on its back, is Viṣṇu;
O fair-faced one, it should have thick wheels and be black in color.
Likewise, a line is seen above the door in the middle; Narasiṃha is tawny, with separate faces and a large mouth. || 607 ||
For householders, three or five drops there are not sufficient;
however, the *kapila* (tawny) Narasiṃha should be like molasses or lac. || 608 ||
With two thick wheels in the center and a very beautiful line at the gate, it should be known as Mahānṛsiṃha, endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics. || 609 ||
The lines are shaped like filaments, and the face is long and terrifying.
Lakṣmīnṛsiṃha is to be known as having four wheels and the bindu. || 610 ||
Endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics and adorned with a forest garland (vanamālā), this Varāha likewise resides in the Śakti-liṅga and the Viṣama-cakra.
It should be thick, resembling a sapphire, and marked with three lines;
that stone which has the form of a boar is known by the name Varāha-pṛthvī. || 612 ||
A single straight line that does not bend at all bestows a kingdom; that stone is to be known as the "Matsya" (fish), adorned with three dots. || 613 ||
That which originates from bell-metal, resembles gold in color, and is long, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The stone known as Kūrma, however, should be circular and elevated on its back. || 614 ||
A stone that is green in color, marked with the Kaustubha gem, and shaped like a tortoise should be known as a Kūrma stone. || 615 ||
Likewise, marked with wheels and circular in shape, she is worshipped as the bestower of stations.
The Hayagrīva [line] is in the shape of a goad, situated near the wheel.
The back, marked with many spots and as dark blue as a rain-cloud, is to be known as the gentle Hayagrīva;
the stone resembling Hayagrīva is likewise [to be known]. || 617 ||
It should be joined with a long line, or it should be a line of that same kind. || 618 ||
He whose face has the form of a horse is to be known as Hayaśīrṣa; or his head may likewise be lotus-shaped, accompanied by a rosary. || 619 ||
Vaikuṇṭha has the luster of sesame seeds, and likewise possesses a single discus and a banner;
a line above the doorway is likewise highly auspicious for the worshipper.
Śrīdhara, however, O Lord, is likewise marked by a forest garland; he has the appearance of a Kadamba flower and is adorned with five lines. || 621 ||
He should be known as Vāmana, who is very short and round; he resembles the flower of the linseed plant (atasī) and is adorned with a dot (bindu) above.
And the one named Dadhivāmana is endowed with wheels above and below; he is of great splendor, short in stature, and the bestower of abundance and security. || 623 ||
Likewise, the god Sudarśana is dark-complexioned and possesses great luster; he has a single disc on his left side and only a single line on his right.
This one named Sahasrārjuna consists of various lines; where there is a row in the shape of a crane, it bestows lost wealth. || 625 ||

One who is stout, whose belly is large, and upon whose center a discus is established; one who resembles the color of dūrvā grass and has a yellow line crowded at the entrance—such a person bestows wealth. || 626 ||
Rādhādāmodara is to be known as that which is joined with the upper and lower wheels.
One whose face is not too long and who has a vertical line in the middle bestows enjoyment. || 627 ||
He who is marked with two discs is to be known as Dāmodara; when worshipped, he is subtle, possesses apertures, and is always the bestower of happiness. || 628 ||
It should be infinite and multicolored, marked by the coils of a serpent; intersected by many wheels, it bestows the fruits of all desires. || 629 ||
He whose names are "Puruṣottama" and who bestows the fruits of the goals of human existence is seen with faces directed toward the cardinal points, the intermediate directions, and upward. (630)
He whose linga is situated upon his head should be known as a master of yoga (yogeśvara).
It is the destroyer of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and the bestower of the perfections of yoga. || 631 ||
Likewise, Padmanābha is red and is joined with a lotus-umbrella;
by worshipping him at Talasī, even a poor person shall become a lord. || 632 ||
Raśmijvāla, Hiraṇyākṣa, Candrābha, and Sphaṭikopama.
Or else, he is born endowed with various lines of gold.
That pervasive Lord Garuḍa is to be known as being in the center of the two wings;
a very long line is seen there, which destroys the poison of serpents. || 634 ||
He whose belly bears four distinct and clearly visible discs (cakras) is to be known as Janārdana; he brings satisfaction to the ancestors. || 635 ||
Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa is to be known as having his chest marked with a forest garland.
The subtle gateway consists of four wheels and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
He who has the form of a half-moon should be known as Hṛṣīkeśa.
Having worshipped him, one shall attain heaven and all desired objects. || 637 ||
Lakṣmīnarahari is to be known as being dark-complexioned with a bindu; on his left side are two symmetrical wheels, and he is the bestower of desired objects upon householders. || 638 ||
He should be known as Trivikrama, dark-complexioned and of great splendor; there are two discs on his left side, while there is a single line on the right.
The black stone, whether with a wheel or without a wheel, should be known as Kṛṣṇa.
He is formed with a clockwise whorl and adorned with a forest garland.
He should be known as four-faced; two wheels are in the middle region, and there are four lines extending to the sides, bestowing the Vedas, Śāstras, and Āgamas. || 641 ||

These are declared to be the manifestations (bhedas) of Viṣṇu; one should invoke Hari right here at this very spot. At the conclusion of the worship, one should perform the dismissal (visarjana), but one should not perform the ritual installation (pratiṣṭhā) here. || 642 ||
Śālagrāmas that are equal in size are to be worshipped; among equals, there should not be two.
Those that are unequal are never to be worshipped by those who desire the fruits of all their wishes.
The man who daily worships the twelve Śilās with devotion shall experience an increase in righteousness and the destruction of sin here in this world. || 644 ||
He who has assumed the form of the *liṅga* should be known by the name Śiva.
He himself possesses the form of the liṅga and is the one who effects the accomplishment of mantras.
He who is adorned with three dots (bindus) is to be known as Tryambaka; likewise, a line in the shape of a trident is a giver of a limited lifespan. || 646 ||

But that on which there are three lines resembling matted locks should be known as belonging to Dhūrjaṭi; where these three are clearly visible, it is the giver of knowledge, accompanied by grace. || 647 ||
Śambhu, however, should be known as pale white, while the bindu at the top of the head is black.
The size of a bilva fruit, radiant, and worshipped, it brings women under one's control. || 648 ||
That Lord is to be known as red, with a drop (bindu) upon his head; he has one wheel or two wheels, and there is a cow’s footprint within and below.
This should be known as the Mṛtyuñjaya [mantra], which indeed destroys untimely death. Below is the discus, and above that is a white line bearing the trident.
This [deity] named Candraśekhara has a crescent moon upon his head; in its center are two wheels, through the service of which diseases are destroyed.
That very moon is to be known as Kapila, moistened at the crown of the head.
A line within the center of the wheel shall destroy the lineage of one's enemies. || 652 ||
Now I shall describe the Śālagrāmas, which are born from insects and belong to the Śakti;
by worshipping them, the goddess Bhavānī becomes well-pleased. (653)
On its base is the Śrīvidyā, and above it the wheel is seen like a parasol;
its head is marked with a bell on the outside, and it is smooth and to be served by all at that time. || 654 ||
She should be known as Mahākālī, endowed with the symbol of the yoke.
All stones that have two holes and so forth, as well as those marked with a triangle, [should be used]. || 655 ||

When the form of a weapon appears within, one should designate that as the Goddess; one should worship that stone of the Goddess, which bears a discus, by means of the right-hand path (dakṣamārga). || 656 ||
Worshipped by way of the left path, she brings happiness to both worlds; one should worship that goddess as a stone who is devoid of a discus. || 657 ||
O Brahmins, one should not touch that stone which causes agitation;
O gods, a solar stone (saurī śilā) is generally difficult to find in the Kali age.
She becomes like crystal; when liberated from phenomena, she is released.
The consecrated woman [beholds] the fire situated above the sun, raining down.
If a false oath is made, she causes leprosy.
A stone endowed with such characteristics as these is considered suitable for the Sun.
He who is marked by a trunk should be known as Gaṇeśa.
Or it may be shaped like a trunk, or even resembling the face of an elephant. || 661 ||

That stone upon which there is a great wheel in its center and a subtle wheel in a particular direction should be worshipped by the ruler of that direction; it bestows sovereignty in that very direction.
Where two fragments are seen in the shape of a half-moon, that is indeed a moonstone (candraśilā);
one joined with three triangles is considered an earthstone (bhaumaśilā).
O gods, the stone of Mercury is to be known by a mark in the shape of an arrow; the stone of Jupiter is considered to be long and quadrangular. (664)
The [orb] of Venus is five-cornered, while that of Saturn is considered to be bow-shaped;
that of Rāhu is winnow-basket shaped, and that of Ketu has the form of a banner.
When the terrible Kali age has arrived, which is intermingled with left-handed practices.
In a place crowded with barbarians, devoid of consideration regarding what is fit or unfit to be eaten, and so forth.

When people are pervaded by lust, anger, and the like, and utterly conquered by women, where is the disciple, where is the teacher, where is the mantra, where is the recitation, and where are the spiritual accomplishments?
When ten thousand years of the Kali age have passed, the Viṣṇuśilā shall leave the earth.
Half of that is the water of the Ganges, and half of that is the stone of the deity.
In the Kali age, the recitation of mantras (japa) is indeed the best means to spiritual welfare, as is the worship of the Śālagrāma stone.
At the time of offering the arghya water to the Sun, one should give gifts to the best of one's means.
The rites beginning with invocation (āvāhana) should be performed; that [rite] is threefold, pertaining to the image (mūrti) and so forth.
First, the invocation should be performed; one should recite the root mantra three times.
Having meditated thus—that the Lord has come from his own world in a subtle form and remains present within the images—the wise practitioner [should do so] by way of the *suṣumṇā* path. (671)

Having brought the splendor from its own place and caused it to emerge through the nostrils, one should place it within the hollowed palms joined like a flower-offering and present it upon the head of the deity.

The splendor of the deity is invoked into that image; with hands joined in *añjali* and well-filled with flowers, this is declared by the best of teachers to be the *āvāhanī* mudrā. One should establish [the deity] while reciting the root mantra; this is the invocation (*āvāhana*).
This is the opinion. || 673 ||
The wise have declared that the installation of the pervasive deity involves a mechanical device (yantra).
Thereafter, one should perform the formal consecration (saṃsthāpana), saying: "Stay here, stay! || 674 ||
At the end of the root mantra, one should recite the name of the deity, and at the end of that, one should display the *āsthāpanīya-mudrā* (the mudrā for stabilization) and meditate upon it. (Note:
That same mudrā, when turned face-downward, is said to be used for the rite of stabilization. 675.
But one should subsequently offer this prayer: "O Lord of Gods, easily accessible through devotion, accompanied by all your retinues... (676)
"Remain well-established for as long as I shall worship you. Having thus prayed to the Lord of Gods, one should perform the ritual of invocation (sannidhāpana). || 677 ||
Having recited the root mantra, one should awaken that deity,
saying twice, "Be present here," so as to bring it into one's own presence.

One should satisfy the deity who is present by means of the *sannidhāpana-mudrā*—[the two fists joined together with the pair of thumbs raised; this mudrā is designated as that for the invocation of presence by those who know the Tantras]. Then, of the deity...
Having uttered the root mantra, one should perform the rite of making it present. || 679 ||
Having fully realized that, one should subsequently utter it while remaining in complete restraint; she herself is proclaimed as being within the thumb during that restraint.
The placement of the six limbs upon the body of the deity constitutes the rite of *sakalīkṛta*. And one should utter twice the word "bhava" (be), filled with compassion.
The state of being obstructed by the sentiment of devotion.
One should contemplate the deity as having become firmly established within the image;
the preceptor, having uttered the root mantra, should cause the deity to face him.
Having fully understood that, he should afterwards say, "Be present before me."
One should meditate upon the God facing oneself, with a most gracious lotus-like face.
"One should display the mudrā that brings [the deity] face-to-face"—thus it is remembered.
The knower of mantras, having recited the root mantra, should perform the veiling of the deity.
It should be shown that, having fully awakened to that [reality], one remains veiled by it.

And the *avaguṇṭhana* mudrā: a fist formed with the right hand, with the index finger extended and pointing downward; this is considered the *avaguṇṭhana* mudrā when it is rotated around. Furthermore, the little fingers and ring fingers are joined and facing one another.
And likewise, the dhenumudrā is proclaimed to be formed with the index and middle fingers.
The best of teachers should perform the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa) with that [substance].

With the thumbs interlaced and the fingers of the hands extended, this is declared by the wise to be the Mahāmudrā for the purpose of supreme transformation (*paramīkaraṇa*). The *Sammukhīkaraṇī-mudrā* is to be known as the pair of fists, in which the two thumbs are released and the deity is established.
"One should show and one should contemplate. || 684 ||

With devotion, [one should worship] the God whose eyes are wide open with wonder; and likewise, one should perform the sakalīkaraṇa (the rite of making the deity complete) within the heart and other parts of the God. (p. 107) 685.

Having performed the placement of the six-limbed mantra (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) and having recited the root mantra, one should awaken the deity; then, having become "entirely formed" (sakalīkṛta), one should speak as follows.
One should meditate upon the limbs [of the deity], and having established the deities of the limbs within the god, one should meditate upon them.
Because there is a single, non-different purpose for those things that possess different intrinsic natures. (687)

Through the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, the limbs [of the deity] become one with the possessor of the limbs. I shall now describe the rite of amṛtīkaraṇa: having established the deity upon the seat (pīṭha), [one should proceed]. (688)
Having properly formed the *dhenumudrā* over the head of the deity, there occurs a showering [of nectar];
and by meditating thus with the water of the *arghya* offering, it becomes nectar. (689)
One should sprinkle it three times with the root mantra, consecrated by the Dīpinī mantra.
Furthermore, it is divided threefold by means of the *mātṛkās* beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with the letter 'kṣa'.
The Vāgbhava [syllable], the pair of words, Vāgvādinī, and the Vāgbhava again; "Klīṃ, O moist one, O wetting one, moisten, O Great Agitation," and so forth. || 691 ||

Perform the pair [of syllables] *kāmabīja* (the seed-syllable of desire), then perform the pair *mokṣa* (liberation). Then *prāsāda* and again *prāsāda*; this consists of thirty-seven syllables. || 692 ||

The mantra called *dīpinī* indeed brings about the increase of the deity. The root [consists of the name of the deity preceded by the root-mantra and ending in the vocative case—meaning "O, such-and-such deity! become nectarized"—in this manner, the process of *paramīkaraṇa* (transformation into the supreme) is performed]. And it ends with the vocative.
"O Gods, you have been made immortal. One should speak thus; this indeed is the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa).

I shall explain the process of perfection (*paramīkaraṇa*) and the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*). One should also bind [the seal] with the following mantra: *Aiṃ vada vada vāgvādini aiṃ klīṃ klinne kledini kledaya mahākṣobhaṃ kuru kuru klīṃ oṃ mokṣaṃ kuru kuru hauṃ hauṃ*. This is the *dīpinī* mantra.

Having recited the root mantra and the deity as before, one performs the supreme unification (*paramīkṛti*). Having said, "May [the deity] become made," one should meditate upon the increase of supreme nectar at the head of the deity while touching the heart of the deity. || 694 ||

One should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (the rite of infusing life-force) using the previously mentioned *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra; however, one should speak thus, substituting the word "mine" (*mama*) with the name of the specific deity (*amukadevasya*). One should likewise utter the name of the deity in its entirety.
And all of that is exactly as before. || 695 ||
Then one should display the mudrās prescribed in the ritual manuals (kalpas) for each respective deity; these truly fulfill one's own joy through the gateway of the body of the Self. (696)

Those mudrās which, by means of effortless application, are considered to be powers (śaktis), they cause delight [to the deities] and dissolve the flood of sins arising from planetary influences and other such sources. || 697 ||

Because they cause delight (*modana*) and melting (*drāvaṇa*), they are therefore proclaimed as *mudga* beans; thereafter, one should worship the God with whatever offerings can be obtained according to one's capacity. || 698 ||
Therein, first of all, worship should be performed with the sixteen types of offerings:
the seat, welcome, water for the guest-offering (arghya), water for washing the feet (pādya), and water for sipping (ācamanīya). || 699 ||
The honey-mixture, water for sipping, bathing, clothing, and ornaments; sandalwood paste, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and prostration—(700).
One should indeed employ sixteen modes of service (upacāra) in worship; the worship with ten modes of service is considered middling, and it is prescribed for householders.
The guest-offering (arghya), the foot-water (pādya), as well as the water for sipping (ācamana), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and again the water for sipping (ācamana).
The ten services (upacāra), beginning with fragrance (gandha) and ending with the offering (nivedya), are traditionally taught.
The fivefold service consists of offerings beginning with fragrance and ending with the food offering.
It should be performed by those intent on their duty, whether they are householders or non-householders. || 703 ||
First, the preceptor should perform the worship with Vedic mantras;
thereafter, a woman or a Śūdra should do so according to the Tantra with Tantric mantras.
Oṃ [Oṃ aṃ haṃ haṃ, take this, this, this, svāhā]. Aṃ haṃ ha, take this, this; [followed by] the two ṭha syllables. This fifteen-syllable mantra is to be employed in all ritual offerings. (705)

Or one may recite it at the end of a Vedic rite; however, in that case, the Vedic practitioner should recite the Tantra-mantra. In all instances, in place of the word "svāhā" (the wife of fire), a Śūdra should recite "namaḥ."
On the left side of the deity, one should offer a seat with the root mantra; it may be made of flowers, wood, cloth, leather, silk, or metal.
The *pauṣpa* [seat] is one fashioned from flowers and the like, combined with *kuśa* grass, *dūrvā* grass, and so forth.
It was of various colors, fragrant, soft, and the granter of all desires. || 708 ||
Whatever [offering] has been made with those flowers which have been declared forbidden for a particular person—
Using only these [faulty seats] destroys the practitioner's aspirations. || 709 ||
One made from sacrificial wood, or from the Bilva tree, or produced from sandalwood, or said to be from Gambhārī or Śrīparṇa, bestows all that is desired. || 710 ||

One should avoid the *tāla* and *śāla* trees when they possess thorns or produce milky sap; likewise, one should avoid the *bibhītaka* tree that grows near a shrine (*caitya*) or in a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*). || 711 ||
Cloth made from wool, from bark, from silk, and from cotton—
these four types of garments are declared to be excellent, each preceding one being superior to the next.
Of lions, tigers, and hyenas; of goats and buffaloes;
and of elephants, horses, and the black antelope skin. || 713 ||
An excellent seat has been prepared; the seats made of reeds and dog-skins are forbidden.
Of the jackal, the wolf, the cow, the hare, and likewise the monkey. || 714 ||

Kuśa, kāśa, śara, granthi, yava, dūrvā, balvaja, vīraṇa, naḍa, and gundra—each subsequent one is recommended in the absence of the preceding. An āsana made from these is considered equal to a yoga-pīṭha; among them, each preceding one is most excellent.
Kauśa is said to be of ten kinds. || 715 ||

Among gold, silver, and copper, [silver is the lowest]; among all base metals, tin is well known [as the lowest]. Furthermore, iron, bronze, lead, and brass are each inferior to the preceding one and are prohibited. (716)
"O God, I have come for the purpose of worshipping you, together with your limbs and your retinue. Having meditated thus, at the end of the root mantra, one should proclaim a welcome. (717)
Then one should offer the *arghya* upon his head; for him, time is considered to be of three kinds: when he has arrived, during the worship, and while seated for the purpose of bathing. (718)
At the conclusion of the worship, one should cause the arghya offering to be presented to the deity who desires to depart.
Reciting the ritual formula (upacāra-mantra) with waters mixed with the materials for the arghya offering, [he should perform the rite].
At the time of arrival, at the time of bathing, and also at the commencement of the food offering—these are the three occasions for the *pādya*; *pādya* is the washing of the feet. || 720 ||

The ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with pure water is proclaimed to be of six kinds: during the offering of water for the feet (pādya), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), bathing, the [offering of] garments and the sacred thread (upavīta), and while eating. || 721 ||
Having prepared honey in a bronze vessel, one should offer it into the lotus-like mouth of the Deity on the day [of the ritual],
while reciting the offering mantra accompanied by curd.
Combined with the powder of nutmeg, cloves, cardamom, camphor, and kaṅkola, one should again offer water for rinsing the mouth into the mouth of the deity. (723) [This refers to camphor.]
Having anointed him with fragrant oils and performed an ablution with fragrant *āmalaka* and other substances,
one should then bathe him with warm water.
And one should perform the consecration with scented water and the root mantra according to one's ability.
[One should offer] milk, curd, clarified butter, honey,
and sugar individually; likewise with coconut water, as well as with the juice of the palmyra fruit, with many fragrant substances, and with scented water.
Even with sugarcane water [i.e., sugarcane juice] scented with camphor and other fragrances.
And one should perform the consecration with pure water and the root-mantra according to one's ability. || 727 ||

Or one may perform the consecration according to one's ability with the fragrant juice of plantain, jackfruit, and *aśvattha*—whether it be a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, or ten thousand times more. 728.
Having worshipped the conch, one who is single-minded should bathe [the deity] with its water;
the conch bestows pleasure upon all, but never upon the Sun.
O Lord, Śiva, having been consecrated with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and waters from sacred fords, attains joy;
thereafter, he does so even more through water from a conch and pure water.
The bath should be performed with the Puruṣasūkta or with the three root mantras [the Puruṣasūkta,
the Mūlamantra, and the bathing mantra]. A primary yellow silken garment should be offered to Viṣṇu.
And for Śiva, Sarasvatī, and Pārśvanātha, a white [or bright] [image].
The blood of Śakti, Arka, and Vighna [8—Devī; 9—Gaṇeśa], as well as that of Bhauma and Saugata [Buddha], [is used]. 732.
The sky of Kṛṣṇa, Bhairava, Kālī, and the others is blue; it is without fissures, free from impurity, and is that which is immediately and exclusively worn.
Whether made of cotton, silk, or wool, it is distinguished as superior.

From one defiled by oil and such substances, disease arises; from one with holes, the status of a *vrātya* or a lack of sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) or a mixture of castes (*saṃkara*) may occur. || 734 ||
From that which belongs to another, poverty arises; from that which is worn out, there is the decay of life.
From one who is burnt, misfortune arises; when the body is supported [by another], servitude is bestowed. (735)
From [an image] pierced by a needle, boils and the like arise; from one that is dirty, there is a loss of luster. (p.
110) When worship and other rites are performed upon one whose hair has been removed, there is the destruction of one's sons. || 736 ||
These may be of various kinds, distinguished by their types such as crowns and so forth.
Furthermore, these should be understood by the discerning according to the distinction between female and male. || 737 ||
Powder, rubbed [substance], essence of smoke, and friction derived from living beings.
Fragrance is to be known as fivefold, providing delight to the inhabitants of heaven.
Those leaf-powders which are combined with excellent fragrances are called "gandha"; this is known as the first type, beginning with powder (cūrṇa). || 739 ||
Sandalwood paste from the Malaya mountains, sal tree resin (a variety of *devadāru*), and *devadāru* wood.
Black agalloch and the kadamba tree—this is proclaimed as the second [type]. || 740 ||
[The oil] is prepared from sandalwood, agallochum, and other ingredients soaked in the juice of śatāvarī (or śatapatrī).
The third [preparation] is perfected in a glass vessel by means of the pippalīyantra. || 741 ||
Black agallochum, sandalwood, deodar, kālīyaka [yellow sandalwood],
bālaka, bhadramusta [hīvera, black agallochum, śatamūlī].
They consume *śilārasa*, *kundara*, *kolaka*, and *vārivāha*; they consume *kāka* and that which is named *turaga* (*aśvakarṇa*). || 742 ||
Having placed [the substance] in a glass vessel joined with clay and rags, and having sealed the opening with iron and non-iron wires,
the essence of smoke is drawn out from it by means of fragrant substances into a hard glass tube.
He is named Mahāmoda, the maker of the intoxication of wine, and likewise the cause of terror for spirits, yakṣas, and serpents.
Situated on the forehead, he removes the fear of fever, loss of appetite, and vomiting,
and he dispels defects of vision.
But when many [deities] are massaged according to their respective portions with fragrant and non-fragrant waters, that is proclaimed as the fourth, known as Sammarda. || 745 ||
One part of musk and two parts of mustaka.
Half of that [quantity] each of lāja, jaṭāmāṃsī, tvak, kuṣṭha, and śilārasa; || 746 ||
A fourth part of *bālaka* and likewise *nakhī* fried in ghee.
Sugandhakokilā [Aśvagandhā], Lohabāṇa [well-known by its respective name], and likewise Rājavacā; || 747 ||
There should be eight parts of keśara and sixteen parts of murā.
And black agallochum and kālīya are said to constitute eight parts of that.
Likewise, one should grind portions of *sevantikā* together; this friction, named *kāmoda*, brings satisfaction to the King of Deities. (749)
Musk, the rut-fluid of the musk deer, is said to be "born of breath. This fifth fragrance was created by the gods and the dānavas.
Flowers are said to be of five kinds: supreme, inferior, excellent, middling, and low; I shall describe their characteristics.
But the supreme golden flower is indeed always worthy of being offered.
It should always be worthy of worship after being first anointed; furthermore, it is proclaimed that [the vessel] may be made of silver or copper. (752)
p. 111) And this [initiation] is always suitable for those who are fit, whether they be three years or one year [of age].
Tulasī, ketakī, padma, karavīra— and mālatī (which is well known as either jātī or mālatī)— [753].

These five are said to be the best, and likewise ten are considered middling: *mallikā* (the well-known jasmine), *kunda*, *mandāra*, *bakula*, *arjuna*, *kiṃśuka*, [4—*maulasirī* in the vernacular], [5—*palāśa*]. || 754 ||
Pārijāta, aśoka, bilva, and campaka—gold that is distinct from these and possesses a destroyed fragrance is called "sugandhahata. || 755 ||

One should worship those [offerings] prescribed in the ritual injunctions for their respective mantras. One should not offer that which has fallen on the ground, that which is lukewarm or hot, or that which has been eaten by insects. (756)

Likewise, that which clings to the body, has been smelled, is withered, stale, or accumulated from a previous day; as well as that which has a pungent odor, lacks fragrance, or has been used for bathing at midday. (757)
A leaf, or even a flower, or a fruit should not be offered with its face turned downward; it is declared to cause suffering. It should be offered exactly as it was produced. || 758 ||

In all types of variegated worship, there is no fault in using what is not prohibited; however, offering flowers face-down is not desired, nor is that [practice] appropriate for the rite of the handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali). || 759 ||

There is no fault in using flowers that have been kept overnight when offered to Tulasī, Bilva, Campaka, lotuses, Bakula, Agasti, or those grown in the garden of a garland-maker (or in a garland-maker’s house).
One should not worship Śiva with *ketakī* or *kuṭaja* flowers; one should not worship Hari with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*);
one should not worship Durgā with *dūrvā* grass, nor the Sun with *bilva* leaves. (761)
And one should worship Lambodara and Tantuṣṭā with these same [offerings], excluding this [specific item].
One should worship the Goddess with arka flowers, and Āditya with tagara.
Red flowers are extremely dear to Gaṇeśa and Sūrya; in the absence of flowers, one may use young shoots, or in their absence, buds.

In the absence of those, one should offer fruits; in the absence of those, leaves; and in the absence of those, *kuśa* grass. [The following are suitable: the wood-apple (*kapittha*), pomegranate (*dāḍima*), jujube (*kola*), [the *bera* fruit], the rose-apple (*jambu*), the tamarind (*ciñcā*), the myrobalan (*āmalaka*), and the mango (*rasāla*). || 764 ||

The *mātuluṅga* (known in the vernacular as *cakotara*, a variety of citron), the *jambīra*, and the *panasa* (the spiny fruit) are said to be excellent. Then, at the conclusion of the flower offerings, one should perform the worship of the retinue (*āvaraṇārcana*). || 765 ||
One should worship the limbs of the deity in sequence with the letters of the Mātṛkā, accompanied by the nasal bindu and enclosed by mantras, using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. || 766 ||
Then, following that, [he should worship] the Mothers in their respective locations as limbs of the dissolution (layāṅga).
First, the enclosure (āvaraṇa) is to be worshipped; at its conclusion, one should sacrifice to the deity.
Having thus worshipped all those aforementioned deities of livelihood.
One should worship the heart-mantra and the others on the filaments, beginning from the southeast corner.

The Eye [of the mantra] is to be meditated upon in the center, and the Weapon [mantra] in the directions; these are the deities of the limbs (aṅgadevatās), possessing rays that are white as snow, crystal, dark, blue, black, and ruddy. (769)
The principal female deities, bearing the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, are stationed in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Asura, Vāyu, and the center, in successive order. || 770 ||

In the center of the deity stands the deity to be worshipped; the space between that deity and oneself should be designated as the eastern direction. In the worship of the enclosures (āvaraṇa-pūjana), the front is to be known as the east.
Then follows the worship of the retinues, proceeding in a clockwise direction. || 771 ||

The limb-mantras (aṅgamantra), however, end with the syllable *oṃ* during worship and end with the syllable *svāhā* during the oblation (*antāhuti*)—that is, those whose final constituent parts end in *oṃ*.
Furthermore, they are positioned facing the deity and conclude with *svāhā*. (772)
Then one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) stationed in their respective directions, and their weapons before them;
now their meditation (dhyāna) is described.
I worship Indra, the sovereign lord of the gods, the all-pervading one seated upon his throne on Airāvata; he has a thousand eyes and two arms, holding a thunderbolt upon his seat. || 774 ||

One should meditate upon Agni, the lord of splendor, red in color, the sovereign who holds a white spear in his hand; he is adorned with ornaments, has a ram for his vehicle, is the god of the gods, and possesses lovely eyes. (775)
Yama, the lord of the pretas, is black and seated upon a buffalo.
He was cruel, wielding the staff of Time (Kāladaṇḍa), and surrounded by terrifying messengers.
And [he beheld] Nirṛti, the lord of the Rākṣasas, seated upon a corpse, smoke-colored, with a sword in hand, and possessing a tawny beard and mustache. || 777 ||

I bow to Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures, who is seated upon a crocodile, resembles lightning, holds a noose in his lotus-like hand, possesses a white body, and has a protruding belly. || 778 ||
The supreme Vāyu is smoke-colored, dear to Prāṇa, and holds a red goad in his hand.
I worship him who has ascended to the stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) and runs with great speed.
And Kubera, the lord of the yakṣas, who is white and holds a white mace.
I worship Him who is seated upon a lion-throne and holds a drinking vessel.

One should visualize the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyādhipa), who holds a blue trident and has a bull for his vehicle; he is three-eyed, bears the crescent moon on his forehead, wears a mass of matted hair, and is white in complexion. || 781 ||
Upon his head is the pale-colored lord of serpents, adorned with a circle of hoods and jewels.
I worship Ananta, the bearer of the discus, who is plump, lofty, and all-pervading.
The Lord of the World, the Creator, auspicious, red in color, and holding a lotus in his hand.
I worship him who is mounted upon a swan and is engaged in the recitation of the Vedas. || 783 ||
Furthermore, regarding the root [offering] for the world-protectors: after the root mantra has been recited, the worship should be performed with this mantra:
"Obeisance to the Goddess, together with her limbs and her retinue. Having fully recited "together with her limbs" and "together with her retinue," and also "to Vārāhī."
One should utter the name of Nāmadevī ending in the dative case.

The practitioner should worship [the mantra] three times with "Namaḥ" and with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. Then, he should mark the incense burner with the Astra-mantra and subsequently worship it.
