Having worshipped the bell with the heart-mantra (the *namaḥ*-mantra) and the weapon-mantra (*astra*), one should ring it. Incense should be offered; guggulu is said to be dear to Gaṇeśa.
Sarja (well known as incense) is for the Goddess, and resin is for Maheśa.
Devadāru is for Viṣṇu; black agallochum is for Viṣṇu; realgar is dear to the Sun-god. (787)
I shall describe the ten-fold formulation of Śakti: Śaileya and sandalwood produced from the Malaya mountains.
One should prepare one part each of nakha, kuṣṭha, and sarjarasa.
Two parts each of *śilārasa*, *aguru*, *jaṭāmāṃsī*, and *bhāgadvaya* are prescribed; six parts of honey and eight parts of white sugar constitute this incense, which is known as *Śaktimohana*.
Harītakī, sarjarasa, murā, and māṃsī are each one part.
Three parts of lac, and four parts each of realgar and musta-grass. || 790 ||
Nail is said to consist of five parts, and kuṣṭha is said to consist of six parts.
For the twelve-year period of Guru, Keśava’s ten-fold incense consists of [half a part of] Madhu, Musta, ghee, Gandha, Guggulu, Aguru, Śailaja, Sarala, Sihla,
and Siddhārtha; this is the ten-fold incense for the remaining deities.
The incense should be held with the left hand, either in front or [to the side], but never on the right. One should not offer the incense upon the ground, nor upon a seat, nor likewise upon a cloth.
Having prepared it in whatever manner is appropriate for the vessel, one should offer it; however, fat, marrow, and bone are not desired for Viṣṇu, as is anything derived from wood.
Having performed worship with one's own mantra preceded by the ringing of a bell, one should offer a lamp with various musical instruments according to one's means. || 795 ||
*Tāra* [Oṃ jayadhvani mantramāne svāhā];
the word *jayadhvani*, *mantramāne*, and *agnigehinī*—this eleven-syllable mantra of the bell bestows all accomplishments. (796)

One should ring the bell during the invocation, the offering of arghya, and the incense; one should also ring it for the flowers, the food offering, and the lamp—especially for the incense and the lamp.
Except at the time of worship, one should not play it on other occasions; nor should one who desires spiritual success perform worship without it.
One should display the lamp high up, using either cow's ghee, oil, or a small wick; it must never be made with substances such as fat.
One should not offer a lamp by mixing various oils such as ghee and others out of greed;
having offered one made from mixed oils, one shall go to the Tāmisra hell.
One should cause it to revolve and display it in the form of a pigeon's circling, like the circling of a dove around a lamp; then one should recite a single verse for each of the deity’s limbs. 801.
A great lamp of perfect illumination, dispelling darkness everywhere, this light which is both internal and external—may this lamp be accepted. || 802 ||
Mustard oil is on the right, and sesame oil is on the left.
A white wick is on the right, and a red wick is on the left. || 803 ||
A lamp should be offered in vessels and never on the ground. A man who, having prepared a spot on the earth, offers a lamp there, attains the hell of Tāpa for a hundred years.
One should not extinguish the lamp, for it causes the destruction of prosperity.
Having offered water for the feet and water for sipping, one should present the food offering.
Having placed a golden vessel together with its lid here within the mandala.
Having established it as a square, one should consecrate it according to the path of the scriptures. || 806 ||

Having sprinkled [the site] with the weapon-mantra (astramantra) and protected it with the wheel-mudrās (cakramudrā), one should join both hands facing each other, well-extended and joined together; with the little fingers and thumbs joined, this is the mudrā known as the wheel (cakrasañjñitā). Having bound the two palms together...

By inserting the ring fingers and little fingers into the thumbs and little fingers respectively, the wheel mudrā (cakramudrā) is formed. One should dry up the defects of touch, sight, and so forth by means of the wind seed-syllable, using the mantra "Yam. || 807 ||
Touching with the tip of the right hand, one should burn it away with the seed-syllable of fire, namely the mantra "raṃ."
Having rendered it nectar with the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, one should then touch that vessel— which has been consecrated by reciting the root mantra eight times— with both hands. || 808 ||

One should touch [the water] with both hands according to the rule after it has been consecrated eight times; then, having displayed the *dhenumudrā*, one should worship it with perfumes and flowers. (809)
Having worshipped the deity, one should offer a handful of flowers with undistracted mind.
Divine, well-prepared, and excellent rice-pudding (paramānna) was placed within a golden vessel. || 810 ||
"Accept this [food] of five kinds, endowed with six flavors, for my success! Having recited the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, one should offer water. || 811 ||
Touching the vessel with both hands at the conclusion of the food offering (naivedya), one should say "namas.
Having offered water into the right hand of the deity, one should recite this: || 812 ||
"Thou art the under-layer of nectar, Svāhā!"—this is the eleven-syllable mantra consisting of the syllables *bhava*.
One should display with the right hand [the gesture] resembling a full-blown blue lotus. || 813 ||
Having displayed the *grāsamudrā*—
the *grāsamudrā* being formed by the fingers of the right hand, which is shaped like an open lotus, making the gesture of receiving—
the practitioner should perform five offerings of breath (*prāṇāhuti*).
The joining of the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb is the mudrā of Prāṇa.
Having taken a morsel with that [mantra], he should recite: "To Prāṇa, Svāhā!"
One should utter the word for "drinking" (*pāna*) joined with the index, middle, and thumb fingers; then one should say [the name] ending in *ṅ* and followed by *svāhā*, and then say "to Vyāna. (815)

One should offer [the oblation] with the ring finger, middle finger, and thumb ending in "svāhā"; for the udāna breath, one should offer it with all fingers except the little finger into the house of Agni.
Having uttered "svāhā" with all [the mantras] combined, one should offer a morsel of food. Then, in a vessel made of gold or other materials, one should offer excellent water using the *dhenumudrā*.

Having consecrated [the food] as nectar (*amṛta*), one should recite this mantra before offering it to the God: "Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, the supreme bringer of all satisfaction. This pure food, offered, remains in its natural state and is most refreshing. (818)
"Filled with supreme bliss, accept this excellent water. Having spoken thus, one should place the water vessel to the left of the deity. || 819 ||
Food prepared by cooking should be offered for the sake of the gods by those of the three castes.
Cooked in ghee, prepared with milk, and refined solely by fire.
It is appropriate that it be made with sugarcane mud; this is praised for a Śūdra. Then, one should offer a handful of flowers as a binding with the Astra-mantra. || 821 ||
Having made the directions a curtain (*tiraskariṇī*), one should place them all around the Lord. (p.
115) One should then utter "Namaḥ" over the nectar-like food offering (*naivedya*). 822.
Then, having displayed the dhenumudrā, one should contemplate the deity as partaking of the food.
Having recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times, he should offer water.
Having offered water for sipping (ācamana) at the conclusion of the food offering (naivedya), one should perform the ritual of the fire oblation (homa).
Having prepared the fire as before, the knower of mantras should invoke the deity.
Having performed worship with the root mantra, one should offer twenty-five oblations of clarified butter,
sacrificial food, sesame seeds, or auspicious milk-rice.
Either with rice mixed with sesame seeds, or even with flowers alone.
One should offer one oblation for each of the deities of the limb-enclosures.
Having dismissed both the deity and the fire, one should then proceed to the place of worship.
Having sat upon his seat, he should then offer the bali-oblation to the spirits with mantras.

Having prepared a mandala in the northeast, one should place there a vessel provided with its base, filled with food, condiments, and water, and adorned with flowers and other offerings. Having worshipped the spirits (bhūtas) therein, one should then offer them a bali-oblation. || 828 ||
Those who are fierce, whose deeds are fierce, and who dwell in fierce abodes.
The yoginīs are also of the nature of fire, as are those who are the lords of the hosts (gaṇas).
May all beings— those who move on the earth, those who move in the sky, and those who dwell in the intermediate space—
accept this offering with minds full of joy.
With the left hand, one should offer a stream of water into that vessel; then, taking a handful of flowers, one should pray to the spirits as follows. || 831 ||
May all those beings who dwell here upon this earth, having accepted this offering presented according to the ritual rules, depart everywhere in satisfaction; homage be to them!
Having offered a handful of flowers and bowed down, let them dwell at their ease. Then, one should dismiss the spirits and other beings with the nārāca-mudrā. || 833 ||
Having meditated that the deity is satiated, and having reflected upon the food offering as being devoid of essence,
one should then place that vessel in the direction of the Rakshasas (the southwest).

Then, one should place the food offering (naivedya) with cow-dung water while reciting the Astra-mantra. Having taken the remains of the deity's meal, one should say: "Salutation to the consumer of the floral remains (nirmālya). || 835 ||
Having placed the hand in the northeast, one should then wash it.
One should again offer water for sipping (ācamana) and likewise a fragrant powder for rubbing the hands (karodvartana).
Having offered pure water for sipping (ācamana), one should scent the hands with fragrant perfumes;
then one should offer twelve-ingredient betel (tāmbūla) to Viṣṇu.
[One should offer] catechu, cardamom, cloves, camphor, cinnamon, tamāla leaves, nutmeg, and jāvatrī, combined with musk and saffron. || 838 ||
Now, the fruit of the *pauṣa* month is declared to consist of ten components for Bhāskara;
however, for Vidheśvara, it is devoid of musk and garlands. (839)
The five-fold [incense] consists of powder, khadira leaves, pūga fruit, and induka; that of the Goddess includes nutmeg, while that of the Great Lord includes the shell of the jātī flower.
Then one should present the crown and other ornaments;
likewise, one should show the mirror and provide the parasol and the fly-whisks.

Having placed dūrvā grass, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and a sacred thread upon the head of the deity, one should then perform the ārātrika ceremony for the attainment of dharma, kāma, and artha. || 842 ||
On a plate made of gold, silver, or bell-metal—captivating to the eyes of the world—one should draw a beautiful eight-petaled lotus with saffron. || 843 ||
One should place a great lamp upon the pericarp and eight lamps upon its petals.
[Offer] those filled with ghee, adorned with the beauty of circular coils, prepared from barley and wheat, and combined with sugar and milk. || 844 ||

Then, having consecrated it with the nine-syllable mantra of Ratneśvarī— namely: *Śrīṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Glūṃ Stūṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Glūṃ Stūṃ Hrīṃ* (this is the nine-syllable mantra of Ratneśvarī)— the practitioner of mantra should then [consecrate it] with *Hrīṃ Glūṃ Stūṃ*.
Then, as before, [the syllables] *śrīṃ* and *hrīṃ* [are placed] in sequence. || 845 ||
Then, having designated Ratneśvarī, one should worship her with the root mantra.
Then, having lifted that vessel, [he should move it] repeatedly up to the top of the head. || 846 ||
One should rotate [the vessel] nine times and display the *cakramudrā*. Then, having prostrated to the deity, one should perform three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). || 847 ||
Then, with the root mantra, one should perform the filling [of the vessel] preceded by the ritual placement (nyāsa).
Either one thousand and eight, or nine hundred and thirty-two.

One should also recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times without sloth. When the recitation is completed, one should place the rosary upon the head. Then, taking water from the vessel of honor (arghyapātra), one should recite this again: || 849 ||
You are the protector of the most secret of secrets; accept this recitation performed by us. O Lord, Master of the World, may success be mine through your grace. (850)

Having offered water into the right hand of the deity, one should present [the offerings]. The rosary used for recitation should be placed in a secluded spot and covered. Then, accompanied by songs of praise and the sounding of a bell— || 851 ||
A Brāhmaṇa [is purified] by Vedic mantras and the like, and a Kṣatriya by the Saṃhitās and so forth.
The Vaiśya [should recite] with the Paurāṇikas and others, while the Śūdra [should recite] with the Prākṛtas and others. || 852 ||
However, at the conclusion of the ritual service, the Vāmins should perform a satiation with liquor;
for them, the fire-oblation is optional, but the practice of satiation is obligatory.
One should sprinkle that remnant with those who follow the Kaulika path together with their Śaktis. If, out of delusion or desire, a Śūdra should recite a Purāṇa or a Smṛti,
that evildoer goes to hell along with his ancestors.
If a Śūdra should intentionally listen to the Vedas or cause the twice-born to hear them, both of them will become miserable in this world and will become denizens of hell in the next. || 855 ||
But he who, out of pride in his authority or even out of pride in his wealth, should cause a Śūdra to hear the Veda, shall become childless and destitute. (856)
If, however, out of ignorance, the Veda has been heard or recited by a twice-born man;
By performing three Prājāpatya penances, the two of them will become completely purified. || 857 ||

Then, taking the vessel for the *arghya* offering and reciting the root mantra, [one should say]: "O Blessed Lord, whether my actions have been well-done or ill-done, whatever has been performed by me—accept all of that as your supreme act of worship. (858)

Having thus offered the water for the *arghya*, the wise one should present a small portion from the right hand; then, having performed the worship, he should bow with devotion to the Lord of Gods and offer [the service] with these verses: || 859 ||
Whatever leaf, flower, fruit, or water is offered with mere devotion, and whatever food offering is presented—please accept that out of compassion. (860)
I do not know the invocation, nor do I know the dismissal; I do not even know the worship itself. You alone are my refuge, O Supreme Lord. (861)
In deed, thought, or word, there is no other refuge for me but you;
O Supreme Lord, you are the witness of all beings through your inner movement.
O Lord, in whichever of the thousands of wombs I may enter,
may my devotion to you always remain steadfast and imperishable.
The God is both the giver and the enjoyer; the God is this entire universe. The God is victorious everywhere;
he who is the God is indeed myself. 864.

Then, one should perform the offering of worship with the water from the *arghya* vessel according to the formula for *brahmārpaṇa*: "Oṃ Tat Sat! Whatever has been done by me—through my vital breaths, intellect, body, and the authority of my duties; in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep;
through mind, speech, and action; internally, or through my stomach and genitals..."
Whatever has been remembered, whatever has been spoken, and whatever has been done—all that becomes an offering to Brahman;
[with the mantra] "bhūḥ svāhā," one should then perform the offering to Brahman according to the Manu-śāstra. || 865 ||
One should recite "Tāraḥ" (Om), followed by "tatsat," and then "prāṇabuddhi."
Having spoken regarding the domain of bodily functions in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, [it is said]: "Then, internally, by means of mind, speech, and action... (866).
Whatever is uttered with the word "Om," whatever is done with the belly, whatever is remembered with the penis, whatever is spoken,
and whatever is performed— all that shall become an offering unto Brahman.
And this mantra, "bhūḥ svāhā," is declared to consist of sixty-six syllables.
Then one should cause the deity to depart together with the assembly of attendants.
Having thus offered a handful of flowers and prostrated, one should contemplate that the entire multitude of rays has dissolved completely before the deity. (869)
Having meditated upon Śiva in the form of light, [one should say] "Forgive me" again and again.
One should then dissolve the deity into one's own heart-lotus through the practice of kṣamā.
Go, go, O best of gods, to your own abode, O Supreme Lord—
that supreme state which even the gods, beginning with Brahmā, do not know.
Having emitted [the breath] with this mantra, one should then [inhale] with the filling air (pūraka);
having meditated with this mantra, one should place her within the heart. (872)
Stay, stay in the supreme abode, O Supreme Lord, in your own place where Brahmā and all the gods abide within my heart. 873.

Having thus established and worshipped [the deity], one should meditate upon oneself as being identical with it. One should prepare a mandala in the northeast at the entrance, excluding the lotus design. (874)
For the purpose of consuming the *nirmālya* during the worship of the five deities (*pañcāyatana*), one should perform exactly five [offerings] and worship beginning with Īśāna. || 875 ||
Lambodara is the splendor of Gaṇeśa, Candra is that of Vivasvat, Viṣvaksena is said to be that of Hari, and Īśvarī is that of Maheśitṛ. || 876 ||
And Caṇḍeśvara should perform such [rites] with the mantras of Bhavānī.
Liquids to be licked, things to be sucked, food, drink, and so forth, as well as floral remains and unguents.
"By the command of Śrī Śiva, I give this to you who consume the remains of the offerings. Having thus given the remainder of the *naivedya*, one should bow and dismiss [the deity]. || 878 ||
Then, for the sake of ensuring the rite is free from defects, one should offer worship to the Sun with the mantra consisting of the seeds *hrīṃ hrīṃ saḥ* followed by *namaḥ*. || 879 ||
Salutations to you, Vivasvat, the radiant one, the splendor of Viṣṇu; to the pure Savitṛ, the progenitor of the world, the bestower of the fruits of action. || 880 ||

Then, with palms joined in reverence and having steadied the mind, one should recite: "Whatever flaw there may be in my sacrifice, whatever flaw in my austerity, and whatever flaw in my worship—by the grace of the Sun-god, may all that be rendered flawless. (881)
Then, having stirred with a little of the arghya water remaining from the previous worship of the scents, one should again consecrate it eight times with the root mantra. || 882 ||

One should sprinkle that place with that water while reciting the root mantra. The practitioner should wear the *nirmālya* (remnants of the offering) upon his head while reciting the root mantra. || 883 ||
After drinking the water for the feet, one should then distribute the food offering.
Having himself eaten with those devoted to him, he indeed dwells happily, being one with them.
But the Śaiva alone is entitled to the grace of the *nirmālya* of Śiva; any other person goes to hell.
There is no fault in the union of the five.

Whether they are devotees of Śiva or not, by performing with devotion the consecration of a linga, a sacred bathing place, or even a temple, they are indeed liberated from the heap of their sins. || 886 ||
One may then worship or bow down to a Linga installed by a Shudra.
One who takes the alms, etc., belonging to such a person shall fall into hell. || 887 ||
Having risen in the morning and recollected the Guru and others, one should properly perform the bath, the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā),
and the libations (tarpaṇa), both according to the Vedic and Tantric traditions.
Having returned home, one should thereafter perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma),
and likewise perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Mātṛkās, as well as that of the meters, sages, and deities.
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of that mantra known as the hands and limbs, and likewise established its presence;
The mantra-bath and the five-fold worship of the deity. || 890 ||
There, within the Vaiśvadeva rite, one should offer five oblations; one should perform the fire-sacrifice there with the root mantra and recite it one hundred and eight times.

The worship ending with the *vaidikī* and *kākabali*, as well as the eating of the remains (*ucchiṣṭabhojana*), should be performed; thereafter, one should pray to the God and perform the evening twilight ritual (*sāyaṃsandhyā*). || 892 ||
While the temple was ablaze, this summary of the daily ritual was proclaimed.
Now I shall describe the afternoon [rite], which occurs in those ten locations. (893)

On a journey, while traveling abroad, on a difficult path, upon falling ill, or when faced with great danger; in an inauspicious prison or place, or when threatened by fear arising from snakes, tigers, and the like—894.

Upon the arrival of an enemy army— the arrival of the military forces of kings from other lands in one's own country is called the "arrival of an enemy army"— one should collect taxes and so forth, however it may be.
There, having performed the mental worship consisting of the visualization of bathing and other rites, [one should proceed]. || 895 ||
Having meditated upon that seat called Yoga within the heart with the mind,
one should perform the worship of the Lord right there, in the center of the earth.
Just as worship with flowers and other offerings is performed externally, so too should it be performed within the heart for the attainment of all aspirations. (897)

And one should perform this oblation mentally during times of adversity; this is the daily ritual (āhnika). Now, therefore, I shall describe the daily ritual for one who is generally in good health. (898)
If the disease is seen to have subsided within oneself by the end of the fasting period, then no worship should be performed upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or before images. || 899 ||
One should not perform bathing, nor the use of a tooth-stick, nor even the fire-oblation.
Having gazed upon the orb of the sun, or else again upon the image; || 900 ||
Having recited the root mantra once, one should offer a flower along with unbroken grains of rice.
Whether overcome by extremely fierce diseases, by old age, or likewise by the failure of the senses, or even by one's own fellow initiates,
one should nevertheless complete what is to be done for oneself.
Then, having returned from the illness and bathed, he worshipped the fire-gods.
And in their presence, he should address these words to the gurus and the Brahmins.
Having prayed, "By your grace, let there be no fault in this worship that has been interrupted for so long," one should perform it again as before. (903)
But as for that fault which arises from the power of disease, one should perform its purification through recitation, meditation, burnt offerings, or even through giving. || 904 ||
Now, for those in a state of ritual impurity (sūtaka), one should always perform the Vedic rites prescribed by the Vedas mentally,
while performing the Tantric worship and other such rituals only with the mind.

If the application is for the sake of desire, then one should act as previously described. Having abandoned the house of the deceased, there is no ritual impurity (sūtaka) in the Vāmācāra tradition. || 906 ||

Having abandoned desire through prior knowledge regarding lineage and the path of Dharma, he who performs the Vāmācāra with devotion may obtain the dharma of meditation; yet he who does not know the reality of the scriptures and the reality of the deity is merely a Guhyaka. || 907 ||
One who seeks happiness resorts to knowledge through the left; therein it is born.
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, one becomes a preta; therefore, one should reflect upon dharma.
The ritual should be performed with water for worship; that [physical] yantra is not required at all. Then one should worship the deity with mental offerings such as flowers and so forth. (909)
Devotion, faith, and meditative cultivation are said to be the life-force of all forms of worship.
I shall now describe the daily ritual for the dull-witted, as well as the procedure for the abbreviated rite.
The jeweled pavilion, the fourfold mandala of Dharma and so forth, and the reddish lotus.
The worship of the root-form and its six limbs is now described.

In the worship of all [the Buddhas], whatever object might not be obtained, one should perform the mental cultivation of its offering within the mind alone; for indeed, there is no [offering] through the mere intention when objects are unavailable.
With pure water alone, one should perform the worship with a steady mind.
In general, worship is threefold: superior, inferior, and middling.
Furthermore, it is divided a hundredfold by way of the qualified persons and the causes. || 913 ||
Worship performed with its full array of requisites is considered the most excellent.
But worship performed with materials obtained as they come is indeed middling.
Worship performed with leaves, flowers, and water is designated as sādharmya-pūjā.
By stainless Brahman-sages who had performed all that is prescribed in the Vedas.

The ancient teachers composed the Tantras, perceiving that those men who possess the defects of the Kali age— such as lust and anger— and whose senses are unsubdued, lack the qualification for Vedic dharma; in those [Tantras],
all those dharmas which are Vedic should be practiced, while furthermore, those [which are not]...

Practices such as animal sacrifice and the left-hand path (*vāmamārga*), which are contrary to the Vedas, were taught solely by some means to encourage the devotion of gods among the ignorant *śūdras* and others;
those who, having understood the intention of the Tantric teachers, follow only those practices contrary to the Vedas—

Those who, considering themselves superior, perform worship or cause it to be performed, fall away from Brahmanic luster and descend into hell; however, that worship which is *sāttvika* bestows liberation.
By royal sages devoted to austerity and who knew the true nature of the Blessed One.
The worship that is performed correctly is royal, and it bestows happiness.
By women, children, the elderly, leaders, and others—devotees whose minds were undistracted. || 917 ||

Whatever worship is performed constantly [in this manner] is proclaimed to be tāmasī (of the nature of darkness). Indeed, people are not capable of performing it according to the Vedas; however, the Tantras exist in every age. || 918 ||
Those brahmins by whom [the scriptures] were proclaimed according to their names arose from a portion of Kali; incited by Kali, those brahmins followed the path of those tantras.
Men seized by lust, greed, and other vices, and devoid of Brahmanical character, will become Mlecchas;
with their merit exhausted, they shall fall into the Raurava hell.
Knowing that [the knowledge] will perish, one must certainly not abandon the Vedic tradition; it is the protection of Viṣṇu through its chapters, a cowherd [of wisdom] devoid of worldly excitement.
Those books composed by chapters are the sacred recitations (svādhyāya) for the twice-born; however, in a system (tantra) composed for a specific purpose, that purpose holds primacy therein.
"However, that which is proclaimed in the Merutantra shall be stable and not otherwise. Thus, O gods, the resolution of your question has been fully explained. || 923 ||
Since an action performed after due deliberation does not lead to suffering, one should indeed perform the action prescribed by the Veda for the sake of the supreme good.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the *Āhnika-prakāśa*, composed by Śiva in the *Merutantra* with the approval of the illustrious Mahāmāyā and Mahākāla. 5.
The Meru Tantra, composed as a dialogue between Śrī Śiva and Śivā,
having been edited by the scholar Ojhā Paṇḍita Raghunātha Śāstrī.
Edited with commentaries such as the *Ṭippanī*,
published by Khemrāj Śrīkṛṣṇadās, Bombay, 1935.
Chapters 6 to 10. The Blessed Goddess said:
O Lord, please explain the meaning of the word *puraścaraṇa* and its ritual procedure.
And all mantras, beginning with those of the Vedas, do not attain success without him.
The Lord said:

I shall declare before you the secret of all mantras, for the sake of the Kali age—the purpose of enjoyment and liberation for those born in this age. That which is the essence of all tantras has been kept hidden. (2)
Mantra is said to be the means for accomplishing dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; that which was practiced in the past for the sake of attaining those goals is what is proclaimed here.
Regarding that mantra which exists from the beginning of the Vedas up to the Śabara [Tantras] and is known by the name *puraścaraṇa*— I shall now describe its method.
Japa, homa, tarpaṇa, mārjana, and the feeding of Brahmins.
Regarding that, some have stated the nature of the five-limbed [prayer] as follows.
Furthermore, there are those with four limbs, three limbs, two limbs, and even those with only one limb.
Mantras reside in the Vedas as well as in the Śabara Tantra.
Some mantras may consist of six limbs; I shall indeed make those who are ignorant of this understand it.
By means of the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn, the offering of water to the Sun, the recitation of mantras, and prostrations.
With the worship of the deity and the five [offerings], these are thus remembered as the five-limbed [rite].
Likewise, sacrifice consists of oblations, worship through ritual action, and the veneration of the wheel.

Through the union with the banner and the linga, by means of recitation (japa) and the offering of oblations (bali), and by the presentation of the great oblation, he becomes possessed of eleven limbs. || 9 ||
The authority over the assemblies of the Kaulikas resides in the sixteen-fold limb.
It shall effect the destruction of all sins, or else it shall bring about an obstruction to spiritual accomplishment.
Having destroyed whatever sin he possesses, one should perform the preliminary rite;
by the path thus described, his success is not far off. || 11 ||
There, the destruction of all sins occurs for those who follow the Vedic path; however, the Tantrikas, the Kaulikas, and the Vāmas do not possess the qualification [for this]. || 12 ||
They have no entitlement to that Vedic ritual action.
The astrologer should be one who studies the Ṛgveda branch, and his procedure is as follows. || 13 ||
Having bathed, performed his ritual duties, and being accompanied by his wife upon a bed of darbha grass, he should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma),
make a formal resolve (saṅkalpa), and worship Gaṇeśvara.

Having established the fire according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, one should take refuge in it; then, having anointed that sacrificial oblation with clarified butter, one brings it forward twice, beginning with the syllable "Oṃ. (15)

O Agni, having recited each verse beginning with "Agni, lead us" (*agne naya*) and so forth, one should offer the *svāhā* exclamation. At the end of the *svāhā*, one should recite the formula: "This is for Agni, not for me. Furthermore, one should perform oblations with the six-verse hymn beginning with "Lead us" (*naya*), saying at the time of the offering after each mantra: "This is for Agni, not for me."
Therefore, I shall now recite the Ṛgvedic verses here, so that there may be no confusion regarding the Vedic branches (śākhās).
Oṃ! O Agni, lead us by a good path to prosperity, O God, you who know all ways.
Fight against us; turn away our sin. We shall offer you the most abundant expression of homage.
Bring forth the oblation and the prayer well-prepared for Agni, whose bright radiance [is yours], he who goes between all divine and human generations with his wisdom.
Clear are the songs and the thoughts seeking the gods, as they beg Agni, their lord, for wealth.

O Agni, you who are beautiful to behold, of fair countenance, the self-existent bearer of oblations, and the messenger of men— drive away from us all diseases and those who, being devoid of fire, have turned their minds against us among the people.
Furthermore, O gods, worthy of sacrifice, together with all the immortals, grant us excellent wealth.
O Agni, as one ever new, do thou carry us across all difficulties with thy blessings.
May Pūṣan and the broad, vast earth grant well-being and security to our children and descendants.
O Prākāravas, being praised by our thoughts, you who seek the gods lead [the sacrifice] toward the gods.
The ladle, moving to the right, dripping with ghee, brings the oblation for Agni.
Then one should offer oblations with the Puruṣasūkta consisting of eighteen verses; one should renounce [the fruit], thinking, "This is for the Puruṣa, the seed of the universe, not for me."

One who is not a Vaiṣṇava [at the end of each mantra, at the time of offering *svāhā*, should say: "This is for the seed of the universe, and not for me"; however, a Vaiṣṇava should utter these words: "This is for Nārāyaṇa, and not for me"].
The Vaiṣṇava hymn belongs to Nārāyaṇa and not to me; that hymn, which is dear to the God of gods, is now being recited. (25)
Oṃ. The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet. Having pervaded the earth on all sides, he transcended it by ten fingers' breadth. 26.
The Person alone is all this, whatever has been and whatever is yet to be.
And he is the lord of immortality, that which grows by means of food. || 27 ||
Such is His greatness, and yet the Puruṣa is even greater than this. All beings constitute one quarter of Him;
His three quarters are the immortal in heaven. 28.
The Puruṣa rose upward with three quarters; his one quarter here again became the world of men. From there he strode out in all directions toward that which eats and that which does not eat.
From him Virāj was born; from Virāj, Puruṣa was born as its lord. Once born, he extended beyond the earth—both behind and before. || 30 ||
When the gods performed the sacrifice with the Puruṣa as the oblation, spring was its clarified butter, summer its fuel, and autumn its offering. || 31 ||
Seven were its enclosing sticks, and thrice seven were the fuel-sticks made; when the gods, performing the sacrifice, bound Puruṣa as the victim. (32)
They sprinkled that Puruṣa, who was born in the beginning, as a sacrifice upon the sacrificial grass; with him, the gods, the Sādhyas, and the Ṛṣis performed the sacrifice. || 33 ||
From that sacrifice in which everything was offered, the speckled butter was gathered together.
He created those animals—both those of the forest and those of the village—which belong to Vāyu.
From that sacrifice in which everything was offered, the Ṛg-verses and Sāman-chants were born; from it the meters were born, and from it the Yajus formula was produced. (35)
From that the horses were born, and whatever animals have two rows of teeth; from that the cows were born, and from that goats and sheep were produced. (36)
When they fashioned Puruṣa, into how many parts did they divide him? What was his mouth, what were his two arms, and what are said to be his thighs and feet? (37)
The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth; the Rājanya was made from his arms; that which was his thighs became the Vaiśya; and from his feet the Śūdra was born. 38.
The moon was born from the mind; from the eye, the sun was born.
From his mouth Indra and Agni were born, and from his breath Vāyu was born. || 39 ||
From his navel the intermediate space arose; from his head the sky evolved; from his feet the earth, and from his ears the directions; thus they fashioned the worlds. 40.
I know this great Puruṣa, resplendent like the sun, beyond the darkness.
Having discerned all forms and having fashioned names, the Wise One remains calling them forth.
Dhātṛ proclaimed it in the beginning, and Śakra, the wise one, [proclaimed it] in the four directions. Knowing this very thing, one becomes immortal here; no other path for traveling is found.
By means of sacrifice, the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice; those were the first ordinances (dharmas). They...
The mighty ones have attained the firmament, where the ancient Sādhyas, the gods, abide.

One should offer oblations there with the hymn beginning with "agnermanve," which consists of twenty-two verses. In those three [verses], the renunciation (tyāga) is to Agni; using the mantra "Agnaye idam na mama" (This is for Agni, not mine), one should offer the oblation by forming and joining the sentence according to this very method even for the minor names [of deities].
And [the thought], "This is not mine. || 44 ||
In the fourth [verse], the renunciation is "to Indra and not mine";
in the fifth and sixth, it is "to Indra and Varuṇa and not mine";
likewise, in the seventh and eighth, it is "to Mitra and Varuṇa and not mine."
[Regarding the seventh and eighth [verses]: (by Vāyu and Sūrya; not by me, but by Agni alone, in this manner).]
"In the ninth and likewise in the tenth [day], it is from Vāyu and Sūrya; and from the Aśvins and the Maruts, it occurs in the eleventh and twelfth. (46)
For the thirteenth and fourteenth [lunar days], [the oblations are] for the Viśvedevas; for the fifteenth, for Anumati, Havyavāha, and Agni. || 47 ||
For Anumati, it should be on the sixteenth day; thereafter, on the seventeenth, it should take place.
And likewise for Vaiśvānara, for Agni, and also for the eighteen [deities]. || 48 ||
"For Dyāvāpṛthivī" is for the twentieth and nineteenth [verses]; now hear those remaining Ṛgvedic verses beginning with "For Agni. (49)
Many [invoke] this Agni, the first and wise one, who belongs to the five peoples.
They kindle [thee] in every clan, or indeed in each individual clan; we entreat thee—do thou deliver us from distress. || 50 ||
I praise Agni, whose alone is this that breathes and blinks, that moves, and all that has been born and is being born; seeking protection, I call upon him repeatedly: may he deliver us from sin. 51.
I consider that the hymns have reached the likeness of the foremost Indra, the wise slayer of Vṛtra;
may he who comes to the call of the donor who performs good deeds deliver us from sin. 52.
He who leads the battle, who is master over the fight, who brings together the three prosperities—I praise Indra; seeking protection, I call upon him repeatedly. May he deliver us from distress.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, I am mindful of you; take note of this, you who possess true power and rise up as destroyers of enemies.
O King, O Charioteer, release us from this path; let us not meet with destruction. || 54 ||

Or he who, as the controller, moving in secret with his rays, approaches together with the one of true law to cause corruption—I praise Mitra and Varuṇa; seeking protection, I call upon them: may they two release us from sin. 55.
We consider the thoughts of Vāyu and Savitṛ to be true—those two who, possessing selfhood, sustain all things and protect them;
those two who have become the encompassers of the universe—may they both release us from sin. 56.
May our most excellent blessings be firmly established in the dharma of the two gods. I praise Vāyu and Savitṛ; seeking protection, I call upon them repeatedly: may those two deliver us from sin. 57.

I invoke for protection the two most excellent charioteers among charioteers, the most beautiful to behold and most eager to sacrifice, with their well-governed horses—those two gods whose vigor among the gods is most unyielding; may you two deliver us from sin. (58)
When you two came with the three-wheeled chariot of Sūryā, seeking a seat together—praising all the gods, I, the suppliant, call upon you both; release us from sin. 59.

I call upon the Maruts; may they speak for us, and may all of them protect this entire speech. May those who are easy to guide come to our invocation for protection, and may they release us from sin. 60.
The divine Viṣṇu, possessing sharp weapons and modesty, is victorious and all-pervading in battles.
I praise the divine Maruts; seeking protection, I call upon them repeatedly: may they release us from sin. || 61 ||
I call upon the gods; may they speak for us, and may all of them protect this entire speech.
O Sūrās, come to our invocation for protection; may you deliver us from sin. 62.
That is to say: "Do not grieve; I praise [thee] with both human and divine [praise]."
Seeking protection, I repeatedly invoke all the gods; may they release us from sin. || 63 ||
May approval follow what has been urged, and may the sacrifice be considered among the gods; and may Agni, the bearer of oblations, be a source of joy for the donor. 64.
O Anumati, do thou follow us and grant us well-being; impel us toward wisdom and skill, and prolong our lives. 65.
May Vaiśvānara come from afar to what has been prepared; may Agni, through our well-spoken hymns, approach us. 66.
Questioned in heaven, questioned on earth, Agni has entered all plants when questioned. May that Vaiśvānara Agni, questioned with power, protect us by day and by night. 67.
Those two who have spread themselves out with immeasurable powers, who have become the two foundations of all treasures.
I praise Heaven and Earth; seeking protection, I call upon you both repeatedly: deliver us from distress.
May the two vast worlds, Heaven and Earth, grant us wide space; may the Mistress of the Field speak for us.
I praise them; seeking protection, I cry out to Heaven and Earth: may you both deliver us from distress. (69)
Whatever offense we, O most youthful one, have committed against men through ignorance, however slight it may be—[forgive that].
Make us sinless before Aditi; O Agni, loosen our bonds on every side through innocence.
Just as the Vasus, the worshipful ones, released Gaurī who had been bound by the foot, so too [did they release her].
O Agni, release us from this distress; prolonging our lifespan, lead us across to safety. 71.

Then, with the four hymns beginning with "yāvāmindrāvaruṇā," [where "hymns" refers to the mantras proclaimed in those hymns], the dedication (tyāga) is always made to Indra and Varuṇa, and not otherwise. || 72 ||
O Mitra and Varuna, by whatever body of yours is to be restrained, release me from this distress.
O Indra and Varuṇa, with whatever powerful bodies you possess, release me from this distress. || 74 ||
O Indra and Varuṇa, by whatever body of yours is demonic, release me from that sin.
(75) O Indra and Varuṇa, by whatever body of yours is radiant, release me from that sin. (76)
Or one should offer oblations with the verse "yo vām indrāvaruṇā" and then with eight [verses].
The renunciation is always "to Indra and Varuṇa," and never otherwise.
O Indra and Varuṇa, whatever sin we have committed against you in the fire, that I expiate for you with this [offering]. || 78 ||
O Indra and Varuṇa, whatever disease there is among your biped animals, that I appease for you with this [offering].
O Indra and Varuṇa, whatever sin of yours is among the plants, that I expiate for you with this [offering]. 80.
O Indra and Varuṇa, whatever sin of yours is in the trees, that I expiate for you with this.
The Pāvamānī Anuvāka, which is known to consist of seventeen verses.
Therein, according to the Śāktas, the first verse consists of sixty-three statements, while the [second] verse consists of three statements.
Those who lack the necessary capacity should state my renunciation [of the ritual] in favor of the Pāvamānī verses. || 82 ||
[One should recite] the Pāvamānī verses and likewise those dedicated to Śiva; for the sake of purification, it must not be otherwise.
May that Pavamāna, the all-seeing one who is the Purifier, purify me today with the filter. 84.

The second [offering] also should be offered to the people, to the Maruts, and likewise to the Viśvedevas from three sentences alone; it is not said that there is an abandonment of "mine" (mama). || 85 ||
May the divine beings purify me; may the mental faculties and intentions purify me; may all beings purify me; O Jātavedas, do thou purify me. 86.
The third [formula] also consists of four sentences: "To Agni Jātavedas, this, not mine"—having spoken thus, the renunciation (tyāga) is also made manifest. 87.
O Jātavedas, purify me with the purifier that possesses the power of purification; O Agni, shining among the gods, purify my intentions according to my will through your pure radiance. 88.
The fourth [formula], however, consists of three statements: "To Agni, not to me," and so forth; the fifth is also a triad of statements, the renunciation being "And to Savitṛ," as in both cases.
That purifier of yours which is stretched out within the flame at its tip—by that, O Brahman, purify us. (90)
O God Savitṛ, purify me on all sides with both the filter and the impulse. || 91 ||
The sixth [chapter] consists of four statements in verse, and its renunciation is now being defined.
She should say, "To the Viśvedevas," and not "to me. Thus it is said. (92)
The goddess, common to all men, purifying, has come—she in whom are many voices and smooth-backed forms.
Rejoicing with her at our communal feasts, may we be masters of riches. 93.
"To Vaiśvānara, to Vāta, to the vigorous one who bestows bliss—to Dyāvāpṛthivī"—thus the renunciation (tyāga) is prescribed in the seventh [verse]. || 94 ||
May Vaiśvānara purify me with his rays; may Vāta, the swift and bliss-bestowing, purify me with his breath.
May Heaven and Earth, the holy ones, purify me with their milk and waters, O Śatāvarī.

The seventh [offering] consists of four sentences, while the eighth is considered to consist of three sentences; "Savitre," "Agnaye," "na mama," and "tyāga" are used on the eighth day, as is the case with the evening offering.
O Agni, purify me with the three great, most excellent, and skillful prayers of the divine Savitṛ. 97.
From this point forward, one should offer [the oblation] to the divine Brahman with four verses; on the ninth day, to the Pāvamānī verses;
and on the tenth day and those following, as they are [prescribed].
By that with which the gods purified themselves, by which the celestial waters were cleansed—by that divine Brahman, purify this Brahman, me. 99.
He who studies the Pāvamānī verses, whose essence has been gathered by the seers, eats everything purified and made savory by Mātariśvan. (100)
To him who studies the Pāvamānī hymns—the essence gathered by the seers—Sarasvatī milks forth milk, clarified butter, honey, and water. 101.
The Pāvamānī hymns are indeed auspicious, yielding easily, and full of nourishment;
they are the essence collected by the seers, and nectar is hidden within the Brāhmaṇas. 102.
May the purifying verses (pāvamānīs) point out to us this world as well as that one; may the goddesses, being concentrated together with the gods, fulfill our desires. 103.
The Pāvamānī hymns are indeed auspicious, yielding great milk and dripping with clarified butter; they are the essence gathered by the seers, and nectar is placed within the Brāhmaṇas. 104.
By that purifier with a thousand streams, with which the gods always purify themselves, may the Pāvamānī verses purify me. 105.
The renunciation is as before; however, for one learned in the Vedas (śrotriya), there is this distinction regarding the sixteenth [year].
Listen to the sixteenth [verse], beginning with "prājāpatyāya" and "pavitrāya. (106)
The purifier belonging to Prajāpati, golden, with a hundred supports—by means of that, we who know Brahman purify the purified Brahman. 107.
One should then say: "To Indra, together with Sunīti; to Soma, together with Svasti; to Varuṇa, together with Samīcī. || 108 ||
One should offer [the oblation] to King Yama together with Pramṛṇā, and likewise to Jātavedas together with Ūrjayantī. (109)

Those men by whom the abandonment of these seventeen [impurities] has been performed on the seventeenth day have effectively performed the ritual cleansing; they have bathed in the waters of the Ganges. 110.
May Indra purify me with good guidance; may Soma purify me with well-being; may Varuṇa purify me with harmony;
may King Yama purify me with those who crush [evil]; may Jātavedas purify me with the *ūrjayantī* plant. 111.
With the hymn "yad devā devaheḍanam" consisting of twenty verses, one should perform the oblation. In that rite, the renunciation (tyāga) belongs to the Ādityas first, and not otherwise. [The mantra:
"O gods, whatever offense against the gods we have committed, O Ādityas, release us from that by means of truth through truth."
Not from me. || 112 ||

In the second [verse], one should say, "To Agni Gārhapatya, not mine"; and according to the Ṛgveda verse, "To Dyāvāpṛthivī and Sarasvatī"—in the third verse, one should utter the formula: "To Dyāvāpṛthivī and Sarasvatī, not mine. || 113 ||

O gods, whatever untruth we have uttered with our speech out of a desire for life, may Agni Gārhapatya release me from that sin and from whatever misdeeds we have committed; may he make me free from blemish.
By Truth, O Heaven and Earth; by Truth, O Sarasvatī, protect our skin.
Guard us from the sin we have committed, whatever falsehood we may have uttered. 115.
To Jātavedas, not to me—thus on the fourth day; and then on the fifth, the renunciation was likewise performed for Agni Gārhapatya. || 116 ||

Whether from a sin committed against one’s own kin, or from a sin against a relative, whether from a greater sin or even from a lesser one— whatever offense has been committed against the gods unknowingly, O Jātavedas, release us from that. 117.
Whatever untruth we have committed with speech, with the mind, with the two arms, with the two thighs, with the knees,
or with the genitals— may Agni Gārhapatya release me from that sin and from whatever misfortunes there are.
Whatever we have done, may he make me free from sin. || 118 ||

One should speak [the offering] for the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* mantras at the sixth and seventh [steps], with the word "bhara" at the sixth and "tyāga" at the seventh; one should speak to Agni Gārhapatya at the ninth and to Agni at the tenth. (119)
Whatever sins I have committed with my two hands while smelling the wealth of mortals—may Dūrepaśyā and Rāṣṭrabhṛt carry them away; may they discharge these debts.

Whatever debt I incurred while not gambling, or whatever I consumed from people while intending to give it away—may Agni Gārhapatya release me from that sin; may he make us free from misfortune and devoid of frailty. 121.

Whatever sin my mother committed while I was in her womb, or whatever my father [committed], may Agni Gārhapatya release me from that transgression and from whatever misdeeds we have done; may he make me free from sin.
When the son, joyfully sucking at the breast, crushed his mother and father—since my parents were not harmed by me, for that reason, O Agni, I become free from debt. 123.
One should recite [the formulas] for Agni Gārhapatya on the tenth and eleventh days; but on the twelfth day, they are for Agni Pathikṛt and for Agni Gārhapatya. 124.

Whatever [sin] I have committed against the atmosphere, the earth, or the sky, or whatever [sin] I have done to my mother or father—may Agni Gārhapatya release me from that transgression; may he free me from whatever misdeeds I have committed, and make me sinless. (125)

Whatever we have done through desire, through negligence, or through excessive desire—whatever sin we have committed, whether new or old—may Agni Gārhapatya release me from that sin; may he free me from whatever misdeeds we have done and make me sinless. 126.

I pass beyond misfortune; I cast off evil and impurity in the highest dwelling-place, where the doers of good go and not the doers of evil—to that world of the virtuous I ascend. The gods cleansed this sin; Trita cleansed it among men. Therefore, if [it should affect] me...
May Gārhapatya, who is free from any sin, release me from that transgression; may he release me from whatever misdeeds we have committed, and may he make me sinless. 128.

On the fourteenth lunar day [and on the fifteenth—that is, on the fourteenth and the fifteenth—there is this statement: "This is not indeed for me from the waters"]; then for two [days], it is for you [the Waters] and for Varuṇa; and on the eighteenth and nineteenth, it is for Agni-Varuṇa. || 129 ||
Those waters born in heaven, those born in the waters, those born from plants, and those born from fire—may they, the purifiers, cleanse us. 130.
Whatever evil we have committed at night, or whatever by day—whether new or old.
Then, O golden-hued ones, purify us. || 131 ||
O Varuṇa, hear this my invocation today; have mercy upon me. Seeking your protection, I call out to you.
I approach you with a sacred prayer, honoring you; the sacrificer, with his oblations, seeks this from you.
O Varuṇa, be mindful of us without anger; do not steal away our long life. 133.
O Agni, you who are wise, may you cause away from us the wrath of the god Varuṇa.

Most excellent in sacrifice, the best of bearers, shining brightly, release from us all those who hate us! O Agni, be such a protector for us with your aids, most near to us at the dawning of this morning.
Be gracious to us, O Varuṇa, being pleased; accept our offering, O merciful one, and be easy for us to invoke. 135.
Then, for Agni, there is the Vaiśvānara hymn consisting of twenty verses;
this group of eight verses dedicated to Agni Vaiśvānara is declared to be the final one. || 136 ||
O Agni, you have been established with this very unwearied mind; bearing the oblation unweariedly, bestow healing upon us. 137.
May Vaiśvānara come to us for our protection from afar; may Agni approach our well-spoken hymns.
We pray for the eternal Dharma—Vaiśvānara, who is true to the cosmic order, the lord of the light of truth. (139)
From the seat of Vaiśvānara, the solitary seer has beheld the great with his far-reaching vision.
Magnifying both his parents, Heaven and Earth, who possess abundant seed, Agni was born.
Sought in heaven, sought on earth, Agni has entered into all plants. Vaiśvānara Agni, sought with power, is our comrade.
May he who protects by day protect [us] by night. || 141 ||
When you were born, O Agni, you surveyed all beings, like a watchful herdsman looking over his cattle.
O Vaiśvānara, find for us the path to Brahman; may you always come to us with blessings.
O Agni, blazing forth with your flame, at your birth you filled the two worlds, heaven and earth.
O Vaiśvānara Jātavedas, by your greatness, you released the gods from the curse. 143.
O Agni, bestow upon us, who are liberal patrons, enduring sovereignty and heroic vigor.
May we win booty consisting of hundreds and thousands, O Agni Vaiśvānara, through your protections. || 144 ||

May the benevolence of Vaiśvānara be for us; he is the king of all beings, the glory of the worlds. Born from here, he beholds this entire universe; as Vaiśvānara, he exerts himself for the sake of the Sun. 145.
Then, having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and having encircled the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), he should take a full water-pot and go to a crossroads in the southwest direction. || 146 ||

Having washed his feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should then, facing eastward together with his wives, observe the auspicious or inauspicious shadow upon that [mirror]. || 147 ||
If my anger is toward a lion, one should then mutter the *premanuvāka* over it; then one should cast [the water] with the mantra: "May the waters and plants be friendly to us. (148)
Afterwards, some water together with a jar should rise up from the ground.
"May those with evil enmity be his—those who hate us and whom we hate. He should cast the water-pot behind him. 149.
In whichever direction his enemy may be, he should cast [the offering] right there;
afterwards, having sipped water, he should then enter his own home. || 150 ||
One should perform this at the three junctions of the day for seven days and observe one's form; when one sees one's reflection clearly in the midst of the water, then it shall become tranquil.
This sacrificer has been well-purified; otherwise, he should perform it again.
Then, having received the words of benediction, he should feed the Brāhmaṇas. || 152 ||
One should observe silence for as long as one performs the ritual action;
one should consume sacrificial food (haviṣya) only once while remaining celibate (brahmacaryabhāk). || 153 ||
Having conquered his senses and sleeping upon the ground, [he was freed] from the evil accumulated in previous births.
He becomes liberated from the one who creates obstacles to the accomplishment of the mantra; it is not otherwise. || 154 ||
Whatever sin has been committed in this life through ignorance or negligence, one should perform oblations with the Kūṣmāṇḍī mantras for the sake of its destruction. || 155 ||
He whose ancestors were steeped in Vedic learning but fell into the Kaulika path due to the fault of [misguided] knowledge, is afflicted by poverty and other such miseries. || 156 ||
If one is constantly tormented by the mind in the pursuit of attaining all happiness, and for the sake of establishing oneself in both worlds, one should also practice that which is secret. (157)
In the case of stealing gold, drinking liquor, killing a cow, murdering a Brahmin, or violating the teacher’s bed,
one should perform this vow for one year.
For theft, for the killing of a fetus, for sexual intercourse with one who is not a wife [or for causing an abortion],
for the emission of semen [in an improper place], for betraying trust, and for misappropriating a deposit [or a trust fund], one should perform ten thousand repetitions.
During the non-attainment of a desired object, during a terrible planetary affliction, during the eclipses of the moon and the sun, in water, or in a temple of Śiva—
Having received the gift, [he gave] ten thousand one by one. || 160 ||
In cases of perjury (or false testimony), usury, extortion, tax collection, and in matters concerning the gods or Brahmins, one should employ the *lakṣa* penance at the end of the period of distress.
In the case of consuming prepared food, approaching a prostitute, slaughtering an animal, or eating food intended for the gods and others [that is,

consuming wealth accumulated for the sake of the gods], or in the omission of the three daily junctions (saṃdhyā), one should shave the hair and beard, bathe in a sacred body of water, and perform [the penance] for one hundred thousand [repetitions] for each day.
And after the portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga), one should perform the oblation with the Kūṣmāṇḍī verses.

And one should daily recite the Sāvitrī and the purificatory mantras (*pavitrāṇi*), such as: "The Gāyatrī with the *vyāhṛtis*: 'Tat savitur vareṇyam... and 'May the divine beings purify me; may the intellects purify me; may all beings purify me; O Jātavedas, do thou purify me. These and other such mantras are the purificatory verses.
And according to one's capacity: a Brāhmaṇa should drink milk, while a Kṣatriya should eat gruel (yavāgū).
[Gruel is prepared by boiling six parts of water; when it has formed thick lumps and is mixed with various thin liquids, it is beneficial for one suffering from fever. 164.
When the Vaiśya is capable, he should consume *āmikṣā*— which is formed by adding curd to heated milk— or he may rely upon boiled rice, parched grain flour, fried grains,
or even clarified butter. (165)

Anything different from this must not be consumed, as previously prescribed for those observing celibacy and other vows. The fire-oblation (homa), however, should be performed with cow's ghee; in its absence, with buffalo ghee.

The first mantra is *yad devāḥ*; one should offer oblations with the mantra "yad devāḥ" (O gods, that which...). Thereafter, one should recite "devebhya āditebhyaḥ" (to the gods, the sons of Aditi). Furthermore, in this same manner, among the recited mantras addressed to Agni, the mention of the names of the gods should be applied.
[This is] *devaheḍanam*. Therein, the offering (*tyāga*) to the gods and the Ādityas is prescribed.

In the second mantra, "to the Viśvedevas" (*viśvebhyo devebhyaḥ*) is stated with the dative case; however, the dative is also expressed [in the sense of the accusative]. As before, the renunciation (*tyāga*) is performed with the instrumental case [in the third mantra:
*dyāvāpṛthivībhyāṃ sarasvatyai ca idaṃ na mama*—this is not mine].
The application [of this rule] is everywhere; and that [mantra] is said to be distinct from the *ṛc*. 168.
O gods, whatever offense against the gods we have committed, O deities...
O Ādityas, therefore release me; by means of truth, deliver me from this through truth. || 169 ||
O gods, whatever untruth we have uttered through our speech out of a desire for life, from that release us here, O Viśvedevas, acting in harmony. 170.
By Truth, O Heaven and Earth; by Truth, O Sarasvatī, protect us from the skin [of sin].
Guard us from the committed sin, whatever falsehood we have uttered. 171.
May there be renunciation unto Indra, Agni, Mitra, Varuṇa, Soma, Dhātṛ, and Bṛhaspati.
That which is now the fourth is called the Ṛk. || 172 ||
Indra and Agni, Mitra and Varuṇa, Soma, Dhātṛ, and Bṛhaspati—may they release us from that sin, whatever falsehood we have uttered. 173.

From a kinsman of equal birth, from a kinsman of equal lineage, or from a superior kinsman, or from an inferior kinsman— whatever sin has been committed unknowingly against us by the gods, from that, O Jātavedas, deliver us; this [is for] Jātavedas, and not indeed mine.
The fifth [vow] is considered to be as previously stated; or else, that which was previously proclaimed as the sixth is "whatever by speech" and "whatever by mind. 174.
The renunciation "Not for Jyotis, mine"; that is declared for the seventh [tithi]. Likewise, the renunciation "Not for Agni, mine" is stated for the eighth. || 175 ||
By which Trita was brought from the waters, and by which he released the sun from darkness.
By that light through which Indra drove away all enemies, by that light of lights, may I attain you, O Eye. 176.
Whatever debt remains unpaid by me here, on account of which I wander as one who owes a treasure to Yama.
O Agni, thus I become free from debt to you; even while living, I restore this to you. || 177 ||
The ninth oblation is that which was previously mentioned as "O Mother, in me," performed as before; the tenth oblation is that which was previously mentioned as "He went to his mother. (178)
The intermediate space and the earth were previously mentioned; this constitutes the eleventh oblation.
When the twelve oblations previously mentioned here were offered with the *yadāśasā* and *niśasā* formulas, [the result was as follows]. || 179 ||

Then, at the beginning of that, there are three Ṛg-verses; thus there are fifteen oblations. "yadāpo naktam" (when the waters [gather] at night) shall be the sixteenth, as previously mentioned. || 180 ||
The renunciation [of the offering] is prescribed in those waters which are golden-hued. The five verses beginning with "imamme varuṇa" have been previously mentioned. || 181 ||
By that renunciation, twenty-one oblations are prescribed; the renunciation for Indra and Agni is the twenty-second, and that Ṛk is now being stated. || 182 ||
O Ugrampaśyā, you who sustain the kingdom, take away these sins: whatever occurred in the gambling match that was not rightfully given.
Therefore, being weighed against his debts and credits, he is bound by a cord in the world of Yama.
"Adīvyaṃ nṛṇaṃ yad aham... and so forth—these six [verses] are as before. Then, here, there is the renunciation of two: "Not indeed for me, but for Varuṇa. (184)
O Varuṇa, we entreat you with homage, with sacrifices, and with oblations for your favor. O Asura, O King of keen insight, loosen for us the bonds of these deeds that have been committed. 185.
Loosen the highest bond of Varuṇa from us, and the lowest, and the middle one as well.
Now, O Āditya, under your law, may we be sinless before Aditi. || 186 ||

In the thirty-first [verse], regarding Śaṅkuśuka, Vikuśuka, Nirṛtha, and Niḥsvana, the abandonment [of disease] is taught; that is now declared by means of this *ṛc*: "Śaṅkuśuka, Vikuśuka, Nirṛtha, and Niḥsvana—those [diseases] which, being innocent, have attacked us..."
They have driven it far, even further away.

Then, in the two [subsequent offerings], there is a renunciation (tyāga) to Agni and Tvaṣṭṛ; in the one immediately following that, a renunciation to Āyuṣmān Agni is prescribed as the thirty-fifth. || 188 ||
Drive away your consumption, as well as your sorcery and destruction. With that [remedy], we drive away whoever seeks to encounter us. 189.
One should [recite] the *duḥśagūṃ* and *sānuśagūṃ* mantras, together with the *ghaṇa* and *anughaṇa*.
Therefore, may both [worlds] come together for us; we offer excellent offspring to him. || 190 ||
With splendor, with glory, and with our bodies, we have come together with a mind that is helpful and auspicious.
May Tvaṣṭṛ provide us with wealth here; may he now smooth over whatever in our bodies is injured.
Bestowing life upon you from every side, may this Agni be most excellent for you; your breath returns to you again—I drive away the consumption from you. 192.
The renunciation for the lifespan and the fire-offering (agnityāga) take place in the thirty-sixth year and the one immediately following it.
To Agni, Varuṇa, Aditi, and the Viśvedevas. || 194 ||
Bestowing long life upon Agni, partaking of the oblation, you who have ghee as your face and ghee as your womb, be present.
Having drunk the ghee and honey from the beautiful cow, protect this man now as a father protects his son.
O Varuṇa, bestow long life and splendor upon him who is immersed [in this]; sharpen his keen vigor together with the *sagū*.
O Mother Aditi, grant us protection like a mother; O All-Gods, may we reach old age. || 196 ||
The offering to Agni Pavamāna is performed in the three [verses] consisting of thirty-eight [syllables];
thereafter, the offering to Agni Jātavedas is said to be in two [verses]. || 197 ||
O Agni, bestow upon us long lives and strength; bring us nourishment and food, and drive far away those who seek to harm us. 198.
O Agni, purify yourself for him with your own splendor and heroic vigor.
Bestowing upon me wealth and nourishment. || 199 ||

O Agni, the seer, the purifying one, the priest of the five peoples—him, the possessor of great wealth, we implore. O Agni, Jātavedas, drive away the enemies already born and repel those yet unborn; shine upon us with a gracious mind, free from anger.
May we abide in your triple-layered protection, O Source of Emergence.
O Jātavedas, driving away our rivals born with great heroism and power, drive away those yet unborn.
Speaking for us with a well-disposed mind, may we be victors, driving away our rivals. 202.
For the forty-third [day], it is "agnaye vṛtraghne"; then again, for the forty-fourth, it is "agnaye," and for the forty-fifth, it should be "uṣase nimuce. || 203 ||
The Agni-born people from all sides—the wolf and the she-wolf—seek to kill us.
O slayer of Vṛtra, strike them down and bring wealth to us. 204.
O Agni, whoever seeks to harm us—whether he be one of our own kin or a stranger—we make him into fuel and offer him up to you, O Agni. 205.
May Dawn and Night both sweep away the mass of all the evils of him who curses us when we do not curse, and him who curses us when we do not curse. (206)
In the forty-sixth [chapter], there is the renunciation [of offerings] to the gods, and in the one following that.
Then there should be the renunciation (tyāga) to Jātavedas and Agni, and subsequently to Agni. || 207 ||
O gods, whatever rival or mortal enemy assails us, let not a trace of him remain, just as nothing is left of fuel that has been consumed by fire. 208.
O Jātavedas, whoever hates me, and whoever I hate, and whoever hates him;
O Agni, burn up all those bonds—both the bonds that I hate and those that hate me.
Whoever acts with hostility toward us, whoever hates us, and whoever reviles us—from all directions, drive them all far away from us. || 210 ||

It is prescribed for a learned Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires, for one who is fifty years of age, for one even older than that, and likewise for the youngest, as well as for Vaiśvānara. || 211 ||
Sharpened is my sacred knowledge; sharpened is my heroic strength.
Sharpened is my victorious sovereignty, for whom I am the domestic priest.
I have raised up their arms, their luster, and their strength; with my sacred word (*brahman*), I destroy the enemies and I exalt my own people. 213.
May my mind come back to me; may my life-span come back to me; may my sight come back to me; may my hearing come back to me.
May my breath come back to me; may my intention come back to me; may my thought come back to me; may my resolve come back to me. 214.
"May Vaiśvānara, the purifier of the body, burn away all my misfortunes.
Having offered the oblation in this manner, one should then stand facing north with fuel-sticks in hand and praise the fire from the south with twelve verses.

We announce this to Vaiśvānara: if we have been debtors or have failed to fulfill our agreements among the gods, may he, who knows how to release these bonds, release us from misfortune and blame. 217.
May Vaiśvānara purify us with his purifiers, as I hasten toward the battle and my desire.
Whatever offense I have committed here through ignorance or by begging with my mind, that I now fully confess. 218.
O fortunate one, these stars in the sky known as the *vṛttas*—may they grant this [liberation], for here is the release from bound desire. (219)
Desire to leave the worlds; loosen your bonds and release what is bound. Like an embryo released from the womb, follow after all things as they are.
Knowing this, let the wise one respond; Prajāpati is the first-born of Cosmic Order.
One should follow that unbroken thread given by us beyond old age;
however, some do not follow that thread for those to whom the ancestral offering has been given as their path.
To those who give to the friendless, who bestow gifts and are able to give—may heaven be theirs!
You two, O Aśvins, protect them; you two, following the path of the Ṛbhus, protect them with ghee upon the common way.

Whatever meritorious work you have performed, whatever has been offered, or whatever has been cast into the fire—for that [deed], O ye two, may you attain the state of being joined with a wife here. || 223 ||

Whatever [sin] we have committed against the intermediate space, the earth, or the sky, or whatever [sin] we have committed against our mother or father—may Agni Gārhapatya release me from that transgression; may he make me free from whatever misdeeds we have done, and render me sinless. 224.
The earth is our mother, Aditi our place of birth; the atmosphere is our brother, our protector against curses.
Like the sky, you are our father; from the father’s path, may you be auspicious to us. Do not seek to exclude us from this world.
Where the well-disposed doers of good rejoice, having left behind disease by means of their own bodies.
"O gods, may we behold our father and son there in heaven with limbs unimpaired and wonderful;
whatever food I eat, whether I shall give it or not give it, or whether I shall perform it or not perform it, [may that be for you]."
Whatever debt I have toward the gods, and whatever I have accepted as a gift—may Agni make me free from that debt. || 227 ||
Whatever food, even in many forms, clothing, gold, or cattle— cow, goat, or sheep— that has come into my possession as an offering to the gods,
and whatever else I have accepted as a gift, may Agni make me free from debt for that. 228.
Having thus worshipped the fire, one should offer a fuel-stick held in the hand with the mantra to be mentioned hereafter; this is indeed the renunciation (tyāga) for Vaiśvānara. || 229 ||
Whatever sin has ever been committed by me through mind or speech—from all that, O Agni, deliver me; for you know everything exactly as it is. Svāhā! 230.
Thereafter, one should perform the recitation of mantras (japa) and the fire sacrifice (homa); this has been described as the atonement that wards off the sins committed in this life. (231)

This has been stated regarding the twice-born; now it is being told for the Śūdras: On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, having performed his daily rites and being pure, [he should proceed]. || 232 ||
On the ninth day, one should likewise practice eating a single meal consisting of sacrificial food (haviṣya); on the tenth day, eating what is unasked for (ayācita);
and on the eleventh day, fasting. || 233 ||

Having performed the shaving of the head on the twelfth lunar day, one should worship the Brahmins and the deities, reciting the mantra beginning with one's own chosen seed-syllable and ending with "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa. (234)

Having received the eight-syllable mantra from the mouth of a guru, one should perform its recitation; eating the remnants of the twice-born's meal and devoted to his service, one should recite it eight hundred thousand times.

One should perform the recitation until midday, sleeping on the ground and observing celibacy; when the recitation is complete, one becomes free from sin, but if it is not, one should perform it again.
I shall now describe the signs of being free from sin here, as well as those pertaining to the previously mentioned fire-offerings (homa).
On the day the sacrifice and other rites begin, [one should prepare] a firm, unblemished vessel made of clay.
One should bring a pure water-pot and place it on a clean spot.
Into that [vessel], one should pour water measured by a jar, originating from sacred fords and other such sources.
One should place cow's urine from Śṛṅgala Island in a glass vessel; one should perform the worship of Hari and Hara with one pala each of these two. || 239 ||
On the day of examination, having performed worship, one should pray to that water:
"The waters are Nārāyaṇa himself; everything is established in the waters. (240)
"By that truth, may my sin be destroyed and may true knowledge be yours.
Having thus prayed over the water, he should then offer a handful of flowers. (241)
One should see the reflection of one's own body in water as well as in a liquid; if it is seen in the liquid just as it is in the water, then the sin has departed.
When the reflection in the water becomes dim, then indeed the sin has not departed; therefore, one should perform an expiation so that the reflection may become perfectly clear. (243)

Thus, one's sins are destroyed, and one becomes a possessor of the success (*siddhi*) resulting from the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*). If any Vedic mantra, even one consisting of a hundred million syllables, is recited [in this manner], [the same result follows]. (244)
The name-mantra destroys the sin committed in a single lifetime; that of Viṣṇu and myself, Gaṇeśa, and the Sun destroys half of that. || 245 ||
The practitioner of Tantra destroys evil, while the ordinary person destroys half of it, and the student destroys a quarter.
The *apadaṃśa* is half of that; this is concealed everywhere. || 246 ||
I shall describe the places for recitation, both artificial and natural, which are kept secret in all the tantras for each respective deity. (247)
Māpura, on the bank of the Narmadā, is the field of Mahāgaṇapati; it is a great cremation ground (mahāśmaśāna) and Māpura bestows the supernatural powers (siddhi) of Gaṇeśa. || 248 ||
Prabhāsa, Kurukṣetra, Puṣkara, and Bhṛguparvata.
On the bank of the Yamunā at Kāśī, the Sun-god bestows success upon his devotees.
Ayodhyā, Mathurā, Māyā, Kāśī, Badarikāśrama, Gayā, the banks of the Gaṇḍakī, and Dvārakā bestow the perfection of Viṣṇu. || 250 ||
Kedāra, Tryambaka, Kāśī, Kāñcī, Avantī, and the forests; the banks of the Gaṅgā, Vaidyanātha, and Rāmeśa, who bestows the perfection of Śiva. || 251 ||
Jvālāmukhī, Prayāga, Kāminī, and the station of Mālikā.
Likewise, the bank of the Sarasvatī brings about the accomplishment of Śākta mantras.
And on the shore of Kamaleśvarī, there is the solitary Yakṣa mountain.
And the regions of Aṅga, Vaṅga, and Kaliṅga bestow the attainment of minor deities. || 253 ||
Kāmarūpa, that place, Hiṅgulā, Vindhyavāsinī, Jālandhara, and Pūrṇagiri are the bestowers of perfection upon the path of the left (vāmamārga). || 254 ||
And the shores of lotus-pools, as well as groves of plantains, sugarcane, and Arka trees.
The region abounding in coral is exceedingly dear to Gaṇeśa. || 255 ||
Then there was that forest of lotuses, as well as groves of oleanders and sunflowers.
Fields of wheat and dūrvā grass, and stones, are dear to the Sun. || 256 ||

In the vicinity of tulasī, aśvattha, dhātrī, sugarcane, śālagrāma, and the like; in a cow-pen, in a village of śrotriyas, or in the presence of one who delights in the Vedas—[these are places for worship]. (257)
In a temple of Śiva where the linga faces west—excluding that of Nandin—at the bank of the Śiva-tīrtha, near a banyan tree, at a confluence, in a forest, or by a lake; || 258 ||
In the forests of *sevantī* and *carcarī* flowers, near the plantain and mango trees, on the banks of the river known as Granthā, there is joy for Śakti in solitude. (259)
At the edge of a pond, in places thick with nimba, kola, śākhoṭa, and madhūka trees, on an anthill, and at a dried-up river, the minor deities (kṣudradevatās) rejoice. (260)
In the father’s house, in the cremation ground, at the triple-pathway, and at the crossroads; in an empty abode or a place strewn with corpses—there the Vāmakas find satisfaction. || 261 ||
In the house, in the cow-pen, likewise in a garden, on a mountain peak, by a river, at a confluence of rivers, or in a temple—the Vedic [rite] shall be superior. || 262 ||
In whatever land there is neither the killing of cows nor the slaying of Brahmins, and where Śūdras do not cause [the Vedas] to be heard, there indeed is Vedic success.
Barbarians, heretics, rogues, kings, ministers, and so forth.
And young women do not frequent that place; there, success is not far off. || 264 ||
One should not dwell in ruined temples, gardens, houses, or trees; nor by rivers, on riverbanks or mountain slopes, nor in cavities in the earth and similar places. || 265 ||
In this manner, the wise preceptor should perform the acquisition of the ground, having worshipped the Earth as Varāha and with the assistance of the son of the Earth (Mangala). || 266 ||
One should say: "For the sake of accomplishing the *puraścaraṇa* of such-and-such a mantra, I accept this ground; may this mantra be perfected. || 267 ||
[One should take] those produced from any one of these trees: the nyagrodha, milk, sasya, or sthava.
One should take ten round pegs, each measuring one *vitasti* in length.

One should drive eight [stakes] into the eight directions starting from the northeast (Īśāna) and proceeding eastward; furthermore, one should bury a ninth in the center with the thought that it is above, and likewise one below.
