Afterwards, one should nail down the yantra with the Astra-mantra in the space between the southwest and the west. || 269 ||

One should perform worship with the weapon-mantra and likewise worship the weapon within them; when the field has been thus pinned down by the mantra-practitioner, he is not overcome by obstacles. || 270 ||
One should offer an oblation of black gram and rice to the guardians of the quarters in the various directions; and in the center of the field, one should worship Kṣetrapāla and Gaṇeśvara. || 271 ||

One should offer the third triple oblation (balitraya) to the Vāstupuruṣa and those [deities] at the end; then, having taken one's station in the middle of the site, one should examine the tortoise-diagram (kūrmacakra). || 272 ||
For one who is ignorant of the tortoise-chakra, great obstacles arise.
The tortoise is of four kinds, distinguished by its being in a foreign land, a village, or a house. || 273 ||

One should construct two squares divided into nine compartments. The seven classes of consonants, beginning with the *ka*-group, should be written starting from the eastern direction, with the two *la*-sounds [placed] at the end. (274)
In the northeast, one should draw two by two [squares] within the central circle;
the vowels are to be written starting from the east, and the seed-syllable of Śrī (Śrī-bīja) is to be placed in the central square.
The outer tortoise is always born facing the east; it is the foremost region among all lands, situated in whichever direction [it faces]. || 276 ||
In that direction, there should be the face of the village-tortoise; however, two faces are to be understood, namely from the vowels and likewise from the consonants. (277)
The face of the house-tortoise should be where the door of the house is located;
on both sides of the face are the forelimbs, and the belly and feet extend from there in their respective directions. (278)

One [digit] is in the tail, then one in the middle, and one in the back; thus it possesses six limbs. In the state of great enmity there is loss of life, and in hostility there is destruction of wealth. (279)
Now, the slight reduction of pleasure resulting from various forms of enmity is being described: *aga*, *ṛccha*, *ḷpa*, *jāha*, *paṣa*, *ena*, *ira*, and *ula*. (280)
Pha-dha-u, bha-ra-u, ya-sa-u, and ce-ti are proclaimed as the great *mahārīs*.
Ja-cha-u, o-ṭū, ya-ḍau, gā-dau, ja-ṭau, rā-khau, bu-dhau, and ra-lau [are likewise]. || 281 ||
In the fifth section, there is enmity; that [enmity] occurs between the letters *ka* and *ya*, as well as between *ca* and *ṭa*, *pa* and *ca*, *ta* and *ra*, and *ra* and *la*. (282)
There is supreme joy in one's own group; therefore, double your own group.
It is said that this, when added to the group of positions and divided by eight, is [the remainder]. || 283 ||

The place-value (sthāna) is doubled and increased by its own square; the remainder when divided by eight is to be assigned to both places. Whichever has the greater remainder is considered superior. || 284 ||

As long as it remains [in its proper place], that [mark] is a giver of wealth; however, if it is misplaced, it does not grant wealth to the practitioner. Success in all matters occurs when it is on the face; minor successes occur when it is on the two hands. If it is on the waist, there is no gain at all; if on the feet or the tail, it signifies death. (285)
One should not contemplate the abode of Kūrma at Kurukṣetra, Prayāga, the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, Mahākāla, or Kāśī. || 286 ||
If even a single initial syllable of the mantras for accomplishing a field (kṣetra) should exist, that mantra will certainly bestow the fruit of all accomplishments. || 287 ||
Amṛta, Vṛṣabha, Śailarāja, and Vāsuki as well.
One who possesses strength should first worship [the deity] in wood and other materials that are capable of fulfilling one's purpose. || 288 ||
One should also place Padmayoni, Mahāśaṅkha, and Chāyā in the middle.
Having constructed a house upon the back of a tortoise, the householder should perform his recitation of prayers (japa).
Now I shall explain the garland; it is of two kinds: stable and moving. The stable [garland] is for those of steady mind, while the moving one is for those of flickering consciousness. (290)
With the letters of the Mātṛkā alphabet, beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa', accompanied by the Bindu.
By means of a garland of syllables fashioned from those situated in both direct and reverse order.
The individual mantras and the pair-mantras should be recited; they bestow all accomplishments. || 291 ||
Furthermore, the Ṛgveda and others, as well as the Sthiramālikā, have been proclaimed by others.

The garland of syllables is said to begin with the letter 'a' and end with the letter 'kṣa'. During the recitation, one hundred and eight repetitions should be performed, followed by the addition of the [mantra] syllable.

Now, the movement of the rosary in the practice of *abhicāra* is described: for the sake of liberation, one should always recite with twenty-five [beads], and for [other purposes] with those numbering the lunar days (fifteen). || 293 ||
The increase of the thirtyfold dharma shall be fifty-four times the desired amount.
From one hundred [recitations] there is equality; likewise, from one hundred and eight, all supernatural powers (siddhis) are attained. || 294 ||
Rudrākṣa beads are considered to grant all perfections and bestow wealth.
The conch brings about the recovery of what has been lost and the acquisition of wealth; crystal is considered to bestow enjoyments. (295)
Those made of coral grant sons and increase prosperity;
those made of pearls are considered to bestow liberation. (296)
Those made of kuśa grass destroy sins, while those made of gold grant all desires.
The increase of desire is achieved through the *tāra* seeds and *indrākṣa* beads; with silver, there is the accomplishment of desired objects.
This is the verse on a favorable reception (*svāgata*). 297.
For the purpose of subjugating women, turmeric is used; for subjugating men, it is made with dārvī.
Lakṣā destroys fever, while conch-shell brings satisfaction to the ancestors. (298)
The worship of the Sun should be performed with *arka* flowers for the purpose of eradication, and with *śrīphala* fruits for the attainment of knowledge.
One made from Padmaka wood is for satisfaction; one made from Devadāru wood is for Nirukti.

Tāmasa action is accomplished with [implements] produced from black wood; for all purposes, those made of ivory are considered suitable, while those made of copper are intended for the purpose of deluding.
For killing, one made of iron is prescribed; for the sake of wealth, one born from a white lotus; for poison, one arising from sandalwood; and for a spear, one made of white wood. (301)
In the practice for achieving the Yakṣiṇīs and others, [the seed-syllables] arise from red sandalwood. || 302 ||

A pillar made of *nimba* wood for a spirit pillar, and one made of *śamī* wood for a human pillar; with *mahānimba* (known in the vernacular as *baka*), *ḍākinīs*, and *bhūnimbas* (*tiktaka*), there is the immobilization of diseases. 303.
From the Indra-tree comes the debt-stump; from the monkey comes the malevolent rite (abhicāra); from the bear comes success in the forest;
and the tiger is its presiding deity. || 304 ||
Rākṣasas are brought under control by human bones, and heroes are brought under control by horse bones.
With the bone of a donkey, one attains minor supernatural powers; with the bones of an elephant, however, one gains honor.
A rosary made of gems set in clay brings success for the Śabaras; a Brahmin should recite with knots of Kuśa grass, and a king with beads of gold. (306)
A Vaiśya should recite with *putrajīva* seeds, while indeed everyone may use lotus seeds.
One should not place anything at all between the rudrākṣa, the crystal, and the indrākṣa. || 307 ||
Placing [the beads] in the middle while reciting the mantra, one destroys both desire and liberation; on the fourth day, one should string the rosary with the mantras of Gaṇanātha.
At midday on the seventh lunar day, or on a Sunday, with his mantras.
On the twelfth lunar day, the Vaiṣṇava rosary should indeed be strung with the mantra of Viṣṇu.
On the thirteenth day, at the twilight hour, one should offer a garland to Śiva with those mantras.
On the eighth, the fourteenth, or the ninth lunar day, O son of the Earth.
The rosary for the Śaktis should also be made according to the prescribed rule on a bright night;
it should be strung with silk thread for the pleasure of the Goddess. (311)
That Vaiṣṇava garland should indeed be made from either [lotus fibers] or from silk threads.
Or with wool, or with bark-fibers, or with threads of *śaivī* cotton. || 312 ||
Listen now to the procedure for the production of the thread for almost all the deities:
the thread should be spun by a meritorious woman of the best of the twice-born and must be free from knots. (313)
Having tripled the threefold [thread] and carefully washed it, it should be taken up.
With one face, two faces, four faces, and five faces;
Or alternatively, they may be made with six faces; however, one should avoid mixing them with one another.
Having joined face to face, one should join back to back;
the face of the rudrākṣa is said to be elevated, while the back is depressed. || 316 ||
The best is equal to an āmalaka fruit; the middling is like a jujube berry.
The lowest [type] has the appearance of chickpeas; inferior even to that, it brings about calamity. || 317 ||
One Meru is to be given there, which is situated everywhere and joined with the small; first the gross, then from that smaller, and then smaller still. || 318 ||
One should fashion it in the shape of a serpent at each *brahmagranthi* bead; alternatively, it may be without knots, provided it is equipped with a firm wheel. || 319 ||
Then, by winding it three times around the middle and once below from left to right, a knot that turns clockwise is called the Brahma-knot. || 320 ||

Having first observed a single meal, the practitioner himself should string [the beads]; having performed his daily rites, being pure and unwearied, he should work with the aforementioned beads. || 321 ||

White, red, golden-hued, and black—these [beads] are for the twice-born and others respectively; among these, the white bead is most excellent for the purpose of making a rosary for recitation. || 322 ||
In the absence of twice-born men, however, those of their own respective castes may be used; for in the Kali age, a Brahmin who abides by his own duty is as difficult to find as a Brahmin at all.
A rudrākṣa that is too large, too small, cracked, fragile, light, split, previously worn, or decayed is considered inauspicious. || 324 ||
From rubbing them against one another, the loss of the recitation (japa) will certainly occur. Knots should be made in the middle; one should not place pearls or other such gems therein. || 325 ||
Śiva has one face; his rosary removes the sins of killing a Brahmin and other such evils for one who recites it, and likewise grants the desires of his devotees and others. 326.
This two-faced [image] named Umā-Śaṅkara removes sins such as the killing of a cow and bestows happiness upon the householder stage of life. || 327 ||
The three-faced one, who has the form of fire, destroys sins such as the killing of a woman.
Dharma, artha, and kāma are accomplished through its retention and even through its recitation.
One becomes four-faced Brahmā, the destroyer of sins such as the killing of a preceptor; all sciences flash forth, and the perfection of speech (vāksiddhi) is also attained. || 329 ||
Śiva, the five-faced one, is manifestly the remover of all sins.
For those of the Śaiva, Gāṇeśa, and Śākta traditions, success in the fire-oblation comes from the recitation of that [mantra].

Kārttikeya, who has six faces and destroys the sin of faltering from one's vows, grants victory in battle through the wearing [of his image] on the right arm according to the prescribed rite. || 331 ||
Then, by the recitation of that [mantra] of the great serpent named Ananta, who has seven mouths, infinite accomplishments are attained, and death from snake venom does not occur. || 332 ||
Gaṇeśa shall be eight-faced, the warder-off of all obstacles; by the recitation of his mantra, all enemies such as desire, anger, and the like, are destroyed. || 333 ||
Bhairava shall have nine faces; the deities who abide on the Vāmamārga become propitiated through recitation alone, as does Oghahā, who resides on the left arm.
Janārdana and the ten-faced Rāvaṇa perish through recitation and through its retention.
Piśācas, grahas, vetālas, brahmarākṣasas, and pannagas. || 335 ||
By wearing this, one becomes Rudra himself with eleven faces;
and through its recitation, one becomes a partaker of the fruits of horse sacrifices and other such rites. || 336 ||
By the retention [of this mantra] and by its recitation, one becomes twelve-faced like the Sun;
one becomes radiant and majestic, and shall partake in the fruit of a horse-sacrifice (gomedha). || 337 ||

He is remembered as having thirteen faces and being the manifest essence of all the Viśvedevas; when held during the time of a Śrāddha ceremony, he grants the ancestors an imperishable state. || 338 ||
Chanted with fourteen faces, it becomes infinite;
one is honored by gods and men and attains an imperishable state. || 339 ||

Now I shall describe the form of the garland; one should wash it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). [The milk] should be from a golden-colored cow, and the cow dung from a white cow. || 340 ||
The cow's urine should be from a copper-colored cow, and the curd from a blue-colored one; the ghee should be from a black-colored cow, and the same applies to the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
Cows of various colors are easily found in many regions; from among them, one should collect the five products of the cow according to their respective colors. || 342 ||
There is no fault in the loss of color (varṇa), but one should avoid that which is deficient in measure (mātrā).
One should give cow urine twice the amount of cow dung, and ghee four times the amount.
Milk is said to have eight qualities, and likewise curd and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Taking cow’s urine with the *Gāyatrī*: [Oṃ tat savitur vareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi | dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt ||] Taking cow dung with the verse beginning "gandhadvārā":
[gandhadvārāṃ durādharṣāṃ nityapuṣṭāṃ karīṣiṇīm ||]
[I invoke here Śrī, the sovereign of all beings. Cow-dung. 344.
"May you swell" (āpyāyasva): "May strength come to you from every side; may your virility increase."
"Be present at the gathering of strength," and "The milk and curd of Kāvya"—this indeed refers to the curd.
You are splendor—[you are splendor; you are seed, you are nectar; protect my life! "Seed" refers to clarified butter.
[In the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan—with the healing medicine of the Aśvins, I sprinkle you for the sake of splendor and spiritual luster.]

With the healing power of Sarasvatī, for vigor and the enjoyment of food, I sprinkle you; with the sensory power of Indra, for strength, prosperity, and glory, I sprinkle you—upon you, with water infused with Kuśa grass. 345.
One should wash it with the five products of the cow and other substances while reciting the *sadyojāta* and other mantras:
"I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutations again and again to Sadyojāta. In every birth, in non-birth, and beyond birth, be my protection; salutations to Bhavodbhava."

With the scents of sandalwood, agallochum, and so forth, one should worship with the Vāmadeva mantra: "Salutation to Vāmadeva, salutation to Jyeṣṭha, salutation to Śreṣṭha, salutation to Rudra, salutation to Kāla, salutation to Kalavikaraṇa, salutation to Balavikaraṇa, salutation to Bala."
Salutation to Balapramathana; salutation to Sarvabhūtadamana; salutation to Manonmana.
One should rub [the powder]. || 346 ||

One should also fumigate with black agallochum and guggulu using the mantra known as Tatpuruṣa: "To those who are not terrible, and to those who are terrible, and to those more terrible than the most terrible;
to all you Rudras, who are the lords of all, let there be salutation to your forms.
And with the mantra of Tatpuruṣa: "To Tatpuruṣa..."
We know [thee], we meditate upon Mahādeva; may that Rudra inspire us.
One should smear [the image] with sandalwood paste and other substances. || 347 ||

"Īśānaḥ [Īśāna, the lord of all sciences, the lord of all beings, the sovereign of Brahman, the overlord of Brahman; may Śiva, the auspicious one, be mine; Sadāśivom!]"—one should recite this mantra for each [of the items], saying "all," a hundred times. By that very [means].
One should consecrate Mount Meru and likewise consecrate it with the Aghora mantra.
Now I shall describe another method for consecrating a rosary, using the leaves of the Aśvattha tree.
When it has been established there in the shape of a lotus with nine [parts], one should deposit [the mantras]. || 349 ||
Then, having washed the gem-string with scented water, one should consecrate each individual gem in sequence with the letters of the Mātṛkā preceded by "Oṃ Hrīṃ. (350)

Having placed the sūtra there and performed worship, one should then offer oblations with sesame seeds and so forth, or with clarified butter alone, using the mantras beginning with Sadyojāta and the others individually. || 351 ||
One should perform [the rite] one hundred times, or eight times, or twenty-eight times, with the five mantras.
In the absence of fire-offerings (homa), recitation (japa) is prescribed; one should then rotate the rosary.
It should be made like a cow’s tail, or single-pointed, or with a central ridge.
Thereafter, one should display the eight mudrās beginning with the invocation (āvāhana).
The washing and other rites are performed as before with the mantras beginning with Sadyojāta. || 353 ||
In the Kaulika and other traditions, this is the distinction: the satisfaction of the *maṇi* with wine;
furthermore, there is a garland of thirty-six [heads] and a necklace of thirty-two [heads]. (354)
Sixteen are said to be at the elbows, and thirty-two at the wrists.
An upper garment (upavīta) provided with one hundred and eight [strings] is prescribed. || 355 ||
Half of that [number] for the chest, one is said for the crest-lock, and six for the two ears; thus the sequence of wearing [the garland] is declared. || 356 ||
One should not wear fewer than the prescribed number, nor is it a fault to have more. By wearing Rudrākṣa in this manner, one becomes Śiva at the end of the body. || 357 ||
One obtains abundant merit and is born fortunate in this world through bathing, giving, recitation, burnt offerings, the Vaiśvadeva rite, and the worship of the gods. || 358 ||
Likewise, during rites of expiation, at a śrāddha ceremony, and especially at the time of initiation.
And having become a wearer of rudrākṣa beads, whatever Vedic rite one performs, [it becomes fruitful]. || 359 ||
Whatever action a learned brahmin constantly performs shall become fruitful if he wears [the sacred thread] around his neck, on his head, on his hand, on his ears, or as an upper garment. || 360 ||
By the mere wearing of rudrākṣas, a human becomes Rudra, even while eating meat, drinking liquor, or associating with those born of the lowest castes. || 361 ||
One who wears a rudrākṣa on the head becomes instantly purified in soul.
Those Vedic animals which nourish the gods are themselves deities in this regard. || 362 ||
For those who kill these [beings] in the Kaula tradition, this Yama is their teacher;
for the sake of protecting them, there is nothing else on earth besides the rudrākṣa. || 363 ||
Rudrākṣas bestow the accomplishment of mantras for all the gods. If a pig dies with a rudrākṣa resting upon its neck, [it attains liberation]. || 364 ||

Even he attains Rudra; how much more so then humans and others? Whether one is impure, engaged in forbidden acts, or bound by all manner of sins, a man is liberated from all evils by wearing the rudrākṣa beads. (365)
One who is devoid of devotion should wear a rosary of rudrākṣa beads around the neck.
Even one who has committed evil deeds is eternally honored in the world of Rudra.
If even a Brahmin, out of ignorance, performs any Vedic rite while not wearing rudrākṣa beads, he does not obtain the fruit thereof. (367)
The consecration of a garland is prescribed for the sake of a Śūdra and for the sake of women.
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, Viṣṇu, Īśa, and Durgā with devotion, || 368 ||
Then, that very garland should be consecrated with the *krom* seed-syllable.
One should place it in the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) for three days, reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.

But on the fourth day, having gathered [the materials] together, one should wash them with the Astra-mantra; having tied them with a knot using the Hṛdaya-mantra, one should place them upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila). || 370 ||
There, one should place the washed garland in a golden vessel, having bathed it with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and with cool water. || 371 ||
Then the practitioner should perform the consecration with fragrant sandalwood, musk, saffron, and other substances, using the *ha sauṃ* mantra. || 372 ||
Having worshipped the nine planets, one should also worship the guardians of the directions.

Then, one should perform oblations according to one's ability with sesame seeds mixed with ghee; furthermore, one should give as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor gold equal in weight to the number of gems. || 374 ||
One should feed Brahmins who are reciters of that mantra or those learned in the Vedas; in the absence of gold leaves, a leaf of the Aśvattha tree may be used. || 375 ||
The consecration of the rosary is said to be the recitation that bestows spiritual accomplishment.
Of those belonging to the Kīkasādi lineages, the Kaulikas, and the Vāmins. || 376 ||
For the sake of accomplishment, I shall describe the consecration rite hidden in all tantras. First, one should worship the artisan with garments, perfumes, and ointments. (377)
Being well-pleased, he should have a garland made, and he should drink honey purified by mantras.
One should prepare [a device] with fifty jewels and insert it into the vulva of a menstruating woman.
Having set aside one night, he should then wash those gems.
One should consecrate [the disciple] with pure water and the juices of vijayā while reciting the root mantra. || 379 ||
Having washed it, one should subsequently fumigate it and thread it with desired cords;
for one's own desired recitation, the cord should be blue, and black for the rite of killing.
For subduing, it is green; for paralyzing, it has the appearance of smoke; for causing enmity, it is the color of a crow;
for pacification and nourishment, it is white; and for inciting hatred, it should be red.
Yellow is for subjugation, while astringent is considered for causing distraction.
Then, having performed the wheel-worship one thousand and eight times,
And with meat, wine, and parched grain, the practitioner [should worship] with the root mantra. || 382 ||

Then, one should cause the bali offering to be presented according to the rules for the buffalo and other animals; furthermore, one should feed as many artisans and practitioners as there are gems. || 383 ||
Having thus properly cleansed the rosary, he should present it to the Guru; with whichever mantra that rosary was made, he should recite that [mantra] with it. || 384 ||
From the recitation of another mantra, a curse from the deity arises; one should fasten a firm thread and perform the recitation while remaining restrained. || 385 ||
When the thread has worn out, one should knot a new thread and recite the mantra one hundred times.
One should not touch the thread with the index finger, nor should one shake or agitate it. || 386 ||
One should not touch [the rosary] with the left hand, nor should one allow it to slip from the hand. When moving the beads, the thumb should not touch the other bead. 387.
At the time of recitation, the wise one should never violate the mantra; at the time of turning [the pages], he should never cause a clashing of sounds. || 388 ||
If there is a rattling sound like "khaṭakhaṭa" or if it sways, there is death while moving; if it moves [otherwise], there is enmity; and if it cracks, the occurrence of disease. || 389 ||

If it falls from the hand, there is a great obstacle; if the thread is broken, there is destruction. Alternatively, one may perform the recitation using finger-beads (aṅgulimālā); that is now described. (390)
Starting from the ring finger and proceeding in order through the little finger, up to the base of the middle finger, this is proclaimed as the hand-garland (karamālā). || 391 ||
One should form the pair of middle joints of the middle and ring fingers as Meru, starting from the base of the ring finger and proceeding in order through the little finger. || 392 ||
There are ten [fingers] counted from the tip of the index finger to the base of the middle finger; or alternatively, one may conceive of Meru as beginning from the first joint of the middle finger.
There, the ring finger and middle finger, as well as the base of the index finger, are prescribed for the counting of recitations;
thus, the recitation is considered to be of three kinds. || 394 ||
In that regard, this previously mentioned threefold recitation has been declared by me at the outset.
Recitation performed with the fingers is declared by me to be one thing, and no other [kind] is mine. || 395 ||
Recitation performed by means of the lines on the fingers is known as *lekhājapa*. One should never separate the fingers during the time of recitation. (396)

Through the separation of the fingers, the recitation (japa) flows out through the gaps; one who possesses the proper qualities should not let the thread cross over, but should slightly contract the palm. 397.

One should not show one's hand at the time of recitation; if one should show it, then the rākṣasas take away that fruit. If one does not show the hand, the rākṣasas seize the fruit. One should abandon the twenty improper actions which cause obstacles to success. 398
One should perform the twenty rites that bring about the perfection of recitation (japa), as well as [the avoidance of] greed, anger, envy, lust, hatred, and violence. (399)
Deceit, causing someone to flee, anointing the body, speaking pleasant falsehoods, singing, instrumental music, honey, and the shade of the *vibhītaka* and *karañja* trees. || 400 ||
A wise man should avoid meat, accepting gifts in the morning, garlands, betel, and sinful speech; now hear from me what ought to be performed. || 401 ||
The mantra, the cessation [of speech], reflection on the meaning of the mantra, and the regular rites; the occasional rites, the Vedic silence, and the avoidance of contact with others. || 402 ||
Sleeping on the ground, bathing at the three periods of the day, daily worship, constant giving of gifts, and the honoring of the guru’s feet and invitation to partake of food. || 403 ||

One should perform bathing with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), wear the purifying thread (pavitraka), offer salutations at the three junctions of the day, and likewise perform the five great sacrifices (pañcayajña) and the libations (tarpaṇa). || 404 ||
(p. 144) Now, the expiation for wearing garments as previously described is stated.
When a word has been uttered once, one should pronounce the *praṇava*.

Even when the word "pāmara" (a low-born person) is uttered, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) once; likewise, upon excessive chatter, one must certainly perform the ritual placement of the limbs (nyāsa) and then recite the mantra. || 406 ||
Even when hungry, or likewise upon touching places that should not be touched, one should abandon silence and either mutter a mantra or remember Hari, the Lord of Viṣṇu.
Upon seeing an outcaste or one of the lowest castes, one should gaze at something radiant.
The sun, fire, the moon, the planets, the sages, the lunar mansions, and the stars. || 408 ||
The learned Brahmins are [the highest], and those others are devoid of splendor.
Upon sneezing, passing wind, walking, or speaking to those who have fallen [from their caste] and so forth; || 409 ||

Having abandoned the recitation and likewise performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and the six-limbed breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should thereafter recite the mantra; in the absence of water, one should meditate upon Hari.
A cat, a cock, a curlew, a dog, a vulture, a bird, and a monkey.
Having seen [an impure thing], one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and then carry out the rite; having touched it, bathing is prescribed.
If, by chance, one has spoken untruth, one should mutter the Raudra-Puruṣa hymn.
Wearing many garments or a single garment, with hair disheveled or hanging down to the throat. || 412 ||
One who wears a turban, one in a bodice, one who is naked, or even one whose head is covered.
Or one whose mind is distracted by anxiety and the like, or who is angry, or filled with hunger within; || 413 ||
Or with his legs hidden, or likewise while seated on a vehicle or a bed;
or lying down with washed feet, or afterwards facing the south. || 414 ||

One whose garment is withered, one whose upper garment is worn, likewise one whose garment is doubled; one whose garment has fallen off, one whose garment is red, one whose garment is oily, and one who wears two girdles. || 415 ||

One with the hem outside, one without an upper garment, one with the hem open, and one with a single hem; one wearing only a loincloth, one with feet thrust forward, and likewise one wearing sewn garments [the root *ṣivu* meaning "to sew"].
If one who is capable of recitation fails due to negligence, the fruit is seized by Rākṣasas; having abandoned that cause, one should perform that recitation again. || 417 ||

If one commits an error through negligence with his own wife, that is a fault; having bathed while still wearing wet clothes and remaining silent, he should [offer] water measured by ten jars. || 418 ||
One should give [the fruit] in the house of a Vedic scholar; for another's wife, it shall be a thousandfold. Japa is the repetition of syllables; that is proclaimed to be threefold. (419)

That which is produced by speech is inferior, while that of the body is middling; however, that of the mind is supreme. [This applies] to those who [speak] with high and low modulated tones, using words and syllables that are clearly articulated. || 420 ||
When a mantra is uttered in a low voice, that is known as vocal recitation (vācika-japa).
One should recite the mantra slowly and move the lips only slightly. || 421 ||

But that which is physical and unsuitable for anyone to hear is the middling [type]. When one utters the sequence of syllables with the intellect according to their proper places, [that is the highest type]. (422)
But that mental recitation (japa) which is preceded by the recollection of the meaning is the most excellent.
One who performs the six rites becomes verbal; one who performs them bodily accomplishes all siddhis. || 423 ||

Through the mental [yoga], one accomplishes liberation; other than that, there is the performer of minor rites. By means of recitation (*japa*), the deity, being constantly praised, becomes pleased. (424)

Success comes from recitation, success comes from recitation; success is not far off through recitation. Just as a person of little merit becomes satisfied with wealth, so too does one attain success through recitation. || 425 ||
In the same way, by means of offerings and worship, minor deities become submissive through great qualities, just as a virtuous lord becomes submissive through his own virtues. || 426 ||

Likewise, O Lord, Viṣṇu, the Sun, and Gaṇeśa—the latter being understood here because the word "ca" (and) implies an unstated inclusion—are the recitations that bestow fruit. Posture is said to be twofold, distinguished by the categories of obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*). || 427 ||
It should be joined with a layer of kusha grass and deerskin on top, four finger-breadths in height, square, two cubits in size, beautiful, soft, and stainless. || 428 ||

This is the perpetual comfortable seat (sukhāsana) that brings about the accomplishment of recitation (japa). Now, the rites for specific desires (kāmya), which lead to the attainment of knowledge and other goals, shall be described. 429.
Tiger skin leads to all accomplishments;
sheepskin [and woolen garments] destroy disease. Silk is said to bring nourishment, while that made from cane increases prosperity.
On a white woolen blanket, the accomplishment of Dharma is declared; on a yellow one, the accomplishments of wealth (artha); and on a red one, the fulfillment of desire (kāma).
Regarding the twice-born among these—[the status of being twice-born applies to] the three [castes], while the others are not;
that is stated by Manu: "The Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya are the three castes who are twice-born."
The fourth is one born of a single caste, namely a Śūdra; there is no fifth. A black blanket bestows liberation. 431.
But for one who is stained by the desire for liberation from suffering, the blue dye is not beautiful.
The wise man should abandon what is forbidden, but he may engage in those things that are not forbidden. || 432 ||
Now, those things that are prohibited will be described: there would be grief if one sits on a wooden seat;
one would become poor if on a bamboo seat; and there would be the destruction of one's position if on a cloth seat. (433)
Likewise, on stone there is eradication (uccāṭa), and on a seat made of clay there will be fever;
[the word "clay" (mṛṇmaya) refers to the general category, since stone and brick are mentioned separately]. || 434 ||

If one sits on a seat of earth, there will be physical pain; if on a seat of leaves, there will be confusion of mind. If one sits on a seat of grass, there will be pain; however, a seat made of bricks is strictly forbidden.
The agitation of the mind that occurs for a householder upon the black antelope skin may lead to success for a student, a forest-dweller, a renunciant, or a graduate. || 436 ||
Having bathed according to the prescribed rule at an auspicious moment, under a favorable constellation, and on a propitious lunar day.
Having diligently gratified the Brahmins with food, clothing, and other such offerings. || 437 ||
Having satisfied one's own guru with land, wealth, clothing, ornaments, and other gifts, one should thereafter begin the recitation (japa) following his permission. || 438 ||
Then, at the place of recitation, one should draw a triangle with a circle outside it.
Outside of that, one should worship a square within that same field. || 439 ||
With such sentences as "Come here," he [brings her] again from the triangle to the front.
One should place the vessel for the bali offering, filled with food, water, and other substances. || 440 ||
O gods, a buffalo should be offered there by the Vāmins, a ram by the Kaulikas, and a sheep by the Siddhāntins, while reciting the mantra. || 441 ||
"Come, come! [Come, come, O Vidraṣī-puruṣa! Victory, victory! Dance, dance, O Vighnavighna!
Mahābhairava! Kṣetreśa! Kṣetrapāla! Accept, accept the *bali* offering, svāhā!
Having uttered 'Vidraṣī,' one should say 'puruṣa' followed by two instances of 'jaya,' and then two instances of 'nartaya.'"
And afterwards, "O Great Destroyer of Obstacles! (paścādvighnavighnamaheti). || 442 ||
One should utter "Bhairavapada" followed by "Kṣetreśa," and then say, "Kṣetrapāla, accept the bali, accept it—svāhā! || 443 ||
This mantra for the offering to Kṣetrapāla consists of forty-three syllables.
One should present the bali-offering to him along with his retinue; one must not consume it oneself. (444)
One should commence the *puraścaryā* on an auspicious day as prescribed for initiation; first, having prostrated before the gurus and the Brahmins, and having fully worshipped Gaṇeśa. || 445 ||
Having performed the *puṇyāhavācana* rite, one with *kuśa* grass in hand should say: "The Sun, the Moon, Yama, Time, the two twilights, the spirits, the day, and the night. (446)
The wind, the lord of the quarters, the earth, the sky, the sky-dwellers, and the immortals.
Abiding by the command of Brahmā, establish your presence here.
Having recited this and placed it in a copper vessel along with kuśa grass, sesame seeds, and unbroken grains (akṣata), he, facing north,
should perform the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) for the year and other periods.
There, one should utter twenty recitations for each of the following:
the year, the season, the month, the fortnight, and the five limbs [of the calendar]. || 449 ||
"The position of the nine planets [should be calculated] according to the day, the portion, and the muhūrta."
Having pronounced the specific names of one's own country, one should utter them together with one's desires. || 450 ||
In each island, continent, and region, one should utter the preeminent lineage name;
then one's own name, followed by a name ending in the [mother’s] caste name, and finally the suffixes *śarman* or *varman*. (451)
I, the servant named Gupta, desiring the accomplishment of the mantra of such-and-such, shall perform the *puraścaryā* consisting of this many recitations. (452)
Alternatively, during these days, provided there is no obstacle, one should form the mental resolve (saṅkalpa) with the mind alone, thinking, "I shall perform [the rite]. || 453 ||
Having spoken his desire with words and having fulfilled it through action, he bowed down to and worshipped his guru, Gaṇapati, and Durgā for my sake. || 454 ||

Having performed [this], one should practice three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) with one’s own root mantra; likewise, having performed the ritual placement of the seers (ṛṣi-vinyāsa) and so forth, as well as the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅga-nyāsa). || 455 ||
One should meditate upon the deity in the heart while placing the rosary in its vessel; having sprinkled it with the arghya water, one should then pray to it as follows: || 456 ||
Oṃ, Māle, Māle, O Great Illusion (Māhāmāyā), you who are the embodiment of all powers! The four aims of human life have been entrusted to you;
therefore, be the bestower of success upon me. || 457 ||
Having performed worship, one should then take the garland in the right hand; first uttering the seed-syllable of Gaṇapati, which is "gaṃ," immediately thereafter—458.
"O Mālā, grant me freedom from obstacles"; immediately after that, he should take it in his right hand and then meditate upon Śiva in his mind. || 559 ||

And one should meditate on the Guru upon the crown of the head according to his respective color and other attributes; one should meditate on the mantra in the middle of the throat, yellow in color and golden.

One should contemplate Mahāmāyā in the heart, oneself at the feet of the Guru, and thereafter the command-wheel (ājñācakra) of the Guru, the mantra, and oneself. (461) [Note: Regarding the mantra *oṃ māṃ*, it should have been recited first here; its omission in this instance is due to the fear of violating the metrical structure.]
Then, having brought [the breath] into union with the Goddess via the path of the suṣumṇā, from there—
One should leap over that single form of the Guru toward each of the six cakras.
Having meditated with effort for a moment upon Mahāmāyā within the six cakras as well.
One should suspend the sixteen cakras beginning with that by means of the root mantra.
The practitioner should contemplate that Goddess, who bestows bliss upon the practitioners, within the sixteen cakras beginning with Ādi;
then he should commence the rite of birth (jātakarman). || 464 ||

Above the eyebrows, the end of the three channels is said to be located. That terminal point is the station of the triple path (tripatha), hexagonal in shape, and four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in extent. || 465 ||
And this wheel is called the *ājñācakra* by those who know the yoga of the *kula*. In the throat of human beings, there exists an encircling of three channels. || 466 ||
The hexagon formed by the Suṣumṇā, Iḍā, and Piṅgalā is six finger-breadths in extent.
It is declared as the Wheel of Reality (tattvacakra), white in color, situated in the middle of the throat.
And there may be oneness in the hearts of even the three gods. In that place, there should be a sixteen-spoked [cakra] measuring seven finger-breadths. || 468 ||
That [state] is the first of the sixteen cakras reached by those previously mentioned yogas, pertaining to the objects of meditation, the mantras, the contemplation, and the recitation. || 469 ||
Since it is the primordial heart, it is therefore called the "First" (Ādi). Therein, the Praṇava was produced first from the First Son. || 470 ||
Just as water flows downward in an instant when it is without a dam,
even so the mantra of the sacrificers flows away in an instant when it is without a dam.
Therefore, in all efforts, those belonging to the four castes and other classes should begin the rite of recitation (japa), having established a boundary on both sides. || 472 ||
The Praṇava is proclaimed as the bridge for the twice-born among all mantras.
The other [mantras] consist of the fourteen vowels joined with the moon (the letter *a*) and the anusvāra. || 473 ||
Having reflected thus, one should place the rosary upon the middle joint of the middle finger; without touching the index finger, one should move the rosary with the tip of the thumb. (474)
If one who is reciting a mantra first touches another jewel with his thumb, that recitation shall always be fruitless for him. (475)
Holding the garland near one's own heart with the right hand, (p. 148)
The garland mantra, however, is "hrīṃ siddhyai namaḥ"; one should pray thus. || 476 ||
O Mālā, grant delight to all the gods and bestow auspiciousness; O Blessed One, bring me well-being and increase my fame and valor. 477.
In this context, regarding the worship of prayer, this is the proclaimed mantra of the rosary.
Then, by means of the five-syllable mantra, one should pray to one's own chosen deity. || 478 ||
You are the protector of the most secret of secrets; accept this recitation performed by us. O God, Lord of the World, may success be mine through your grace. 479.
Having recited the root mantra, one should offer it into the hand of the deity;
and at the time of midday, one should likewise offer this recitation with the water of the arghya.
For that purpose, one who knows the ritual procedure should bathe as before, but with special care.
One should perform all the previously mentioned ritual actions, concluding with the rite of nyāsa.

Then, after completing everything up to the worship and the fire-oblation, the twice-born man should begin his recitation (japa). Having bathed again at the conclusion of the day, he should then proceed further. || 482 ||
Having performed the twilight worship as before, he should again worship the deity; having dismissed [the deity], he should always take his meal at the rising of the stars. || 483 ||

One who eats the fruits and roots of the six medicinal plants, one who subsists on the alms of the virtuous, one who eats sacrificial oblations (haviṣya), or one who observes the milk-vow—these are the best; their characteristics are now described. || 484 ||
The root of the lotus, piṇḍāraka, and kaseruka promote longevity.
A red elephant, a conch, and a sweet lotus-root are said to be the most excellent. || 485 ||
Grapes, mangoes, rose-apples, jackfruit, wood-apples, dates, pomegranates, and coconuts.
The fruit of the parūṣaka, the kṣīriṇikā, the plantain (kadala), and the dhātrī is indeed purifying. || 486 ||
Patramūla, tvacāmūla, vimūla, pañcamījaṭī, akavāku, and kuvāku—these, when used at the root, bring about purification. || 487 ||
Of those who are endowed with Vedic conduct, pure, prosperous, and virtuous.
For those born into noble families and high castes, he is one who subsists on alms. || 488 ||
Rice-cakes, roots, fruits, milk, curd, alms-food, and barley-meal— these seven kinds of food obtained through begging are to be consumed by those established in their vows.
There were fifty oblation-worthy white rice grains, steamed and grown in the Himalayas.
Rice grains are considered to be of three kinds: those produced from the ṣaṣṭika, nīvāra, and śāli varieties. || 490 ||
Mudga beans, barley, black sesame, boiled rice, and even tripuṭa grains.
And millet, horse-gram, barley, wild rice, and śikā. || 491 ||
Kālakaṃsa, vāstūka, karambū, hilamocikā, cakravartin, cakramarda, palaṅkaṣa, and śatapuṣpikā. || 492 ||
The root produced in winter, white mustard, black gram, and sesame.
Mṛṇālamusalī, ghoṇṭā, śatamūlī, and vidārikā. || 493 ||
All types of *piṇḍālū*, as well as *padma*, *vāravaṣā*, *āyuṣkara*, *kañcuka*, *śṛṅgāṭaka*, and *kaseruka* [are beneficial]. || 494 ||
Sea salt, rock salt, curds, clarified butter, and milk from cows, buffaloes, and other animals;
sweet milk containing its essence, and whatever other milk has its seeds intact. (495)
Having abandoned the breadfruit, mango, myrobalan, tamarind, molasses, jaggery, sugarcane products, sacrificial ghee, all medicinal substances, fish, liquor, and meat; 496.
Cow's milk is said to be the best, that produced by the Surabhi cow is middling, and buffalo milk is the lowest;
furthermore, all other types [of milk] are forbidden for those observing a vow.

He who abandons forbidden food and other such things according to the scriptures is considered middling; he who avoids what is forbidden by reason of place or family, but consumes what is otherwise praised, is remembered as inferior.
Now, the twenty-seven prohibited items are being described:
white lentils (*mudga*), lentils (*masūra*), *kodrava* grains, and three types of chickpeas (*caṇaka*). (499)
Māṣa beans, soil-salt, and whatever else has acquired a different taste; honey, alkaline substances, onions, garlic, and food from a glass vessel—these are forbidden. (500)
Meat that has been steamed with salt, asafoetida, and stalks;
food that is stale, oil, betel-leaf, and small grains. || 501 ||
Also the patola, the vṛntāka, the radish, and the kaliñjaka; burnt food, food cooked twice, rice with jaggery, and the fruit of the palmyra palm. || 502 ||
O gods, listen to the distinction according to the divisions of caste and stage of life: sesame oil purified by mantra is sanctifying and difficult even for the gods to obtain. (503)

After massaging [the body], the householder must always perform a bath; the twice-born, however, should take their meal after spreading the under-layer (upastīrya) and pouring the clarified butter (āvidhārya). 504.
One should purify it with Vedic mantras through rites such as sprinkling; then, having consecrated it again with the root mantra, one should eat while reciting the heart-mantra (hṛdayāṇu). || 505 ||
When thirsty during a meal, one should drink water consecrated with the root-mantra; one should eat from a Palāśa leaf, while other leaves are to be avoided. (506)
In the absence of those, he may do so on a plantain tree, or on a Madhūka or Sarjaka tree; having eaten, he should sleep upon a very clean bed or on the surface of the earth. || 507 ||
On a pure seat spread with an unwashed cloth and woven with a border, consecrated by the root mantra, he who has conquered anger and subdued his senses [should sit]. (508)
Meditating upon his chosen deity, he should sleep at night with his head toward the east; then, having risen at midnight and performed the cleansing of his feet, [he should proceed]. (509)
Having sipped water and worshipped the God, and having quickly touched [him] as before, one should perform recitation according to one's ability and likewise offer it to the Lord.
But one who has seen a dream while sleeping should report that dream to his guru;
this recitation is indeed prescribed for forest-dwellers who are exponents of the Veda.

If it must be performed at will due to fear of calamities such as those arising from one's country, this is said to be the appropriate time; and it is also prescribed when [the practice] is mandatory. || 512 ||
Recitation until midday is best; that during the three middle watches is middling.
One who has failed in the necessary duties for three and a half watches is said to possess the aforementioned characteristics.
The procedure for bringing the recitation to completion is said to be fivefold. The first method is that one should perform the recitation every day until midday. || 514 ||
One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with the substances prescribed for the Kalpa, using a tenth part of that [number].
Having performed the libation (tarpaṇa) and the ritual purification (mārjana), as well as the feeding of Brahmins (brāhmaṇabhojana).
This first ritual procedure (kalpa) is said to consist of one-tenth of that;
this second ritual procedure, however, requires one hundred thousand recitations (japa). || 516 ||
Having performed the fire oblation and other rites for him, one should commence the first hundred thousand recitations. This is the third ritual procedure;
one should perform the full number of recitations. || 517 ||

When the *homa* is complete, one should perform the libations (*tarpaṇa*) and other rites exactly as before. As for the fourth method, it is that those who are poor should perform double the number of recitations (*japa*). [This is the remainder of the sense. || 518 ||

In the absence of fire-offerings and other rites, it should be performed by multiplying [the number] by three and so forth, using the king and others as multipliers; furthermore, the fifth method is that which is dear to whichever deity it may be.
That very same [offering] should be made double for the swift gratification of the deity.
All the goddesses are fond of recitation; on the left-hand path, they are fond of offerings.
Mahādeva is fond of the fire-oblation (homa), and Bhāskara is fond of libations (tarpaṇa); the cleansing (mārjana) belongs to Gaṇeśa, while the feeding of Brahmins belongs to Viṣṇu. || 521 ||
But if an expiation is performed, then the twice-born becomes pure.
Through fourfold *puraścaryā*, Kṣatriyas and others [attain success] by means of three, two, and so forth.
Alternatively, the *puraścaraṇa* is described in another manner: having first fasted and being pure, one should undertake it on the day of the sun or the moon. || 523 ||
Standing in water reaching to the navel in a river flowing toward the ocean.
With a concentrated mind, one should recite the mantra from the stage of touch (sparśa) up to the stage of liberation (mukti). || 524 ||
One should recite the mantra in this manner for that duration, and thereafter perform the fire sacrifice (homa) and other rites.
Afterwards, one should feed the Brahmins; this is the procedure for the preliminary rite (puraścaryā). || 525 ||

Expiation is the destruction of the transgression resulting from the performance [of a rite]; for those [mantras] whose number of recitations and oblations is not prescribed in the Tantras, [this applies]. || 526 ||
And therein, this preliminary practice (puraścaryā) is concealed in all tantras; likewise, another [practice] for the left-hand path (vāmamārga) of mantras is now described. || 527 ||
Beginning from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
one should meditate upon the deity and recite the mantra forty thousand times.
Afterwards, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) ten times the number [of recitations], and then offer libations and perform the consecration.
O gods, because the guru is unaccomplished, the disciple's accomplishment does not arise. || 529 ||

Then one should employ the means which is now described as that which is to be kept secret: [the practice] with the letters of the Mātṛkā, beginning with *bindu*, in both direct and reverse order. || 530 ||

One should recite the mantra encapsulated [by the seed syllables] every day one hundred times for one month; thereafter, the mantra becomes perfected through the performance of fire oblations (homa) and other rites. || 531 ||
One should perform the entire daily routine as prescribed for the *puraścaraṇa* rite; thus, for the sake of attaining mastery over a Vedic mantra, [the practice] should be accompanied by the vowels.
The letters, joined with the bindu, should be assigned both in direct and reverse order.
The vowels *a*, *i*, *u*, and *ṛ* are considered to be of three kinds through the distinctions of short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), and protracted (*pluta*). || 533 ||
The short and the protracted *ḷ* are considered to be of two kinds each, and the diphthongs (*ec*) are likewise considered to be of two kinds.
Indeed, through the distinction between long and protracted [vowels], and by means of the anusvāra and visarga; || 534 ||
Thus, twenty-four vowels have been declared along with the letters ña, ma, and ha; there are four consonants beginning with ka, and the letter ka joined with the jihvāmūlīya.
Thus, the ka-group is tenfold, and the first fifteen [vowels] are traditionally taught.
The letter *pa* is joined with the *upadhmānīya*; therefore, there are six [syllables] therein.
If eight Mātṛkās are proclaimed in the Veda regarding the sacrifice,
two additional *ḷ* and *kṣa* are found in the *Ṛks* (the *Ṛgveda*), and an even greater number is recorded in the *Atharvaṇa*.
And one should perform the recitation one hundred and eight times every day for a period of exactly one month.
Having avoided the days unfit for study, [he should do so] likewise for forty days.
Having obtained all [the mantras] beginning with those for the fire-oblation (homa), one should always employ them; however, one should enclose a mantra of a minor deity with the Bhūtalipi. || 539 ||
One should perform one hundred recitations in both forward and reverse order; success will be attained within a month. [The vowels:
aṃ, iṃ, uṃ, ṛṃ, ḷṃ, eṃ, aiṃ, oṃ, auṃ, haṃ; [the consonants: yaṃ, vaṃ, raṃ, laṃ, kaṃ, ṅaṃ, khaṃ, ghaṃ, gaṃ, caṃ, ñaṃ, chaṃ, jhaṃ, jaṃ, ṭaṃ, ṇaṃ, ṭhaṃ, ḍhaṃ.
Ḍaṃ taṃ naṃ thaṃ dhaṃ daṃ paṃ maṃ phaṃ bhaṃ baṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ; [the letters] ha, ya, va, ra, la, together with the second and fourth from the beginning and the end. (540)
And one should recite the letters of the groups in sequence for the third [time], and likewise the three sibilants;
thus, with forty-two syllables— || 541 ||

Thus, one thousand and eight recitations of the mantra dedicated to Ugradaivata should be performed at the three times of day with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings; furthermore, this should be done again at midnight.

If she is worshipped for six months by those belonging to the Kaulika and other traditions, she becomes well-pleased; however, this is not the case for the unqualified who have merely obtained the status of an Ācārya or other rank from a Guru. || 543 ||

It is not said that the preliminary practice (puraścaryā) must be performed merely according to the general instruction; rather, it is as [prescribed] for kings, fortunate persons, or those who are delicate. 544.

Success will thus be attained; I shall now describe the preliminary rites for the medicinal herbs according to their colors. That [practice] is to be understood as sevenfold, granting success through the months corresponding to those colors. (545)
One should fashion auspicious pills from mantra-syllables, medicinal herbs, and wood.
These have been declared according to the sequence of the castes, both in direct and reverse order.
And from roots and other sources, many jewels should be fashioned accordingly.
The garland should always have the form of two snakes; one should then recite [the mantra]. || 547 ||
This first recitation is said to consist of a number of beads equal to the [total] count of the rosary;
all the beads should be strung together with threads corresponding to their respective syllables.
This second [method] is that the garland for the neck should always be worn around the neck; likewise, one should worship those [beads] which are strung upon a thread as they shine. || 549 ||
This third method proceeds by way of those who are like gods;
the fourth is the daily bath with a decoction of medicinal herbs. || 550 ||

The fifth [type of bath] is performed with cow's ghee from [substances such as] pigments, medicinal herbs, water, and so forth; one should apply its powder as an ointment, and this is proclaimed as the sixth.
"One should perform the wearing of that ash constantly"—this is the seventh [verse].
If there is hatred toward Brahmins, hatred toward one's guru, or hatred toward women, success will not arise. (The word "success" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. || 552 ||
Or, due to a curse or because it is pinned down, there should be eight means in that case.
Heating, nourishing, liquefying, awakening, and subjugation; || 553 ||
Oppression, nourishment, and drying, as well as burning—these are said to be its functions. Having obtained birch bark, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus. (554)
With eight kinds of fragrant substances, or with *rocanā* and sandalwood paste, one should write the mantra interwoven with the letters of the practitioner's name. (555)

One should continue until the completion of two [circles], and write the name of the practitioner, preceded by the syllable *Tārā* (Oṃ), at the beginning and end; then, one should write it upon the eight petals.
Two by two, the vowels should be written there, while meditating correctly upon the nectar-natured seed-syllable *vaṃ*.
Having encircled that with clay, a Brāhmaṇa or others should properly wrap it around. || 557 ||
Thereafter, one should wrap it with a fine cloth that is white or other such colors.
One should cast that into a small earthen vessel containing the three sweets.
One should place that small vessel into a new jar filled with milk.
Having established the sacred fire, he should place that jar in its vicinity.
One should establish [the deity] with the three sweets and perform the fire offering (homa) with the root mantra.
One should pour out one thousand and eight vessels of water for the sake of perfecting the rite.
Having completed the fire sacrifice (homa) and cast that pitcher into a body of water, one should satisfy one's own guru and the Brahmins with food, sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), and other offerings.

This is said to be for the purpose of pacifying or nourishing [the deity], provided that success has not yet been attained; however, one should then perform the rite of liquefaction (drāvaṇa), the method for which is described here.
Having bound it with the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, one should write the mantra upon birch bark.
And with uśīra and rocanā, as well as with śilā, karpūra, and kuṅkuma. || 563 ||
One should place that written [mantra] in the midst of milk, clarified butter, honey, and water; through worship, recitation, and fire-oblation, it becomes melted and yields its fruit. || 564 ||
If he is not mastered even after being melted, one should cause him to be awakened; having encased him with the Vāgbhava seed-syllable (Aiṃ), one should recite it.
In this way, one becomes a perfected Buddha; otherwise, one should perform the rite of subjugation using kucandana, mahādāru, turmeric, and realgar.
A mantra written with these [substances] upon a beautiful birch-bark leaf, when worn around the neck, brings one under control;
otherwise, it will cause suffering.
One should recite the first [syllable] with an anudātta accent, the second with an udātta, the third with an anudātta, and the fourth with an udātta. (568)
In this manner, the practitioner of the mantra should recite all the words.
While pronouncing the words with the anudātta accent, one should meditate on the God situated below.
Standing upright, one should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times with an elevated tone;
thereafter, one should write [the mantra] on birch bark with the milk of a cow that has calved for the first time.
One should step upon that mantra with the left foot and then perform the fire oblation; when the mantra has been thus afflicted one hundred and eight times, it becomes propitious. || 571 ||
If it is not established, then it is called "to be nourished" (poṣya); its ritual procedure is now described.
One should write the mantra, encased within the seed-syllable *soma*, upon a leaf of birch bark.
One should apply *rocanā* and *kuṅkuma* with curd and milk;
this is called nourishment (*poṣaṇa*), and now drying (*śoṣaṇa*) is described. || 573 ||
Having written the desired mantra upon a birch leaf with the ashes of a sacrifice, interspersed with the seed-syllable of Vāyu, one should wear it around one's neck. || 574 ||
This is called "drying"; now "burning" is being described. [One should perform it] with the individual mantras arranged separately in the four directions. (575)
One should draw [the diagram] with the seed-syllable *raṃ* and the oil from the seeds of the *palāśa* tree on a birch leaf;
that should then be worn around the neck—this is the procedure for burning. || 576 ||
Now, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for the Śabara mantras is described. In the region known as Kāmarūpa, where the deity Kāmākṣā resides— || 577 ||
Where that Kāmaśāla is, it is called the Kāmapīṭha;
there, one should indeed inscribe the mantra upon the bamboo frame in the proper sequence. || 578 ||

He should be made to recite by the Guru, and afterwards he himself should recite the mantra. In the absence of a Guru, [he should do so] at the foot of that very mountain on a festival day (parvan). || 579 ||
Having written it down, one should recite the mantra; the Guru is considered the seat of desire (Kāmapīṭha). Or else, it is certainly on the Yoginī Hill in the southern direction. || 580 ||
Having written there the mantra of that goddess Yogāmbā, one should recite it.
Or near Jvālāmukhī, or at Hiṅgulāja. || 581 ||
Having written it down, one should recite the mantra; otherwise, it will not be successful. Primarily, the grasping of the mind occurs near a woman at the seat of desire (kāmapīṭha). || 582 ||
Alternatively, it is said that the reception of the mantra may take place in all locations. One should write the mantra on palm leaves and place them inside a full water-pot. || 583 ||
Having meditated upon the Sun as his Guru, the Sun-god himself recites [the mantra] three times for the Guru.
Now, hear about the initiation (dīkṣā) for Tantric mantras without a Guru. 584.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight, when endowed with the strength of the moon and the stars,
one should go into the presence of Dakṣiṇāmūrti and worship Him.

Having performed the installation of the water-pot (kalaśa), one should scatter [offerings] before it; then, having written the mantra and the name of the deity on a palm leaf, one should worship the deity. || 586 ||
Having meditated upon the mantra as the deity and the guru, one should clearly recite it.
And the reception of the mantra is said to consist of one hundred and eight [repetitions]. || 587 ||

This reality has been fully declared; it must be kept secret like a lover's affair with one's mother. Greed and other such faults reside in the Guru; therefore, people shrink away from him. Thus, having made the Guru his scripture, Manu [proceeded] from Dakṣiṇāmūrti. (588)
O Goddess, when the mantra has been thus accomplished, those things which bind one to the path away from liberation [are overcome].
And many supernatural powers arise that cause the depletion of one's ascetic merit. || 589 ||
If one is immersed in the attainment of minor powers, then the [eight] supernatural faculties such as *ṛddhi* will not arise.
If one is immersed in the powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest, news of liberation is extremely difficult to obtain.
Minor austerity perishes in an instant, and even moderate austerity perishes through pride.
This gateway to accomplishment for him is described by me as its characteristic.
If, whether in a dream or before one's very eyes, something wondrous that causes great joy should suddenly occur, it must not be told to anyone except the Guru. || 592 ||

One who desires mundane success should never disclose [this] anywhere. He who, out of delusion or impatience, reveals the bliss born of mantra, finds that the accomplishments (siddhis) which were near to him depart far away. (593)
Sufferings and various sorrows also arise; yet there is little eating, very little sleep, and constant clarity of mind. (594)
And a sentence endowed with clarity and truthfulness arises; for one capable of accomplishing the mantras, this first occurs within the first three years. || 595 ||
Many obstacles arise that cause one to abandon their observances; yet the practitioner does not experience agitation, provided he remains steadfast in action and mind. || 596 ||
Then, after three years had passed, the kings and the lords of the earth [assembled].
Even those who are proud and full of self-respect make requests out of compliance with [another's] insistence. || 597 ||
"O Lord, let favor be granted; be the cause of my deliverance. They behold [him] blazing with splendor and majesty. (598)
Therefore, you are unable to speak in detail to that tiger among sages.
After the ninth year, the king of mantras becomes spontaneously effective.

One who has accomplished the desires of speech and mind is indeed a giver and an enjoyer, yet remains a non-seeker. Now I shall explain how the accomplishment of mantra may come about even for a poor person. (600)
For a Brahmin who is unable to perform the fire-sacrifice (homakarma), the recitation (japa) is doubled; for the other castes, however, a threefold increase and so forth is prescribed. || 601 ||

If the fire-oblation (homa) is performed, the libation (tarpaṇa) becomes complete by means of twice that number of recitations. If the purification (mārjana) has not been performed, it is said that the recitation must be double the number of libations. || 602 ||

A substitute for the feeding of Brahmins is nowhere heard of in any Vedic scripture; therefore, one should by all means feed the Brahmins in order to ensure the successful completion of the rite with all its constituent parts.

By the mere act of propitiating a Brahmin, that which is deficient becomes complete. Whatever rites may be lacking [in merit] due to the failure to feed the twice-born, they become as fruitless as seeds sown in saline soil. (604)
Thereafter, one should satisfy the Guru with gold, garments, and other offerings; for when the Guru is pleased, the mantra becomes satisfied and grants success to the practitioner. || 605 ||
A mantra heard by chance, or even one recited through deception or force, or a verse prompted by others—that recitation of such does not accomplish any purpose. (606)
Those who recite mantras after looking at them written in a book are proclaimed to have a sin equal to that of killing a Brahmin. (607)
(155) Even a wise man becomes distracted while contemplating millions of mantras;
yet a single mantra received from the mouth of a guru shall bestow all accomplishments. 608.
Born into a noble family, he follows the conduct of his lineage and is honored by all practitioners.
He who is equal toward all living beings is fully endowed with the characteristics of accomplishment.
He for whom enemies act as friends and who reveals all paths—he alone should be made one's guru, and never anyone else in the Vāma tradition. 610.
In this world and in the next as well, the Kaula falls if he acts otherwise; however, for one who is skillful, even in the absence of supernatural power (siddhi), the destruction of sin occurs. 611.
Through the practice of the fourfold set [of the four M’s and so forth], hell indeed lies to the left. Thus has the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) been described; what else do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the sixth chapter, the Purashcharya-prakasham, in the Merutantra composed by Shiva with the approval of the illustrious Mahamaya and Mahakala. || 6 ||
The illustrious Goddess said:
In this terrible Kali age, people will become excessively arrogant due to their very meager accomplishments;
how can there be stable accomplishment for them? (1)
The growth of the lineage at its head, as well as the grace of the gods upon that lineage—O ocean of mercy, tell me how liberation is attained by the practitioner. || 2 ||
The Lord said:
Through the abandonment of egoism and the relinquishing of actions performed for the sake of desire.
By the practice of one's own duty, everything arises without effort.
If one is unable to do this, one should at least avoid what is forbidden; one should perform the prescribed duties, and thus there will be success extending to one's sons and grandsons.
In that regard, I shall first describe the prohibited places; listen, O beloved:
in a temple, in the abode of a guru, in a cremation ground, and at a crossroads.
One should avoid using sandals, sitting on a seat, voiding excrement or urine, engaging in sexual intercourse, and so forth [while wearing the sacred thread]. || 5 ||

One should not revile a woman of the lowest caste who is intoxicated, a maiden in her menses, one whose breasts have fallen away, one who is deformed, one with disheveled hair, or one afflicted by passion.
A maiden’s vulva, sport with cattle, nakedness, and exposed breasts.
One should not look upon the property of others, and one should avoid the wives of others.
One should never stretch out one's feet toward grain, cattle, a teacher, a deity, fire, a brahmin, or a book, nor should one step over these things. || 8 ||
One should avoid laziness, intoxication, delusion, curses, malice, and strife; one should also avoid envy, self-adulation, and the censuring of others.
A Brahmin who bears the sectarian marks (liṅgin), observes vows (vratī), and is well-versed in the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, and the Saṃhitās.
One should not defile, even in thought, the Purāṇas, the Āgamas, and the Śāstras.
A pair of wooden mortars, a pestle, a stone, a rope, a hearth, a mortar, a winnowing basket, a broom, a staff, a banner, and indeed a musical instrument as the eleventh weapon. || 11 ||
The water-pot, the chowrie, the parasol, the mirror, and likewise the ornament.
And whatever other sacrificial materials are suitable for enjoyment, || 12 ||
One should never step over objects in sacred places or in temples, nor objects declared to be divine, nor indeed those possessed by spirits; one must never touch these with one's feet. (13)
That social gathering which is despised by the world, and that which proceeds according to one's own whims;
And that which consists of harming others—he should never engage in that at any time. || 14 ||
One should not accept gifts out of a desire for one's own enjoyment.
One should acquire wealth through effort, even by means of giving, for the purpose of honoring the deities and guests. (15)
One should not take shelter in the shade of the *bibhītaka*, *karañja*, *arka*, or *snuhī* trees.
[The same applies] to pillars, lamps, humans, and likewise to other living beings. || 16 ||
One should avoid from afar the water used for washing clothes that has been shaken off by the tips of nails or hair, as well as the dust raised by donkeys and goats. || 17 ||
One must never step over the area where the linga stands, nor over its floral offerings (nirmālya);
rather, one should cast all such things into a river, or give them to one who has received initiation into the Śiva tradition.

One should not transgress the command of the guru, nor should one speak back to him; likewise, one should avoid saying what is unpleasant, especially at the wrong time, as well as desire and anger. (19)
One should never speak with an uncovered mouth in the presence of the guru; one should avoid monologues and the worship of deities in the presence of the guru. (20)
The practitioner should not step over, touch, or wear the guru’s insignia, such as his sandals or meditation belt, in the guru’s presence. (21)
Likewise, one should not lie on a couch, nor crawl on one's hands and feet, nor stretch one's limbs, nor engage in playful gestures in the presence of the Guru. || 22 ||
A disciple should not step over the shadow of his teacher, nor should he walk in front of him; nor should a disciple display his own prowess in the presence of his teacher.
One should not harbor egoism, nor should one maintain an arrogant physical posture. In the presence of one's superior, a wise person should never prostrate before his own guru.
Seeing him intent on performing prostrations, the Guru should restrain him; he should not issue a command to him, nor should he say "you" and so forth. || 25 ||
In addressing or speaking to him, one should say, "The venerable Lord Śrīnātha. When some misfortune has occurred, one should utter an oath known as that of the Guru.
One should not perform [the rite] with the name "Śiva," unless it is done out of favor; for that purpose, one should diligently complete the worship, recitation, and oblations at the end.
But if he fails to fulfill that purpose for which the oath was sworn, [he shall pay the fine].
One should perform the atonement for the root mantra by reciting it one thousand times.
One should never utter speech that causes distress to the world, that cuts into the vital organs, or that causes agitation regarding one's stability. || 29 ||
One should never adopt an appearance that is loathed by the world, even if the forest is radiant and desired by the mind. (30)
By respectfully practicing those other conducts prescribed in the Tantras, both pertaining to this world and the next, the initiated person attains peace. (31)
Even in times of great calamity, practitioners should never employ their own mantra for the protection of others, even if it has already been mastered. || 32 ||
Whether by the words arising from his guru, out of fear, for his own sake, or through supreme compassion, he should always practice mercy toward those who are helpless. || 33 ||
In whichever cities, O Guru, envy is heard of, one should not dwell there;
rather, one should depart while keeping [the teaching] in mind within the heart.
One should certainly not dwell in that place where there is censure of Viṣṇu, Śiva, the scripture, the Veda, the Sun, Gaṇeśa, or Bhavānī. || 35 ||
One should not, through action, mind, or speech, desire the wives of others; rather, one should speak truthful words and maintain good character, equanimity, and fortitude. (36)
Always [consider] power, compassion, the state, and divine power.
One should perform going and coming after having prostrated before the sandals of the Guru.
One should depart from the teacher's house with the right foot first, having offered a prostration.
Free from impurities and the like, he [is purified] by the plucking out of his hair and beard. || 38 ||
And [one should meditate on her] situated above the moon and sun, and positioned in the midst of the cow, the Aśvattha tree, and so forth.
One should meditate upon the deity Viṣṇu as residing within the bodies of the guru and the brahmins.
One should serve one's mother and father, as well as Viṣṇu, one's beloved, and guests;
Viṣṇu, the refuge of the universe, should be known as the Self, and the Self should be known as being like Viṣṇu. 40.
However, one should conceal all actions performed in one's own practice; and the secrecy of the mantra must always be maintained for the sake of attaining success in the mantra. 41.
One should not utter the name of the guru; however, when it must be spoken, one should do so preceded by "Oṃ Śrī" and followed by the name of the deity. (42)

Having joined his palms at his head once more, he should utter the name of Hari, ending with "namaḥ," together with the word "pāda" and the number of syllables corresponding to the lunar day. || 43 ||
The daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and desire-based (kāmya) [worship] depend upon each preceding one; otherwise, O Goddess, such worship brings about a succession of calamities. || 44 ||
The worship performed every day is proclaimed as "nityā" (daily); the "naimittikā" (occasional) worship on the following day is equal in number to those five.
Even in the absence [of specific causes], this occasional worship might sometimes occur; however, this occasional worship is pure and is said to be of twenty varieties.

The lunar festival days (parvan), the Mahāyogas, Vyatīpāta along with Vaidhṛti, the beginnings of the Manvantaras and Yugas, and whatever limb of his has originated from a deity—[all these are auspicious]. || 47 ||
The Puṣya asterism, Sunday, the day of one's own birth among the three elders, the day of initiation, and the Navarātra—these are auspicious. || 48 ||
Now listen to the days of the *gaṇḍāntas* and the necessary days for worship—those days on which a special worship performed becomes fruitless. (49)

Likewise, when going on a journey of ten days, upon seeing a hero or one's own kinsmen, during an eclipse of the moon or sun, upon gaining a profit, at a fire sacrifice, and during a great festival; || 50 ||
On a sacred seat (*pīṭha*), at a holy pilgrimage site (*tīrtha*) frequented by those who travel to such seats, and upon beholding the deities of the ford.
In diseases, calamities, faults, evil associations, and inauspicious omens; || 51 ||
One should perform worship according to the time, according to one's faith, according to the materials available, as is appropriate, according to one's strength, and according to the place. 52.
Regarding the times for occasional worship, they occur at dawn, midday, and also at twilight;
and [the deities to be worshipped are] Vighneśa, Ravi, Viṣṇu, Īśa, and Śakti.
And he who does not worship the God with Damanaka during the middle of the month, the Lord of Desire (Kāmarāj) takes away the fruit of that person's worship performed throughout the year. || 54 ||
The three months beginning with Caitra are most excellent in successive order; likewise, the eighth, ninth, full moon, new moon, and fourteenth days [of the lunar fortnights]. || 55 ||
But during this period, on a certain previous day at dusk, [he performed the rite].
Having performed his daily rites, being pure and joined by those who observe the conventional rules. || 56 ||

Having approached Damanaka, one should sit upon a seat; then, having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the sages and other elements. || 57 ||
O water-born one, nourished by the sun, you have arisen from the ashes of desire.
Salutations to you, who delude the sages, gandharvas, gods, and others. || 58 ||
For the sake of accomplishing the perfection of the annual worship, O Damana, come hither; forgive me, and salutations be unto you! || 59 ||
"O you who have arisen from the grace of Śiva, be present here indeed! When the task of Śiva arises, you must depart by the command of Śiva. (60)
Having thus addressed Damana, Kāmadeva, and Rati, the practitioner should worship Prīti there as well, each with their respective mantra. || 61 ||
*Tāra* (Oṃ), *klīṃ kāmadevāya namaḥ*—this is the nine-syllable mantra. Having uttered *śrīṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ kroṃ*, followed by *ratyai namaḥ*, this eight-syllable mantra is for the Heart of Rati. (62)
At the place of pleasure, this eight-syllable mantra beginning with the word *prīti* [should be recited]. Then, on the second day, he should return to his own home. || 63 ||
