Having performed his daily obligatory rites and being joined with his own desired [virtues], he should approach self-restraint.
One should uproot or cut [the enemy] by means of one's own root-mantra and the weapon-mantra. || 64 ||
Having brought [the disciple] into the house, one should sprinkle him with water while reciting this mantra: "Oṃ aghore aiṃ ca oṃ ca ghore hrīṃ"—thus one should proclaim. || 65 ||
"Ghoraghoratare Śrīṃ, and to all from every side, to all from all; obeisance to you in your Rudra-forms, Hrīṃ Śrīṃ"—this is remembered as the mantra. || 66 ||

One should cause that [mantra], consisting of thirty-four syllables, to be placed in the Damana [rite]; and in the place of worship, on the pedestal and so forth, one should fashion for it a ninefold division.
Having fashioned an eight-petalled lotus, one should arrange the divisions therein.
And one should smear them with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and red sandalwood. || 68 ||
Having worshipped each of those seed-syllables individually with the syllables "Ānandeśī," along with the bindu and the word "namaḥ" at their ends,
one should here recite the mantra and ask for forgiveness.
One should construct a Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala at the place of worship.
In its eight directions, jars fashioned from gold and other materials should be placed.
Alternatively, if one is unable [to set up many vessels], one should then place only a single jar in the center;
there, one should perform the worship beginning with the worship of one's own seat (svāsana) and ending with the Yoga-pīṭha. || 71 ||
To the south of that, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus with vermilion, encircled by two circles and a square enclosure (bhūpura). || 72 ||
Having drawn an Aśoka flower upon the pericarp with powders of five colors,
and having made a petition to it, one should worship it with sandalwood and other offerings.
Salutations to you, O Aśoka, the destroyer of the sorrow of desire and women; remove my affliction of grief forever and produce joy within me. (74)
Then, on a similar mandala to its south, one should worship Kāla, who holds an excellent sword and is variegated with five colors. || 75 ||

Salutation to Him who is the self of Time, the one of great power whose form is time, beginning from a moment (truṭi) and ending with the dissolution of the universe, and who impels the entire world. || 76 ||
Then, below that Aśoka tree, in an auspicious triangular mandala.
One should perform the worship of the sacred seats (pīṭhapūjā), beginning with Maṇḍūka and ending with Jñānātman. || 77 ||
Outside of that, on the eight petals, the worship of the eight Śaktis is prescribed: Saubhāgyā, Hṛdyā, Vṛṣā, Dhṛti, and Rati. (78)
Having invoked the springtime joy called Nirvāṇa, which is full of longing in its midst,
and then Kāmadeva, one should proceed with the Gāyatrī of that [deity] thereafter.
We know Kāmadeva; we meditate upon the one with flower-arrows; may that Anaṅga inspire us. 80.
Having performed the rites up to the installation of life-force (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), one should then display the mudrās.
Thereafter, one should meditate upon those designated as the noose, the goad, the bow, and the arrow.
Clad in red garments, red in complexion, and anointed with red perfumes and unguents; wearing a red garland, youthful, and joined by [the two hands] on the left and right. (82)
In her lower hands, Rati holds a bow made of sugarcane and flower-arrows; above them is a noose. Thus, these three should be worshipped with the previously mentioned mantras.
One should meditate upon the auspicious Rati, fair-complexioned, clothed in red garments, adorned with all ornaments, and holding two lotuses in her hands. || 84 ||
She is dark-complexioned, wears red garments, and is adorned with all ornaments.
One should enjoy the love of her whose mouth is filled with betel and whose hands shine with water-jars and flowers. 85.
In front of Kāmadeva, one should worship Vasanta; [Vasanta] holds a jar of nectar in his left hand and a flower-weapon (kusumākara) in his right. 86.
One should meditate upon Vasanta, who stands in the midst of a Kadamba forest, clothed in red garlands and garments, fair-limbed, handsome, and enchanting to the world. || 87 ||

The heart-mantra of Vaṃvāsanta consists of seven syllables. Thereafter, for the purpose of worship and other rites, [one should worship] from the southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, and the center. || 88 ||

Having recited the seed-syllable of the Aṅga [Nārāyaṇa]—which consists of the syllable *vaṣaṭ* joined with four long vowels—in the four directions, one should worship the six limbs, beginning with the heart. || 89 ||
On the eight petals at its tip, starting from the face of the deity and proceeding clockwise, [one should worship] Kāma, Bhasmaśarīra, Anaṅga, and Anmatha. (90)
And I remember the friend of spring, the wielder of the bow of sugarcane, with his flower-arrows;
and before him, the weapons of the world-protectors.
Then, one should perform the recitation according to the sequence with the Kāma-gāyatrī; one should pray to Vasanta and Kāmadeva with two verses. || 92 ||
Salutations to you, O Spring, beloved of trees, shrubs, and creepers; salutations to you, who provide a thousandfold pleasure and can assume any form at will.
Salutations to the one whose arrows are flowers, who brings joy to the world; to Manmatha, the eye of the universe, and the beloved of Rati and Prīti. || 94 ||
Then, having bowed to Kāmadeva, one should perform the root-assignment (mūlanyāsa).
One should invoke the deity into the central jar and worship him along with his limbs (attendants).
O Lord of Gods, O All-pervading One, you have been invoked by me at this very moment; by your command, I shall perform the full festival according to my means as it ought to be done. 96.

Thus, one should then worship the God along with His retinue using *damanaka* flowers; having offered incense, lamps, and other offerings, one should perform the daily fire-sacrifice (*nityahoma*). || 97 ||

The fire sacrifice (homa) performed with substances prescribed for the gods is three times more efficacious than recitation (japa). Then, having completed the remainder of the worship, one should pray to the deity as follows: || 98 ||
O Lord of all forms, O bestower of the fruits of desired objects, O God, O Lord of the lords of desire, fulfill the desires residing within my heart. 99.
Having thus prayed to the Lord of Gods and then dismissed the Guru, [he should proceed].
One should satisfy the Brahmins with substances and other offerings and feed them; such is the rule for that [rite]. || 100 ||
A boon was granted by Śambhu to the serpent named Pavitra: "The fruit of that [merit] which has not been obtained by those who have performed the Pavitrāropaṇa shall be yours. (101)
One should perform [the rite] from the transit of Gemini until the transit of Libra. Āṣāḍha is the best month; Śrāvaṇa would be the middling one. (102)

The month of Bhādrapada is inferior; the bright fortnight is middling, while the dark fortnight is excellent. On the eighth, the fourth, and the fourteenth day, the Pavitraka rite should be performed.

On the ninth day as well, it should be performed according to the sequence starting with the Kṛta age; [the vessel] should be made of gold, silver, or copper, but in the Kali age, an auspicious one made of cotton [is prescribed].
But for householders it should be made of silk, while for forest-dwellers it should be made of bark.
For the followers of the Sugata, a lotus-born [seat] is prescribed; for Śūdras, a linen garment is desired. || 105 ||
For boys, it should be made of darbha grass; for Vaiśyas, however, it should be made of hemp.
For those established in vows, [the seat] is made of muñja grass; for those seeking battle, it is made of wool.
A pavitra made of one hundred and eight strands of new thread is declared to be supreme; half of that is remembered as middling. (107)
The smallest [should] be twenty-seven finger-breadths long.
The wise one should fashion [the offerings] equal to those of the deities of the worship-enclosure.
Thirty-six finger-breadths for the best [image], and twenty-four for the middling.
There should be exactly twelve [strands] in the smallest [pavitraka], and furthermore, there is another pavitraka.
From the shoulder down to the navel, provided with ten knots; that is declared to be the purifier for disciples who possess knowledge of the sequence. || 110 ||
For others, one may fashion them according to one's own wish, provided they are joined with small knots.
The wrapping of the knots is best when performed with twenty-six threads;
the middling is with twenty-four, and the inferior is recorded as being with twelve in number. The knots should be made with the *varma* mantra on the day prior.
At night, one should bring forth the sacred objects together with those who have taken the initiatory pledges.
And here at the place of worship, with vermilion, saffron, and red sandalwood; || 113 ||
One should decorate it with musk, camphor, lac, red ochre, and other pigments. [Camphor.]
Having established it upon the seat at the locations of the knots within those nine threads.
Devatā, Navakampa, Oṃkāra, Candramas, Vahni, Brahmā, Nāga, Guru, Ravi, as well as Śiva and Aśiva; || 115 ||

All the gods should also be worshipped; one should consecrate them with the *śiras-mantra* [the *svāhā*-mantra]. One should sprinkle them with the *hṛdaya-mantra* and secure them with the *astra-mantra*.
Within their ten knots (*granthi*), the ten Śaktis should be worshipped, as well as Kriyā.
Pauruṣī, Vīrā, Gāyatrī, and Aparājitā. || 117 ||
Vijayā, Jayā, Muktikā, Sadāśiva, and Manonmanī—these are to be worshipped with the root mantras and the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) during the purificatory rites. || 118 ||
One should place the first purifier (pavitra) and likewise the great purifier into the jar;
having performed the ritual depositions (nyāsa) and so forth there as before, one should arrange the worship. || 119 ||

Having invoked the deity into the pitcher, one should worship him along with the surrounding deities (āvaraṇas). The offering of the sacred thread (pavitra) is performed with the root mantra of the deity. || 120 ||
One should offer purifying oblations to the deities and satisfy the poor and the helpless; having given these abundantly, one should thereafter eat while remaining silent.
The procedure for the Pavitrāropaṇa has been declared here very clearly. I shall now describe the rites performed for specific desires; among those, peace (śānti) is first explained. 122.

Peace (śānti) is the destruction of diseases, sorcery, and the like for human beings. Having divided the day and night into six parts, the rite of peace (śāntika) is performed during the fifth portion. || 123 ||
In the winter season, one should perform [the rite] when the wind moves downward;
at that time, water is the essential element (tattva), and one should perform the pacifying rite (śāntika) therein.
Having fashioned a square mandala with a white color,
One should perform worship with sandalwood and other offerings using the seed-syllable *vaṃ* for the pacification of enemies.

Facing north, one should perform the rite of pacification (*śāntika*). At the beginning of the pacification rite and others, Rati is to be worshipped, as well as the lotus mudrā (*padmamudrā*)—[the lotus mudrā is formed when the two thumbs are joined in the palm;
one should bring the two hands together with the fingers held close and raised].
One should show [it]. || 126 ||
Having bound [the posture]—the characteristics of the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) were explained first.
One should place the right foot upon the left knee and the left foot upon the right knee;

thus one should remain in the *padmāsana* (lotus posture). For rites of pacification (*śāntika*), the mantra ends with "Namaḥ. Regarding pacification, *kuśa* grasses [are used]; for the rite of pacification, it should be understood from another text that the seat is a cowhide (*gocarmāsana*).
Furthermore, the worship with sexual union (ratipūjana) is prescribed by the Tantra; one should accept it and perform the fire offering (homa) with the deer-mudrā.
Where the oblation is offered while excluding the little finger, that becomes the Mṛgī mudrā.
On the three Uttarā lunar mansions, there should be rites for pacification among the twice-born.
Now, moreover, I shall explain that which brings others under one's control.
Of gods, rākṣasas, kings, the world, serpents, women, horses, and elephants. || 129 ||

In the first part [of the day, i.e., the first division of the day], the rite of subjugation (*vaśyakarma*) succeeds during the spring season. At that time, the wind does not flow upwards; rather, the fire-element (*agnitattva*) flows.
The rite of subjugation is performed with the triangle, using the seed-syllable *raṃ* for the worship of Fire, which is of red color.
Having performed the rite of subjugation, one should proceed facing the east.

One should worship Vāṇī for the purpose of subjugation (vaśya) and display the Pāśa-mudrā. Having placed the left index and middle fingers facing upwards, and the two right fingers facing downwards and well-aligned with each other,
this Pāśa-mudrā is formed by pressing them against one another.
Having assumed the svastika posture, one should recite the mantra ending with "svāhā" for those two. || 132 ||
For the purpose of subjugation (vaśya), one should perform a fire sacrifice with the skin of a goat [in another text, the skin of a rhinoceros];
one should sacrifice with the mudrā of a deer. In this rite, the sacrificial materials should be red, and the visualization (dhyāna) is held to be reddish. 133.

However, under the asterisms of Mṛgaśīrṣa, Antya (Revatī), Citrā, Amitra (Śatabhiṣaj), Viśākhā, and Kṛttikā, I shall now describe the ritual for the pillar, which prevents obstacles to its undertaking. || 134 ||
In the winter season, that sixth part of the day is said to be for immobilization; it is [effective] against fire, water, an army, an enraged person, and venomous fanged creatures. || 135 ||
One should bring water mixed with the blood of a ram for the purpose of satiation; then, having knelt upon the ground, one should perform the rite of immobilization (stambhana).
The suppression of the diseases of lovers and Buddhists is the Dharma; [it is likewise] the protection against ghosts, spirits, and other demons.
If the wind becomes fixed and attached to the bridge of the nose, it results in the arising of the earth element. || 137 ||
Then one should perform the rite of immobilization (stambha) using the seed-syllable *laṃ* for the Earth; one should worship her within a yellow mandala provided with eight corners. || 138 ||
Facing the east, one should perform the rite of immobilization (stambhana) and worship Ramā there.
[Seated in the vikaṭāsana posture, one should place both arms between the knees and the shanks;
this is defined as the vikaṭāsana by the sages. For the Goddess, the mace-mudrā (gadāmudrā) consists of the two arms straightened with the fingers interlaced and the thumbs [joined].
When the middle fingers are joined together and well extended, one should display [this mudrā]. || 139 ||
The mantra for the rite of immobilization (stambhana) is proclaimed to end with "vaṣaṭ" during the fire-oblation (homa).
The elephant-hide posture is likewise used for the pillar, the mace, and the mudrā-offering. || 140 ||

In this rite, the oblation (homa) should be performed with yellow substances, and one should oneself wear yellow garments and so forth. For the purpose of immobilization (stambhana), the asterisms are Bharaṇī, Citrā, Rohiṇī, and the three Uttaras. 141.

Now I shall describe the rite of inciting enmity; it causes the destruction of affection between two people. Enmity should be incited during the summer season, specifically on the second part of the day. (142)

When the wind is situated in the middle of the nose at the rising of space [the arising of the element of ether], hatred is prescribed. One should worship space within a circular mandala of smoky color.

Then, with the seed-syllable *haṃ*, one should perform the rite of inciting hatred while facing the southwest. Dhūmāvatī—the elder goddess—is to be worshipped; for hatred, the mudrā is the *musala* (the pestle-mudrā, which consists of placing the right hand over the left).
One should form a pair of fists with the two hands; that is the destroyer of obstacles. || 144 ||
In this rite, one should enter the *homamantra* ending with *phaṭ* while seated in the cock posture (*kukkuṭāsana*).

[Having first assumed the squatting posture (*utkaṭāsana*), then placing both feet evenly together, and finally placing both hands between the knees—that is declared the cock posture. For the purpose of inciting hatred (*vidveṣa*), one may use the skin of a jackal or even an iron seat.
The offerings should be made with smoke-colored substances, and the practitioners should likewise wear smoke-colored garments and so forth.
The four Ārdrās and Mūla, along with Jyeṣṭhā, are considered suitable for the rite of causing enmity.
Now I shall describe the rite of eradication (uccāṭana), which is the expulsion of enemies; for the eradication during the rainy season, the third part of the day is recommended. (147)
But when the wind has moved horizontally, the wind blows [the air-element]; and there, indeed:
One should perform the eradication of an enemy; one should worship that [deity] with the seed-syllable "yaṃ."
The mandala of Vāyu is hexagonal, black in color, and marked with six dots.
In that [rite], deerskin and so forth are used for the ritual of Vāyu.

One should worship Durgā and display the Aśani mudrā— the Aśani mudrā is considered to be that formed by joining the little finger and the thumb in a triangular shape. Seated in the vajrāsana posture— having placed the feet successively upon the thighs with the fingers turned inward toward the knees— one should hold the two hands...
One should place the verb [therein], the unsurpassed Vajrāsana; and the mantra for the oblation ends with *phaṭ*. || 150 ||
For the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*), one should perform meditation on a smoky-colored deity and likewise offer oblations with black substances.

Such a rite of eradication is praised when performed during the *kṣipra* nakṣatras—namely Hasta, Aśvinī, Puṣya, and Abhijit. Furthermore, that which is declared as the "killing" (*māraṇa*) of enemies—that is, the taking of their lives—is prescribed for the rite of killing. Regarding killing:
One should avoid other Brahmins as well as those who are highly righteous.
One should employ [this] against enemies of the king, excluding women and children; or, out of anger, one may take it away for the sake of protecting the people. || 153 ||
But a mantra-practitioner should never perform a rite of killing out of greed or fear; O Goddess, an expiation must be performed for the pacification of that fault. 154.
One should recite the mantra ten thousand times and likewise perform as many oblations with milk-rice mixed with ghee, or with black sesame seeds combined with ghee. || 155 ||
The wise should always perform self-protection at the time of performing the rite; specifically during the fourth or sixth part of the day for the rite of killing in autumn. (156)
In rites of subjugation and killing, worship and other rituals should be performed within a fire-mandala.
Facing south, one should perform the rite and worship Bhadrakālī.
One should display the sword mudrā (*khaḍgamudrā*):

having extended the three fingers beginning with the index finger of the raised left hand, one should join the other two—the thumb and the little finger—mutually; this is declared to be the sword mudrā.

She who cuts down all enemies should enter the auspicious seat (bhadra-āsana). Having placed the pair of ankles very firmly on either side of the perineum (sīvinī), one should bind the heels beneath the scrotum with both hands. The channel which lies between the anus and the genitals—
It is called *sīvinī* when, having placed the ankles below the testicles and having positioned the forefeet [there], one binds the forefeet with both hands; this is the *bhadrāsana*.
One should offer oblations with the mantra ending in *huṃ*, using either buffalo flesh or iron [substances]. (158) p. 164)
The posture is the Śūkarī-mudrā, which arises from the contraction of the hands. One should perform meditation on the black-colored [deity] and worship with black substances. || 159 ||
Regarding the fierce (*ugra*) and sharp (*tīkṣṇa*) [natures]: 2.
*Pūrvā-phālgunī*, *Pūrvā-āṣāḍhā*, *Pūrvā-bhādrapadā*, *Bharaṇī*, and *Maghā* are fierce; 3. *Ārdrā*, *Āśleṣā*, *Mūla*, and *Jyeṣṭhā* are sharp. Of one's own [natal asterism].
When the strength of the moon, stars, and so forth is lacking, and when the enemy's strength is likewise absent, one should stand upon a single foot. || 160 ||
Warm water with black pepper is for the purpose of satiation, but [it is used] for killing in [the case of] māraṇa.
While standing, one may perform the rite of killing, or else place one's foot upon the ground. || 161 ||

Standing with his left foot placed [there], he should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) at that spot; furthermore, miscellaneous rites and malevolent spells (abhicāra) will be explained therein. || 162 ||
Facing south and seated upon the skin of a ewe, or else seated upon an iron throne or a sow, one should perform the oblation with the mudrā. || 163 ||
One should perform the rite that accomplishes wealth while facing westward.
In the Mṛga, Antya, Citrā, and Maitra [nakṣatras], meditation on the gods is of the nature of passion (rājasa). || 164 ||
One should recite the mantra ending with "svāhā," beginning with "gocarmaṇāsanam" for delusion.
One should employ water mixed with turmeric for the purpose of libation.
Svātī and Rohiṇī are also excellent for that, as is a comfortable seat;
furthermore, one should accomplish all fierce rites under the constellation Raudra. || 166 ||
In various types of rites, the tiger skin is prescribed.
With a steady mind, one should meditate on the form of the All-Protecting Lion. || 167 ||
It was joined with a shower of nectar and possessed a radiance equal to that of the full moon.
Or rather, the practitioner should meditate upon Him in this manner during all ritual activities. || 168 ||
For the attainment of long life, one should listen [to the teaching] and meditate upon the deity Rājasī; for the conquest of untimely death, the three Uttaras as well as Pūrvā are prescribed. (169)

One should meditate on the deity presiding over the royal assembly; the mantra for the oblation should end with "vaṣaṭ," and one facing the southeast corner should perform the rite of attraction (ākarṣaṇa). || 170 ||
Everything stated for subjugation (vaśya) should be understood as applicable to attraction (ākarṣaṇa) for the sake of accomplishing one's purpose.
For the sake of accomplishing all-knowledge, one should face Īśāna. || 171 ||

In all ritual actions involving consciousness, a white woolen blanket serves as the seat; for the accomplishment of nourishment and other such rites, the mantra is joined with the *vauṣaṭ* exclamation and the sprout-syllable. || 172 ||
The Haṃsī mudrā is formed by releasing the index finger; this mudrā is used for the nourishing (pauṣṭika) fire sacrifice.
In rites for nourishment (pauṣṭika), one should perform meditation on the deity as previously described. || 173 ||
For the destruction of fear everywhere, the mantra for the oblation ends with "vaṣaṭ."
Indeed, meditation conjoined with great bliss shall become fearless. || 174 ||

In rites for the destruction of mantras, the mantra used in the oblation (homa) ends with *vaṣaṭ*; however, in the case of breaking [the mantra], it should end with *phaṭ*. The visualization (*dhyāna*) in this instance is of a tamasic nature. (175)
For the sake of happiness, one should perform the recitation while facing north upon the skin of a ruru deer.
In battle, one should meditate upon the Lord as being of the nature of darkness (tāmasa), like the fire at the end of an aeon. || 176 ||

Now I shall describe the deities who are to be worshipped at the beginning of rites for specific desires; one should always worship Vighna (Gaṇeśa), the lords of the days of the week, and the lords of the lunar days.
Then the lords of the lunar mansions, who are the presiding deities of their respective rites, should be worshipped.
Then one should worship the chosen deity, and thereafter perform the fire sacrifice (homa).
In due order, [the lords of the gates are] Sūrya and Śiva, Soma and Ambikā, Guha and Aṅgāra, Jña and Viṣṇu, and Caturvaktra and Bṛhaspati. (179)
O Goddess, Venus and Jupiter, Saturn and Rāhu are declared to be the deities to be worshipped on Sunday and the other days, respectively;
now hear from me concerning the lords of the lunar days (tithis). || 180 ||
Brahmā, the Creator, Viṣṇu, Yama, the Moon, Guha, Indra, the Vasus, the Nāgas, Dharma, Śiva, and the Sun; || 181 ||
Kandarpa, Kali, the Viśvedevas, and likewise the Pitṛs; the two Aśvins, Yama, Vahni, Brahmā, Candra, Śiva, and Aditi. || 182 ||
The Guru, the serpents, the ancestors, Bhaga, Yama, and the Sun; Tvaṣṭṛ, Vāyu, Indra and Agni, and Mitra, the lord of the gods. || 183 ||
Nirṛti, Jala, the Viśvedevas, Vidhi, and Hari;
the Vasus, Varuṇa, Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, and Pūṣan. || 184 ||
These are the twenty-eight lords of the lunar mansions, including Abhijit.

[They should be addressed] beginning with the syllable *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending in the dative case, accompanied by the word *namaḥ*—for example: *Oṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*, *Oṃ vidhātre namaḥ*, and so forth. || 185 ||
The name-mantras of these [deities] should be employed in the practice of worship and other rites. (186)
One who has mastered the mantra should perform rites for specific desires, and not otherwise;
if they are performed perversely, one will fall into hell. || 187 ||
Devoted to the guru, pure, bathed, and knowing the procedure for rites performed for specific desires, one should perform the rites for desired ends both for oneself and for others. || 188 ||
The best of mantra-knowers should perform the six rites for the sake of others; he should perform them only for these [six classes] and never for anyone else. 189.
Whether for a king, a prince, a wealthy man, or anyone else—provided they are a believer, devoted, and possess wealth acquired through righteous means. (190)
The preceptor should perform the rite for one who is grateful, generous, a worshiper of the guru and the gods, virtuous in conduct, and deeply devoted. || 191 ||
The king, or another person acting as the patron, should bow down to the practitioner.
Then, one should choose the performer of the rite according to the procedure prescribed for initiation.
The practitioner should be self-restrained, a twice-born man, contented, and pure.
Having conquered his senses and subdued his anger, he is free from the agitation of pride. || 193 ||
One who is devoted to the obligatory and occasional rites may perform various kinds of desired actions;
however, having performed the cruel rite as prescribed, one should then perform the ritual anointing (abhyaṅga). || 194 ||
Having bathed, one should worship one's chosen deity together with its enclosures and limbs.
And for the sake of protection, one should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times.
Having said, "Protect me, protect me! and having bowed to the deity, one should dismiss him;
however, one should have protection from harm performed by other very affectionate friends.
By means of mantras such as the Mṛtyuñjaya and others, through service to the Sun and the offering of arghya water.
And by means of recitation, burnt offerings, worship, and so forth, as well as by the propitiation of Brahmins and similar acts. || 197 ||
One should perform the ritual application correctly, having learned it from a guru and likewise from the scriptures;
for by performing the applications otherwise, one will surely encounter suffering. || 198 ||

Then the king, having caused [the rite] to be performed, should satisfy the practitioner with wealth; bowing down repeatedly, he should act in such a way that the practitioner attains complete satisfaction. || 199 ||
For one whose mantra is perfected, the six rites are accomplished without a doubt;
for one whose mantra is not perfected, they are not accomplished at all, and he shall incur the curse of the deity. || 200 ||
For those who perform rites for the sake of desired rewards, there is no world beyond.
The accomplishment of their practice alone is their fruit; nothing else exists. || 201 ||
Through oblations, libations, mantras, and various specific meditations, one should effectively accomplish the six rites for both oneself and others. || 202 ||
The practitioner of mantras should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, employing the yoga of meditative visualization and ritual placement.
For the sake of pacifying defects in the ritual application and for the sake of self-protection. || 203 ||
If he does not obtain the fruit [of his labor], he shall incur the curse of the deity.

One should declare all matters—whether auspicious or inauspicious—based on the fire's radiance, smoke, color, sound, fragrance, the shape of its flames, and the movements and other behaviors of the messenger. || 204 ||

Having performed the consultation and the subsequent connection characterized by the entry of the deity into the body and so forth, devotion to the Guru must always be practiced, especially at the time of ritual action. || 205 ||
For those seeking benefits in this world and the next, the Guru alone is the supreme refuge. [But] rites such as killing and driving away belong to the base practitioners of the left-hand path. (206)
Minor deities accomplish [only trivial things]; they are not capable of bestowing true happiness.
But for those who are devoted to the supreme goal of others, this is the highest state. || 207 ||
The consecration, wealth, and so forth should be exactly as prescribed;
the people of the South never perform anything censurable here. || 208 ||
For those men who are pure by birth and have been consecrated according to the rites prescribed for the eon, there is the attainment of power and the eternal world beyond. || 209 ||
If they fall on the left, what sin could be greater than this? This has been declared as the "northern" practice;
what else do you wish to hear? || 210 ||
Thus ends the seventh chapter, the Illumination on the Stabilization of Siddhi, in the Merutantra composed by Śiva with the approval of the illustrious Mahāmāyā and Mahākāla. || 7 ||
Śrī Devī said:
Tell me the characteristics of the mudrās, those which are identical on the left and the right.
And those [mantras] which are dear to all the gods and bestow the fruitfulness of worship. || 1 ||
The illustrious Śiva said:
Indeed, you shall explain the characteristics of the mudrās from the beginning; for him who performs them constantly, all the gods shall become bestowers of happiness. || 2 ||
The mudrā called Aṅkuśa is formed with the ring finger and little finger behind, the index finger curved over the thumb,
and the middle finger straight.
That throat-seal (kaṇṭhamudrā) binds all throats with both hands.
In this [mudrā], the right thumb is joined with the left [thumb] to form a single fist.
The Vahniprākāra-mudrā consists of both hands with the tips of the tridents [formed by the index fingers] crossed and placed on either side of the fire; it is also called the Astra-mudrā. || 5 ||
As for the finger-mudrās, one should touch the five fingers in successive order.
With the thumb [touch] four [fingers], and with the index finger [touch] the thumb itself.
The mudrā called "Heart" consists of the fingers with the thumb excluded, all extended.
Four fingers apart at his heart, [he should do so] according to the mantra.
That is to be known as the Śiromudrā, with the palm extended along the side.
And four fingers were also extended and held by the head. || 8 ||

That should be known as the Śikhā-mudrā; having formed a fist with the thumb extended like a sprout, and having touched the crest-lock (śikhā) with it while reciting the Śikhā-mantra, by the practitioners (sādhakas). 9.
This mudrā is indeed called kavaca; the fingers are joined together like a tube.
The movement of the hands should extend as far as the shoulders. || 10 ||
This is known as the Trinetra-mudrā; the index finger is placed at the right eye, while the middle and ring fingers are on the forehead and the left [eye] respectively for the three-eyed deities.
This is known as the Dvinetra-mudrā (the two-eye gesture): the index finger is placed on the right eye and the middle finger on the left eye, [used] for the various [deities] such as Sūrya and Viṣṇu.
The eight mudrās have been fully described as warding off all misfortunes;
they are proclaimed by means of the tips of the thumbs and index fingers of both hands.
These are the seals of the six limbs for both the daily (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites. Now, I shall describe the characteristics of the six seals for the optional (kāmya) rites. 14.
The two thumbs are joined at their sides, and the two index fingers are straight and joined together.
The middle fingers are joined back-to-back, and the other [fingers] are likewise positioned.
Some [place the hands] with the backs of the palms touching each other and raised high;
this is proclaimed as the *namaskāra-mudrā* of Lalitā. || 16 ||
Having made the two index fingers straight, the remaining fingers are joined by their nails.
The two thumbs placed upon the middle joints of the little fingers are considered the *kṣobhiṇī* [mudrā]. || 17 ||
With the index fingers straight and the little and ring fingers joined, and with the tips of the little fingers placed upon the thumbs, this shall be the Drāviṇī mudrā. || 18 ||
The little finger, middle finger, thumb, and two index fingers are bent; the two middle fingers are straight, while the remaining [fingers] are joined at the tips and drawn forward. || 19 ||
This heart-mudrā is used in rites for desired ends, as well as in the Śaiva Āgamas.
Having formed the fists with the hands, one should place the two thumbs upon the heart.
The head-mudrā is formed by placing both hands, joined in fists, at the tip of the forehead.
One should form [the mudrā] with the two index fingers (tarjanī) joined by the thumbs (jyeṣṭhā), their tips directed upwards and slightly hooked.
The Śikhāmudrā is formed by the two hands being released from the fist-position; the two index fingers have their tips joined, while the two little fingers are positioned upwards. || 22 ||
The mudrā called Kavaca and the one called Prasakta are formed by placing the two thumbs like a triangle.
With the two index fingers, one should bring [the mudrā] to the head, the face, the sides, the hands, and the heart.
The Netramudrā consists of the middle, index, and ring fingers held straight; when a bow is unavailable, the thumb and little finger are joined at their tips. (24)
The *astramudrā* follows that as well, performed by the clapping of both hands; one should then produce a sound with the two index fingers, the tips of which are bent toward each other. (25)
The gālinī mudrā consists of the little finger and the thumb joined with one another.
The index, middle, and ring fingers of the two hands are joined and not bent. || 26 ||
For the bow mudrā, one should interlace the little fingers and ring fingers of both hands and display the index and middle fingers upon the right shoulder. || 27 ||
The conch mudrā, however, consists of the left thumb placed within the right fist.
When the tip of the left index finger is joined with the right thumb, it is produced. || 28 ||
The *yonimudrā* is formed by joining the little fingers and index fingers of both hands, while the palms remain separated;
the remaining fingers—the thumbs and ring fingers—are kept extended. || 29 ||
The fish-seal (matsyamudrā) has the left hand facing downwards; placing the right hand in the same manner above it, one should move the two thumbs. || 30 ||
The invocation mudrā, however, is formed by joining the two hands in the añjali gesture.
Then, one should place the two thumbs upon the root-joints of the painless [fingers].
That [mudrā] is the Sthāpanī; this same one is the Āvāhana-mudrikā. If it is turned face downwards, it is capable of establishing everything. || 32 ||
The *sammukhīkaraṇī* (face-to-face) mudrā should be known as the pair of fists; that which is used for the installation of the deities is the one with both thumbs released.
That which is performed as the assignment (nyāsa) of the six limbs upon the deity—wherein the limbs are assigned once to the possessor of limbs—is declared to be the sakalīkaraṇī mudrā. || 34 ||
The Avaguṇṭhana-mudrā consists of the left hand formed into a fist with the index finger extended long and pointing downwards; one should then rotate that [finger]. 35.
That which is designated as Mahāmudrā is indeed that which brings about the state of supremacy.
With the fingers of the hands extended and the thumbs interlaced with one another. || 36 ||
The mudrā for causing the appearance [of wealth] is the union of two fists;
if both thumbs are properly formed and raised upward, it is so. (37)
That mudrā, however, is the obstructing one (saṃrodhinī), wherein the two fists are inserted within each other.
If the two thumbs are joined in a fist and there be no gap between them, [it is the mudrā]. || 38 ||

The *dantamudrā* (tooth-gesture), born of the right hand, is dear to Gaṇeśa; it has the palm facing upward with the fingers pointing skyward, the middle finger held straight, and the fist clenched. || 39 ||
But for the left [hand], the one called the noose is on the index finger, [to which] the right index finger [is joined].
Having thrown [the hands] and bound the two fists, there is the joining of the two index fingers with the two thumbs. || 40 ||
The fingers of the hands are interlocked and joined with their tips pointing downwards;
the two thumbs are raised and joined—this mudrā is considered "subjugating" (vaśakarī). || 41 ||

With the two hands extended, one should join the tips of the little fingers together; then, having firmly bound them with the two middle fingers, one should join the tips of the ring fingers. || 42 ||
One should place the two index fingers at the tips of the ring fingers—[the letter *a* being elided]—above the middle fingers.
The Unmādinī mudrā is considered to be that in which the two thumbs are joined together. || 43 ||
The other fingers, the little fingers, are firmly bound together by the two middle fingers.
When the ring finger and the thumb are joined while the others are straight, it is the mahāṅkuśa mudrā.

When the *vighnamudrā* is long in form, with the middle fingers pointing downward, and the thumb forms a fist emerging from the joint of the index and middle fingers; [this is the *vighnamudrā*]. (45)
And the mudrā of the axe (paraśu) is formed by joining the fingers obliquely.
The hands are extended and joined, with the palms brought together.
The mudrā called Laṇḍḍuka is formed by raising the right hand with its palm facing upward.
The fingers are spaced apart and bent, and the palm of the hand is likewise depressed. || 47 ||
When the left fist is turned upward with the seed-vessel (bījapūra) filling it, there are the six mudrās of Gaṇeśa beginning with Danta; the Aṅkuśa-mudrā is the seventh. || 48 ||
That mudrā is called Varā; it consists of the fingers being very closely joined. Having placed the right hand palm upwards, one should slowly bend it downwards. (49)
This is declared to be the mudrā of Abhaya, which bestows fearlessness; it is formed by turning the left hand away with the thumb and little finger joined. (50)

When the middle finger and index finger of the right hand are extended and joined, and the left hand is stretched out horizontally with its movement bent inward— this is considered the Seal of the Leather (Carmamudrā), beloved by Śakti. 51.

The bow mudrā consists of joining the tip of the left middle finger with the tip of the index finger; the tips of the little fingers are placed on the left shoulder and pressed by the right thumb. (52)
The mudrā called the pestle (musala) occurs when the right hand is placed over the left.
One should form a pair of fists with the hands to destroy obstacles. || 53 ||
As for the Durgāmudrā, one should form fists with both hands and apply them such that the right hand is placed upon the left on the head. || 54 ||
The arrow-mudrā is formed by the long index finger of the right fist. The eight [mudrās] beginning with Varada, along with the noose and the goad, are recorded as the ten mudrās of Śakti. || 55 ||
Having placed the palms of the hands facing downwards, one should insert the two thumbs between the little fingers and the ring fingers. 56.
The *gadā* [mudrā], however, consists of the two hands straight with fingers interlaced; furthermore, the two middle fingers are extended and joined at their tips.
When the two thumbs are joined together in the palm, one should bring the two hands facing each other with the fingers pressed together and raised. 58.
The flute mudrā is formed by joining the left and right little fingers with the thumbs.
The remaining [fingers] are within the belly of the left thumb, and the little finger is curved upward. || 59 ||
The two hands joined together, with the middle, ring, and thumb fingers bound, form the Śrīvatsa mudrā.
If the two index fingers are placed at the base of the two little fingers, [it is so]. (60)
The Kaustubha mudrā is formed by the middle fingers and the thumbs joined with their tips pointing upward.
The knuckles of the little fingers and the index fingers should be joined, with the two hands placed face-to-face horizontally.
The mudrā called Vanamālā consists of a fist formed by the thumb and index finger;
with both hands, one should touch [the body] like a garland from the neck down to the feet.
The wisdom-seal (jñānamudrā) consists of the index finger and thumb joined together and placed upon the heart.
Or, if he should place his left lotus-hand upon his head; || 63 ||
The Viśvākhyā [mudrā] consists of the right thumb encircling the left hand, which is raised upward.
One should place the fingers of both hands, fixed upon that [thumb], against the heart.
And having wrapped around the forearms, the wrists, and the elbows.
Having joined them correctly, one should wrap them well with the two index fingers in the middle. || 65 ||
Having joined the two middle fingers in the yoga [mudrā], the two thumbs [should be placed] upon the other fingers.
When they are mutually interlocked at the edge of the right ear, that is considered Khecarī.
In the first joint, one should properly join the two little fingers together;
then, below that, one should join the two ring fingers at their middle joint.

One should join the tips of the nails of those [fingers] above the ring fingers; having left a space between the two "elephant trunks" (the middle fingers), there is a joining of the index fingers and the thumbs. || 68 ||

This mudrā, known as the source of boons (varayoni), is considered to be called the seed (bīja). Without the seed-mantra (bījavidyā), all [practices] such as worship and recitation are in vain. || 69 ||
The mudrā of Garuḍa consists of the two hands joined together with the little fingers interlaced;
the two index fingers are likewise joined to each other, while the two superior fingers (the thumbs) are placed at the level of the feet.
In the Nṛsiṃha-mudrā, the chin and the lower lip [are brought together], while the hands, fixed at the knees, are placed between them.
If the tongue of the wide-mouthed one quivers while repeatedly licking the lips, and the eyes are terrifying, this is the seal of Narahari; if all the fingers are turned downward, it is likewise.
And with the two thumbs of the hands, one should press upon the two little fingers.
Vārāhī [is placed] on the right hand, which is extended and supine; the left [hand] is inverted above it.
Having joined the tips of the fingers, one should bend them downward. || 73 ||

In the Hayagrīva [mudrā], the fingers of the left hand are equal and facing downward; having restrained them with the middle finger, one should bend the middle [finger]—thus it becomes that [mudrā]. || 74 ||

When the hands are joined in the *kāma* (love) gesture, with the two middle fingers placed on the back [of the other hand], and the two index fingers resting upon the middle fingers, while the pair of thumbs is likewise positioned [on the backs of the middle fingers]. (75)
The Trailokyamohinī mudrā is formed by placing the fists with the thumbs inside upon the head.
And these [weapons] of Hari, beginning with the discus and ending with the bow and arrow. (76)
In the Vidhumudrā, the two hands, resembling lotuses, have the middle fingers joined; one should hold the other fingers together and display them at the tip of the moon.
The solar mudrā consists of the left hand placed below with the palm facing upward and the fingers pointing toward the top.
The lotus-shaped mudrā and [the other] should both be [performed] by those dear to the Sun. || 78 ||
One should encircle the mudrā called liṅga, which is on the right, with the left thumb.
One should wrap the two left fingers with the right ones; that is beloved by Śiva.
The mudrā called Triśūla (Trident) is formed by joining the thumb with the little finger and then extending the remaining three fingers. || 80 ||
One should firmly tie the tips of the thumb and forefinger together in the garland mudrā.
One should extend three fingers for the successful accomplishment of recitation (japa). || 81 ||
The deer seal consists of the index finger and the little finger with their tips raised.
The tips of the ring finger, the thumb, and the middle finger are joined crosswise. || 82 ||
The Khaṭvāṅga-mudrā, having six faces, becomes exceedingly dear to Śiva. If the five fingers of the right hand are joined and raised upwards, [it is the Khaṭvāṅga-mudrā]. || 83 ||
The Kapālinī mudrā occurs when the left hand is placed upon the left shoulder like a bowl; she is the beloved of Bhairava. 84.
The ḍamaru [mudrā] is formed by making a loose fist with the middle finger raised.
One should move these ten near the ear; they are considered [the ten] by Śūlin.
The mudrā called āsana is performed while sitting comfortably on a pleasant seat; the two hands, placed upon one's respective knees, face downward like buds. 86.
If the two hands are raised, swayed, and shaped like hoods, each positioned in its respective direction, this is the mudrā known as Kuśalā. (87)
Having firmly formed the left fist, one should extend the index finger.
Or one should bring that auspiciousness-bestowing mudrā to the left ear.
One should form a fist with the right hand, with the thumb tucked inside.
This mudrā, known as Ripujihvāgraha, is the destroyer of enemies. || 89 ||
The mudrā called Sāgatā occurs when the two hands are separated by a span (vitasti).
The man should likewise remain bent over, with his thighs extended and positioned near [the woman]. || 90 ||

That should be known as the *arghyamudrā*; it must be firm and without gaps. When the two hands are joined in *añjali* and the fists are positioned near the ears, [it is the *karṇapūraṇamudrā*]. || 91 ||
The *pādya* mudrā is indeed the same as the *arghya* mudrā, with this specific distinction.
The joining of the thumbs and index fingers should be performed with both hands.
The *mudrā* known as *ācamana* consists of the palms joined together with the hollows facing downward;
it is formed by the three fingers excluding the little finger, with the tips of the thumbs joined to the index fingers. (93)
This shall be the mudrā for the madhuparka offering, provided it is turned face downwards.
If the tips of the ring finger and the thumb are joined together, [it is formed]. (94)
If the mudrā of bathing consists of the right hand in a fist turned downwards and joined with the little finger, it bestows infinite fruit through that bath. 95.
For the mudrā of clothing, one should turn the right hand upward and touch the middle finger with the thumb;
this is used for the giving and wearing of clothes.
If this [mudrā] is turned face downwards, it becomes the mudrā of ornaments;
if the tips of the ring finger and the thumb are joined together, [it is so]. (97)

The bathing mudrā is fully described as being formed by the joining of the little finger and the thumb; it is used for the performance of the sacred thread (upavīta) and in cases where its wearing has been interrupted. || 98 ||

The mudrā for fragrance should be understood as follows: one should perform the gesture with the hand turned palm-upward; by touching the tip of the little finger with the tip of the thumb, it is used for the offering of fragrance. 99.
The mudrā called Puṣpa is formed by turning the hand downward and joining the tips of the index finger and the thumb; this is used for worship. 100.
The incense mudrā, however, is fully extended for the incense offering to the gods and others; one should touch the tip of the index finger with the tip of the thumb as before. || 101 ||
Now, the lamp-mudrā is taught; it brings everything dear to the lamp. One should touch the tip [of the lamp] with the tips of the thumbs and the middle fingers as before. 102.
The offering mudrā for the deities is proclaimed to be as described previously.
One should join the tip of the ring finger with the tip of the thumb.
The *grāsamudrā* consists of the right hand formed in the shape of a full-blown lotus.
One should demonstrate the five winds; they are called the five mudrās. || 104 ||
Now I shall describe the Prāṇamudrā; one should display it at the beginning of a meal.
One should properly join the little finger and the ring finger with the tip of the thumb.

The mudrā of drinking [air] should be understood as the joining of the index finger and the middle finger; by the sight of this, the yogi is liberated through the obstruction of the vital winds. || 106 ||
That is to be known as the Vyāna-mudrā, formed by joining the middle and ring fingers; upon seeing it, the vital air (vāyu) pervading the entire body becomes well-pleased. || 107 ||
The mudrā of the udāna wind should be performed with the thumb.
The ring finger, middle finger, and middle toe dispel all diseases. || 108 ||
When the five fingers are joined together, it is the mudrā of the samāna wind.
The mantras beginning with the syllable *praṇava* (Om), ending in the dative case, and concluding with "namas" are [to be used] for the names. || 109 ||
In the union of the little finger and the thumb, the other three fingers are held straight.
The mudrā called Mahāyoni bestows the bliss of Sundarī. || 110 ||
Having joined the two hands together with the fingers interlaced with one another.
Having raised the two hands joined at the inner palms, the two index fingers are made straight. || 111 ||
Thereafter, one should perform a salutation with the mudrā for raising the Śakti;
by this, the Śakti that has been brought forth shall go to her own place as a bestower of boons.
The mudrā called Saptajihvā consists of the two hands with the fingers extended.
The pair of little fingers and thumbs, as well as the two wrists, are joined together.
The mudrā of Bhūtabali is said to be the joining of all the fingers, with the hollow of the hand at the end and the mouth resembling a crow’s beak. || 114 ||
One should bring the left hand to the front of the arrow and the right hand to the back;
gradually straightening them, the other fingers [except] the two index fingers are joined in a seal. || 115 ||

The hand called *saṃhāra* is turned downward; the fingers of the left hand are thus knotted above those of the right. When both hands are thus inverted and bound, it is the *visarga* mudrā, which brings satisfaction to the deities of the offerings and so forth. (p. 173) 116.
That mudrā is named Aśani; with the left index finger pointing upward and the other [right index finger] facing downward, joined together therein, it is the destroyer of enemies. 117.
If the fingers are joined in the form of the moon-mudrā, it is indeed the fist-mudrā.
One should employ the joining of the index finger and the thumb in the rite of fulfillment (pūrṇakarma). || 118 ||
It becomes the Kālakarṇī mudrā when the two thumbs are raised from the fists.
And at that time, two others were also attached to the sides, facing toward him.
The *mudrā* known as Vismaya shall produce a state of being overcome by wonder.
The right fist is tightly clenched, with the index finger placed against the nose. || 120 ||
If the thumb is held within the fist by the index finger, this is the Nādamudrā; it should be practiced by those who practice restraint, for it brings about the manifestation of Brahman. 121.
The mudrā called *prārthanā* (supplication) is formed by placing both hands at one's own heart.
The two [hands] should be seen with fingers extended, joined together, and facing each other. || 122 ||
This supreme Lakṣmī-mudrā indeed bestows all prosperity. Having joined the two hands together with the fingers extended, [one forms this mudrā]. || 123 ||
Having extended both hands to the region of the navel, one should touch them facing downwards with the two index fingers; that is the Annākhyamudrā, which bestows food. 124.
Having first formed the fang-mudrā and the wheel-mudrā, one should press [the thumb] with the two middle fingers and the two index fingers; this destroys all sins. 125.
The pṛṣṭhaka-mudrā is formed by extending the right hand; it is placed at the level of the navel or in the space before one, and then gazed upon. || 126 ||
The mudrā called Gajakarṇa consists of joining the backs of the two hands together; then, turning the hands upward, a knot is formed by the two thumbs. (127)
The mudrā for shaking the garment consists of the left little finger and forefinger.
At the tips, the roots, and the backs of both the middle and ring fingers, those two [should be placed]. || 128 ||
The Vāpī mudrā is formed by placing the middle finger of the right hand upon the left;
the index and little fingers of the right hand should be above those of the left. 129.
The mudrā called Śakaṭa is formed when the two middle fingers press against each other from behind, while the index and ring fingers [are held] as before. (130)
Now, the twenty-four mudrās of the Gāyatrī will be described; one should display them at the beginning of recitation, as well as their presiding deities and their fruits. || 131 ||
The two hands joined at the tips with the fingers slightly curved are called Sumukha; the Śakti associated there is Prahlādinī, who bestows bliss upon Sumukha. || 132 ||
The hands, joined together like two lotus buds, form the *sampuṭa* [mudrā]. Its power is Nityaviśvā, who brings great joy to the universe. 133.
The two hands joined together with the fingers not extended are called *hṛdayā*;
that is the power which reaches the hearts of all.
When the two hands are joined together with the fingers mutually released and spread wide, it is the Vimalā Śakti; by its power, one becomes stainless. (135)
The mudrā called Dvimukhā consists of the joining of the two little fingers (kaniṣṭhā) when the two hands are held facing each other;
its constant name is Śakti. || 136 ||
The mudrā called Trimukhā consists of the two ring fingers joined together in both hands, while the remaining fingers are separated; this is the Śakti Prabhāvatī. || 137 ||
He has four faces and two arms joined at the waist, with the luster of the midday sun.
But when the remaining fingers are joined together, it is proclaimed as the *līlā* mudrā. || 138 ||
Likewise, when the two index fingers are joined together while the other fingers are spread apart, that five-faced mudrā is Śakti; it brings peace and bestows tranquility. || 139 ||
This shall be the Ṣaṇmukha-mudrā, consisting of the joining of all the fingers.
Excluding the two little fingers, Śakti is proclaimed as Durgā. || 140 ||
The mudrā named Adhomukha consists of the two hands turned downward; with their tips slightly bent and joined together, its presiding deity is Sarasvatī. 141.
The mudrā named Vyāpakāñjali consists of the hands being positioned in that same manner; however, the distinction here is that they are turned upward, and the deity is Viśvarūpā. 142.
The mudrā named Śakaṭa consists of the two hands with the fingers interlaced at the tips; they are turned downwards with the fists clenched.
Here, however, the Viśākhā-śakti is present. (143)
When the two hands, with fists clenched, are joined together as the noose of Yama, and the two index fingers are joined there, Lopāmudrā is the deity in that [mudrā]. 144.
If the fingers are knotted together, joined at their mutual joints, with the thumbs raised and turned upward, this is declared to be the Vāmā-śakti mudrā. (145)
The Sammukhonmukha mudrā consists of two hands with their fingers interlaced; the right hand is turned downwards, while the left is turned upwards, forming the Āpyāyinī.
The mudrā named Vilamba consists of two hands with their palms turned upward and their tips raised;
its power is proclaimed to be Vimalā. || 147 ||
But when the two hands are joined together in fists with palms facing upward, that is declared to be the Śakti mudrā consisting of Tamas. || 148 ||
But when the fish has come face to face with the joined fingers reaching to the crown of the head, [it is the time for the rite].
The fingers with their tips joined upwards form the golden spear (śakti). || 149 ||
The tortoise is downward-facing; the left [hand] is grasped at the back by the right. His power (śakti) completely overcomes that [state]; she is subtle, the accomplisher of subtle goals. 150.
Vārāhī has her right hand raised upward and her left hand with the palm facing up.
Having placed it face downwards, she who is the source of the universe should bend it.
The mudrā called Siṃhākrānta consists of fingers made into sprouts; one should display it before the Goddess, and it is proclaimed to have the form of a spear and a mace.
One should never display the mudrā in a gathering of many people; the deities will become agitated with him, and his performance will become fruitless. || 153 ||
Just as mothers rejoice upon seeing the performance of a child, so do the deities rejoice upon seeing a mudrā performed with devotion. (154)
The deities proclaimed in the Uttarāmnāya are pleased by the fifth [offering]; however, if even a single ritual element is omitted, they curse the practitioner. (155)
For the deities of the Western Tradition, the drinking of liquor may or may not be performed.
They maintain that there are four macas, and they curse those who hold otherwise. || 156 ||
The flesh of the deities mentioned in the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya), whether prepared or unprepared.
There are five essential mantras; without them, they are cursed.
The fourfold [set] beginning with Ma is forbidden for the deities of the Southern Tradition (Dakṣiṇāmnāya); even without one of them, they curse the practitioner. || 158 ||
Therefore, the mudrās should be learned according to the tradition; one who knows the mudrās attains liberation everywhere—of this there is no doubt. (159)
Thus, everything that is concealed in all the tantras has been explained to you—the supreme reality of the mudrās. What else do you wish to hear? || 160 ||
Thus ends the eighth chapter, the Illumination of the Characteristics of Mudrās, in the Merutantra composed by Śiva with the approval of the illustrious Mahāmāyā and Mahākāla. || 8 ||
The goddess Śī said:

Through his practice, he seeks the next world for the sake of others' welfare, not for the sake of happiness in this life; in the Kali age, the disciple seeks success, and the guru seeks wealth. || 1 ||
Likewise, the gods desire worship, and the mind desires sense-objects.
If even the accomplishment pertaining to this body is far from us, how could that which pertains to another [body] possibly come to be? || 2 ||
Therefore, if there were some means by which success could be attained both in this world and the next without preliminary rites (*puraścaryā*) and the like, and without censure, please tell me that.
The Lord said:
They come and go, yet they are not considered [as such] by all living beings;
those texts composed by my own portions and called Āgamas have been spread abroad.
When two thousand five hundred years of the Kali age had passed, O gods.
At that time, however, the surface of the earth was abandoned by all the hosts of gods.
The Veda, Nārāyaṇa himself, will remain for a period of ten thousand years.
Even that region described in the scriptures will become inaccessible.
And for the sake of uplifting the virtuous, by the command of Mahākāla, I have related this worship of the earthen linga to those who are long-lived.
I shall now fully proclaim its ritual procedure; O gods, listen with reverence! In this world and in the next, spiritual perfection rests within the palm of one's hand.
In that regard, this is the procedure for the worship of earthen liṅgas: having bathed and performed the daily rites at the outset, the wise one should go to a pure spot of ground. (9)
The clay situated in these eight locations bestows the accomplishment of all aims.
At the root of an Aśvattha tree that has a Śamī tree at its heart, or on the bank of a river in a solitary place.
On a mountain peak, at a sacred ford, in a cow-pen, or in a grove of *tulasī* trees.
There, beneath the banyan tree, one should consecrate the ground and offer a prayer. || 11 ||
"Hrīṃ, obeisance to Earth"—this is declared to be the six-syllabled mantra. Having worshipped the Earth with this, one should offer a prayer. || 12 ||
For you, O Earth, are the support of all; protect me with this clay.
I shall accept you; being well-pleased, always become for me the object of my linga-worship.
Then, taking clay that is free from gravel, one should prepare it properly;
one should place it daily in a thoroughly purified vessel for the purpose of worship. || 14 ||
Or from one's own heart, or from the true guru, or from the sun, or from another deity.
Likewise, one should take seven [offerings] for the worship of Guha and Gaṇeśa.
In the taking of the earth, "Tāra" (Oṃ) followed by "Harāya namaḥ" is used; with "Maheśvarāya" following "Tāra," there should be a conjunction with "namaḥ. || 16 ||
The mantra for dismissal should be: *Tāro ṅentaḥ śūlapāṇir namaḥ*.
On a seat covered with cloth and other materials: Oṃ, salutation to the wielder of the Pināka bow. || 17 ||

One should establish [the image] with the mantra that bestows auspiciousness and grants liberation; there, one should meditate upon the Lord Śiva according to the specific difference of one's desire. (18)

One should bathe [the deity] with the mantra: "Oṃ, obeisance to Paśupati. Having worshipped with the fivefold offerings (pañcopacāraka) while reciting "Oṃ, obeisance to Śiva," [he is to be honored]. || 19 ||
One should dismiss [the deity] with the mantra: "Oṃ, salutations to Mahādeva. Hrīṃ gaṃ gloṃ gaṇataye glauṃ gaṃ hrīṃ is the syllable of Bhava. || 20 ||
Aiṃ huṃ kṣaṃ klīṃ kumārāya namaḥ; this ten-syllabled mantra should end with "namaḥ."
Having taken these mantras, one should recite them eight thousand times.
Having offered incense and meditated on the Guru in the heart for the sake of attaining success in his mantra.
Then, on an auspicious day, for the sake of attaining his desired goal, he— having performed his daily rites and being pure—
should offer the *arghya* water to the Sun.
Taking clay and water, one should consecrate them with the *vaṃ* seed-syllable; having sprinkled [the clay], one should knead it into the desired size and place it in a vessel. || 23 ||
Then, having recollected the time and the desires dwelling in his heart, he said, "Let us worship these earthen lingas here with such-and-such a number. || 24 ||
Having thus made this resolve, the wise man should take a small amount of clay from the lump of earth.
One should fashion the Gaṇeśvara of the gateway by means of the mantra of Gaṇeśvara.

Having fashioned [the deity] with hands shining with a fruit and the gesture of granting fearlessness, pot-bellied and seated upon a mouse, the Brahmin should place him on the pedestal and then perform the ritual. || 26 ||
The ritual placement (nyāsa) of Rudra, performed according to the rules and accompanied by the encapsulation (sampuṭīkaraṇa).
Listen to the secret ritual of placement (nyāsa) for the worship of the earthen image, which must not be disclosed to those who lack wisdom.
Of this mantra known as Śrīpārthiva, which is a wish-fulfilling gem of knowledge.
The performer of restraint and favor: [Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā, the Ṛṣi, on the head;
Oṃ, salutation to Gāyatrī, the Chandas, on the mouth; Oṃ, salutation to Kāmadughā, the Devatā, on the heart;
Oṃ Hrīṃ Hrauṃ, salutation to the Bīja, on the private parts; Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to the Śakti].
At the feet: *Oṃ namaḥ*; at the navel: *namaḥ kīlakāya*. Brahmā is declared to be the sage (*muni*);

the deity (*devatā*) shall be Kāmadughā; Gāyatrī is said to be the meter (*chanda*). *Oṃ hrīṃ hrauṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*); *hrīṃ* is the power (*śakti*); *namaḥ* is called the pin (*kīlaka*). (29)

For the sake of accomplishing one's desired aims, there is the injunction for the worship of the *liṅga*. One should properly perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) by placing the mantras preceded by the seeds *oṃ*, *hrīṃ*, and *hrauṃ*. (30)

At the end, one should utter "śivāya" as the supreme [seed-syllable], and then recite the limbs (*aṅga*) and so forth. For the mantra-installation (*mantranyāsa*), the three seed-syllables—*oṃ hrīṃ hrauṃ*—should be joined before [the name]. Thus: *oṃ śivāya sarvajñāya aṃguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*; *oṃ śivāya*... [and so on].

Oṃ, salutation to Śiva, who is all-satisfying, with the two index fingers; Oṃ, salutation to Śiva, whose power is eternally undiminished, with the two middle fingers; Oṃ, salutation to Śiva, whose power is all-knowing wisdom, with the two ring fingers; Oṃ, salutation to Śiva, whose power is eternal bliss.

"Salutation to the two little fingers; oṃ, salutation to Śiva, the infinite power-Śiva, to the palms and backs of the hands. Again, one should perform the *nyāsa* of the heart and other limbs with these very same mantras. First, [salutation] to the one who satisfies all.
And the reply: || 31 ||
To Him whose power is eternally undiminished, who possesses the power of all knowledge, who possesses the power of eternal bliss, and who is Śiva of infinite power. || 32 ||
Having performed the placement of the fingers, one should apply [the mudrā] to the heart and other parts.

There, a pure Vedic scholar (śrotriya) [should apply] the earth with the Sadyojāta mantra. [The five mantras beginning with Sadyojāta are mentioned in many places; therefore, they are not stated here. || 33 ||
Having taken it up with the Vāmadeva mantra and offered water, one should knead it; one should fashion the liṅga with the Aghora mantra and worship it with the Tatpuruṣa mantra. || 34 ||
Having established [the deity] with the Rudrasūkta, one should perform the dismissal with the Īśāna mantra. Having first honored Gaṇeśāna, one should seat him in the center of the pedestal. || 35 ||
Afterwards, one should fashion the ritual marks as desired, making them equal [and reciting "Hrauṃ"].
It should be larger than the size of a thumb and beautiful, measuring up to the span of a vitasti.
One should fashion the earthen liṅga neither deficient nor excessive in size in any respect.
It has the appearance of a ripe jambu fruit and bestows the fulfillment of all desires. || 37 ||
If it is excessively thick, there is poverty; if flat, the occurrence of disease; if larger than the prescribed measure, there will be separation;
and if too small, success does not arise. (38)
If there are two segments, death will occur; if in a non-womb (viyoni), there will be no happiness.
One should fashion the boy from the remaining clay, accompanied by the appropriate mantra.
One should install it up to the liṅga and worship it with its own mantra.
By worshipping the earthen linga, one shall partake of the fruits as previously described. || 40 ||
With those [mantras] beginning with the five seed-syllables: *tāra*, *hrauṃ*, *hrīṃ*, *jūṃ*, and *saḥ*.
A practitioner of Tantra who desires fruit should worship Śiva with the month-mantras.
One who follows the left-hand path (vāmamārgī) should worship with the Prāsāda mantra preceded by the seed-syllable (bīja).
One should worship with those Kaulika [substances], such as the seed-syllables of Parā-prāsāda and others. || 42 ||

At the time of invocation, one should meditate upon Śiva as having arrived in such a manner; however, that [meditation] should be performed according to the specific difference in one's desires once He is established in the liṅga. || 43 ||

Meditation may be of various kinds; one should worship the source according to one's desire. In that regard, this meditation is to be understood wherever it has not been specifically mentioned. || 44 ||
Then the wise one should contemplate himself as the self of Śiva, five-faced.
Having three eyes and four arms, adorned with all ornaments. || 45 ||
He has a blue neck, is marked with the crescent moon, and resembles pure crystal.
And he has a tiger skin as an upper garment and a serpent as a sacred thread. || 46 ||
The Lord, the God, holding a water-pot and endowed with a rosary of beads.
With hands granting boons and fearlessness, he bestows the highest boons upon those who bow before him. || 47 ||
Mounted upon the back of a bull, bearing Umā as half of his body, with matted hair and tawny in hue,
he illumines the world with the radiance of his teeth and nails.
It was divine, bathed in nectar, endowed with celestial enjoyments, accompanied by the deities of the directions, and saluted by gods and demons. || 49 ||
It is eternal, perpetual, pure, constant, imperishable, and undecaying.
To Rudra, the all-pervading Lord, who indeed possesses the form of the universe.
Having meditated thus correctly, the twice-born should then begin the sacrifice:
"You are propitiated by men, by the Siddhas, and by the gods, Asuras, and others. (51)
I propitiate you with devotion; accept me, O Maheśvara.
O Lord, O Sovereign of the entire world, until the conclusion of the worship.
"Until then, remain present in this linga with a spirit of affection.
Having thus entreated the Lord of Devas, one should then worship the earthen linga. || 53 ||
One should worship each liṅga one by one and dismiss each one as well. At the end, Kārttikeya is to be worshipped; this is declared to be the supreme mode of worship.
Because all the lingas are worshipped quickly in one place, that worship is declared by those who know the rules to be the "middling" (madhyamā) worship at that time. || 55 ||
One should perform meditation individually upon each [deity], offering incense and flowers separately for each.
One should offer incense, lamps, food offerings, and so forth, according to one's means.
One should worship the eight [deities] in the directions by circling counter-clockwise starting from the east:
[Oṃ Śarvāya kṣitimūrtaye namaḥ in the east; Oṃ Bhavāya jalamūrtaye namaḥ in the northeast corner;
Oṃ Rudrāyāgnimūrtaye namaḥ in the north; Oṃ Ugrāya...]
Oṃ, salutation to Vāyu in the form of wind in the northwest corner; Oṃ, salutation to Bhīma in the form of space in the west;
Oṃ, salutation to Paśupati in the form of the sacrificer in the southwest corner;
Oṃ, salutation to Mahādeva in the form of the moon in the south; Oṃ, salutation to Īśāna in the form of the sun.
Homage in the southeast corner; likewise in the eight directions: Bhava, Rudra, Ugra, Bhīma, and Paśupati. (57)
Likewise, one should worship Mahādeva and Īśāna, who are sequentially the embodied forms of earth and the other elements.
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, the sacrificer, the moon, and the sun. || 58 ||
Earth and the other elements become Śarva and the others; from that, one should worship Indra and the rest.
By means of incense, lamps, food offerings, and so forth, as well as prostrations and circumambulations. || 59 ||
Then one should perform the recitation: *Oṃ hrauṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ oṃ namaḥ śivāya prasannāya pārijātāya svāhā*. One should utter *hrauṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ*.
"Oṃ namaśca śiva," ending with the suffix -ṅe, one should utter this for the sake of the Gracious One (Prasanna). || 60 ||
"To the Pārijāta, svāhā!"—this consists of twenty-one syllables.
At the conclusion of the worship, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times with undivided attention.
One should offer either a bilva fruit or a bilva leaf, smeared with ghee and mixed with sesame seeds.
Afterwards, he should offer eleven oblations and prostrate himself upon the ground like a staff.

[One should worship] with the names preceded by *praṇava* (Oṃ), ending in the dative case, followed by "Ananta-deva" and "namaḥ" [e.g., Oṃ Anantadevāya namaḥ]; and likewise, the name of his wife joined with the genitive case, ending in the feminine suffix *-ī*, followed by "namaḥ" [e.g., Oṃ Anantadevasya patnyai namaḥ]. || 63 ||
Furthermore, the libation (tarpaṇa) should be performed with those very same names.
With words ending in the dative case, I offer libations with bilva leaves, water, and unbroken rice grains.
Bhava, Śarva, Īśāna, and the fourth is considered Paśupati.
Rudra, Ugra, Bhīma, Mahat, and Tvaṣṭṛ—these eight are proclaimed as the Great Ones (Mahāntaḥ).
One should always feed a married couple with the intention of honoring Pārvatī and Śambhu;
or, in their absence, one should feed a single person who is most learned in the Vedas.
For a person who worships the supreme earthen linga in this manner, perfection shall be attained within just one month;
there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
If one worships another deity without having fashioned a linga of earth, that worship—along with rites such as ritual bathing and giving—is in vain. (68)
This procedure should be performed for rites undertaken with desire; listen now to the specific detail.
One who seeks knowledge, however, [should perform] a thousand [offerings] with flour produced from rice.
If one performs the worship of these two together in a single place for one month, one will certainly obtain the vidyā; its meditation is now described. || 70 ||
By this very procedure, one should worship that which is born of fresh butter; thus, knowledge and likewise fame shall instantly arise in the four directions.
I bow to Maheśa, who is served by gods and siddhas, the bestower of knowledge, whose gaze is fixed upon his book.
I always meditate upon that Lord, whose lotus feet are worshipped by devoted people and who grants all desires. || 72 ||

Thus, a liṅga of white agallochum (śvetāguru), when worshipped, increases the intellect; likewise, a liṅga of black agallochum (kṛṣṇāguru), when worshipped, bestows meditative concentration (dhāraṇā).
As before, a linga made of the flour produced from chickpeas should be fashioned with intelligence.
Having fashioned a linga made of rice as before, one should strike it while the speech falters. 74.
Those desiring knowledge should meditate upon the supreme Hari, who holds the axe and the gesture of wisdom (jñānamudrā) in his hands and is seated at the foot of a banyan tree.
She should worship five hundred earthen lingas every day, each one individually;
by doing so for a month, she becomes Sarvatomukhī (the one facing all directions).

May he who possesses the luster of the moon protect us— he who, bowed down by the three worlds, rests upon the lap of Dakṣa with his elephant face being wiped by his right hand, while on his left thigh sits Guha in the lap of the daughter of the mountain; and who holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in his two other hands.
Blue-throated and three-eyed. || 77 ||
At the junction of two opposing men, one should perform [the rite] ten thousand times.
And one should worship those [images] with clay brought from both banks of a river. || 78 ||
There, Hari-Hara, the bearer of the conch, the lotus, and so forth, as well as the trident, is to be meditated upon.
Resembling a sapphire and the autumnal moon, he was adorned with a multitude of ornaments. || 79 ||
For the purpose of denoting the couple, he is remembered as Ardhanārīśvara.
He holds a jar filled with nectar, as well as a noose and a goad.
One desiring a son should prepare one thousand five hundred [offerings] made from rice flour.
Alternatively, one may make earthen [liṅgas] numbering half a lakh (fifty thousand). || 81 ||
The meditation and the worship are each performed separately, [visualizing her] seated on the lap of Dakṣa.
As for the food offering (naivedya), it may consist of rice with curd, or here, one may use flour-based sweets according to one's desire.
One seeking beauty should consume five hundred [pills] produced from the flour of *āḍhakī*.
Alternatively, one may make earthen [liṅgas] numbering half a lakh; two by two, they are to be worshipped separately. Herein, the meditation is described. (83)
White as camphor, the descent of compassion, the essence of cyclic existence, adorned with a necklace of lordly serpents.

I bow to Bhava, who always delights in the lotus of the heart, together with Bhavānī. For the purpose of subduing [an enemy], one should fashion seven hundred lingas made from hair and bone; or else, lingas made of iron or even from chaff.
One should worship the thousand signs of the sugarcane staff for the purpose of eradication.
For the purpose of inciting enmity, one should employ earth from a cremation ground. || 86 ||

One should perform worship according to the requirements of the task, from a thousand up to a hundred thousand [repetitions]. Furthermore, for the rites of eradication, killing, and creating enmity, he should be meditated upon in this same manner. || 87 ||
Supported by the lotus-hand of Kālī, he impaled the multitude of his enemies upon his trident;
his neck was radiant with a garland of severed heads, and his roar terrified all beings. || 88 ||
Liberation arises for men even without [this specific] knowledge; at that time, one should worship ten million liṅgas—this is called meditation (dhyāna). || 89 ||

I meditate upon that Lord of the Universe, who bestows upon men the knowledge that rests upon all things—a knowledge otherwise obscured by the power of yoga-māyā; he is the destroyer of the sins of the Kali age, embraced by Śivā, and possesses eight forms. 90.
One who desires enjoyments, however, should make one hundred thousand [offerings] consisting of flowers.
One obtains divine enjoyments; meditation is now described herein.
I bow to Maheśa, who is served by gods and Siddhas, who dwells in the forest of the Kalpa-tree, and who is gracious.
Seated upon his throne together with the Daughter of the Mountain, he is delighted by the beautiful songs and dances of celestial maidens.
For the sake of dwelling in Kāśī without obstacles, and out of a desire to conquer both worlds.
There were ten thousand liṅgas made from the wood of the dhātrī fruit.
He who worships the Liṅgas of Pittalyā even once a day, or at the three junctions of the day, or even just once, obtains land extending for a thousand [yojanas] as he desires. || 94 ||
One who desires beauty should worship three thousand liṅgas made from *gorocana* (bovine gallstone);
