In a fire kindled with wood from a poisonous tree and adorned with variegated garlands, one should perform a *tāmasa* rite;
therein, such action succeeds without a doubt. The *tāmasa* rite consists of killing (*māraṇa*), driving away (*uccāṭana*), and creating enmity (*dveṣa*). (This is a collective dvandva compound.)
There may be the state of a piśāca. || 742 ||
By means of an oblation of *rājī* and salt, the attraction of women occurs. Having first ensured one's own protection, one should thereafter accomplish the ritual acts. || 743 ||
One should draw a triangle, a hexagon, an eight-spoked wheel, and a square enclosure.
On page 228 of the *Citra*: one should write the root mantra in the center, accompanied by the name of the person for whom the rite is intended. || 744 ||
One should place the six limbs in the six corners and the vowels in the filaments; the consonant groups on the petals, and the mantra in the four corners of the square earth-house.
And one should draw it with powders of five colors, so that it is pleasing to the sight.
One should install pitchers containing one, three, six, eight, and four parts respectively, in due order.
From the center to the end of the square, one should place twenty-two pots in sequence;
or alternatively, eighteen, ten, seven, four, or one.
The unstable jewel, the network of veins, the clay, the flesh, the blood, the water, the skin as clothing, the tuft of hair, the beard, and the coconut fruit as the head. (748)
One should worship the deity of the pitcher (kalaśadevatā), who is conjoined with the vital breath of the mantra;
she consists of the three forms (trimūrti) along with the Mothers beginning with Aṃśā, accompanied by the Bhairavas. || 749 ||

Having duly worshipped the Guru, Vighneśa, Durgā, and Kṣetrapati in the intermediate directions, as well as [the deities] within the pitchers, according to the rules, that best of mantra-knowers— || 750 ||
One should consecrate the beloved disciple for the pacification of all sins.
Longevity, prosperity, beauty, good fortune, knowledge, health, and so forth shall come to pass. || 751 ||
One consecrated as king obtains the earth bounded by the four oceans.
One who is consecrated while possessing nothing shall indeed attain great sovereignty.
A barren woman, when consecrated, obtains a son endowed with all virtues.
Elemental spirits, untimely death, diseases, and so forth will undoubtedly perish. || 753 ||
O Goddess, having written this supreme yantra either on the three metals or on birch bark, when it is worn and worshipped, it shall provide protection from all [evils]. || 754 ||
Akula is said to be Śiva, and Kula is proclaimed to be Śakti.
O Dear One, the Kaulikas are those who are skilled in the continuous investigation of the Kulākulā.
Because it is the beginning of all paths and because it sets in motion the joy of the mind, [the vowel *u* is used; this is an archaic grammatical usage].
Because it is the cause of all things, such as sacrifice and so forth, it is celebrated as the Āmnāya.
Thus has this exposition of the Kaulika path been demonstrated. Those who are devoid of the Vedic dharma are the ones qualified for this dharma. || 757 ||
Because the senses are difficult to restrain and because desire, greed, and other passions arise, this Kaula path generally leads to hell in the Kali age. (758)

O gods, in the Kali age there will be the destruction of Dharma by the Kaulika, the destruction of wealth by the Rasika, the destruction of desire by the Phiraṅga, and the destruction of liberation by the envy of people;
there will be hypocrisy and sin in every house. (759)
For nothing whatsoever is produced by Primordial Matter (prakṛti) without a Puruṣa;
likewise, the Lord is not able to do anything without Śakti. 760.
For without power, a deity is indeed not capable of bestowing the fruit; therefore—
Therefore, having formed a union with a man, one should accomplish the mantra. || 761 ||
In the Kaulika and Vāmamārga traditions, a male practitioner does not attain success as a deity; rather, he should meditate upon himself as Śiva and the deity as being of the nature of Śakti. (762)
His deity is well-pleased and sports with the five *makāras*. One should regard women as mothers on the path of the Dakṣas, and as sisters on the Kaulika path. (763)
But for him whose [faith] has become even firmer, the deity is truly pleased.
This secret has been declared; it must be guarded like a lover's affair with one's mother.
I shall declare another most secret [teaching], concealed in all tantras;
I shall now proclaim how a deity herself would bestow a mantra. 765.
Know that the letters recited in the Veda are the designators of the moon and other such objects.
These are joined with a set of four notes, increasing in number progressively.
This convention regarding the ancient deities has been proclaimed by me.

In this context, the letters beginning with the nameless one (Anāmā) are to be taken along with their numerical values; likewise, in the Southern Tradition (Dakṣiṇāmnāya), the letters are devoid of the nameless initial. Two, two, then one, and again two—these are the groups that signify the conventions.
The letters [are arranged] according to the sequence of tradition, and likewise the mantras and so forth;
the vowels (acaḥ) follow that same sequence for the deities of the West and the North. || 769 ||
The unification of the groups of letters according to the conventions of the four traditions (āmnāyas) should be performed in the Upper Tradition (ūrdhvāmnāya);
however, nothing at all [of that] should be done by one following the Vedic tradition.
In whatever order and in whatever location those letters have been proclaimed, those letters, numbering one and so forth, should be grasped in that very same order. || 771 ||
When the combination of the syllables of the mantra, joined with the mark of one's own name, reaches its root, then a dream arises. || 772 ||
In the absence of a root mantra, one should again employ the name-designations of the deity; when the root mantra itself cannot be taken, the name-designation should be joined with the seat (pīṭha).

When one no longer returns to the root [of worldly existence], then dreams do not arise. Even if a mantra has been received from a guru, it will fail to be effective [if this condition is not met]. (774)
[One should draw] squares equal in number to the root-digits, extending north-south and east-west.
Having written down the letters starting from one and so forth, there would be counting; [the root *likh* belongs to the *bhūvādika* class, though this is an archaic usage]. For example: || 775 ||
The method for arranging them so that they are equal in number on all sides is now explained: the western [line] is to be written first, and likewise the one near the middle in the north.
The second [line] should be drawn with the gait of a horse, and after that, with the gait of a minister; thereafter, one should draw from beginning to end with the gait of a horse as before.

Then, upon the obstruction of that [movement], there should be the movement of the king according to the movement of the minister; one should again perform the movement of the minister, and then again the movement of the horse as before. (778)
In this manner, one should practice again and again according to the path shown by the Guru; thus, the fulfillment of the limbs occurs completely and in due order.
One should write the mantras equally within the four compartments of the grid; having thus prepared this center, one should then place the final mantra in the Māheśī [cell].
Likewise, one should place the penultimate [syllable] from the southeast in the southwest as the first.
The second [deity] should be in the northwest, so that the number may be as it should be. || 781 ||
In the same way, O Ambika, the single units (ekaka) should be maintained in the Kāṣṭhā as full.
Those who rival them should be stationed in the direction that rivals theirs.
In this way, however, the completion of those with equal leaves is proclaimed.
Alternatively, one should write down the sequence of the dividend, the divisor, and the leaves (quotients).
It is known that [the fruit] is obtained without a preceptor, just as the entire divine [realm is attained] without [effort]; having bathed on a Sunday before the rising of the sun, thereafter— 784.
At sunrise, having offered those arghya oblations and bowed down, one should enter the house; one should not look at anyone lower than oneself, nor should one utter any harsh word.
Within a single muhūrta, the entire yantra should be [inscribed] upon birch bark or a copper plate.
One should draw [the deities] upon the petals or within the mandala using the eight fragrances appropriate for each respective deity. || 786 ||
Having first worshipped Gaṇeśa, and then the planets and the lords of the directions,
one should draw the yantra in a secluded place and observe silence on that day.
The celibate student, subsisting on sacrificial food, should not look upon forbidden substances. He should inscribe the mantra above the yantra, or else two *ṭha* syllables facing north.
One should draw two ṭha-s on the right side of the area to be accomplished;
likewise, [the wheel] is on saffron-colored, yellow, black, and white garments. (789)

Upon a blue surface measuring one span, one should encircle the yantra of the deity of the lineage (āmnāyadaivata) situated within the palace; there, oil produced from a *kuḍava* measure [should be used]. || 790 ||
One should arrange sesame oil, buffalo ghee, the fat of this [animal], and likewise khākhasa, cow's ghee, and muscle fat in the directions starting from the east. || 791 ||
One should likewise draw an eight-petalled lotus on the ground with unbroken grains of rice.
Then, one should worship the host of Vighnas and Gaṇeśa in the pericarp to the north.
Having worshipped one's chosen deity (iṣṭadeva) in the center and Kṣetrapāla to the south, and having worshipped the eight lords of the directions (digīśas) upon the petals, one should dismiss them.
Thereafter, one should place a beautiful lamp upon the pericarp;
having established the lamp there, one should light it and then worship it. || 794 ||
Remaining vigilant there, he should sleep— [the root *svap* being Vedic in its bhūvādika class]—
on that day which is the head of the Vedas and the gods; thus purified of sin,
he shall attain the assembly of the deities.
One should meditate upon the guru in that very form in which the deity bestows the mantra, and one should honor those who belong to that same lineage. || 796 ||
If the Sun is in the first house, one becomes a sinner of middling degree; if in the second, a perpetrator of many sins; but if in the third, a mortal free from sin shall attain the mantra.
In the fourth [house], he is of middling sin; in the fifth, a great sinner; in the seventh, a Rakshasa who is sinless;
and in the sixth, he is a middling sinner. || 798 ||
One certainly attains the mantra on the seventh day of the sun; this most secret [teaching] has been proclaimed, hidden within all the tantras. (799)
It should also be given even to a Mleccha who is devoted to his own dharma.
O gods, it must not be given even to a Brahmin who has abandoned his own duty.
He who, out of greed or desire, should give [it away], falls from both worlds.
Now I shall declare the most secret mystery concerning the origin of the sacred seats (pīṭha); by knowing which all practitioners attain perfection, and not otherwise. || 801 ||
There are fifty-one seats (pīṭhas), and the deities residing in the five traditions (āmnāyas) dwell there; O gods, they number thirty-three. 802.
Regarding those secondary seats (upapīṭhas) which are declared to be the deities in the Sixth Tradition (Ṣaṣṭhāmnāya), their location is specified there as being above the heart. 803.
The followers of the Veda reside where Teṅgapāta was born; likewise, the Southern Path leads to success there, while the Northern Path does so elsewhere.
The letter *A* is said to be the primordial seat (*ādipīṭha*) known as Kāmarūpa; it is at that seat, O Goddess, that the path of the Kula was set forth by me. (805)
Having seen her, they fell into that womb, and thus their beloved deed was accomplished.
The Kula scripture, however, bestows liberation upon the Kaulas who possess true knowledge. || 806 ||

Success is swiftly attained by the five [classes], but for others it does not arise at all. Indeed, those desiring the supernatural powers (siddhis) such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest should go there to behold it. || 807 ||
The root of Śrīvidyā, however, is the menstrual flow that issues month after month; if there is a lapse on the part of a Kula-siddha, the suppression of that flow occurs. (808)
By your instruction, its two subsidiary seats (upapīṭhas) have arisen on all sides from the hair of the one called Vaṃśa;
the accomplishment (siddhi) therein is Śābaracerakī. || 809 ||
The seat of Kāśikā, which was given by you, has fallen into a state of division; yet because it does not perish even at the time of universal dissolution (pralaya), he is called Maheśvara.

Where there is neither sin nor merit, and where the supreme state is attained beyond the abandonment of the body—therein lie these two fruits; liberation is found at its subsidiary seat (upapīṭha). || 811 ||

"In that sacred seat (pīṭha), there is a terrifying torment at every step; I am unable to drink from your jar-like breasts there. Hold back the pair [of streams] that have issued forth, for you have become like Varuṇa with your sword. (812)
One yojana outside of Kāśī is known as Devabhūmi; there, the mantras practiced yield their fruits at that very time. (813)
In their respective places in the four directions, the deities of the sacred tradition (āmnāyadevatās) reside;
by the mere performance of the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa), those gods grant success.
The portion of Kāśī on the opposite bank of the Gaṅgā is most sacred; yet, due to the curse of Vyāsa, it became the wondrous Gardabhakṣetra. || 815 ||
At that time, the perfection of the traditional teaching arises there.
Upapīṭha is on the bank of the Asi; Sāranātha, however, is to the south. There, the mantras of the Southern Path (dakṣiṇamārga) bestow spiritual accomplishments (siddhi). || 816 ||
To the north of Varuṇā and likewise to the north of Sāranātha is that Upapīṭha;
it bestows great accomplishment upon those on the path of the Left (Vāmamārga). || 817 ||
O Pārvatī, the letter *i* is indeed Nepāla, and it is secret therein;
therefore, that is said to be the root location of the left-hand path (vāmamārga). (818)
There are fifty-six lakhs of Bhairavīs as well as Bhairavas; two thousand Śaktis and three hundred Pīṭhas. || 819 ||
Fourteen cremation grounds are situated there, and on the path of Dakṣa, eight seats (pīṭhas) that bestow spiritual accomplishments (siddhi) are also located there. || 820 ||
The efficacy of Vedic mantras resides in those four sacred seats (pīṭha); wherever their impurity fell, there an upapīṭha was produced. || 821 ||
To the east of Nepal, that region is surrounded by Kirātas; indeed, there are thirty thousand beings of divine origin there.
The place of origin for the vowel *ī* is Raudraparvata;
that great seat where your left eye fell is so called. (823)
Success arises from the recitation of any mantra whatsoever; therein, through the left-hand practice (vāmācāra), there is the vision of the deity. || 824 ||
The place of origin of the syllable *ukāra* is said to be Kashmir; because the ear fell there on the left side, it is therefore that most excellent sacred seat (*pīṭha*). || 825 ||
Whatever deity's mantra a person may recite, he shall become one who has reached the further shore of all sciences and likewise become a knower of reality. || 826 ||
O Goddess of the Gods, for those who have fallen away from the Vedic, Kaulika, Smārta, or Dakṣa paths, there are indeed means of expiation. || 827 ||
The sacred fords established by me grant immediate conviction as well.
In the Kali age, when the world is overrun by barbarians, I shall make them exceedingly well-concealed.
The place of origin for the letter Ū would be Kānyakubjaka; there, your right ear fell, appearing exceedingly beautiful. (829)
Between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, that region known as Antarvedī was indeed ordained as a dwelling place for those who drink the Soma. || 830 ||
There, the gods beginning with Brahmā established their respective sacred fords (tīrthas). There, the deities attained the perfection of Vedic mantras at every step.
O Goddess, from his impurity was born that secondary sacred seat (upapīṭhaka) known in the world as Indraprastha, situated on the bank of the Yamunā. || 832 ||
By the power of that very seat, the Vedas were forgotten by Brahmā.
Then, having been regained, there arose a sacred ford (tīrtha) that provides awakening to the community.
There Kālī performed penance, saying, "Those who shall please me—even if they are unqualified in the fifth [aspect]—let that be according to their desire for a boon. (834)
Having obtained that boon from Mahākāla at that time, she then impelled the world toward the fifth [element], and she manifested and bestowed perfection (siddhi). || 835 ||
The letter *Ṛ* became Pūrṇagiri, and there the nose fell; therefore, the complete perfection of Yoga arises there. There, the deities presiding over the mantras become directly manifest. (836)
The place of origin for the vowel ṛ is Mount Arbuda; from there it descends to the left, and for that very reason, it is beloved (vallabha).
There, the Power named Ambikā is always fond of her own specific conduct.
If even a single *puraścaryā* is performed at the time of enjoyment, liberation shall occur in that very seat through union with a thousand vulvas. || 838 ||
O Pārvatī, that place belongs to the celestial women; it is the abode of the descent of those very goddesses. A great vow was made by that goddess together with me. || 839 ||
That man who shall spend twelve years in celibacy within my field (kṣetra) shall alone become my husband. || 840 ||
Even a Buddhist falters there for one year minus three days; indeed, while the Vāma system succeeds there, obstacles arise in the Dakṣa system.
The letter *ḷ* originated where Āmrātakeśvara is located; Dakṣagaṇḍa fell upon that sacred seat (*pīṭha*), which is a great marvel. || 842 ||
The Yakṣas such as Dhanada and the Yakṣiṇīs such as Dhanadā dwell there;
for one who recites [mantras] there, spiritual accomplishment (siddhi) arises. || 843 ||
In ancient times, the origin of the letter *ḷ* occurred at Ekāmra; there, many nails were shed by the Vidyādharas as they performed intense penance.
For students, however, that seat bestows their desired knowledge;
even a text not previously heard is understood there through the recitation of the Sārasvata mantra.
In the three streams of your single birth, the three folds of skin have been cast down; [the absence of the final *t* is an archaic Vedic usage].
A garment produced during the three winds falls in the east, west, and south.

Those three are the secondary seats (upapīṭhas); there the householder attains success. Only a twice-born man, and no other caste, [attains it]; the Manus are established in the rite of nourishment (pauṣṭika). || 847 ||
The letter Ai became Kāmakoṭi; there, indeed, your [mantra] falls.
There, all mantra-kāmas are accomplished; of this there is no doubt. || 848 ||
Having propitiated you, the desirable one, who are situated on the bank of the Chāchika river.
He shall possess the capacity for the enjoyment of sixteen thousand women. || 849 ||
O Pārvatī, secondary seats (upapīṭhas) have arisen there in the four directions; that is the abode of the Apsarases, where the mantras concerned with women reside.
All of them attain accomplishment there very quickly; of this there is no doubt. Even by merely seeing it, one obtains the desired and delightful accomplishment. || 851 ||
Having become the syllable *oṃ* on Kailāsa, in the valley of the Himālaya mountain, her fingers fell there and,
by means of their joints, attained the state of being lingas.
Whatever mantra the twice-born person recites there with his rosary, [that becomes effective].
By the mere performance of the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa), the deity becomes pleased. || 853 ||
In ancient times, the origin of the vowel *au* occurred at Bhṛgupīṭha; there those teeth fell, and thus that seat became a great wonder. (854)
All Vedic mantras and those declared in the Kalpas remain there in their essential form; indeed, through service to them, they become immediately effective.
Let this dakṣa, produced from the field (kedāra), fall upon your palm;
for when it has fallen upon that seat (pīṭha), the supernatural powers (siddhis) are held within the hand. || 856 ||
To its south is a secondary sacred seat (upapīṭha) known as Agastyāśrama; there a ring fell, which bestows all supernatural powers (siddhis). || 857 ||
After that, an extraordinary seat (pīṭha) arose from your mudrā;
it is named Indrākṣī, which was formerly worshipped there by Indra himself. || 858 ||
After that, your bracelets fell upon the bank of the Revatī; even one who has fallen shall be liberated by [the mantra] "O Sovereign Lady of the Kings of Kings. (859)
Even there, success arises quickly through the practice of the left-hand path; indeed, by mere recitation, the Yakṣiṇīs become visible to one's sight.
The syllable Aḥ became the left cheek, fallen in Candrapura;
there all mantras are perfected, of this there is no doubt. || 861 ||
At the Śrīpīṭha, however, there was the letter *ka*; your head has fallen there. Generally, in the Kali age, it is difficult for those with sins to go to that place. || 862 ||
When all powers sport there at will during the night, they do not afflict the vigilant one,
but rather consume that which is contrary to dharma.
From that, Karṇābharaṇa was born, and Upapīṭha is situated to the east;
there resides the power Brāhmī, who illuminates the knowledge of Brahman. || 864 ||
From the ear-ornament [of the deity] in the south-eastern corner arose the Upapīṭha; there, the Śakti is considered to be Māheśvarī, who effects the purification of the mouth. || 865 ||
Then those leaf-patterns fell upon its right side; there, the secondary seat (upapīṭha) was the power (śakti) Kaumārī, the bringer of victory. || 866 ||
But the Kaṇṭhamālā [pīṭha] has fallen in the south-west, and it is an upapīṭhaka.
Established in the Vaiṣṇava state, it has arisen as a magical illusion that bestows perfect accomplishment.
The nose is the Mukta, and that which falls after it is the Upapīṭhaka.
Blessed by Vārāhī, it became the crusher of enemies. || 868 ||
The head-ornament and the secondary pedestal have fallen in the northwest wind.
It became presided over by Cāmuṇḍā and grants the attainment of the powers of minor deities. || 869 ||
From the ornament of hair (Keśābharaṇa), there arose the Upapīṭhaka in the northeast;
it is presided over by Mahālakṣmī for the attainment of success in the Sūktas. || 870 ||
The letter Kha became the syllable Oṃ in the sacred field of Amarakaṇṭaka.
From the falling of your arm, Pīṭha became established upon the Narmadā. || 871 ||
There, all the best of sages, bowing down along with their lay disciples, performed great austerities;
thus they became great ṛṣis liberated while living. || 872 ||
And to the north of that, the secondary seat (upapīṭha) arose from the falling of Kañcukī;
this is the abode of Jyotiṣmatī, illuminated by the mantra of Light (jyotis).
Where his chest fell, a most wonderful seat (pīṭha) was produced; it became famous there as Jvālā, and by the fire (Vahni) penance was performed. || 874 ||
Having attained the state of being the mouth of the deity, he remained upon its pedestal;
that fire, renowned as Jvālāmukhī, is the mouth of the god. (875)

A fire sacrifice (homa) must be performed there with the substances prescribed for the *puraścaryā* ritual, using the number of recitations specified for that *puraścaraṇa*; thus, the perfection of the mantra (*mantrasiddhi*) is produced. || 876 ||
In ancient times, Gorakṣa attained the eight supernatural powers (siddhis) at that very place.
Merely by seeing it, it bestows all accomplishments upon men. || 877 ||
The Mālava [tune] of the letter *gha* is situated here on the left shoulder;
it is worshipped by the Gandharvas and is known as Āgajñānaka. || 878 ||
At the end of the *kula*, the letter *ṅa* arose; your armpit has fallen away.
In that [place], ritual applications for hatred, eradication, and death grant success. || 879 ||
And at Koṭṭaka, the letter Ca became established as the left armpit;
there, the Rākṣasas obtained the siddhi known as Devajayā. || 880 ||
The origin of the letter *cha* is proclaimed to be at Gokarṇa; where the belly fell, that is the most wonderful sacred seat (*pīṭha*). || 881 ||
The letter *ja*, which bears the name of the Lord of the Mother—therein is your offering (*bali*). The first [letter] has fallen upon the seat (*pīṭha*) that reveals the mantra of Śiva. (882)
Aṭṭahāsa is the location of the syllable Jha; there, the supreme offering fell for that Gaṇeśa, which is considered to bring about the perfection of mantras.
The letter ja, however, is the place of virajas; there, the supreme offering is made.
There, the accomplishment of all Viṣṇu-mantras is not far off.
His birth took place in Rājagṛha, and there your delivery occurred.
Below that, a small bell has fallen, and it is the secondary pedestal (upapīṭhaka). || 885 ||
That which is called the "little bell" (ghaṇṭikā) is declared to be a well-known form of sorcery (indrajāla).
Likewise, the accomplishment of the meaning of the Upavedas shall take place in the royal palace. || 886 ||
On the great highway, the porter with the high hips has fallen down because of you.
There, the twice-born who were defiled by birth surrendered their own bodies. || 887 ||
Having attained another birth, those destroyers of the Vedic path—Aghora and others—have set their own paths in motion during the Kali age, which grant physical pleasure. || 888 ||
The syllable *ḍa* was at Kollagiri; your thigh fell there.
For all the forest deities, spiritual perfection is not far off there. || 889 ||
In Elāpura, the letter Ḍha became your right thigh as it fell. (890)
At Kāleśvara, the letter *ṇa* became your left thigh as it fell.
However, the mantras for conquering death and bestowing long life are perfected there. || 891 ||

Jayantī, however, is the location for the letter *ta*; there, the knee is placed down. By reciting [the mantra] there, Dakṣa attained perfection in the science of archery; of this there is no doubt. (892)
In Ujjayinī—[the word "fell" is to be understood as the ellipsis]—the letter *tha* became the left knee;
for the sake of success with armor-mantras (*kavacamantṛa*), it is called Avanti. (893)
The origin of the Dasyu [occurs] in the Yoginī; there the Jaṅghā was cast down. (p. 236) The Kaulika and Vāmaka mantras are perfected there, and no others. 894.
The syllable *Dha* is located in Kṣīrikā; there, O you whose left shank is [marked], the Vaitālika mantras and the Śābara mantras attain perfection. (895)
The origin of the letter *na* is proclaimed to be at Hastināpura; for there, O Dakṣa, your ankle fell along with your anklet. (896)
The secondary seat (upapīṭha) born from that is known as Nūpurārṇava.
There, at the primary and secondary seats (pīṭha and upapīṭha), the mantras as numerous as the suns attain accomplishment.
The sacred seat (pīṭha) of the letter Pa is called Uḍḍīśa; there, Vāmaka’s ankle fell, bestowing success upon the practitioner. 898.
In that place, the great tantra known as the Uḍḍīśa becomes accomplished; where the anklet fell, there is the Ḍāmara and the Upapīṭha. (899)
Prayāga is the location of the letter *pha*, and Deharasa is its site; wherever it has fallen, white clay is seen there. (900)
Between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, as well as on both their banks—in such places the bones were dropped by the best of the twice-born. || 901 ||
Those [sites] created within the earth became sacred seats (pīṭhas) there; and to the east of the Gaṅgā is the most wonderful secondary seat (upapīṭha) of Bagalā.
To the north, however, is the most wonderful secondary seat (upapīṭha) beginning with Cāmuṇḍā.
Between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā is Rājarājeśvarīśvara.
Bhuvaneśī is established on the southern bank of the Yamunā.
From Prayāga, it is called Tīrtharāja and Pīṭharāja. || 904 ||
The Lord of the Sixth (Kārttikeya) is the presiding deity of the letter *ba*, and you two are located there.
O Goddess, the southern side has fallen; here, however, is the accomplishment of the sandals (pādukāsiddhi).
The left heel fell at Māyāpura, while that [other] part fell upon Bhasthala.
The illusory powers of gods, dānavas, and gandharvas are indeed accomplished there. || 906 ||
In the sacred seat (pīṭha) called Malaya, which consists of the syllable *ma*, blood fell there.
That is the place for the accomplishment of mantras for the followers of the Buddha, such as those who wear red garments.
O Ambikā, on Śrīśaila there is a Yakṣa named Āruha; there, O Mother, all mantras are indeed perfected, especially those of the Vaiṣṇavas. || 908 ||
The peak named Meru on the Himavat mountain is indeed the seat of Rasthāna; your fat, having fallen there, became Siddha-svarṇākarṣaṇa-Bhairava. || 909 ||
The letter *la* originated at that mountain seat where your tongue-tip fell; by reciting [the mantra] there, the perfection of speech is certainly attained. (910)
The station of the letter *va* belongs to Mahendra; marrow fell from you there. There, without a doubt, is the accomplishment of all *śakti*-mantras. (911)
The position of the letter Śa, however, is the Vāmana [tīrtha], which arises from the thumb; by reciting [the mantra] there, one shall even attain preeminence among practitioners of mantra. || 912 ||
The letter Śa, born from Hiraṇyapura, arose on the left; its seat originates from the thumb and became preeminent in the left-hand path. || 913 ||
At the seat of Mahālakṣmī as well, the syllable *sa* became your desire;
having fallen from your body there, all perfections (*siddhi*) are produced. (914)
The letter *ha* arose in the place of Atri, and there the *dhamanī* fell; whatever *siddhis* were present within the range of vision remained stationed there. || 915 ||
On the seat of shadow (chāyāpīṭha), the letter *la* appeared; thus, your shadow was seen by me. Having assumed the guise of a virtuous wife (satī), it therefore became known as Chāyāpīṭha. || 916 ||
The letter *kṣa* has arisen upon the seat of the umbrella as a mass of hair; O Goddess, wherever it has fallen for you, there success is not far off. || 917 ||
O Goddess, this secret concerning the origin of the sacred seats (pīṭha) has been proclaimed by me.
Now I shall proclaim another secret, most wonderful.
In the Kali age, however, gurus are greedy and disciples are merely desirous of attaining supernatural powers;
therefore, there is no success anywhere, but only destruction day after day.
Therefore, for the sake of accomplishment, I shall declare that which is hidden in all tantras; it should be given to a devoted and excellent disciple, and never elsewhere. 920.

Preceded by the seeds *tāra*, *māyā*, *ramā*, and *kāma*—namely, *oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ rāmāya namaḥ*—this mantra, when recited by members of the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*), bestows swift accomplishment.
Alternatively, for a Brāhmaṇa, *oṃ rāmāya namaḥ*; for a Kṣatriya, *hrīṃ rāmāya namaḥ*.

Likewise, it should be recited by a Kṣatriya as "Śrīṃ Rāmāya Namaḥ," by a Vaiśya as "Klīṃ Rāmāya Namaḥ," and by a Śūdra as "Rāmakam. Furthermore, those beginning with Brāhmaṇas should recite [the mantra] ending in the dative case and concluding with "Namaḥ. (921)

This should be received from an elderly Brahmin; on one occasion, he should satisfy him with a gift. This mantra is declared to be perfected; it must be kept secret like a lover's affair with one's mother. 922.
Furthermore, one should perform the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) using the first seed-syllable.
One should first perform the placement (nyāsa) of the aforementioned mother-syllables (mātṛkās). || 923 ||

In the elephant-faced one, the divine source, and in Gaṇeśa, there are the Mātṛkās; in the Śākta [tradition], there are the short vowels; and among the Śivas and others, there are Śrīkaṇṭha and the rest.
Keśava and the others are proclaimed as the deities for Viṣṇu, Sūrya, the planets, and so forth. As for the placement of the seats (*pīṭhanyāsa*):
[Aṃ, salutation to the seat of Kāma; on the head. Āṃ, salutation to the seat of Kāśī; in the mouth. Iṃ, salutation to the seat of Nepāla; in the right eye. Īṃ...]
Salutation to Raudraparvatapīṭha on the left eye; salutation to Umakāśmīrapīṭha on the right ear; salutation to Oṃkānyakubjakapīṭha on the left ear.
This should be performed everywhere for the purification of the body. 925.

The worship and other rites shall be as before, and the preparatory rite (puraścaryā) likewise; however, for one who is devoted, those six rites and that hymn shall become manifest within him spontaneously.
One should likewise meditate upon the enemy in the place of destruction and the deity in one's own place;
all ritual applications will succeed, and in the end, one shall attain liberation.
One must never abandon one's own duty; one should support those who are dependent on one. One should never do what is unpleasant to one's mother, nor likewise to one's father.
One should serve this [teacher] as one would a god; thus has the secret been revealed. The giver of the mantra is always miserable, and the receiver of the mantra is destitute. (629)
In the Kali age, there will generally be a lack of discrimination between teacher and disciple. Having understood the scripture, one should choose a teacher; then one shall attain happiness. (930)
Thus has the procedure for initiation been proclaimed, endowed with the Kula practice. O Goddess, what else do you wish to hear, apart from this explanatory praise? || 931 ||

In this work composed by Śiva and revealed by Meru, which has become like Mount Meru among all tantras, there is the definitive determination of the preliminary rites (puraścaryā) and other matters. || 932 ||
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Kaula Conduct for Puraścaryā," in the Merutantra composed by Śiva with the approval of the illustrious Mahāmāyā and Mahākāla. 10.
The Meru Tantra, composed as a dialogue between Śrī Śiva and Śivā,
having been edited by the scholar Ojhā Paṇḍita Raghunātha Śāstrī.
Edited with commentaries such as the *Ṭippanī* by Khemarāja Śrīkṛṣṇadāsa, Bombay:
Part Two: Chapters 11 to 15.
The Śrī Devī said:
O Mahādeva, in this most terrible Kali age, where will the Vedic sages remain, what Manus will exist, and which Kalpas will yield their fruits? || 1 ||
And how much Vedic ritual is described in the Brāhma and the Pādma [Purāṇas]? Which branches will remain, and likewise which sub-branches? (2)
The illustrious Maheśvara said:
In the Kali age, human intellect is extremely difficult to find for Vedic rituals, just as men desire to reach the far shore of the ocean without a boat. || 3 ||
Therefore, O Goddess, in the Kali age, those who out of ignorance show devotion to the Vāma and Kaula [paths] are ignorant of the true reality;
they perish and are deprived of human status. || 4 ||
But some, having been instructed by deceivers in the yoga of devotion to you, abandon Vedic ritual and are born as lords of the Yavanas. || 5 ||
During ten thousand ages of Kali, Viṣṇu will abide in a central region;
that Lord manifests in the Vindhya mountains or somewhere on the Himālaya.
It shall remain until the junction of the Kali age is complete; beyond that, it will no longer exist.
In a world devoted to women, meat, and liquor, and turned away from the Dharma.
For all those mantras are established within the four Vedas; they shall remain in the midst of the earth as long as the Kali age is not yet complete.
At the twilight period of the Kali age, all thirty mantras will be established on earth;
then the birth of Viṣṇu in the form of Kalki will take place.
O Goddess, I shall now describe the means of accomplishment for those who abide in the Kali age.
At the beginning of the practice of private Vedic study, there are indeed fourteen vows.

Having shaved his hair and beard, he should act with purity according to the teacher's command; or else, being freed from sin by the previously mentioned rule, he should practice [the recitation]. 11.

O Goddess, at the evening hours, the disciple, having been purified, should recite those lessons in a solitary place while standing before the teacher with humility, by the teacher's command. || 12 ||

Three days one should eat in the morning, three days in the evening, three days one should eat food obtained unasked, and for another three days one should not eat at all; this indeed is the Prājāpatya vow. (13)
One should eat only a single morsel for three days each, as previously described; then one should fast for the final three days—this indeed is the Atikṛcchra vow.
One should bathe and perform the twilight devotions every day according to the prescribed rules.
And fasting for seven days is the Śiśusāntapana vow. || 15 ||
For three days each, one should drink hot water, milk, and ghee; being composed and bathing once [daily], this is the vow known as the Taptakṛcchra. || 16 ||
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with kuśa grass.
A fast for one night is the Kṛcchra-sāntapana vow. || 17 ||
One should consume the cow-urine and other substances for three days at a time, and then again for three days.
Then the fast is declared to be the Mahāsāntapana vow. || 18 ||

One should decrease the morsels one by one during the dark fortnight, with no eating on the new moon day; likewise, one should increase them during the bright fortnight—this is declared to be the Cāndrāyaṇa vow. (19)
One should increase the morsel by the measure of a *pala* during the bright fortnight; it should be decreased during the dark fortnight.
This middle *cāndrāyaṇa* vow is thus established.
Having performed his daily rites, a Brahmin should eat four morsels in the morning.
When the sun has set, the Śiśucāndrāyaṇa vow consists of four [mouthfuls]. || 21 ||
Restraining the self, one should eat eight morsels of sacrificial food (haviṣya) when the sun is at the meridian;
this is the Yati-cāndrāyaṇa vow.
Having performed the ritual bathing, the twilight prayers, and other duties, one shall not eat for twelve days.
With a steady mind and free from negligence, this is the vow known as Parāka.
Consuming, in sequence over six days, oil-cake, honey, fermented gruel, water, and barley meal—this is the excellent vow known as the Saumya-kṛcchra. || 24 ||
Thus, by practicing each one according to the rule for three nights.
Like the Tulāpuruṣa rite, this vow is a threefold path of spiritual practice. || 25 ||
One who is self-controlled and firm in his vow should eat three morsels at a time.
The Ṛṣicandrāyaṇa vow consists of the distribution of sacrificial food (haviṣyānna).
Likewise, one should drink cow's milk for seven days, seven days, and three days; or for six days, subsisting only on air—this is the Stomāyana vow. || 27 ||
With water containing leaves, dūrvā grass, barley, śirīṣa, bilva leaves, and kuśa grass; [and with leaves, udumbara, and rājī].
By drinking each of these individually every day, this is indeed the Parṇakṛcchra vow.
By these vows, his soul purified, he should be devoted to the service of the Guru;
subsisting on alms or sacrificial food (haviṣya), he should maintain silence while eating. || 29 ||
The Pratilomas, the Puṣpavartins, the Yavanas, the Bauddhas, and the Kaulikas.
Upon seeing those devoid of proper conduct or Śūdras, one should not recite the Śruti.
In the fourth watch of the night, having performed the washing of the feet and other rites, and having seated himself on his seat,
he should recite the Veda as he has learned it.
One should not engage in the censure or praise of anyone, nor speak falsehoods; upon seeing a beautiful woman, one should meditate upon the eternal Viṣṇu. (32)

One should recite [the mantra] at the beginning and at the end of the chanting of Hari’s names; likewise, one should perform a prostration with eight limbs (sāṣṭāṅga-namaskāra) to the Guru at the beginning and at the end.
In the first watch of the night, one should worship Gaṇeśāna and Sarasvatī; since [the deity] goes forth during the night, therefore the Lord of the Gaṇas should be worshipped. (34)
In the fourth watch of the day, having performed worship, one should dismiss Sarasvatī after she has been gratified, and likewise Gaṇeśa who has returned. || 35 ||
Having meditated, "She is situated within my mouth," during the fourth watch of the night, one should recite [the mantra] again;
however, if it is a time unfit for study (anadhyāya), one should not cause the recitation to take place. || 36 ||
If the seventh watch of the night has passed at the half-watch (sārdhayāma), then Sarasvatī goes near Kārttikeya; therefore, one should worship her before singing. || 37 ||

One should meditate upon Skanda accompanied by Sarasvatī, and through her power, one should maintain [the practice]; then, having meditated again during the remainder of the night, one should recite [the mantra] once more, ending with the word "svāgata. || 38 ||
If the thirteenth lunar day clearly occupies the first half of the night, then the voice [of the deity] is present.
Performing the Pradoṣa vow, she goes dancing to Kailāsa. || 39 ||
Therefore, for the sake of propitiating Śiva, one should certainly not recite it there.
If one recites it by force, it merely comes to naught.
At this time of dusk, intent upon her worship and meditation, or practicing breath control and observing silence, a devotee of Śakti attains perfection within three years.

One should never, under any circumstances, neglect the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā). The morning twilight is said to be that which occurs while the stars are still visible, and the evening twilight is that which occurs when the sun has risen. || 42 ||
Beyond five muhūrtas and within twenty, in whatever manner [it occurs].
The time for the attainment of enlightenment has arrived; it is most excellent, indeed most excellent in every respect. || 43 ||

Due to the omission of the twilight prayer (saṃdhyā), there is a lapse in the primary fire-ritual; for this, a single expiation (prāyaścitta) must be offered, and if it is further exceeded, more is bestowed. || 44 ||
When the time has passed beyond the subsequent twilight (parasandhyā) by more than that duration, the recitation of the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times is prescribed there. || 45 ||
Or if he has been detained by the king, or has gone away for an absolutely necessary task.
Having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas), one should recite the Gāyatrī mantra one hundred and eight times.
And at the end of the meal, such blameless food is prescribed as the expiation.
Now I shall speak of the Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas, among the mantras. || 47 ||
By her, Brahman with attributes is sung and expounded;
without her, liberation does not arise for anyone. (48)
Mahākāla himself should recite that which is the very nature of Mahāmāyā.
By whose power you and I have been born like another Kāla. || 49 ||
The sage of the Gāyatrī is declared to be the ascetic Viśvāmitra; its meter is said to be Gāyatrī, and Savitṛ is remembered as its deity. (50)

Having placed the seven *vyāhṛtis*, beginning with *bhūḥ*, in sequence upon the heart, the two shoulders, the two thighs, and the abdomen, this is known as the first ritual placement (*nyāsa*). || 51 ||
It should be at the toes and the ankle joint, and it should be at the joint between the ankle and the foot.
Likewise at the joints of the ankles and knees, and at the joints of the knees and thighs. || 52 ||
One should sequentially assign the phonemes to the genitals, the navel, the heart, and the throat.
At the joints at the base of the fingers of the hand, at the wrist, and at the elbow; || 53 ||
At the base of the arms, on the face, on the nose, and also on the two cheeks; on the pair of eyes, on the two eyebrows, on the head, below the topknot, and on the left ear. (54)
One should place the syllables in sequence on the right ear, the mouth, and the head; this is proclaimed as the second method, the placement of the syllables of the Gāyatrī. || 55 ||
The ten syllables of the Gāyatrī are located at the head, between the eyebrows, the eyes, and the mouth.
Then one should place [the mantras] at the throat, heart, navel, and ankles, as well as on the knees and feet.
The third [placement] is the placement of the head (śironyāsa) of Gāyatrī upon the region of the head;
the heart is declared for Brahmā, and the head is said to be for Viṣṇu.
The *śikhā* is declared for Rudra; the *kavaca* is proclaimed for Īśvara; the *netra* is said to be for Sadāśiva; and the *astra* is remembered as belonging to the Soul of All. || 58 ||
This is proclaimed as the fourth, the six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa).
And on the knees, the shanks, the navel, the heart, the throat, and the forehead. || 59 ||
The vyāhṛtis should be assigned in sequence, and the Supreme Brahman at the head.
Furthermore, this fifth [method], the Nyāsa of the Vyāhṛtis, has been proclaimed.
"Tat savitur" is for the heart; "vareṇyam" is likewise for the head; "bhargo devasya" is the tuft (śikhā);
and "dhīmahi" is remembered as the armor (kavaca). || 61 ||
"The weapon called Netramukta, which is the leader of our intellects, has been described by Śeṣa. This is the sixth Nyāsa; these six are the removers of sin. (62)
Having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma), one should then practice meditation. I shall now describe here the meditation on Gāyatrī, which is delightful to the devotee. || 63 ||

One should meditate upon Gāyatrī, who possesses three eyes with faces having the luster of pearl, coral, gold, sapphire, and white [crystal], who wears a crown bound by a crescent moon, whose nature consists of the syllables representing the meaning of reality,
and who holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, a goad, a whip, a pure skull, a cord, and a conch.
I worship her who carries a discus and a pair of lotuses in her hands. || 64 ||
Then one should worship the Goddess together with her eightfold enclosure; having first worshipped the Queen of the Gods, one should thereafter worship at the tips of the corners.
In the fire-corner of the triangle, the deities are arranged in a clockwise direction: Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, and Vaiṣṇavī constitute the first enclosure. (66)
In front of him, one should worship eight [deities] in the eight directions in sequence.
Āditya, Ūṣas, Ravi, Prajñā, Bhānu, and likewise Prabhā;
And Bhāskara and Sandhyā—this is the second enclosure.

Then one should worship the six limbs upon the filaments of the eight-petaled lotus; and one should worship these [deities] mentioned in the third [section] of the Gāyatrī in the middle of the petals.
The eternally radiant one who brings delight, the consort of Bilva-Rudra, the playful one.
Prabhāvatī, Jayā, and Śāntā—this is the fourth enclosure.

Then, one should worship on the tips of the petals, in order, Kānti, Durgā, Sarasvatī, Viśālā in the form of Bilva, Īśānī, and Vyāpinī; and Vimalā is declared [to be worshipped] in sequence—this indeed is the fifth enclosure (pañcamāvaraṇa). || 70 ||
In the eight-petaled lotus immediately following that, these Śaktis are to be worshipped: Tamohāriṇikā, Viśvayoni, and Jayāvahā are to be worshipped. (71)
Padmālayā, Parāśobhā, and Padmarūpā constitute the sixth [enclosure]. (p.
242) In front, there shall be the enclosure consisting of the seven Mothers beginning with Brāhmī; the eighth is declared to be Aruṇā.
This, indeed, is the enclosure that has been described. || 72 ||
The Sun, Venus, Mars, Rāhu, Saturn, the Moon, Mercury, and Jupiter.
And this is the eighth enclosure, located in the eight directions of the square.
The guardians of the directions are proclaimed in the seventh [chapter], and likewise their weapons in the eighth. In this manner, one should worship the Goddess and display her mudrās.
One should always recite the Gāyatrī mantra conjoined with the three Vyāhṛtis.
Twenty-four hundred thousand [recitations] are said to constitute the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa). || 75 ||

For the sake of attaining mastery over the mantra, one should offer a thousand oblations of each individual substance: milk-rice, sesame seeds, dūrvā grass, cooked rice, and excellent sacrificial fuel sticks. || 76 ||
Then, having performed the libations and other rites, one should diligently satisfy the Guru.
The wise one should practice the applications preceded by permission for them. || 77 ||
The mantra practitioner should offer oblations of sesame seeds for thousands of times the number of principles (tattvas).
Freed from all evils, he attains a long life. || 78 ||
And for the sake of longevity, one should offer an oblation of clarified butter alone, or even of ghee.
The mantra-practitioner should offer three thousand oblations with sesame seeds mixed with dūrvā grass.
Then, for six months, the twice-born man, with his senses restrained, should offer oblations for each substance ten thousand times with Aruṇārka and Śvetārka flowers.
And for the sake of the glory of Brahman, one should offer oblations with flowers produced from the Brahmavṛkṣa tree.
One desiring liberation should recite the Gāyatrī joined with its fourth foot.

"Parorajase sāvadom"—thus the fourth [pāda] is proclaimed. Vimala is its seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is its metre (chandas), and the Supreme Self (Paramātman) is remembered as its deity (devatā)—this is how it connects with what follows. || 82 ||
The Supreme Self should first perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Praṇava.
One should perform the nyāsa of the seven vyāhṛtis, the gāyatrī, and so forth, as previously described.
The heart belongs to the Self that is Brahmā, and likewise the head to the Self that is Viṣṇu.
"Śikhā to the Self that is Rudra," and "Kavaca to the Self that is Īśvara"; "Netra to the Self that is Sadāśiva," and "Astra to the Universal Self. || 85 ||

There is no mantra higher than this, and no austerity higher than this; all mantras, beginning with the Mahāvidyās, are regarded as mere straw in its presence. (This is an epithet of "mantra" [in verse 85]). 86.
Now I shall declare that which is to be kept secret—secret as one would keep a secret from a mother or a paramour—that which brings about the complete perfection of all Vedic mantras. (87)
If one utters [this] to one who is greedy, ungrateful, an atheist, or deceitful, or to one who is arrogant or hostile toward their guru, they shall incur a curse. || 88 ||
For those Vedic mantras whose application is indicated by ritual action.
One should always recite the Gāyatrī together with its Tān, Ādi, Pāda, and Sahitāṅga. || 89 ||
Likewise, there are one thousand and eight protective mantras; those joined with the middle foot are for protection, while those joined with the last foot are for destruction.
"Success is inevitably attained through the splendor of the Gāyatrī. Thus has this secret procedure of the Gāyatrī been briefly proclaimed. (91)

One should draw an eight-petalled lotus with the syllable *hrīṃ* situated in the pericarp; one should write two vowels on each petal, corresponding to the cardinal and intermediate directions. || 92 ||
Upon the filaments at their tips, one should place the syllables of the Gāyatrī three by three.
But one should draw [the remaining elements] within the space between that pair of outer circles. || 93 ||
Likewise, [the syllables] beginning with *ka*, as well as Umā, water, light, essence, nectar, and Brahman.
And the mantra "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ om" is a yantra that grants the accomplishment of all aims.

Fear of death, however, is constant for all people in all their actions; but when that [fear] is conquered, a person may accomplish everything from the attainment of the gods up to liberation. || 95 ||
For that purpose, I shall fully proclaim the mantra named Mṛtyuñjaya; through its worship, therefore, there shall be long life for our lineage. (96)
We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant one who increases prosperity; may he deliver us from death, as a cucumber is released from its stem, yet not from immortality. 97.
Vasiṣṭha is its sage, the Anuṣṭubh its meter, and Tryambaka its deity.
With three, four, eight, six, five, and three syllables: [Tryambakaṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ,
yajāmahe śirase svāhā, sugandhiṃ puṣṭivardhanaṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ, urvārukamiva bandhanāt kavacāya hum, mṛtyormukṣīya].
*vauṣaṭ* to the three eyes; *phaṭ* to the weapon from the nectar. This is the six-limbed rite (*ṣaḍaṅgakam*).
[In the east, west, south, and north-east corners: *tryaṃ* in the east, *baṃ* in the west, *kaṃ* in the south, *yaṃ* in the north, *jāṃ* in the southeast, *maṃ* in the southwest.]
He [is] at the northwest; *suṃ* in the northeast corner; *gaṃ namo* at the navel; *dhiṃ* at the heart; *puṃ* at the throat;
*ṣṭiṃ* at the belly; *vaṃ* at the genitals; *rddhaṃ* at the anus; *naṃ* at the base of the right thigh; *uṃ* at the base of the left thigh; *rvāṃ* in the middle of the right thigh; *ruṃ*...

*Vaṃ* is in the middle of the left thigh; *kaṃ* is on the right knee; *miṃ* is on the left knee; *vaṃ* is on the curve of the right knee; *vaṃ* is on the curve of the left knee; *ndhaṃ* is on the right breast; *nāt* is on the left breast;
*mṛṃ* is on the right side; *tyoḥ* is on the left side; *muṃ* is on the right foot.
KṢĪM on the left foot, YAṂ on the right hand, MĀṂ on the left hand, MṚṂ on the nose, and TĀT on the head; immediately after that.
One should likewise perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the limbs, specifically at the navel, heart, throat, and belly. || 99 ||

On the penis, the anus, as well as on the two thighs, the two roots of the thighs, the middle of the thighs, then on the two knees, the pair of knee-circles, and likewise on the two breasts. || 100 ||
One should place [the syllables] on the two sides, the two feet, the two hands, the nose, and the head;
this is the second nyāsa, consisting of the individual letters of the mantra. || 101 ||
There are exactly eleven words: "O Tryambaka" on the head; "we worship" on the eyebrows;
"the fragrant one" on the eyes; "the increaser of prosperity" on the mouth; "like a cucumber" on the cheeks;
"from the bond" on the heart; "from death" on the belly; "may he release us" on the thighs; and "he who is beyond" on the knees.
[The threefold placement is: on the two ankles, from the feet up;
on the two eyebrows and the eyes; again on the face and the pair of cheeks; and again on the heart and the belly. (102)
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) in this manner upon the ankles, thighs, knees, and feet. Thus one should perform the three types of nyāsa, preceded by the mātṛkā-nyāsa. || 103 ||
With two hands he was filling two jars with the essence of nectar, with two others he held those two deer-eyed bracelets upon his head, and with the remaining two he bore the Supreme One.

I worship the three-eyed Lord Śiva, who is as beautiful as Mount Kailāsa, who resembles clear water, who wears a crown of the eternal moon, and whose two hands placed upon his lap are filled with nectar.
One should worship the Bull-bannered Lord on the seat (pīṭha) described by the five-syllabled mantra, using the root-mantra for the form.
Having made a resolution by means of the path that will be described. || 105 ||
Having first worshipped the limbs, one should afterwards worship the form.
Starting from the east and proceeding clockwise, [one should offer] to Īśāna, who is the form of the Sun.
One should utter "To Mahādeva, Soma" for the form of the Moon; "To Bhava, the earth-form" and "To Śarva, the water-form. || 107 ||
To Rudra in the form of Agni, and to Ugra in the form of Vāyu.
To Bhīma, whose form is space, and likewise to Paśupati ending in the suffix -ṅ. || 108 ||
Then one should worship at the tips of the petals with the mantra "yajamānamūrtaye ca. [One should worship] Ramā, Rākā, Prabhā, Jyotsnā, Pūrṇā, Pūraṇī, and Sudhā. (109)
These belong to the third enclosure, while these belong to the fourth enclosure: Vidya, Viśvā, Sitā, Yuktā, Sārā, Sādhyā, Śivā, and Niśā. || 110 ||
Noble Wisdom, Radiance, Delusion-Dispeller, Peace, Beauty, Fortitude, and Intelligence.
These belong to the fifth enclosure, and then those belonging to the sixth enclosure. || 111 ||
Dharā, Māyā, Satī, Padmā, Śāntā, Māgha, and Dvayāmalā;
in the seventh [patala] are the world-protectors (lokapālas), and likewise their weapons in the eighth. (112)
One who has conquered the senses should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times while meditating in this manner.
One should perform ten thousand oblations with these ten substances mixed with clarified butter.
Bilva, palāśa, khadira, and vaṭa wood, as well as sesame and mustard seeds, milk-rice, curd, and dūrvā grass—one thousand of each of these [should be offered]. || 114 ||
Having gratified and consecrated them, one should then satisfy the Brāhmaṇas and the Guru. When this is done, this great mantra becomes fit for ritual application. || 115 ||
A wise person should offer ten thousand oblations with bilva wood fuel-sticks for the attainment of prosperity.
One should offer oblations with the fuel-sticks of the Brahmavṛkṣa for the sake of Brahmanic splendor.
Having offered ten thousand oblations with *khadira* wood, one shall obtain peace and prosperity.
And one should offer oblations according to the prescribed rule with fuel-sticks of the vaṭa tree.
By ten thousand oblations, the practitioner shall become prosperous with wealth and grain; by offering that same number of sesame seeds, he is liberated from all sins. || 118 ||
Having offered ten thousand oblations with *siddhārtha* seeds, the king conquers his enemies;
by this very procedure, there shall be no untimely death. || 119 ||

An oblation (homa) performed with milk-rice bestows protection, prosperity, fame, and beauty. Furthermore, by offering cooked food prepared with cow’s milk into the fire, one may destroy the effects of a magical spell (kṛtyā). 120.
This very oblation is considered to bring about peace, glory, and prosperity; by means of an oblation of curd, one may cause a reconciliation between two enemies.
Every day, the mantra-practitioner should offer one hundred and eight blades of dūrvā grass into the fire.
Having conquered all diseases, one shall attain a long life. || 122 ||
On one's birth day, one desiring blameless prosperity, health, and great fame, should perform oblations with milk-rice mixed with clarified butter.
One who desires mastery over others should offer oblations with dūrvā grass smeared with cow’s milk and ghee;
the wise person who performs this correctly one hundred and twenty times on his birth day shall be freed from all diseases and live happily for a hundred years. 124.
One should offer three hundred oblations each of *kāśmarī* wood, clarified butter, milk, and cooked rice.
One should perform the oblation and afterwards feed the Brahmins with sweet food.
One should respectfully gratify one's own guru with various kinds of grain and other offerings; thus, one attains freedom from illness, long life, and prosperity. || 126 ||
By offering oblations of milk-rice mixed with ghee on every lunar festival (parvan), one attains royal splendor within six months; of this there is no doubt.
And with pure parched grains, one should perform oblations for the sake of obtaining a bridegroom.
By performing oblations with fuel-sticks of milk-tree wood, one shall bring Brahmins and others under one's control.
Having bathed, one should mutter the mantra a thousand times while facing the sun.
Freed from mental and physical ailments, one shall attain a long life; by means of this mantra, one shall accomplish everything desired for oneself. || 129 ||
Now, for the destruction of poverty, I shall declare the mantra of the Lord of Wealth.
The sage is declared to be Medhātithi, and the meter is said to be Gāyatrī. || 130 ||

Having performed the ritual placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa), one should perform the recitation (japa) of the deity Sadasaspati for forty thousand times during the month. || 131 ||
For the propitiation of the deity, the recitation of the mantra should be performed for six months.
This shall constitute the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa), consisting of feeding Brahmins according to one's own capacity.
I salute Kubera, the lord of the Gandharvas, who is mounted upon a horse, holds a spear in his hand, is beloved by Citriṇī, is the master of treasures, and is golden-hued. || 133 ||
Now follows the mantra.
I establish for you this prayer, a wondrous lord of the assembly, beloved by Indra and desirable as a gift.
The man who recites it forty thousand times every month shall become a great treasurer; for him, this [mantra] brings about the destruction of poverty. || 135 ||
I shall describe that which accomplishes all aims and bestows victory in battle.
Listen to that which I remember regarding the slaying of Jalandhara. || 136 ||
Let us press the Soma for Jātavedas, so that he may burn away the wealth of the stingy enemy.
May Agni carry us across all difficulties, as one crosses a river with a boat, beyond all misfortunes. 137.
The metre is Triṣṭubh, and its sage is considered to be Marīci Kaśyapa; the deity is Agni Jātavedas, and one should perform the six ancillary rites (ṣaḍaṅga). || 138 ||
With nine, six, seven, eight, and seven finger-letters [of the mantra]: *Oṃ jātavedase sunavāma*—homage to the two thumbs; *somamarātīyataḥ*—homage to the two index fingers;
*nidahāti vedaḥ*—homage to the two middle fingers; *sa naḥ pariṣadati*.

Salutation to the two ring fingers; salutation to the two little fingers with the mantra "durgāṇi viśvā nāveva"; salutation to the palms and backs of the hands with the mantra "sindhuṃ duritātyagniḥ."
Thus is the placement of the heart and other limbs (*hṛdayādinyāsa*). Now follows the placement of the syllables (*akṣaranyāsa*):
*jā* on the right big toe; *ta* on the left big toe; *ve* on the right ankle;
*da* on the left ankle; *se* on the right calf; *su* on the left thigh; *na* on the right knee.
Or [the syllables] *vā* on the left knee, not on the right thigh; *so* on the left thigh; *ma* on the hips; *ma* on the penis;
*rā* on the navel; *tī* on the heart; *ya* on the right breast; *to* on the left breast; *ni* on the right side; *da* on the left side; *hā* on the back; *ti* on the right shoulder; *ve*...
On the left shoulder, *daḥ*; between the right shoulders, *sa*; between the left shoulders, *nā*;
on the right forearm, *pa*; on the left forearm, *ri*; on the right upper arm, *ṣa*; on the left upper arm, *da*;
on the right elbow, *duḥ*; on the left elbow, *gā*.
*ṇi* on the left forearm; *vi* on the right wrist; *śva* on the left wrist;
*na* on the palm of the right hand; *ve* on the palm of the left hand; *va* on the mouth; *siṃ* on the right eye; *dhuṃ* on the left eye; *du* on the right ear; *ri* on the left ear; *tā*.
In the middle of the eyebrows is *tya*, at the top of the head is *ma*, and on the crown of the head is *gni*.
On the two thumbs, on the two ankles, on the two shanks, and likewise on the two knees; || 139 ||
On the thighs, the hips, the genitals, the navel, the heart, and likewise on the breasts; || 140 ||
And likewise on both sides, at the back, and between those two shoulders.
And likewise on both the upper arms, the forearms, and the two elbows. || 141 ||
And likewise on both forearms, as well as on both wrists; on the palms of the hands, on the face, on the nose and eyes, and on the ears. || 142 ||
And for the eyebrows, it is *māstikye*; for the head, it is the second, *mūrdhani*. For the crest-lock (*śikhā*):
[Now the placement of the steps (*padanyāsa*): *oṃ jātavedase* at the crest-lock; *sunavāma* on the forehead;
*somaṃ* on the eyes; *arātīyataḥ* on the ears; *nidahāti* on the upper lip; *vedaḥ* on the lower lip.]

May he [Agni] be upon our tongue and in our throat; may he dwell in our arms with the *ṣa* and *riṣat* syllables; in our heart all difficulties; in our belly like a boat; in our hips like the secret parts; in our thighs the river; in our knees the transgressions; across our shanks; and Agni in our feet—and also on our forehead and in our eyes.
Likewise, on the two ears. || 143 ||
On the lower lip, the tongue, the throat, the two arms, and likewise in the heart;
This placement of the feet on the belly, the hips, the secret place, the thighs, the knees, the shanks, and the feet is proclaimed; now meditation is described. || 144 ||
She possesses a radiance equal to a garland of lightning, stands upon the shoulders of the king of beasts, appears terrifying,
and is attended by maidens whose hands gleam with swords and shields.
I worship Durgā, who holds in her hands the discus, sword, shield, arrow, noose, goad, and the threatening gesture; she whose nature is fire, who bears the moon, and who possesses three eyes.
Having prepared the auspicious mandala called Sarvatobhadra as previously described,
Upon its pericarp, within a hexagon, one should worship Maṇḍūka and the others.
One should worship those aforementioned supreme principles (paratattvas) in the filaments; and in front of them, one should worship Jayā, Vijayā, Bhadrā, Rudrā, and Kālī, starting from the east.
One should worship Sumukhī, Durmukhī, Candramukhī, and Siṃhamukhī, as well as Durgā in the center; afterwards, one should worship the lion-seat with the lion-mantra.
Having uttered *tāra* [i.e., *oṃ*], [the mantra for the worship of the Lion is:
*oṃ vajranakhadaṃṣṭrāya mahāsiṃhāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*.
Then, the seventeen-syllable heart-mantra is: *vajranakhadaṃṣṭrāya ca mahā siṃhāya huṃ phaṭ hṛd*.

Having conceived the form by means of the root mantra, one should invoke [the deity] into it and worship. One should worship the six limbs in the filaments, and again on the eight petals starting from the east. || 150 ||
Jātavedas, the seven-tongued, is the second bearer of oblations; thereafter [he gave] Udaraja, who possessed the splendor of Vaiśvānara and Kumāra. || 151 ||
Upon the pedestal in the four compartments, one should [worship] Viśvamukha, Devamukha, Dharātmā, Jalātmā, Vahnyātmā, and Nirātmaka. || 152 ||
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and Śānti are the secondary [kalās].
Then Pūṣā and Vāṇī, as well as Vīthī and Śacī, whose nature is water. || 153 ||
She is considered to be Nityā, Dayāvatī, and Aṣṭamīkāriṇī; likewise, she is called by the name Navamī and Tiraskriyā. || 154 ||
Furthermore, Devamātā and Damana-priyā are described later;
likewise, Nandinī, who crushes the bodies [of enemies], is to be propitiated. || 155 ||
Padmā, Daṇḍinī, Tigmā, Durgā, and Gāyatrī; beyond these, Niravadyā, Viśālākṣī, and Saumyā are described for the evening. || 156 ||
Svarodvāhā, Nādinī, Vedanā, Vahnigarbhiṇī, Siṃhavāsā, Dhūmrā, and Durviṣahāriraṃsukā. || 157 ||
Outside of that [is the mantra] "tāpaharā tyaktadoṣānissapatnā."
One should then complete the worship of the world-protectors (lokapālas) and their weapons as before. || 158 ||
One should recite the mantra for thousands of syllables and perform the fire oblation separately for each.
[One should perform the rite] with sesame, white mustard, and various grains, numbering four times the number of the Vedas and oceans (four hundred and thirty-two). || 159 ||

With roots and sacrificial fuel-sticks—according to the opinion of Bhāguri, these take the feminine suffix ṭāp—from the *vaṭa*, *udumbara*, and *pippala* trees, as well as those originating from the *arka* and *plakṣa* trees, and with ghee, oblation, and various foods. || 160 ||

One should offer oblations with all [the aforementioned substances] mixed with ghee, and at the end, offerings of sesame seeds with ghee. Then, having gratified [the deities] with sesame seeds and performed one's own ritual ablution, || 161 ||

Having propitiated the Goddess of the Earth (Dharādevī), one should satisfy one's own Guru. When the mantra has been mastered through such means as recitation (japa) and others, the most excellent practitioner— || 162 ||
One shall be the master of the Āgneya weapon; its ritual procedure is now declared. That which is called the Āgneya weapon is a mantra renowned for its reverse order. || 163 ||
The same six limbs previously mentioned, beginning with the sage and so forth, [are assigned] in reverse order.
Having pronounced "gnityatāridudhuṃ siṃ," the heart [mantra] is considered to be here. || 164 ||

With the *va* syllable, the horses emerge; this is proclaimed as the placement of the head (*śironyāsa*). Know that in the same way for what follows: [“*tidadharipanaḥ sa śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*"], by reversing the previously mentioned syllables. || 165 ||
The placement of the letters (varṇanyāsa) is likewise performed with the same number of syllables as previously stated;
similarly, the placement of the words (padanyāsa), the recitation (japa), and the worship (pūjā) are to be done as before. || 166 ||
For the accomplishment of that [rite], one should offer caru well-cooked with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), four thousand, one hundred, forty, and four [times]. || 167 ||
One should perform the fire-oblation as before, and the recitation [of mantras] in reverse order; in all cases, the preceptor should perform a recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra twice its usual length.
One should perform cruel rites according to the reverse order; rites for pacification and nourishment should be performed according to the natural order. || 169 ||

*gnyādyaḥ* [daḥ vetihādani kavacāyahūm toyatī rāmamaso netratrayāya vauṣaṭ mayānasu sedavetajā astrāya phaṭ]. The arrangement of the feet is performed by means of the syllables of the mantra in reverse order. The first foot consists of five syllables.

The first [element], consisting of the five colors beginning with smoke, is to be known as having the nature of the organs of knowledge—namely, these five: the ear, skin, tongue, nose, and eye. The second consists of the nature of the organs of action. (170)
The third mantra, beginning with the letter ŚVA, consists of five syllables and is known to be composed of all beings—the five great elements: earth, water, fire, air, and space.
First, there are the seven constituent elements (dhātus): skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen.
These seven elements constitute the fourth foot, which consists of seven syllables and has the form of an element.
The fifth quarter, beginning with *daḥ*, consists of six syllables and has the form of a wave (*ūrmi*).
Another [quarter], beginning with *ta*, likewise consists of six syllables and is considered to be composed of the six sheaths (*ṣaṭkauśika*). || 172 ||

Another [form] preceded by "sa" consists of five colors and is said to be composed of sound and the other [sensory objects]. That is to be known as the eighth, beginning with the letters [of the alphabet], consisting of speech and so forth. || 173 ||
Thus, through the union with reality (*tattva*), the arrangement [of the feet] has been described (or, according to another reading, "the arrangement of the feet has been described").
The fire-deities, such as Tārā and others, arise from the respective syllables of the feet;
they are the images of the primary forms, their splendor impelled by their own respective functions.
With blazing hair and garments, possessing formidable fangs, they were terrifying.

The deities born from the sense-faculties (indriya) are said to have upward-gazing eyes. The deities arising from the feet of the Bhūtas are proclaimed to have horizontal eyes (or, according to another reading, horizontal faces). || 176 ||

Those born from the letters of the *dhātu*-forms are considered to have the appearance of both [male and female]; those born from the waves (*ūrmi*) have upward faces, while those arising from the *kośa* have horizontal faces. || 177 ||
The deities produced from the number of objects have two faces;
all these are traditionally known as neuter, while those born from the objects of the senses are female. || 178 ||
By means of these, the mantra-practitioner may burn the kingdom along with its mountains and forests;
a wise person should commence the weapon-mantra during a human asterism.
One should employ [rites] against the Asuras; one should remove auspiciousness from the deities. One should commence [an action] on the Nandās, and one should discharge weapons on the Riktās. (180)
One should perform the bringing of auspiciousness and the highest rites such as recitation (japa);
one should begin on Tuesday and conclude on Saturday. || 181 ||
The withdrawal [of the ritual] may occur during the period of Jupiter or Venus;
the commencement should take place when the planets are in fixed signs, and the dismissal should occur when they are in movable signs. || 182 ||
The wise one should perform the withdrawal of the weapons for both; he should employ the weapon during the dark fortnight and release it again with the moon.
One should again withdraw the weapon into oneself according to the sequence of the bright fortnight;
the wise one should perform the emission and withdrawal by means of the Sun during both fortnights.
Facing the west, one should accomplish all ritual activities.
[He should draw] all the constellations and trees, together with the names of those to be accomplished and their respective rites. || 185 ||
Having become self-restrained, one should offer seven thousand sesame seeds individually with castor oil;
the enemy shall go to the city of Yama. || 186 ||
One who is wearing wet clothes during the time of rain should offer oblations for seven nights with black pepper mixed with the oil of white mustard seeds, while reciting this mantra. (187)
Having written the name of the enemy according to the prescribed rite upon a palm leaf, he is seized by a fever equal to the fire of universal destruction. || 188 ||

Having enveloped [the target] with the Āgneya weapon, he is buried in the middle of the sacrificial pit; enraged, one should strike him with black pepper, and he will become overcome by fever. || 189 ||
Taking that, one should cast it into cold water; he shall become submissive. Likewise, sea-water, asafoetida, poison, cumin, and red ochre [are used]. (190)

Having prepared a doll made from the wood of the *nakṣatra* tree while the [substance] is boiling, one should cast it face-down and pierce it with a staff made from the wood of a poisonous tree. || 191 ||
One should strike that head while reciting the mantra in reverse order.
Within seven days, the enemy, deluded by fever, meets his death.
His feet were seized by the lordly serpent of the sun’s chariot, his body was enveloped by its poison, he stood naked with limbs smeared with oil, and was scorched by the rays of the sun. || 193 ||
Having meditated upon one's own enemy with his face turned downward, [one should strike him] with boiling water.
Having looked at the sun while performing the libation, one becomes beloved even to death. || 194 ||
One should meditate upon her who bears a pestle and a trident, possessing the luster of a dark cloud at the end of time.

Having wrapped [the offerings] in cotton seeds and leaves, and having offered oblations soaked in sheep’s ghee, the preceptor, having taken [the substance] with his fingernail, shall cause the enemy to be driven into hatred. (195)
Having meditated upon Durgā, who is terrifying and holds a threatening forefinger and a trident,

one who offers oblations with sprouts from poisonous trees drenched in buffalo ghee causes the enemy's great army to be eradicated in an instant. (Alternatively, "he eradicates the army" is a variant reading.)
One who knows the mantras. || 197 ||
Having meditated upon the Goddess as previously described, [one should worship her] with sacrificial offerings (caru) mixed with black pepper.
One should offer oblations for three days smeared with the blood of a goat; this will effect the eradication of an enemy's army—of this there is no doubt. || 198 ||
Having visualized the goddess Durgā as being filled with fiery spikes, blazing like the fire of universal destruction,
one should offer oblations of seeds produced from the *dhattūra* plant mixed with mustard oil—
or alternatively, with black pepper and mustard— into the fire, and thereby cause the enemy to be utterly deluded. || 199 ||
One should meditate upon Durgā, who resembles black collyrium and holds a trident and a sword in her hands.
One should offer oblations with the best sacrificial fuel-sticks produced from the *nakṣatra* trees, known as the *vraṇa-vṛkṣa*;
by doing so, one shall conquer an enemy within a month.
Mounted upon a lion, she is rushing forward toward the fleeing enemy.
Arrows released from bows, with the tips of their flames appearing like fire.
Recalling Durgā as she releases [the waters], one should offer libations with warm water.
By beholding the orb of the sun, the eradication of the enemy shall occur. || 202 ||
One should visualize her as being exceedingly difficult to approach, with a spear and a mace in her hands that are unfailing.
Shining like thousands of streaks of lightning, [it was offered] with oblations drenched in buffalo ghee.
One should offer oblations with the aforementioned excellent fuel-sticks of *nimba* and *vibhītaka*, as well as *kodrava* grains;
thus, the immobilization of the enemy's army shall occur. || 203 ||
One should constantly meditate upon Durgā, whose limbs are adorned with a network of arrows and goads.

Having kindled a fire with wood suitable for sacrificial rites, one who knows the mantras should offer oblations of salt and sweet substances at night for seven days; thus he shall bring kings under his control.
One should meditate upon Viśvadurgā, who is red in color and holds a noose and a goad.

The practitioner of mantra who performs oblations at night with the flowers and fruits of the *phalinī* plant, sprinkled with sandalwood water, shall bring the entire universe under his control. || 205 ||

Having meditated upon Sindhu-Durgā— who resembles the autumn moon, who is the radiant supreme nectar (or, according to another reading, from whom nectar flows), and who holds a noose and a goad in her hands— with the best of sacrificial fuel;
One should offer oblations with cane-sprouts sprinkled with honey for the attainment of a livelihood. || 206 ||

One should meditate upon Agnidurgā, who resembles a hibiscus flower; one who knows the mantra should offer oblations with an effigy made of salt mixed with the three sweets. Thus, one shall attract the desired object of practice; of this there is no doubt. (207)
The first [mantra] beginning with "atidurge" and ending with six syllables is proclaimed; likewise, another beginning with "du" and ending with "varṇā" is known as Gāni Durgā. (208)
And because she begins with the word "viśva" in this mantra, she is proclaimed as Viśvadurgā.
That which begins with Sindhu and ends with Sāvakāra is called Sindudurgā.
The wise know that Agnidurgā is likewise composed of fire and the other elements.

Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in the courtyard, one should daily worship the Goddess there with fragrant flowers and other offerings, following the very path previously described. || 211 ||
One should offer the bali-oblation with caru at night; it bestows all accomplishments.
