This shall destroy sorcery, disease, fear, malice, and malevolent spirits.

Having duly propitiated the fire with fragrant and captivating flowers, the practitioner, standing before it with one-pointed mind, should recite the mantra. This recitation leads to all accomplishments; there is no need for hesitation in this matter. || 213 ||
Facing the west, one should offer oblations of salt sprinkled with sweet substances.
By means of the number of syllables in the mantra, the practitioner of mantra should bring the enemy under his own control. || 214 ||
Having washed and thoroughly cleaned the śāli rice, one should make the grains pure.
Having placed [the offerings] in the five products of the cow, [he should offer them] into the consecrated sacrificial fire.
And having descended [the deity], the wise and clear-minded one should again cook [the oblation] while reciting the mantra, after having worshipped in the kindled fire as before. || 216 ||

One should offer oblations with sacrificial porridge (caru) and clarified butter (ājya) eight thousand times; then, having performed the "heating" rite upon a leaf, the Guru should have the subject consume it.
One should honor that disciple with water poured down in the middle of the courtyard.

The force of malevolent spells (*kṛtyā*) perishes along with elemental spirits (*bhūta*), seizing demons (*graha*), and diseases; moreover, a spell that has been repelled by others may devour those very same people. || 218 ||
With rice, with oblations, with milks, and with the best fuel-sticks from milk-exuding trees.
One should offer one thousand oblations separately with clarified butter mixed with the three sweets, accompanied by the respective mantras.
One should perform oblations; that becomes the ground for success, and the practitioner will certainly attain it. || 219 ||
When the sun was situated in the sign of Aries, on a day endowed with the qualities of mantra-knowledge, he went to a river and constantly chanted the mantra in its abundant waters.

Having dug them up, taken them, and purified the sand, one should thoroughly cleanse it. Having placed that [sand] into the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) within the produced sacrificial fire, one should fry it with a ladle made from the wood of the Brahma-tree, using the mantra for the sake of success. || 221 ||
When the Sun is situated in Leo, Aries, or Sagittarius, on the eighth lunar day of the dark fortnight.
Likewise, under Viśākhā, Kṛttikā, Mūla, Hasta, the three Uttarās, and Maghā. || 222 ||
A wise person should perform the installation of the sand on the Rohiṇī or Śravaṇa asterisms, or on a Saturday or Thursday; one should avoid other [asterisms] for this rite. || 223 ||
For the protection of houses, villages, and kingdoms, auspicious sands [should be used].
These measures—the *prastha*, *āḍhaka*, and *ghaṭa*—are used for the medium and lower [weights] respectively. || 224 ||
Having recited the mantra, one should cast [the offerings] into the nine [vessels] and worship them in sequence.
The preceptor [should worship] the goddesses beginning with Madhyā and the weapons ending with the skull-cup.
The discus, conch, sword, shield, arrows, bow, and trident.
Having worshipped the skull with its own respective mantra, one should finally offer the bali oblation.
One should offer oblations to the lunar mansions, the planets, the zodiac signs, and the lords of the worlds; where protection is thus established, there prosperity increases. (227)
Minor planets, great diseases, fear, spirits, and reptiles—all these go to destruction by this rite; of this there is no doubt. (228)

There should also be sixteen *kuḍavas* of pure sand—[a *kuḍava* is said to consist of four *palas*]. These are placed in a vessel made from the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree, which has been mixed with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). (229)
Wherever one deposits [the wealth] according to the prescribed rite, there prosperity remains; it increases day by day along with untimely rains and other such blessings. || 230 ||

Great portents, sorcery, malice, diseases, and planetary seizures are destroyed. One should perform the installation of the sacrificial porridge, cow-products, and stones according to this procedure. || 231 ||

There should be one *prastha* of cow urine [one *prastha* consists of sixteen *palas*], and cow dung should be half of that. Milk should be seven times the amount of clarified butter (*ājya*), and curd should be three times the amount of cow urine. (232)

Clarified butter should be mixed with cow urine in equal proportions, or all [the ingredients] are said to be equal. The cows should be tawny, white, or possess the luster of white, smoke-colored, or reddish-brown. || 233 ||
And in their absence, all [the materials] should be white, or everything should be derived from Kapila.
On a board consisting of forty-nine squares, [the positions] of Brahma's tree are established. || 234 ||
Having left the corner squares, one should write "hrīṃ" in the central square.
Starting from that upper cell, one should write [the letters] in a clockwise direction.

Having invoked the Goddess there, one should worship her with ritual offerings. Having performed the fire-oblation (homa), one should bury the remnants (sampāta) as previously described. One should offer the bali-offering as before;
the fruit for that has been stated previously. || 236 ||
One should draw a very beautiful square diagram consisting of nine compartments.
One should write the syllable Māyā, accompanied by the name of the person to be accomplished, in the central square.
Starting from the square below that, one should write [the syllables] in a clockwise direction; and outside of that, one should write the eight previously mentioned quarters of the root mantra.
But within the space between the two verses, one should encircle it with the letters of the Mātṛkā.
Outside of that, there should be a square, containing the wondrous mantra of dhāraṇā.
It removes the fear of all beings and bestows auspiciousness, fortune, fame, and long life. || 239 ||
The man who knows the rites of discharging and withdrawing the fiery weapon (āgneyāstra) is the most excellent among those possessed of qualities;
the three worlds are dependent upon him. || 240 ||
I shall now declare the Atidurgā-mantra, which is called the "Day-Arrow" (dināstra); by reciting this mantra in reverse, it is designated as the "Arrow" (astra). || 241 ||

Agni crosses over all difficulties and even the impassable rivers; he carries us across all misfortunes. Let us press the Soma for Jātavedas; may he burn away the wealth of the enemy and protect us on every side. 242.
The previously mentioned *aṅganyāsa* is called *varṇanyāsa*; by this sequence, the placement (*nyāsa*) of the syllables and words is prescribed. (243)
And the meditation for the Kṛtyā-weapon was previously taught in reverse order.
Likewise, the sage [performs] the ritual placement (nyāsa) and meditation (dhyāna), as well as the chandas, as before. || 244 ||

I shall now proclaim all the ritual applications, beginning with the preliminary service (puraścaryā): one should visualize the enemy situated within the solar disc, in the center, distorted and struck down by poison. || 245 ||
The wise one should contemplate it as being swallowed by Kuṇḍalī, who has risen from the root.
If he should contemplate his own death immediately even at the root-support (mūlādhāra), [he will attain liberation].
Within two days, the enemy, overcome by fever, shall give up his life.
With his body pierced by the weapon of Time (dināstra), the enemy has come under one's own mastery.
One should meditate on his body as consumed by a fire kindled by the five vital winds (vāyus) and mutter the mantra;
immediately he shall become beloved of Yama. || 247 ||
Meditating on the enemy situated in the Maṇipūra [cakra], with his body blazing with fire and consumed by the weapon-mantra, one should recite [the mantra];
he shall fall under the power of death. 248.
The enemy, unassailable [by others] yet slain by him, is consumed by the fire of mantras;
bound with a noose, he is swiftly led away by the servants of Yama. || 249 ||
An enemy who has gone to a pure place, yet is overwhelmed by the five arrows of the sun (the five senses), is said to be head-downward;
he shall quickly become lifeless within three days. || 250 ||
One should burn an enemy situated within one's own command with the fire of an arrow through the power of the intellect.
Accompanied by his sons, friends, wife, and others, he shall meet with death. || 251 ||
Standing in water reaching up to the navel, one should meditate on the orb of the Sun;
by reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times while visualizing the enemy with all his limbs consumed by fire, he goes to the world of Yama within seven days. || 252 ||
Beginning from Monday, one should recite the mantra for seven days.
From the time of sunrise until sunset, the enemy shall be overcome by a severe triple-dosha fever and seized by Yama. || 253 ||

Having stayed in the abode of Durgā for three nights while abstaining from food, or on a single day, the mantra-knower should intensely contemplate the enemy as being struck by disease; by reciting this mantra, the enemy shall become afflicted with fever and go to his death. || 254 ||
Having seen Durgā, one should constantly recite the mantra while keeping one's enemy in mind.
With his body impaled on a trident and tormented by the weapon of Time, seized by a great fever, he becomes a guest of Yama. || 255 ||
The enemy who had entered the solar disc was bitten by the serpents that were his chariot.
One should meditate on [the victim] whose entire body is burned by the fire of poison as being bathed with warm water.
If one satisfies [the deity] with five hundred oblations daily, he shall become dear to Yama. || 256 ||
Having visualized the enemy with his body consumed by flames issuing from the solar disc, one should recite the mantra;
he shall go to the presence of Yama. || 257 ||
The frontal orb of the planet seized by the grahas is pierced with arrows consisting of mantras.
The knower of mantras should recite ten thousand times against an enemy who has transgressed the path;
he quickly leads that enemy to the abode of Yama by means of Yama’s messengers.
Resembling the fire of universal dissolution, like another Night of Doom, she was terrible, bearing a trident and a noose, and seated upon the shoulders of a lion. || 259 ||
[He should contemplate her] situated within the orb of the sun, arising from the three red eyes.
She was burning her enemies with sparks, their bodies thrown into utter confusion.
Her lower lip was bitten by her own fangs, and her face was terrifying with dancing frowns.
Threatening her own enemy with a finger in a terrifying gesture. || 261 ||
Illuminating the quarters of the sky with a network of rays from her fangs, she was terrifying as she tore open the chest of her enemy with her trident. || 262 ||
The wise one should recite it for three days and shall slay his own enemy.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) with weapon-mantras, he possessed a radiance equal to the fire of universal dissolution. || 263 ||
Wearing red garments, she is wrathful and adorned with three red eyes.
Mounted upon a lion, she was running toward a fleeing enemy;
having severed his head with her sword, she instantly ascended to the expanse of the sky. || 264 ||
Having meditated upon Durgā, one should recite the mantra for three days while abstaining from food;
by this very procedure, the enemy shall become dear to death. One should perform these rites during the day, but not at night. || 265 ||
Therefore, the weapon for the day has been described; now the weapon for the night is being taught. Having placed a living buffalo facing westward in front [of him], || 266 ||
Having dug a triangular pit upon its head,
the most excellent preceptor, according to the rules, [should act] when the fire therein has been kindled.

The mantra-syllables, arranged in triangles and joined with the name of the person to be accomplished, should be sprinkled with blood from one's own arm and used as excellent *kāraskara* fuel-sticks; having meditated upon the Goddess within the solar orb, one should offer them into the fire a thousand times. || 268 ||
Terrible like the fire of universal destruction, she is adorned with thirty-two arms.
Dancing upon the head of a lion, she is brilliantly illuminated by her uplifted weapons.
With great tusks, most terrifying, with flaming hair and a roaring mouth.
Clad in garments of fresh, blood-drenched flesh, with three fierce eyes rolling, (270)
By this rite, the enemy, afflicted by a great fever, shall abandon his own body along with his sons, friends, and others. || 271 ||
Then the mantra-practitioner, having suspended the serpents with their faces turned upwards, [proceeds].
Durgā, who was situated within the orb of the sun and resembled a thousand suns.
She who has a thousand hands and feet, and a thousand eyes, heads, and mouths.
Her limbs were bound by a thousand serpents, and she struck terror into the three worlds. || 273 ||
Meditating with that very mantra, one should offer libations with warm water;
thus restrained by the noose of Time, the enemy shall relinquish his own life. || 274 ||
Resembling ten thousand midday suns, she roared like Narasiṃha.
Seated upon a formidable lion-throne, she was most terrifying to behold.
Meditating on the enemy impaled upon a stake, one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind.
If one offers warm water at the mouth of the serpent for three days, that enemy shall go to the abode of Yama;
of this there is no doubt. || 276 ||
Then, having placed the image made of *ṛkṣa* wood into hot water so that it is permeated by the wind [of steam], one should squeeze it according to the prescribed ritual. || 277 ||
Resembling the sun, the moon, and fire, she holds a sword and a shield.
[She was] crowded with hundreds of sparks issuing from the meeting of her three eyes.
Seated upon a lion, richly adorned with serpent ornaments, she who inspires fear in the three worlds.
Meditating on the enemy as being cut down by a sword, one should mutter the mantra ten thousand times;
by this procedure, the enemy becomes joined with death. || 279 ||
Having fashioned an excellent triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the temple of Durgā, [he should offer] into the fire kindled there an oblation made from the dung of a buffalo.
One should place a small doll, red in color, with its vital breath firmly established.
Having repeatedly cut [the offerings], one should offer them at night, provided they are not dyed with red.
Having meditated upon Durgā, who is dancing upon the chest of Mahiṣa, of terrible appearance, and piercing the body of Mahiṣa with her trident; 282.
Terrifying with loud bursts of laughter arising from her mouth, she was served by the gods.
Resembling a blazing fire, she was endowed with three wandering eyes. || 283 ||
Her lower lip was bitten by [her own] fangs, and her lotus-face was terrifying with its tusks.
She was surrounded by young maidens equipped with swords and shields. || 284 ||
By this method, the enemy goes to the abode of Yama. Thus has the weapon for the day been described; now the weapon of the Kṛtyā for the night is being told. || 285 ||

The goddess Kuṇḍalī, who has the form of a serpent, having risen from the foundation (ādhāra), then proceeds through the path of the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) to the region of space (vyomasthala). || 286 ||
Having seized the enemy with her mouth, she returned toward her own home.
Having visualized [the enemy] as blazing with the kindled fire of Time (Kālānala), one should recite the mantra; within seven days, the deluded enemy meets his death. || 287 ||
On a Tuesday, one should offer a *kuḍava* measure of white mustard seeds, nourished with mustard oil, into the funeral fire;

having consecrated them with recitation (*japta*), one should sacrifice them with the mantra of the victim. By the flame of the *kṛtyā*-weapon, the enemy shall immediately go to the city of Yama. || 288 ||
On the fourteenth day, at midnight, the practitioner [should collect] the bones from the funeral pyre here.
Then, one should offer oblations into the funeral fire after anointing them with wound-oil; by this rite, the cowardly enemy shall meet his death. || 289 ||
Having ground the husks of grain and fashioned an effigy of the enemy,
one should offer it into the fire at night, after anointing it with wound-oil and attributing life to it.
Having repeatedly cut [the enemy] with the blood of an old man, the enemy dies within seven days. || 290 ||
Having touched sand from a cremation ground mixed with unbroken grains of rice, one should recite the mantra with fixed concentration.
However, water boiled with [the mantra] and recited over it in a secluded place such as a pond, when drunk, quickly destroys all diseases. || 291 ||
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, with the ashes of a deceased person recited over [with mantras],...
With buffalo ghee combined [with the offerings], according to the number of syllables in that mantra. || 292 ||
Having fashioned this image and properly consecrated it with breath-visualization (samīraṇa),
one of firm resolve should offer oblations into a fire kindled with funeral wood.
Before the three fourteenth days [of the lunar fortnight], an enemy shall fall under the power of death. || 293 ||

One should cast the ashes of a cremation ground and white mustard seeds into the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). One should then meditate upon the Goddess, whose radiance is like a blazing fire, as she rides upon a buffalo.
Reciting the mantra, one should roast [the offerings] in a fire kindled with poison-wood; then, an expert in weapons should offer ten thousand oblations with this mantra in the temple of Durgā.
Taking up that ash again, one should throw it into the enemy's army;
that army will be split in many ways and utterly bewildered by fever.
Having abandoned his weapons and fled at the time of battle, he shall swiftly effect the eradication of those who have been cast into houses, villages, and the like. || 397 ||

On the seven days of the week, at the dwellings of Durgā belonging to the Kulika [astrological period], one should take sugar-grains from the directions starting with the seventh and ending with that of Indra (the east), and then recite the mantra. (298)

First, one should satisfy a buffalo with the five products of a female buffalo. Having recited [the mantra] further, one should cast these [substances] into a house in a village or city; that region will quickly perish, consumed by the forest fire of the mantra.

Having taken the three—brahmadaṇḍī, markaṭikā, and vajrakaṇṭakikā—at the time of Kulika on a Saturday, one should recite the mantra; then the destruction of the enemy occurs along with his sons, wife, and others. || 300 ||
The practitioner of mantras should dig in one place alone; that spot shall be within the mandala.
One should bury a doll made of six sets of six dots, accompanied by cooked rice.
Having touched it, one should recite the mantra from noon on the eighth day of the dark fortnight.
One should bury this [image], inscribed with the name of the enemy, in a cremation ground; the enemy will quickly perish along with his family and kinsmen. || 302 ||

The practitioner of mantras, having touched those fragments of skull with the number of syllables of the *kṛtyā* weapon-mantra, should recite that weapon-mantra after first performing the rite of establishing the vital breath (*prāṇasthāpana*). || 303 ||
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, in a cremation ground consisting of poisonous trees.
Then, one should offer oblations smeared with human blood into the blazing fire of the *kṛtyā* weapon; thereupon, the enemy, utterly deluded by a great fever, shall go to the city of Yama. || 304 ||
One should cast a snake into a jar filled with blood, cover it with a skull-cup,
and conceal it with a red cloth.
One should worship with red flowers and other offerings, and having touched it, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times.
On Tuesday, being composed as before, [he should do so] in the middle of the directions, starting from the east. || 306 ||

When the fire has been kindled with *kāraskara* wood and intensified by the *kṛtyā* weapon-mantra, one should offer ten thousand oblations of "wound-oil" (*vraṇataila*); at the conclusion, that cloth [should be treated] again. || 307 ||

Having uprooted [the plant] together with its head, the wise practitioner intent on malevolent rites should offer it as an oblation according to that ritual procedure; within three days, the enemy shall die.
A beautiful prastha of buffalo ghee, consecrated with the mantra.
With all its limbs bound with kusha grass, it was established by the power of its vital breath.
Having performed a fire sacrifice (homa) with fuel from the *kāraskara* tree mixed with oil for wounds in a fire, the knower of mantras,
with a restrained mind, should further offer cloth as an oblation; within a single day,
the enemy shall go toward the city of Yama.

When the fire has been placed in a triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and kindled with the mantra, the wise practitioner, having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, should perform ten thousand oblations (juhuyāt). || 311 ||
Then, for seven days, one should daily [perform the rite] with oils made from sesame seeds devoted to Raji.
When the queen has reached the time of childbirth and her vital breath (anila) has been stabilized,
one should touch her while she is honored with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and recite that mantra.
One should offer oblations into the fire with fuel, starting from the head and ending at the yoni; when this is done, a Kṛtyā arises, blazing from the sacrificial fire.
One shall devour the enemy, even if protected by the Lord, before long. || 313 ||

Furthermore, desiring even the agent [of her own creation], she enters again into the fire. He who, being the best among those who know mantras, should perform such rites, must recite mantras such as the Mṛtyuñjaya for the sake of self-protection. (314)
(p. 257) Now, for the purpose of accomplishing the mantra of the Three Powers (triśakti), one should perform the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa):
the recitation (japa) of the Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛti), as well as the fire-oblation (homa) and the libation (tarpaṇa).

Having recited the mantra preceded by the syllable *oṃ* ten thousand times, one should offer oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) one thousand times; thereafter, one should perform the libations (*tarpaṇa*) and other rites. || 315 ||
When this is performed, there shall be the propitiation of all the gods and the attainment of capability; without this, however, the accomplishment of the mantra of Triśakti does not arise. (316)
Oṃ bhūr! To Agni and to the Earth, and to the Great One, svāhā! Oṃ bhuvaḥ! To Vāyu and to the Atmosphere, and to the Great One. || 317 ||
Oṃ, to the Sun, to the auspicious, to the sky, and to the Great One. Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, to the Moon, to the constellations, to the quarters, and to the Great One, svāhā! 318.
But the attainment of the fruit to be described hereafter is common to thousands.
According to the place and time, however, it is most excellent when performed with ten thousand oblations. || 319 ||

Just as one desires, such a result arises from a hundred-thousand-fold oblation (lakṣahoma). Now, I shall describe that process in sequence: one becomes radiant through an oblation of clarified butter (ghṛtahoma). || 320 ||
By means of fuel-sticks of the Udumbara tree, one gains the capacity to accomplish all rites; desiring cattle and the like, one should offer either milk or curd. || 321 ||
For the purpose of pacifying all portents, by offering Apāmārga grains and Arka fuel-sticks as oblations,
one shall obtain gold according to one's desire.
Having tied a pair of jasmine creepers together and soaked them in ghee, one should [use them].
One should perform the oblation ten thousand times; he shall always obtain prosperity.
One desiring a daughter should offer oblations with handfuls of sesame seeds and rice;
one desiring a son should offer oblations with fuel-sticks of Apāmārga.
To bring [someone] under one's control, one should offer fuel-sticks of *palāśa* or *aśoka*; one desiring long life, with *dūrvā* grass; and one desiring wealth, with flowers. (325)
Having combined the fuel-sticks of the *vyādhighāta* tree with the blood of a goat, the practitioner of mantras should offer them as oblation;
thus, the malevolent rite (*abhicāra*) succeeds. || 326 ||
For those already born or being born, the Lord is everywhere wrathful; one should offer oblations there with all kinds of grains out of reverence, or [perform the rite for] death.
One should perform seven oblations with abundant rice and dūrvā grass.
An oblation performed with the feathers of an owl and a crow causes enmity. || 328 ||

In the case of grasping by a dream-demon, one should perform a thousand oblations of tawny cow's ghee; having set aside the ghee from the final residue, one should stir it with *vacā* root. By consecrating [the woman] with this, she becomes possessed of sons and is born wise. 329.
Having stood facing the sun for exactly one month, if one constantly recites [the mantra] ten thousand times every day, one obtains a virtuous son. || 330 ||

Whatever object is most beloved, one should perform a homa with that very thing; by offering ten thousand oblations mixed with ghee, its attainment is brought about. Whatever is suitable for the homa is a means for achieving success, like a son. || 331 ||
Now I shall describe the practice for the mantra of the Three Powers (Triśakti), by whose grace Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and likewise Hari attained perfection. (332) p. 258)
The *gāyatrī* is "tatsavitur... (RV 3.62.10); the *āgneya-astra* is "jātavedase... (RV 1.50.1);

and the *traiyaṃbaka* is "tryambakaṃ yajāmahe... (RV 7.59.12). By the combination of these three Vedic verses, a mantra of one hundred syllables is produced. This *gāyatrī* mantra is named "Triśakti."

By reciting "vareṇyam" in place of "japya" at the time of chanting, the mantra's completion as a hundred-syllabled one is achieved; likewise, there is the Āgneya weapon-mantra and the Traiyambaka mantra.
This triad is declared to be the mantra known as Triśakti, consisting of one hundred syllables.
The three sages have been mentioned, as well as their respective meters;
his supreme splendor is beyond the senses and is to be known through the Vedas, and its presiding deity is the Supreme.
With all the Rudras, likewise with thirteen,
with eleven, with twenty-two, with the Kṛtyās, with the Akṛtyās, with the lunar days (tithis), with the clouds (ghanas), and with the syllables of the mantra.
One should perform the six limbs and the preliminary ritual placements (prāṅnyāsa).

He is the grain devoid of human agency, the primordial cause of the world according to the words of the Vedas, pervading all that is moving and stationary, and meditated upon by the best of sages whose senses are restrained.

We bow to that supreme splendor, which consists of twelve thousand rays, whose body is composed of the hundred-syllable mantra, who is the essence of Tārā, who is eternal, the abode of the qualities of perpetual bliss, and the highest reality.
There, in the Saura-pīṭha, one should worship with the six limbs as the first enclosure; thereafter, one should worship the three enclosures with the Gāyatrī-śaktis.
The fifth enclosure is to be made, and within it, in the form of a pathway.
The powers (śaktis) that have arisen as musical instruments are forty-four in number. || 338 ||
Indeed, the fourfold group of Śaktis mentioned in the Āgneya-astrology has been declared; their worship within the enclosures (āvṛtis) is performed with the Śaktis spoken of by Mṛtyuñjaya. || 339 ||

One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) and their weapons in the tenth and eleventh enclosures; then, one should offer milk oblations and satisfy them with food offerings and other gifts.
When the mantra has been thus perfected, the practitioner shall become like the sun.
One should offer oblations of pieces of guḍūcī, produced from a plaster of sudhā, combined with milk. || 341 ||
Indeed, one attains a long life, free from mental and physical ailments.
One shall obtain that very same fruit by offering dūrvā grass sprinkled with ghee. || 342 ||
One should offer oblations with reddish lotuses combined with the three sweets.
One who knows the ritual procedure attains great fortune within six months.

One should offer oblations with red lotuses smeared with the three sweets for the sake of all prosperity; one should offer oblations with *śrī* flowers [or bilva flowers], and one will become the abode of *Ramā*.
One should constantly offer a thousand oblations of milk-rice and auspicious sesame seeds.
One should daily feed twice-born men, numbering as many as the sun (twelve), with foods accompanied by sweets.
Completely liberated from all sins and entirely freed from all diseases.
Having conquered all malevolent spells, treacherous spirits, and planetary influences, he lives a long life. || 346 ||
Constantly devoted to the morning bath, he should always mutter [the mantra] one hundred times each.
One who beholds the sun with perfect concentration shall live for a hundred autumns.
One should daily recite the mantra beginning with the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times for the attainment of the supreme good (niḥśreyasa) and for liberation from all sins. (348)

For the destruction of all enemies, one should recite this mantra beginning with the *triṣṭubh* verse, namely "Oṃ jātavedase" (which is the first mention of the mantra). For the increase of longevity and health, one should recite the mantra beginning with "tryambakaḥ". (349)
Now, the ritual procedure for Tvaritarudra is being described. Neither in the Vedas nor in the Āgamas is there a mantra such as this that bestows swift accomplishment. (350)
Rudra who is in the fire, who is in the waters, who is in the plants—Rudra who has entered all beings, to that Rudra let there be homage. 351.
The sage is declared to be Atharvaṇa, and the meter is said to be Anuṣṭubh;
its deity is Rudra, and one should apply the six limbs in their proper sequence. || 352 ||

In this context, the five-limbed ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is performed with fifteen syllables: "Oṃ yo rudro agnau, to the thumbs, salutation; yo apsu, to the index fingers, salutation; ya oṣadhīṣu, to the middle fingers, salutation; yo rudro viśvā bhuvanā viveśa... [and so on].

"Salutation to the two ring fingers; salutation be to that Rudra with the two little fingers. In this same manner, the placement (nyāsa) of the heart and other limbs is also performed. Now follows the placement of the syllables (akṣaranyāsa): *Oṃ* on the head, *yo* on the forehead, *ru* between the eyebrows, *dro* in the right eye, *psu* in the left eye, and *yaḥ* [on the nose].
Oṃ at the right ear; ṣa at the left ear; dhī at the nose; ṣu at the right cheek; yo at the left cheek; ru at the mouth; dro at the right arm; vi at the left arm;
śvā at the palm of the right hand; bhū at the palm of the left hand; va at the back; nā at the... [anus].

*Va* is on the chest; *u* on the belly; *ve* on the navel; *śa* on the hip; *ta* on the right thigh; *smai* on the left thigh; *ru* on the right knee; *drā* on the left knee; *ya* on the right shank; *na* on the left shank;
*mo* on the right foot; *a* on the left foot; and *stu* on all the limbs.

Thus is the placement of the syllables (akṣaranyāsa). Having placed the phonemes (varṇas) upon the body and other parts, beginning with the thumbs, one should perform the meditation (dhyāna). || 353 ||
Four-armed and three-eyed, resembling pure crystal, with two hands filled with nectar in the form of jars. || 354 ||
With both hands forming the mudrā of yoga, he sat in a steady posture.
To Śaṅkara, the lord of the fruits of all desires, the ocean of compassion; || 355 ||
He has a fierce form for his fierce deeds, with eyes like blazing fire; he is two-armed, with a serpent for a hand, holding a trident in his hand, and wearing matted hair.
During the preliminary rite (puraścaryā), one should sleep on the ground once [per day], eat only sacrificial food (haviṣya), observe celibacy, and speak the truth. || 357 ||

One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, perform fire oblations with sacrificial wood and clarified butter, and conduct libations, purificatory sprinklings, and the feeding of Brahmins for the sake of attaining mastery over the mantra. (358)

Regarding the worship of the earthen liṅga: whatever worship was prescribed for a specific desire during the earthen worship, one should perform it there in that very same manner. One should perform the daily rites as before.
When the mantra has been mastered in this way, the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) is fit to perform the ritual applications (prayoga). || 359 ||
The accomplishment that is attained through twenty thousand homas is thus described.
One desiring food should [use] udumbara wood, but one desiring splendor should use khadira wood. || 360 ||
Through the oblation of Apāmārga fuel-sticks, the affliction caused by malevolent spirits is destroyed.
For the destruction of afflictions caused by the planets, one should recite [the mantra] in the presence of an Aśvattha tree.
(260) Those [seats] made from the Bodhi tree have three corners, their tips smeared with curd mixed with salt.
Dry fuel sticks are offered; one should utter the mantra ending with "svāhā. || 362 ||

Having offered fifteen oblations, one should utter "Go, go! as long as the homa and the bali are being given, equal in measure to the essence of the Puruṣa. When this is properly performed, he indeed releases that Puruṣa.
One who offers lotus petals with a joyful heart shall obtain his desired object; by an oblation of parched grain (lāja), one seeking a maiden obtains a beautiful daughter.
Furthermore, parched grain mixed with sacrificial porridge, or white flowers, when offered in a green place, shall bring the entire universe under his control. || 365 ||
That [mark] should be raised on the left for subjugating women, but not on the right.
For the sake of pacifying the enemy army, [one should offer] sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter.
And having placed a single water-filled jar at the site of the fire sacrifice (homa),...
Having recited the mantra eight thousand times, one should scatter those bowls there.
And having sprinkled their hall with those consecratory waters, he circumambulated it clockwise.
For the sake of pacifying the influence of planets, spirits, and so forth, one should likewise perform this for the sake of the kingdom as well. (368)
The worship of the site (vāstupūjā) should be performed with the auspicious sixty-four squares.
An offering (bali) should be made to Īśāna, as well as to the Lord of Beings (bhūtānāṃ pati);
when this is done, one shall obtain peace for both cattle and progeny. || 370 ||
During all kinds of portents, one should sit outside the village at night and quickly recite the Rudra mantra together with many others. || 371 ||
The fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed with Palāśa wood mixed with clarified butter;
one should offer the oblation (bali) to Īśāna in whichever direction that miracle occurred. || 372 ||

Then, desiring prosperity, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times before the Lord of the Quarters and likewise before the Lord of Beasts, accompanied by an oblation of sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter. || 373 ||
And an offering and worship should be performed for Śiva and Varuṇa, provided that one has the capacity for any such undertaking whatsoever. || 374 ||
Then, one should quickly recite from fifty thousand up to one hundred thousand times.
One obtains all desires through the grace of Tvarita. || 375 ||
One who desires prosperity or one who desires peace should then recite this [mantra] one hundred thousand times.

One desiring prosperity should offer oblations with *bilva* fuel-sticks, while one desiring peace should offer oblations with wood made of *śamī* (as is understood from the context), mixed with clarified butter; likewise, there should be libations and ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*). Thus it is for all [rites].
In ritual activities, an oblation should likewise be performed with barley.
One desiring a son should offer one hundred thousand oblations with milk-rice (pāyasa);
likewise, one desiring knowledge should do so with bilva fruits, and one desiring long life with dūrvā grass.

One desiring splendor should offer sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter, or with ghee alone; one desiring nourishment should offer rice grains, and likewise one desiring satisfaction should offer those same grains.
In all rites for the fulfillment of desires, milk-rice mixed with sugar should be offered as an oblation.
Honey, lotus, clarified butter, and mango leaves [are used] for the destruction of violent fever.

For the destruction of all diseases, one should recite [the mantra] facing the sun—one thousand, ten thousand, or a hundred thousand times—according to the relative severity of the patient's condition. || 381 ||
At the conclusion of the recitation, one should also perform the placement (nyāsa) of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), which is called "supreme" (parā).
In the five, three, and five Rudras, the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) is performed with eight, eight, six, eight, eight, seven, and six syllables respectively. For example:
"In these firm lands, *namaḥ* to both thumbs (*aṅguṣṭhābhyām*). Thus.
One should perform all the nyāsas according to the previously stated method; the six-limbed [nyāsa] is performed with the four syllables.
[The placement on the feet, shanks, knees, thighs, and private parts. Now the deposition of syllables (*akṣaranyāsa*) is described as follows:
*dhru* at the tip of the right foot; *vā* at the tip of the left foot;
*su* at the base of the toes of the right foot; *tvā* at the base of the toes of the left foot; *su* at the right ankle.

*Kṣi* on the left ankle; *ti* on the right knee; *ṣu* on the left knee; *kṣi* on the right thigh; *yaṃ* on the left thigh; *to* on the anus; *vya* on the penis; *sya* at the *mūlādhāra*; *tyā* at the navel; *sa* on the right side of the abdomen; *va* on the left side of the abdomen; *ru* on the back; *ṇo* in the heart. *Mu*.
*Va* on the chest, *kṣa* on the throat, *mo* on the tip of the right hand, *na* on the tip of the left hand,
*ra* at the base of the fingers of the right hand, *t* at the base of the fingers of the left hand,
*vo* on the right wrist, *nvā* on the left wrist, *nā* on the right elbow, *di* on the right arm, and *te* on the left arm.
*Ru* on the mouth; *pā* on the right cheek; *da* on the left cheek; *yā* in the right nostril;

*yaṃ* in the left nostril; *yā* in the right eye; *ta* in the left eye; *sva* in the right ear; *sti* in the left ear; *bhiḥ* between the eyebrows; *sa* on the forehead; *da* on the crown of the head; *naḥ*.
[Perform] the placement on all limbs (*sarvāṅga*). Thus is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*): *Oṃ*, to Rudra who is in the fire, salutation to the heart;

to him who is in the waters, *svāhā* to the head; to him who is in the plants, *vaṣaṭ* to the crest-lock; to Rudra who has entered all worlds, *hūṃ* to the armor; to that Rudra, [salutation] to the three eyes.
*vauṣaṭ*, *namo astu astrāya phaṭ* [at the penis]; then in sequence at the navel, the abdomen, the heart, the throat, the mouth, and the nose. (383)
One should place the sixteen words of the mantra upon the two eyes, between the eyebrows, on the forehead, and on the head; this is the Tvaritarudriya. || 384 ||
The ritual application of this verse addressed to Varuṇa is now duly described: wherever its worshipper resides, there drought shall never arise. (385)
Dwelling in these firm settlements, Varuṇa has driven away all hostility and released the men.
Having spoken thus from the lap of Aditi, go you always with blessings to us.
The seer is Vasiṣṭha, the metre is Anuṣṭubh, and Varuṇa is the deity.
The assignment of the limbs is performed with eight, eight, eight, seven, six, and five syllables. || 387 ||

Likewise, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the tips of the feet; the remainder is that one should perform the placement with the sixteen words of this very mantra, in sequence, upon the locations mentioned in the root text. [Specifically:
*yaḥ* on the two feet, *rudraḥ* on the two shanks, *agnau* on the two knees, *yaḥ* on the two thighs, *apsu* on the private parts, and *yaḥ*...

"Rudra has entered into the *liṅga*, into the plants, into the navel, into the belly; Viśva has entered into the heart, Bhuvana into the throat, and [Viśvakarman] into the mouth; [he has entered] into the nose, into the two eyes, into Rudra in the middle of the eyebrows, salutation to him on the forehead, and let there be [salutation] on the head"—such is the placement of the words (*padanyāsa*).
Also at the two bases of the toes of the feet, as well as at the two ankles, the two knees, the two thighs, and the anus and the genitals. (388)
In the mūlādhāra, as well as in the navel, the belly, the back, and the heart; in the chest, the throat, the tips of the hands, and the roots of the fingers. || 389 ||
Likewise, on the pair of wrists and the pair of elbows, on the two roots of the arms, on the face, on the pair of cheeks, and on the two nostrils. (390)

Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the syllables of the mantra in sequence upon the two eyes, the two ears, between the eyebrows, on the forehead, on the crown of the head, and on all the limbs, one should practice meditation. || 391 ||
Candraprabha is seated upon a lotus, holding a bow, a goad, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of boon-granting.
For the sake of prosperity, one should meditate upon the serene bestower of boons, whose entire body is adorned with ornaments of pearls.
One should properly worship Varuṇa on the seat (pīṭha) conceptualized as Dharma.
Having performed the worship of the limbs, [one worships] Vāsuki and Takṣaka as the remainder. || 393 ||
Karkoṭaka, Padma, and Mahāpadma beyond that; Śaṅkhapāla, Kulika, and the weapons of Indra and the other gods. || 394 ||
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform a fire sacrifice with milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with clarified butter, using a tenth part of that amount;
thereafter, one should perform the libations and other rites.
To be freed from debt, one should recite the mantra every day one hundred and eight times;
by this recitation, one obtains esteemed and imperishable prosperity.

The practitioner of mantras should offer oblations of pieces of sugar-cane soaked in clarified butter for four days, one thousand times each, for the sake of liberation from debt and for great prosperity. || 397 ||
For three days, [one should offer oblations] with fuel-sticks of reeds standing in water, smeared with milk.
One who knows the mantra and has conquered the senses should perform the oblation for the successful attainment of rain.

By this method, when the sun has entered the asterism Śatabhiṣaj, the mantra-practitioner who is in debt should offer four hundred oblations of milk-rice mixed with ghee. An oblation performed with milk-rice on a Friday leads to the destruction of debt, the attainment of prosperity,
and the increase of subjugation and health.
Having performed a great rite with ghee, one shall deliver [the practitioner] from all calamities.
(399) A wise person, remaining hidden within the body, having offered four hundred oblations for three days with rice mixed with ghee while facing west at sunset, shall paralyze the enemy troops.
Having propitiated the Fire-god, the practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra four hundred times; thus he shall be liberated from all calamities. 400.
The mantra-practitioner, having turned his face toward the west, should offer libations with pure waters.
For the destruction of all calamities and for the attainment of prosperity at all times. || 401 ||
What is the use of saying more here? By means of this mantra, the practitioner [attains success].
One who is devoted to recitation, fire-offerings, and other rites shall accomplish all desires. || 402 ||
Reciting it ten thousand times, one who is bound is liberated; there is no doubt about this. By reciting it by day and by night, accomplishment is attained immediately. || 403 ||

Remaining thus for a day and night, fasting and pure in his conduct, may his iron fetters break, and especially his wooden fetters. This [mantra] should never be given to one who is non-Vedic, nor ever to a Tantrika. (404)
I shall now declare the mantra of Annapati, which is devoid of ritual placement (nyāsa), mudrās, and so forth, and which lacks formal worship;
by its mere recitation, one never becomes destitute of food. (405)
Grant us food that is well-prepared, free from disease, and full of vigor. Further the giver; bestow strength upon our two-footed and four-footed creatures. 406.
With this, one should daily offer food one hundred and eight times; thus the food becomes unfailing, even when it has been burnt by fire or rained upon. (407)

Then, having established the fire in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) equipped with all necessary utensils, one should offer food one hundred thousand times until [the merit] becomes inexhaustible for as long as one's birth lasts. || 408 ||
When he had gone to the forest and performed [the rite] according to the procedure for cooking a sacrificial pot (sthālīpāka),...
And having kindled the fire, he should offer it along with a fuel-stick of udumbara wood. || 409 ||
If one performs oblations in his field, the grains known as rice shall become inexhaustible.
And what is so wonderful about good rain, when [these things] occur even during a drought? (410)
Now, the procedure for the mantra of salt is being declared: at the end of the supplementary words, one should likewise offer oblations of salt. || 411 ||
You are established in the salt waters; you are fierce, O Heart.
The Earth is the mother of the salt ocean, and Varuṇa is its father. 412.
While salt is being offered as an oblation, whence can there be sleep, and whence delight? Salt burns; salt cooks;
salt cuts; salt breaks. 413.
Burn the limbs of such-and-such a person; burn me, burn my skin! Burn my skin, bones, and marrow;
from the bones, burn my enemies! 414.
"Even if he dwells a hundred yojanas away, or at the distance of a hundred rivers, bring fire to me quickly, blazing with the brilliance of salt. || 415 ||
In this very city, which has iron walls and hundreds of black serpents for its bolts, let [the enemies] come under control, preceded by the salt-mantra. 416.
That night of yours which is the Great Night (Mahārātri), that night of yours is the Deep Midnight (Mahāniśā). The sage is declared to be Aṅgiras, and the meter is said to be Anuṣṭubh. || 417 ||
The deities are Agni, Rātri, Durgā, and Bhadrakālī.
In the five, three, and five Vedas, with the two-syllabled mantras born from the Ciṭi-mantra. || 418 ||
One should perform the six limbs; that mantra is now being declared: [The mantra with the *tāra* is said to be:
*oṃ ciṭi ciṭi cāṇḍāli mahalyahali amukaṃ me vaśam ānaya svāhā*. After the two *ciṭis*, [comes] *cāṇḍāli*.
Immediately after that. || 419 ||
One should indeed say "mahalya hali," then "amukaṃ me padaṃ tataḥ," followed by "vaśamānaya" and the pair of "ṭha"s;
this mantra consists of twenty-four syllables. || 420 ||
Thereafter, one should perform the meditation on the quartet beginning with Agni; listen attentively as those meditations are now described. || 421 ||
I worship Agni, who resembles fresh saffron, who has three eyes, and who is adorned with hundreds of beautiful ornaments.
Holding a sacrificial ladle (sruva), a spear (śakti), a boon-granting gesture (vara), and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) in his arms, he is seated upon a red lotus.
She possesses the luster of a dark rain-cloud, is reddened by the moon, and is endowed with breasts beautified by strings of pearls.
I bow to Yāmavatī, who holds a skull, a noose, a goad, and a trident in her hands, who is clad in blue garments, and who has the luster of a dark rain cloud;

she whose crest is adorned with the young moon, and who is richly endowed with a sword, a conch, a trident, and a shield. I remember her, the formidable one with three eyes, who has conquered the host of enemies.
Skilled in the destruction of the enemies of Durgā.
Holding a ṭaṅka, a skull-bowl, a hand-drum, and a trident,
adorned with a crescent moon, with tawny hair standing erect and terrifying white fangs— may Bhadrakālī grant me prosperity. (425)

One should properly recite the five Ṛks ten thousand times, and then offer oblations into the consecrated fire with clarified butter sprinkled over sacrificial grain, using one-tenth of that number as the portion for the homa.

Having thus performed the preparatory rites (puraścaryā), one becomes skilled in the practical application (prayoga). For the rites of subjugation and attraction, one should meditate on Agni and Yāmavatī; for the rite of killing, the mantra-practitioner should remember Durgā and Bhadrakālī. || 427 ||
Standing in water reaching the knees, one should recite the mantra at night; by this means, the desired object of accomplishment becomes a servant in an instant. || 428 ||
Standing in water reaching up to the navel, one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind.
Whoever performs this one thousand and eight times, that person for whom it is intended shall come under their control.
Standing in water reaching up to the neck, the practitioner of mantra should recite the five verses.
Within seven days, one shall bring kings under control by means of this rite.

Having written that [mantra] on a palm leaf, interwoven with the name of the person to be influenced, and having placed it in water mixed with milk, one should boil it at night; the person to be influenced will become submissive to him—no doubt should be entertained in this matter. || 431 ||
Having written this on a palm leaf, one should bury it in the house of Bhadrakālī;
this is declared to be the practice for bringing all living beings under one's control. || 432 ||

Having written the mantra interwoven with the name of the person to be influenced upon a palm leaf, one should heat it in a fire of khadira wood; within a month, that man shall become submissive. || 433 ||

Having approached a triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) that possesses the characteristics correctly described in the scriptures, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) therein upon the consecrated bearer of oblations (havyavāhana).
The wise person, having washed it with curd and milk, should thoroughly cleanse the salt.
One should offer well-ground powder as an oblation; within seven days, one shall bring the world under control.
Likewise, one should offer oblations with rock salt that has been sprinkled with curd, honey, and clarified butter.
One shall subjugate all the gods without delay; how much more so mortal kings? || 436 ||
A *prastha* of pure salt, divided separately into five parts.
One should reverently offer each portion with a *ṛc* verse for five days; by this ritual, the person whose name is used shall quickly come under one's control.
Taking pure salt mixed with honey, one should offer oblations;
by offering fifty oblations, one brings whatever is desired under control. By offering daily oblations of pure salt, one shall bring even enemies under subjection. (438)
With salts well-ground and mixed with the three sweets.
One should offer oblations and thus bring under control women, men, and even kings.
One should recite the mantra from the second day of the dark fortnight until the eighth day. One should fashion five effigies, complete with their primary and secondary limbs, uniform and auspicious.
One should be made from the wood of the tree to be accomplished, while the other is considered to be made of flour.
One [image] may be made of clay with a wheel in its hand, while another is made of sand.

One *kuḍava* of salt produced from a ship, ground and purified, should be sprinkled with milk, curd, clarified butter, and honey in succession; then, it should be thoroughly mixed again with this [mixture] combined with jaggery, clarified butter, and honey. || 442 ||
One should fashion a gentle effigy, beautiful in all its limbs.
With the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantras, one should project the vital breaths into its heart; having quickly established the breaths, one should worship it with flowers and other offerings. || 443 ||
Afterwards, when only one watch of the night of the eighth day of the dark fortnight has passed, having performed the Mātṛkā-nyāsa immediately following the mantra. || 444 ||
The twenty-four [deities] who have arisen from the *ciṭi* mantra.
Being composed, one should place the syllables beginning with Tārā in these locations.

On the crown of the head: OṂ; on the head: CI; on the forehead: BHALE; on the right eye: ṬI; on the left eye: ṬI; on the right ear: CĀṂ; on the left ear: ḌĀ; on the right nostril: LI; on the left nostril:
MA; on the mouth: HA; on the chin: LYA; on the throat: KA; on the right breast: HA; on the left breast: LI; on the navel: A.

The placement of the mantra syllables (*mantrākṣaranyāsa*) is as follows: *mu* on the right side of the abdomen, *kaṃ* on the left side of the abdomen, *pe* at the navel, *va* on the right hip, *śa* on the left hip, *na* at the genitals, *ya* on the two thighs, *svā* on the pair of knees, and *hā* on the pair of feet. [Then, *bhā* on the forehead.]
In the two eyes, the two ears, the nose, the mouth, and the chin; in the throat, the two breasts, the two sides of the chest, the two flanks, the navel, and the two hips. 446.
Having placed the remaining four syllables on the penis and the anus, [one should place them] on the two thighs,
the pair of knees, the pair of shanks, and the two feet.

Having thus performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) on all his limbs, being adorned with red garlands and unguents, wearing red garments, and being pure, he [should fashion] a doll of formidable appearance made of wood. || 448 ||
One should dig an image made of flour with its face downward into the sacrificial pit beneath the seat;
likewise, one should step upon it with the foot along with one's own [image]. || 449 ||
One should suspend a sand image above the fire-pit; thereafter, while touching an effigy made of salt, one should recite the mantra. || 450 ||

Having combined the five *ṛks* as arranged according to the *aṣṭottarasahasra* [list], one should again perform the placement of the syllables of the *cit-mantra* upon the limbs of that salt doll. For example:
*Oṃ*, place [the syllable] on both thumbs...
Aṃ at the two thumbs; ṭi at the two soles of the feet; ci at the two calves; ṭi at the two knees;
cāṃ at the two thighs; ḍā at the anus; li at the penis; ma at the navel; ha at the abdomen; lya at the heart; ha at the right breast;
li at the left breast; a at the neck; mu at the chin; kaṃ at the mouth; me at the [forehead].

One should place [the syllables] *va* on the right nostril, *śa* on the left nostril, *mā* on the right ear, *na* on the left ear, *ya* on the right eye, *svā* on the left eye, *hā* on the forehead, and *ṃ* on the crown of the head. One should place [the syllables] on the two breasts,
the joints of the thumbs, the forefeet, the calves, the knees, the thighs, and the hips, and in the region of the genitals.
Again, at the navel, in the abdomen, and in the heart-lotus. || 452 ||
One should place [the mantras] upon the two breasts, the neck, the chin, and likewise the face; on the two nostrils, the two ears, the two eyes, the forehead, and the crown of the head. || 453 ||

Having taken fire and kindled it with wood corresponding to the constellation of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), one should worship the deity mentioned in the mantra within that fire using a silver vessel. || 454 ||
Having offered the arghya with water containing kusa grass, lotuses, and rājīpuṣpa flowers, the wise person should prostrate.
With these mantras, at the beginning and end of the ritual application, one whose mind is fully restrained— || 455 ||

Then, having consecrated salt with the mantra at night, [one should offer it] into the fire at night, saying: "Be satisfied by this [salt] which has been recited over with the mantra, together with her. (456)
O Jātavedas, Great God, with the luster of molten gold; O Lord of Svāhā, consumer of all things, burn the salt, O slayer of enemies! 457.
O Śarvarī, O Śarvāṇī, you alone rule over the universe; by you the world is swallowed and released. O Mahādevī, salutations to you; O giver of boons, be the fulfiller of our desires. || 458 ||
O Great Goddess, composed of darkness, devoted to the Great God; you are dear to me—having slain this man, bring him under my control, O Goddess! 459.

O Goddess who dwells in the inaccessible yet is free from all difficulty, you who are the bolt that secures the attainment of what is hard to reach; O Goddess who bears the discus and the conch, you who strike down wicked enemies! 460.
Salutations to you! Burn my enemies and bring them under my control, O Caṇḍikā! O Great Goddess Śākambharī, O sinless one, be my refuge. 461.
O Bhadrakālī, bestower of the desired accomplishments of Rudra, destroy, utterly destroy my rivals; wither them and burn them, burn them! 462.
Having cut [them] with spears, swords, javelins, thunderbolts, and other weapons, bring them to the abode of Yama! O Great Goddess Mahākālī, protect us, you whose nature is the imperishable! 463.
Having recollected the object to be accomplished, one should again split the effigy into seven pieces.
Having recited the five verses, one should offer oblations into the fire fueled with wood.
First the right foot, and immediately after that, the hand.
The head is declared to be the third, and after that, the left hand.
The fifth should be above the middle, and the sixth is said to be below the shoulder.
The seventh [segment] shall be the left foot; such is the remembered sequence of divisions. || 466 ||
Or else, one may divide each [of those] into seven parts according to the rule prescribed for the aforementioned [mantras].
Having performed this and worshipped the fire, one should then prostrate like a staff.
The sacrificer should gratify his own preceptor with wealth and grain; by this rite, the practitioner of mantra shall bring both asuras and suras under his control.
How much more so, then, for men, kings, ministers, and royal women? For their killing, one should employ the four effigies previously described. || 469 ||
The supreme adept, knowing the ritual procedure, should install [the deities] as before; he should arrange the other [elements] according to the procedure that will be described hereafter. (470)

One should prepare a modification [of the mantra] using *balā*, *mūla*, *nakhī*, sesame, the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), and asafoetida (*rāmaṭha*), along with the dust from the feet of the person to be subdued (*sādhya*), for the purpose of achieving subjugation (*vaśya*). || 471 ||
Having properly prepared an effigy with the aforementioned salts ground together with buffalo urine, one should perform the rite of infusing life (prāṇapratiṣṭhā). || 472 ||

One should perform all rites, such as recitation (japa) and worship (pūjā), according to the previously mentioned method. Then, at night, in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) equipped with an altar, where the fire is blazing— || 473 ||
And having propitiated either Durgā or Bhadrakālī according to the prescribed ritual,
The practitioner should hold a sharp weapon with his left hand. || 474 ||
Beginning with the left foot and ending with the right foot, one who has conquered the senses and abstains from food should offer oblations, cutting [the flesh] again and again. || 475 ||
Beginning from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
By this very procedure, the wise one should perform the fire-oblation (homa).
By practicing this for three weeks, one may cause the destruction of one's own enemy. || 477 ||
The Nakṣatra tree, Kāraskara, Āmalakī, Udumbara, Jambū, Khadira, Kuṣṭha, Vaṃśa, Pippala, and Nāgara. || 478 ||
Rohita, palāśa, plakṣa, vaṭa, śilābhava, pārtha, vaikaṅkata, bakula, and sarala follow in sequence. || 479 ||
Sarja, vañjula, panasa, arka, śamī, kadamba, nimba, āmra, madhūka, and lodhra—this is the ritual procedure for the mantras. || 480 ||
And for him who performs the twilight devotions at the three junctions of the day preceded by a thousand recitations, I shall declare the easily accessible *ṛc*s for his success. || 481 ||
One should recite that mantra eight thousand times, even without the deity, ṛṣi, nyāsa, meditation, and so forth;
in those [mantras], success is not far off. || 482 ||
For the benefit of the entire world, I shall here relate those Ṛgvedic verses.
As they descend from heaven, the plants have spoken: "The living man whom we reach shall not come to harm. (484)
Having offered oblations of all medicinal herbs, one always obtains sweet food.
One should offer the items from the treasury into the fire by means of a fourth part. || 485 ||
Within a year, those [results] become complete; of this there is no doubt. He who performs this three times in this manner obtains the imperishable fruit of ten thousand [offerings]. || 486 ||
The essence of concentration is honey; it has been revealed as new honey. I shall speak honey-sweet words;
I shall utter to the gods speech full of honey, and that which is worthy of being heard by men.
May the gods protect me for the sake of splendor, and may the ancestors rejoice in my food. 487.

When a disease born of great malevolent magic has not been pacified and there is transgression, one should offer a thousand oblations of clarified butter with this [mantra] for its pacification. || 488 ||
Homage be to the serpents, whichever ones are upon the earth; to those in the intermediate space and those in heaven—to all those serpents, homage! 489.
One should offer ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa) into the fire at the location of the serpent with this [mantra] for one month, a thousand times;
thereafter, gold is produced. || 490 ||
Homage to those serpents who are the arrows of sorcerers, or those who dwell among the trees, or those who lie within holes. || 491 ||
Having seen a snake that has entered its hole, one should perform the fire-oblation right there.
By performing a thousand oblations of clarified butter with that [mantra], one obtains a hundred pieces of gold. || 492 ||
Put forth your vigor like a wide-spreading net; go forth like a powerful king with his retinue. Praised for your triple-reaching net, strike down the Rākṣasas with your most scorching weapons.
He who, being wise, should constantly recite this Ṛgvedic verse three times a day—at dawn, noon, and sunset—[attains success].
The suffering caused by fire falls upon that enemy. || 494 ||

"Rise up toward the north! Spread yourself out against the other enemies, O you of sharp weapons! He who has committed hostility against us with his fuel—that one you shall burn down like dry wood. One should take poison, black mustard seeds, and red thorns, and offer them as oblations into the fire of the enemy. Having taken [them]...
The destruction of his enemies' villages occurs for him. || 496 ||
To destroy the anger caused by what has been done, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times; for the subjugation of a man, one should offer a thousand mustard seeds as oblations for a month.
Growing from joint to joint, from stalk to stalk, O Dūrvā grass, spread forth for us with a thousandfold and a hundredfold increase. 498.
O divine brick, you who spread yourself with a hundred [parts] and grow forth with a thousand—we shall worship you with an oblation. 499.
One who desires subjugation should offer ten thousand oblations of young durvā shoots with these two [mantras];
by doubling the number, one may slay a village headman or a killer standing before him.
One should destroy the regional pestilence with three-fold [remedies], and great diseases with six-fold ones.
One may destroy the Māraka pestilence arising in various regions by means of a hundred-thousandfold oblation (lakṣahoma). || 501 ||
May our forest tree be full of sweetness; may the sun be full of sweetness; may our cows be sweet for us. 502.
With whatever desire one should offer fuel-sticks of the Udumbara tree smeared with clarified butter ten thousand times, or a hundred thousand, or ten million, from that [desire] he shall succeed.
Swift, sharpening his weapons like a terrifying bull, the striker, the agitator of the people; the roaring, unblinking, sole hero, Indra, conquered a hundred armies at once. (504)

With Indra— the shatterer, the one who provides sustenance, the victorious, the one who stirs the battle, the unshakable, and the bold— conquer with him, O men, and prevail in combat with that bull who holds arrows in his hand. 505.

He is the self-controlled one with arrows in hand and quivers at his side; he is Indra, the creator of hosts, victorious in battle with his troop. He is the winner of the gathered host, the drinker of Soma, whose arms are worthy of praise, who wields a fierce bow, and who shoots with well-aimed missiles.
O Bṛhaspati, fly around with your chariot, slaying the Rākṣasas and driving away our enemies.
May he who shatters the enemy host in battle, conquering them, be the protector of our chariots. || 507 ||
The elder, the great hero, powerful, vigorous, victorious, and fierce.
O preeminent hero, O bull among beings, possessing irresistible power, mount Indra’s victorious chariot for the sake of winning the cattle!
This lineage [produced] Govinda, whose arms are like thunderbolts, who is victorious and crushes the enemy hosts by his might.
Born for the sake of the bull, follow after the hero; O friends, go forth with Indra as your companion. Pounding through the cow-pens with force, Indra is the heroic victor of a hundredfold wrath.
May Duścyavana, the subduer of armies, the one who fights, protect our host in the battles.
May Indra be their leader; may Bṛhaspati, the sacrificial fee, the sacrifice, and Soma go before them.
May the Maruts go at the head of the divine armies as they crush [the enemies] and achieve victory. 511.
The fierce host of the showerer Indra, of King Varuṇa, of the Ādityas, and of the Maruts—
the roar of these high-minded, world-shaking gods has arisen as they triumph. (512)
O Maghavan, brandish your weapons and stir the spirits of my warriors!
O slayer of Vṛtra, let the vigor of the vigorous steeds rise up; let the shouts of the victorious chariots go forth.
May Indra be with our banners when they are gathered together; may those arrows which are ours be victorious.
May our heroes be superior; O gods, protect us in the battles. 514
Enchanting their minds, take hold of their limbs; go elsewhere!
Advance and burn them with heart-rending sorrows; let the enemies be enveloped by blinding darkness.
Released, fly away toward the target, sharpened by the power of Brahman!
Go and seek out enemies; do not leave even one of them remaining.
May the spirits be victorious; may Indra, the lord of men, grant you protection. May your arms be powerful so that you may remain invincible. || 517 ||
Where arrows fall like boys with shorn hair, may Indra, Bṛhaspati, and Aditi grant us protection; may they grant us protection at all times. 518.
I cover your vital organs with armor; may King Soma clothe you with immortality.
May Varuṇa make your chest broader; may the gods rejoice as you are victorious. || 519 ||
Having consecrated both himself and his weapons with this Anuvāka, one should go forth to battle;
victory will certainly be attained. || 520 ||
A thief, a tiger, a buffalo, a lion, a serpent, and a rākṣasa.
Having heard it at that place, the Anuvāka was meditated upon mentally by the twice-born.
One should go to that auspicious place, or else throw unhusked grains or *kuśa* grass consecrated with mantras, [saying]: "May there be protection from this. (522)
Seven are your fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven your tongues, seven your seers, and seven your beloved abodes; with seven officiating priests they worship you in seven ways;
fill the seven wombs with clarified butter, Svāhā! || 523 ||
Having offered oblations of ghee from one thousand up to one hundred thousand with this [mantra], one becomes radiant; if one offers them ten thousand times, one attains even greater splendor.
And by offering fuel-sticks of *audumbara* wood smeared with clarified butter, one shall obtain gold.
Within six months, [the result] up to seventy *tolakas* is certain. || 525 ||
O Prajāpati of the world, you whose dwellings are above and whose [dwellings] are here—grant great protection to this Brahman and to this Kṣatra; Svāhā! || 526 ||
One should offer clarified butter here with the sacrificial formula, "Svāhā to Indra! By performing this one thousand and eight times, one is liberated from the defects of the dwelling site.
In that house, there is no untimely death, and no mental agitation arises; even a woman in childbirth does not suffer pain, and one shall have no fear when alone. (528)
O Agni, you purify our lives; bestow upon us strength and nourishment within these [waters].
Drive far away misfortune.
Having offered a thousand oblations of clarified butter with this [mantra], one should go to the enemy's house. || 529 ||
Therefore, the bestowing [of the gift] should be preceded by right joy, like that of a friend.
I invoke Savitṛ, the golden-handed, for protection—the conscious one who knows the station of the gods.
(530) With this [mantra], ten thousand sticks made of Udumbara wood as well as those born of Arka are [offered].
For the sake of attaining success in the increase of gold, one should offer oblations of fuel-sticks smeared with clarified butter.
I call upon Indra, the protector, Indra, the helper; at every invocation, I call upon the hero Indra, who is easy to invoke.
I invoke Śakra, the much-invoked Indra; may the bounteous Indra bestow well-being upon us.
We call for protection the great Earth, the mother of those who observe sacred vows, the consort of Ṛta.

By the mere recitation of this mantra—*tuvikṣatrām ajarantīm urūcīm gūṃ suśarmāṇam aditim gūṃ supraṇītim*—one shall swiftly cross over even that which is difficult to traverse. Just as one standing on a raft or situated upon a boat does not sink in the water, so too shall one not perish. (534)
We invoke you, the Lord of hosts, the sage among sages, possessed of the most exalted fame;
the supreme ruler of sacred prayers, O Brahmaṇaspati—listening to us with your protections, sit upon your seat. 535.
With this, the mantra-practitioner should offer oblations of whole barley grains, sesame seeds, as well as fuel-sticks of Apāmārga and likewise of Udumbara. (536)
In this manner, wealth increases individually by as much as one prastha up to a hundred thousand;
then, one should perform a fire sacrifice at a crossroads.
By means of leaves produced from the *picumanda* tree, two [people] are suddenly brought under control;
and having fashioned a linga from the clay of an anthill, one should likewise bathe it. || 538 ||

O Gods, may we hear with our ears what is auspicious; O Holy Ones, may we see with our eyes what is auspicious. With firm limbs and bodies, praising you, may we attain that lifespan ordained by the Gods. 539.
If one with impaired faculties recites this two hundred thousand times, he becomes one with complete faculties and is liberated from impotence. (540)
Having understood these words, may the gods be favorable toward us from every side.
May the increasing ones increase with the aged; may the delights be pleasing. || 541 ||
Standing in water reaching up to the neck, one should recite this verse day and night without weariness;
then rain will fall even out of season. || 542 ||

That divine power which goes far away from one who is awake, likewise returns to him when he is asleep; that mind of mine, which is the far-reaching light among lights, may it be intent upon auspicious resolve. 543.
That by which the wise and skillful perform their rites in sacrifice during the assemblies—
that which is the unprecedented, mysterious power within living beings— may that mind of mine be of auspicious intent.
That which is wisdom, as well as consciousness, steadfastness, and the immortal light within living beings— may that mind of mine be of auspicious intent.
Since no action whatsoever is performed without it, may that mind of mine be of auspicious intent;
by which all this—past, present, and future—is encompassed through the immortal;
by which the sacrifice is extended with its seven priests, may that mind of mine [be of auspicious intent].
May there be auspicious resolve. || 546 ||

In which the Ṛg-verses, Sāman-chants, and Yajus-formulas are established, like spokes in the hub of a chariot wheel; in which all the thoughts of living beings are woven together—may that mind of mine be of auspicious intent. || 547 ||
May that mind of mine, which is established in the heart, swift, and most rapid— like spirited horses led by a skillful charioteer with reins— be possessed of auspicious intentions. 548.
One should recite these ten thousand times, and stability of mind arises. Having invoked the supreme earthen linga on a Monday, || 549 ||
One should perform the daily rites thereafter, [offering] one hundred and eight grains.
Having thus embraced them while they are still unbroken, they should be placed in the four positions.
Having formed a resolve in his mind, he should worship the earthen linga;
at the conclusion of the worship, having recited a single verse from the Rig Veda, he should offer unbroken grains of rice (akṣata).
In the first watch, at the beginning of the lunar phase, upon the head of the liṅga.
In the second watch and subsequent watches, one should place [the deities] in the southern and other directions.
In the middle of this, he should recite [the mantra] at night; he shall behold his desired object. When it is not yet evening, he should perform the ritual and then consume [it]. || 553 ||
One should arrange three grains each in the four directions.
These auspicious verses should be recited eight thousand times.
A dream necessarily becomes true and not otherwise;
it is seen as something past, present, or even future. || 555 ||
O Agni, you who know, may you cause away from us the wrath of the god Varuṇa.
Most excellent in sacrifice, the best of carriers, blazing brightly, release from us all hatreds and enmities. 556.

Those desiring sons should offer clarified butter with this mantra from one thousand up to one hundred thousand oblations, and they shall obtain excellent sons; likewise, those desiring cattle shall obtain them. Now, I shall describe the Śrīsūkta, the most excellent of all mantras, along with its ritual procedure for the Kali age.
Likewise, for the destruction of poverty, there is nothing else whatsoever for men.
O Jātavedas, bring to me Lakṣmī, who is golden-hued, tawny, adorned with garlands of gold and silver, moon-like, and made of gold. 559.
O Jātavedas, bring to me that fortune which never departs, through which I may find gold, cattle, horses, and men. (560)
I invoke the Goddess Śrī, who has horses for her front, a chariot for her middle, and is awakened by the trumpeting of elephants; may the Goddess Śrī be pleased with me. 561.

I invoke here Śrī, who is accompanied by smiles, whose ramparts are of gold, who is moist, radiant, satisfied, and bestowing satisfaction; she who dwells in the lotus, who has the color of a lotus—her I invoke here.

I seek refuge in her who is moon-like, radiant, blazing with ascetic power, the noble Śrī cherished by gods and men; I approach that lotus-eyed one for protection—may my misfortune perish, for I choose you. || 563 ||
O you who possess the color of the sun, born from ascetic heat, your tree is the Bilva, the lord of the forest.
By its fruit, may my inner and outer magical illusions (māyā) and misfortunes (alakṣmī) be dispelled through austerity;
may the friend of the gods (the Moon) and Fame dwell with me along with this jewel. Having appeared in this kingdom, may it grant me fame and prosperity. (565)
I destroy the supreme impurity of hunger and thirst, as well as misfortune.
Drive away from my home all misfortune and lack of prosperity.
She whose door is fragrance, who is invincible, eternally nourished, and rich in sacrificial offerings.
I invoke here that Śrī, the sovereign of all beings.
May we obtain the desire of the mind and the intention of speech; may the form of cattle, the essence of food, prosperity, and glory rest within me. 568.
"O Kardama, progeny have come into being through your seed; O Kardama, take birth within me! Cause Śrī, the mother garlanded with lotuses, to dwell in my lineage."
May the waters create unctuous things; cling closely to me in my house. O Niṣadevī, dwell in my home as the mother Śrī. 570.
O Jātavedas, bring to me Ārdrā, Puṣkariṇī, Puṣṭi, Suvarṇā, Hemamālinī, Sūryā, Hiraṇmayī, and Lakṣmī.
Ārdrā, Puṣkariṇī, Yaṣṭhi, Piṅgalā, and Padmamālinī.
O Jātavedas, bring to me the golden Lakṣmī who is like the moon.
O Jātavedas, bring to me that Lakṣmī who does not depart;
through her, may I obtain abundant gold, cows, female slaves, horses, and men. || 573 ||
For this verse beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇām," Lakṣmī is considered the seer (ṛṣi).
Ānanda and Kardama were the lords of the fourteen [worlds]. || 574 ||
Cilki, Ta, Lakṣmītanaya, and Catvāra are considered to be the sages.
The meter of the three verses beginning with "hiraṇya" and "aditi" is declared to be Anuṣṭubh. || 575 ||
May the *kāṃsosmitārcas* *bṛhatī*, which possesses the luster of the moon and the sun, and the *triṣṭubh* meter, approach me today along with the eight verses of the gods. (576)
"The meter is declared to be Anuṣṭubh; bring that to me"—thus [he recites] the Ṛg-verses.
Prastārapaṅkti is declared [to be the meter] for the deities Śrī and Vibhāvasu. (577)
The consonants are said to be the seeds (bījas), the vowels are the powers (śaktis), and the nasal points (bindus) are declared to be the pegs (kīlakas);
this constitutes the six-limbed [mantra] beginning with the thumbs. || 578 ||
Salutation to Hiraṇyā with the two thumbs; salutation to Candrā with the two index fingers; salutation to Rajataprabhā with the two middle fingers;
salutation to Hiraṇyasrajā with the two ring fingers; salutation to Hiraṇyākṣī.
"Salutation to the two little fingers for Hiraṇyavarṇikā;
salutation to the palms and backs of the hands. Thus is the Nyāsa of the thumbs and other fingers.
And likewise, Candratṛtīyā has the luster of silver. (p. 273)
Hiraṇyasraj, Hiraṇyākṣī, and likewise Hiraṇyavarṇikā. || 579 ||
With these mantras ending in "namaḥ," one should perform the assignment of the limbs.
One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) thus upon the fifteen limbs from the head down to the feet—namely, on the head, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, throat, chest, hands, and navel.
Regarding this, it is said: "The golden-colored one" (*hiraṇyavarṇām*) is for the head; "bring her here" (*tām āvaha*) is for the [eyes].
