With "aśvapūrṇām" for the two eyes, and "etad" for the two ears; in this manner, the others are also to be understood.
One should place the Ṛg-verses on the anus, the rectum, the pair of thighs, the knees, and the shanks. O Goddess, one should perform these two types of nyāsa and thereafter practice meditation.
Seated upon a red lotus, her complexion the color of a mass of its pollen,
she holds in her lotus-like hands the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness along with a pair of lotuses.
May Śrī, the Mother of the World, adorned with nets of ornaments such as various jeweled crowns, be ever present for our prosperity. || 582 ||
Having drawn a hexagon in the center, the deities of the limbs (aṅgadevatās) are to be worshipped therein.
Likewise, from the southeast corner, on the eight petals outside of that, are these [deities].
Seated on a lotus, lotus-colored, standing upon a lotus, and lotus-eyed; she is both the one who gratifies and satisfaction itself, blazing forth immediately thereafter. || 584 ||
There shall be the designation of the golden ramparts, the weapons of Indra and the other [guardians], as well as the invocation, the seat, and the offerings of water for honor, feet, and sipping.

The honey-mixture (madhuparka), the consecration (abhiṣeka), clothing, ornaments, sandalwood paste, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and finally the dismissal (udvāsana)—these are the sequence. || 586 ||
One who knows the mantras should indeed perform these with the fifteen Ṛg-verses; then, having offered fruit and betel, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for Śrī.
Then one should offer clarified butter (ājya) with these fifteen verses; having offered water for sipping (ācamana) to the Goddess, one should worship her with the mantra "tām ma āvaha". || 588 ||
One should dismiss [the deity] into one's own heart and recite with palms joined in reverence; this Śrīsūkta is the daily worship and is called the *puraścaraṇa*. || 589 ||
One should always sprinkle [the image] three times with those same hymns during the ritual of bathing.
Facing the sun, having recited [the mantra], one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for as long as [desired]. || 590 ||
Starting from the first lunar day (tithi) of the bright fortnight until it reaches the eleventh day.
One should recite it twelve thousand times with a steady mind.
Delighting in the practice of celibacy, with pure garments, teeth, and so forth, he is wise.
With lotuses mixed with the three sweets, and with milk-rice soaked in ghee. || 592 ||
One should offer three hundred oblations every day with ghee and the sacred *samit* fuel-sticks.
Furthermore, on the twelfth lunar day, one should feed twelve Brahmins;
by that means, the mantra becomes perfected—of this there is no doubt to be made.

The *kunda*, *mandāraka*, *kumuda*, *mālatī*, *padma*, and *ketaka*; the flower called *nandyāvarta*, the *jātī*, *kalhāra*, and likewise the *campaka*; and flowers such as the red lotus (*raktotpala*)—these are exceedingly dear to Lakṣmī. || 594 ||
The practitioner of mantra should offer oblations three times daily according to the prescribed rite; he who performs this for six months shall himself become a lord of a hundred thousand.
One should place the fresh butter (navanīta) upon a lotus that is merely beginning to bloom;

in the center, on the filaments, on the petals, and likewise correctly between the petals. Having taken that [butter] from a well-kindled fire, the wise one should offer it as an oblation (hunet). (596)
Having worshipped [the deity], one should perform the recitation one hundred and eight times on a Saturday.
With forty [verses], his great fortune shall be unshakable. || 597 ||
One should offer eleven oblations of clarified butter with the fourth verse;
by doing so, great prosperity shall come to him within six months.
He who desires the goddess Śrī, the bestower of boons, to be eternally established in his family, should, becoming pure and beloved, offer clarified butter as an oblation every day. (599)
One desiring prosperity should constantly recite the fifteen verses of the Śrīsūkta.
One should invoke Śrī into a lotus or, alternatively, into gold with five [mantras].
One should present offerings consisting of cooked rice, solid foods, milk, and curd;
and one should prepare a *sthālīpāka* of *śāli* rice with milk.
One who has disciplined oneself through the Cāndrāyaṇa vow shall attain prosperity from whatever source it may come.
Having bathed with decoctions and infusions prepared from all medicinal herbs, even those that have been boiled; || 602 ||
"May the friend of the gods approach me"—this [verse] is for the consecration of a king; "The desire of the mind"—this is for the consecration of one desiring cattle. (603)
And one who desires offspring, being pure in his vows, should bathe well while reciting, "Who am I? (kāṃsosmi).
One who desires a kingdom should, with a concentrated mind, bathe at the place called Aśvapūrṇa.

Once the hide has been prepared, the Brāhmaṇa should bathe according to the prescribed rule; the King (Kṣatriya) on a tiger skin, and the Kṣatriya on a Ruru deer skin; for the Vaiśya, it should be on a goat skin. Immediately thereafter, the fire-oblation (homa) must be performed.
A twice-born man should offer lotuses with clarified butter, reciting the mantra "candrāmi."
By means of this verse beginning with "ādityavarṇa," the oblation of wood-apples (bilva) is prescribed.
The fire produced from *bilva* fuel should be used, and the twice-born should offer *śāli* rice as oblations.
A sacrifice of ten thousand oblations is proclaimed for one who desires prosperity; having first offered these correctly, one obtains infinite wealth.
Having offered ten times ten thousand oblations of clarified butter with the Sūktas, he should perform the rite.
One attains eternal prosperity that is unspoken and undifferentiated.
In the event of inability—[the word "of him" is to be supplied as the remainder]—recitation alone is declared to be the superior alternative, consisting of ten thousand repetitions.
By reciting it correctly ten million times, one obtains infinite prosperity.
Having recited it ten times ten thousand times, one attains prosperity;
moreover, one should certainly offer lotuses as oblations daily, even ten thousand times.
Having worshipped with the supreme bilva fruits, the wise man indeed sustains himself on them; eating bilva,
dwelling among bilva trees, and offering bilva fruits with clarified butter, he attains supreme perfection within twenty-one nights.
With whatever desire one performs the oblation while having restrained senses—whether it be lotuses or bilva fruits—that desire shall be fulfilled. (612)
One should never, out of miserliness for the sake of wealth, summon prosperity;
nor should one ever perform a fire-oblation (homa) out of desire for anything whatsoever.

Furthermore, whether by one seeking greatness, or by one desiring clarified butter, or again by one praying for something else such as jewels, prosperity is certainly attained through these [offerings]. || 614 ||
At the conclusion of the principal satiation (*tarpaṇa*), it should be understood that the same applies to the other names as well:

one should join the word *namaḥ* to the end of each name beginning with *oṃ* and ending in the dative case, and then utter the word *tṛpyatu*; having joined the word *namaḥ*, one should pronounce the phrase "may [he/they] be satiated."

Just as: *Oṃ śriyai namaḥ, śrīs tṛpyatu* (Om, salutation to Śrī; may Śrī be satisfied), in this same manner, the other names are to be understood. These Śaktis are to be gratified, beginning with the Praṇava (Oṃ) and ending with the Hṛdaya (namaḥ): Śrī, Lakṣmī, Varadā, Viṣṇupatnī, and Vasudā.
She has the form of Vasu and is golden. || 615 ||

Padmā, Mālinī, and Ramā are said to have the luster of silver; Pragrahā is golden, as is Svarṇaprākārā and Padmamālinī. Indrā, Viśvapriyā, Aiśvaryā, Bhukti, and Pramuktiyuk are likewise [golden]. 616.
Viśuddharddhi, Samṛddhi, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, and the one called Dhana;
Bhuvaneśī, Śuddhā, Bhoginī, and likewise Bhogadā. || 617 ||
The thirty-two powers, namely Dhātrī and Vidhātrī, have been thus proclaimed.
One should satisfy [the deities] with salutations preceded by the Praṇava and ending in the dative case. || 618 ||
One should offer the oblation with these names, saying, "O Bali, eat me! At the conclusion of the worship, a daily observance is prescribed. || 619 ||
He should sleep on a bed, either alone or with a young woman; he should never be unclean, nor should he eat despicable food. (620)
One should never step over a water trough, a lotus-pond, a bilva tree, or a lotus flower; for these are always dear to Lakṣmī, and therefore a wise person should avoid them.
One should always wear upon one's head sahadevī, indravallī, śrīdevī, viṣṇuvallabhā, kanyā, jambū, and pravāla. || 622 ||
O Earth, be pleasant to us, thornless, and a place of rest; grant us wide-spreading shelter, and may she burn away our sin. 623.
The Brahmin who, being pure, recites this verse every day, obtains vast land that is free from rivals and devoid of thorns. || 624 ||
The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, like an eye stretched across the sky. 625.
In the accomplishment of mantras, the faults of eating the food of others are indeed obstacles; by reciting this verse over water, their destruction is brought about. 626.
Advancing with the dark dust, he establishes both the immortal and the mortal.
On his golden chariot, the divine Savitṛ comes, beholding all beings. || 627 ||
With this [mantra], one who has conquered the senses should worship the Sun for three days until success is achieved.
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times; thus, one shall be freed from disease and attain a full lifespan.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times while meditating on the Sun at night, and having offered clarified butter into the fire with this [mantra], one shall obtain a long life. (629)
I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutations indeed to Sadyojāta! In every birth, do not lead me beyond existence;
be my protector! Salutations to Bhavodbhava. || 630 ||

Salutation to Vāmadeva; salutation to the Eldest; salutation to the Most Excellent; salutation to Rudra; salutation to Time; salutation to the Maker of Time; salutation to the Maker of Strength; salutation to Strength;
salutation to the Destroyer of Strength; salutation to the Subduer of All Beings; salutation to Him who transcends the mind.

To those who are non-terrible, and to those who are terrible, and to those who are more terrible than the most terrible—to all of them, to all the lords (Śarvas), let there be salutation to you in your forms as Rudras. || 632 ||
Let us know that Tatpuruṣa; let us meditate upon Mahādeva. May that Rudra inspire us.
He is the Lord of all sciences and the Sovereign of all beings.
May Brahmā be my sovereign, may the Lord of Brahmā be my sovereign; may the auspicious Brahmā be mine; Sadāśiva! 634.
[Tryambakaṃ yajāmahe sugandhiṃ puṣṭivardhanam | urvārukamiva bandhanān mṛtyormukṣīya mā'mṛtāt ||] These are the sixty [verses] ending with Mṛtyuñjaya.
And one should mutter [this mantra] day after day. That woman shall always obtain peace for herself, her husband, and her cattle from Śaṅkara.
With this very six-verse hymn, one should offer oblations of clarified butter daily. And for the sake of prosperity, one should conceive of the fire as Raudra on the five festival days (parvan).
The rays of light bear up that god, Jātavedas, the Sun, so that everyone may behold him. 637.
Whoever daily worships the sun with this mantra at the three junctions of the day, for him heart disease is destroyed and supreme health is increased. (638)
O Soma, being in harmony with the ancestors, you have now spread yourself across heaven and earth.
That greatness of yours—be pleased with that for us; be auspicious to our bipeds and quadrupeds.
(639) A man, with fuel in hand, should worship the Moon at night with this *ṛc*;
for him who does so, his suffering shall go to dissolution. (640)
One who, being composed, worships the rising sun on the full moon day shall obtain garments and attain the same world as the Moon. || 641 ||
I shall now proclaim the heroic deeds of Viṣṇu, who measured out the earthly realms;
he who, the wide-striding one, propped up the highest station as he strode across the three worlds. 642.
Thou art the forehead of Viṣṇu; thou art the razor of Viṣṇu; thou art the needle of Viṣṇu;
thou art the fixed point of Viṣṇu. Thou belongest to Viṣṇu; for Viṣṇu, thee! || 643 ||
Behold the deeds of Viṣṇu, from which you behold his sacred vows; he is the close ally of Indra. 644.
Having paid homage to Indra and Viṣṇu with these three verses, a man, becoming pure and holding fuel in his hand, should perform worship every day.
Dharma, intelligence, wealth, sons, health, and spiritual luster.
One attains the supreme station, which is eternal and of the nature of light.
Display your power like a wide-spreading net; go forth like a king with his host, as these [men] are ours.
Following our swift course with the wooden vessel, pierce the Rākṣasas with your most burning shafts.
O you who blaze forth, boldly touch those flames of yours that fly swiftly; pursue them with daring.
O Agni, with your tongue of flame, cast forth your heats like winged insects; let loose your firebrands in every direction.

Discharge your arrows, become the swiftest one, and protect the life of this people. O Agni, let no affliction from you reach him who is far away today, nor him who is near. Let no distress overcome us.
Arise, O Agni! Spread yourself out against him; burn him up with your sharp weapon, O Mitra-like one—him who has acted as an enemy toward us, even though we were close to him.
Burn him down like dry wood.
Arise, O Agni, and having penetrated [the truth], reveal to us the divine things.
Render the followers of the sorcerers unstable; crush their kin and those who are not kin.
He, the youngest, knows your good intention; he has granted a path for your prayer.
For him, the noble one, the steward of wealth has shone forth all auspicious days and splendors.
May he who has brought you with oblation and hymns be fortunate and a liberal giver; may there be no distress for him.
He desires to please him in his own life and in his home; for him, that sacrificial session with all its auspicious days is well-established.
I worship your benevolence; let the sound be directed hitherward, and may this cow cross over the waters.
May my own horses and fine chariots win for me; may they maintain my kṣatriya powers day after day.
May many a man here seek you as a wife; may he shine upon you at night, following after you through the days.
Playing with you, well-disposed toward the living, those men of noble spirit have stood firm in their glory;
he who possesses fine horses and fine gold, who approaches us with a chariot laden with wealth.
You are his protector and his friend; may those human Ādityas take pleasure in him.
I celebrate our kinship with words; let that not depart from the father Gotama. O Hotṛ, most youthful and of noble power, take heed of this our speech, for we are not deficient. 657.
The covers are sleepless-born and very gracious; the wolves are unwearied and have not been stirred to harm.
O Agni, may those [flames] of yours, which have been accumulated through the practice of the *tejas* path, protect us here. || 658 ||
O Agni, those evildoers who go against me—you, seeing [the truth], have protected them from misfortune.
The All-Knowing One protected those whom he had made; though they desired to deceive him, the seekers of power could not deceive him.
Blessed by you with food, protected by you, may we, through your guidance, attain spoils of war.
Both of you possess the noble path that leads to the arising of the good. || 660 ||
Drive away the female camel, drive away the male camel; and so, O Agni, may we offer fuel to you.
Accept the hymn being recited.
Protect us here from the sorcerers, from the malicious ones, and from the reviler, O you who are great as a friend and free from reproach. 661.
I offer oblations to the slayer of demons, the vigorous one; I approach for protection Mitra, the most extensive.
May Agni, sharpening his weapons and kindled by our rites, protect us from harm by day and by night. 662.
Agni shines with great and radiant light; he makes all things manifest by his majesty.
He overcomes the godless, evil-wishing illusions; he whets his weapons to pierce and strike down the Rakṣasa.
And indeed, the roars of Agni’s sharp-armed [flames] resound in heaven to slay the Rakṣasa.
No one can withstand his splendors; the godless obstructors do not prevail against him.
When a Brahmin is surrounded by robbers, he should recite this hymn;
it shall take away the lives of his enemies, and no fear whatsoever shall arise.
With the Lord of the Field as our ally, we conquer by that very means; having caused us to proclaim [the victory] over cattle and horses, may he be gracious to one such as this. 666.
The twice-born man who, being pure, daily recites this verse while constantly gazing at the sun, obtains an excellent field belonging to the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrapati). || 667 ||
I shall declare the ritual procedure for the Puruṣasūkta, which is concealed within the Tantras. This hymn consists of Anuṣṭubh verses, with its final verse in Triṣṭubh; its deity is [Puruṣa]. (668)

The Puruṣa who is the seed of the universe is remembered as the seer Nārāyaṇa. Having bathed according to the prescribed rule, facing eastward with a purified mind, [one should worship him]. || 669 ||
One should place the first [mudrā] on the left hand and the second on the right hand;
one should place the third on the left foot and the fourth on the right.
The fifth [mudrā] is on the left knee, and the sixth on the right knee;
the seventh is indeed on the left hip, and the eighth on the right hip.
One should place the ninth [syllable] at the region of the navel, the tenth at the heart;
the eleventh at the region of the throat, and the twelfth on the left arm.
One should place the thirteenth [syllable] on the right arm, the fourteenth on the region of the face, the fifteenth on the two eyes,
and the sixteenth on the head.
Having thus performed the rite of placement (nyāsa), one should thereafter perform the worship.
In the waters, in the fire, in the heart, in the sun, on the sacrificial mound, and in images. || 674 ||

The fitness for the perfect worship of Hari is declared in these six [elements]. Since water is His abode, therefore Hari is always present within them. For those engaged in ritual action, Viṣṇu resides in the fire; for yogis, Hari resides in the heart. (675)
For the wise, Hari is the sun; for those who have cultivated their selves upon the bare ground, he is the sacrificial altar.
For those of small intellect, these [images] are remembered as being of six types. || 676 ||
There are indeed images of Hari that are both uncrafted and crafted, as well as immobile and mobile; they are both lifeless and endowed with life.
Listen, O Goddess, I shall describe their characteristics in due order. It is of two kinds, both being unartificial; the Śālagrāma is exceedingly purifying. (678)
In its absence, the discus of Dvārakā is likewise purifying. (p. 279) These ten artificial [liṅgas] are proclaimed; they are superior in descending order from the first to the last. || 679 ||
The first may be fashioned from jewels, and it may also be made of gold, silver, copper, brass, crystal, red lead, wood, or clay; and these are described in order as having various forms. || 680 ||
For those in the form of sacred fields are indeed immovable, like Haridvāra and Gayā; whereas those images which have been fashioned by deities are both movable and immovable.
Jagannātha, Veṅkaṭeśa, Pāṇḍurābhra, and others—these are living Brahmins; the Pippala tree is considered lifeless. || 682 ||
Having first performed the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa) upon one's own body and upon the deities.
Having assigned the limbs [of the body] to the syllables of the Gāyatrī, one should worship the imperishable Viṣṇu.

One should invoke the deity with the first verse of the *Puruṣasūkta*— beginning with "Oṃ, the Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet," and so forth, according to the sixteen Vedic verses recited as such.
Among those, the invocation is performed with the first verse, the seating with the second verse, and so on, following the sequence stated in the root text.
They perform the worship of the Blessed One Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person.
One should offer a seat with the second [verse] and offer water for the feet with the third.
The *arghya* should be offered with the fourth [mantra], the water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamanīyaka*) with the fifth; one should perform the bath with the sixth, and the clothing with the seventh.
On the eighth day, the sacred thread (yajñopavīta) should be offered; on the ninth, unguents (anulepana); on the tenth, flowers (puṣpa);
and on the eleventh, incense (dhūpaka).
On the twelfth day one should offer a lamp; on the thirteenth, an offering of food (naivedya); on the fourteenth, a prostration;
and on the fifteenth, a circumambulation. || 687 ||

One should offer water for sipping (ācamanīya) after the bath, the clothing, and the food offering; furthermore, one should perform the final dedication with a sixteen-fold offering according to one's capacity.
Then one should perform circumambulation and, with a concentrated mind, perform recitation; having recited the hymn according to one's ability, one should offer it to him. || 689 ||
To the right side of the deity, there should be either a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or a leveled mound (sthaṇḍila).
One should perform [the rite] with the first [mantra], but with the second, the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa).
With the third [verse] he should place the fire, and with the fourth he should kindle it.
With the fifth [verse], the cooking of the clarified butter (ājya) and likewise the cooking of the sacrificial porridge (caru) are performed. || 691 ||
With the sixth [syllable] alone, one should fashion the fire-drill and the lotus seat.
One should meditate upon the Lord of the Gods, whose splendor is equal to the fire of cosmic destruction.
Then one should offer incense, flowers, and the smoke and light of lamps; having obtained permission, one should then perform the rites beginning with the seventh day in their proper sequence.

First, one who has performed the ritual sprinkling should offer as many fuel-sticks as there were [previously]; then one should offer with clarified butter, and after that again with the sacrificial oblation (caru). || 694 ||
Having offered the oblation in this manner, he should then take leave of him in due order.
One should recite the hymn of praise in the presence of that blessed Agni. || 695 ||
Victory to you, O lotus-eyed one; salutations to you, O creator of the universe! Salutations to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, Great Being, Primordial One.
The pair of your feet is the common presiding deity for both gods and dānavas; I always go to you for refuge. (697)
You alone are the creator of the world and likewise its destroyer; you are unmanifest, the witness, devoid of qualities, yet veiled by Māyā.
Having obtained refuge in you alone, the wise cross over the terrible ocean of saṃsāra, which is a vessel for endless afflictions. || 699 ||
You have no form, nor appearance, nor weapons, nor abode; nevertheless, you manifest in the form of a person for the sake of your devotees.
O Lord, you are not beyond the perception of anyone, yet you are not perceived by anyone either;
and for no one is you to be attained through effort, except through devotion.
The cause of all effects is the first; the object of speech is the supreme. Yogis know that to be the ultimate perfection and the highest state.
"I am afraid, O Lord of Gods, in this world of great terror; protect me, O Lotus-eyed One, for I do not know the supreme state. (703)
O Acyuta, at all times and in all directions, and even within my own body,
a great fear has come upon me and persists.
Apart from your lotus feet, there is nothing else for me even in future births—neither this realization that has been attained, nor this which is devoid of knowledge. (705)
"O Lord, may there never be a depletion of this [merit] for me even in another birth; even if I am born into a miserable state, may my heart's desire remain fixed upon you. (706)
If one does not experience destruction [of the self], then from that state one is always a doer of good deeds; one should desire only the feet of Viṣṇu throughout all births.
This hymn of Puruṣa, dedicated to Hari, is pure, auspicious, and brings renown.
This knowledge of the self is meritorious; this knowledge of yoga is supreme.
Having thus praised the bearer of oblations, one should thereafter dismiss him;
by this very act, a person becomes free from sin. (709)

Having understood [the procedure] as before, one should commence its application upon mercury (pārada). When it is the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) on an auspicious weekday during the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), [one should begin]. || 710 ||
The husband and wife should observe a fast in the temple of the gods; on the twelfth day, for one desiring a son, they should prepare a Vaiṣṇava sacrificial oblation (caru).
Having properly worshipped Janārdana with sixteen Ṛg-verses,
one desiring a son should cause him to consume the sacrificial oblation (caru) while reciting the Puruṣasūkta.
He shall indeed obtain a Vaiṣṇava son who is capable of perpetuating the lineage without delay. He should properly offer twelve *carus* on twelve twelfth lunar days (*dvādaśīs*) with milk.
[First, he should offer that *caru* with the Puruṣasūkta; the remainder the woman should eat. || 713 ||
He who offers oblations indeed goes to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
And Keśava is to be worshipped in succession during the months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa.
Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, Govinda, and Viṣṇu; Madhusūdana is mentioned, as well as Trivikrama and Vāmana; Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, and Gadādhara. || 715 ||
Having performed worship, one should then recite the hymn one hundred and eight times.
And one should perform the fire-oblation as before; thus one shall attain all desires.
To her who is childless, whose sons have died, or who has given birth only to daughters—I shall now declare the means by which she may obtain a virtuous son. (717)
One should offer one hundred and eight fuel-sticks of the *aśvattha* tree, each accompanied by a verse (*ṛc*), along with clarified butter;
then one should worship the Fire-god.
Having worshipped Viṣṇu once again, one should perform an oblation of ghee; being pure and restrained in speech, one should perform it one hundred and eight times every day.
Having set aside the ghee for the *sampāta* offering, he should give it to his wife to consume;
she, having paid homage to Viṣṇu, her husband, should eat it. || 720 ||
Having properly gratified the twice-born and received their blessings, he should enter his home; by performing this at least seven times, she will certainly become pregnant. (721)
One should dwell constantly in the forest and perform ablutions three times a day.
One should recite this hymn one hundred and eight times during the three periods of the day.
For one month he should subsist on fruit, and for one month he should satisfy [the ancestors] with water.
One should constantly worship the Sun with this mantra; having offered a thousand oblations of clarified butter, one should recite it for three years every day.
Devoted to Him, with his mind fixed on Him, disciplined, and having no other object of devotion, he beheld that very Lord Nārāyaṇa, free from all affliction, after ten years.
Now I shall describe the means for the liberation while living (jīvanmukti) of householders:
he who is devoted to his own duty, whose conduct is righteous, and who is pure in his vows. || 725 ||
Having abandoned sleep at midnight, having become pure, and restrained in speech;
When the worlds are fast asleep, the knower of yoga should practice yoga.
Having prepared a seat in a level place, free from wind and devoid of noise, and having placed the left foot upon the right knee and the right foot upon the left knee,
remaining upright and fixing his gaze on the tip of his own nose, he should recite the syllable *oṃ* together with his mind.

Having drawn in the breath, one should fill the abdomen; immediately thereafter, one should lead the breath from the navel-center to the heart, then to the chest, then bringing it to the throat, and then having placed it between the eyebrows,
one should lead it to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) very slowly with the mind fixed on the syllable Om.

One should recite [the mantra] for as long as one is able to restrain the vital breaths (prāṇas). Then, having slowly released the breaths again and again, through practice according to the aforementioned method, the unstruck sound (anāhata-śabda) is manifested tenfold.

Furthermore, if even a person bound by all sins attains the Supreme Brahman through the recitation of the syllable *Oṃ* in the heart and mind, then what need is there to mention the attainment of that state for those who have performed meritorious deeds? [One should place] the right foot upon the knee.
Then he should cause [them] to lie down. || 727 ||
Having drawn back the right foot, he places it upon the left knee.
With palms joined in reverence, composed, and with eyes closed in yoga. || 728 ||
One should contemplate "Oṃ" thus within one's own heart without hesitation; there, one should concentrate the self, as well as the senses and the mind. (729)
One would not awaken, nor would one see, hear, or perceive anything else.
Having restrained the vital breaths while seated, one should then contemplate with an undisturbed mind.
Then, having caused the mind to go to the navel together with the breath itself, |||
And thus breathing repeatedly, one whose mind is fixed on that should practice yoga.
One should lead the mind into the heart so that it neither sees nor hears; then one should lead that consciousness upward from the heart.
The collarbones, the mouth, the two nostrils, the two eyes, and the two eyebrows are equal [in measure]. The supreme place is in the middle of the eyebrows; therein lies the path of its gateway.
Having held it at the region of the forehead, one should then lead it to the head; one should exhale at the proper time, and then exhale again from the navel. || 734 ||
This is declared to be the supreme abode of Brahman, the Supreme Self;
thus disciplined, one attains the Great Soul, the Self. (735)
Whether one is thus a doer of good deeds and pure, or a doer of evil, by perceiving the Supreme Brahman and knowing the goal, one becomes pure. || 736 ||
Even one who is bound by all sins, if he recites [the mantra] with self-restraint from beginning to end, shall attain the supreme goal even after conquering the Equal One (Viṣṇu).

One should always perform concentration (*dhāraṇā*) separately according to that same rule; one should fix [the mind] upon the sun, fire, the moon, or the tops of trees, or on a mountain peak, in the ocean, or wherever the mind finds delight. (738)

One should not, under any circumstances, maintain a sense of existence upon encountering sense objects; one should recognize that there is much suffering in this process of maintenance which culminates in destruction.
One who has fallen from yoga is born into a pure family of righteous people; by the power of such recitation, one attains Brahman at the crown of the head. || 740 ||
Then, with his head, the yogi should lead the supreme light upward along the path of the stars;
having attained the Lord of Yoga, who is beyond duality and higher than the highest.
Devoted to Hari, one should perceive the Self by means of the Self everywhere;
having bathed, one should also mutter the vowels—this is the supreme purifier. || 742 ||

Even one joined with great sins may become virtuous through time; thereafter, being constantly devoted to that [practice], truthful in speech and free from malice, a Brahmin reciting that Ṛc will, in time, become virtuous. (743)
Whatever desire one recites that verse for, that desire shall always be fulfilled for the person of faith who performs it. (744)
Whether one performs a fire sacrifice (homa), or recitation (jāpya), or an unsurpassed offering (upahāra), whatever desire one has, its fulfillment arises thereby. || 745 ||
The supreme goal, attainable through knowledge, is established as the all-pervading reality.
Through this statement, with the utmost effort, one attains the eternal Brahman.
The Sahasraśīrṣa Sūkta, moreover, bestows the fruit of all desires.
He who possesses a body that is the womb of the Vedas is indeed remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, and Parjanya are well-established within this hymn. By remaining here, one shall behold after death the entire world, both stationary and moving. || 748 ||
Even if one does not attain [the desired goal], one should not abandon devotion; for the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, is heard to be compassionate toward his devotees. || 749 ||
For the sake of worshipping that deity, he [should offer] wild flowers gathered by himself.
One should offer the sacrificial porridge (caru) every day according to the rules for forest-dwellers (āraṇyaka).
One should offer the oblation with the mantra "Nārāyaṇāya svāhā"; by doing so, he bestows divine vision upon the hotṛ priest there, up to a thousand times.
Alternatively, one may offer a thousand carus with a single mantra; having performed that oblation, one obtains the fruit of all desired wishes.

Endowed with a full human lifespan, he shall wander the earth as a perfected being (siddha). There are millions of hymns, but this one is supremely dear to Him by whom Hari—the Lord of all, who is affectionate toward His devotees—is sung. (752)

Nārāyaṇa, who dwells in the center of the solar disc, seated upon a lotus throne, adorned with armlets, shark-shaped earrings, a crown, and necklaces, possessing a golden body and bearing the conch and the discus— He should always be meditated upon. (753)
But he who, having prostrated before the venerable feet of Nārāyaṇa, recites this very hymn alone, through that recitation of the Supreme Eternal One,
attains the abode of Viṣṇu, which is free from old age and death. (754)
The wise worship Hari eternally with oblations in the fire, with flowers in the water, with meditation in the heart,
and with silent recitation within the solar orb.
The bilva leaf, the śamī leaf, and the leaf of the bhṛṅgarāja plant.
And the leaves of *mālatī* and *kuśa* grass bring immediate satisfaction to Hari. || 756 ||
Whatever is not attainable through mere mental meditation is attained through the grace of the Discus-wielding God of gods.

With leaves, flowers, fruits, and water—whether obtained through trade or always given by the virtuous—one should exert effort toward liberation in that Ancient Person who is accessible solely through devotion; why is such effort not made? (758)
Thus, O Goddess, the lords of sages joyfully spoke this procedure for the worship of the image of Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person.
This was for the sake of awakening [beings] to the single path of liberation, and certainly not for the sake of worldly desires.
(759) Those herbs that have Soma as their king, which are spread across the earth—
Impelled by Bṛhaspati, bestow that vigor upon her. || 760 ||
As they fall down from heaven, the plants cry out: "The living man whom we reach shall not come to harm. (761)
Those creepers which hear this, and those which have gone far away— let all of them come together and bestow their power upon this one.
May the digger not suffer harm, nor he for whom I dig you.
May our bipeds and quadrupeds all be free from disease.
The plants converse together with Soma the king: "O King, we shall carry that man across for whom a Brahmin performs [this rite]. (764)
That man who constantly recites [the mantra] only on the festival days for six months [attains the fruit].
The physician shall have the nectar in his hand, while another shall perform the rite for well-being. || 765 ||
Having performed a sacrifice to Rudra in the autumn, one should always recite the mantras of the medicinal herbs; for such a person, diseases do not arise, nor do the five types of indigestion.
Having taken refuge in the medicinal herbs, the Brahmin, being composed, should always recite this hymn seven times over the course of seven nights. (767)
And she should inform them, "Come here from the field of the enemy";
for by sacrificing to Varuṇa in one's own field, one obtains the medicinal herbs belonging to the enemy. || 768 ||
O Bṛhaspati, that which belongs to the enemy, which is glorious and wise among men, surpass it.
"O you who have been born from the Truth (Ṛta), bestow upon us that wonderful wealth which has shone forth through your power.
[769] "One desiring rain should approach Bṛhaspati with controlled diet, provided with an offering of milk-rice (pāyasa) and accompanied by burnt offerings (homa). [770]
Afterwards, a wise man desiring rain should employ this verse;
by paying homage to Parjanya, he obtains auspicious rain. || 771 ||
In the Kali age, for the sake of protecting the Dharma, these Ṛks will appear here and there among various Brahmins in various regions, and indeed other [mantras] as well shall exist upon the earth.
"This reality has been proclaimed here, though hidden in all the tantras. Beyond this, O Goddess, what more is to be said by the gods? Let that be told. (773)
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of Mantras with the Ritual for the Kali Age," in the *Merutantra* composed by Śiva with the approval of the illustrious Mahāmāyā and Mahākāla.
Śrī Viṣṇu said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, you who bestow grace upon your devotees! You are Time for all the worlds, and this supreme power is the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā). || 1 ||
But what mantras and hymns (sūktas) are pleasing to you both? Tell me that, by which there may be both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and indeed no suffering at all.
The illustrious Śiva said:

"O Viṣṇu, that which was asked by you is to be kept secret; it must not be spoken to a twice-born who is a follower of Tantra. Furthermore, while the nature of Tantra is tāmasa, what was asked by you is indeed sāttvika."
Know that Śatarudriya of mine to be the sole abode of enjoyment and liberation, the most excellent among the four Vedas, and the Lord of Mantras and Stotras.
The meters for this [mantra] are the Anuṣṭubh and others; its sage is considered to be Aghora;
its deity is Rudra, Āditya, and the Supreme Puruṣa. || 5 ||
That which is called your *rudraśikhā* is the head in this [mantra] "maha"; the *sahasrāṇi* is on the forehead, and the *haṃsa-ṛk* is between the eyebrows.
O Rudra, that auspicious form of yours which is not terrible and does not cause suffering—O Lord of the Mountain, look upon us with that most peaceful form! 7.
Upon this great ocean, in the intermediate space, you dwell; we brandish our weapons at them a thousand leagues away. 8.
Those thousands upon thousands of Rudras who dwell upon the earth—to them we extend our bows a thousand leagues away. || 9 ||
Ha gūṃ saḥ; the pure-dwelling Vasu, the dweller in the intermediate space, the Hotṛ priest.
The guest seated at the altar, dwelling in the house. 10.

Tryambaka: "We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity; may I be liberated from death like a cucumber from its stem, but not from immortality. And with the mantra *namaḥ* (salutation), he should worship the two eyes; with *stutyāya* (to the one worthy of praise), the two ears; with *mā nastoke* (do not harm our offspring), the nose; and with *avatatya*, the mouth.
One should place [the syllables]. || 11 ||
Homage to the one worthy of praise and to the one who brings prosperity; homage to the one of the furrow and to the one of the irrigation channel.
Homage to the one belonging to the stream and to the one belonging to the lake; homage to the one belonging to the river and to the one belonging to the pond.
O Rudra, do not harm our children or our grandchildren, nor our life-span, nor our cattle, nor our horses.
Do not slay our heroic men who are full of wrath; bearing oblations, we invoke you forever. 13.
O thousand-eyed one, wielder of the hundred quivers, having drawn your bow and sharpened the points of your arrows, be auspicious and well-disposed toward us. 14.
One should place two Nīlagrīvas sequentially on the neck and the vicinity of the neck; "namaste" and "ayā te" are the two *hetis* (weapons) to be placed on the arms and the forearms. || 15 ||
Those blue-necked, white-throated Śarvas who roam upon the earth below—to them we unbend our bows at a distance of a thousand yojanas. 16.
The Rudras with blue necks and white throats have taken refuge in the sky;
we unbend their bows at a distance of a thousand yojanas. 17.
Salutations to you, the weapon that is unstrung yet bold; salutations to both your arms, and salutations to your bow. 18.
That missile which was in your hand, O most bountiful one, and that bow of yours—
With that [strength], which is all-pervading and free from disease, do thou protect us on every side.
Those who wander among sacred fords, carrying spears in their hands and wearing quivers—we unstring their bows at a distance of a thousand yojanas. || 20 ||
One should place this Ṛc upon the fingers of both hands, beginning with the thumbs; one should then place these five mantras, beginning with Sadyojāta, upon the heart.
Homage to you, O Kirikas, the hearts of the gods; homage to those who are scattered abroad, homage to those who search out, homage to those who have been driven forth. 22.
One should assign "Salutation to the Gaṇas" on the back, and "Salutation to Hiraṇyabāhu" on the sides; likewise, one should assign "Salutation to the Takṣas" on the two flanks. || 23 ||
Homage to you, the hosts, and to you, the lords of the hosts; homage to you, the troops, and to you, the lords of the troops. Homage to you, the clever ones, and to you, the lords of the clever;
homage to you, the multiformed, and to you, the all-formed. 24.

Homage to him of the golden arms, the leader of armies, and the lord of the quarters; homage! Homage to the trees with greenish-yellow hair, the lord of animals; homage! Homage to the one tawny as young grass, the radiant one, the lord of the plains; homage! Homage to the one with greenish-yellow hair who wears the sacred thread!
Salutations, salutations to the Lord of the Nourished; salutations to the one who dwells in the waters. || 25 ||

Salutations to the carpenters and to you, the chariot-makers; salutations to the potters and to you, the smiths; salutations to the Niṣādas and to you, the Puñjiṣṭhas; salutations to the dog-keepers and to you, the hunters. || 26 ||
The *vijyā* mantra is on the belly; the *hiraṇyagarbhaka* is at the navel; the *miḍhuṣṭama* is on the hips; and those [mantras] belonging to the beings are on the secret parts. (p. 286) 27.
The bow has lost its string, O Kapardin; he is free from arrows, though he was once an arrow-bearer.
His arrows have vanished, and his quiver has become empty.
In the beginning, Hiraṇyagarbha arose; once born, he was the sole lord of all that exists.
Whoever always supports the earth and this heaven—to which god shall we offer worship with our oblation?

O most bountiful one, O most auspicious one, be gracious and well-disposed toward us. Having placed your weapon upon the highest tree and wearing a skin as your garment, come hither; bearing the Pināka bow, do not be heedless. 30.
Those who are the lords of beings, devoid of locks of hair, yet wearing matted locks;
We bow to those whose bows extend for a thousand yojanas. || 31 ||
The five mantras beginning with *jātavedase*, joined with the head-mantra (*śiras*), [are placed] on the *apānaka*; one should place *mā no mahāntam* on the thighs and *eṣa te* on the knees.

Let us press the Soma for Jātavedas; he shall lay low the wealth of those who act with enmity. May Agni carry us across all difficulties, as one crosses rivers with a boat, beyond all misfortunes. 33.

May that Indra, the bull with his bull-like powers, the fulfiller of desires, the sovereign ruler of heaven and earth, whose strength is true, who is to be invoked in the battles—may he, accompanied by the Maruts, be our protection. 34.
He whose course is unassailable like that of the sun, who possesses the strength of a slayer of Vṛtra in every battle.
May Indra, the most excellent bull, accompanied by his own friends and his Maruts, be our protection with his aids.
Whose paths, like those of the seed of heaven, go forth encompassed by power as they pour down.
May Indra, who overcomes hatred, who is victorious through his manly deeds, and who is accompanied by the Maruts, be our protection with his aids.
Thus, being the best of the Aṅgirasas, he became the bull among the bulls, a friend to his friends.
May Indra, the eldest, accompanied by the Maruts, together with the fires, the Ṛg-verses, and the paths, be our protection.
Do not harm our great ones, nor our small ones; do not harm our growing ones, nor our grown ones.
Do not slay our father, nor our mother; O Rudra, do not injure our dear bodies. 38.

O Rudras, come hither with the spring; pass beyond the Mūjavat mountains. With bows unstrung, carrying your Pināka staffs, clad in skins and wearing serpents as ornaments, come as auspicious ones. 39.
And [he placed] *sagūṃsṛṣṭa* on the two calves, *jijjaṅghya* on the two shanks, and *viśvambhūta* on the two ankles;
*ye pathāṃ* on the two feet, and *pathiraṅghryaḥ* and *adhyavocaḥ* on the armor (*varmaka*). || 40 ||

O Bṛhaspati, you who conquer the gathered hosts, whose arms are swift, who hold the bow aloft, and who shoot with far-reaching arrows— fly around as the charioteer of the gods, slaying the Rākṣasas and driving away the enemies. All that exists, the world, the friend, whatever has been born and whatever is being born in manifold ways— [all this do you protect].
For this entire world is Rudra; let there be homage to that Rudra. || 42 ||
Those who protect the paths on the journey, the sons of Ilabrida, who fight for their own lives.
We stretch their bows to a length of a thousand yojanas. || 43 ||
The first divine physician has spoken as the one who speaks over [the patient];
crushing all serpents and driving away all sorceresses who move upon the earth. 44.
One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) on the third eye with "upavartmane 'mo 'vilmi" and "namo astu ca netrayoḥ," and then with "pramuñca dhanvanaḥ" on the two eyes. || 45 ||

Homage to the one with the helmet and to the one with the armor; homage to the one clad in mail and to the one who possesses a chariot-shield. Homage to the one renowned and to the one with a renowned army; homage to the one who is the drum and to the one who is the striker. 46.
Homage be to the blue-throated one, the thousand-eyed, the bounteous giver; and also to those who belong to him.
Homage to those who have made beings free from slaughter. || 47 ||
Unstring the bowstring from both ends of your bow. O Blessed One, cast away those arrows that are in your hand. 48.
Thus, the first placement (nyāsa) of the twenty-six limbs has been described. Then, one should perform the binding of the directions (digbandhana) with the mantra "ya etāvantaḥ. || 49 ||
The Rudras, possessing great power and vast forms, have spread themselves out through the quarters of space.
We stretch their bows to a distance of a thousand yojanas. || 50 ||
Indeed, he has acquired the authority for the recitation of all mantras.
One who performs this nyāsa does not perish even in fire.
*Tāra* is *oṃ*. The ten-syllable mantra is proclaimed as: *namo bhagavate rudrāya*. With this, one should perform the salutation at the conclusion of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). || 52 ||
Thereafter, one should perform the ritual placement (*varṇanyāsa*) of the syllables of this very mantra: *Oṃ* on the head; *na* on the nose; *mo* on the forehead;
*mā* on the face; *le* on the throat; *ga* on the heart; *va* on the right hand; *te* on the left hand; *ru* on the navel; *drā* on the two feet; *ya* on the two feet. Thus.
The placement of the mantra-syllables: [on] the nose, the forehead, the mouth, the throat, and likewise the heart.
In the right hand, the left hand, the navel, and likewise in both feet. || 54 ||
One shall become authorized for all mantras through this second nyāsa;
now the third nyāsa is also proclaimed here—listen to it. (55)
In this third nyāsa, the verses beginning with Sadyojāta are to be placed on the feet, heart, mouth, and head; through this nyāsa, the Śaiva splendor shall enter [the practitioner].

One should utter "I am that Haṃsa" and contemplate it likewise with the intellect; then, one should install the guardians of the eight directions in their respective quarters with their respective mantras.
I call upon Indra, the protector, Indra, the helper; I call again and again upon the hero Indra, who is easily invoked.
I invoke Śakra, the much-invoked Indra; may Indra, the giver of joy, bestow well-being upon us.
O Agni, you who know, may you remove from us the wrath of the divine Varuṇa.
O most excellent sacrificer, best of bearers, shining brightly, release from us all those who hate us and all enmities. 59.
May he make our path auspicious and free from fear, on whichever lunar mansion King Yama goes.
Upon him the gods poured the consecration; we worship that wonderful power of his with this oblation. (60)
Seeking him who does not breathe out and does not sacrifice, follow after that thief with your weapon.
"May you desire someone other than us; O Goddess Nirṛti, let there be homage to you! || 61 ||
I approach those principles, worshipping with sacred prayer; the sacrificer, with oblations, prays for them.
O Varuṇa, be mindful here without being indolent; do not steal away our wide-reaching life.
O Vāyu, come to our sacrifice with your teams of horses by the hundreds and by the thousands for this rite; rejoice at this libation. Do you all protect us evermore with blessings.
Not so. || 63 ||
O Vaya Gūṃ, abiding in your Soma-vow and maintaining our minds within our bodies, may we, possessing progeny, remain united with you. || 64 ||
We invoke that Īśāna, the lord of the moving and the stationary world, who quickens the intellect.
May Pūṣan, the undeceived guardian who watches over our wealth, be with us for our well-being.
May the Rudras, the liberal ones, and the mountains be in harmony with us at the invocation during the slaying of Vṛtra.
May the gods, with Indra as their chief, protect us—those for whom the thunderbolt has been established, who recite and praise.

With this [mantra], one should pay homage both above and upon the surface of the earth. One should perform [this] with the Earth-mantra (dharā-mantra), and thus he becomes freed from sin: "O Earth, be propitious to us, free from thorns, providing a dwelling; grant us wide protection, O Goddess, you who are pure and free from sorrow. (RV 1.22.15)
Upon seeing one who possesses the ritual placement (nyāsa), disturbances such as ghosts, thieves, and other calamities [do not arise] here.
Unable to endure him as he blazed forth, they fled to a great distance.

One should assign *manojyotis* to the secret place, and likewise *abodhyagni* to the belly; having assigned the head to the heart, one should likewise assign the vital points (*marmāṇi*) to the mouth. (69)
May the light of the mind enjoy the clarified butter; may it restore the interrupted sacrifice and make it whole.
Those dawns which were seen at their setting, those I join together with oblation and praise.
Agni has been awakened by the fuel of men, as one goes toward the approaching dawn like a milch-cow.
Like great birds rising up to the branch, the rays have sent forth light toward the sky.
The gods have generated from their own mouths Agni Vaiśvānara, the head of heaven, the steward of earth,
born of Truth— the sage, the sovereign, the guest of men, the vessel for the sacrificial seat. 72.
I cover your vital organs with armor; may King Soma clothe you with immortality.
May Varuṇa make your chest broader; may the gods rejoice in you as you conquer. 73.
The fourth Nyāsa is declared to be *jātavedas* on the head. || 74 ||
Whether you are Jātavedas, or Pāvaka, or Vaiśvānara, or Vaidyuta—grant welfare to all creatures and to the sacrificer; bestowing the world, strength, and nourishment, descend into this place.

The *Śivasaṃkalpa* is for the heart, the *Puruṣasūkta* for the head; the verse beginning with "From the waters was born" (*adbhyaḥ saṃbhūtaḥ*) is considered the armor (*varman*), and the *Pratiratha* hymn is likewise regarded as such. || 76 ||

Drawn forth from the waters and from the essence of the earth, he came into being in the beginning from Viśvakarman. Tvaṣṭṛ, fashioning his form, entered him; that was the entire birthplace of the Puruṣa in the beginning. 77.
I know this great Puruṣa, resplendent like the sun, beyond the darkness.
Knowing Him alone, one becomes immortal in this very world; there is no other path for proceeding.
Prajāpati moves within the womb; being born, he is manifested in many ways. The wise perceive his source; the seers seek the station of the rays of light.
To him who shines upon the gods, who is the domestic priest of the gods, who was born before the gods—to that radiant one belonging to Brahman, let there be homage! || 80 ||
Generating splendor for the Brahmin, the gods spoke thus in the beginning: "The gods shall be under the command of that man who knows the Brahmin in this manner. (81)
Śrī and Lakṣmī are your two wives; day and night are your two sides; the stars are your form;
the Aśvins are your open mouth. Bestowing [blessings], bestow them upon me; bestow the whole world upon me. 82.
The Śatarudriya shall be the weapon; now the five-limbed [rite] is described. This fifth [limb], known as Nyāsa, is proclaimed as the accomplisher of all desired goals. || 83 ||
You are Rudra of Agni at the onset; you rule over the host of the Maruts, the great heaven, and the sacrificial power.
You travel with the ruddy winds for the welfare of the household; and as Pūṣan, you yourself protect us. 84.
O gods, take your place among the gods; as the first, take your place among the second. As the second, take your place among the third; as the third, take your place among the fourth. 85.
Take refuge in the fourth [stages] within the fifth; take refuge in the fifth within the sixth. Take refuge in the sixth within the seventh;
take refuge in the seventh within the eighth. 86.
Take refuge in the eighth [stages] within the ninth; take refuge in the ninth within the tenth.
Take your stand, you who are ten, upon those who are eleven; take your stand, you who are eleven, upon those who are twelve;
take your stand, you who are twelve, upon those who are thirteen; take your stand, you who are fourteen, upon those who are fifteen;
take your stand, you who are fifteen, upon those who are sixteen. Take your stand!
The sixteen [syllables] are in the seventeen [syllables]. || 88 ||
Take refuge in the seventeen; take refuge in the eighteen. Take refuge in the eighteen;
take refuge in the nineteen. Take refuge in the nineteen; take refuge in the twenty. Take refuge in the twenty; take refuge in the twenty-one. 89.

Take refuge in those who have twenty-one qualities by relying on those with twenty-two; take refuge in those who have twenty-two qualities by relying on those with twenty-three. Take refuge in those who have twenty-three qualities by relying on those with twenty-four; take refuge in those who have twenty-four qualities by relying on those with twenty-five.
gūṃ in the Śeṣas. || 90 ||
Take refuge in those with five super-knowledges; take refuge in those with six super-knowledges, O you who possess three super-knowledges!
Take refuge in those with seven super-knowledges; take refuge in those with eight super-knowledges, O you who possess seven super-knowledges! Take refuge in those with eight super-knowledges.
In twenty-nine [verses]. || 91 ||
Take refuge in the twenty-nine within the thirty; take refuge in the thirty within the thirty-one. Take refuge in the thirty-one within the thirty-two;
take refuge in the thirty-two within the thirty-three. 92.
Take refuge, O gods, you who are thrice eleven and thrice thirty-three;

may you be on our side. May those whose path is upward and whose essence is upward be with us. Whatever desire I have for which I offer this oblation, may that be fulfilled for me; may we be masters of riches.
Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā. || 93 ||

Having thus performed the placement of the five limbs (pañcāṅganyāsa), one should bow to Śiva with the eight limbs (aṣṭāṅga). Then, having offered the recitation (japa) to Rudra, one should perform the ritual attendance (upasthāna) once again.
In the beginning, Hiraṇyagarbha arose; once born, he was the sole lord of all that exists.
He who always supports this earth and this heaven—to which god shall we offer worship with our oblation?
By his greatness, through his breathing and his blinking, the one Indra became the king of the world;
under whose control are his bipeds and quadrupeds—to which god shall we offer worship with oblation? 96.
The knowledge of Brahman, born in the beginning, from the east, from the boundless expanse, Vena has perceived you, the radiant ones.
The heights of heaven are his foundations; he has disclosed the womb of both the existent and the non-existent.
May the great sky and the earth sprinkle this sacrifice for us; may they fill us with nourishments.

Cause the earth and the sky to resound; let the world, established in many places, take heed of you. O drum, in harmony with Indra and the gods, drive the enemies far, even to the furthest distance. 99.
O Agni, lead us by a good path, you who know all divine ways, away from those who are not our kin.
Drive away from us the crooked sin; we shall offer you the most abundant speech of homage.
O Agni, with that body of yours which is worthy of sacrifice, come and ascend to yourself. Creating for this man many noble riches, become the sacrifice and sit upon the sacrifice in your own womb.

O Jātavedas, being born, you have become [the light] as it were; Svāhā! To Agni with oblations rich in clarified butter. With those immeasurable days of ours, O Agni, protect us with a hundred fortresses made of iron. 102.
Sit upon this seat of Yama, in harmony with us, together with the Aṅgiras and the Fathers.
May the mantras recited by the sages bring you hither; O King, rejoice in this oblation.
Having thus performed the ritual attendance before the deity, one should practice the yoga of the deities: "May Īśa abide in the nose, and the Moon and Sun in the eyes. (104)
May the Aśvins also abide in my ears, and the Rudras in my penis;
may the Ādityas abide in my head, and Mahādeva be situated upon my crown. || 105 ||
May Vāsudeva be at the crest-lock and Pinākin at the back;
may Śailī stand in front, and Śiva and Śaṅkara on both sides. (106)
And on all sides there is wind, and beyond that, on all sides, is the exterior.
And let garlands of flames of fire stand before me in great numbers.
"May all my deities abide in all my limbs. Having said, "Abide in me," one should mentally offer the phenomenal world (prapañca) as an oblation. || 108 ||
Fire is established in my speech, speech in my heart, the heart in me, and I in the immortal Brahman. || 109 ||
The wind is established in my breath; the breath is in the heart; the heart is in me; I am in the immortal; the immortal is in Brahman. || 110 ||
The sun is established in my eye; the eye is in the heart; the heart is in me; I am in the immortal; the immortal is in Brahman. || 111 ||
The moon has taken refuge in my mind; the mind in the heart; the heart in me; I in the immortal; and the immortal in Brahman. || 112 ||
The quarters of space are supported by my ears; the ears are in the heart; the heart is in me; I am in the Immortal; and the Immortal is in Brahman. || 113 ||
The waters are supported in my semen; the semen is in the heart; the heart is in me; I am in the immortal; the immortal is in Brahman. || 114 ||
The earth is supported by my body; the body is hidden within the heart; the heart is in me; I am in the immortal; and the immortal is in Brahman. || 115 ||
The herbs and trees are established in my body hairs; the body hairs are in the heart, the heart is in me;
I am in the Immortal, and the Immortal is in Brahman. 116.
Indra is established in my strength; strength is hidden in my heart; the heart is in me; I am in the immortal; the immortal is in Brahman. || 117 ||
Parjanya is seated upon my head; the head is in the heart; the heart is in me;
I am in the Immortal; the Immortal is in Brahman. || 118 ||
Īśāna is established in my fury; fury is in the heart; the heart is in me; I am in the immortal; the immortal is in Brahman. || 119 ||
The Self is resorted to by me within the self; the self is in the heart; the heart is in me; I am in the Immortal; and the Immortal is in Brahman. || 120 ||
Again has my self returned, again has life returned; again has breath returned, again has intention returned.
Vaiśvānara, having grown strong with his rays, stands within as the guardian of immortality;
having thus performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should then meditate upon the Self as the Lord.
Then one should perform the worship of the *liṅga* according to the method described by the King.
"You have been propitiated by humans, by the Siddhas, and by the gods, asuras, and others; I propitiate you with devotion—accept me, O Maheśvara! (123)

May the bay horses with their well-trained companions bring you here day after day with white, radiant steeds; O Śarva, protect me quickly with winds that are powerful and swift as thought for my oblation. 124.
O Rudras, pass us by with the spring; go beyond the Mūjavat mountains. With bow unstrung and Pināka in hand, clad in a skin and slithering like a serpent, pass us by as one who is auspicious. 125.
He has four horns, three feet, two heads, and seven hands.
Bound in three ways, the bull bellows loudly; the great god has entered into mortals.
Be gracious, O Lord of Gods; be well-disposed, O Śaṅkara. Be peaceful here, and be turned toward me.
O Lord, Sovereign of the entire world, remain present within this *liṅga* with a spirit of affection until the conclusion of the worship. || 128 ||
Then one should perform the consecration with the five nectars in due order;
afterwards, with pure water, and then one should begin the worship. || 129 ||

One should perform the Raudrīndhārā at the end; that is declared to be its ritual procedure. And with the two chapters beginning "Obeisance to you, O Rudra, Agni, Viṣṇu," [the rite is completed]. || 130 ||
This is declared to be the "āvartana," which bestows the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā; indeed, that man who performs the ablution of the āvartana every day [attains that merit]. (131)
The sin incurred on that very day, as well as that born of fate, shall go to destruction.
If that [sin] arising from a previous birth has been exhausted through the performance of the twilight devotions (sandhyāvandana), [then one is purified]. || 132 ||
One recitation is "namaste," and the subsequent section belongs to the other; may they remain for our prosperity, as far as "nā" and likewise the single verse on Viṣṇu. || 133 ||
This is declared to be the Rudriya hymn, which cuts away fierce sins. Whoever performs the consecration of the Linga with this every day— || 134 ||
The sin committed in birth after birth perishes year by year; when the sin accumulated over seven births is destroyed, prosperity increases.
The lineage attains stability and his fame reaches the ends of the quarters. Just as his form appears in mercury (pārada), so too is it seen in water. 136.
The first Rudra is proclaimed by means of the eleven Rudrīs. Those by whom [the Linga] is sprinkled with this do not behold the son of the Sun (Bhāskari). || 137 ||
By these eleven [verses], Mahārudra is proclaimed.
It bestows wealth upon the poor and destroys even the greatest of sins. || 138 ||
The oblation performed with this [mantra] bestows the fruit of the Soma sacrifice;
for one who is otherwise ineligible for initiation, it effects the destruction of his sins. || 139 ||
Atirudra is proclaimed to consist of eleven Mahārudras; by its very sight, it shall be an expiation that removes even the most heinous sins.

Betrayal of trust, treachery toward one's master, unjust punishment, ingratitude, and the destruction of those who have sought refuge despite having the power to protect them—[these are the causes of downfall]. || 141 ||
Even in a cursed land, if one performs penance and commits no improper act, even the five most heinous sins shall be destroyed by Atirudra. || 142 ||
But in whichever branch both of these [recensions] are studied according to their respective traditions;
In that manner, he should cause them to be recited, but he should not have the branch cut into pieces.
Rudra does not belong to that branch in which one might recite the Taittirīya; rather, the branch of the sacrificer is established through the medium of the Brāhmaṇa. 144.
Or else, among the Taittirīyas, no other recensional branch (śākhā) is honored.
An action performed with mixed branches would bring destruction upon the sacrificer. || 145 ||
That fool who, out of greed for wealth, consecrates me for the sake of another should be known as a Cāṇḍāla; he shall remain penniless for seven births. || 146 ||
If my worship is performed with effort by a householder for the sake of wealth through recitation and charity, that shall be the atonement for this portion of Rudra. || 147 ||
A crow becomes a consumer of the property of a Brahmin, while a cock becomes a consumer of the property of Śiva.
The monkey who eats the food of a goddess and the mouse who consumes the wealth of Viṣṇu [are both reborn as such]. (148)
O twice-born ones, likewise, the remains of offerings (nirmālya) from Caṇḍī and Caṇḍīśa, as well as those from Vaināyaka [should not be used].
And they do not accept a gift at any time unless it is given by their own hand. || 149 ||
Those who, in another birth, did not honor me with wealth according to the prescribed rule, yet have now become my worshippers, they indeed bring me unsurpassed happiness. (150)
But he who possesses the *Pariśiṣṭas* along with [the text] in the branch of Rudra—indeed, he [is a true scholar].
One whose own Vedic branch has been lost should indeed recite that very Rudra-text from the Taittirīya.
Now, the Rudrādhyāya accompanied by the application of mantras shall be explained. It must never be recited for one who is unrefined or for a Tantrika. 152.
Oṃ, salutations to you, O Rudra, for your wrath and also for your arrow;
salutations be to your bow and salutations to your two arms. 153.
That arrow of yours which is most auspicious, and that bow of yours which has become auspicious, and that name of yours which is auspicious—O Rudra, with those, grant us mercy. 154.
O Rudra, with that body of yours which is auspicious, non-terrible, and free from causing sin—O Lord of the Mountain, look upon us with that most peaceful form. 155.
O Lord of the Mountain, you carry this arrow in your hand to shoot; O Protector of the Mountain, make it auspicious, do not harm the person or the world. 156.
O Giriśa, we address you with auspicious words. One should offer one hundred thousand oblations of bright cow-ghee here. (157)
Mādhvīka wine, madhuka, honey, and sesame seeds combined with curd.
Whatever task one has in mind, its accomplishment comes to pass. || 158 ||
In the same way, if one performs a thousand oblations on the eleventh day, the spirits that kill children in the village will undoubtedly perish. || 159 ||
The Kumāramāraka demon perishes within twelve days;
furthermore, a fire offering for fifteen days destroys calamities to the kingdom. || 160 ||
Through twenty nights of burnt offerings, the calamities of the country are destroyed; through a month of burnt offerings, the calamities of the earth shall perish. (161)
When a calamity has befallen the cows, one should then perform the oblation in the middle of the cow-pen.

By offering ten thousand oblations of *vaikaṅkata* fuel-sticks—a specific type of thorny tree—peace arises. By performing ten thousand *rudra*-oblations, great peace (*mahāśānti*) will certainly be attained. (162)
So that this entire world of ours may be free from disease and well-disposed toward us.
If one recites it ten thousand times, liberation from the curse occurs; by reciting it one hundred thousand times in the water at dawn during the winter season, one shall become happy. || 163 ||
The first divine physician, the Adhyavaktṛ, has spoken;
may he destroy all serpents and all sorceresses, and drive away those who move upon the earth.
(164) One hundred thousand recitations for the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) should be performed as a fire-oblation (*homa*) with ghee and mustard seeds. (p. 294)
And now, another application for the destruction of diseases is described as follows. || 165 ||
Having consecrated seven mustard seeds with mantras, one should scatter them in the four directions of the afflicted person; thus protection arises from the ten directions.
Having consecrated seven mustard seeds with mantras, one should constantly scatter them in the ten directions while walking on a path; thus, safety is produced on the road. (167)
One possessed by Brahma-rākṣasas, yakṣas, and others, or by piśācas, pretas, and bhūtas, should be struck with mustard seeds consecrated seven times with mantras. || 168 ||
Having first recited the mantra again and again, those seeking wealth depart after taking the wealth—indeed, sandalwood itself—in their hands. 169.

Having stepped upon the crest-lock, one should mutter [the mantra] and strike with white mustard seeds; throughout the entire night, the afflictions caused by Skanda and other planetary spirits are destroyed. || 170 ||
Having thus consecrated it with this mantra, one should administer the medicine prescribed in the scriptures;
for its efficacy at that time will be as it is on any other lunar day. || 171 ||
Having consecrated the water with mantras, one should give it to alleviate the suffering of all sentient beings within existence.
And one should remove [the obstacles] by means of mustard seeds and likewise by blows. || 172 ||
One shall conquer all suffering arising from living beings by wearing the sacred ash. Likewise, one should consecrate a trident with mantras during both day and night. (173)
Having taken a thousand [of them], one should throw them into a lake inhabited by nāgas.
By means of the trident, those serpents, their force destroyed, go to their destruction. || 174 ||
Having consecrated the ashes with mantras, one should place them in a temple frequented by serpents.
One should cast it with the sound of clapping hands; thus there shall be the eradication of serpents.
To him who is copper-colored, ruddy, and tawny, the most auspicious; and to those Rudras who are stationed by the thousands around him in all directions—to them we pray for freedom from wrath. 176.
He who glides along, blue-necked and deep red—him the cowherds have seen, and now they see him clearly;
him all beings have seen, and may he, being seen, grant us mercy. 177.
He worships the Sun at both its rising and setting with these two [verses].
For him, for three years, there shall be inexhaustible wealth—[this is the ellipsis]. || 178 ||
One should bathe Śiva with milk over which a thousand recitations have been performed; by doing so for one year, he becomes pleased, and from the flowing of ghee, there is rain.
One should offer flowers of the linseed plant (atasī) ten thousand times; even one who is independent will become submissive, and the Sun-god shall become a granter of boons. || 180 ||
One should offer into the fire ten thousand oblations of *arka* wood-sacrificial fuel that have been soaked in milk produced from the roots of the *arka* plant;
if one is capable, one should recite the mantra over water.
At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, the Lord Sun releases rain; it does not happen otherwise. For those who devote themselves to these two mantras, he bestows the desired accomplishment. 182.

"Salutation be to the blue-necked one, the thousand-eyed, the bountiful; and likewise to those who are his attendants, let us offer salutations. Having prepared milk-rice with ghee near the edge of the sacrificial mound, (183).
Starting from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
one should daily offer a thousand [coins] consecrated with mantras; one should present a thousand *kārṣāpaṇa* coins to the deity.

From diligent effort, profit arises; there is no doubt when the mantra is perfected. But if it is unperfected, the profit shall be half of that, even from [the sale of] sun-crystals, bulls, and so forth. Furthermore, through offering, there is a gain of one hundred thousand, with a pre-eminent honor.
The fire sacrifice, however, performed with milk-rice and clarified butter, is a practical application that cannot be fully described.
Release the string from both ends of your bow; O Blessed One, cast away those arrows that are in your hand.
O thousand-eyed one, wielder of the hundred quivers, having drawn your bow and blunted the points of your arrows, O Śiva, be well-disposed toward us. 187.
The bow of the one with matted hair is strungless, and his quiver is without arrows;
his arrows have vanished, and his scabbard has become harmless. 188.
That missile which was in your hand, O most bountiful one, and that bow of yours—
With that [protection], which is all-pervading and free from disease, do thou protect us on every side.
Homage be to your weapon, which is unstrung yet bold; homage also to both your arms and to your bow. (190)
May the missile of your bow avoid us on every side; and whatever quiver you have, place that far away from us. 191.
Having consecrated the weapons with mantras and having recited this five thousand times, one should bind them and cast them away;
then the enemies will flee. || 192 ||
One who desires to incite hatred [in another] should offer ten thousand darbha thorns;
having pronounced the name of the enemy with honey in his mouth, he should sacrifice while remembering that name. || 193 ||
By means of the rite known as *japākhya-savana*, one may forcibly destroy an enemy; by performing the complete *ahaṃ-japa*, one may even destroy an entire army. || 194 ||
The king should destroy [the sin] in a day and night, or in half a day; a Vaiśya in one-fourth part, and a member of a single caste (Śūdra) in one-sixth part. || 195 ||
Of the Palāśa, Aśvattha, Bilva, and Apāmārga, in that order.
One who desires to bring Brahmins and others under one's control [should offer oblations] combined with curd, honey, and clarified butter. || 196 ||
One hundred thousand fuel sticks should be offered for the accomplishment of the task.
To bring under one's control those of low caste, as well as Varuṇa, Arka, and Vetasa trees.
And one should offer oblations of śākhoṭaka wood two thousand eight hundred times.
He offers *saugandhika*, blue lotuses, and *agnikumuda* flowers. || 198 ||
One should oneself mark the linga with sandalwood paste applied with devotion; by means of these six mantras used individually, a king who has been deprived of his kingdom shall regain it. (199)
One who seeks wealth shall obtain riches by worshipping Śambhu in this manner.
He who places one hundred thousand *ekantila* seeds individually upon Śiva; || 200 ||
He shall place [the enemy] upon the heads of his foes and stand forever above them.
He who offers ten thousand oblations of fuel-sticks from the *rājavṛkṣa* tree [attains this]. (201)
He who offers six thousand pieces of guggulu resin in the presence of Dakṣiṇāmūrti shall swiftly conquer his enemy in battle, in the royal court, or at a game of dice. || 202 ||
Whatever purpose for which one performs the oblation, its accomplishment arises swiftly.
Even that which is incurable shall be accomplished by holding [the mantra] eight thousand times.
Just as one would offer cooked food from a kitchen, so too should one offer it.
Eight thousand of these substances become inexhaustible. || 204 ||
A single *ṛc* from this remainder shall be proclaimed hereafter;
listen with careful attention for the benefit of the world. (205)

Salutations to you, O Blessed One, the Lord of the Universe, Mahādeva, Tryambaka, Tripuruṣa, the Destroyer of Tripura, the One of the Three Times, Kālāgnirudra, Nīlakaṇṭha, the Lord of All, Sadāśiva, the illustrious Mahādeva; salutations!
He who is honored by the world should recite this ten thousand times and offer oblations with bilva leaves smeared with ghee, one thousand for each name. || 207 ||

Homage to Hiraṇyabāhu, the leader of armies and lord of the quarters; homage, homage! Homage to the trees with golden hair, the lord of animals; homage, homage! Homage to the one tawny like young grass, endowed with brilliance, the lord of paths; homage, homage to the golden-haired one who wears the sacred thread.
Salutations again and again to the Lord of the nourished. || 208 ||

Salutation to Babhluśa, the lord of various diseases; salutation, salutation to Bhava’s weapon, the lord of the worlds. Salutation to Rudra, the archer, the lord of fields; salutation, salutation to Sūta, the unslayable, the lord of forests. 209.
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for this [mantra] is said to be one thousand recitations. One who has entered into battle should mutter this for the sake of skillfulness. || 210 ||
By the power of recitation, he is not afflicted by weapons, missiles, or even by enemies.
The first [portion] has been told for the sake of the Sūta; now the remainder is being declared. || 211 ||
Homage, homage to the Lord of those who protect with playful grace; homage, homage to the Lord of those who protect with various faces.
Homage to Rohita, the architect, the Lord of trees; homage, homage to Bhuvanti, the creator of space, the Lord of herbs. 212.

Salutations again and again to the minister, to the merchant, to the lord of the quarters; salutations again and again to the one of loud roar, to the one who cries out, to the lord of lords. || 213 ||
Homage, homage to him who is completely clothed, who runs toward [his prey], the lord of beings;
homage, homage to the victorious one, the piercer, the lord of those who pierce; homage, homage!
Homage to the one who carries a quiver, the preeminent one, the lord of thieves; homage, homage to the one who carries a quiver and possesses a bow-case.
Salutations again and again to the Lord of thieves. || 214 ||
Five thousand recitations of this are said to be its preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*). For one who has chanted this, there is no fear in the forest from tigers, thieves, and the like. (215)
Homage to the deceiver, to the one who utterly deceives, to the lord of thieves; homage, homage!
Homage to the prowler, to the one who wanders about, to the lord of the forest-dwellers; homage, homage!
Homage to those with quivers, to those who strike, to those who exist, to the lord of robbers; homage, homage to the kindled ones!
Salutations again and again to those who roam at night and to the Lord of the Carvers. || 216 ||
