Homage again and again to the one with the turban, who wanders the mountains, the lord of the Kulañcas;

homage to those with arrows and to those with bows. Homage to you who are stringing [the bow] and to you who are placing [the arrow]; homage to you who are drawing [the bow] and to you who are releasing [the arrow].
Salutations again and again. || 217 ||
Eight thousand recitations of this [mantra] are prescribed as the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa). It is taught that its recitation is a destroyer of severe pain from wounds and the like. (218)

Salutations, salutations to you who are releasing [the breath], and salutations to you who are wise; salutations to you who are sleeping, and salutations to you who are waking. Salutations to you who are reclining, and salutations to you who are sitting;
salutations to you who are standing, and salutations to you who are running. || 219 ||
Salutations to you, the members of the assemblies and the presiding lords of the assemblies; salutations to you, the horses and the masters of the horses. 220.
Its preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) consists of nine thousand repetitions; one should recite this for the pacification of the fourfold army. || 221 ||
Homage to you who are disease-free and to you who pierce through; homage to you who are in troops and to you who slay the thieves. || 222 ||

Homage to you, the hosts, and homage to you, the lords of the hosts; homage to you, the troops, and homage to you, the lords of the troops. Homage to you, the skillful ones, and homage to you, the lords of the skillful;
homage to you, the multiformed ones, and homage to you, the all-formed ones. 223.

Homage to you who are great and to you who are small; homage to you who are charioteers and to you who are lords of chariots. Homage to you who are armies and to you who are army commanders; homage to you who are warriors and to you who are charioteers; homage to you who are great.
And salutations to you who are like children. || 224 ||
Homage to the carpenters and to you, the chariot-makers; homage to the potters and to you, the smiths. Homage to the hunters and to you, the Niṣādas;
homage to the arrow-makers and to you, the makers of bows. Homage!
Homage, homage to you who are hunters and to you who are fishermen; homage, homage to you who are dogs and to you who are masters of dogs. || 225 ||

The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for this consists of sixteen thousand recitations; having offered an oblation to the malevolent planets and having recited [the mantra], one becomes free from disease. || 226 ||
Homage to Bhava and to Rudra; homage to Śarva and to Paśupati. Homage to the blue-necked one and to the white-throated one; homage to the one with matted hair and to the one with shorn hair. 227.

Homage to the thousand-eyed and to the one with a hundred bows; homage to the mountain-dweller and to the one pervaded by rays. Homage to the most bountiful and to the wielder of the arrow; homage to the short and to the dwarf;
homage to the great and to the more extensive; homage to the aged and to the increaser.
One should perform ten thousand preliminary rites (*puraścaryā*) for the sake of its full manifestation.
He who recites this thus at the three junctions of the day shall become fortunate within a year. (229)

Homage to the foremost and to the first; homage to the swift and to the rapid. Homage to the quick and to the hasty; homage to the one of the waves and to the one of the waters. Homage to the one of the currents and to the radiant. 230.
Five thousand repetitions are said to constitute the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa); this is the view held by others as well, according to which the host of deities attains satisfaction.
Homage to the eldest and to the youngest; homage to the first-born and to the later-born.
Homage to the middlemost and to the modest; homage to the last-born and to the foundational one. 232.
Homage to Sobhya and to Pratisarya; homage to Yamya and to Kshemya.
Homage to the one who dwells in the verses and to the one who dwells in the dwellings; homage to the one who dwells in the fertile fields and to the one who dwells in the threshing floors. || 233 ||
Homage to Vanya and to Kakṣya; homage to Śrava and to Pratiśrava.
Ten thousand repetitions are said to constitute the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa).
One attains preeminence among kinsmen through recitation alone; of this there is no doubt. || 235 ||

Salutations to the one who possesses swift arrows and to the one who possesses a swift chariot; salutations to the one with arrows and to the one who pierces through; salutations to the one clad in armor and to the one possessing a protective fender; salutations to the one wearing a helmet and to the one wearing a breastplate;
salutations to the one renowned and to the one whose army is renowned. 236.

The preliminary rite (puraścaryā) for this is prescribed as five thousand repetitions; by it, lameness is destroyed according to one's birth, and one attains the perfection of the sandals (pādukāsiddhi). || 237 ||
Homage to the one who is like a drum and to the one who strikes it; homage to the bold and to the one who touches [the enemy];
homage to the messenger and to the one who is sent forth; homage to the one who carries a quiver and to the one who possesses a bow-case.
Homage to the one with sharp arrows and to the wielder of weapons; homage to the one who follows the sacred tradition and to the one who follows the path.
Homage to Kāṭya and to Nīpya; homage to Kulya and to Sarasya.
Homage to Nādeya and to Vaiśanta! || 239 ||
A recitation of twenty thousand [verses] is prescribed as its preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa); this Anuvāka is proclaimed to bring victory in battle. || 240 ||

Homage to the one who dwells in wells and to the one who dwells in pits; homage to the one who is excellent and to the one who is not excellent. Homage to the one who is pure and to the one who is in lightning; homage to the one who possesses the senses and to the one who is untruthful. 241.
Homage to Vātya and to Reṣmya; homage to Vāstavya and to Vāstupā.
The Sun, presided over by the planet, has six thousand as its preliminary rite (puraścaryā).
Having consecrated it with this [mantra], he releases the water by means of that.
Salutations to Soma and to Rudra; salutations to the copper-colored one and to the dawn-red one; salutations to Śaṅgu and to Paśupati; salutations to the fierce one and to the terrible one. || 244 ||
Homage to the one who strikes from nearby and to the one who strikes from afar; homage to the slayer and to the more deadly slayer.
Homage to the trees with tawny hair; homage to Tārā! || 245 ||
Homage to Śambhava and to Mayobhava; homage to Śaṅkara and to Mayaskara; homage to Śiva and to Śivataras. || 246 ||

One should recite the mantra ten thousand times as the preliminary rite (puraścaryā), followed by one hundred and eight repetitions. Three times a day, one should consume ashes mixed with water and likewise smear them upon the body.
Consumption (rājayakṣmā) perishes after three months, and leprosy (kilāsa) after a year;
it certainly vanishes, while a minor disease becomes divine [incurable] after three days.
Homage to the one who is beyond the ford and to the one who is at the bank; homage to the one who is obstructed and to the one who is unobstructed.
Homage to the one who carries across and the one who brings forth; homage to the teacher and to the one who inflates. || 249 ||
Homage to Śaṣpa and to Phenyā; homage to Sikatya and to Prabāhya.

One should recite [this mantra] six thousand times while performing the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) for six months at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*). One obtains the fruit of that sacred ford as described, even in this very birth. || 251 ||
Homage to Iriṇya and to Pramathya; homage to Kiṅguśila and to Kṣayāṇa; homage to Kapardin and to Pulasti. || 252 ||

Homage to him who is in the cow-pen and to him who is in the house; homage to him who is on the bed and to him who is in the home. Homage to him who is in the wood and to him who dwells in the abyss; homage to him who is in the heart and to him who is in the dwelling.
Homage to Pāgūṃsavya and to Rajasya; homage to Śuṣka and to Haritya; homage to Lopya and to Colpya. || 254 ||

Nine thousand repetitions are said to constitute the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa). By its grace, even the alchemical practice of transmuting base metals (dhātuvāda) belonging to the passionate nature (rājasa) is accomplished. || 255 ||
In this regard, there is indeed only one remaining anuvāka; one should recite it at the beginning of the *Rajasīya*, ending with the word "namaḥ. (256)
Homage to the Nearest and to the Lean-bodied; homage to the Further and to the Farther.
Homage to the Supreme and to the Smoke-colored; homage to the Seizer and to the Savior.
Homage to the Dwarf and to the Deer-marked; homage to the Auspicious and to the Golden-haired.

Eight thousand recitations of this [mantra] are prescribed as the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa). By sprinkling water with *barhis* grass, the child-seizing spirits (*bālagraha*) are destroyed. || 259 ||
Homage to the Wide One and to Sūrya; homage to Parṇa and to Parṇaśada.
Homage to him who raises [the weapon] and strikes down; homage to him who draws out and tears away.

The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for these nine thousand [mantras] is now declared: having consecrated water with the mantra, it should be given to one who is grieving for the sake of pacifying their sorrow. 261.
"Obeisance to you, the Kirikas, the hearts of the gods everywhere."
And whoever should recite this supplement even during ritual applications here, [he shall attain success]. || 262 ||
By performing ten thousand oblations of sesame seeds, one shall obtain a thousand palas of gold from the king, and within a year, one shall also attain royal consecration. || 263 ||
Eleven thousand pieces of honeyed sugar-cane and indeed eleven cows, smeared with clarified butter, should be offered. (p. 300) 264.
If one performs the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa) and offers one hundred thousand oblations of sesame seeds and rice grains,
the royal fortune (rājalakṣmī) shall dwell of her own accord in that person's home.
And thus, through oblations of sesame and grain, prosperity shall become stable.
Having fashioned an image made of a hundred flowers, resembling the form of a king.
If a king offers a thousand oblations, he brings his subjects under his control. By offering one hundred thousand oblations of lotuses and water-lilies, he shall obtain royal splendor.
One should offer one hundred thousand pills of guggulu incense as an oblation, using chickpeas as the measure for each.
He shall surely obtain the kingdom of the neighboring vassal kings, and not otherwise. || 268 ||
If one performs [the recitation] for a hundred days with oblations in the presence of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, then he shall obtain a kingdom consisting of one hundred thousand vassal chiefs. || 269 ||

A *liṅga* made from the earth of an anthill should be placed at a great crossroads. One should bathe it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), consecrate it with the *Rudrādhyāya*, and offer the sacrificial oblation while reciting the *Mānastoka* mantra. The offering consists of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with ghee.
And likewise, one should offer an oblation to the elemental spirits.
Having performed this for three months, one shall attain great sovereignty;
[one should offer] either a *pala* or half a *pala* in the presence of Dakṣiṇāmūrti. || 272 ||
Having ground white cloth (śvetāmbara) and placed it in a copper vessel, one should stir it with tawny clarified butter (kapilājya) that has been consecrated with the Pradīpinī mantra. || 273 ||
Then, one should drink eight thousand [measures] with this mantra; his speech will certainly become unimpeded everywhere. || 274 ||
One should offer ten thousand oblations of *udumbara* wood fuel-sticks smeared with clarified butter;
such a master shall possess many cows, and his milch-cows shall never diminish. (275)
One should likewise offer eight thousand fuel-sticks of bilva wood into the fire.
One who has not attained perfection indeed obtains eight pieces of gold, or eight pieces of silver.
In the absence of bilva, however, one should use āmalaka; in its absence, udumbara;
in its absence, haimavatī; and in its absence, vibhītaka. || 277 ||
One hundred thousand lotuses, smeared with sandalwood paste and cow's ghee.
Prosperity comes to him of its own accord as he fasts. || 278 ||
O Drāpi, O Lord of the Soma-juice, O wearer of the blue and red garment! Do not fear for these men, nor for these cattle; do not let anything whatsoever cause us distress. 279.
With this [mantra], one should offer clarified butter in a number up to ten thousand;
in that manner, his garments shall become inexhaustible.
O Rudra, that auspicious body of yours which is benevolent to all and healing, which is the auspicious healer of disease—
that with it, O gracious one, protect us for life.
And the woolly creatures abandoned their bodies while still alive. || 281 ||
One should prepare eleven strands for each individual thread;
having thus completed a thousand, eleven knots are prescribed.
Having thus worshipped that rope and offered incense, one should bind it.
If he places it in the left hand of a pregnant woman, she will give birth to a son easily. || 283 ||
The child remains comfortably in the right hand;
if one should bind the thread, it must be consecrated with the mantra itself. || 284 ||
A wealthy person might wear this around his upper arm or on his neck.
At times, indeed, no fear arises for him from a creditor. || 285 ||
To Rudra, the powerful one with matted hair, the ruler of heroes, we offer our prayer,
so that there may be peace for our bipeds and quadrupeds, and so that everything in this village may be nourished and free from disease. (286)
One should offer sesame seeds one thousand and eight times every day; by this, unasked-for wealth is indeed obtained from all the worlds.
But he who should offer ten thousand blades of young dūrvā grass smeared with clarified butter, [attains success].
Even when afflicted by a great fever, he lives as if he were dead.
Being pure, one should offer ten thousand oblations of honey mixed with milk-rice and clarified butter.
One is liberated from great planetary afflictions, fevers, and the like, as well as from malevolent sorcery. || 289 ||
One should offer ten thousand fuel-sticks of *vaikaṅkata* wood with clarified butter; the affliction arising from fever and other ailments will perish instantly. || 290 ||
When someone is being oppressed by others for the sake of wealth and other such things, he should then offer ten thousand oblations of husks; thus his happiness increases. || 291 ||
One should offer a hundred thousand oblations of fuel-sticks of *vaikaṅkata* wood, as well as *udumbara* wood and sesame seeds, with this [mantra]; it is remembered as bestowing all powers. || 292 ||
If cattle or other animals have been harmed in that place,
one should establish a fire there and offer oblations of *vikaṅkata* wood fuel soaked in clarified butter.
For him, there shall be peace through ten thousand [offerings], and likewise ten thousand of palāśa leaves.
One should offer oblations of [substances] smeared with ghee; thus the planetary spirits, headed by Mahājvara, [are appeased]. || 294 ||
Rākṣasas, bhūtas, vetālas, pretas, and even piśācas, having left behind people, elephants, or horses, depart to a great distance. || 295 ||
In whatever house the birth of people occurs, or where there is childbirth, death, or loss, the performance of propitiatory rites (śānti) is prescribed therein. || 296 ||
A twice-born man should offer ten thousand oblations of sesame seeds smeared with ghee; in that place, there shall indeed be no fear of pestilence, tigers, or other such dangers. || 297 ||
Wherever there is agitation among the gods, I declare that one should perform pacification; specifically, one should carry out the installation of the fire in the central part of the city. (298)
Furthermore, four men, fully armed and well-guarded, should be stationed in the four directions;
thereafter, one should perform the ritual with full attention. (299)
One should offer one thousand and eight sesame seeds smeared with clarified butter.
Then, at the time of midnight, [he should offer] boiled rice with ghee and sesame seeds.
Then, in various places throughout the country, the wise man should offer as an oblation (bali) ground flour, black-gram rice, kṛśara, and excellent cooked rice. || 301 ||
On a Palāśa leaf, one should [offer] to the Rudras and then to the Rākṣasas; by doing so for one fortnight, all calamities will be destroyed. (302)
O gracious Rudra, make us well-prepared; we shall worship you with reverence, O Lord of heroes.
That which Manu, his father, offered as both sacrifice and oblation, that same [offering] was performed by Amata for Rudra’s guidance.
One should recite [the mantra] a thousand times in the water and worship Śiva on the bank; whatever is desired will surely be met within three days, even if it be at a great distance.
Do not harm our great ones, nor our small ones; do not harm our growing ones, nor those already grown. Do not slay our father, nor our mother; O Rudra, do not injure our dear bodies. (305)
One should offer *tila* oblations for the sake of the health of one's attendants and children; by offering ten thousand, health arises instantly from diseases such as *śītala*. || 306 ||

"O Mānastoka! Do not harm our offspring, nor our life-span, nor our cows, nor our horses. Do not slay our heroic sons who are free from pride. Bearing oblations, we invoke you at every session. This is the mantra; and another follows: "Do not [harm] our great..."
"Do not [slay] our child, nor our youth, nor our grown man; do not slay our father, nor our mother, O Rudra. Do not harm our beloved bodies.
This great [teaching], hidden in all the Tantras, I shall declare to the sage of the gods.
For the sake of accomplishing the task. || 307 ||
Having first purified oneself through the *atikṛcchra*, the *kṛcchra*, or likewise the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance, one whose body is cleansed should perform the recitation (*japa*). || 308 ||
Reciting this, he should eat either vegetables, barley-gruel, or milk.
And for him, there should be ten thousand recitations of the *bhikṣāñjya* mantra. || 309 ||

When one thousand recitations of the mantra have been performed, the mantra becomes fit for practical application (prayoga). At the conclusion of the application, however, recitation (japa) should be performed continuously for a full day and night. || 310 ||
One should offer oblations of *audumbara* wood soaked in clarified butter, numbering one-tenth of that [total].
Thereafter, one should offer clarified butter with the Mahāvyāhṛtis for that same duration.
Having consumed the portion of the residue according to the prescribed practice, one shall attain imperishability;
yet one should perform the ritual action again and again, and the expiation likewise again and again. || 312 ||
And one should bathe with sesame oil that has been consecrated seven times with mantras.
Through the ritual applications for death and so forth, there shall be liberation from sin. || 313 ||
One who desires spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa), however, should offer eight thousand oblations of fuel-sticks smeared with ghee;
for medicinal herbs are used in all ritual acts.
One who desires prosperity, or one who desires a vision of Śiva, should offer ten thousand oblations of lotuses smeared with ghee after fasting for ten nights. || 315 ||
Or one should offer ten thousand grains of Apāmārga rice smeared with ghee for the fulfillment of all aims. || 316 ||
For the sake of obtaining a thousand cows, one should offer oblations of clarified butter (ājya) eight thousand times with devotion, either using cow-dung or [cow-urine]. || 317 ||
Having fasted for ten days, one should offer bilva fruits smeared with ghee;
by offering ten thousand, one shall obtain eight thousand [merits].
When the mantra is mastered, one obtains gold; when it is not mastered, silver.
For this purpose, one who is pure should offer oblations, saying, "May such-and-such a woman become my wife. || 319 ||
And *jātī* flowers combined with clarified butter and honey; furthermore, when a tawny cow (*kapilā*) has calved, or even a cow in heat accompanied by a bull. || 320 ||
Having taken clarified butter and milk, one should indeed cook the sacrificial pap (caru) with that.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations, and likewise eight thousand.
Having consecrated it with mantras, he should eat it together with his wife while moving about.
And she shall give birth to eight sons of long life; of this there is no doubt. || 322 ||
One should offer oblations of fresh durvā shoots combined with curd, milk, and ghee.
One who desires long life obtains a lifespan of eight thousand years.
Of flowers smeared with curd, honey, and ghee, and of kuśa and kāśa grass;
If one desires minor animals, one should offer eight thousand oblations.
Having fasted for three nights, one should go to a great crossroads; likewise, having fashioned an image out of cow dung facing the deity. || 325 ||
Having performed worship, one should offer one thousand and eight oblations upon the ground; by that rite, the king will undoubtedly become submissive. || 326 ||
With that sharp oil, which has been consecrated seven times with mantras, [he should rub] both hands.
When correctly touched by that [mantra], whoever is touched shall come under its control.
One who desires spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa), however, by offering a hundred thousand oblations of Bilva fuel-sticks mixed with curd, honey, and ghee,
shall become a treasury of splendor.
And one should offer oblations of udumbara wood fuel-sticks, combined with curd, honey, and clarified butter.
By offering eight thousand fuel-sticks, the eradication of the enemy shall occur. || 329 ||
For the purpose of destroying all calamities, one should take seven pieces of sugar, consecrate them by reciting the mantra a thousand times,
and then scatter them in the four directions.
Near its top and bottom is the destroyer of all calamities;
by performing this [rite] while traveling on the road, one removes the fear of thieves and tigers. || 331 ||
O you who strike down cattle and strike down men, hail to you, the ruler of heroes; let there be well-being for you.
Protect us and speak for us here, O God; then grant us shelter, you who are all-pervading.
Praise the famous one, the youth seated upon the chariot-throne, who is formidable, impetuous, and fierce.
O Rudra, being praised, be gracious to the singer; let your missiles pass us by. 333.
May the missile of Rudra spare us; may the ill-will of the impetuous evildoer pass us by.
Make [your protection] firm for the liberal patrons; O you who are to be praised, be gracious to our children and descendants.
O most bountiful, most auspicious one, be gracious and well-disposed toward us. Having laid aside your weapon upon the highest tree and wearing a skin, come hither bearing your Pināka bow.
When great fear has arisen—such as the fear of tigers, thieves, and so forth—one should remember these four [verses] in one's mind; they are the destroyers of that fear. || 336 ||
O you whose blood is scattered and flowing, homage be to you, O Blessed One!
May those thousand-fold rays of yours rain down [blessings] upon us. (337)
If one utters ten thousand curses against those who oppose him, the great people will come under his control, and great affection will arise. || 338 ||
Thousands upon thousands are the weapons in your two arms; O Blessed One, as their master, turn them away from our faces.
But when there is great death or some calamity involving the king, then one should perform a fire-oblation with the finest fuel-sticks of the *vaikaṅkata* tree.
With fruits of the udumbara tree, or with śālmalī wood, or even with sesame seeds or barley.
Having consecrated each one eleven times, he then [consecrates] the earth.
Then one should offer kṛsara or even pāyasa to the spirits.
One should offer an oblation of cat meat; thus all calamities perish. || 342 ||
Those thousands upon thousands of Rudras who dwell upon the earth—to them, whose bows are drawn to a distance of a thousand yojanas, we pay homage. || 343 ||
Those belonging to other Vedic branches should recite the *Pariśiṣṭaka* at the end of the passage.
In this great ocean, you likewise protect him from the demon. || 344 ||
Those with blue necks and white throats, the Śarvas who roam upon the earth below.
We bow to those whose bows extend for a thousand yojanas. || 345 ||
The blue-necked, white-throated Rudras have taken refuge in heaven.
We stretch their bows to a length of a thousand yojanas. || 346 ||
Those who are tawny like young grass upon the trees, with blue necks and deep red [throats].
We bow to those whose bows extend for a thousand yojanas.
Those who are the lords of beings, wearing braided hair and matted locks.
We bow to those whose bows extend for a thousand yojanas. || 348 ||
They pierce the vessels as the people drink from them.
We bow to those whose bows extend for a thousand yojanas. || 349 ||
Those who are the guardians of the paths, the sons of Ilabṛd, the warriors for life.
We bow to those bows of theirs, which extend for a thousand yojanas. || 350 ||
Those who wander among the sacred fords, carrying spears in their hands and bearing quivers.
We bow to those whose bows extend for a thousand yojanas. || 351 ||
And as many of these fearful Rudras as have taken their stand in every direction.
We bow to those bows of theirs, which extend for a thousand yojanas. || 352 ||

One should recite these nine verses along with the supplementary portions; when accompanied by them, they are considered bestowers of enjoyment, but when devoid of them, they are regarded as bestowers of knowledge. || 353 ||
Homage be to the Rudras who are upon the earth, whose arrows are food! To them, ten [fingers] to the east, ten to the south, ten to the west, ten to the north, and ten upwards.
Homage be to them; may they protect us, may they be gracious to us. Whomever we hate and whoever hates us—him we place within their jaws. || 354 ||
Homage be to the Rudras who are in the intermediate space, whose arrows are the winds;
to them [be homage] ten times in the east, ten times in the south, ten times in the west, and ten times in the upward direction. || 355 ||
Homage be to the Rudras who are in heaven, whose arrows are the rain; to them [be homage] ten times toward the east, ten times toward the south, ten times toward the west, and ten times upward. (356)
And at midday, one should offer clarified butter along with thorny wood into the fire with these mantras.
One should perform the ritual of the mantra of Pratyaṅgirā; this is the mantra. || 357 ||
The conclusion of this [rite] is performed with the mantra "namas te" from the Mṛtyuñjaya [hymn].
And there are seven supplements (pariśiṣṭa) in the Taittirīya branches. || 358 ||

The five verses beginning with *sadyojāta*—namely, "I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutations indeed to Sadyojāta," and so forth—were previously written in the section on Brahmā. Together with the six verses beginning with "We worship Tryambaka," these are called the *Artharudra*.
May Agni, the descendant of Aṅgiras, increase me for the enjoyment of the essence of knowledge;
he has emerged with brilliant strengths. || 360 ||
Standing at the conclusion of the twilight prayers (sandhyā-vandana) at the three periods of the day, one should perform the recitation (japa) constantly.
By reciting [the mantra] one thousand and eight times for six months, one becomes truthful in speech.
May my strength and my impulse, my exertion and my penetration, my study and my resolve, my tone and my fame, my sacrificial ladle and my sacred revelation,
my light and my heaven be perfected through sacrifice. 362.
May my out-breath and my in-breath, my diffused breath and my life-force, my consciousness and my learning, my speech and my mind, my eye and my ear,
my skill and my strength— may these be perfected through sacrifice. 363.
May my vital essence and my strength, my self and my body, my shelter and my armor,
my limbs and my bones, my joints and my physical forms,
as well as my life-span and my old age, be perfected through sacrifice. 364.
And may my preeminence and my lordship, and my indignation and my wrath, and my might and my victory, and my greatness and my vastness,
and my breadth and my width, and my height and my length, and my growth and my increase be [granted] through sacrifice.
May they be successful. || 365 ||
May truth and my faith, the world and my wealth, the universe and my greatness, my play and my joy, what has been born and what is yet to be born,
my well-spoken hymn and my good deed, be perfected through sacrifice. 366.

May my cosmic order and my death, my consumption and my disease, my life-force and my long-livedness, my friend and my fear, my happiness and my bed, and my prosperity be made perfect through sacrifice. || 367 ||
May my controller and my supporter, my security and my steadfastness, my all-pervasiveness and my greatness, my consciousness and my discernment, my procreation and my productivity,
my plough and my repose, prosper through sacrifice. 368.
May peace and prosperity for me, joy for me, what is dear to me, my desire for food, my longing, mental well-being for me, fortune for me, wealth for me, auspiciousness for me, excellence for me,
higher good for me, and glory for me— may these be fulfilled through sacrifice. 369.

May my vigor and my pleasant speech, my milk and my juice, my clarified butter and my honey, my eating together and my drinking together, my agriculture and my rain, my victory and my prosperity through cultivation, be perfected by means of sacrifice. 370.
May my wealth and my riches, my nourishment and my prosperity, my pervasiveness and my lordship,
my fullness and my greater fullness, my grain and my dwelling, and my food and my hunger be perfected through sacrifice. 371.
May my wealth and what is to be known, my past and my future, my good state and my wholesome path,
my prosperity and my power, my arrangement and my accomplishment, my intellect and my excellent wisdom, be perfected through sacrifice. 372.
May my rice and my barley, my beans and my sesame, my mung beans and my lentils, my millet and my panic seed, my wild rice and my *śyāmāka* grain,
my wheat and my lentils be perfected through sacrifice.
May my stone and my clay, my hills and my mountains, my sands and my trees, my gold and my iron, my lead and my copper, my tin and my pewter, be perfected through sacrifice. || 374 ||
May Agni be mine; may the waters be mine; may the creepers be mine; may the herbs be mine;
may the crops ripening in tilled soil be mine; may the crops ripening in untilled soil be mine; may the domestic animals be mine;
may the wild animals be mine; may my wealth be mine; may the acquisition of wealth be mine; and may the past be mine.
And may prosperity be ordained for me through this sacrifice. || 375 ||
May my wealth, my action, my power, my purpose, my desire, my arrival, and my goal be perfected through sacrifice. 376.
May Agni and Indra for me, Soma and Indra for me, Savitṛ and Indra for me, Sarasvatī and Indra for me, Pūṣan and Indra for me,
and Bṛhaspati and Indra for me be perfected through sacrifice. 377.
May Mitra and Indra for me, Varuṇa and Indra for me, Dhātṛ and Indra for me, Tvaṣṭṛ and Indra for me, the Maruts and Indra for me,
and all the gods and Indra for me— may they be perfected through my sacrifice. 378.
May the earth and Indra for me, the intermediate space and Indra for me,
the sky and Indra for me, the years and Indra for me, the lunar mansions and Indra for me,
and the quarters and Indra for me be perfected through sacrifice. 379.
And my Agūṃśu, and my Raśmi, and my Dābbhya, and my Dhipati,
and my Upāgūṃśu, and my Antaryāma, and my Aindravāyava,
and my Maitrāvaruṇa, and my Āśvina, and my Pratiprasthāna, and my Śukra.
May both my churning-stick and my sacrifice be successful. || 380 ||
And my Āgrayaṇa, and my Vaiśvadeva, and my Dhruva,
and my Vaiśvānara, and my Aindrāgna, and my Mahāvaiśvadeva,
and my Marutvatīyas, and my Niṣkevalya, and my Sāvitra, and my Sārasvata.
May my Pālīkīvat and my Hāriyojana prosper through this sacrifice. || 381 ||

And my *sruva* ladles, and my *camasa* cups, and my *vāyavya* vessels, and my *droṇakalaśa* vat, and my *grāvāṇa* pressing-stones, and my two *dhiṣaṇā* sounding-boards, and my *pūtabhṛt* filter-vessel, and my *ādhavanīya* mixing-vessel,
and my altar, and my sacrificial grass, and my purificatory bath, and my cry of "Svadhā"— with these, may I be united through sacrifice.
May they be successful! || 382 ||
May Agni and Dharma, Marīci and Sūrya, Prāṇa and Aśvamedha, Pṛthivī and Aditi, and Diti and Dyau, as well as my fingers, the Śakvarī verses, and the quarters, be harmonized through sacrifice. 383.
May my *ṛc* and my *sāman*, my *stoma* and my *yajus*, my initiation (*dīkṣā*) and my austerity (*tapas*),
my sacrifices (*kratavaḥ*) and my year (*saṃvatsara*), my day and night, my thighs and knees,
and my *bṛhat* and *rathantara* chants be perfected through sacrifice. 384.

May my male calves and my female calves, my one-year-old males and my one-year-old females, my two-year-old males and my two-year-old females, my three-year-old males and my three-year-old females, my four-year-old males and my four-year-old females, prosper through the sacrifice.
May my bull and my cow in heat, my ox and my barren cow, my stud-bull and my large one, my draft-ox and my milch-cow— may these attain fullness of life through the sacrifice. 386.
One for me and three for me, three for me and five for me, five for me and seven for me,
seven for me and nine for me, nine for me and eleven for me, eleven for me and thirteen for me,
thirteen for me and fifteen for me, fifteen for me.
And seventeen for me, and seventeen for me; nine and ten for me, and nine and ten for me; twenty-one for me, and twenty-one for me; twenty-three for me, and twenty-three for me; twenty-five for me.
Twenty-five for me, twenty-seven for me,
twenty-seven for me, twenty-nine for me, twenty-nine for me,
thirty-one for me, thirty-one for me, and thirty-three for me.
May they be made ready through sacrifice. || 387 ||
Four for me and eight for me; twelve for me and sixteen for me;
twenty for me and twenty-four for me; twenty-eight for me and thirty-two for me; thirty-six for me and forty for me.
May my forty-four and my forty-eight be made perfect through sacrifice. || 388 ||
May Vāja, Paśu, Kratu, Mūrdhan, Vyaśniya, Antyāyana, Antya, Bhauvana, Bhuvana, and Adhipati be perfected through sacrifice. || 389 ||
O Uddhava, this much has been declared to you, which bestows the fruit of all desires.
The recitation of the Rudrastotra, with its syllables clearly articulated, leads to peace.
May Iḍā, who calls the gods, Manu, who leads the sacrifice, and Bṛhaspati, strengthen our hymns and our exhilarating songs.
May all the gods, speakers of well-spoken words, grant us favor. O Mother Earth, do not harm me; I shall conceive honey, I shall bring forth honey, I shall speak honey—honey!

I shall speak honeyed words; may I utter speech that is pleasing to the gods and worthy of being heard by humans. May the gods protect me for the sake of splendor, and may the ancestors rejoice in me. Om. Peace! Peace! Peace! 391.
One should then mutter the remainder; this is remembered as the ritual procedure for Rudra.
One should perform the consecration for the sake of prosperity, while one who desires pacification should perform the fire oblation (homa).
One desiring success should recite [the mantra] according to the number of syllables; indeed, in this very world, one becomes Śiva himself, enriched by many Rudras, and not anyone else. || 393 ||
From the recitation of the mantra with a rhythm equal to the words, even direct realization (*vijñapti*) arises.
By reciting the Vākyatulyāvṛti, all sin is destroyed. || 394 ||
By the recitation of the prescribed number of Ṛgvedic verses, all minor sins are destroyed.
Having recited this section (anuvāka), one shall conquer the afflictions caused by malevolent planets.

I shall proclaim the Devīsūkta, which bestows all desired objects. It is said that one who is incapable [of performing the ritual] should recite it before Rudra, even without this [preliminary]. || 396 ||
Now follows the Devīsūkta.
I move with the Rudras and the Vasus; I am with the Ādityas and the Viśvedevas.
I sustain Mitra and Varuṇa in my radiance; I am Indra and Agni, and I am the Aśvins in my radiance. 397.
I, O Soma, am Manahsā; I bear Tvaṣṭṛ, as well as Pūṣan and Bhaga.
I bestow wealth upon the one who offers oblations, upon the sacrificer who presses the juice and is skilled in the sacred rite.
I am the sovereign ruler, the gatherer of treasures, the wise one, the first.
Her, the one worthy of sacrifice, the gods have distributed in many places—she who has many abodes and causes many to enter. 399.

He who perceives, he who breathes, and he who hears what is spoken—by me he is fed. The breathless do not wait upon those who possess breath. Listen, O you who have heard; I speak to you, the faithful one.
I myself declare this, which is favored by both goddesses and men: whomsoever I desire, him I make fierce; him I make a Brahman, him a seer, and him a man of great wisdom. 401.
I bend the bow for Rudra, so that his arrow may slay the one who hates sacred knowledge. I stir up conflict among the people; I have entered heaven and earth. 402.

On the morrow, I shall place my father upon his head; my womb is within the waters, in the midst of the ocean. Thence I spread out across all worlds, and I touch even that highest heaven with my summit.
I alone blow forth like the wind, setting all worlds in motion. Beyond...
By day he is equal to the earth; so great has he become in his majesty. || 404 ||
This Devīsūkta has been proclaimed as the most excellent among all sūktas; it is celebrated as the foundation for the accomplishment of mantras for the twice-born. (405)
Now I shall proclaim the hymn of Viṣṇu and that of Gaṇapati, without which all mantras are obstructed by impediments. (406)
Therefore, having first propitiated Gaṇeśāna, one should perform the practice of the deity again; thus it will be accomplished without obstacles. (407)
Sleep, laziness, hunger, anger, greed, delusion, passion, negligence, and disease—these and others are known as the obstructors of mantra. || 408 ||
Therefore, that hymn is being recited here according to the prescribed ritual, by which the functions of the knowers [of the mantras] shall remain unimpeded. (409)
Regarding this [hymn] of twelve verses dedicated to the high-souled Gaṇeśa, the seer is Gṛtsamada and the deity is proclaimed to be the Lord of the Gaṇas. || 410 ||
And for the first three triplets of verses, the meter is proclaimed to be Triṣṭubh.
And for the nine Uttara hymns, the Gāyatrī metre is said to be used. || 411 ||
Mahāgaṇapati is proclaimed as its presiding deity; the application (viniyoga) should be declared according to the specific purpose at hand. || 412 ||
We invoke you, the Lord of hosts, the sage among sages, possessed of most exalted renown;
the supreme ruler of sacred hymns, O Brahmaṇaspati, hearing us, sit upon your seat with your protections. 413.

Seated among the hosts, O Lord of the Gaṇas, they call you the wisest of the sages. Nothing whatsoever is done without you; O great one, worship the wondrous, exhilarating, and intoxicating [Soma]. 414.
May they not perceive your radiant host, with conch and other weapons in hand, who maintain their vows and are the protectors of the earth through me. 415.
O Indra, seize for us a most auspicious and wondrous course with your great right hand! 416.
For we know you to be a shaper of forms, a finder of wealth, and one who bestows great bounty.
With aids that are truly firm. || 417 ||
For neither gods nor mortals can restrain you, O Hero, when you desire to give. They call upon the Terrific One for cattle;
come, let us praise Indra, the sovereign lord of wealth and self-rule. May he not neglect our desire for bounty. 419.
He shall chant the *prastāva*, he shall respond with the *upagīti* to the *sāman* being sung; he has chanted for us the strength of the host.
O Indra, do not exclude us from our share of wealth through the right hand, nor through the middle, nor through the left. 42.
O bold one, bring near the onset of the people who are most skilled in their knowledge;
O Indra, whatever vigor you possess for the inspired singers, let that thunder forth from heaven. May that which has been praised by us be present here;
may all the gladdening spoils of battle be ours. And of strength...
May he quickly grow old. || 424 ||
For the *Gaṇas*: "Of the hosts" (*gaṇānām*)—homage to the two thumbs; "let him sit down" (*niṣusīda*)—homage to the two index fingers;
"the brilliant host, with conch and other items in hand" (*tveṣaṃ gaṇaṃ tava śaṅkhādi-hasta*)—homage to the two middle fingers;
"then indeed Indra, the well-portioned" (*ātū na indraḥ sumam̐sam*)—homage to the two ring fingers.
"Salutation; for we know you indeed as the one who strides across," with these words, one should perform salutation with both little fingers (*kaniṣṭhikā*).
"For not even the gods [can overcome] you, O Hero," with these words, one should perform salutation with the palms and the backs of the hands.
In this manner, one should again perform the placement (*nyāsa*) on the heart and other parts, repeating the complete mantra.
One should recite the *pūrṇa* [hymn], as well as "tvā niṣusīda tveṣaṃ gaṇam," and likewise "ā tū na indra vidmahi" and "na hi tvā śūra. || 425 ||

Beginning from the tip of the thumb, one should place [the mantras] on the back of the hands and so forth; with the mantra "gaṇānāṃ tvā," one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅgaka) externally and on the heart and other locations.
Having thus performed the two types of placement (nyāsa), one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) with six [verses]. Then, one should perform the placement here with twelve verses. 427.
On the head and the face, on the two eyes as well as the two ears, on the nose, the throat, the heart, the arms, the belly, and in the middle of the navel. || 428 ||
And for the two ankles and the two feet, there are twelve verses each respectively.
And with the syllables of the king of mantras, the third placement (nyāsa) is performed. || 429 ||

Then, one should perform the fourth placement (nyāsa) with the six-syllabled mantra alone; and with ten verses, one should perform the binding of the directions (digbandha), placing one [verse] on the feet and one on the head.

Having thus performed the rite of ritual placement (nyāsa), one should worship with the ancillary limbs and the surrounding enclosures; having worshipped with the Tantric mantra, one should likewise do so with the twelve Ṛgvedic verses.
With the sixteen modes of service, including the deities of the limbs, the throne, and so forth.
With various kinds of food offerings, such as sweetmeats (modakas) and prepared laddukas.
One should satisfy the Leader of the Gaṇas with milk-rice and pieces of sugar-candied milk.
With pieces of sugarcane, sugarcane juice, plantains, jackfruit, and so forth. || 433 ||
With coconuts, pomegranates, and various other kinds of fruits, along with betel leaves containing camphor and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) on all sides; || 434 ||
Having performed worship at midday, one should then begin the recitation (japa). First, the wise practitioner should recite the King of Mantras twelve times. || 435 ||
And then, one should recite the twelve verses with complete alertness.
But in the intermediate twelve-fold recitation, one should again mutter the King of Mantras.
In this manner, O Hari, the chanting of Vedic mantras should be performed in succession; this chanting, which brings about complete perfection, must always be practiced day after day. (437)
By the recitation of the hymns and mantras, one shall quickly attain all accomplishments; or else, the recitation of Vakratuṇḍa should be performed first. (438)
By repeating twenty-six times, one places the *Gaṇeśvara-sūkta* in the center; again, by repeating twenty-six times, there is the six-syllabled mantra of Vakratuṇḍa: *Oṃ vakratuṇḍāya hūṃ*. (439)
And having thus performed the conjunction, one should mutter the twelve-verse hymn.
Having thus performed one hundred and eight recitations of the hymn, O Hari, chant the prayer.
The preliminary rite for the hymn is said to consist of twenty-one thousand [recitations]. From ten times the number of recitations, there shall be a fire-oblation of milk-rice and ghee. (441)
And with sugar, the five kinds of edible foods, and karavīra flowers.
With bilva leaves, sugarcane stalks, pomegranates, and plantain fruits. || 442 ||
One should offer water-soaked laddukas and charming sweets fried in ghee; however, in the absence of all these materials, one should perform the oblation with sesame seeds and clarified butter.
One should satisfy [the deities] with the tenth part of the oblation and with cow’s milk;
or else with sugarcane juice, and in its absence, with jaggery-water. || 444 ||
One should perform the purification with auspicious water using a tenth part of the libation;
and using a tenth part of that purification, one should feed many Brāhmaṇas. || 445 ||
With milk-rice, sugar-candies, sweetmeats, and prepared *laḍḍukas*.
With cakes such as maṇḍakas and others, accompanied by ghee and sugar.
Likewise, with the juices of mangoes (sahakāra) mixed with ghee, and with plantain fruits;
When the hymn has been thus accomplished, it is declared to be fruitful.
One attains great and incomparable sovereignty, wisdom, knowledge, fame, strength, and perfection of speech;
and at the end, one shall go to the city of Brahman.
Whatever action is performed with a specific purpose in view is called *purojapa*.
By the grace of that respective Gaṇapati, it will certainly and surely be accomplished. || 449 ||
In matters of binding and eradication, in hatred and killing, in the liberation from bondage, in subjugation, in debate, during great portents, and likewise in fear of a hostile army; || 450 ||
One should recite it in a great forest, in battle, amidst a throng of enemies, or in times of peril.
For binding, eradication, and hatred, [one should use] mustard seeds combined with iron. || 451 ||

One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in a desolate forest at night using the feathers of an owl and a crow; for the purpose of killing, one should perform the recitation (japa) with wrath while standing in a cremation ground at night.
With sesame seeds, mallāṭa flowers, and black mustard mixed with salt.
Furthermore, a homa performed with the wool of a ewe will certainly result in the killing [of the enemy]. || 453 ||
And likewise, one should perform the recitation at night in a cremation ground with a sense of wrath.
For the purpose of attracting those to be accomplished, [one should use] the seeds of the *unmatta* fruit. || 454 ||
Then, one should offer oblations with vulture feathers and milk released by the sun.
Up until the end of seven days, there shall then be an attraction.
And for the purpose of subjugation, one should perform recitation especially in a temple of Śiva.
Starting from sunset until sunrise occurs. || 456 ||
One should recite the root mantra with the *sampuṭa* method for three nights; during that time, the fire-oblation (*homa*) should be performed by day using honey, flowers, and fruits.
And likewise, with *mālatī* leaves combined with ghee.
With modakas mixed with red sandalwood, along with ghee and sesame seeds. || 458 ||
One should satisfy [the deity] with sugarcane juices; this is considered an immediate means for subjugation. Kings, princes, and royal ministers [are thus won over]. || 459 ||
Even Īśvara falls under the power [of karma]; what need is there to mention human beings?
For the sake of liberation from bondage, one should perform recitation at night in a temple of Śiva.
Constantly observing the vow of fasting, practicing celibacy, and having his senses subdued.
There shall be twenty-one thousand oblations by day in the temple of Śiva.
With milk-rice mixed with ghee, the release from bondage will certainly occur; for this oblation, common to all, should be performed according to the rule for each image.
At the beginning, one should offer twelve oblations with the mantra twelve times.
Thereafter, the wise one should offer oblations for each individual image according to the division of mantras.
And for twelve days prior, there shall be a fire-offering (homa) with the king of mantras; in this very manner, it applies to all common types of recitation (japa).
Thus, the *gaṇeśasūkta* of the *sampuṭa* is produced; likewise is the procedure for Rudra, and the *devīsūkta* in the same manner. (465)
Since no difference has been declared between you and Viṣṇu, therefore, let that which you desire beyond this be asked. || 466 ||
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Revelation of the Vedas and Mantras for the Conviction of the Kali Age," in the Merutantra, authorized by the illustrious Mahāmāyā and Mahākāla. 12.
The Goddess said:
Alas! In the Kali age, these wicked people generally always bestow misery;
what kind of worship is there for them according to the Vedic path, and who is their Manu? || 1 ||
How is it that faults such as illusion (māyā) and affliction do not affect men? Furthermore, tell me according to the Vedic path the determination regarding their worship. || 2 ||
The illustrious Śiva said:
"Excellent, O Goddess, is the question you have asked regarding the determination of the worship of the planets;
for indeed, without [proper] timing, they afflict everyone with suffering. || 3 ||
Planets situated in exalted positions humiliate even a universal monarch.
When those established in a low state regard the son of a universal monarch as a slave, || 4 ||
The Sun is said to be the soul of Time, and the Moon is called its mind; Mars is its essence (sattva), Mercury its speech, and Jupiter its knowledge and happiness. || 5 ||
Sita is desire, Śani is suffering, Chāyā is Rāhu, and Śikhī is the crest-lock.
Through the worship of Kheṭa, a mortal becomes a knower of the three periods of time. || 6 ||
But those who worship the planets according to the Vedic path enjoy happiness in the world of the planets together with the planets themselves. || 7 ||
In that regard, for the mantra of Bhāskara, Hiraṇyastūpa is the sage; the Triṣṭubh is the meter, and Savitṛ is proclaimed as the deity. || 8 ||
With "Ā kṛṣṇena" (with the dark dust), salutation to the two thumbs;

with "vartamāno niveśyan" (moving, settling), salutation to the two index fingers; with "amṛtaṃ martyaṃ ca" (the immortal and the mortal), salutation to the two middle fingers; with "hiraṇyayena savitā" (Savitar with the golden), salutation to the two ring fingers.

"Salutation to the one who goes by means of his chariot, O god"—thus with the two little fingers; "salutation to the one beholding the worlds"—thus with the palms and the backs of the hands; in this manner, one should also perform the placement (nyāsa) on the heart and other parts. Now follows the placement of the words (pada-nyāsa): "Ā" on the head.
With Kṛṣṇa [as the sun] in his eyes, with dust in his ears, placing [the sun] in his nose,
with nectar in his mouth, with mortality in his throat,
with gold in his arms and hands, with Savitṛ in his navel, with the god on his chariot in his anus, and in the pair of his thighs.
He goes through the two knees, through the two shanks, and beholding the worlds with his two feet;
such is the placement of his steps. Moving along with the dust of the earth, establishing both the immortal and the mortal, the divine Savitṛ travels through the worlds upon his golden chariot.
Beholding. || 9 ||
One should practice while distributing the six syllables to the six limbs, beginning with the thumb.
Then, one should perform the placement of the steps (padanyāsa) for the mantra of the universe.
Then, in place of the verses spoken in the Śrīsūkta, one should meditate upon the Sun.
He was born in the land of Kaliṅga, seated in the lotus posture, with hands like lotuses, possessing a splendor equal to the interior of a lotus, and having seven horses and seven swords. || 12 ||
Viśvāmitra is the Āryaka, Triṣṭubh is the metre, and Kāśyapa is the lineage-born.
Wearing red garments and adorned with red ornaments.
His limbs were smeared with red perfumes and unguents; he bore red banners and flags, wore a diadem and armlets, and was adorned with a red parasol.
His left side, mounted upon the chariot, is presided over by the fire-god Agni as the presiding deity.
And it should be joined with the left [hand] by the presiding deity of each [limb], facing the east.
Having meditated thus, one should worship the Sun with full-blown flowers and unbroken grains of rice.
And upon a seat made of śrīparṇa wood or similar materials, measuring twelve finger-breadths [in height].
Here, one should worship the presiding deity as well as the corresponding secondary deities;
one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with a tenth part of that number. || 17 ||
If the oblations (homa) are very few, one should perform recitation (japa) for the presiding deity and the subordinate deities, using flowers such as karavīra mixed with red sandalwood. 18.
The libation for the Lord of Day (the Sun) should be performed with dūrvā sprouts and unbroken grains of rice.
Madhucchandas is the sage, Gāyatrī is the meter, and Agni is the deity. || 19 ||
One should also proclaim the application (viniyoga) as being for the propitiation of Savitṛ. || 20 ||
I praise Agni, the domestic priest, the divine ministrant of the sacrifice, the invoker, the bestower of treasures. 21.
The sage is Vāmadeva, the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is Rudra; one should proclaim that the application (viniyoga) is for the propitiation of Savitṛ. || 22 ||
To you two kings of the sacrifice, the Rudras, I call the Hotṛ-priest who performs true worship for both worlds.
Before the thunderbolt strikes, invoke Agni, whose form is golden, for protection. || 23 ||
The fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed with *arka* fuel-sticks; in their absence, with lotus seeds (*kamalākṣaka*);
in their absence, with barley, sesame, and ghee, or with the three sweets (*madhuratra*). || 24 ||
One who has not seen the sun should not eat at night on a Sunday;
one should also renounce salt, buttermilk, sleeping during the day, and sexual intercourse.
One should recite this hymn three times a day and worship it especially; when the mantra has been thus perfected, kings shall become his servants.
By the mere water from his feet, the multitude of diseases dissolves away; even one whose mantra has been mastered, if about to die, perceives his own shadow as headless.

But a practitioner afflicted by diseases such as leprosy should offer oblations with the *ṛc*s; for the sake of health, he himself should do so with the quarters of the verses, or even with groups of three verses. (28)
Having thus sacrificed with twenty-four [oblations], one should indeed satiate the Sun.
Then, like the sun, he destroys even those who are difficult to subdue by means of the [mantras] beginning with Trikālā.
Flowers of the *karavīra*, red sandalwood and [ordinary] sandalwood, *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), tips of *kuśa* grass, and sesame seeds—these three together [are offered]. (30)
These they call the essential requirements for worship and sacrifice, each succeeding one being superior to the preceding; having placed musk, saffron, and camphor into a copper vessel, || 31 ||
Or else, with the Gāyatrī mantra, he should kneel upon the earth.
Having seen the sun and paid homage, one should offer the arghya with undistracted mind.
And one should sprinkle water upon the head with the verses (ṛcas) while the water is being offered; one should abandon everything previously mentioned, especially on Sundays.
Major diseases such as leprosy and others are brought to destruction within six months.
And those [afflictions] such as skin diseases (upakuṣṭha) and so forth, which occur even when both twilights have been observed.

Even by worshipping at a single twilight, Sūryāvarta and others have attained [success]; some, however, [attained it] in seventy days, and some in three times seven [days] through the maṇḍala. || 35 ||

Moreover, on the seventh day as well, one should investigate the gradations [of the lunar days] for a single day; one should sleep only when they have risen, and by worshipping them, one shall obtain what is desired. || 36 ||
Rising today, O Mitra, ascending to the highest heaven, O Sūrya, destroy my heart-disease and my jaundice. 37.
We place my yellowness upon the parrots, we place it upon the *ropaṇākās*; moreover, we deposit my yellowness upon the *hāridravas*. 38.
This sun has risen together with all its majesty; may it subject my enemy to me, and may I not suffer the evil of one who hates me. 39.
The sage of this hymn consisting of eleven verses is Hiraṇyastūpa.
The meters are considered to be Triṣṭubh and Jagatī, and the deity is Savitṛ. || 40 ||
I invoke Agni first for well-being; I invoke Mitra and Varuṇa here for protection.
I invoke Night, who brings rest to the world; I invoke the god Savitṛ for our protection—He who, moving through the dark realm, establishes both the immortal and the mortal.
On his golden chariot, the god Savitar travels, beholding all living beings. || 42 ||
The god goes down the slope, he goes up the ascent; the worshipful one goes with his two bright bay horses.
May the god Savitṛ come from afar, driving away all difficulties. 43.
Enveloped in pearls, multiform, with golden pins, the worshipful and great Savitṛ,
of wondrous luster, has mounted his chariot, bestowing power upon the dark regions. 44.
The dark, white-footed mares, drawing the golden-yoked chariot of the Immortal One, carry him along.
Evermore, all people and all beings abide within the lap of the divine Savitṛ. 45.
Three are the heavens of Savitar; two are his lap, and one among his worlds is the one that prevails over heroes.
Like a bolt on a chariot-pole, he stands firm upon immortality; let him who knows declare what is beyond that.
The double-winged bird has traversed the mid-air; the Asura, the good leader, is like a deep abyss.
Where now is the sun? Who can perceive it? To which heaven has his ray extended?

Hiraṇyākṣa, the god Savitṛ, has come forth, bestowing desirable treasures upon the donor; he has measured out the eight directions of the earth, three hundred yojanas across the land, and the seven rivers. (48)
Savitṛ, the golden-handed, the all-beholding, moves between both heaven and earth.
He drives away disease and brings forth the sun; with his dark radiance he reaches the sky.
May the golden-handed Asura, the good leader, the most gracious and self-reliant, come hither toward us.
Driving away the Rākṣasas and the Yātudhānas, the god has stood firm, being praised at every twilight.
Those paths of yours, O Savitṛ, which are ancient, dustless, and well-prepared in the mid-air;
By those easy paths, protect us today and speak for us, O God.
Karavīra, japā, musta, devadāru, and manaḥśilā.
With saffron, cardamom, lotus wood, madhūka flowers, and bālaka,
one who recites this mantra should daily perform a bath with water mixed with these substances for the satisfaction of the Sun,
even if the Sun is unfavorable to him. || 52-53 ||
A saffron-colored garment, gold, a ruby, or likewise a cow.
A constant devotee of the Sun-god should give either everything or one thing alone. || 54 ||
If he is unable [to fast], he should give wheat; likewise, one afflicted by the Sun should always eat food with jaggery and wear the root of the Arka plant.
Now I shall declare the mantra of Candra; Gautama is considered its sage, the Gāyatrī is said to be its single metre, and Soma is proclaimed as its deity. (56)
Swell up, O Soma; let virile strength gather from every side for you; be present at the gathering of nourishment. 57.

The six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅgaka*) is performed with the letter *sakāra* (sa) joined with the six long vowels and the bindu. Furthermore, there is the placement of the feet (*padanyāsa*): *sāṃ aṃguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*, *sīṃ tarjanībhyāṃ namaḥ*, *sūṃ madhyamābhyāṃ namaḥ*, *saiṃ anāmikābhyāṃ namaḥ*.
"Salutation to the thumbs and little fingers; salutation to the palms and backs of the hands.
In this manner, one should also perform the assignment (*nyāsa*) on the heart and other limbs. It should be performed on the limbs mentioned by Rudra and in the cardinal directions. (58)
Wearing a diadem, clad in white garments, possessing ten horses, and adorned with white ornaments.
Him with two arms, holding a noose in his hand, born of the lineage of Atri.
And he was born in the land of the Yavanas, anointed with white fragrant unguents.
Abounding with white banners and flags, it was adorned with armlets and jewels.

[The water is the presiding deity (adhidevatā) of the moon; Mā is its counter-deity (pratyadhidevatā). One should [visualize him] as having a white form, mounted upon a chariot, joined with that counter-deity, and likewise joined with the counter-deity facing the northwest (vāyavya). 61.
Having meditated thus, one should worship the Moon, accompanied by two deities, upon a square altar of twenty-four finger-breadths made with white unbroken rice grains.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; this is the procedure for all of these.
The entire procedure, beginning with the recitation (japa), for both the presiding deity and the secondary deity is as before. || 63 ||

One should satisfy [the deity] with white unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), flowers, sandalwood (*śrīkhaṇḍa*), and a conch shell, accompanied by white *dūrvā* grass; one should then offer oblations of *palāśa* wood fuel. || 64 ||
In the absence of those, however, they are prescribed for the bridegroom; if one is unable or if even that is unavailable, one should recite the mantra ten times the required number of oblations.
Medhātithi is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi), the Anuṣṭubh is cited as the meter (chandas); the waters are the deity here, and the application (viniyoga) is for the propitiation of the Moon. 66.
Soma has told me that within the waters are all healing medicines, as well as Agni, who brings welfare to all. 67.
The seer is declared to be Dīrghatamas, the meter is said to be Jagatī, the deity is proclaimed to be Umā, and the application is for the satisfaction of the Moon. 68.
Gaurī has lowed, fashioning the waters; she is one-footed, two-footed, and four-footed.
Eight-footed, ten-footed, desiring to become, thousand-syllabled, she dwells in the highest heaven.
On the full moon day, fasting, one should worship the moon in the evening.
One should offer the arghya with milk from a conch shell for the satisfaction of the God.
The hymn (sūkta) of the Moon is to be recited as before until the moon's libation;
[the worshipper becomes] peaceful, self-controlled, of good renown, illustrious, generous, and handsome. (71)
Gautama is considered the sage (ṛṣi) of this hymn consisting of twenty-three verses.
The meter is proclaimed to be Triṣṭubh, and the deity is the Moon. || 72 ||
O Soma, you are discerning through your wisdom; you lead us along the straightest path.
Through your guidance, O Soma, our wise fathers, like Indra among the gods, have shared in the treasure.
You, O Soma, have become one of excellent wisdom through your powers of will; you, the all-knowing, have become one of great skill through your abilities; you are the bull.
By means of his bull-like powers, through his greatness, and through his splendors, he, the observer of men, became resplendent. || 74 ||
Thy laws are not those of King Varuṇa; O Soma, thy domain is vast and profound.
Thou art pure, dear as a friend to us; O Soma, thou art like Aryaman, worthy of being honored. 75.
Those abodes of yours which are in heaven, those on earth, on the mountains, in the plants, and in the waters.
With all these [powers], O King Soma, being well-disposed and without malice, accept our oblations.
You, O Soma, are the lord of the good, you are the king and the slayer of Vṛtra. You are auspicious, you are the sacred will;
and you, O gracious Soma, we bring as our very life. You are the beloved one of praise, the lord of the forest.
O Soma, you bestow great fortune; you grant skill for life to the youth who follows the cosmic order. 79.
O Soma, O King, protect us from all sides against those who wish us harm; a friend like you shall not suffer ruin. 80.
O Soma, those exhilarating draughts of yours which bring bliss to the donor—with those, be our protector.
Accepting this sacrifice and this speech, come hither. O Soma, be for our prosperity; O Soma, we who know the sacred words shall exalt you with our songs. Be our benefactor.
Enter! || 83 ||
Increasing our cattle, dispelling disease, finding wealth, and increasing prosperity—O Soma, be a kind friend to us. 84.
O Soma, take delight in our hearts like cattle in the pastures, as [a husband does] in his own home. 85.
Whosoever, whether god or mortal, delights in your friendship with Soma—he is skillful and he is your seer. 86.
Protecting us from reproach, O Soma, deliver us from distress; be a most gracious friend to us. 87.
Swell up; let virile power come to you from every side, O Soma; be present at the gathering of strength. 88.
Swell up, O most exhilarating Soma, with all your rays; become for us the most glorious friend for our prosperity. 89.
May the flowing streams come together, may the strengths come together, and may the virile powers that overcome the assailants come together.
Swelling for the sake of immortality, O Soma, place in heaven the highest glories and renown.
May those abodes of yours which they worship with oblation encompass all our sacrifice.
Increasing our wealth, furthering us, accompanied by brave sons, do you, O Soma, who slay the enemy, proceed to the dwellings.
Soma bestows a milch-cow; Soma, a swift steed; Soma grants a hero who is skillful in action.
He who has offered oblations to us [obtains] a dwelling fit for the assembly, fit for the sacrificial session, and fit for the council, bringing renown to his father. 92.
In battles difficult to withstand, he is the beloved protector of the waters, the winner of the prize, and the deliverer from distress.
O Soma, may we rejoice after you, who bring victory in battle, who provide a secure dwelling, and who possess great renown.
O Soma, you have generated all these plants; you have generated the waters and the earth.
You have stretched out the wide mid-air; you have dispelled the darkness with light.
O divine Soma, with a divine mind, O powerful one, strive for our share of wealth! Let it not fail you;
you are the master of this heroic power. As the most effective healers, provide for both sides. 95.
Having cast the five products of the cow, silver, pearls, conch-shells, mother-of-pearl, and white water-lilies into the water,
one should perform a bath for the satisfaction of the Moon.
A white bull, a jar of clarified butter, a conch shell, and a vessel of bell-metal.
And according to one's means, one should offer a pearl necklace or a string of large pearls, as far as one is able. || 97 ||
One who constantly performs service to the Moon should eat milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with white, fragrant fruits, and one should wear the root of the Soma plant. 98.
Thus, whoever performs worship of the Moon and the Sun.
He, however, is capable of destroying the diseases born of the great sins (mahāpātaka). || 99 ||

One should perform the ritual application of the resolve (saṅkalpa) accompanied by white flowers; having first uttered the name of the disease, one should then recite [the mantra] for its destruction. || 100 ||

Having uttered the place, time, and so forth, preceded by the lineage (gotra), conduct (ācāra), and so on, one should then recite the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) in the genitive case, according to the ritual procedure (kalpa) and the sacred verse (ṛc). || 101 ||
"I shall offer the arghya," or he should say, "I satisfy [the deity]."
Then, having performed the binding of the topknot (śikhābandha), one should carry out the expulsion of the spirits (bhūtotsādana).
Having prayed for the earth, he should sit upon his own seat; then, with the mantra of Sudarśana, he should perform the binding of the directions.
p. 318) For the warding off of all diseases:
"Obeisance to Sudarśana, the king of weapons, the iron-arrowed Śārṅga bow.
This is the Sudarśana mantra. One should utter the word "Śārṅga."
To the King of Weapons together with his arrow—[this] Sudarśana [mantra] ending in the dative case. || 104 ||

This mantra, consisting of twenty-seven syllables ending with the heart [seed-syllable], is thus declared. Then, having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should practice the installation of the vital breaths (prāṇasthāpana). || 105 ||

Having touched one's own limbs with a *ṛc* verse, and likewise the Guru and the Supreme Guru, and having meditated upon the Guru who is higher than the highest, one should thereafter perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
"O Mitra, rising today with great splendor, place [your hand] upon my right hand; whatever has been done by me here, may Mitra protect me from that. (107)
And one should place it in the left hand while ascending to the higher heaven.
May the Sun always protect me from the sin arising from the non-performance of prescribed duties. 108.
"O Sūrya, [take] my heart-disease"; thus one should place [the mantra] in the heart. "May Sūrya always protect me from the sin committed through ignorance. (109)
One should place *harimāṇa* on the nose and above the head;
may the Sun protect me at all times from all beings. || 110 ||
May he place my jaundice upon the parrots and upon my right foot.
May the two Suns always protect me from the sin of going where one is forbidden to go. || 111 ||
In which [vessel] do we place the dye? One should apply it to the left foot.
May Pūṣan protect [him] from the sin arising from sexual union with a woman during her fertile season. || 112 ||
Then, one should place [the mantra] upon the *hāridrava* [lines] at my navel region: "May Hiraṇyagarbha always protect me from the darkness-born sin. (113)
We deposit the yellowness; one should place it upon the tongue and in the mouth.
May Marīci always protect me from the sins arising from the mouth and the tongue. || 114 ||
One should place this [mantra]—"The risen sun, may the Sun-god always protect me from the sin arising from the eyes"—upon the right eye. || 115 ||
One should place [the mantra] "viśvena sahasā saha" upon the left eye. May Savitṛ protect that which ought to be seen but was not seen from that sin. 116.
Subduing my enemy, one should place it upon the armor.
May the Sun protect me from the sin arising from [the cutting of] skin and hair. || 117 ||
Then I shall cast my sin upon the hater, and likewise upon his weapon.
May Bhāskara always protect me from the sin of causing enmity. || 118 ||
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Puruṣasūkta upon the image of the deity; then, having performed it upon one's own body as before, one should meditate upon the Sun-god. 119.
Then one should worship with the Puruṣasūkta consisting of sixteen verses.
One should employ only red flowers, along with perfumes, unbroken grains, and the like. || 120 ||
The food offering is said to be milk-rice (pāyasa); Kaṇva, known by the name Praskaṇva, is considered the sage of these three verses, the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and [the same] is the deity. || 121 ||
Then, on the white [fortnight], one should say "O Śrīsūrya, this arghya for Mitra," and likewise, on the other [dark fortnight], it is said: "I satisfy Mitra. (122)
In this same manner, it should be further conceptualized for both Ravi and Sūrya thereafter.
One should also say, "O Mitra and Ravi, this is the arghya for you," at the half-verse mark.

In this manner, the three [mantras] for all the deities should be inferred by the wise through their own intelligence. One should say "Kṛṣṇa" everywhere, but for the Sun, one should say "tarpayāmi" (I satisfy). || 124 ||

He should be fully gratified even with every kind of worship; this specific rule has been proclaimed. It must be performed on the day of the planet Mercury (Pratibhānu), and not on any other day. || 125 ||
Minor diseases are destroyed if one feeds twelve Brahmins; however, for a major disease such as a great fever characterized by coldness and other symptoms, one should feed a thousand.
When a calamity has arisen in the country, if one again offers a thousand *arghya* oblations to the Sun, all the people here become free from disease. (127)
His son, wife, and friend are born free from disease;
he attains vast prosperity and attains the Brahman that is free from ailment. || 128 ||
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, under the asterism Viśākhā, on a Friday.
The illustrious Sūrya was born from Kriyā; therefore, worship is especially distinguished there.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, under the asterism Kṛttikā and on a Thursday, the Moon was born in that field; therefore, worship there is especially distinguished. (130)
I shall now proclaim the mantra of Bhauma; Virūpa is considered its sage (ṛṣi), Aṅgāraka is its deity, and Gāyatrī is declared to be its meter. || 131 ||
Agni is the head of heaven, the summit, the lord of this earth.
He quickens the waters and the plants. || 132 ||

The six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) should be performed with the seed-syllable *am*, as well as the placement upon the fingers; the second [stage], the placement of the steps, should be performed in the locations of Rudra. || 133 ||
Clad in red garments, red in complexion, and anointed with red perfumes and unguents; being worshipped with red flowers, he has four arms and wears a crown. || 134 ||
Holding a boon-granting gesture, a shield, a mace, and a trident in his hands, he stands upon a ram.
Born of the Vasiṣṭha lineage, he was the sage Jamadagni, the son of Kuru. || 135 ||
He has the Jagatī meter as his vehicle, a curved form, and red flags and banners.
Having meditated upon the God born in the land of Avantī, one should worship Him. || 136 ||
Having prepared a triangular mandala with rice mixed with red sandalwood,
one should invoke and worship [the deity] there, together with the presiding deity Earth and the six mothers, as well as the secondary deity (pratyadhideva). || 137 ||
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, combined with the three sweets (*madhuratraya*). For the fire-oblation (*homa*), fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of *khadira* wood are used;
the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and other rites are as before. Medhātithi is the sage (*muni*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandas*), and Earth (*bhū*) is the deity (*devatā*). (138)
Be pleasant, O Earth, free from thorns, a place of rest; grant us wide-spreading shelter. May it drive away our sin with its light. 139.
The sage is declared to be Dīrghatamas, and the meter is cited as Triṣṭubh; Skanda is the deity, and the application is for the purpose of recitation to please Mars. || 140 ||
When you were first born, crying out as you rose from the ocean or from the primordial waters.
The wings of a hawk, the forelegs of a deer—great indeed is your birth, O steed worthy of praise.
A man seeking the favor of Bhauma (Mars) should consume sacrificial offerings.
One suffering from disease should always wear gojihvā on a Saturday.
When the mantra of Kujā is fully perfected, one shall be victorious in battle; enemies, appearing like fire reflected in the eye, will perish of their own accord. || 143 ||
For this hymn consisting of thirty verses, the seers are Virūpa and Aṅgiras; the meter is specified as Gāyatrī;
and the deity is Agni for the satisfaction of Kujā. (144)

Honor Agni with fuel; awaken the guest with clarified butter. As the invoker, offer the oblations into him; enjoy my hymn of praise. Grow strong through this birth, O you who take delight in the recited hymns. 146.
I place Agni at the forefront as my messenger; I invoke him, the bearer of oblations. Bring the gods here to sit upon these seats.
O Agni, the great, bright rays of you who are kindled rise up toward the heavens.
May the ladles filled with ghee, which are dear to you, approach you, O beloved one; O Agni, accept our oblations. 149.
I praise Agni, the lowing one, the priest of the sacrifice, the many-rayed, the source of light—Agni who shines like the dawn. 150.
The ancient, desirable Hotṛ-priest, the beloved Agni, the seer and the power of will.
The glory of those who are below. || 151 ||
Accepting [the offerings], O best of the Aṅgirases, bring our oblations in due order; O Agni, lead the sacrifice with wisdom. 152.
O you of bright luster, desiring our fuel, bring hither the divine folk, you who are wise.
We implore the wise Hotṛ priest, the guileless one, whose banner is smoke, the radiant one—the banner of sacrifices. 154.
O Agni, protect us; do thou ward off those who seek to harm us, O God, along with our companions and our strength, O thou who art made victorious. 155.
May Agni, the seer, together with the inspired singer, adorn our own body with his song of praise for our increase. 156.
I invoke the descent of vigor, the impetuous one, the purifier with his flame, at this well-performed sacrifice.
O Agni, you who are great like Mitra, sit upon the sacred grass (*barhis*) with the gods through your bright radiance.
He who delivers this god Agni to me—that very one shall shine forth wealth for us.
Agni is the head of heaven, the summit, and the lord of this earth.
He quickens the secret powers and the vital energies. || 160 ||
O Agni, your pure, bright, and radiant flames rise upward; your lights and your rays of splendor surge forth. 161.
For you, O Agni, Lord of Light, are the master of the gift of desirable wealth; may your praiser abide in your protection. 162.
O Agni, the wise ones impel you with their insights; may our songs increase your strength. 163.
We firmly maintain friendship with Agni, who is ever the messenger of the one rushing along the paths, running forward from afar. 164.
Agni, whose vows are most pure, is pure; he is the pure sage. Pure, he shines brightly when offered oblations. 165.
And may my songs ever increase your strength; O Agni, be mindful of our friendship. 166.
O Agni, whether it be my greatness or whether it be yours, may there be blessings here through the fulfillment of our prayers. 167.
For you are a Vasu, the lord of wealth; you are the radiant one at the beginning. May we abide in your benevolence.
O Agni, for you whose vows are steadfast, our songs surge forth like rivers toward the ocean;
we adorn Agni with our hymns—the youthful lord of the people, the seer, who is ever-present and swift to hear. 170.
For the charioteer of sacrifices, for the one with sharp teeth and fierce roar—[we pray] for nourishment with hymns to Agni. O Agni, let this singer be dear to you; be gracious to him, O Purifier.
For his wise protector is ever victorious and never sleeps; O Agni, shine forth at every dawn, before calamities and before battles, O Sage! May he extend our life and all our strength. [Ginger.
