Sandalwood, asafoetida, and *asanapuṣpa* [asafoetida]. [Asafoetida.]
A bath with *phalinī* and *bakula* flowers brings satisfaction to Mars. || 175 ||
Tāmra is produced from reddish water, while pravāla and masūrikā are coral.
A deep red garment for Tuṣṭi, and the flower of the aśvārī plant for Puṣṭi. || 176 ||
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, under the lunar mansion named Pūrvāṣāḍhā and on a Wednesday, he was born; a great festival was held there on that occasion. (177)
I shall now proclaim the mantra of Buddha; its sage is considered to be Bauddha. Its meter is Triṣṭubh, and its deity is Buddha, who is regarded as the bestower of wisdom. || 178 ||
Awake, O Agni! Be watchful! May you two unite this sacrifice with the merit of past rites and future offerings.
O All-Gods and the sacrificer, sit down together upon this higher common seat.
(179) His meditation is described by means of the seed-syllable *bum* and the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*): [he is] clad in yellow garments...
Yellow in color, anointed with yellow perfumes and unguents. || 180 ||
He was being worshipped with yellow flowers; he held a sword, a shield, a mace, and a lotus in his hands, and he was born of the Atri lineage. 181.
The descendant of Bharadvāja was born in Ārṣaka, and Kirīṭin was born in Magadha.
It was adorned with the Bṛhatī meter as its canopy, and possessed umbrellas, banners, and flags. || 182 ||
I meditate upon Mercury, who is enriched by the splendor of the jewels on his armlets, joined with Viṣṇu as his presiding deity and with that [deity] as his counter-presiding deity. || 183 ||
Having meditated thus upon the square mandala shaped like an arrow, fashioned from turmeric and *akṣata* rice, one should duly invoke and worship Jña (Budha). 184.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times according to its syllables and perform the fire oblation (homa) with a tenth part of that number.
Then one should perform the libations with fuel-sticks of Apāmārga.
That Viṣṇu who is named Trivikrama is the presiding deity of Mercury.
The sage Medhātithi is declared to be its seer, and the Gāyatrī is said to be its metre. || 186 ||
Vishnu strode across this [universe]; he established his foot in three places upon the gathered dust. Svāhā! || 187 ||
Now, as for the presiding deity of each [element], it is Viṣṇu, known by the name Nārāyaṇa.
The sage is declared to be Dīrghatamas, and the meter is said to be Triṣṭubh. || 188 ||
I shall now proclaim the heroic deeds of Viṣṇu, who measured out the earthly realms;
he who, the wide-striding one, propped up the highest station as he strode across the three worlds in three steps. 189.
One should eat milk-rice, but never a gourd;
one should not wear soiled clothing, nor likewise the matted locks made from the wood of the vṛddhadāru tree.
When the mantra of Budha is fully accomplished, one becomes eloquent and wise; invincible against adversaries, he himself becomes a conqueror in this world. || 191 ||
In this hymn of twelve verses, the Viśvedevas are the deities and likewise the Ṛṣis;
the meters are Bṛhatī, Triṣṭubh, Jagatī, and Gāyatrī. || 192 ||
Awake with one mind, O friends; kindle Agni together, you many who are united.
For the sake of wealth, I invoke for you Dadhikrā, Agni, and the goddess Uṣas, along with Indra. 193.
Make the chants resonant; extend the prayers; make the boat one that carries us across with its oars.
Prepare the path; make it a continuous stream. Lead the sacrifice forward, O friends! (194)
Yoke the ploughs, stretch out the poles; when the furrow is prepared, sow the seed here. Through our song, may the harvest-yielding rain come to us;
may the ripened grain approach even closer than the sickle.
The wise yoke the ploughs; they stretch out the yokes separately, the steadfast ones, seeking favor among the gods. 196.
Make it free from leakage; provide it with a secure fastening. Let us pour from the well that holds water, which is well-supplied and overflowing. 197.
I pour out the well-prepared, inviting, well-clothed, and easy-to-drink [milk], full of water and inexhaustible. 198.
Satisfy the horses, for then you shall conquer; thus make the chariot one that carries you safely.
Pour out the water-jars, the stone wheel, and the leather buckets for the kings! Let them flow down to the lowest depth.
Prepare the cow-pen, for you are the protectors of men; sew together many wide shields.
Make iron fortresses, unassailable; let not your vessel leak, but make it firm. 200.

O divine gods, worthy of sacrifice, turn our prayer toward this rite for our protection; may that great goddess, worthy of worship, yield for us like a cow who has come for our aid—a mighty cow with a thousand streams of milk. (201)
Sprinkle the tawny one with water upon the lap of Indra, and fashion him with stone-made axes.
Embrace both poles with ten girth-straps; yoke the two draft-animals to the pole.
The draft-animal, being bound to both poles, moves within like a bird in its nest.
Establish the Lord of the Forest in the wood; sit down and dig out the spring.
O men, bestow the prize-winning steed upon us; urge him on and strike for the winning of the spoil.
O Nishṭigrya, urge on your son; let him, a subduer of foes, come here for the drinking of Soma with Indra.
Harītakī, with *kaliphala*, cow dung, *akṣata*, and *rocanā* [or *vidhītaka*], combined with gold, *āmalaka*, and pearls, along with honey—what water [is not purified] by this?
As it has been said: "In the head, the mind, water, the body, the mouth, Brahman, and the vital breath; in desire..."
The word *kāśa* denotes time, gold, wealth, and sound.
Thus, in the *Anekārthadhvanimañjarīkośa*: "snapet" [should be read as] "snapayet" || 205 ||
One should give blue cloth, mung-bean rice, gold,
and woolen cloth for the pleasure of Mercury, or else offer *mālatī* flowers.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Nabhasya, on a Monday, Budha was born to Tārā from the Moon;
this is his festival here.
I shall declare the mantra of Bṛhaspati; its sage is Gṛtsamada, its meter is Triṣṭubh, and its deity is indeed the Lord of the Gods (Indra). || 208 ||
O Bṛhaspati, that which surpasses the enemy, worthy of honor, resplendent, and full of wisdom, shines among the people.
That which has shone forth as the Truth born of power—bestow that wonderful wealth upon us.
One should perform the six-limbed nyāsa and other rites here using the seed-syllable *bṛm*. Listen, for I shall now describe the meditation upon this Bṛhaspati. (210)
The god holds a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), bestows boons, and carries a staff and a rosary; he is yellow in color and resplendent with a golden crown. || 211 ||
To the noble Vasiṣṭha, born in the land of Sindhu, who was clothed in yellow garments.
It has the Anuṣṭubh meter, belongs to the Aṅgiras lineage, and is praised by the gods.
Abounding with banners and flags, it was adorned with yellow parasols and ointments.
Abounding in the splendor of armlets and bracelets, it was joined with the presiding deity of Indra.
Having meditated upon him as joined with Brahmā as the presiding deity, one should invoke him. || 313 ||
In a long square measuring six finger-breadths, fashioned with mantras.
One should worship him in a mandala prepared with turmeric and unbroken grains (akṣata). || 214 ||

One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with *pippala* wood sticks mixed with the three sweets, and the libation (tarpaṇa) with five yellow flowers. || 215 ||
The sage is Gṛtsamada, the metre is Triṣṭubh, and Indra is the deity. || 216 ||
The higher conception consists in the application [of oneself] for the satisfaction of that Guru. || 217 ||
O Indra, bestow upon us the most excellent riches, the insight of wisdom, and good fortune;
grant us the increase of wealth, the safety of our bodies, the sweetness of speech, and the auspiciousness of our days. 218.
The sage is said to be Gṛtsamada, the deity is Brahmaṇaspati, the metre is Triṣṭubh, and this is declared to be the presiding deity of the Guru. || 219 ||
O Lord of Prayer, you are the controller of this inspired hymn; quicken the son of the awakener.
All that is auspicious which the gods protect; may you, O Bṛhadvad, proclaim it for me, O seekers of light.
He should give curd-rice, gold, yellow garments, and so forth; he should always wear [the mantra] on his arm, but he should maintain the root-mantra of Brahmā.

When the mantra of the Guru has been thus perfected, the perfection of speech arises; there is the manifestation of power within the body, or the comprehension of meaning through one's own power. || 222 ||
(324) Vāmadeva is considered the sage (ṛṣi) of this hymn consisting of eleven verses; Jagatī is said to be the meter, and Bṛhaspati is the deity here. || 223 ||
Bṛhaspati, who stands in the three seats, has by his roar swiftly propped apart the ends of the earth;
him, the ancient seers, the inspired poets of old, meditating with fervor, established as one whose tongue is resonant.
O Bṛhaspati, those who shake the world, rejoicing in their clear insight, have extended their praise toward you.
O drops, bestow the moving, gliding, and powerful [soma] upon the womb of Bṛhaspati, which is protected by him.
O Bṛhaspati, from that highest distance, the touchers of *ṛta* have sat down.
For you the wells and springs dug by Atri flow with milked sweetness on every side, rich in poison.
Being born as the lowest [priest] for Bṛhaspati, [he rose] from the great light in the highest heaven.
Seven were born from her by means of his roar; with seven rays, the Sun dispelled the darkness.
With his well-praising, hymn-chanting host, he shattered the fruit-bearing forest with his roar;
Bṛhaspati, through his splendor, impelled the lowing cows that yield the oblation.
Thus let us worship the Father, the bull of all the gods, with sacrifices, with the mind, and with oblations.
O Bṛhaspati, may we have excellent offspring and heroic sons; may we be masters of riches.
That Indra, the king, has established all things born of the intellect through his vital strength and heroic power.
He who supports the well-performing Bṛhaspati, praises him, and honors him as the one who receives the first portion.
He dwells there, well-established in his abodes; for him, the white one, the nourishing food is always ready at every time.

To him the subjects bow down of their own accord, he upon whom the royal power preceded by the sacred word (*brahman*) rests. Unopposed, he conquers the treasures of his enemies as well as those of his own kin. The gods protect that king who, being heroic, bestows gifts upon the suppliant who possesses the sacred word.
Indra and Bṛhaspati, rejoicing at this sacrifice, purify the Soma, O you who possess bull-like wealth. May the waters enter us; bestowing upon us wealth consisting of all-heroic sons, grant it to us.
O Bṛhaspati and Indra, strengthen us; may that benevolence of yours both be with us.
He has entered our thoughts, he has seized the stronghold with his wisdom; the enemy of those who strive has been struck down by the arrow.
The sprouts of the *madayantī*, the *madhūka* flower, and white mustard seeds.
One should also satisfy the guru with a bath using *mālatī* flowers. || 234 ||
Turmeric, sugar, yellow cloth, gold, and brass should be given for the satisfaction of Guru;
in their absence, chickpeas may likewise be offered. || 235 ||
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, under the Puṣya asterism and on a Friday, when Jupiter is born, his festival should be celebrated there. || 236 ||
I shall proclaim the Śukra-mantra; Bharadvāja is considered the sage (ṛṣi), Triṣṭubh is declared the meter (chandas), and the preceptor of the Daityas is the deity (daivata). || 237 ||
One of your forms is bright, the other is worthy of sacrifice; on two days of different appearance you are like the sky.
For you protect all wondrous powers, O self-dependent one; auspicious is your bounty here, O Pūṣan. 238.

Having performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the seed-syllable *śuṃ*, one should perform the meditation: [He is] clad in white garments, white in color, and anointed with white perfumes and unguents. (239)
He saw the son of Śunaka, adorned with a crown, being worshipped with white flowers; he had four arms and carried a staff, a rosary, and a water-pot. || 240 ||
[This word "paṅkti," though ending in a vowel, is treated as ending in a consonant (d) due to Vedic usage. Likewise, one should worship Varada and the one born in the Kīkaṭa country.
He possessed white umbrellas, banners, and flags, and was born of the Bhārgava lineage.
Having thus meditated upon him wearing armlets, mounted on a chariot, and adorned with white ornaments, within a white-colored, five-cornered [mandala] measuring nine finger-breadths; || 242 ||

Indrāṇī is the presiding deity (adhidaivata), and Śakra is the counter-presiding deity (pratyadhidaivata). Then, one should worship the preceptor of the Daityas together with those two within the mandala. || 243 ||
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with fuel-sticks of the Udumbara tree mixed with the three sweets;
the libations and other rites, however, are like those for the Moon. || 244 ||
The sage is declared to be Vṛṣākapi; the meter is cited as Pakti; Indrāṇī is declared the deity; the application is for the satisfaction of Śukra. || 245 ||
Among these women, I have heard that Indrāṇī is the most fortunate; for her husband shall never die from old age nor by any other cause. Indra is superior to all. 246.
Madhucchandā is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi), the Gāyatrī is said to be the meter (chanda), and Śukra is its presiding deity; this is the injunction for the satisfaction of Viśvataḥśukra. || 247 ||
We invoke Indra for you from all sides, setting him apart from other people; may he belong exclusively to us.
For the constant satisfaction of Śukra, one should eat prepared rice; one should wear white garments and carry the root of a sage, namely the root of Agastya. || 249 ||
When the Śukra-mantra has been mastered, the signs will be that women come under one's control.
Success in one's journey, renown, and the subjugation of internal kings shall occur. || 250 ||
For the hymn of the Nigama-Ṛc, the sage is considered to be Bharadvāja.
The Triṣṭubh and Jagatī are the meters, and Pūṣan is said to be the deity. || 251 ||
One [form] of yours is the seed, the other is the sacrificial offering; you are like the sky on two days of different forms.

For you protect all wondrous powers; your self-sustaining power is auspicious, O Pūṣan, and here is your bounty. Goat-faced, the winner of cattle, you have quickened the prayer; you are established throughout the entire world. 252
O Pūṣan, you are the goad; driving away the parched earth, the god moves along, surveying all the worlds. || 253 ||
O Pūṣan, those golden ships of yours which move within the ocean;
Or rather, by means of those [verses], we desire that the fame of Sūrya be established through his own will. || 254 ||
Pūṣan is the close kinsman of heaven and earth, the lord of nourishment, the bounteous one whose splendor overcomes the Dasyus.
O gods, that which you gave to Sūryā was the desire-fulfilling [gift] of the powerful one. 255.
Triphalā with its roots, elā, keśara, and manaḥśilā;
One should bathe with these waters for the satisfaction of Bhārgava.
A white horse, as well as silver, sandalwood, and white clothing;
One should offer clarified butter for the satisfaction of Śukra; in its absence, however, one should offer rice grains.

And on the ninth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Madhu, Rāma Bhārgava was born; furthermore, Rāma [Dāśarathi] was born under the asterism Punarvasu when Venus was in Maghā—this is the interval between them. || 258 ||
I shall now proclaim the mantra of Śani; Sindhudvipa is considered the sage (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is said to be the meter (chandas), and the deity is Śanaiścara. || 259 ||
May the divine waters be auspicious for our protection and for our drinking; may they flow toward us for our well-being. 260.

One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the seed-syllable *Śam*, and then one should practice meditation: [one should meditate on the deity] who is seated upon a moon, bearing a trident, possessing a luster like sapphire, born in the land of Saurāṣṭra, the bestower of boons, and having a vulture as his vehicle. (261)
He was of the Kāśyapa lineage, adorned with a crown bearing the crest-jewel of Bhṛgu.
He was dressed in black garments, was black in complexion, and was anointed with black perfumes.
The god whose meter is Gāyatrī, adorned with black ornaments.
Wearing armlets and a crown, and likewise clothed in black garments.

Having meditated upon [the deity] seated upon a lotus together with Prajāpati as the presiding deity (adhideva), and joined with the lotus as the counter-presiding deity (pratyadhideva), one should worship him. || 263 ||
In a mandala fashioned from black powder mixed with musk, |||
The fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with *śamī* fuel-sticks, and the libation (tarpaṇa) with an iron arrowhead.
One should offer sandalwood with black flowers, and aloe-wood with *kālīya* flowers.

The sage is Hiraṇyagarbha, and the Triṣṭubh meter is declared for this [mantra]. Its application is for the sake of pleasing Śani and for the destruction of various afflictions. One should recite the mantra "brahma jajñānam" here. || 265 ||
Press the Soma for Yama; offer the oblation to Yama. To Yama indeed goes the sacrifice, well-prepared, with Agni as its messenger. 266.

A man who is a constant devotee of Śani should eat *kṛśara* (rice and pulse porridge). The roots of the *vyāghrī* (or *śrībṛhatī*) plant should be worn around the neck, and anointing the body with oil should be performed daily.
When the mantra of Śani is mastered, all mantras are mastered for him.
All diseases perish by a mere blowing upon them. || 268 ||
For this hymn of nine verses, Sindhudvīpa is considered the sage; it is proclaimed that its meter is Anuṣṭubh, and its application is for the purpose of binding or for firm establishment. || 269 ||
The meters are the deities, the waters are the application for the satisfaction of Śani.
For one who recites these nine verses, the evil born of desire is destroyed. (270)

O most purifying waters, you who bring well-being, grant us strength for our nourishment. Grant us a share here of that most auspicious essence of yours, so that we may behold great delight. Like longing mothers, come to him whose dwelling you quicken; O Waters, give birth to him.
May the divine waters be auspicious for our protection and for our drinking; may they flow toward us for our well-being and prosperity. (274)
The sovereigns of precious things, who dwell among the people—I beg the waters for medicine. 275.
Within the waters, Soma has declared to me all healing remedies, as well as Agni, who brings welfare to all. 276.
O Waters, bestow healing medicine as a protection for my body, so that I may long behold the sun.
O Waters, carry away whatever evil is in me—whatever wrong I have committed, or whatever falsehood I have spoken. (278)
I have followed after the waters today; we have united with their essence. O Agni, come hither full of milk;
endow me with that splendor. 279.

Rasāñjana, black sesame seeds, śatapuṣpā, ghana (cloud), balā, and water mixed with lajjālū and lodhra— bathing with these brings joy to Śani. Black cows, buffaloes, iron, oil, and lead bring him satisfaction.
If one is unable [to give the prescribed gift], one should give iron or even maraṭas for Saturn.

On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha, on the day of Asṛk (the blood-constellation), when Rohiṇī was conjoined with the Sun, Śani was born; worship of him therein leads to joy. (282) I shall now proclaim the mantra of Rāhu; Vāmadeva is considered the sage, and Gāyatrī the metre.
Thus it was said; however, the deity is Saiṃhikeya. || 283 ||
With what aid will he, our wondrous friend who ever prospers us, come to us? With what most powerful host? (284)
The six limbs [of the deity] are formed with the seed-syllable *rāṃ*; now his meditation is described: he has a terrifying face and holds a great sword, shield, and trident. 285.
He was dressed in black garments, was black in complexion, and was anointed with black fragrant unguents.
He was being worshipped with black flowers, adorned with armlets and a crown.
The cruel mustard oil from Āntīra, produced in the eastern region.
Born of the Pāṭalī lineage, it is composed in the Anuṣṭubh meter and constitutes a compendium. || 287 ||
Mounted upon a chariot with a black umbrella, and possessing a black banner and pennants.
It is joined with the serpent as its presiding deity (adhidevatā) and Time as its secondary presiding deity (pratyadhidaivata). || 288 ||
Having reflected thus, [he should worship] in the southwest, in a mandala shaped like a crocodile.
One should worship with blue akṣata grains on a surface twelve finger-breadths wide. || 289 ||

The fire-oblation for him is prescribed with dūrvā grass smeared with honey; here, the libations and other rites should be performed with these substances, and he should gratify the Kaulika Brahmins. || 290 ||
The sage is declared to be the King of Serpents (Sarparāja), the meter is said to be Gāyatrī, and the deities are said to be the serpents; the application is for the satisfaction of Rāhu. || 291 ||
This spotted bull has come; he has gone before his mother and his father, proceeding toward heaven. 292.
The sage is declared to be Kaṇva-ācārya; the meter is said to be Gāyatrī; the deity shall be Time (Kāla); and the application is for the propitiation of Rāhu. || 293 ||
May Nirṛti, who is difficult to overcome, not strike down those who have gone far away, together with their craving for what is desired. (294) p. 328)
One should always eat black gram (māṣa) and wear the root of dūrvā grass; one should not revile those engaged in censurable actions and should perform the ritual release of captive birds. || 295 ||
When the mantra of Rāhu is perfected, the Daityas, Rākṣasas, and Guhyakas always carry out the command of the practitioner, and victory in battle is assured. || 296 ||
For this hymn of fifteen verses, Vāmadeva is considered the sage;
the metre is Nivṛt-gāyatrī, and the deity is the Leader of the Gods (Śiva). || 297 ||
By what means has he, the wonderful, ever-prospering friend, become our messenger? By what most powerful assembly is he encompassed? 298.
Which true one among the exhilarations, most delightful, shall intoxicate me with the soma-juice? He who breaks open even the firmest wealth. 299.
Be the protector of your friends and the guardian of those who sing your praises; may you be present with a hundred aids. Turn toward us, like an unobstructed wheel that has not been turned back.
Not by the weapons of the people. || 301 ||
For with great power, O Mahādeva, you go forth; I have been consumed by the Sun, and he too.

O Indra, your wrathful powers have been stirred; the wheels have rolled together. Even when the sun had sunk below, you sped forth; for they call you, O Lord of Might, the bountiful Maghavan, the giver who shines with undiminished luster.
Therefore, to him who exerts himself and presses the soma, you, the Vasu, instantly bestow great wealth upon the one who strives for glory.
The Asuras chose a hundred forest-dwellers for Mahīṣmati; they will not cause his vital breaths to fail. 306.
May your hundred aids protect us, may your thousand protections guard us; may all our desires be fulfilled for us. 307.
Choose us here for friendship and for well-being—for great wealth and for divine wisdom. O Indra, grant us all-encompassing wealth from every side.
With all your protections, [protect] us. || 309 ||
Grant us those waters from the dwelling place of the sun, which are rich in cattle.
With the nine protections of Indra. || 310 ||
May our chariot, bold and radiant, O Indra, be unshakable.
From the city of Gavyūtapura. || 311 ||
O Sūrya, among the gods, establish for us supreme renown, as lofty as the highest heaven above. 312.
By means of betel vine, *nāgabalā*, *kumārī*, *cakrā*, and *bhāskara*.
A bath with vacā, guḍūcī, and tagara should be performed using four vessels.
One should give lead, woolen cloth, gold, and a sheep for the sake of satisfaction.
In the absence of this [Rāhu], however, one should cause three pieces of *guggulu* from Tripura to be offered;
[the meaning is that "three pieces" refers to the second member of the compound in the bahuvrīhi].
On the full moon day of Āśvina, under the asterism Bharaṇī, [one should worship] the son of Siṃhikā.
He caused him to be born therein; one should worship him with special reverence for the sake of joy. || 315 ||
I shall now proclaim the Ketu-mantra; Madhucchandas is considered its sage (ṛṣi), the Ketus are declared its deity, and the Gāyatrī is said to be its meter. || 316 ||
Making a banner for the bannerless, O men, providing form for the formless.
You were born together with the dawns. || 317 ||
The six limbs are performed with the seed-syllable KAṂ; the meditation here is now described.
With arms like those of Dhūmrākṣa, they held nooses and possessed distorted faces. || 318 ||
Wearing crowns, borne by vultures, born in the Middle Country, and firm.
They were clad in variegated garments, possessed diverse colors, and were anointed with fragrant perfumes. || 319 ||
The first [group], consisting of various meters, comprises the Gotamas and those born of the Jaimini lineage; they bear black and tawny banners and flags, and likewise wear crowns.
Wearing armlets and mounted upon chariots, they were massive, with Brahmā as their presiding deity.
And one should contemplate the secondary deities known as Citragupta and the others. || 321 ||
When a mandala in the shape of a banner, measuring one and a half finger-breadths, has been made in the northwest;
Having invoked [the deity] there with multicolored unbroken grains and flowers, one should worship him. || 322 ||
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform an oblation of kuśa grass.
One should worship with various substances combined with the three sweets (madhuratraya). || 323 ||
The sage is declared to be Vāmadeva, and the meter is cited as Triṣṭubh; Brahmā is its deity, and the application is for the propitiation of Ketu. || 324 ||
The knowledge of Brahman, first born in the east, Vena revealed from the boundless, shining expanse.
The comparisons for this are "sabundhyā," and it reveals the source of both the existent and the non-existent.
Praskaṇva is declared to be the sage; the Bṛhatī is said to be the meter; Citragupta is the deity here; and the application is for the satisfaction of Ketu. 225–226.
O Uṣas, bring us splendid strength among the human race;
with that [strength], bring the well-performed sacrifices to us—the priests who sing your praises.
He should always wear the dress of a Brahmin and should never sit on a lower seat.
One who is intent on serving the Ketu should not eat food that has been burnt or otherwise spoiled.
When the mantra of Ketumān is perfected, the sign is universal respect; however, that supreme practitioner remains hidden in many ways and is not visible.
The sage of this ten-verse hymn (sūkta) is remembered as Madhucchandas; its deities are Candra and the Maruts, and the meter is said to be Gāyatrī. || 330 ||
They harness the ruddy, rushing steed who moves about; those who stand around him behold him. The luminaries shine in the sky. 331.
With the creatures dwelling in the hollows of the wood, and with Indra and Agni within the cave, you found the splendor along with them.
Seeking the gods according to their wisdom, the Giris have approached the possessor of wealth;

they have praised the great one, the swift-moving, for he is indeed seen by the fearless sacrificer. O you who are joyous, moving among men, blameless ones, overcome the swift [foes] with these [songs]; strike them down, consume them, and destroy their splendor with the hosts of Indra.
By means of those rites performed for specific desires. || 335 ||
Therefore, O all-pervading one, come hither from the luminous realm of heaven; our songs of praise find delight in you alone.
From here we invoke the god, whether he be from the earthly realm or from the great expanse of the mid-air. (337)
Sahadevī, lajjālubalā, mustā, and priyaṅgu;
By bathing in water prepared with this, the Fire-god is always propitiated. (338)
One should give woolen cloth, a goat, a banner, and a small flag—yellow in appearance—for the satisfaction of Ketu, or alternatively, one may give black gram (rājamāṣaka). || 339 ||
In the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, during the asterism Raudra (Ārdrā), the comets appeared; therefore, the great festival of the comets should be performed on a Sunday. || 340 ||
Thus has the worship of the planets been described according to the Vedic path; for those who perform it constantly, success rests in the palm of their hand. || 341 ||
For those whose nature is to propitiate the planets, there shall be happiness in this world and in the next; what more need I say? Let the deities themselves declare it here. || 342 ||
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, concerning the method of describing the nine planets, in the Merutantra composed by Śiva with the approval of the illustrious Mahāmāyā and Mahākāla. || 13 ||
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, if a mantra is given by a wise preceptor out of greed, then suffering is obtained from it. || 1 ||
Then, O Lord, what should be done when happiness does not arise, so that happiness may be obtained both in this world and in the next? (2)
The illustrious Mahādeva said:
O Goddess, in the Kali age, spiritual teachers are generally possessed by greed.
For disciples who desire happiness but lack devotion do not attain success anywhere.
Therefore, the grasping of mantras through mere effort leads only to suffering;
for that purpose, I shall explain that which is hidden in all the tantras. || 4 ||
Having first performed the abandonment of the mantra, one should resort to Pratyāṅgirā.
I shall describe the procedure for the renunciation of mantras, by which happiness is produced.
Having recognized him as a learned Brāhmaṇa, fully established in the Tantras.
Having gone to his house in the morning, one should report one's own suffering.
Then, he should perform the supreme rite for the renunciation of the mantra. First, in a beautiful dwelling, he should prepare the water-pot according to the rules of initiation.
Having placed it within the mandala, it should be joined with auspicious waters from sacred fords (tīrtha).
Having invoked one's chosen deity there with the mantra of the reverse tantra, || 8 ||

Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa and having worshipped [the deity], one should worship the surrounding deities (āvaraṇa). Thus, the practitioner of mantra, having thoroughly worshipped the chosen deity together with its retinue, [should proceed].
Then, with the *hunedviloma* mantra, one should offer a thousand oblations of cow-flesh, or one hundred and eight;
thereafter, one should satisfy that [deity] with libations.
By means of the offering to Brahman—

[that which is performed] with the mind, speech, or action, internally or through the stomach or the generative organ, during the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, and throughout the authority of the vital breaths, intellect, body, and dharma— whatever [is done].
Whatever has been remembered, whatever has been spoken, and whatever has been done—all that becomes an offering to Brahman;
*bhūḥ svāhā*. Then, one should offer the *bali* to the deities with the *manu*.
And with barley-meals and milk-rice, [he should worship] in the cardinal and intermediate directions, below and above. || 11 ||
"Come, O Indra, Lord of the Suras, Śatamanyu, Lord of Śacī! Salutations to you;
accept this offering of flowers, incense, and other gifts. (12)
Come, O Lord, with your splendor, O bearer of oblations, bestower of boons! Accept these flowers, incense, and other offerings presented as this bali.
O Lord of the Pretas, come here, you who possess a luster like crushed collyrium! Accept this bali offering and, being well-pleased, become a granter of boons. 14.
Salutations to you, O Lord of the Rakshasas, Nirṛti; you have come here. Accept this offering, worship, and other gifts presented by me with devotion. 15.
Come, O Guardian of the Western Quarter, Lord of the Waters; salutations unto you! Accepting this worship offered with devotion, may you attain happiness. || 16 ||
O Prabhāñjana, Lord of Life, come here with your retinue; accept with respect this offering presented by me according to the prescribed rite. || 17 ||
"May Kubera and the Lord of the Stars (Rudra), those best of gods, come here; being pleased by flowers, incense, and other offerings, may they grant me boons. (18)
O Lord, come, O Blessed One, refuge of all knowledge, O Master!
Honored with flowers, incense, and other offerings, be pleased for the sake of our prosperity. 19.
Come, O Lord of all worlds, O Brahmā; accept this worship, O foremost of all Brahmins! Salutations to you, the Creator of the universe. (20)
Come, O best of givers of boons, O Viṣṇu, leader of the universe! Being worshipped with supreme devotion, may you become the bestower of happiness upon me. 21.
Then, whoever should worship the deity of the mantra along with his retinue using flowers, incense, and offerings, but with the mantra reversed; || 22 ||
Then the wise one should pray to the worshipped deity of the mantra.
Having considered the secondary alternatives and so forth, this was done by me of unsteady intellect. || 23 ||
The mantra, when appropriated, bestows suffering; remove that defect. May my sin be destroyed, and may there be eternal welfare for me. (24)
"May devotion alone, which is purifying, extend my welfare"—having thus prayed to the Lord of Mantras, one should [place] the mantra in reverse order upon the yantra. || 25 ||
Having drawn [the design] with black aloe-wood, camphor, and sandalwood paste, one should offer it, placing it upon the water-pot (kalaśa) while endowed with supreme devotion. || 26 ||
Having bound that machine to one's own head, one should bathe with water from a jar.
Furthermore, one should fill another jar with waters purified by mantras. || 27 ||
Having placed the mantra and the yantra within it, one should then fill that pitcher [with water] from a river or in some other pure reservoir. || 28 ||
Then he should dismiss the Brahmins and honor them according to his capacity. For one who has thus performed this difficult rite, the affliction of the mind [is removed]. (29)
They perish without a doubt, and through this process, clarity of mind gradually arises.
It is born exceedingly prosperous, and that family always flourishes. || 30 ||
Now I shall describe Pratyāṅgirā, who is the very essence and the bestower of happiness; by the mere glance of one devoted to her, the spirits, ghosts, and presiding deities [are subdued]. (31)
Sometimes they do not approach; yet the accomplishment of the goal is produced. It bestows peace, nourishment, and prosperity upon the practitioner. (32)
One who knows the two families, the self, and so forth; who is skilled in the knowledge of the meaning of mantras; who is endowed with right conduct;
and who is pure in speech as well as in mind—(such a person is qualified). || 33 ||
With a tranquil intellect and a serene soul, he has conquered anger and subdued his senses.
Free from hypocrisy, egoism, delusion, and the like, he was the foremost among those possessing knowledge.
Established in the yoga of meditation, he is the accomplisher of all desired goals.
Having obtained this king of mantras, he becomes a lord of the earth. || 35 ||
Now I shall explain the ritual application (viniyoga) as well as the forty verses: Pratyaṅgirā is declared to be the sage (ṛṣi), and Anuṣṭubh is proclaimed to be the meter (chandas). || 36 ||
Whether it be the fierce deity Kṛtyā, or Mahādeva, or Hari—such is the application [of this mantra] in all one's desired objectives. || 37 ||

First, for the sake of purifying the body, one should perform the Prājāpatya vow; having purified it with water mixed with Kuśa grass, one should further purify it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

While consuming the sacrificial oblation (caru) consisting of sacred food, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Then, after three days, the perfected mantra should be employed in ritual activities. || 39 ||
Having fully understood the ritual procedure for the guardians of the directions, the mudrās, the seats, and the sprouts, one should recite the excellent mantra.
Otherwise, his mantra will not attain success; for this king of mantras is indeed eternally pure.
One shall leap over all adversaries, and indeed that which is desired comes to pass.
However, a mantra employed against a Brāhmaṇa becomes contrary in its result. || 41 ||

Whether at the beginning of recitation (japa), at the commencement of a ritual application (prayoga), or likewise during preparatory rites (puraścaryā), one should first perform a rite of pacification (śānti); its procedure is now declared. || 42 ||
The sage is Bārhaspatya Śānti, the Viśvedevas are considered the deities, and the meter is said to be Śakvarī; its application is for the purpose of pacification. || 43 ||
We choose that auspiciousness for our bodies, a path for the sacrifice, a path for the Lord of Sacrifice;
may divine well-being be ours. 44.
May there be well-being for human beings; may the healing medicine ascend upward. May there be peace for our bipeds and peace for our quadrupeds. 45.
Homage to Brahman; homage be to Agni. Homage to the Earth, homage to the plants;
homage to Vācaspati, homage to the great Viṣṇu I offer. May our mind be auspicious even toward the wind. 47.
Uttering "Śānti" at the end of the mantra, preceded by the three Tārās.
Having recited the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times, one should perform the ritual action.
Furthermore, at the conclusion of the ritual action, one should likewise perform this and complete the rite. For all mantras, the seed syllable is *oṃ* and the power (*śakti*) here is *hrīṃ*.
All [mantras] should be recited encased by *tāra* (oṃ) and *māyā* (hrīṃ), for they will not succeed if recited alone;
this is the definitive conclusion regarding mantras in the tantras.
The two Aśvins are declared to be the sages (*ṛṣi*), and the *anuṣṭubh* is said to be the meter (*chandas*). Thus it is here... [kṛtyātra]
And the deity is his command for the attainment of desired success. || 51 ||
Of this mantra, Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the *anuṣṭubh* is the meter (*chandaḥ*),
Pratyaṅgirā is the deity (*devatā*), *hrīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *kṛtyānāśane* (for the destruction of sorcery) is the application (*viniyoga*).
This thirty-seven-syllabled mantra is encapsulated by the two seed-syllables *oṃ* and *hrīṃ*.

It is as follows: one should perform the *aṅganyāsa* with mantras consisting of eight, three, four, four, five, and eight syllables, beginning with the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) and ending with *hrīṃ*. For example: *oṃ yāṃ kalpayanti norayaḥ hrīṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*; *oṃ krūrāṃ kṛtyāṃ...* [and so forth].

*Hrīṃ*, svāhā to the head; *oṃ vadhūmiva hrīṃ*, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock (*śikhā*); *oṃ tāṃ brahmaṇā hrīṃ*, huṃ to the armor (*kavaca*); *oṃ apanirṇughna hrīṃ*, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes (*netratraya*); *oṃ pratyakkartāramṛcchatu hrīṃ*, phaṭ to the weapon (*astra*). — [The mantra for] the head.

One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) with the mantra-syllables beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *hrīṃm*. "May the cruel sorceress (*kṛtyā*), whom the fools fashion like a bride, be driven away by Brahmā; let her return to her creator. (52)
In the [years] eight, three, four, four, and four Vedas, by means of the eight letters beginning with *dhruva*.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) of the mantra, ending with the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*.
In the head, between the eyebrows, in the mouth, in the throat, in the two arms, and in the heart.
One should not place the feet upon the navel, the thighs, or the knees; nor should one place them upon the feet.
The practitioner, having recited the mantra fourteen times encased between the *tāra* (oṃ) and *māyā* (hrīṃ),
should then meditate upon the lion-faced goddess with disheveled hair and naked.
She was dark-complexioned, wielding a sword and shield, with fangs protruding from her mouth, terrifying to all.
Devouring the enemies with intense splendor—this is declared to be Dhyāna. || 56 ||
One should recite the mantra ten thousand times; the fire oblation for it is one-tenth of that amount.
The oblation should be performed with fuel-sticks of Apāmārga and with offerings such as clarified butter.
One should worship the Goddess in the triangle, and perform the worship of the limbs in the six petals.
One should worship the world-protectors and their weapons in this manner; such is the ritual of adoration.

The practitioner who has thus accomplished the mantra should recite it one hundred times during the ritual applications; he should also perform one hundred oblations and offer a bali-offering in the ten directions with the ten mantras.
Whatever evil has previously entered me through this wicked deed here— may Indra, the king of the gods, shatter it, smear it, delude it, destroy it, and kill it;
let him offer an oblation to that [evil], and may there be well-being for me, may there be peace for me.

May there be well-being through this mantra; one should first worship Indra with the words: "May the evil that has preceded me be shattered here by this ritual act. Having uttered the name of the god Indra, one should say at the end of the king's name: "May it break! (60)

Having uttered "añjayatu" (let him anoint), one should then utter "mohayatu" (let him delude); after that, the word "nāśayatu" (let him destroy), and from there, "mārayatu baliṃ" (let him kill the offering).
"May he grant me what is done [for me] and may there be auspiciousness at my end. Thus is the bali-mantra proclaimed, which brings peace and prosperity. (62)
One should offer the bali-oblation with that very [mantra] consisting of sixty-eight syllables beginning with the Praṇava.

In this mantra, in place of the first word, one should say "Agni" and so forth; then again, in the same manner, having joined the words beginning with "Vahni" in place of the word "Śakra," one should utter the word "Dik" (Direction) for the sake of offering oblations (*bali*) to the guardians of the directions in their respective quarters. || 63 ||
In place of "Indra" and so forth, one should recite "Agni" and so forth. Thus there shall be ten mantras; one should offer the bali-oblation in those respective directions.
When this has been done, the *kṛtyā* spell performed by an enemy is swiftly destroyed. || 65 ||
Pratyaṅgirā is declared to be the sage; Anuṣṭubh is proclaimed as the meter; Kṛtyā is its deity, and its application is for the subjugation of enemies. 66.
She who possesses a head, who possesses ears, who is the form of Viṣṇu, and who is terrifying—
he who sent her here today, you must always unite him with blessings.
Vāmadeva is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi), and Gāyatrī is said to be the meter (chandas). Kṛtyā is the deity; as before, the application is for the turning back of enemies. 68.
"By whom you have been seen here, O you who bestow full satisfaction—turn back to him alone; let me not be the one to harm the innocent. (69)
The sage is Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha; its meter is proclaimed to be Anuṣṭubh;
the deity here is Kālāgni-Rudra; and the application is for the destruction of enemies. (70)
By those [weapons], he forcefully cast down the performer of the Abhivarta sacrifice, as well as the life-span and progeny of that man-eater who was cutting them down.
The sage of this [mantra] is declared to be Ūrdhvāsya; the meter is stated to be Anuṣṭubh. The deity is Yātudhānī, and its application is for the destruction of malevolent sorcery. || 72 ||
"O Kṛtyā, go back to him who fashioned you here; return to your source! May all the malevolent Yātudhānīs perish for the destruction of these spells. (73)
I shall now describe the wondrous ritual application (*prayoga*) of these five [hymns] on this earth.
One should perform this hymn (*sūkta*) consisting of five verses on the eighth day of the bright fortnight (*śuklāṣṭamī*). (74)
And on the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should [offer] a level [oblation] made of udumbara wood.
One should bring a single staff, equal in length to a man's height.
Remembering the hundred names and taking up the staff, one should recite the hymn one hundred and eight times;
then his misfortune is consumed by the great planets.
If one should perform this rite from the commencement of the first lunar day (pratipad).
But the staff, made of vibhītaka wood, should be eight spans in length and straight.
Having taken up and uttered the name of the enemy, one should then recite the hymn; at that time, the enemy [is subdued].
Seized by a great disease, he dies; there is no doubt about this. || 78 ||
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations for seven nights into the fire, using fuel-sticks from the *kāraskara* and *arka* trees produced at the mouth of the fire, smeared with oil.
Either the destruction of the enemy occurs, or else by mere recitation, if one performs this for one month, the enemy shall meet his death. (80)
One should write the enemy's name on a palm leaf using wood from a cremation ground, with the letters of the name interspersed within the mantra, in the temple of Īśvara.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, [one should place it] on the ground at a distance of one span.
At that very moment, a fever arises in the enemy. || 82 ||
At that very moment it goes to destruction; however, at the conclusion of the ritual, the fees [are given].
One should give cows, land, gold, and so forth according to one's ability; such is the rule for that [gift]. || 83 ||
Mahādeva is declared to be the sage, the Anuṣṭubh is proclaimed as the meter, Kṛtyā is its deity, and its application is for the subjugation of enemies. || 84 ||
"Return quickly to the house of the very performer of the rite."
Destroy his cattle as well, and utterly annihilate his virility. || 85 ||

Agastya is declared to be its sage (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is proclaimed as its meter (chandas), Kṛtyā is declared as its deity (devatā), and its application (niyoga) is for the destruction of enemies. || 86 ||
But as for him who, though learned, employed you here as an instrument against his own kin— turn back against him and cut off his very body, just as one cuts down a tree.
Vasiṣṭha is declared to be its sage (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is proclaimed as its meter (chandas), and Rudra is declared to be its deity; its application is for the cutting down of enemies. 88.
Praticitvāvasa, Dhātubrahmaṇa, Viṣṇumitrah, Agni, Kṛtya, Rakṣohā, Ojas, and Ekapāt. (89)
Brahmā is declared to be its sage (ṛṣi), the Anuṣṭubh is proclaimed as its meter (chandas);
Kṛtyā is said to be its deity (devatā), and its application (niyoga) is for the cutting down of enemies. || 90 ||
Just as the ancient Aṅgirases, the Bhṛgus, the Atris,
and Vasiṣṭha exerted themselves, so too do not you neglect me.
Agni is known as its sage (ṛṣi), Triṣṭubh is proclaimed as its meter (chandas), Kṛtyā is declared as its deity (devatā), and its application (niyoga) is for the destruction of enemies. || 92 ||
He who established its joints with wisdom, like the parts of a chariot.
Because the light of the people's knowledge has entered the umbrella of the Tantra. || 93 ||
Now I shall describe the auspicious ritual for this aforementioned hymn of five verses: while consuming the milk of a tawny cow, one should recite the Anuvāka for three days. (94)

Free from the dualities of hunger and thirst and the like, one should be devoted to celibacy (*brahmacarya*). In this practice, however, desire, anger, and other such [afflictions] are to be recognized as obstacles. 95.
With fuel-sticks of palāśa wood, soaked in sweet curd.
By reciting it eight thousand times, one becomes endowed with the splendor of Brahman.
In this rite, a cow is declared the sacrificial fee; one should offer oblations with fuel-sticks of Palāśa wood.
The planets [are propitiated] by reciting one hundred and eight [verses] smeared with milk over the course of seven days.
The subordinate planets flee and peace arises everywhere;
by thus offering oblations with fuel-sticks of the Pippala tree, one shall attain glory. || 98 ||
On a riverbank, in a cremation ground, or even in the temple of Bhadrakālī, having made a heap of those ashes and meditated upon [the deceased] by name in one's mind, || 99 ||
If one recites it eight thousand times, after seven days one becomes an immortal. That same ash, consecrated with the mantra for a day and night, should be cast into a cow-pen.
There, happiness arises for the cow immediately; of this there is no doubt.
Then, having fasted on the full moon night, [one should offer] a ring during the night.
And for the sake of self-protection, one should maintain the vow and recite it eight thousand times; by the command [of the deity] and through his power, he shall become equal to a great king. 102.
One should daily recite the mantra one hundred and eight times in the temple of Viṣṇu.
Within six months alone, his heart's desires shall be fulfilled;
(this is the implied meaning). By reciting this for a year, one becomes equal to Brahmā.
One should give a hundred loads of sesame seeds as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to that reciter. (p. 336) 104.
Bhṛgu is the sage, Anuṣṭubh is the meter, and Kṛtyā is the deity; its application is proclaimed to be for victory in battle. || 105 ||
O Goddess, whoever—whether a person engaged in hostile rites, one standing in battle, or any other individual—harms us, pierce his body with fire by means of your own weapon. 106.
The sage is declared to be Agastya, the meter is said to be Anuṣṭubh; the goddess is Kṛtyā, and its application is for victory in disputes and the like. (107)
The mind of Śaryāta, which dwells within this oblation, is directed toward the one who acts for the sake of the ritual.
"Sarasvatī"—this is its name; it has no other part whatsoever. 108.
Mahādeva is the sage, Kṛtyā is the deity, and Anuṣṭubh is declared to be the meter;
its application is for victory in disputes and the like. || 109 ||
"Whether he be far away or standing near, let him drink the blood from his heart, for he is some great enemy who stands as a guarantor against my mind. || 110 ||
The sage is Agni, the metre is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is Kṛtyā.
The application of this [mantra] is proclaimed for the sake of accomplishing difficult tasks. || 111 ||
May that thunderbolt of his, discharged by the power of his own fury, shatter him who sent you on this mission under a pretext, out of a desire to slay us.
Gautama is declared to be the sage; Anuṣṭubh is its meter, and it has the deity as its divinity.
But for the destruction of thieves and others who stand upon the path of evil deeds, there is the application [of this rite]. || 113 ||
He who is our dwelling and our departure goes away to the furthest distance.
O Goddesses, through their agency, cause us to pass this night; do not cut us down.
Now, the practical application of this section (anuvāka) is being proclaimed.
One should recite it every day, beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight. || 115 ||
One should perform one thousand and eight [recitations] until the full moon day.
One should consume the milk of a tawny cow and also sacrificial rice (haviṣyaudana).
Or one may seek alms at the house of a Vedic scholar, provided that all other duties are not thereby obstructed.
If this is so even from the mere observation of capacity, what need is there to speak of that which has already come into being? (117)
Likewise, one shall conquer untimely death, as well as yakṣas, gandharvas, and rākṣasas.
Likewise, [he destroys] diseases such as the seizing of the aggregates (skandagraha), brahmarākṣasas, and apasmāra.
All diseases perish, and there is indeed progress and increase further and further.
Indeed, all calamities shall be pacified within the abode of the practitioner.
Having daily offered one hundred and eight oblations of rice grains smeared with ghee,
There shall be the destruction of all diseases, and indeed only auspiciousness day after day.
One should offer one thousand and eight oblations of sesame, black gram, and sacrificial porridge (caru) smeared with ghee;
this is known as the swift pacification of all diseases.
Having offered one hundred and eight Palāśa flowers and sesame seeds mixed with fragrant ghee for a month, all suffering is removed.
There shall be pacification of great portents, and likewise one shall live for a hundred years;
a gold ring and other such gifts should be given as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the reciter of the mantra.
The sage is declared to be Aṅgiras, and Gāyatrī is said to be the meter.
The application of the fire of the gods, however, is for the destruction of all enemies. || 124 ||
If you go to our two-legged youths today, and do not remain with us for four paces, we shall not allow you to enter our eight-paced houses. || 125 ||
The sage is Jvara, the Lord; Triṣṭubh is declared to be the metre. Mṛtyu is the deity, and the application is: "May old age befall the enemy. || 126 ||
"Whomever we hate, and whoever hates us—the malevolent one of whom there is no doubt—to him I shall speak as if to a dog;
I shall address him for our own death. || 127 ||
Brahmā is declared its seer (ṛṣi), the Anuṣṭubh is proclaimed as its meter (chandas); Agni is the deity, and it is intended for the incitement of hatred toward enemies. || 128 ||
O Lord, whatever sacrifice, oath, or curse comes toward us from me— [may it be for our welfare].
[He saw] Brahmā, Acyuta, Rudra, Śiva, and the Lord of the World. || 129 ||
The deity is declared to be Bhauma, and the sage is said to be Kaśyapa. The meter is specified as Anuṣṭubh, and its application is for the flight of enemies.
Whether he be a kinsman or a stranger, whoever plots against us with evil intent—may the serpent Tārkṣya, the finder of wealth, cause him to sink down. 131.

The ritual application of this hymn of five verses, along with its wealth-bestowing power, shall now be declared. Having gone to a river flowing toward the ocean, one should recite it one hundred and eight times. || 132 ||
One should recite [the mantra] daily, day and night, while offering handfuls of water.
One should give twenty-eight [offerings] in number and likewise recite [the mantra] again.
Within seven days, his enemy or his sick person will die; of this there is no doubt.
And having taken up a staff made of *bibhītaka* wood, measuring exactly one span (*prādeśa*). || 134 ||
Constantly remembering the name of the enemy and holding it in mind, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times;
thus the host of enemies, whether known or unknown, shall perish.
But he who hates without cause is born as one afflicted with leprosy.
He who, seeing the sun and remembering his enemy, recites [this mantra] twenty-eight times every day, will have that enemy tormented by fever. || 136 ||
An oblation of eight hundred fuel-sticks smeared with sesame oil should be performed; by this, the enemy's sons, wife, horses, elephants, and so forth, shall perish. || 137 ||
One should give gold as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and at the conclusion of the rite, a propitiatory ceremony (śāntika) should be performed.
One should perform penance again, and thus one becomes freed from fault. One should never do anything displeasing to the twice-born who are devoted to the gods. (138)
The deity is the Lord Kālāgnirudra; the sage is said to be Tūpamanyu; the meter is prescribed as Bṛhatī;
its application is for the destruction of enemies. || 139 ||
"Go quickly, O you of auspicious countenance, with the chariot yoked; the enemy does not remain for long in his purpose, like a wolf from a house that has been overcome. (140)
The sage is said to be Sabhyatapas, the meter is declared to be Bṛhatī, its deity is Jvalana, and its application is in the routing of enemies. || 141 ||
Like fire consuming a lake, burn us by the curse of our elders;
strike down our enemies alone, as the thunderbolt strikes a celestial tree. (142)
The sage is Aṅgiras, the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is Kṛtyā.
The employment of elephants, goats, horses, and so forth serves to delude the enemy. (143)
Make us free from rivals in the east; grant auspiciousness in the south. Grant constant fearlessness in the west, O Bearer, and prosperity in the north within our home. 144.
The sage is said to be Kaśyapa, the meter is declared to be Bṛhatī, and the deity is Kṛtyā;
its application is for the purpose of terrifying enemies. || 145 ||

Do not remain indifferent toward the duties of others; lead them to the state of serving the elders. A deer should act like a deer even toward a predator, for one ought to perform the duties appropriate to one's own condition. 146.
Now the application of this very Anuvāka is being proclaimed: beginning from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the eighth day of the bright fortnight. (147)
Having worshipped the Māheśvara Liṅga and reciting [the mantra], one destroys in an instant malevolent rites such as *abhicāra* and *kṛtyā*, as well as the diseases of horses and elephants. || 148 ||
Having worshipped Rudrakālikā, one may destroy even a great disease.
If he does not chant [the mantra], his enemy will perish even if he is protected by the Lord.
Facing south, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times from Rudra;
one should likewise recite it daily for a period of twenty-one days against an enemy.

There may be the loss of wife and other such things; therefore, two blankets should be given as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and self-protection must be performed with careful attention to the Rudra-nyāsa. || 151 ||
The sage is Śarva, the lord of all gods; the meter is proclaimed to be Anuṣṭubh; and his function is likewise to be the burning of cities and the like. || 152 ||
"O you who are fierce even with fire as your mouth, though he be a man destined for destruction, yawn!
Accept this, for it is indeed a marvelous thing for his undoing. (153)

The deity is Arka, the sage is a Muni, the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and Kṛtyā is its presiding deity. Its application is for the pacification of the anger of kings and others who are exceedingly enraged. || 154 ||
You are Indra, Yama, and Varuṇa; you are the waters and also the wind and the chariot. You are Brahmā, Rudra, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Prajāpati as well. 155.
The meter is considered to be the goddess Gāyatrī, and the deities are the Aśvins; the sage is Indra, and the application is for the swift destruction of disease. (156)
Turn hither, turn back, O seasons and years!
Likewise, the days and nights, the years, the cardinal directions, and the intermediate directions are mine. || 157 ||

The sage is declared to be Gālava, and the deity is proclaimed to be Mitra. The metre is Triṣṭubh, and the application is to be performed for the sake of one who has performed wondrous deeds. || 158 ||
Having summoned Yama, Varuṇa, Soma, the Waters, Agni, and likewise Vāyu, you bring forth cattle here and create wonders. || 159 ||
The sage is Viṣṇu, the deity is Viṣṇu, and the meter is said to be Anuṣṭubh;
its application is declared for the sake of protecting anyone at all. || 160 ||
Those who abandoned the Person, the benefactor of the universe, as he lay within the womb of Mount Meru.
The foremost of men [goes] to the Kumbhīpāka hell, and likewise a man who has not drunk the Soma for five years. || 161 ||
Those who constantly recite this section of five verses here shall dispel the fear of mental anguish and physical disease arising from past karma. (162)
Now, one verse remaining here is being proclaimed;
by constantly reciting it, a person is not overcome by women. (163)
O Agni, when will the exhilarated and unrestrained prayers of me, the sacrificer, reach you?
The sage is Śukra;
the deity is Brahmā; the meter is declared to be Anuṣṭubh. This injunction is proclaimed for the purpose of deluding women. || 164-165 ||
Not abandoned, red, unadorned, and carrying misfortune from all sides;
likewise, those of the same kind as the *kṛtyās* are for the purpose of slaying enemies with a focused mind. 166.
The Vasus are declared to be the sages, and the Supreme Self is the deity.
The application of this Anuṣṭubh meter is for the destruction of enemies who are difficult to slay. || 167 ||
Just as a man who sits facing eastward remains there even if struck once, so too, with you as our ally, we shall remain firm against his mobile and immobile [forces]. 168.
Agni is declared to be the deity, and the Moon is proclaimed to be the sage.
Furthermore, its application in the Anuṣṭubh meter is for the destruction of enemies. || 169 ||
Arise, O you who are not devoid of manliness; if you desire [victory] through the fires that have been kindled, or whatever rites you have begun, let there be a counter-attack against them. 170.
The sage is said to be Śāntāyana, and the supreme deity therein is Devatā.
The application of the Anuṣṭubh meter is for those who create obstacles to one's ascetic penance. || 171 ||
Or else, greed, laziness, and other such things which are seen to be obstacles to austerity [are present]. (172)
One should recite this "Śamit" mantra against those who create obstacles to austerity or during the study [of the Vedas], while wielding one's own weapons.
Your weapons are not lacking, nor are your enemies; yet such obstacles as these are harsh for you.
With those various whetstones, you sustain the lives of your sinful enemies.
The sage is Bhagīratha, the deity is Brahmā, and the meter is declared to be Anuṣṭubh; its application is for the destruction of the sins of those who are enemies of sin. || 175 ||
May you not leave behind the two-footed man, nor the four-footed beast; may you not abandon the kinsman, O swift-moving ones, for the sake of the human being. 176.
Whoever should constantly recite the five-verse section one hundred and eight times and worship Rudra, for him there shall be the destruction of his enemies. || 177 ||
It brings about the pacification of all malevolent rites and the subjugation of the entire world; by reciting it one thousand times in a temple of Rudra, one may eliminate disease. || 178 ||
Having offered eight thousand oblations of cotton seeds, salt, and ghee into the fire while facing the sun twenty-eight times, [one attains the desired result]. || 179 ||

Through the recitation [of this mantra], there is the paralysis of sight; one may even dry up the ocean. By the practice of reflection upon this very [mantra], the state of a learned scholar (vidvattā) is easily attained. || 180 ||
The sage is said to be Aṅgiras, and the two deities are Kāla and Mṛtyu.
The application of the Anuṣṭubh meter, however, is extremely difficult to accomplish.
"You were sent by those acting as enemies against me; therefore, he who followed you likewise has been subdued for my sake. (182)
The sage is said to be Aṅgiras, and Mahādeva is its deity. Niyoga is declared to be the metre; Niyoga is for the performance of meritorious deeds. (183)
"O Goddess, since we have been thus treated with such disrespect by Brahmā in every way, he shall surely perish upon reaching us, for his mind is indeed evil. (184)
The sage is declared to be Aṅgiras, the meter is proclaimed to be Anuṣṭubh, and the goddess is Kṛtyā;
its application is considered to be for the withering of enemies. || 185 ||
Just as a tree struck by lightning withers away from its very roots, so does he who seeks to do me harm utterly wither away. 186.

Kaṭha is the sage, Mahādeva is the deity, and the Anuṣṭubh is declared to be the meter. One who has performed malevolent magic (abhicāra) and the like by means of a woman should recite this at every watch of the day. || 187 ||
Just as a wooden puppet, having become a likeness, runs back toward its operator, so may the evil run back to him who intends evil against me. 188.
Bhṛgu is declared to be its sage, and the Viśvedevas are its deities; the metre is Anuṣṭubh, and it is likewise employed for yoga and for happiness in times of distress. || 189 ||
May the gods who are in our eyes, and those who are in our nostrils, drive away all [evil] that seeks to strike us down; may the Veda be my armor, syllable by syllable. || 190 ||
The application of this group of five verses will now be explained.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations of sesame seeds and rice grains smeared with ghee.
Within eight months, there will be a great increase in food and other provisions; one who desires long life should offer one hundred and eight oblations of nectar to the Goddess.
On this day of his own birth, he conquers untimely death; all his sins are destroyed, and peace of mind arises. || 193 ||
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of *palāśa* flowers, that bull among the twice-born—
His body, consisting of Brahmanic splendor, shines with extreme brilliance.
With fuel-sticks of the *brahmavṛkṣa*, with *bakula* flowers, and with unbroken grains of rice (*akṣata*).
Having offered eight thousand oblations with [the wood] smeared with ghee, there is the destruction of sins.
Whoever performs the worship of the fire with this very Anuvāka, the destruction of all his sins occurs within the course of a year. || 196 ||
Having recited the mantra one thousand and eight times, one should conclude the rite.

One should feed Brahmins capable of propitiating the deities with divine foods numbering as many as the syllables of the *Manoratha* hymn—which brings pleasure to the gods—as described hereafter. In their absence, one should feed those learned in the Vedas, for the Manu is composed of the Vedas. (198)
In the absence of those engaged in that tradition, however, one should feed others. Thus has the abandonment of the guru been described, which is concealed in all the Tantras. (199)
How can one who is himself unaccomplished deliver his disciple? I shall now proclaim the abandonment of the deity, which is concealed in all tantras. (200)

Having performed his daily obligatory rites, he should perform the worship of the deity; then he should make a formal resolve (saṅkalpa), preceded by the offering to the deity and other preliminary acts. 201.
Having uttered his own name and lineage and mentally recollecting Hari, he should pray to the God, whether in the absence or in the presence of the Guru. (202)
O Lord of the three worlds, O Sovereign of the universe, you are Maheśvara;

with the wondrous, peaceful consciousnesses from the bellies of tens of millions of my beloveds, forgive those hundreds of offenses of mine committed by this small-minded one who meditated upon you as having two arms and other such forms. (203)
You are the very embodiment of the sun, the moon, fire, Śiva, Gaṇeśa, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Indra, Śakti, humans, and serpents;
yet You have been meditated upon in a limited manner and worshipped with limited objects— may that be forgiven as my hundredfold transgression.
O Blessed One, forgive me. || 204 ||
Neither the gods, nor humans, nor even Sarasvatī know you;
what is the use of much speaking here to one of dull intellect? O Maker of Compassion, Friend of the Wretched, forgive this slight offense and this sin committed by me through my meditation. 205.

I perform meditation with the mind, yet I do not perceive form; I contemplate this which consists of the syllables of the mantra as being your very form—what the Vedas proclaim. Accomplishment comes from recitation, and not from external acts such as ritual worship.
Having thus prayed to the Lord of Gods, he prostrated himself again like a staff.
One should offer everything—the mantra, the image, and so forth—to the guru. || 207 ||

In the absence of that [image], one should cause it to be given to a worshipper who is devoted to it; and on that day, one should perform double the number of recitations (japa) in every case. || 208 ||
And as before, one should feed the Brahmins and also satisfy the preceptor and others;
thus has the abandonment of the deity been explained by me to you. (209)
Thus, in this Kali age, I have declared the rule for well-bred people by means of Vedic mantras;
what else do you wish to hear? || 210 ||

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Illumination on the Recitation of the Pratyangirā Mantra," in the Merutantra composed by the venerable Śiva, with the approval of Rīma, Mahāmāyā, and Mahākāla. || 14 ||
The Goddess said:
O Lord, I have heard the mantras declared in the Vedas that grant success even in the Kali age.
I wish to hear about the yantras that bestow one's desired objects.
The illustrious Śiva said:
For Brahmins, no other path exists apart from the Vedas.
The Smṛtis are the refuge of kings, and likewise the Purāṇas are the refuge of the Vaiśyas.
And for Śūdras as well, their intellect [is directed toward] tantras due to the influence of the defects of the Kali age.
Craving stands above all [afflictions]; by it, suffering is produced. || 3 ||
In the Kali age, a Brahmin who delights in Vedic rituals is undoubtedly Brahmā himself.
But one who is devoid of Vedic knowledge and ritual action should be known as a Brahmarākṣasa. || 4 ||
Performing the twilight devotions at the three periods of the day and being entirely devoted to service for the guru.
He failed to recite during forbidden times and neglected his compassionate teachers and kinsmen.
Having brought them under control, one should serve them constantly, being intent upon meditative study.

(342) One who avoids eating the food of others and has abandoned the acceptance of Śūdras succeeds merely by performing it, even without recitation (japa) or worship (pūjā). That rite is to be performed with Vedic mantras, and never by anyone else.
Now, first of all, I shall fully describe the supreme Gāyatrī yantra: one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with the syllable *hrīṃ* situated in its pericarp.
One should draw two vowels for each cardinal and intermediate direction on every petal;
and upon the filaments and their tips, one should write the syllables of the Gāyatrī three by three.
One should draw [the remaining parts] within the intervals between the pairs of outer lines.
Likewise, [the syllables] beginning with *ka*, as well as *oṃ āpo jyotī raso 'mṛtaṃ brahma*.
"Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ oṃ"—this is called the Gāyatrī Yantra. Having fashioned it in gold or even in metal, one should bind it upon the hand. || 10 ||
Attainment occurs without effort, the mind delights in dharma, one’s lineage remains unbroken, and one’s fame increases. Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the great wonder of Sarasvatī. (11)
There, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus as a yantra that bestows intelligence.
In its pericarp, one should write the Praṇava together with the sādhya within a hexagon;
in its center, or within the six corners, one should write the Vāgbhava seed-syllable. 12.
May he who is the bull among the meters, the all-pervading one, who arose from the immortal meters—may that Indra strengthen me with wisdom; may I become a bearer of the immortal, O God. 13.
One should write its five syllables upon the eight petals; or else, the mantra-syllables on the petals, with four *vṛtta*s (circles) on the outside. 14.
One should place two verses within each of the two internal paths; these should be written in sequence, and the outer *vṛtta* should be filled with the letters of the Mātṛkā.
May my body be keen of sight; may my tongue be most sweet. May we attain the desire of the mind and the truth of speech. 16.
He who is the first of the gods, the sovereign lord of all, Rudra, the great seer.
He beholds Hiraṇyagarbha being born; may that God endow us with auspicious mindfulness. || 17 ||
Having constructed a city-walled enclosure outside of that, one should draw [the symbols] in its corners.
And the seed-syllables Aiṃ, Klīṃ, Sauṃ, and Hrīṃ [should be inscribed] on one made of cloth, gold, or other materials.

Having painted it on an auspicious day, one should wear it according to the prescribed rite; [the wearer] becomes intelligent, a retainer of what he has heard, free from disease, and pleasant of speech. (19)
He shall become highly learned even in the Vedas and Āgamas through gradual practice; for one who possesses all-knowledge, such mastery certainly arises through constant application.
Now, the Traiyambaka Yantra, which brings about supreme accomplishment, shall be described.
Having drawn an eight-petaled lotus, one should place the *tāra* (the syllable Om) within its pericarp.

In its belly, one should place the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) joined with the desired rite of the practitioner; two vowels on each of the filaments, and the three syllables of Tryambaka on the pericarp.
On the outside, it should be encircled four times with the syllables of the mantra.
The one to be accomplished [should recite] the verse that is about to be mentioned, adorned with the letters of his own name.
One should wrap the yantra with that [cord] and likewise write it within it.
The sage is Gṛtsamada, the metre is Triṣṭubh, and the deity is Rudra. || 24 ||
O Mother, you who possess the Rudra-wheel, the wise one; homage be to you, the fierce avenger, who dwells with the bull!
Bestow heroic strength through your remedies; I hear that you are the most skilled physician among physicians. 25.
In the first [circle] of the earth-puraka and others, the seed-syllable *ṭhaṃ* is in the cardinal directions, and likewise the seed-syllable *baṃ*.
This Traiyambaka Yantra must be guarded with great effort.
It bestows long life, health, good fortune, and the fruits of dharma, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.
What need is there for much speaking here? By the power of this yantra, one obtains one's desired object and supreme prosperity; of this there is no doubt. (28)
On a wooden board consisting of forty-nine squares belonging to the Brahma-tree,
one should write the syllable *hrīṃ* together with the name of the practitioner (sādhya) in the central square.
One should worship with supreme devotion, offering sesame seeds and rice grains smeared with ghee.
But by offering oblations for eight months, even greater accomplishment is attained. || 30 ||
One who desires long life should offer one hundred and eight oblations of nectar into the Goddess.
On this day of his own birth, he conquers untimely death; there is the destruction of all sins, and peace of mind arises. || 31 ||

Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with *palāśa* flowers, O bull among the twice-born, his body shines forth, radiant and composed of the splendor of Brahman. (The word "he" is to be supplied as the subject. || 32 ||
With fuel-sticks of the Brahmavṛkṣa tree and hundreds of Bakula flowers, |||
Through eight thousand oblations of offerings smeared with clarified butter, there is the destruction of sins.
Whoever performs the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite with this very hymn, the destruction of all sins occurs for him within the course of a year. || 34 ||
Whoever, facing the sun, stands and recites [the mantra] twenty-eight times, shall then obtain the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā. || 35 ||
Whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others, one should recite [the mantra] in water reaching up to the knees.
The afflictions caused by all malevolent planets are not able to torment him. || 36 ||
One should place sandalwood mixed with saffron and camphor in front.

Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one should sprinkle [the patient] with bundles of kuśa grass; then the affliction caused by planets and secondary planetary influences shall perish. || 38 ||

Afflictions caused by spirits such as *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and *piśācas* perish at that very moment; diseases such as epilepsy and the like [are destroyed—this is the ellipsis]. A barren woman obtains a son;
a maiden finds a husband; and one seeking a daughter obtains a daughter. (39)
Standing in water reaching up to the navel, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times at sunrise and sunset;
then, within days, a great rain will fall from the mountains.
One should offer eight thousand oblations with fuel-sticks of *vañjula* wood.
If [the oblation] is smeared with milk, a great rain will arise within seven days; likewise, an offering (havana) should be performed with ghee for the attainment of all happiness. 41.
The deity of the upcoming Anuvāka consisting of five Ṛcs is Kṛtyā;
its metre is Anuṣṭubh, and the sage is considered to be Pratyāṅgiras. || 42 ||
O Karālī, you who are at my main gate, you who are in my dwelling; you who are in my hair, in my nails, in my ointment, and in my tooth-cleansing wood. (43)
Like a young prince who has escaped from his father's house, shatter their heads and seize their royal insignia! 44.
By this, O Sañjaya, the sons of Nūna have now become masters of the honeyed fire; let the wealth of the highest one be revealed, for his supreme food has been consumed. 45.
O Agni, those mortals who have practiced deceitful ways, speaking as if they were immortal, have abandoned you.
And with your flame, O Jātavedas, consume their lives, as you would dry straw or chaff.
O Rudreśī, whose nature is that of Rudra, O dark-complexioned one, O terrifying one! O Goddess of gods, O Great Goddess, may my great enemy be destroyed!
(47) Having touched an Aśvattha tree, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
On a Saturday, one shall obtain long life, health, and sovereignty.
And having recollected the Sage, the Vedic meters, the deities, and so forth, thereafter the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the mantras must be performed; such is the settled conclusion. || 49 ||
Khaṃ phaṭ! O you who possess a radiance equal to smokeless fire, perform your task for me! O Goddess of goddesses, O Great Goddess, may my enemy be destroyed! 50.
At the beginning, one should perform [the rite] with a quarter-verse, a half-verse, and a verse joined with a name.
I shall now describe the six limbs and the finger-assignment (aṅgulinyāsa), stating their names in due order.
To Kṛṣṇāmbara at the heart, to Siṃhavāhinī at the head, to Mahābalā at the crest-lock, and to Mahābhairavī as the armor. || 52 ||
"O gods, it is declared for the eyes as 'the destroyer of all duties';
likewise, for the weapon-mantra, it is 'the destroyer of mantras that transcend all'. (53)
One should perform self-protection, the binding of the directions, the purification of the elements, and the stationing of the weapon-mantra.
And one should perform all the Mātṛkā-nyāsas beforehand.

One should first recite the Gāyatrī, and afterwards mutter this mantra [“tryambakaṃ yajāmahe”]. Then one should recite the Jātavedas [“jātavedase sunavāma somam”], and again recite the Gāyatrī. || 55 ||

Again, the root [the root is Tryambaka]. Then, I take refuge in that goddess Durgā, who is fire-colored, blazing with ascetic power, the daughter of Virocana, devoted to the fruits of karma— O you whose essence is white, grant me easy passage across the ocean of existence.
[Salutation: The verse beginning with "tapasā" (RV 10.154.1). Preceded by the Gāyatrī, the root mantra is first, then the mantra "tvam pāraya" (RV 8.42.3), and also "pāraya" (RV 8.42.2). || 56 ||
