Furthermore, he recites that Ṛk verse beginning with "tām agnivarṇām" as the root mantra; then the root mantra preceded by the Gāyatrī, and the verse beginning with "yajñāyajñiyam. (57)
In this manner, one should recite the mantra from one thousand up to a million times, having considered the relative intensity of the desired objective.
Whatever desire one may long for, that very thing one attains in every way; when the ritual application is performed, the desire is surely accomplished—of this there is no doubt. (59)
The ritual applications of the Anuvāka consisting of five Ṛcs have been previously described.
With five verses one performs the five-limbed rite, and with the fifth [verse] again the weapon-mantra.
In every case, at the beginning of the recitation, one should mutter this verse one hundred and eight times;

O Granthikarṇī, O Virūpākṣī, O Stambastanī, O Mahodarī!

The sage is Aṅgiras, the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is Kṛtyā.
This application is for the purpose of destroying all diseases and for the increase of prosperity.
O Kubera, may your fierce face bring joy and bliss to Nandi; O Imperishable One, destroy death, fear, anger, and poison at the gateway.
Then, using two feet [of mantras] joined with the names "Kṛṣṇa," "Ambara," and so forth, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) beginning with the fingers as before. || 67 ||
One should maintain [the protection] as before, as well as the protection of oneself and so forth.
That [system] is considered to have been composed previously by those who hold the views of the Gāyatrī and other such schools, just as before.
One should recite it one thousand times, or eight thousand times due to the gravity of the task; success in the undertaking will inevitably arise, for this is the meritorious power of words. (69)
Distraction is a fault of the mind; being tormented by a grave fault is mental anguish; and mental and physical ailments arise from divine displeasure;
therefore, one should avoid that [divine displeasure]. || 70 ||

The renunciation of the mantra has been explained previously; now the renunciation of the Guru is likewise described. On whichever lunar day (tithi) a particular deity's mantra was received, on that same day it should be performed on earth.
One should form the resolve to abandon one's guru, preceded by the recognition of his faults, thinking: "I shall take another guru," whether that be a human or even a deity. (72)

One should select a single preceptor from among the eight deities who have been purified by the calculation of the zodiacal signs (rāśikūṭa); in the absence of the former, one should choose the next best.
For water is indeed Dakṣiṇāmūrti, as are the sun, the moon, and the fire.
And the deities of the mantra-obscuration, the deity of birth, and the Lord of the Family (kuleśvara). || 74 ||
O local deity, these eight men, or one endowed with the auspicious marks, having worshipped the pair of the Guru, should prostrate like a staff upon the ground. || 75 ||
Having pronounced the names of the deities, one should worship the substance by means of those names. [This should be done] with a three-leaved palāśa leaf, positioned to the right of the front fist.
And here, having spread kuśa grass upon a surface measuring a span, one should place a jar filled with water to the east and one filled with milk to the west.

In the north, however, it is proclaimed that this [vessel] is filled with wine in due order. Having reflected thus—that the consciousness of the former guru has entered into the new guru—the wise disciple should have an altar constructed. (78)
Therein, having set aside the four corners which are endowed with the syllables of the mantra, one should invoke the Goddess, worship her, and perform the fire-oblation (havana). || 79 ||

One should pour the remnants of the oblation (*sampāta*) onto the yantra with clarified butter while reciting the root mantra; thereafter, one should bury that yantra in the earth one hundred and eight times.
And for the sake of protecting houses, villages, and so forth, as well as kingdoms, in their respective locations.
One should offer an oblation to the constellations, the planets, the zodiac signs, and the lords of the worlds.
Wherever this protection is established, there prosperity increases.
Minor planets, great diseases, thieves, malevolent spirits, and reptiles—all these go to destruction by this rite;
of this there is no doubt. || 82 ||
This yantra of the Jātavedas mantra has been declared; it must be performed by those following the Vedic tradition alone, for otherwise it would result in suffering. || 83 ||
I shall now describe the yantra for those gods who are designated as the portions and feet of the Jātavedas mantra in its reverse order. || 84 ||
One should construct a square maṇḍala consisting of nine compartments.

One should draw the *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) along with its junctions in the central compartment; then, starting from the compartment situated below that, one should write the eight quarters of the mantra in sequence.
One should draw [the design] outside that, proceeding clockwise, within a pair of circles. || 86 ||

This weapon and machine on earth is the warder-off of elemental spirits and diseases.
One should write this, which bestows protection, longevity, fame, intellect, and prosperity, upon a plate made of gold or other precious materials.
One should wear it at the base of the arm, or on the neck, or even on the head. || 88 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the threefold power (triśaktika) yantra beginning with Gāyatrī, which bestows all goals; therein, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus. (89)

In its center, one should draw a hexagon, and within that, the *tāra* (OM) joined with the *sādhya*; then, one should surround it with the seven *vyāhṛtis*. Within the six corners, one should place the syllables beginning with the *tāra* for the five-syllabled mantra of Śiva.
Each single syllable should be written in front of them, according to its purity.
And one should write the first half of the Gāyatrī on the first leaf.

Having uttered "so'haṃ vaṃ ṭhaṃ namaḥ," one should then say the word "śivāya. Then [the mantra] "māyā laṃ ye" [is for] the throat; likewise, the Tāra (oṃ), Māyā (hrīṃ), and the Dhruva (namaḥ). || 93 ||
This mantra consists of twenty-nine syllables and is located in the fourth square.
The northern half of Tryambaka, however, is the fifth northern half.

This seventeen-syllable [mantra] shall indeed be the head of the Gāyatrī.

Agni, Brahmā, Vṛṣa, Nidrā, and likewise Akṣigata; then Śakra, followed by the Moon, and the great peak of the Cintāmaṇi. (98)

Having recited [the mantra] many more times, this very yantra was installed in cities, villages, mines, and other places; it bestows cattle, truth, health, and nourishment. || 102 ||
When worn constantly by men either on the neck or on the right arm, it shall provide them protection from the fear of enemies, tigers, and other such dangers. || 103 ||

Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme Varuṇa yantra: having fashioned a six-cornered figure within the pericarp of an eight-petaled lotus, one should write the Praṇava together with the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) in the center of that hexagon. || 104 ||
"Salutation to Varuṇa" is declared as the six-syllabled mantra of Varuṇa; one should write each syllable of this mantra in the six corners. (105)

In the second [case], it is cast upon the earth; and in the third, the syllables beginning with *to*.
But having forgotten his hope, he drew Varuṇa on the fourth [square], and Varuṇa released him.

One should write "Śarva" in the seventh [segment] and "Indra" in the eighth;

Then, one should encircle it with a *bhūpura* (fortified city diagram), which brings about subjugation and good fortune.
It is supreme, bringing about all forms of prosperity, such as gold, jewels, grain, and so forth.
One should wear it, encased in gold, either at the root of the arm or on the neck; for this is dear to Gaṇeśa and likewise bestows the power of speech. (115)
First, I shall proclaim the mantra that brings about great prosperity; it is Vedic, belongs to the consort of Viṣṇu, and is especially distinguished for devotees. (116)
One should draw a four-petalled lotus, and then one should write that [mantra] within the pericarp.

One should write the name of the sādhya within the *tāra* (syllable Om) on the petals, and likewise the *ṛc* mantra, starting from the eastern petal and proceeding clockwise around the four petals. || 117 ||
The sage is Vāmadeva, the meter is Triṣṭubh, and the deity is Bṛhaspati.
And this application of the mantra is for the sake of accomplishing one's desired goal. || 118 ||
He appropriates for himself the Father Śva and the Viśvedevas; let us worship him with sacrifices, with homage, and with oblations.
"May we be the offspring of Bṛhaspati, possessing heroes; may we be masters of riches.

O Maruts, you who are fond of the chase, bring us toward better fortune, as swift steeds carry their riders.

Thus may Indra and Agni drink of this pressed soma; bestow all prosperity upon us.
May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aditi, Sindhu, Earth, and Heaven grant us that.

Having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus outside of that, one should then inscribe there, in sequence, the syllables of the verse "tvaṃ soma," numbering five, nine, five, four, five, and six [respectively]. (124)
The Vedas are six; from their tips, the six were produced, as were the Ṛks.

Agni is considered to be Gautama, Soma the Triṣṭubh, and so forth, beginning with Agni.

O Soma, you have made clear the path with wisdom; you, the most skillful, have fashioned the way.
Under your guidance, our wise ancestors, like Indra, the god, have partaken of the sacrificial food. 127.
O Prajāpati, none other than you has encompassed all these created beings.
Whatever has been offered as a libation, may that be ours; may we be masters of riches. || 128 ||
Having excluded two verses from the outside, the Mātṛkās, together with their bindus, should be written between them, arranged in the form of an enclosure around it. || 129 ||
And outside of that, in the corners, one should write this seed-syllable: Śrīṃ Śrīṃ.
If one should wear it on the root of the arm, or on the neck, or on the head; || 130 ||
Then he obtains the earth, abounding in cattle, elephants, horses, buffaloes, and crops, as well as a lineage of progeny distinguished by sons, grandsons, and other descendants. || 131 ||
Now, O gods, I shall further describe another yantra that bestows prosperity.
In the center of the hexagon, one should write the Praṇava joined with the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya). || 132 ||
One should write the seed-syllable of Śrī (Śrīṃ) in the corners and draw an eight-petaled lotus on the outside;
in its filaments, one should write the vowels in pairs in their proper order.
May that Lakṣmī, born from the ocean, the cow of plenty, the ancient treasure, the goddess Viśvāvasu, always delight in our home. || 134 ||
One should write the four groups of four syllables of this ṛc upon its petals; having drawn two circles on the outside, one should encircle them within those two. 135.
With the verse beginning "aśvadāya," one *vṛtta* is formed, and that is outside of it.
One should cause the center to be entered by the letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa'.
Outside of that, one should draw a square and write the Śrī-bīja located at its corners.
And prosperity is dear to him in whichever temple this Yantra has been installed. || 137 ||
Having filled it constantly with wealth, various kinds of grain, and other things such as horses and cattle, Ramā indeed takes delight right there. || 138 ||
Now I shall describe the yantra of Bhāratī, which grants all desires.
In the center of the hexagon is the Praṇava, containing within it the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya). || 139 ||

And in the six directions starting from the east and the corners, one should write "aiṃ klīṃ sauṃ" in sequence; then, in that space, one should again draw an eight-petaled lotus with "sauṃ klīṃ aiṃ. || 140 ||
Then, one should write the lines of the two verses to be recited upon each petal;
the sage is Soma, the deity is Vāyu, and the meter is proclaimed to be Triṣṭubh. || 141 ||
Whatever the conscious beings speak with their voice, the Goddess of the Gods, the Delighter, has sat down among them.
She milked out four nourishing streams of milk; has anyone indeed reached her highest point?
The gods generated divine speech; cattle of every form utter it.
May that cow, Speech, who yields for us pleasant food and vigor, come to us with praise.
Having drawn five squares of verses on the outside, one should form four paths.
The seer is Dīrghatamas, the metre is Triṣṭubh, and the deity is Vāṇī. || 144 ||
There are four measured quarters of speech; those Brahmins who are wise know them.
Three, hidden in the cave, they do not set in motion; humans speak only the fourth quarter of speech.
One should then write this Ṛgvedic verse on the second path of the current day. Viśvāmitra.
The sage is Triṣṭubh, the meter is Triṣṭubh, and Vāk is considered the deity. || 146 ||
Driving away the sluggish female serpent, she, bestowed by Yama and Agni, has grown great.
The daughter of the Sun has spread her fame; she has won immortality among the gods.
One should write this ṛc afterwards, and then one should write it on the third [day].
As before, for all [the goddesses] beginning with Muni, there is the ritual application (niyoga) for the accomplishment of the site (vāstu).
Sasarparī brought forth nourishment for these people among the fivefold tribes.
May she, who bestows long life along with her kin, whom the Palastis and the Yamadagnis gave to me—may she protect me.
Then, having surrounded the fourth [syllable] with the Mātṛkā letters, one should write the Vāgbhava seed-syllable in the corners of the square (bhūpura) outside of that. || 150 ||

In this manner, one should inscribe this supreme yantra upon a leaf made of gold or other materials; having invoked Speech (Vāc) therein and worshipped her according to the prescribed rite, [one should proceed]. || 151 ||
Having joined it with the Ṛṣi and other [limbs], one should wear it on an auspicious day; such a person shall become a sovereign emperor among poets and logicians. || 152 ||
Having ground *vacā* and written this with the juice of *nāgavallī*, speech emerges resembling the surging waves of the celestial river. (153)
Today I shall describe the supreme yantra of the *kadṛc* which brings about subjugation (*vaśya*); one should draw it within the pericarp of an eight-petaled lotus. (154)

In the center of that [hexagon], one should write the syllable *hrīṃ* together with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Then, in the six corners starting from the east, one should write *aṃ*, *śrīṃ*, *hrīṃ*, and *klīṃ* in sequence. (155)
Having inscribed the seed-syllables *glauṃ* and *gaṃ* upon the first petal of the lotus.
The first *kūṭa* of the Śrīvidyā is "ka-e-ī-la" and "hrīm. || 156 ||
One should write [the mantra] on the second leaf; however, O slayer of Vṛtra, whatever [is prescribed] today, one should write the second *kūṭa* of the Śrīvidyā on the third [leaf]. (157)
"asakadalahrīṃ"—this is what has been proclaimed; one should write "udagā adhisūrya" on the fourth petal. || 158 ||
One should write the third *kūṭa* of the Śrīvidyā on the fifth petal as "sakalahrīm";
then, one should again write it on the sixth petal.
"O Indra, all that is under your control; [this is for] the seventh Gaṇapati. O Giver of Boons, this is the inscription on the eighth leaf. (160)
"Bring all people under my control, svāhā!"—thus one should write it together.
Outside of that, one should encircle the two *vṛtra*s within with the letters of the Mātṛkā.
Then, in the corners of the *bhūpura*, one should place *śrīṃ*, *hrīṃ*, *klīṃ*, and *glauṃ* in sequence.
And one should draw the subduing [deity] upon a golden cloth or similar surface with a golden needle.
Now I shall describe the yantra of Gaṇeśa according to the Saṃvādasūkta: upon a four-petalled lotus, there is a six-petalled [lotus] in the pericarp. (163)
One should write the *praṇava* (oṃ) along with the name of the one to be accomplished (*sasādhya*) in the central square; then, one should write "aṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glaum gaṃ" on the eastern petal.
To the south of Gaṇapati, one should write "O Bestower of Boons" (vara-varada); in the third [quarter], on the ocean, one should write "Bring all people under my control, svāhā. (165)
Outside of that, one should fashion an eight-petaled lotus and write half-verses (of the Ṛgveda) on each petal;
therein, the hymn of dialogue (saṃvādasūkta) is now being proclaimed. || 166 ||
O God, kindled by all men, bestow upon us in the assembly all the riches of the noble one for our delight. 167.
Gather together, speak together; let your minds be in harmony. Just as the ancient gods, being of one mind, attend to their portion. 168.
Equal are our mantras, equal our assembly; equal is the mind, most closely united among them. With this measure of equality, I address you with mantras. 169.
I offer for you with a common oblation; may our threefold intention be one and our thoughts be united.
May your hearts be united; may your minds be in perfect harmony with one another.
The sage Saṃvartana is traditionally remembered as the seer of this hymn of dialogue.
The deity is Agni, and likewise, the name Ājāyasañjñāna applies to the others as well. || 171 ||
The meter of the third [verse] is Triṣṭubh, while for the others it should be Anuṣṭubh.
Having drawn three circles outside that, one should write two paths (vīthi). In the first path, with the verse "jātavedase sunava" (RV 1.99.1), once again— (p. 351) 172.
One should encircle [the mandala] with the letters of the Mātṛkā and cause it to enter the outer paths.
Having constructed a city outside of that, one should place four feet there.
And that which is to be written in the corners and sub-corners is now described. || 174 ||
May it be well with our wind and with the mind of the Maruts; Svāhā! "Indra is the king of all"—may there be peace for us bipeds and peace for our quadrupeds. 175.
It is the supreme means for creating friendship among mortals who are divided; it deludes the world, brings others under control, and bestows radiance, good fortune, and nourishment. (176)
Now the yoga yantra of Gāyatrī Bhuvaneśvarī is described. One should draw an eight-petaled lotus, and in its center, one should write "saṃ" in the corners. (177)

Six beautiful triangles [should be drawn] according to the path of the six gurus; within that hexagon, however, in its center, one should place the object of accomplishment (sādhya) joined with the practitioner’s ritual action (sādhaka-karma). || 178 ||
One should write the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* and encircle it with [the letters] in reverse order.

Likewise, with the three vyāhṛtis, the wise man should write the mantra either in the middle or again with the three vyāhṛtis; [the absence of the feminine suffix -tisraḥ is an archaic Vedic usage]. || 179 ||
Likewise, one should write the two seed-syllables *khaṃ* and *īṃ* upon the twelve petals of the triangle;
furthermore, one should write them again on both sides outside of the triangles. || 180 ||
One should write two syllables joined with a *bindu* in reverse order of the Mother of the Gods (Gāyatrī) by way of circumambulation; then one should write them again. || 181 ||
One should write the seed-syllable of Śani at the front of the three triangles, joined with the syllable Tāra (Oṃ).
With lines in the form of chains, one should also [draw] the intermediate spaces with each [line]. || 182 ||
And thus, there are two chains with six seed-syllables on the outside.
One should draw two squares there, and the lines of the path should be written in reverse order.
Each syllable of the Jātavedas mantra should be provided with a *bindu*. Outside those two circles, one should construct four pathways (*vīthī*).
One should indeed write the letters of the alphabet, together with the bindu, sequentially along the first row.
On the second [day], one should construct an outer eight-cornered figure in reverse order.
One should draw the *cintāmaṇika* and *kakūṭaka* in the eight corners; outside of that, one should fashion sixteen tridents. 186.
This is the machine of those who know the Vedas, which brings about the successful accomplishment of all undertakings.
It generates all good fortune and brings about the destruction of all enemies. || 187 ||
The worship of the Bhuvaneśī mantra upon this yantra shall be supreme; therefore, the worship of the yantra must be performed with Vedic mantras for the sake of its perfection. 188.
I shall now fully explain its procedure: this yantra should be well-drawn upon a leaf made of gold or other materials, using saffron and similar substances, according to the Vedic rite. (189)
One should worship the Goddess upon the yantra; one should draw three paths (vīthīs) on the outside.
On the first [path], one should place the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), and on the second, the four cardinal directions. (190)
One should worship Hṛllekhā, Gaganā, Raktā, and Karālikā.
In the third path, Brahmā and the others are to be worshipped in the eight directions.
Having drawn a sixteen-petaled lotus outside of that, one should worship these [deities] there: Karālī, Vikarālī, Dhūmā, Sarasvatī, and Śrī. (192)
Furthermore, outside of him, he [beheld] Durgāmukhī, Lakṣmī, as well as Śruti, Smṛti, and Śrī; and again, Śraddhā, Medhā, Mati, Kānti, and Āryā. || 193 ||
Having fashioned a lotus with thirty-two petals, one should worship these [deities] therein.
Vidyā, Hrī, Puṣṭi, Prajñā, Sinīvālī, and likewise Kuhū. || 194 ||
She is auspicious, bestowing success, nourishing with the bliss of the light of the Rudra-path, and full of splendor.
Kālarātri, Bhadrakālī, Mahārātri, and Kapālinī. || 195 ||
Vikṛti, Daṇḍamuṇḍinī, Duḥkhaṇḍā, and Śikhaṇḍinī.
The destroyer of Niśumbha and Śumbha, the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura. || 196 ||
Indrāṇī, Rudrāṇī—who forms half the body of Śaṅkara—Nārī, Nārāyaṇī, Triśūlinī, Pālinī, Ambikā, and Hlādinī:
these are the thirty-two Śaktis. || 197 ||
But outside of that, having fashioned a sixty-four-petaled lotus, one should worship these: Piṅgalākṣī, Viśālākṣī, Samṛddhi, and Vṛddhi. (198)
Śraddhā, Svāhā, Svadhā, Māyā, Nidrā, and Vasundharā;
Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, and Tridaśeśvarī, the sustainer of the three worlds. (199)
To Surūpā and Bahurūpā, who are fond of those fallen from the mere aggregates (skandhas); then to Vimalā, Śyāmalā, Aruṇī, and likewise Āruṇī. || 200 ||
[He knows] primordial nature, transformation, creation, maintenance, and indeed dissolution.
And Sandhyā, Mātṛkā, Haṃsī, Satī, Somarddhikā, and Parā.
[He worshipped] Devamātṛ and Bhagavatī, as well as Devakī and Kamalāsanā. || 202 ||
She has three faces or seven faces, crushing both gods and demons;
she has protruding lips, half a face, many penises, and a slender waist. || 203 ||
Ratharekhā, Śaśirekhā, Parā, Gaganaveginī, Kṣitavegā, Pātālavegā, and Madanāturā—[these were the daughters]. (204)
And likewise Anaṅgā, Anaṅgamadanā, Anaṅgamekhalā, Anaṅgakusumā, Viśvarūpā, and Daityabhayaṅkarā. || 205 ||
[One should worship] Akṣobhyā, Satyavādā, and Śucivrata in the form of Tandrā; also Varadā and Viśveśī, and outside of that, the lords of the directions.
This procedure for worship has been declared as the foremost for the worship of weapons;
even a practitioner of Tantra attains his desired object through this sacrifice. || 207 ||
Now I shall describe the Jātavedas-Durgā yantra, which grants all desired objects.
Having drawn an eight-petaled lotus, one should write the syllable *dhruva* (oṃ) in the pericarp. 208.

In its center, one should write the syllable *hrīṃ*, and in the middle of that, the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Then, one should duly inscribe the syllables *tāra* (oṃ), *hrīṃ*, and *ī* upon the petals. (209)
Having placed the three *vṛtas* outside, one should write each individual syllable of this mantra, "Salutation to Durgā," in the eastern path as before. (210)
On the second [layer], one should place the letters of the Mātṛkā along with the mantra of Jātavedas; outside of that is a square—this is remembered as the Yantra of Durgā.
It wards off epilepsy, malevolent spirits, and minor planetary influences; it grants victory to men and bestows sons upon women—of this there is no doubt. (212)
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme yantra born from the Śrīsūkta.
Having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus with the seed-syllable *śrīṃ* in the center of the lotus.
One should write the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) accompanied by [the seed-syllable], and inscribe it upon the eight petals.
Then, for the five verses beginning with "kardama," one should recite half a verse at a time for ten times.
The person who goes forth for the sake of glory, and who bestows glory upon his singers.

One should write the fourth half-verse of the two *ṛc*s beginning with "śrīyam vasānā amṛtatvam āyan bhavanti satyā samadhā asme tat" and "śriya eva". For the mantra beginning with "śrīśca te", there should be one half-verse for each [of the two parts]. (216)

One should draw two squares outside of that to form the first enclosure (vīthikā); the first [verse] is with the verse to be mentioned hereafter, and the next is with the letters of the Mātṛkā. || 217 ||
One who desires prosperity, having become pure and self-restrained, should offer clarified butter as an oblation every day and should constantly recite the fifteen-verse hymn to Śrī. || 218 ||
Outside of that, one should draw a square and inscribe the Śrī-bīja;
in its four corners, however, one should write the Vedic mantra of Śrī.
I have proclaimed this yantra; whoever should wear it according to the prescribed rule, [shall attain success].
Having obtained abundant prosperity consisting of sons, health, the earth, grain, wealth, cattle, and rice, one shall live for a hundred autumns. || 220 ||
Having written this on a copper plate, one should recite it one hundred and eight times.
Having offered twenty-eight oblations, he should sprinkle them with the residual drops.
Having established her in the middle of the courtyard, one should invoke Lakṣmī and worship her.
One should propitiate Lakṣmī, together with her retinue, by means of the offering of oblations. || 222 ||
When this is done in that place, all forms of prosperity increase: sons, wives, friends, servants, grain, chariots, elephants, cows, and bulls; indeed, immeasurable happiness arises there. || 223 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the yantra born from the Pauruṣa Sūkta.
In the center of the pericarp of the six-cornered [lotus], one should place the Tāra mantra together with the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya). || 224 ||
One should place each syllable—*sahasrāra*, *huṃ*, and *phaṭ*—upon each petal.
One should draw [the lines] right there at the junctions, starting from the eastern point and proceeding in a clockwise direction.
The six mantras end with *svāhā*, and the first is "to Acakra. The fourth [mantra] is for Vicakra, Sucakra, and Dhīcakra. (226)
"Saṃcakrāya" and "Jvālācakrāya" constitute the sixth [mantra].
Outside of that is a four-petalled lotus, and upon its filaments— (227)
In the four directions, one should sequentially write the syllables "klīṃ kṛṣṇa klīṃ."
And there are three sets of three syllables each of the mantra of Vāsudeva.
One should write the mantra on its leaves; one should likewise utter "Oṃ" and "Namaḥ. "To the Blessed Vāsudeva"—this is the twelve-syllable *aṇu* mantra. (229)
Outside of that, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus, and upon its filaments, one should write "saṃ".
Each single syllable is *tāra*, *namaḥ*, and *nārāyaṇāya*. || 230 ||
On the petals, one should write the four syllables of the Nārasiṃha-mantra: "Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Jayalakṣmī," [addressed] to the beloved who is eternally joyful. (231)
One should indeed say "to Manasā, whose body is half-white with Lakṣmī. "Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Namaḥ" is the twenty-three-syllable mantra of Nṛsiṃha. || 232 ||

Outside of that, one should write a sixteen-petaled lotus; on its filaments, one should inscribe in sequence: "Tāraṃ namo bhagavate mahāsudarśanāya" (Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, Mahāsudarśana). || 233 ||
One should place this sixteen-syllable mantra, *huṃ phaṭ*, sequentially upon the petals; outside of that, one should draw two concentric circles for the verses of the Puruṣasūkta. || 234 ||
One should encircle the intermediate path within that with the letters of the Mātṛkā.
Outside of that, with all [the letters] accompanied by the nasal bindu, there is the city of the earth (bhūpura) in all four [directions]. [This is connected to what follows later. || 235 ||
One should well-draw the yantra in the corners; it is called the Pauruṣa. It removes all sins, is meritorious, and bestows sons, long life, beauty, and fame. || 236 ||
Having smeared the yantra with fresh butter (haiyaṅgavīna) and recited the Puruṣasūkta one hundred and eight times, he should feed the woman who has bathed after her menses. || 237 ||

Just as a woman bears the butter produced from that churning apparatus within her womb, so too is a son born who is eloquent and proficient in all the scriptures. Likewise, *haiyaṅgavīna* [fresh butter] is used for one afflicted by poison or suffering from a *sannipāta* disorder. (238)
In cases of colic, wasting, anemia, and similar conditions, freedom from disease arises from its consumption.
In cases of skin diseases (kuṣṭha) and secondary skin ailments (upakuṣṭha), ulcers, fractures, and fistula-in-ano;
In cases of syphilis, fever, and similar conditions, one shall obtain relief through scraping. || 239 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the yantra of the hymn consisting of five verses beginning with "Of the Lord of the Field," which bestows the accomplishment of all aims. 240.

Having fashioned a six-petaled lotus within the pericarp of an eight-petaled lotus, one should write the Praṇava (Oṃ) in its center, and upon that, one should inscribe the seed-syllable Huṃ. || 241 ||

One should write the name of the person to be accomplished within the seed-syllable, and write one letter from each syllable of the thousand-spoked wheel mantra "sahasrāra huṃ phaṭ" in the corners. || 242 ||
One should write the six previously mentioned mantras in the junctions of the hexagon; furthermore, one should write four letters each upon the eight petals.

At the end of the Varāha-mantra, on the leaf, there are five syllables: "Tāra" (Oṃ), "namo bhagavate varāharūpāya" is declared; then the Vyāhṛtis ending in "ṅe" (dative case) are proclaimed, and one should utter the word "pataye. (244)
"Grant me the status of a sovereign," she said, and at the end, the wife of Agni caused it to be given.
This mantra of Varāha is remembered as consisting of thirty-three syllables. || 245 ||
Outside of that, on the sixteen petals, one should write half-verse after half-verse.
I shall recite those Ṛgvedic verses here; listen with full attention. (246)
O Lord of the Field, milk for us the wave of the honeyed mantra, as a cow yields her milk.

Like well-purified clarified butter dripping with honey, the lords of immortality show us mercy. With the Lord of the Field, as if with a benefactor, may we worship so that he may grant us cattle, horses, and maidens for our desire.
May the plants be full of sweetness; may the heavens and the waters be sweet for us; may the mid-air be sweet.
May the Lord of the Field, who is full of sweetness, protect us; may we approach him with our own self. 249.
May the draft-animals be auspicious, may the men be auspicious, and may the plough furrow auspiciously. May the leather thongs be fastened auspiciously;
may they lift up the goad auspiciously. (250)
O Śuna and Sīra, may you both take pleasure in these words; if you have drawn apart [the furrows], do not sprinkle me with that milk of yours. 251.
Turn toward us, O auspicious Sītā; we pay homage to you, so that you may be fortunate for us and so that you may bear us good fruit. 252.
May Indra accept her; may Pūṣan deliver her up. May she, rich in milk, yield for us in the coming year. 253.
May our ploughshares furrow the earth auspiciously; may the plowmen follow with their draft-animals auspiciously.
May Parjanya [bestow] auspiciousness through honey and waters; O Śuna and Sīra, bestow auspiciousness upon us. 254.
The deity of the field (kṣetra) is the god Vāmadeva, who is remembered as the sage.
In this hymn, the seer is Pulastya, and the meters are Anuṣṭubh and Triṣṭubh.
Having drawn three outer lines, there shall be two pathways therein.
One should encircle the first path with the seed-syllable *glauṃ* and the letters of the Mātṛkā.

Outside of that, in the corners of the second city (bhūpura), one should write "glaum," and in the cardinal directions, the seed-syllable "huṃ"; this is the yantra, [to be drawn] on an auspicious day. || 257 ||
Having inscribed it upon a copper plate with a golden needle according to the prescribed rite, it should be installed at the gateway of a house, or in a sacred field, or even in a city. || 258 ||
Or in that region, all prosperities increase day by day.
With elephants, horses, cows, buffaloes, bulls, camels, mules, and so forth; || 259 ||
There shall be a reunion with wealth, grain, land, crops, dwellings, jewels, ornaments, and other such riches that bring delight. || 260 ||

Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the Yantra of the Āgāva-sūkta: one should well inscribe the Kāma-bīja, conjoined with the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), within a hexagon. || 261 ||
Each syllable should be written within the six corners as "dhruvo namaḥ kṛṣṇāya";
having written this at the front, one should fashion a four-petalled lotus.
Within the squares, one should well-inscribe the syllables *klīṃ*, *kṛṣṇa*, and *klīm*.
Three by three, the letters representing the mind of Vāsudeva are to be written upon the petals.
Having fashioned a lotus with eight petals outside of that, and upon its filaments, [one should place] the ten-syllable mantra: "gopījanavallabhāya svāhā. (264)
Having written two syllables at a time on its petals— namely *māyā* (hrīṃ),
*ramā* (śrīṃ), *gopāla*, and then *viṣadharāya* (to the serpent-bearer)— 265.
"Vāsudevāya huṃ phaṭ svāhā"—this mantra consists of twenty syllables. Outside of that, having fashioned a sixteen-petaled lotus, one should write the vowels there. (266)
Then, one should write the verses to be described upon the filaments and the petals, half a verse on each petal, so that it may be beautiful. (267)
The cows have come; they have brought auspiciousness; let them sit down; let them low near us.
Abounding in offspring and many-formed, dwelling here, they yield abundant nourishment for Indra.

Indra bestows his favor upon the sacrificer who gives; he grants us the fruit [of our offerings], yet he robs us of it. Increasing his wealth again and again, he places the god-seeking man within an unbroken field of solitude. 269.

They do not perish; neither the thief nor the enemy, nor distress, assails them. With those [cows] by which he gives to the gods and to you, with those he dwells for a long time; he, as lord of cattle, is with you.
Those [cows] do not [flee] like a horse that has stumbled in dust; they are prepared for that, and there they are released.
The cows of that mortal sacrificer roam about following him, the wide-striding one who grants fearlessness.

The cows are Bhaga; the cows have appeared to me as Indra. Without the cows there is no partaking of the first Soma. These cows that belong to the people, O Indra—I desire them with my heart and even with my mind.
O cows, grant them to me; you make even the emaciated beautiful and even the unlovely fair.
O you of auspicious speech, make our home beautiful; your great vigor is proclaimed in the assemblies. 273.
May they be prolific, grazing on good pasture, and drinking at their easy passage.
May the wicked one, who utters evil, not master us; may we cross over to the further shore, free from all obstacles. || 274 ||
The swift arrow has approached this target; you shall be struck down. The seed of the bull is here, as is your own heroic power, O Indra. 275.
Having excluded two squares from the outside, one should write the letters beginning with 'ka' in that path.
One should correctly draw those ending in the letter 'a' outside of that, and then the square enclosure (bhūpura).
Having written "glauṃ" in the corners, one should write "bhūḥ" in the cardinal directions.
For this Gopālāyantra, when installed in the home according to the prescribed rite, [bestows these benefits].
There, the cows are indeed full of milk, accompanied by bulls, free from disease, possessing full udders, of many forms, and large in stature. || 278 ||
Then, Lakṣmī and Kīrti, abounding in wealth, grain, land, and jewels, shall dwell perpetually and steadfastly in his mansion. || 279 ||
Now another machine will be described, which brings great prosperity to cows and other livestock.
In the center of the eight-petaled lotus, one should write the Praṇava together with the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya). || 280 ||
Having placed one verse at a time from the hymn beginning with "ā gāvaḥ" upon each petal, and having set aside two verses, one should perform the surrounding of the Mothers along that path. (281)
Outside of that, one should fashion a square; this yantra, when installed in the house, shall always be filled with cows, horses, bulls, and other livestock. || 282 ||

Now I shall describe the Yantra of the Sun (Dineśa), which wards off disease. One should then well-inscribe the object of the rite (sādhya) together with the Praṇava in the center of a hexagon. || 283 ||
In the corners, one should write in sequence the syllables *tāra*, *hrīṃ*, *sohaṃ*, and *haṃsa*. Outside of that, there is a four-petaled lotus, and upon its filaments— || 284 ||
One should write "hrīṃ hrīṃ" and "haṃsa" on all the petals, beginning from the east.
One should draw the feet of the verses as they rise today; one should write them outside of that.
One should draw an eight-petaled lotus with filaments in sequence; *ghṛṇi*, *sūrya*, and *āditya*—each of these is a single syllable. (286)
Some maintain that one should place the verses beginning with "śukeṣu" on each petal; outside of that are two circles, and in the pathway (vīthī) is the surrounding of the Mothers.
Outside of that, on the spokes of the city-gate (bhūpura), one should write: aṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ saḥ.
This yantra of the Sun, moreover, shall destroy all malevolent planets.
It increases splendor, fortune, enjoyment, majesty, and fortitude.
One should draw this on a surface smeared with cow dung using slightly reddish sandalwood paste. || 289 ||

Having properly invoked [the deity] upon the ground with a copper needle, one should worship him. At the conclusion of the worship, a distinguished arghya offering is prepared and presented to him. || 290 ||

For the pacification of leprosy, consumption, and other ailments, and for the destruction of minor diseases, this yantra, having been written on a copper plate, should be installed in the home. || 291 ||
By worshipping [it] daily according to the prescribed rules, one shall destroy diseases such as leprosy, epilepsy, amnesia, and even those diseases resulting from malevolent spells. || 292 ||
Having written [the mantra] on a golden leaf, one should cast it into the midst of oil; one should then recite the three-verse hymn beginning with "udyannadya" one thousand times.
For one whose body is incapable [of other treatments], this very yantra should be drawn upon fresh butter to destroy the disease of leprosy. (294)
Having recited the three verses one hundred and eight times and having extracted [the essence], one should consume it;
for the sick person, there shall be the pacification of disease—this is the truth, there is no doubt. || 295 ||
Now I shall further explain another matter: the yantra of the Gāyatrī and the solar mantra, which destroys all diseases and is beloved by the Sun. (296)
Having drawn a circle, one should write the Praṇava together with the sādhya in its center.
Outside of that, one should draw a triangle known as the "mantra-house. || 297 ||
One should draw a circle again outside each corner; there, one should write the five syllables of the mantra "yakṣarājāya. || 298 ||
Outside of that, however, one should write one syllable each within the six corners; then, one should write "sahasrāraṃ huṃ phaṭ" within the eight corners. (299)
One should draw Ghṛṇi, Sūrya, and likewise Āditya in each individual square; furthermore, one should write the two seed-syllables "Śrīṃ" and "Hrīṃ" on the tips of the petals. (300)
This solar yantra is declared to bestow the increase of longevity and health; it grants the birth of sons to barren women and confers good fortune upon women. || 301 ||
It bestows victory upon kings and completely destroys the diseases of the sick; what need is there for much speaking?
When held in the hand according to the prescribed rite, it grants all fruits.
In that very way, I shall proclaim the supreme essence of essences; having understood that which was declared by me as the essence of the Atharvaṇa.
"Assuming the form of a Śabara and wandering the earth, I shall see that in the Kali age all people will be intent on achieving only desire and wealth. (304)
[This occurs] through the mantras of false gurus, whether seen [directly] or [found] in books and the like.
They have fallen away from the conduct of their commitments, they are distracted, and they are destitute. || 305 ||
Likewise, others will become possessed by spirits through unrighteousness.
For the sake of those seized by great planetary afflictions and diseases such as malevolent spells and sorcery,
this divine yantra has been revealed by me.
One should fashion the head of the deceased, excluding [the rest], resembling a mṛdaṅga drum.
And the nose and the other [senses] are situated in the middle of those four sense-faculties.
One should draw a horizontal line extending outward from the top of the *muṇḍa*; likewise, two tridents (*śūla*) should be made at both sides of the two tips.
And the upper line below that should be equal in width to the trident; it is called the "Muṇḍa" or "Hand" [line], and one should make its middle part like the trident. || 309 ||
In the place where the sense organs are concealed, one should draw a line with five forms;
one should place two tridents, joined with pedestals, in the position of the feet.
Having thus assumed the form of a preta, one should inscribe these seed-syllables: on the head, the hand, and the right arm, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus facing upward. || 311 ||
One should likewise write the half-part of the line as *muṇḍam*, ending in *ṅ*, and similarly write *ḍam* and *nam*.
And above the left arm, the two syllables "ho ma" [are placed]. || 312 ||
On the half-portion of the head, one should draw eight [lines]; the topknot (śikhā) should be made at the location of the heart, always extending both horizontally and upwards. || 313 ||
One should write this in the middle portion and on both sides; in the nine divisions in sequence, the first would be the letter 'a'. (314)
The seed-syllable *bhū* should be in the second [position], and *ahīna* in the third;
*sarāhīya* is the fourth, while *vihaka* is the fifth. || 315 ||
*Trayāka* would be the sixth, and likewise *nāmbuda* the seventh; *trayāka* would be the eighth, and *naḥtaraṃ* not so at the end. (316)
Outside, one should construct a group of six compartments beginning with two.
In the upper row, one should likewise write the groups of six, three, and two in sequence.
In the lower row, within the seven-fold enclosure, one should always write the mobile [beings] in the Peśī.
Outside the muscle, below my heart-muscle, on the right side. || 318 ||
One should write the name of the person to be accomplished at the side of the foot, and that mantra on the left;
this yantra is to be drawn upon a blue cloth with ink. (319)
She, having become the wick called *kuśa*, should wrap [it] perfectly.
On Sunday, in the evening, one should smear [the ground] with cow dung.
In that place, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with white unbroken grains of rice.
One should first worship Gaṇādhipa in its pericarp.
On its very southern side, one should worship the Lord of the Field.
One should worship Indra and the other deities in the petals, but Dīpikā in the pericarp.
One should properly place it above that and set down a vessel of oil;
in that [vessel], there shall be a *kuḍava* measure of sesame oil. || 323 ||
One should prepare such a vessel made of clay or metal; having worshipped it with lamps and other offerings, one should seat [the deity] there in the evening. || 324 ||
Demonstrating that, one should hold the fire-drill while looking at the lamp.
For the gratification of the presiding deity of the lamp, together with his retinue. || 325 ||
One should give uncooked food to a Vedic scholar who maintains a family;
and as long as the lamp burns, one should watch it with vigilance.
When a calamity from the gods has arisen, the lamp itself speaks: "Whatever task must be done quickly, peace will surely be attained. || 327 ||
When the humors (doṣas) of a rakshasa or similar being are within the body of one who speaks the truth, then and there they must be dealt with, so that the patient may attain happiness. || 328 ||
In rites such as those for malevolent magic (abhicāra), a trembling of the lamp arises; indeed, it trembles in an instant, and even greatly from moment to moment. || 329 ||
By one Sunday, minor faults are destroyed; by two Sundays, the destruction of the faults committed through black magic occurs. (330)
Even that which has not been practiced by the practitioner shall go to destruction through the three defects.
May the fault of consuming mantras be destroyed by these four lamps. || 331 ||
By the life-force mantra of the *kuguru*, the six defects are destroyed; even disease is destroyed by the *saptadvīpa* [mantra]—this is truly a great marvel. (332)
One should go oneself to the three marks; in the case of piercing, there are three at the window. Inside, either a dark mark or even a fissure is visible. || 333 ||
If it arises with three points, or two colors, or lacking luster;
Having declared the full span of his life, that sick person does not live at all.
This is declared to be the Siddhayantra, which bestows accomplishment upon practitioners of Tantra.
Wise men should certainly not employ a mechanical device for those who have abandoned their own duty. || 335 ||
One should abide in the Brahmanical Dharma; for that, there is no need for external ritual honors.
In this state, both the yantras and the mantras accomplish their results spontaneously; of this there is no doubt. (336)
The eighteen Purāṇas were indeed composed by Vyāsa; and that Nyāya which was propounded by Gautama is a means for achieving dharma. (337)
In the Kali age, there will arise various fallacious arguments that destroy the Vedas; by studying those, a twice-born man becomes once again a ghost or a Brahmarākṣasa.

That Mīmāṃsā which acknowledges a Lord (Seśvarā) accomplishes the goals of human beings; whereas that which denies a Lord (Nirīśvarā) and is devoted solely to ritual action bestows the enjoyment of heaven. || 339 ||
Eighteen Smṛtis have been proclaimed; in this list, the first is Parāśara.
Śaṅkha, Likhita, Vyāsa, Vasiṣṭha, and the sage Kaśyapa; || 340 ||
Agastya, Yama, Mahārīta, Divodāsa, Prajāpati, the venerable Paiṭhīnasi, Jamadagni, and Gautama; || 341 ||
O Bhāradvāja, these are declared to be the founders of the Dharmaśāstras; their differences of opinion should likewise be understood according to ten divisions. || 342 ||

In some cases, however, the word of the Sage exists according to the distinction of time; therefore, having ascertained the birth, family, and country [of the person], one should prescribe the Dharma. (343)
Śikṣā, Kalpa, Vyākaraṇa, Nirukta, and Chandas; Gaṇita, Saṃhitā, and Horā—thus is the threefold Jyotiṣa. || 344 ||
These six Vedāṅgas and the four Vedas—these fourteen are indeed declared to be the means for accomplishing dharma. || 345 ||
But when that [place] is perfected, the Siddhas, Ṛṣis, and others indeed become perfected by themselves.
That which is contrary to this cannot be the means for accomplishing the dharma of the social classes.
Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, Gāndharvaveda, as well as the sciences of polity (nīti), the arts and crafts, mathematics, and omenology—these are the seven. || 347 ||
And the treatises on statecraft have been proclaimed [as authoritative] because of the certain practice of what they prescribe.
Whatever is shown therein is capable of accomplishing the goals of human endeavor.
Literature, traditional scripture, aphrodisiacs, and the practice of sexual conduct—thus the science of love (kāmaśāstra) is fourfold, to be acquired from the teacher and the scriptures. || 349 ||

The fulfillment of desire should be accomplished without contradicting dharma, artha, and the other goals of life; for without a teacher and without wisdom, the purpose of human existence perishes. || 350 ||
The Yogaśāstra and Vedānta—these two are the means for liberation; other books that are merely worldly and which present a semblance of dharma, O gods, are not so. || 351 ||
In this terrible Kali age, when people are devoted solely to their genitals and bellies, there is perhaps one among ten million who increases all virtuous deeds.

"One should become intent upon the Buddha and the Dharma; for that purpose, this is said. One should produce a virtuous son who is a lamp for the lineage—this is what is called the 'procedure' (vidhāna). (353) [The word "procedure" is to be understood as the remainder of the sentence.]
One should perform the sacrament known as *garbhādhāna* during the first menstrual period.
The Sīmantonnayana rite should be performed, as well as the Puṃsavana, so it is remembered. || 354 ||
These three sacraments (saṃskāras) are the makers of the state of being the womb of Brahman. He who is born through these very rites is consecrated by the seed of Brahman. || 355 ||
The birth-rite and others, as well as the first feeding of solid food—these four sacraments for the child are for the attainment of Brahman [for the increase of spiritual luster]. (356)

The tying of the sacred thread (vratibandha), the return home (samāvarta), and the study of the Vedas according to the prescribed rules—these three purificatory rites (saṃskāras) in childhood bring about the state of Brahman. || 357 ||
Thus, he who is purified by the ten purificatory rites and performs the ten duties—he alone is to be known as a Brāhmaṇa; all mantras are under his control. || 358 ||
Seeing that, the heroic Rākṣasas and Mlecchas were unable to cause any harm.
Having seen those ten [deities], the karmas flee far away.
The acquisition of wealth through one of ten modes is said to be the primary task for the maintenance of a family. (360)
Having performed sacrifices for those entitled to them, one should first acquire wealth; having taught a worthy disciple, one should acquire a second reward as a gratuity. || 361 ||
Avoiding a wicked donor, a time of famine, an improper gift, and an unsuitable location, one should accept a gift as the third means of acquiring wealth.
That which is obtained through the order of inheritance and accumulated is known as the fourth; however, whatever wealth is acquired within this lineage is recorded as the fifth. (363)
Those means for attaining wealth that have been proclaimed—by means of them, the sixth [chapter] has been accomplished.
That which is obtained through the instruction of the true mantra is the seventh.
One should practice agriculture according to the prescribed method; that is considered the eighth [means of livelihood].
In accordance with the occasion, this ninth reward has been obtained. || 365 ||
But each preceding gift is superior, and it should be considered double [the value] of the one that follows.
This first activity is proclaimed as that called "the acquisition of wealth. (366)
The duty of supporting dependents is the second [duty], beginning first with one's own body; thereafter comes the devoted wife, and then the mother who gave birth. (367)
Brothers, elders, sons, daughters, and likewise maternal grandfathers.
One's mother-in-law, this circle of dependents, and whatever is obtained in times of misfortune; || 368 ||

Having equalized one part from each, he should cause it to be given to those at the end of the shares. Here, having performed the equalization of the maintenance of that share which belongs to the son, he should be colored by the Brahmin;
because of his Brahminhood, he does not fall away. (369)
The third [duty] is daily bathing; one who does not bathe becomes a Śūdra.
These ten baths are augmented by their respective qualities: first is the bath of the tree of one's caste, and the second is that with oil. || 370 ||
Haimodaka, Mātra, that which is called Bhumā, and Vibhūtimat; likewise Gāyatra, Vāyavya, Kāyika, and Mānasa. || 371 ||
The fourth is the rite of the twilight (sandhyā-karma); thus it is proclaimed to be tenfold.
The worship, preceded by the display of mudrās, is performed according to the method previously described.
And a recitation of one thousand and eight is considered the primary [method]. || 372 ||

Thus, from the practice regarding two or one [deities], three types of junctures (saṃdhyā) are recognized. One is accompanied by worship and a mudrā, while the other is likewise without a mudrā. || 273 ||
One thousand and eight, as well as one hundred and eight.

There are twenty-eight or eight [repetitions]; there are four variations regarding the recitation (japa). In the absence of recitation, the arghya offering for the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) is not presented with the Gāyatrī mantra. || 374 ||
This would be the tenth twilight; by omitting it, one becomes a Śūdra.
Two types of worship of the gods are proclaimed: the daily (nitya) and the optional (kāmya), making five;
and the five great sacrifices (pañcayajña) likewise make five; thus it is celebrated as the tenfold duty (daśakarma). || 375 ||
According to the distinction of gods, spirits, sages, humans, and ancestors, they too are said to be of five kinds,
beginning with the most excellent of the excellent.

These are divided into five types through the omission of each one. Regarding that, the method for the sacrifice to the gods (devayajña), which is the propitiation of the deities, is now described. || 377 ||
The Vaiśvadeva oblation, the oblation of the daily domestic worship (nityopāsana), the Agnihotra oblation, and likewise the recitation (japa) of that hymn; || 378 ||

The bali offering is declared to be threefold; at the conclusion of purification, one should discard water with the mantra "tathā ca vaiśvadevānte yanmatrā" (and likewise at the end of the Vaiśvadeva, whatever [is prescribed]). || 379 ||
That which remains as the residue of one's own leftovers is proclaimed as the third;
this, moreover, is the sacrifice to beings (bhūtayajña), which wards off minor afflictions. || 380 ||
One should daily recite the Aṣṭaka at the conclusion of worship with a restrained mind; in its absence, one should simply meditate or recite the Ṛgvedic verses.
In its absence, the daily recitation of one's own Veda is prescribed; by that, a Brahmin shall perform the sacrifice to the sages (ṛṣiyajña) in birth after birth. || 382 ||

Raw food should be given again in the morning according to one's ability; this sacrifice, performed at the beginning of a ritual and at the end of the Vaiśvadeva offering, is known as the human sacrifice (mānuṣa-yajña). Libation (tarpaṇa) and the offering of food (hantakāra) are considered the two-fold ancestral sacrifice (pitṛ-yajña). || 383 ||
Just as the recitation of a child is for the sake of another's excellence, so too is the mind of those born of noble lineage fixed upon the path of the Vedas. 384.
In the Kali age, the mind of men generally delights in the Kaulika path, which is charming with food, drink, and women;
therefore, human birth is difficult for them to attain. (385)
An ignorant Kaulika who falls [from his practice] becomes a pig; a knowledgeable one who has fallen from the left-hand path (vāmācāra) attains the state of a dog. || 386 ||
Whether in the Vāma or the Kaula path, or in both, there shall be worldly accomplishment for one who is well-guarded and daily devoted to offerings, worship, and the like. (387)
Or else, O gods, in the Kali age one is often treated with contempt and excluded from all the world; there is loss of wealth through the practice of alchemy. || 388 ||
There is censure in the Tantric path, and manifold sufferings in the Kaulika way.
Due to hatred toward Śaivas, Vaiṣṇavas, and others, they go to hell. || 389 ||
I have seen this one pure path of the Vedas, which bestows the fruits of both worlds; it provides accomplishment in this life and the supreme goal in the next. || 390 ||
Thus has this reality been declared to you, which is concealed in all the tantras. For the benefit of all in the Kali age, what else do you wish to hear? || 391 ||
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Illumination on the Description of Vedic Yantras," in the Merutantra composed by Śiva with the approval of the illustrious Mahāmāyā and Mahākāla. || 15 ||
The Meru Tantra, composed as a dialogue between Śrī Śiva and Śivā,
having been edited by the scholar named Ojhā, Paṇḍita Raghunātha Śāstrī.
Edited with commentaries such as the *Ṭippanī*, published by Khemrāj Śrīkṛṣṇadās at Bombay;
Part 3: Chapters 16 to 20.
The Goddess said:

O God, whether a mantra is given to a disciple by an unaccomplished guru, or the guru himself is unaccomplished, the mantras will not be perfected by other means, just as the guru is not perfected. || 1 ||
O Lord of Gods, when a disciple belonging to one lineage worships the deity of a different lineage, what kind of accomplishment (siddhi) would come to him? || 2 ||
Īśvara said:
If the Guru belongs to the Southern Tradition (Dakṣiṇāmnāya), he must be initiated into all the traditions.
Likewise, one who follows the Upper Tradition (Ūrdhvāmnāya) [is established] among others, and one who follows the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya) among those on the other side.

Of the two, however, one follows the Western Tradition (paścimāmnāya), while the other belongs to the Northern (uttara) or Lower (adhara) tradition. In the Lower tradition, no authority as a Guru is observed anywhere at all. || 4 ||
A devoted lay follower who dies while standing upright shall attain union [with the Divine].
In that manner, the former [attains] the state of a deity, while the latter attains similarity of form (sārūpya).
But another [type of person], having gone to the lower world, attains proximity [to the deity] as a fruit of this life.
For the renunciation of greed is indeed a benefit that brings about a favorable result even on the lower path.
And when one has attained perfection in another mantra, the guru bestows that mantra [upon the disciple].
Through practicing as instructed, accomplishment arises for that disciple.

When the Guru, out of compassion, bestows a perfected mantra, then even without recitation and without worship, the accomplishments (siddhis) reside in the hands of that disciple. A mantra given by a Guru who has not attained perfection will bring many obstacles. (8)
Therein, first one should accomplish the mantra of Vighnarāja; thereafter, for one who is free from sin, the supreme mantra will be perfected through the *puraścaryā* practice by itself.

In that regard, I shall declare the obstacle-removing mantra (*vighnamantra*), which consists of a single seed-syllable and has been concealed in all the Tantras due to the diversity of their traditions, yet bestows purity. (10)
In that regard, first of all, for the Vaidikas, the letter *ga* alone is considered [the seed-syllable]; for the Dakṣiṇas, it is joined with a bindu;
and for those of the Eastern Path, it has two bindus.
Subsequently, joined with these two, "gauṃ" is [the mantra] in the Ūrdhvāmnāya; "glauṃ" is in the Uttara, and "gauṃ" is declared in the Pātālāmnāya. || 12 ||
The *gaṇapoṣya* is the meter of the sages (*municchanda*), and the deity is Nivṛdvighna. "To Gaṇa for victory, Svāhā! To the one with a single tusk in the heart, Huṃ Phaṭ! [This is for the head. 13.
"Salutation to Acalakarṇin" is declared as the crest (śikhā), and then the armor (varma); likewise, "Salutation to Gajavaktra" is uttered as the eye (netra). 14.
To the one with great, fierce teeth, *huṃ phaṭ*—this is the weapon against enemies.
The practitioner of Tantra should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) using the seed-syllables joined with the six long vowels.
Then, with speech restrained and a tranquil mind, one should meditate upon Gaṇapati as having red garments, a red complexion, and being anointed with red perfumes and unguents. || 16 ||
He worshipped the pot-bellied one who wears the moon on his crest, the three-eyed dwarf, the lord of obstacles, the venerable Śuṇḍin, who was being honored with red flowers. || 17 ||
Holding nooses and kusha grass in his two hands, one on the left and one on the right.
One should meditate upon Vighnavināyaka, adorned with all ornaments, seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana). || 18 ||
One should worship with saffron and other substances upon a pedestal made of *śrīparṇa* wood and similar materials.
The wise man should construct this auspicious yantra consisting of three squares.
In the center of that, one should prepare the worship-seat (pūjā-pīṭha) of the Lord of Gaṇas;
there, one should arrange the pavilion and other structures according to the previously mentioned procedure.

One should draw the earth up to the ocean and so forth, consisting of the [six] tastes such as sugar-cane juice; and beyond that, the Jewel Island and so forth, within the form of the eight petals of the lotus.
One should worship the deity in the pericarp, and indeed upon the petals in due order:
Tīvrā, Jvālinī, Nandā, Bhogadā, and Kāmarūpiṇī. || 22 ||
Ugrā, Tejasvatī, Satyā, and the ninth, Vighnanāśinī; [these are] the beginning, the middle, and likewise the end of the mind—now hear the mantra of the seat (pīṭha). || 23 ||
"Oṃ, salutation to the lotus-throne of all powers"—with this [mantra], one should worship the pedestal and Gaṇādhipa in the four directions, beginning with the east. (24)
Then, one should worship Gaṇeśāna, who is white in color; Gaṇanāyaka, who is red; and Gaṇakrīḍa, who is blue in color, within the filaments. || 25 ||
In the southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, the center, and the intermediate directions, one should meditate upon the six limbs of this mantra and their corresponding deities. || 26 ||
Possessing the lusters of frost, crystal, dark-blue, black, and ruddy.
The principal female forms hold the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. || 27 ||
Vakratuṇḍa and Ekadaṃṣṭra, Mahodara and Gajānana;
The two formidable ones named Lambodara and Vikaṭa, as well as Vighnarāja and Dhūmravarṇaka.

The goddesses beginning with Brāhmī are to be worshipped on the petals starting from the east; I shall now describe their visualization (dhyāna) as it has been taught, following the clockwise order. || 29 ||
Brahmī should be meditated upon as white in color, adorned with a deer skin.
Holding a rosary, a staff, and a water-pot in her hands. || 30 ||
One should meditate upon the auspicious Maheśī, whose body is as white as the moon, holding in her hands a trident, an axe, a hand-drum, and a human skull. || 31 ||
Holding in her hands a rosary, a water-pot, a staff, and a goad.
One should meditate upon Kaumārī, who is as red as an indragopa insect and is an abode of compassion.
One should meditate upon the goddess Vaiṣṇavī, who possesses a luster like a dark blue cloud and holds a sword, a conch, a skull, and a bell in her lotus-like hands. || 33 ||
The practitioner of mantra should meditate upon Indrāṇī, blue in color and beautifully adorned, her lotus-like hands joined with a thunderbolt, a goad, and a vajra-marked lightning bolt. || 34 ||
One should meditate upon the Śakti Vārāhī, who resembles a mountain of collyrium and holds a plow and a pestle, as well as a sword and a shield, in her arms. || 35 ||
Holding a trident, a shield, a skull-cup, and a human head in her hands.
One should meditate upon Cāmuṇḍā, who is blood-red in color and adorned with a garland of severed heads. || 36 ||
The wise man should meditate upon Mahālakṣmī, who holds a golden rosary and a citron in her hands, as well as a lotus. (37)
One should worship the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) and their weapons within the pair of paths situated inside the three squares, for the sake of removing obstacles to the worship. || 38 ||
Whoever worships Gaṇeśa, the destroyer of obstacles, in this manner, that mantra shall become a bestower of success even if it was previously unaccomplished. (39)
Having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times, one should perform oblations with a tenth part of that amount.
With sweetmeats (modaka), flattened rice (pṛthuka), parched grain (lāja), roasted barley flour (saktu), and pieces of sugarcane (ikṣu-parva). || 40 ||
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) separately with coconuts, sesame seeds, and plantains, numbering one thousand, two hundred, and fifty respectively. || 41 ||
Now, the fire-oblation (homa) with sesame seeds smeared with the three sweets is described; furthermore, an oblation with milk-rice mixed with ghee bestows the desired fruit. 42.
One desiring prosperity should offer four hundred coconuts on the fourth lunar day.
Starting from the beginning of the bright fortnight, one should offer oblations daily in sequence.

Then, by using [the mantra] ending in the dative case, all living beings come under the control of men. An oblation (homa) performed with sesame seeds mixed with ghee bestows prosperity, influence, and fame. (44)
One seeking a daughter shall obtain a daughter, and one seeking a son shall obtain a son, by offering parched grain (lāja) mixed with the three sweets for a period of seven days. || 45 ||
One should offer oblations for four days with salt sprinkled with curd; at midnight, in rites for subjugation and the like, the desired object shall become subdued.
Having understood whether the task is weighty or light, achievable or indeed unachievable,
one should determine the number of oblations starting from a thousand.
In this manner, the very limit [of the number] should be understood where no specific count has been mentioned.
With the roots of the white Arka tree and excellent pieces of Kucandana wood. || 48 ||
Having fashioned an image of Gajākṣatroṭin from ivory for the sake of the elephants, and having worshipped that obstacle-maker (Vighna) and questioned him, one should mutter the mantra. || 49 ||
Having fasted and purified oneself during a lunar eclipse, one should extract that [mantra]; by wearing it on the crest-lock (śikhā), one will be victorious in legal disputes and in battle. || 50 ||
Then, by means of this powder of *rocanā* (cow bezoar), a mark (*tilaka*) was made by Manu; consequently, all kings and all people would always remain under his control.
Having written the name of the person to be accomplished in fresh butter in the forward direction, and the seed-syllable of obstacles (vighna-bīja) in the reverse direction,
that [butter] is placed within water.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, he should then consume it silently.
Within seven days, the object of the rite will certainly come under the control of the practitioner. || 53 ||
One should satisfy Gaṇeśa with water offerings as before, according to the requirements of the task at hand.
Through the maṇḍala and other means, one attains this mantra which begins with the syllable Om.
And for the sake of worshiping a renunciant (saṃnyāsī), that which ends with the Heart-mantra is proclaimed. O gods, you shall then speak of Lakṣmī-Gaṇapati in the Dakṣiṇāmnāya.
This yoga, endowed with the glory of an elephant, is exceedingly difficult to attain. Having uttered "Śrīṃ Gaṃ" for the sake of the gentle one, as well as "Mahāgaṇapati," [one should proceed]. (56)
Having uttered "ṅenta" and having uttered "varavara," one should say to all people: "me vaśamānaya svāhā"; this [mantra] consists of twenty-nine syllables. || 57 ||
The inner controller is the sage; the meter is Gāyatrī accompanied by the Trivṛt stoma;
the deity is Lakṣmī-Gaṇeśa, with the two initial seed-syllables.
One should cause the limbs to be fashioned with the six long [vowels] joined with the [seed-syllables of the] birth [castes]. || 58 ||
Golden-hued, clad in yellow garments, and holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and the gesture of fearlessness.
Beginning from the upper right hand and ending with the lower right hand. || 59 ||
Holding a golden pitcher upon a lotus with his trunk.
And on his left side, he was embraced by Viṣṇu and Lakṣmī with his right arm.
One should worship on the previously mentioned pedestal, which possesses the nine powers beginning with Tīvrā.
Upon a pair of eight-petaled lotuses, radiant with pericarp and filaments.
It is provided with four gates and surrounded by three squares. || 61 ||
Having conceptualized the form with the root mantra, one should invoke it into that [form] and worship it.
The first manifestation is by means of the limbs, such as Vakratuṇḍa and others; the other [manifestation] is likewise.
Aṇimā, mahimā, and likewise laghimā, garimā; as well as īśitva, vaśitva, prākāmya, and prāpti come first. || 63 ||

On the fourth day, one should first [worship] the Mothers and the weapons of the World-Protectors; one should recite the mantra a hundred thousand times and offer oblations of bilva wood fuel sticks soaked in honey. Then, having performed the libations and other rites, one should accomplish the desired objectives.
And indeed, performing thousands of oblations with *śrīphala* fruits mixed with honey brings about great fortune;
this *homa* bestows sons, friends, and a wife. || 65 ||
Having satiated them with pure water four hundred and forty times.
Within forty days, the practitioner of mantras obtains the desired prosperity. || 66 ||
This [mantra] beginning with Tārā and lacking Ramā likewise consists of twenty-eight syllables.
The ritual placement (nyāsa), meditation (dhyāna), and so forth are as before; now the different varieties of worship are described.
First the limbs, then Balākā, Vimalā, Kamalā, Vanamālā, Bibhīṣikā, and Mālikā. || 68 ||

One should worship Vaśaṅkarā and Vasumālā on the two sides, as well as Śaṅkha and Padmaka; one should also worship the Lokapālas and their weapons—this is declared to be for the fulfillment of specific desires. (69)
Standing in water reaching only to the chest and meditating upon the solar disc, for one who recites [the mantra] three hundred thousand times, an increase in wealth arises. || 70 ||
Having taken one's stand at the root of a bilva tree, the fruit is indeed obtained when that [mantra] has been recited [the required number of times].
When the fire is kindled with aśoka wood, [one should offer] rice grains smeared with clarified butter. || 71 ||

Through oblations, one may bring the entire world under control; likewise, by offering fuel from the *arka* tree, or through oblations of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) in a fire of *khadira* wood, a king obtains prosperity (this is the implied sense). 72.
The single-syllable mantra "Śrīṃ" is proclaimed; its meter is considered to be Nivṛt.
The sage is Bhṛgu, while the deity is Lakṣmī, who is considered the bestower of all things.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) joined with the six long seed-syllables. || 73 ||
Seated upon a lotus, golden-hued, with her two upper hands holding lotuses,
she grants fearlessness with her lower right hand and bestows boons with her left.
She was being sprinkled by four elephants resembling snow-clad mountains, who held jars of nectar at the tips of their trunks; she was clad in silken garments and wore a diadem. || 75 ||
One should meditate upon the goddess, the beloved of Hari, who is eager to bestow grace upon her devotees.
On a pedestal fashioned from the Dharmas and so forth, enriched with a square enclosure and eight petals.
Having invoked Rāmā, one should then worship her with perfumes and other offerings in the pericarp.
Vibhūti, Unnati, Hṛṣṭi, Kīrti, and Sannati. || 77 ||
Vyūṣṭi, Utkṛṣṭi, and Ṛddhi are to be worshipped in sequence in the eight directions;
likewise, the Lion Throne (siṃhāsana), which consists of all powers, is to be worshipped in the center.

One should offer the seat beginning with the seed-syllable (bīja) and fashion the form (mūrti) by means of the root-mantra (mūla). Having worshipped the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), one should again worship the eight petals.
And in the four directions starting from the front of the Goddess, he should place Vāsudeva and Halāyudha, as well as Pradyumna and Aniruddha,
in due order in the intermediate directions.
Dāmaka, salila, guggulu, and kuraṇṭaka.
One should worship the treasure known as Śaṅkha at the tip of the goddess’s right hand. || 81 ||
Then, on the second petal to the left, one should likewise place Padmanidhi, followed by Balākā, Vimalā, Kamalā, and Vanamālikā. || 82 ||
The Bibhīṣikā, the Mālikā, the Śāṅkarī, and the Vasumālikā.
These weapons of the world-protectors have been declared; this is the worship of Śrī.
One should recite that [mantra] one hundred thousand times for the Sun, and then perform a fire sacrifice of one thousand oblations.
With lotuses joined with the three sweets, and also with twenty-seven wood-apples (śrīphala). || 84 ||

Or, having performed the satiation (tarpaṇa) and other rites with three [offerings] smeared with honey, the practitioner, whose mantra is thus perfected, shall accomplish his own desired goal. || 85 ||

Standing in water reaching up to his chest, having consecrated the splendor residing in the sun with this mantra, he should recite it for three hundred thousand times; in a very short time, he is completely liberated from poverty. (86)

And having sat upon a *bilva* leaf in the house of Madhusūdana, the practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times; within a year, it bestows desired objects. (The remainder of the sentence is: "this mantra shall belong to him. He obtains an abundance of wealth beyond measure.
Not otherwise, before long. || 87 ||
If a practitioner of mantra offers oblations of rice mixed with ghee into a fire kindled with *aśoka* wood, he shall bring the entire three worlds under his control; it cannot be otherwise.
When the fire has been properly kindled according to the ritual rules with fuel-sticks of khadira wood and lotuses, [one should proceed].

The best of those who know mantras should offer oblations with rice grains mixed with the three sweets; by that, the royal court becomes submissive, and he shall become possessed of wealth and prosperity. || 89 ||
The practitioner of mantras should offer oblations into the fire of the sun with well-purified rice grains;
he will certainly obtain royal fortune, long life, sons, and happiness.
A wise person should offer one hundred thousand lotuses endowed with the three sweets;
the mortal accompanied by misfortune will certainly attain prosperity, and the practitioner becomes satisfied with an abundance of wealth, grain, and other riches. || 91 ||
Having planted a *bilva* tree in the house of a Brahmin, one should cause it to grow; one should recite the *Śrīsūkta* and likewise offer oblations there again. || 92 ||
With flowers and fruits endowed with the three sweets, as well as with excellent sacrificial fuel.
Even while standing at its root, a man may destroy it by breaking apart its constituent parts.
If Lakṣmī is pleased by an oblation mixed with bilva fruits and sacrificial offerings, she will manifest herself before him;
how then could misfortune ever exist in his family? (94)
One should recite the mantra of the group of Śaktis: *hā*, *hrīṃ*, and then *hrīm*.
This [mantra] consists of three syllables; its meter is Virāṭ, and it is said that Bhārgava is its sage. || 95 ||
One should perform the worship of the deity, Śakti, Gaṇeśa, and the six limbs.
Then, by means of the six long conjunct syllables of the word *gaja*, one should meditate upon the elephant-faced deity.
In the right upper hand he holds a goad, and in the left upper hand a noose; in the lower left hand likewise [is a noose].
That very citron fruit itself, golden in color, is on the right. || 97 ||

One should worship on the previously mentioned pedestal, which possesses nine Śaktis starting from the east, [the deity] holding a lotus and sweetmeats (modaka) in his hands and long chowries at his ears. 98.
The deity is situated upon an eight-petaled lotus surrounded by three squares; the first enclosure is said to consist of the limbs (of the deity), and the second likewise consists of the Mothers.

The third [night] should be with the world-protectors (lokapālas), and the fourth also with floods of weapons. One who has conquered the senses and eats sacrificial food (haviṣya) should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times. 100.
One should perform a fire sacrifice with ten parts of that [number] using cakes soaked in ghee;
thus, having perfected the mantra, the practitioner of mantras should accomplish the rites for desired ends. 101.
And having worshipped Vināyaka on the fourth day of the bright fortnight, [one should proceed].
With cakes mixed with jaggery and cooked foods drenched in clarified butter. || 102 ||
The mantra-practitioner should offer three thousand oblations in the presence of the deity, using a mixture of *marica*, *kṣuraka*, and *saindhava*. || 103 ||
Within seven days, one's speech will certainly become composed of both prose and verse. One who desires subjugation should bring a king under control by performing oblations with honey. 104.
One seeking a maiden should offer oblations of parched grains (lāja) while reciting the mantra containing her name; he should feed seven maidens, or else he shall obtain that one alone. || 105 ||
One should likewise consecrate with mantras either one *karṣa* or one *pala* of gold during a solar eclipse as well as a lunar eclipse. || 106 ||
Then, one should divide one thousand and eight [grains] into seven parts; one part should be kept in one's own home while meditating upon the deity. || 107 ||
On the second day, one should drink the remaining portions, one by one, in successive order.
Preceded by meditation, that [offering] to the deity should take place every morning. || 108 ||
In intellect he is like Budha, in wisdom he is equal to Guru, in poetic skill he is like Kavi, and in debate he is like Śani. || 109 ||
Having worshipped Vināyaka on the day of the ritual bath at the end of the menstrual period, [one should proceed].
And likewise, one should take turmeric and sweet flag (vacā) in the measure of half a niṣka and a pāda respectively.
Kuṣṭha ground with cow urine and consecrated a thousand times— having fed this to a barren woman or a maiden along with various kinds of food and drink,
and having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to her preceptor, that woman should drink the medicine herself. 111.
