Then she obtains a son endowed with all auspicious marks—one who is long-lived, handsome, intelligent, and possessed of glory. || 112 ||
This four-syllable [mantra] beginning with *tārā* is said to have the *gāyatrī* meter.
And as before, he has six limbs, is golden-hued, and wears golden garments. || 113 ||
He had large knees, a protruding belly, long arms, and was eyeless.
In his upper right hand he holds a noose, and in his lower left hand a rosary. || 114 ||

I meditate upon Gaṇeśa, who is endowed with power and worshipped by the universe; he holds his own tusk at the lower right [hand] and a goad in the upper arm, while carrying a lotus and a sweetmeat (modaka), and is adorned with golden ornaments. (115)

The worship is prescribed as before; one should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times. Then one should perform the fire sacrifice with sesame seeds smeared with ghee, followed by the libations and other rites.
One who offers oblations daily with clarified butter and cooked rice shall become a man possessed of food; by offering milk-rice, a person attains great prosperity. || 117 ||
This ten-syllable mantra, ending with *hṛd*, is for the sake of swift propitiation; its seer is declared to be Gaṇaka, and its meter is said to be Virāṭ. || 118 ||

The deity Vināyaka, who quickly bestows grace, has been described. A wise practitioner should perform the ritual assignment of the limbs (*aṅgakriyā*) using the seed-syllable (*bīja*) endowed with the six long vowels. || 119 ||
The meditation mudrā is for all [deities]; starting from the upper left, it proceeds clockwise.
Holding a noose and a goad, as well as a sprouting leaf-tip, with his hands, may he shine forth.
May Gaṇeśvara, who holds a citron in his hand, possesses three eyes, wears red garments, and always bears the full moon upon his crest, protect you. 121.

One should worship on the previously mentioned pedestal, which is endowed with the nine powers (nava-śakti). Having conceived the form by means of the root mantra (mūla-mantra), one should worship Vighneśvara within it. The first enclosure (āvṛtti) should consist of the limbs (aṅgas), and the second of the eight Gaṇas. || 122 ||
Vighna, Vināyaka, Śūra, Vīra, and likewise Varada.
Ibhavaktra, Ekadanta, and Lambodara, in that order. || 123 ||

The worship of the Mothers should take place at the edge of the petals, and the weapons of Lokeśa should be placed in front. One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with sesame seeds mixed with the three sweets.
Or else, one should then perform the libation and other rites with the eight substances previously mentioned.
The wise one should offer oblations with clarified butter mixed with sugar.
An oblation with pure clarified butter alone brings mastery over the world;
one who offers that [oblation] smeared with ghee shall become a possessor of fortune. || 126 ||
Then, for forty days, the practitioner of mantra should offer coconuts into the fire.
There shall be an abundance of all prosperity, fulfilling one's desired aims every single day. || 127 ||
For the attainment of one's desired object, there should be a fire-oblation with eight substances—namely, salāja, kaṅgu, and pṛthuka—each soaked in the three sweets (trimadhu). || 128 ||
And by offering it as food, one shall bring even kings and their women under one's control.
One who is unwearied [should recite] the four hundred and forty-four [verses]. || 129 ||
Every morning, however, with waters and the mantras of Vighneśa, [one should perform the rite].
One should satisfy [the deity] with excellent fuel-sticks; his purpose will be accomplished, of this there is no doubt.
When Gaṇeśāna has arrived from the solar orb toward the east and so forth, one should contemplate him as situated in the center of the previously mentioned wheel and then perform the libation.
The practitioner should also perform here the ritual applications described for the three-syllable mantra. || 131 ||
Oṃ Ṭhāṃ, "Salutation to the four-colored Heramba"—this is considered the mantra. The sage is said to be Gaṇaka, and the meter is declared to be Gāyatrī. || 132 ||
Heramba, who has a lion as his vehicle, is the deity of this five-syllable mantra.
By means of the six long seed-syllables, according to the method of the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅgavidhi). || 133 ||
With faces resembling pearls, lightning, clouds, milk, and saffron.
Endowed with five [faces] like an elephant, he wears a diadem and holds a sword in his hand.
And the goad, the trident, the mallet, and the skull-bowl.
He himself [bestowed] fearlessness, as well as the boon and the sweetmeat. || 135 ||
Holding an axe and a rosary with his lotus-like hands.
One should meditate upon the imperishable Ganesha, who resembles ten million suns.
Having fashioned an eight-petalled lotus surrounded by three squares.
One should first worship the seat there, which is provided with four doors.

Oṃ huṃ hūṃ ca mahāsiṃhāya gaṃ herambaṃ uccaret | āsanāya namaḥ ceti proktaḥ saptadaśākṣaraḥ || 138 || Oṃ huṃ hūṃ ca mahāsiṃhāya gaṃ herambāya āsanāya namaḥ; this is declared to be the seventeen-syllable mantra.

With this [mantra] one should offer a seat, and with this very [mantra] one should perform worship; using the seed-syllable joined with Dhruva (Oṃ), one should effect the manifestation of the form. || 139 ||

Having first worshipped the limbs (aṅgas), one should again worship the world-protectors (lokapālas); outside of them, their weapons are to be worshipped, and the worship of Heramba is prescribed there.
Having performed three hundred thousand recitations and offered oblations with sesame seeds in the tenth part [of that number], |||
One should perform the libations and other rites with substances combined with the three sweets. || 141 ||

Once the mantra has been thus mastered, the practitioner of mantras should then perform the ritual applications. On the fourteenth, eighth, and sixth lunar days, the wise one should offer oblations one by one with cakes, *kṛsara* (rice and peas), and sweetmeats (*modaka*) for the attainment of his desired goal. 142.

The knower of mantras should also offer oblations with the substances previously mentioned during the festival days (parvan). Whatever the practitioner desires, he shall accomplish all of that therein.
Or one should perform the practices taught for the swift attainment of faith. || 143 ||
The Tāra (Om), followed by Gaṇeśa (Gaṃ) and Hṛt (Namaḥ), is declared to be the seven-syllabled mantra.
This [mantra] consists of eight syllables ending with the Praṇava (Oṃ), or it may also begin with the Śakti-bīja (Hrīṃ). || 144 ||

The seer (ṛṣi) is declared to be Agni, and Gāyatrī is said to be the meter (chandas). The deity of this [mantra] belonging to Manu is Vināyaka, accompanied by the Brahman-worshipper (sabrahmaṇya). One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) with the long-voweled seed-syllable of Agni. 145.
Clad in red garments, red in complexion, and anointed with red perfumes and unguents; being worshipped with red flowers, he is the remover of the sins of his devotees. || 146 ||
And likewise a mallet, a spear, a lotus, and a goad.
Holding [objects] with his hands, moon-faced, and adorned with various ornaments. || 147 ||
Having thus meditated upon the Lord who destroys enemies, the leader of the host of Subrahmaṇyas,
one should then worship the All-pervading One on the consecrated seat.
Then, one should place the six limbs upon the filaments, and subsequently on the eight petals starting from the east.
Jayanta, Agniveṣa, and Kṛttikāputra as well. || 149 ||
Likewise, Bhūtapatisenānī, Guha, and Hemasūtraka.
And Viśālākṣa is also proclaimed; these [deities] hold a spear and a trident in their hands. || 150 ||
Immediately thereafter, one should worship these on the tips of the petals, starting from the east: Deva-senāpati, Śakti, Vighna, and Kukkuṭa. || 151 ||
Then [he should worship] Medhā, Mayūra, Vajra, Dhī, and the Lokeshvaras.
Then, having worshipped the weapons, this is the worship of Subrahmaṇya.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times with ghee, milk, and food; the practitioner of the mantra should offer ten thousand oblations and satisfy the most eminent of Brahmins.

When the mantra has been thus perfected, the practitioner of the mantra should accomplish his desires as he wishes. Day after day, he should satisfy [the deity] with sweet foods and edibles; he should properly worship the celibate [sage] as a god, with the thought that he is a god. 154.
Those who perform the perfect worship of Subrahmaṇya Manu,
They obtain enjoyments pertaining to this world and the next; there is no doubt in this matter. || 155 ||
Having uttered "Oṃ huṃ gaṃ glauṃ haridre," one should say "to Gaṇapati"; having said "vara varada" (O bestower of boons), one should say "sarvajanapada" (to all people). || 156 ||
"Stambhaya dvandvaṃ svāhā" consists of thirty-two syllables.
The seer is declared to be Madana, and the meter is said to be Anuṣṭubh. || 157 ||
The deity Haridrāgaṇapa should perform the six limbs [of ritual protection].
It is proclaimed for the Brahmins and the other castes by means of the seed-syllable joined with the six long vowels. || 158 ||
I shall now describe the ritual procedure by which this mantra is received: when the fourth day of the bright fortnight has arrived, the knower of the mantra [should proceed]. (159)
Having brought pure turmeric and grinding it well with water from a virgin girl, one should smear it over all the limbs and then bathe with pure water. || 160 ||
Endowed with supreme devotion and a serene inner self,
one should first worship the lotus feet of the Guru according to the prescribed rite.
With masses of golden rings, necklaces, ornaments, and auspicious garments. || 161 ||

Therefore, according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should take up this auspicious mantra; furthermore, one should worship it with fragrant scents and flowers, regarding it with the thought that it is a deity. || 162 ||
Clad in yellow garments, yellow in complexion, and anointed with yellow perfumes, he was being worshipped with yellow flowers while seated upon a jeweled lion-throne. || 163 ||
Yellow-hued, with three eyes and six arms, displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Holding the Krodhamudrā, a goad, a noose, and an axe in his hands. || 164 ||
The mantra-practitioner, with a pure mind, should meditate upon the Lord Gaṇeśa, who is tawny-hued.
On the previously mentioned seat, one should worship with the limbs, the Mothers, and the Lords of the Directions, [or with the "Single Syllable" mantra].

Having recited one hundred thousand Vedic mantras, at the conclusion, one should offer oblations into the fire with rice mixed with turmeric powder in a quantity equal to one-tenth [of the recitation], and should also feed the Brahmins. || 166 ||
Having recited [the mantra] more than a thousand times, one should perform the ten-part oblation in the fire.
One should properly perform oblations outside with cakes filled with ghee and jaggery. || 167 ||
p. 372) One should then, with devoted intent, offer libations to Gaṇeśa of the turmeric hue; one should likewise feed a young maiden and a celibate student. || 168 ||
One obtains the desired fruit; there is no need for deliberation on this point. With parched grains (lāja), one obtains a daughter, and a daughter likewise obtains a husband. || 169 ||
A barren woman, having bathed after her menses, should worship the Lord of the Gaṇas.
Sindhuvāra, vacā, and niśā, ground together with cow's urine measuring one pala, [should be used]. || 170 ||
Having fed young brahmins with sweetmeats, she should consecrate a maiden a thousand times with the mantra;
by drinking that medicine, she obtains a son who is an ocean of virtues. 171.
When this mantra is practiced, it brings about the paralysis of speech and the paralysis of enemies.
One may even ward off water, fire, lions, thieves, missiles, and other such dangers. || 172 ||
These eight are declared to be the lords of the Gaṇas who belong to the Dakṣiṇāmnāya. || 173 ||

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Revelation of the Mantra of Gaṇapati according to the Southern Tradition," in the Merutantra composed by Śiva with the approval of the illustrious Mahāmāyā and Mahākāla. || 16 ||
The Lord said:
In the Ūrdhvāmnāya, I shall proclaim the Gaṇeśas who bestow spiritual accomplishments (siddhis).
Hear now concerning Mahāgaṇapati, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

The syllable *tāra* (oṃ), the seed-syllable *śrī* (śrīṃ), *hṛllekhā* (hrīṃ), *kāma* (klīṃ), and the earth-seed-syllable (*laṃ*); then the seed-syllable of Gaṇeśa (*gaṃ*), followed by "to Gaṇapati, O best of the best" (*gaṇapataye varavarada*). || 2 ||
"Then bring all people under my control, O wife of Agni! she said.
This [mantra] consists of twenty-eight syllables; its presiding deity is considered to be Gaṇaka, and its sage is Mata.
The metre is Nivṛdgāyatrī; the deity is Mahāgaṇapati; 'gaṃ' is the seed-syllable (bīja) and 'hrīṃ' is the power (śakti);
and the syllable 'ga' is joined with the six long vowels.

One should perform [the ritual] by joining the six seed-syllables beginning with *Tāra* individually; one should also practice the six limbs of this mantra, conjoined with the [six] castes (*jāti*). || 5 ||
Or else, it is preceded by the syllable TĀRA and joined with the six long vowels.
One should perform the placement on the fingers with their respective seed-syllables, as well as the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga).
The twenty-two syllables of the mantra, beginning with Gaṇapati, are to be assigned to the Brahmarandhra,
the two ears, the two eyes, the nose, and the mouth.
At the base of the right arm, first, in the middle, at the wrist, at the base of the fingers, and at their tips;
and likewise on the left arm. (8)
One should place the preceding letters first, and then the letters following them; [one should place] those following them in Maṇipūra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, and Mūlādhāra.
One should place Tāra on the heels, Śrī on the mouth, Hrīṃ on the heart, and Śrīṃ on the anus.
The *glau* syllable is at the two feet, and furthermore, the seed-syllable itself is at the heart and each limb.

One should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) upon the body with the remaining portions of the mantra. Having thus performed the rite of placement, one should meditate upon the deity within the heart. (11)
On the auspicious island of sugarcane juice in the ocean, which is composed of the nine precious gems.
When the cool surface of the earth had been washed by the waters flowing with its waves, [he rested].
It was served by breezes carrying the fragrance of water and endowed with its qualities, and it was beautifully adorned by masses of flowers falling from the wish-fulfilling trees.
It was strewn with various flowers, resplendent with various birds, filled with many fruits, and frequented by hosts of apsarases. (14)
Abounding with thousands of garlands of flames and filled with rising moonlight.
Upon a ground made red by a mosaic floor of shimmering clusters of rubies.
In that place, which is charming with the humming of bees dwelling upon the flowers of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpapādapa), one should visualize the Pārijāta, the kalpataru,
in the center.

One should visualize his throne as being adorned with a jeweled fillet inlaid with six gems and beautified with flowers; beneath that, one should meditate upon a lion-throne made of the nine precious gems. || 17 ||
In the center of that is a lotus of letters with six petals; in its middle, within the pericarp, is Gaṇeśa, and situated there is Mahāgaṇa.

He is the elephant-faced one with a single tusk, enriched with ornaments of various jewels; he bears in his lotus-like hands a discus, a goad, a lotus, and so forth, as well as a citron, a mace, a bow, and a trident.
The supreme Lord is embraced by Śakti, whose hands are raised with lotuses.
He has the crescent moon upon his crest, possesses three eyes, is radiant, and is compassionate.
[They were] falling from the mouths of jars filled with a flood of jewels extracted from the Puṣkara lake.
He repeatedly poured forth a stream of jewels, pearls, corals, and other treasures.
On all sides, before the practitioner, he repeatedly warded off with the flapping of his ears a swarm of bees that were greedy for the water of his own ichor.
He was served by both gods and asuras, resplendent with a crown of excellent jewels, possessing a trunk as long as his thighs, having the face of an elephant,
and adorned with various ornaments.
Having meditated thus, one should worship Gaṇapati with all the ritual offerings upon the previously mentioned seat fashioned from Dharma and the other virtues,
which possesses the nine powers beginning with Tīvrā.
The worship diagram of Gaṇeśa is called the Mātṛkā-padmam.
It is provided with four gates and surrounded by three squares. || 25 ||
In its pericarp is a hexagon, and within that is a triangle; in front of the deity, outside the triangle, one should worship the gods with mantras.
"Salutation to Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa"—this mantra, preceded by *oṃ* and *śrīṃ* and ending with the heart-mantra (*hṛt*), is used to worship Him;
one should meditate upon Him as seated at the foot of a bilva tree. (27)
Lakṣmī has a single digit upon two lotuses; Hari holds the conch and discus. "Oṃ hrīṃ gaura-hirābhyāṃ" ending with "hṛt" (namaḥ) constitutes the nine-syllable mantra. || 28 ||
One should worship them while meditating thus: "They are situated to the right of the God, beneath his matted locks, possessing the luster of gold and silver. (29)
The Goddess holds a noose and a goad; Hara holds an axe and a trident. "Tāraḥ klīṃ" [followed by] Ratikāmābhyāṃ and ending with "hṛt"—this is the nine-syllabled mantra. || 30 ||
One should worship the two who desire pleasure beneath the Pippala tree situated at the back.
They were joined by two blue lotuses, a bow, and a flowery arrow, which were not attached to a base.
"Oṃ glauṃ mahīvarāhābhyāṃ hṛdantaḥ"—this ten-syllable mantra [is used]. Then, one should worship Mahī and Kola (the Boar) beneath the Priyaṅgu tree in the north. || 32 ||

His two excellent arms are adorned with the seed of Śukra (a lotus), a bow, a spear, and a discus. "Oṃ Gaṃ, [obeisance] to Lakṣmī and Gaṇaka," ending with *namaḥ*—this is the ten-syllable mantra. || 33 ||
In front of the Deity, one should worship the group of eight Lakṣmīs within the three syllables.
In the six corners, one should worship the mantra beginning with "Oṃ" and ending with "Hṛt. (34)
One should worship Āmoda, accompanied by Siddhi, in the eastern corner.
One should worship Samṛddhi, accompanied by Āyus, in the southeast corner, bringing forth joy.
One should worship Sumukha, endowed with splendor, in the northeast corner; one should worship Durmukha with Madanāvatī in the west corner. || 36 ||
One should worship Vighna, accompanied by Madadravā, in the southwest (naiśācara) corner;
one should worship the Maker of Obstacles (Vighnakartṛ), together with Drāviṇī, in the northwest (vāyavya). || 37 ||
The Vidyās and Śaktis hold nooses and goads, and bestow fearlessness.
Clad in red and non-red garments, adorned with ointments and ornaments, they were overwhelmed by intoxication. || 38 ||
Outside the hexagon, one should worship the deities on the right; likewise, one should worship the Śaṅkha-nidhi accompanied by Vasudhārā on the left.

That meditation is said to consist of a lotus-treasure (padmanidhi) joined with Vasumati; therein, the first [lotus] has the luster of a pearl and the other the luster of a ruby, both constantly raining down wealth and prosperity upon the worlds like clouds.

The worship of the limbs (aṅgapūjā) should take place on the filaments; Brāhmī and the others are situated within the petals. In the square, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) and their weapons as before.
In this manner, one should worship the deity thus endowed with the six enclosures.
Having recited eleven thousand one hundred times with devotion—[the absence of the vowel *i* is an archaic Vedic usage]—one should proceed.
One should offer oblations ten times [the number of recitations] using the eight substances prescribed for the single-syllable mantra.
Having performed the libation with a tenth part [of the mantra], he is then consecrated by means of that mantra.
One should properly feed the Brahmins with food of six flavors and give abundant sacrificial fees;
having done so and bowed down, one should dismiss them, and thus the mantra becomes perfected.
Then, having prostrated according to the rules and having diligently gratified the guru, one should perform the rites for specific desires;
otherwise, the accomplishments (siddhis) will not arise. || 44 ||
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa with red flowers, one should recite the mantra.
At the conclusion of this, one should offer eight thousand oblations made from karavīra flowers.
With one-tenth of that amount of flowers consecrated with the three sweets, the king then becomes a spy, accompanied by his ministers and attendants. || 46 ||
Likewise, by performing oblations with *palāśa* flowers saturated with the three sweets, all obstacles will undoubtedly become subject to his control. || 47 ||
A self-controlled and eminent minister should likewise offer clarified butter as an oblation; he shall attain vast fame that endures for a long time. || 48 ||
Having thus offered grain soaked in clarified butter as an oblation, one is born as a minister.
Having recited the mantra one thousand and eight times, one should perform the fire oblation (homa).
And having purified his ashes with salt, clarified butter, and liquor, || 49 ||
Taking ghee in his hand, he should strike the woman with it.
Until the end of her life, she remained more submissive than even a slave-girl.

From a hundred thousand recitations performed in a temple of Śiva, a fire sacrifice (homa) consisting of a tenth part [of that number] using milk-rice mixed with the three sweets always grants the practitioner of the mantra various riches; he shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 51.
Having offered one thousand and eight oblations with *jāti* flowers, the practitioner attains the intelligence for composing the meaning of the Vedas. || 52 ||
He who should offer thirty thousand oblations of dūrvā grass with clarified butter;
For him, minor deaths, diseases, and the like perish, and his lifespan increases. || 53 ||
Having become absorbed in meditative concentration (samādhi), one should offer yellow flowers mixed with clarified butter.

One shall paralyze the enemy army, along with its servants, elephants, and warriors; one shall effect the suspension of rain-showers and the suspension of speech—of this there is no doubt. One should offer three tens of thousands of oblations with fuel-sticks of *bibhītaka* and *samī*.
One shall expel hosts of enemies, as well as villages, countries, cities, and so forth.
Having offered one thousand and eight fuel-sticks made from the aruṣka tree into the fire,
a widow shall be brought under his control, both by her life and by her wealth.
Having written the names of the two persons to be acted upon upon two neem leaves—
one with the blood of a horse and the other with the bile of a buffalo— [this is done because, even though the former term is included within the compound,
there is a conceptual separation and subsequent reference to the latter term]. || 57 ||
One should perform twenty thousand oblations with mustard oil; at the end of the mantra, one should utter this: "Such-and-such [person] by means of such-and-such."
Then, one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) in a secluded place with the mantra "dveṣaya svāhā. Through this, enmity arises between those two friends, leading to the destruction of their lives.
[One should prepare] a stake eight finger-breadths long from human bone, having wrapped it with the hair from a corpse's head.
And one should recite that mantra one thousand and eight times.
During the Muhūrta of Kulika at night, one should perform worship at the gate of the enemy; within seven days, he will certainly become a guest of Yama. || 61 ||
One should recite this mantra, which has a hundred thousand syllables for the entrance to the Naga's cave; then thousands of Naga maidens will come before him.
Shameless and longing for enjoyment, they offer an elixir.
And various gems and jewels—whatever may be most desired. || 63 ||
The practitioner of mantra, firm in his vows, should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times on the summit of a mountain.
One obtains the perfection of the sword, which is sought after even by gods and asuras. || 64 ||
Having combined camphor, the sensitive plant (lajjālu), white mountain-ear (śuklagirikarṇikā), nandyāvarta, and madhupuṣpī, one should grind them well. || 65 ||
Having prepared a pill, one should consecrate it twenty thousand times; by anointing the eyes with it, one certainly beholds hidden treasure.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, and having blown three times upon the patient afflicted by suffering, one shall remove all that affliction; there is no doubt in this matter.
In a secluded and beautiful place smeared with cow dung, the practitioner, having bathed, [should place] a new pitcher anointed with sandalwood and other [unguents]. || 68 ||
Having filled it with fragrant water, one should cover it with a shallow bowl; likewise, one should place a lamp filled with tawny cow's ghee upon it.
One should worship him, as well as the young girl and the young boy, with ritual offerings; having sat there and touched him, one should mutter [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
Then, upon seeing the lamp, the boy shall tell everything.
It was past, it is present, and it will be future; of this there is no doubt. || 71 ||
Having meditated upon Mahāgaṇapati, or else in the presence of a lamp, one should mutter [the mantra]; then Gaṇeśa will declare in a dream both the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Standing in the midst of water during the *grahaṇa*, one should recite the mantra; then there will be the complete accomplishment of attracting grain, cattle, and women. || 73 ||
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred thousand times at the foot of a banyan tree, the yakṣiṇī named Vaṭā arrives and,
having drawn forth wealth and other riches, bestows them.
Having fasted during the night and bathed according to the prescribed rites, one should bring the *sadvacā* plant,
worship Gaṇeśa, touch it, and recite the mantra ten thousand times.
Having set that powder aside, one should take a quantity of exactly one karṣa.
A wise man should drink [the mixture] with seven oblations of ghee from a tawny cow every morning for seven days.
This must necessarily be connected with what precedes; now hear the procedure for mercury.
First, one should purify the mercury on a piece of cloth one hundred and eight times.
And one should rub it for one day with the fibers of cotton leaves.
Then, for the Kumārikā and Kāśavallī [mudrās], it becomes equal to silver. || 78 ||
One should add an equal portion of pure copper to this.
One and a half parts of copper, half a part of gold, and one part of iron [should be used]. (79)
This cotton-plant maiden, possessing the luster of collyrium, is growing by means of the juices [of other plants].
Having ground it in *āranāla* for one day, [place it] in *āranāla*.
Having formed it into a pill, one should place it there and then go to the abode of Śiva; one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, and then it becomes perfected. || 81 ||

Holding it in his mouth, the practitioner of mantras shall be victorious in battle; he becomes incapable of being slain by any living beings and remains invulnerable even against weapons and missiles. || 82 ||
Having drunk that, one certainly does not die from poisons originating from snakes and the like.
By its power, one possessing a vajra-body attains movement in space. || 83 ||

Her shadow vanishes, she becomes invisible, and she even becomes hidden within water. Wherever she resides in a house, there Lakṣmī shall remain steadfast. And by the will of the practitioner, she may bind the sight of the people. 84.
One should take the *brahmadaṇḍī* and the *lajjālu* under the asterism Puṣya and when the sun is shining.
One should thoroughly rub together vajra-dust and the three metals with those two.
When it has become like collyrium, then one should prepare the pill.
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa, one should take this auspicious pill;
having reflected thus, one should take it in one's own hand and mutter that mantra. || 87 ||
One should wear it on the face, the crest-lock, the hand, or the shoulder;
by its power, thieves, tigers, serpents, and the like do not approach. 88.
He is not overcome by obstacles in the presence of the practitioner. (The word "he" is to be supplied as the subject.)
Kings come under his control, for he is exceedingly dear to beautiful women. (89)
Dhattūra, Rocanā, Śaṅkhapuṣpī, white Aparājitā, Sahadevī, Brahmadaṇḍī, snow (hima), and black agallochum (kṛṣṇāguru) in equal parts. || 90 ||
Then, having pressed it thoroughly, one should fashion a pill according to the prescribed method.
When that tilaka has been applied, one should perform twelve thousand recitations; by the power of Gaṇeśa, delusion arises among the people. || 91 ||
One should grind together Dīrghatuṇḍā, Amṛtā, and Grāhyā under the Puṣya asterism on a Sunday.
Having smeared his two hands with that powder, [he should perform] one thousand and eight [recitations].
Having recited the Manu-mantra, one should display those two hands toward the elephants; then even the elephants equal to Airāvata will flee. || 93 ||
If the king then desires to capture elephants, he should have a strong stable for binding elephants properly constructed within the elephant forest. (94)
One should construct a large, square enclosure provided with a firm perimeter;

therein, one should properly prepare a level ground that is square and elevated. On its northern side, one should fashion a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) as prescribed, having first drawn the *Sarvatobhadra* mandala there.
One should worship [it]. || 95 ||
One should perform the external installation of Gaṇeśa with various ritual offerings.

One should offer oblations three times each with the seed-syllables of Tāra, Śrī, Māyā, and Kāma; one should also perform the homa with the two syllables *glauṃ* and *gaṃ*, and with the word *gaṇapataye*.

Then one should also perform oblations with the words "varavarade," and with this [mantra]: "Bring all people under my control, svāhā. Twenty-seven oblations should be offered as sacrificial offerings using fuel-sticks and cow's ghee.

Then, one should perform three oblations with the *samṛddhi* mantra and this [mantra]: "Bhur Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ," and thereafter "Agni Jātavedas. Then, one should offer nine oblations with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). || 98 ||

One should recite the entire root-mantra a number of times equal to the total count of its syllables; then, one should offer oblations of clarified butter and the eight substances accompanied by the three sweets.
Then, every day, according to the number of deities stationed in their respective shrines.
He should feed many Brahmins, and then he shall be increased by their blessings.

One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru consisting of fifty elephants, or else their value, or even a tenth part of that; having thus gratified the true guru by giving this, [one should proceed]. || 101 ||
Of the four pairs [of months], [the first] belongs to the six Gaṇeśas, and the pair [following] to the two Nidhis.
One should offer oblations of clarified butter with the mantras of the guardians of the limbs, the mothers, and the lords of the directions.
Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, Gaurī and Hara, as well as Kāma and Rati, and Pṛthvī and Varāha—these are the four pairs. || 103 ||
Siddhimodā, likewise Ṛddhipramodā, and Kāntisaṃyutā; Sumukhā, Durmukhā, Priyoktā, and Madanāvatī. || 104 ||
Vighna joined with Madanadravā, and Vighnakartā joined with Drāviṇī—these six are proclaimed as the Gaṇeśas, along with the two Nidhis. || 105 ||

The conch and the lotus, their respective mantras, their seed-syllables, and likewise their names and hearts [should be recited]. Having thus completed the fire-offering (homa), one should then present the food offering (naivedya). || 106 ||
Having worshipped Vighneśa once more, together with his limbs and his retinue, and having dismissed him into one's own heart, one may move about as one pleases. (107)
Then, after days equal to the number of Vedas, indeed hundreds of elephants and likewise young elephant calves fell down by the power of Vināyaka. || 108 ||
And a herd of female elephants falls [into the pit] like water into a jar;
one should properly worship Gaṇeśa in the aforementioned pit, according to the prescribed form. || 109 ||
Having established the fire there, one should perform oblations numbering one hundred thousand, using flowers mixed with milk and ghee,
as well as sugar.
Each of these substances, along with honey and the bark of the agaru tree, should be applied separately.
And the pill known as Vetāla emerges from the midst of the sacrificial pit.
Having attained the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest, one shall become a leader. Having risen at the hour of Brahmā during the new moon festival when the moon has waned, || 112 ||
Having taken a lotus-clump and cow-dung from a tawny cow, and having recited the mantra ten thousand times,
one should block the entrance of the pit.
Regarding tigers, boars, fierce thieves, and the like, there is no need for deliberation here. (113)
Jātī, dhattūra, mañjiṣṭhā, pracaṇḍā, and hastayojinī.
The [mantras] beginning with the *śikhā* and ending with the one called *karṇikā* are formed by means of the impurities (*mala*) of the skin, tongue, and eyes.
Having properly prepared a pill from substances produced by smelling with the nose, and having touched it, one should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times. || 115 ||
One should have her lick a dose the size of a *guñjikā* or a barley grain; even half a mustard seed, when consumed by a woman, acts as a subjugator. (116)

With his senses conquered, he should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times; he should offer oblations consisting of parched grain, fried rice, and flowers, numbering one-tenth of that amount. He shall obtain a maiden from a noble family;
then, he should meditate upon Vināyaka. 117.
Having worshipped him with perfumes and other offerings, one should recite that mantra one hundred thousand times.
Why is one released from fetters? Now, [regarding] the flower of the bilva tree: || 118 ||
One should saturate these—tagara, devadāru, priyaṅgu, agaru, candana, and nāgakeśara—equally with honey. || 119 ||

Having made it into a pill and touched it, one should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times; that pill becomes a perfected pill (siddhaguṭikā), and from its incense comes the destruction of disease.
From this incense, even one who is destitute shall become wealthy and beloved by the people;
an unfortunate woman shall become fortunate, and a maiden shall obtain a husband at a reservoir of water. || 121 ||
From one hundred thousand recitations, rain shall fall within seven days. Now, hear the desired procedure for its hundred-thousandfold fire-oblation (lakṣahoma). || 122 ||
A twice-born man should offer oblations with curd for the sake of cattle, with honey for the sake of gold; he should offer with ghee for the sake of prosperity, and with milk for the sake of sugar.

An oblation with curd leads to all prosperity; with rice cooked in ghee, it leads to an increase in food; with parched grain, the oblation leads to fame; and with sesame seeds and rice, it is for the sake of wealth. (124)
One should perform a fire-oblation with safflower or oleander flowers for the sake of obtaining garments; with barley one may subjugate a king, and with blue lotuses, his queen.

Having fashioned dolls and other such objects from *kairava* flowers for that minister, as well as items derived from his father, the bride should perform the oblation (*homa*) using wood from the *vaṭa*, *plakṣa*, and *udumbara* trees for the sake of subjugation (*vaśyā*). (126)
And having taken sacrificial fuel from somewhere, one should perform the oblation.
One should subdue the castes beginning with the Brahmins; lack of rain [is brought about] by an oblation of salt.
Then, for the sake of the Great Lord of Gaṇas, there would be excessive rain; I shall now declare his syllables, which one should recollect for rites performed for specific desires. 128.

One should visualize [the deity] as yellow for paralyzing, ruddy for subjugation, smoke-colored for eradication; black for killing, reddish for summoning, and pale-red toward an enemy. One should likewise meditate on [the deity] as green for the attainment of wealth and white for liberation. 129.
I shall now describe the libation to Gaṇeśa, which bestows the fruits of all desires; it is equal to the three Vedas and its form is clearly revealed here. (130)

In a solitary, secluded, and delightful place, free from all disturbances, the practitioner of mantra, having performed his ablutions and other rites, should be endowed with the ritual placements (nyāsa) as previously described. || 131 ||
Having visualized a forest of blooming lotuses in the middle of the pond, he should imagine a great lotus in its center,
resembling the rising sun.
The practitioner of mantra should meditate upon it as suddenly blossomed—elevated, rich with fragrance, delightful, and captivating—just as prescribed by the previously mentioned mantra. || 133 ||
He beheld a pure silver staircase leading down from the solar disc.
Having emerged and descended, he spoke [to the one] situated in the center of the pericarp.
Having meditated thus, one should again offer libations to Mahāgaṇapati along with his retinue—[the word "I satisfy" (tarpayāmi) is to be understood as the remainder].
One should worship him with excellent perfumes and flowers, together with his retinue, as before. || 135 ||
Having placed the lotus-mouth upon the head of the preeminent practitioner, one should meditate on [the deity] raining down streams of jewels upon the head of the god. || 136 ||
With a tranquil mind, one should propitiate the God of gods with supreme devotion using water mixed with camphor, sandalwood, saffron, and musk. || 137 ||
At the end of the name as prescribed, one should say, "I satisfy.
Listen now to this procedure for libation (tarpaṇa), the Vedic libation. || 138 ||

At the end of this, the Vedic practitioner should utter "svāhā"; however, the other [the householder] should say "namaḥ," and one of left-handed conduct (vāmācārī) should likewise say "namaḥ. || 139 ||
Having first uttered the root mantra, one should then satisfy Mahāgaṇapati upon the head of the deity ten times. || 140 ||

Furthermore, it should be known that the libation (tarpaṇa) is to be performed four times in each instance everywhere. Having uttered one syllable of the root mantra, one should perform the libation. || 141 ||
Again, one should perform the libation four times with the complete root mantra. In this manner, there shall be libations numbering six, five, and four. || 142 ||
Having again gratified them with the root mantra, one should then gratify the couples. In this regard, the ritual procedure should be as follows:
"I gratify [Name] together with [Name]"—this is the remainder [to be supplied]. Then, saying "I gratify [Name]," one should gratify them once more with the root mantra. 143.
"I satisfy such-and-such [deity] with what was offered by such-and-such [person]," and then he should pay homage.
Furthermore, the root mantra should likewise be used for the libation four times.
In this manner, between each of the six groups of deities and their respective consorts, one should perform the libation with the root mantra four times, equal in number to the [four] skins. 145.
Vasumatī shall be the wife of Vasundharāśaṅkhanidhi as well as of Padmanidhi;
between those two, she should be worshipped eightfold with the root mantra.
The libation (tarpaṇa) should be performed with the root mantra, and one should perform the libation again;
thus it is measured by the four sets of four earth-syllables (bhūbīja), which are [further] determined by the Vedas and the Vedas (i.e., forty). || 147 ||

I shall now describe the procedure for libation (tarpaṇa) which is beneficial for practitioners of Tantra: first, having performed the libation with the root mantra, one should perform the libation with the syllables of the mantra. (148)
Bhū-bhū-bhū-bhū-kubhū-pañca, and five with two directions.
And by means of the root-mantra of the intermediate directions, the fourfold pedestal is thus accomplished. || 149 ||

Then, having satisfied [the deity] with the root mantra, one should perform the satisfaction of Gaṇeśa and his weapons; for this is the sequence of the weapons by means of the intermediate *śūla* mantra. 150.
First, having uttered its seed-syllable (bīja) and then the Praṇava (Om), one should then say "to the self named so-and-so" and "salutation to [the deity] named so-and-so. || 151 ||
"Namaḥ mukam tarpayāmi svāhā"—this is declared to be the mantra. [In the phrase "vighnaṃ bhūmau," the absence of the vowel *u* in *bhūmau* is an archaic Vedic usage.
Then follow *ramām*, *māyām*, *śrīṃ*, *hrīṃ*, *klīṃ*, *vasudhām*, and *gam*. (152)

In the eleventh [chapter], one should also state the six seed-syllables (bīja) of Gaṇeśa; thereafter, one should speak of the mantra, its fruit, its power (śakti), and the binding of the vital breaths (prāṇabandha). || 153 ||
The pervasion of the wheel (cakravyāpti), the Tāra, the Earth-knowledge (bhūvidyā), and the three worlds (trilokaka)—these are said to be the forms of the Self;
I shall now state their names. || 154 ||
And the citron fruit, the axe, the bow, and the trident.
A wheel, a lotus, a noose, and a blue lotus, together with the trunk-tip and the tusk of an elephant calf. 155.
Thus is the determination of the weapons: a jewel-pitcher is placed upon the trunk; everything is produced in a number of twenty-two, including the libation (tarpaṇa). || 156 ||

At the end of the six seed-syllables, one should utter each respective name in the dative case. Having recited the entire root mantra, one should say "Amukagaṇapam" (the name of the specific Gaṇeśa). The mantra ends with the word for fire's wife (*svāhā*), interspersed within the intervals of the root mantra. (157)
Vighna, Vināyaka, Vīra, Śūra, and Varada; likewise Ibhavakra, Ekadanta, Lambodara, and Gaṇeśvara. || 158 ||
Kṣipraprasādana and likewise Mahāgaṇapati—thus there should be four groups of twenty; thereafter, one should offer libations to the pairs.
One should first utter the pair of seed-syllables (yugmabīja) of Gaṇeśa, and after that [the following].
Having addressed that pair as before, [the mantras] are interspersed with the root mantra.
Śrīṃ, Hrīṃ, Klīṃ, and Glaum—these are the four seed-syllables (bīja) in their respective order. In this manner, there are sixteen such groups of four. || 161 ||
One should also offer libations to the Vināyakas, preceded by the seed-syllable of Śrī Gaṇeśa and ending with the word "vināyakān."
And four squares, equal in number to the Jinas, are likewise interspersed with the Mūla-mantras. || 162 ||

One should perform the libation according to the rules as before, interspersed with the root mantra; likewise, Hrīṃ Gaṃ Vasundharā and Śaṅkha are to be offered libations as previously described. || 163 ||

In this case, at the beginning is the female seed-syllable and at the end is the male; there is a reversal of the two seed-syllables. Glauṃ gaṃ is the seed-syllable for the Earth and the Lotus-Treasure during the libation.
In this manner, one should perform eight libations with the root mantra at the end; thus, there are libation sequences numbering four hundred and four (404).
First, one should then satisfy [the deity] four times with the root mantra.
One should thus satisfy the pairs [of deities], beginning with their respective seed-syllables and ending with *svāhā*. || 166 ||

Then, one should satisfy the pair of treasures (Nidhis) within the group of six; in between each [pair], the root mantra is recited four times in this sequence. This is declared to be the "lighter libation" (laghutarpaṇa), totaling one hundred and eight [recitations]. || 167 ||
Mahāgaṇapati, Puṣṭi, and the four pairs.
The six Gaṇeśas and the pair of Nidhis—thus these are thirteen. (168)
Now, these [mantras] are also recited individually at intervals during the root-satiation (mūlatarpaṇa);
furthermore, two hundred and eight [recitations] are performed at the beginning and the end.
Then, however, the root [sum] becomes two hundred and sixteen.
This is considered the middling *tarpaṇa* rite for Mahāgaṇapati. || 170 ||
Alternatively, as before, one should first perform the libation with the root mantra; then, one should perform it with each individual syllable of the root mantra. (171)
One should perform this four times each within the interval of the root mantra.
And thereafter, it becomes like a young elephant being trained. || 172 ||
Furthermore, it arises that one should satisfy [the deity] by means of the intermediate method; this is the complete tantric-vedic libation (tarpaṇa) of Mahāgaṇapati. || 173 ||
Now, the libation according to the divisions of the limbs of desire shall be described. One should offer libations to the deity at Puṣkara with pure waters for the sake of liberation. (174)
One desiring prosperity should satisfy Gajānana with cow's milk on the head; for the sake of desire, one should satisfy the Lord with honey in the secret region. 175.

For the purpose of attraction and for subjugation, one should satisfy that deity with honey on the eyes; for the subjugation of kings, one should satisfy the deity with clarified butter on the back. 176.
Likewise, there is the satiation with castor oil and the dew of a widow.
For the increase of joy, one should satisfy the Lord with milk in the section on the aggregates (skandha).
With milk, curd, and honey, it brings about the increase of one's sons when applied to the beak. Thus, for whoever worships Gaṇeśa, my beloved, properly, both worldly enjoyment and liberation arise;
of this there is no doubt. (178)
By this very lord of sūtras, Divodāsa was exiled after he had fashioned a path outside the Vedas, which is dear to the Kali age. || 179 ||
And the deities of the great Dakṣa-āmnāya were brought here; by worshipping them, people have come to despise their own respective duties. (180)
One who does not know the taste of the *pṛkṣasthavāruṇī* fruit longs for its result; one afflicted by hunger rejects the *kaśeruka* root found upon the ground. (181) p. 382)
But when the people of Divodāsa saw this with swift curiosity, they internalized the Dharma, such as that of the Kaulikas and others, within their own hearts. || 182 ||
The subjects enjoy the king's righteousness, but the monarch suffers for the subjects' sins.
By virtue of that merit, this king was sent from Kāśī to heaven; and by the grace of my son, I have established my residence in Kāśī. (183)
Whichever deities have been assigned by the calculator to the left-hand path.
Desiring the purpose of entering Kāśī, they were gratified by others.
In that regard, the propitiation by the Cīnāgaṇa deities through the left-hand path was requested by them and granted by me;
it is set forth in the tantras. || 185 ||
Heroes such as Kṣatriyas and others are born devoted to that path; women become Yoginīs—O Brahmin, one should avoid them. 186.
At the end of King Divodāsa’s reign, when the Kali Yuga had arrived, the twice-born were oppressed by them and turned away from the path ordained by the Vedas. || 187 ||
Out of fear of those wicked people, they took refuge on the Himālaya mountains; even there, they pursued them, intent on causing the destruction of their dharma. || 188 ||
Then I was praised by many Brahmins with Vedic hymns of praise.
From the midst of them emerged my linga, endowed with a face.
Beholding him, those heroes prostrated themselves with all eight limbs and spoke:
O God of gods, [this is] according to what was spoken by you.
This is a transgression of the path. || 190 ||
This is being performed by foolish Vaidikas; for the sake of their upliftment, this [work] is a purifying cause even greater than the water of the Gaṅgā. 191.
"More pure, delicious, and nourishing than bulbs, roots, fruits, and the like—this meat we offer for the sake of redeeming our three births. (192)
Produced from various sacred fords and consecrated by many rites, these fish bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation; I am prepared to give them to you. (193)
For in this essence-less cycle of existence, the essence is the fawn-eyed woman;
she who was placed by you, O Lord, upon your own body and by Viṣṇu within his heart. (194)
O dear one, we are indeed compassionate, and we are prepared to grant these boons upon the lap of Brahmā and upon the throne of the Lord of the Gods. || 195 ||
Together with the gods, they [performed] six months of meat-eating, six types of food, and visited six sacred fords.
The six fragrances and the six flavors, along with the mudrās, were prepared to be offered. || 196 ||
These people do not grasp them at all, just as one does not grasp sacrificial animals.
Having abandoned the supreme food contained in golden vessels, they subsist on grass.
Then, for the sake of protecting the feet of Dharma, I spoke these words: "O heroes, listen to my words, which are filled with compassion for all living beings. (198)
In this sinful Kali age, people must not be led onto the Kaulika path.
In the ten types of extremely lowly wombs and so forth, only one is born.

Among those born from the wombs of worms, there are ten [species] beginning with the *undurū* (mole/rat); and from among those ten beginning with the *undurū*, the *viḍāla* (cat) and others are produced. (200)
Among those ten, however, one is born as some kind of bird;
among those [ten], one is born among the species of wild animals. || 201 ||
And among those ten, there may be a buffalo or a bull; or among those ten, there may be a donkey or a young camel. (202)
In that group of ten, there might be someone among the species of horses and so forth; indeed, in that group of ten, there might be a man or an elephant. (203)
May they always nourish this life of the noble one with time;
and from among those very men, one is born [as such]. (204)
Having placed some dharma before them, the thought "I am liberated" arises; yet, within the midst of those ten [qualities], some coloration is produced. (205)
Among those ten, perhaps one person may be born in accordance with the natural order; among those ten, perhaps one man may attain the status of a twice-born. (206)
Among ten Brahmins, perhaps one becomes a true Brahmin through great difficulty; among ten of those, perhaps one is born devoted to ritual action. (207)
Among ten performers of ritual action, there might be one man who possesses virtuous conduct; among ten such men, however, there might be one child-like yogi. || 208 ||
Among ten yogins, one is born as a man of knowledge (jñānin); among ten men of knowledge, perhaps one becomes liberated, or perhaps not. || 209 ||
Thus, liberation is very difficult to achieve, for this cycle of existence has persisted for a long time. Indeed, all those who have set out upon the Kaulika path would become liberated.
And the creation and destruction of Brahmā will occur very swiftly.
Thus deceived, the heroes, deluded by intoxication, danced; crying "We are liberated!
We are liberated!", they struck one another with vigor.
Then, all of them, greatly rejoicing, spoke these words: "Alas! You people are like cattle; you have gone to the supreme hell. (212)
"Request a boon from us for the sake of your own deliverance in a future birth.
Then, this boon was requested by the delighted Brahmins. (213)
"This one who is seen here as the bearer of the skull, in the form of a *liṅga*—may our minds, unwavering, take delight therein. (214)
Having heard this, the heroes then spoke these words: "Let that which was requested by the animals here be true. (215)
Of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others, as well as the Śaktis, the Sun, and the celestial dwellers.
"O Lord, having abandoned us today, why indeed do you seek [protection] from the beasts? (216)
For the hero, there are wine, mantra, mudrā, fish, and meat. Oh, what wretchedness!

The Kaulika people grant worldly enjoyment, [the fruits of] action, and liberation. For us, liberation comes through enjoyment; that [liberation] has been abandoned by those who are like beasts. || 217 ||
Whatever pleasure is obtained by placing the male organ within the female organ—
By worshipping this inner self with that, one becomes liberated at that very moment. || 218 ||
If the inner self is satisfied by that which is offered into the digestive fire after being prepared through various rites, one is liberated. (219)
When wine, which is sweeter even than nectar, reaches the heart, at that very moment all afflictions go to their destruction and one is liberated. || 220 ||
When the fragrance of the mudrā flows toward the nose, this essence of the nectars is proclaimed as the Śaphara. || 221 ||
If immortality results from enjoying those [pleasures], then what is the use of the Vedic path? Oh, let the beasts listen to these words, the essence of the Tantra! (222)
Whether wise or foolish, whether initiated or uninitiated, by forming even a hundred thousand mudrās, one shall attain liberation. || 223 ||
Furthermore, the performance of the mudrās should always be learned in this manner.
The great goddesses beginning with Cāmuṇḍā, and the ones of great power beginning with Bhairava. || 224 ||
They are satisfied by mudrās alone, not by worship with flowers and other offerings. He by whom the eight mudrās are performed has performed the great worship (mahāpūjā). || 225 ||
Neither Brahmā nor Śaṅkara can attain that state which he attains; liberation will certainly occur simply from seeing a thousand vulvas. || 226 ||
In ancient times, indeed, a censure of the Kaulika path was made by Viṣṇu.
By the power of that sin, I was born as the son of Daśaratha.
Because his power was thus disparaged, Sītā was abducted by the Rākṣasa; he has experienced sorrow, and this separation is to endure for a long time. || 228 ||
Having obtained a body of great power, he performed penance once again; then he was born in a family of cowherds, always devoted to Śakti. || 229 ||
With half his body possessed by powerful beings, he was a constant consumer of fermented liquor.
He was born from the sight of the vulva of sixteen thousand women. || 230 ||

O bound souls who are eligible for liberation, listen to these words for your own benefit: [practice] without meat, without [eating] for a month, without fish, and without sexual intercourse. || 231 ||
Without one or another mudrā, there can be no accomplishment of the desired goal.
That which was requested by the animals—what indeed is that? It is precisely this. || 232 ||
When this was said by the heroes, the sages of praised vows, their faces blooming within with joy, spoke words preceded by peace. || 233 ||
We, however, are like cattle; the wise have observed that our life-force consists of food. You are lions, and like lions, you always subsist on meat. || 234 ||
Just as the satisfaction of cattle arises from grassy meadows alone, so too is ours through food; we are not capable of eating meat. (235)
Just as meat is the food for lions, but never grain.
In the same way, it is said that meat and other such foods are the sustenance for lions.
Having heard these words of theirs, they spoke to Maheśvara: "These animals, in the form of brahmins, desire to serve you. (237)
"Therefore, you too, O Paśupati, remain firm here in Nepāla. Having spoken thus, they drank wine again and became intoxicated. (238)
Then, indeed, I was gratified by the brahmins with various kinds of hymns of praise. At that time, I said to them, "Choose, choose! (239)
And they said again, "O Lord, how may liberation be attained in the Kali age? O Master, tell us that dharma by which our welfare may be secured. (240)
Having heard these words of theirs, I explained the truth:

"In this world, there is no liberation without knowledge, and indeed, knowledge does not exist without dharma. Therefore, O twice-born ones, the rites prescribed in the Vedas must be performed constantly. (241)
Just as a hook is concealed within flour and cast down for the purpose of catching fish, so too is the practice of the Tantras. || 242 ||
If, by the turn of fate, there should be no fish-eater to consume the powder, then his satisfaction arises and he may continue to live. (243)
In the same way, on the left-hand path (vāmamārga), those whose impurities have been burnt away by knowledge become liberated, and no others; therefore, one should avoid that path. || 244 ||
One should not respect the words of those who, following paths outside the Vedas, are devoted to the left-hand path (vāmamārga) and yet praise their own dharma alone. || 245 ||
In this terrible Kali age, he who practices the path of the Vedas to the best of his ability will have no further birth in the Kali age. || 246 ||
Neither in the world of Yama, nor in hell, nor even in the netherworld (pātāla) is there such a place; that birth as a Brahmin in the Kali age is itself considered to be hell. || 247 ||
Hereafter, I shall describe those deities who were defeated by Gaṇeśa for the sake of the true purpose and for the sake of emptying Divodāsa [of his city]. 248.
They were indeed brought here by me and are dear to Pārvatī as well. By the command of Gaṇeśa, Kāma, though burnt, has risen again. || 249 ||
Residing in the heart of everyone within the palace of Divodāsa, I shall proclaim his mantras, which bestow the fruits of both worlds. || 250 ||

In the beginning, its one-syllable mantra is considered to be the form of the seed-syllable *klīm*. Sammohana is the sage (*muni*), the *chanda* is *chaṃdas*, and the deity (*devatā*) is Smara. One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) using the seed-syllable endowed with the six long vowels. || 251 ||
Clad in red garments, red in color, and anointed with red perfumes and unguents.
It was auspicious, adorned with ornaments and crowns consisting of a multitude of various jewels.
Holding in his hands a noose, a goad, a bow made of sugarcane, and flower-arrows.
One should visualize Kāmadeva seated upon a red lotus. || 253 ||
Having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus, one should worship the limbs (aṅgas) in the center; one should worship the limbs in the pericarp, on the six petals, and in the corners. || 254 ||
One should worship from the front of the deity up to the center, and also upon the filaments [of the lotus]: Mohinī, Kṣobhiṇī, Trāsinī, and then Stambhinī. || 255 ||
Ākarṣiṇī, Drāviṇī, Hrādinī, Klinnā, and Kledinī.
On the six petals are Madana, Anaṅga, Manmatha, and Kusumāhvaya. || 256 ||
For she is both distressed by the flower-weaponed god of love and yet cooled by that same god.
Then follow Anaṅgamekhalā and Anaṅgadīpikā. || 257 ||
All those to be meditated upon have lotuses in their hands and are adorned with ornaments; outside of that, on a sixteen-petaled lotus, one should perform worship starting from the front. (258)
Yuvatī, Vipralambhā, Jyotsnā, Sūrumadadravā, Suratā, Vāruṇī, Lolā, Līlā, and likewise Saudāmanī. || 259 ||
Kāmacchatrā, Candrarekhā, Śukī, Madanāhvayā, Yoni, and Māyāvatī—these were the young women with smiling faces. || 260 ||
Afflicted by desire, they held white water-lilies in their hands and placed attendants upon the tips of the petals.
One should worship the delusion and sorrow of Kāma as his grace and amorous play. || 261 ||
Madanātura, Apatrapa, Yuvan, Candana, Ratipriya, Cūtapuṣpa, Grīṣma, Tāpana, and Ūrjaka. || 262 ||
During both the Hemanta and Śiśira seasons, the flower-arrowed gods revel;
their quivers are slung upon them, and their minds are attached to women with crimson complexions. || 263 ||
Outside of that, one should worship the sugarcane bows upon the eight petals;
then [the deities] Parabhū, Sārasākṣa, Śuka, and Megha. (264)
And one should worship these four in the corners of the underground chamber: Āpāṅgī, Uruvilāsā, Hīnacīrā, and Ratipriyā. || 265 ||
Mādhavī, Mālatī, Hariṇākṣī, and Madotkaṭā.
With beautiful white chowries in their hands, they were dark-complexioned and adorned in body. || 266 ||
Then, one should worship Indra and the other deities, as well as the vajra and the other implements, on the exterior.
In this manner, he who propitiates Smara with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings—
He obtains incomparable good fortune, the fulfillment of desires, and great prosperity.
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for this is said to be one hundred and twenty thousand [recitations]. || 268 ||

One should offer oblations with *kiṃśuka* blossoms smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*) amounting to one-tenth of that [number]. Having performed the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*), one should also feed the Brahmins. || 269 ||
Then, having worshipped the Guru and bowed down along with the Brahmins, he should satisfy them well;
thus, once the mantra has been mastered, the practitioner of mantras should perform the ritual applications (prayogas). || 270 ||
He who offers one thousand and eight oblations for three days with *aśoka* flowers smeared with the three sweets shall become beloved by all. || 271 ||
The knower of mantras, having properly worshipped the fire, should offer one hundred and eight oblations well-saturated with cow's ghee while reciting this mantra. || 272 ||
O beloved, he who indeed feeds his own wife with a pouring of clarified butter [attains this].
In birth after birth, she shall remain obedient to his command.
By offering oblations of parched grain mixed with curd every day until a mandala is completed, the practitioner of mantra obtains his desires,
and that maiden also obtains a beloved husband.
I shall proclaim the garland-mantra (mālāmantra) that grants success to Kāmadeva:
[the heart-mantra] for Kāmadeva, who is beloved by all people. (275)
To delude all people, one should say it consists of blazing fire; one should cause [the mantra] to blaze and proclaim my fame to all people. || 276 ||
"Vaśaṃ kuru kuru svāhā" is the mantra composed of Nāga syllables.
The ritual of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) is declared by means of the six long and horizontal *klīṃ* seed-syllables. || 277 ||
First, one should contemplate these syllables of Kāma upon the fingers of the hands:
the goddess Drāviṇī beginning with *drāṃ*, and also Kṣobhiṇī beginning with *droṃ*. (278)
One should assign the syllable *klīṃ* as the Enchantress (*vaśīkarī*), and the Great Goddess (*maheśvarī*) beginning with *krūṃ klīṃ*.
And he [recited] the first, the Ākarṣiṇī, and the Sammohinī, beginning with the Hā. || 279 ||
Kāma, Anmatha, Kandarpa, Makaradhvaja, and Mīnaketu—these should be assigned to the five limbs and to the fingers. || 280 ||

One should place the forty mantra-syllables, beginning with the letter 'A', in their respective locations; then, one should likewise place them upon the limbs of the Mātṛkā, starting from the nose and proceeding through the other limbs. (281)
One should assign the three syllables to the five locations—the belly, the heart, the throat, the face, and the nose—and assign the remainder as the all-pervading [vyāpaka]. || 282 ||
Again, one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) with the complete mantra; thereafter, one should perform the extensive placement (bṛhannyāsa) of the letters of the Mātṛkā.

Having uttered the syllable that unfolds the seed of desire (Kāma-bīja) along with the pair [of vowels], and having pronounced the end of "Bhī" followed by "Namaḥ," one should perform the ritual placement (vinyāsa) upon the limbs of the Mātṛkā.
One should place Kāma, endowed with passion and bestowing desire, together with Prīti; and likewise Kāntā, joined with desire, together with Mohinī, who is full of splendor. || 285 ||

One should install Śyāmalā, who possesses the limbs of desire, is joined with Kamalā, moves according to her will, is playful, is endowed with passion, is the embodiment of creative imagination, is accompanied by a lover, has a pure smile, and is united with the Increaser of Desire (Kāmavardhana). || 286 ||

[He meditated upon] Viśālākṣa joined with Ramā, Ramaṇa with Lolajihvikā; Digambara as the Lord of Rati, and Ramā who is exceedingly dear to Atirati; Rātrinātha with Kubjikā, and Aramākānta with his beloved. || 287 ||
He was sporting eternally with Kalparūpā, who is like the moon; he was joined by Nandaka and Bhoginī, and by Nandana and Kāmadā; and he was delighting Sulocanā, Nandin, and Pralāpinī. (288)
Pañcabāṇa and Madanī, Ratibhaṅga and Kalipriyā; Puṣpadhanvan and Mṛgākṣī, Sumukha and Mahādhanus; Kramaṇa joined with Nalinī, and Bhramaṇa joined with Yajinī. || 289 ||
Manmatha is joined with Madanā; Morbhaṅga is also joined with Mālā; Śānta is joined with Mugdhā; and Bhrāmaka is joined with Ramā. || 290 ||
Śṛṅga is joined with Bhramā, while Bhrāntācāra is joined with Lolā.
And she brings delusion with her flickering, long-tongued, enchanting [glance]. (291)
Ratipriyā, Modaka, Mohākṣī, and Lolā.
Mohavardhanī, Śṛṅgiṇī, Madanā, and likewise Pāṭalā. || 292 ||
And also Manmatha, Madana, Mālā, and Mātaṅga.
Bhṛṅganāyikā, Haṃsinī, Gāyaka, and Viśvatomukhī. || 293 ||
One who knows song, one who brings joy to the world, a dancer, a woman, a jester, one endowed with splendor, a madman, and a sweet-voiced bird. || 294 ||
Having placed the [deity] intoxicated, joined with Vṛkodara, the dark-complexioned one who delights in sport, accompanied by Sarvottamā, and who increases greed, one should meditate upon him. (295)

As before, one should perform the worship and other rites, and likewise worship [the deity] upon the seat of Kṛṣṇa; furthermore, the ritual applications (prayoga) originating from Kṛṣṇa-Gopāla should also be performed. || 296 ||
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight, on a Monday, one thousand and eight betel leaves,
chewed by the trunk of an elephant, [should be offered].
One attains manhood [through this], and one may cause a beloved wife to bear a virtuous son. Now, the Gāyatrī of Kāma, along with its worship and other rites, is proclaimed.
The sage Vātsyāyana is considered to be like the single syllable of renunciation. || 298 ||
We know Kāmadeva; we meditate upon him who has flowers as his arrows; may that Anaṅga inspire us. || 299 ||
Sixty thousand recitations of this are prescribed; one attains all desires and, even in the next world, a favorable rebirth. || 300 ||
First, however, he was sent by Gaṇeśa into the inner apartments of King Divodāsa and captivated the hearts of the women. || 301 ||
And having cast aside that dharma, it entered the heart of the king—that dharma which was weak, which had been cursed, and which had then been banished from Kāśī. || 302 ||
Therefore, in the assembly of the Gaṇas, there is another desire even greater than mine; since Viṣṇu is composed of desire, therefore desire is the refuge of the virtuous. || 303 ||
When Kāma had entered the inner apartments [of Divodāsa], the leader of the Gaṇas, being scorched by his splendor, exerted himself to become his ally. || 304 ||
Then, having meditated upon Mahākāla and the eternal Mahāmāyā, he beheld his supreme Lord through their power. || 305 ||
Within him there arose a certain sequence of syllables belonging to a proponent of Brahman;
and reciting that very sequence, he remained for the duration of a year for the sake of liberation.
When the supernatural powers (siddhis) manifested on the bank of Maṇikarṇikā, he became renowned in Kāśī as Siddhivināyaka. || 307 ||
For the sake of the accomplishment of human beings, he may assume various forms.
He caused all [the afflictions], such as greed and hatred, to dwell there.
That mantra, which denotes only the boar, is the bestower of liberation.
By whose grace Divodāsa was protected and Guptasena brought to light. || 309 ||
Therefore, this mantra of the phenomenal world has been revealed in the tantras.
This Gāyatrī has been declared by me for the sake of the upliftment of those who are not Brahmins.
O gods, all mantras indeed bring about union with the divine; yet those five mantras which have been composed by me are contained within that [supreme mantra]. || 311 ||
Now I shall declare that mantra which is the subject of the five traditions (pañcāmnāya): the mantra of Mahākāla, which begins with the Praṇava, is the Manu. 312.
The second is proclaimed as Hṛllekhā, which expresses "great illusion" (māhāmāyā); the third consists of two syllables, "haṃsa," which expresses the "living soul" (jīva). || 313 ||
That which is declared by the wise to be the knowledge that severs the karma of the individual soul—if one says "I am indeed He," that is the fourth mantra consisting of four syllables. || 314 ||
Since it is from which the manifold world arises and which brings satisfaction to the deities, the two-syllabled mantra *svāhā* is proclaimed as the fifth. (315)
Thus has this eight-syllabled king of mantras been described;
since Brahmā, the source of the phenomenal world and all else, is remembered as its sage (muni). || 316 ||
Because it protects while singing, it is declared to be the Gāyatrī metre;
and because even though it is one, no limit to its splendor can be found, it is called the Supreme State, the Supreme Light, and the Deity. || 317 ||
But first, the placement of the Mātṛkās alone is traditionally taught as the very first step.
The second [type] is proclaimed as the nyāsa of the Mātṛkās together with the bindu. || 318 ||
The third [type of] nyāsa is proclaimed as the Kalādimātṛkā-nyāsa.
The fourth placement (nyāsa) for the Mothers, beginning with Keśavī, is now described.
The fifth placement (nyāsa) taught here consists of Śiva and Śakti.
The sixth is called the Mātṛkā-nyāsa, beginning with the seed-syllable of Māyā. || 320 ||
The seventh nyāsa, beginning with the seed-syllable of Śrī for the Mothers, is now described.
The Mātṛkā-nyāsa, beginning with the seed-syllable of Kāma, is considered the eighth. || 321 ||
The ninth [set] consists of the Mātṛkās preceded by the seeds Hrīṃ, Ramā, and Kāma.
The mantra of the Mothers, preceded by the *prapañca*, is recorded as the tenth. || 322 ||
And because time is all-pervasive, there is neither meditation nor worship.
Eight hundred thousand recitations of this mantra are said to constitute the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa).
Ugratārā and others are exceedingly fierce, as are Tārā and the rest, who are practitioners. || 324 ||

If this [mantra] is recited while encased [by the protective syllables] for one hundred thousand repetitions, the deity of the mantra will arrive and become a servant to the practitioner. By the power of Mahākāla, he shall not be inferior to those in heaven;
indeed, he shall be no different from them. 325.
The sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh), however, should be produced from the banyan, the plakṣa, the pippala, and the udumbara trees.
Sesame seeds, white mustard seeds, clarified butter, and oblation-materials—these are considered the eight substances for the fire-offering (homa). || 326 ||

One should honor the Brahmins for the sake of the fire-oblation (homa); thereby the mantra becomes perfected. All undertakings will succeed; the ritual application (prayoga) is now being described. || 327 ||
One should perform ten thousand recitations according to the prescribed rule, or alternatively, half of that.
And according to the specific purpose, one should offer oblations with the eight substances.
Then, one should offer four hundred, or half of that, or half of that again, [into the fire] for protection against the dangers of thieves, enemies, disease, serpents, and rākṣasas. || 329 ||
When minor diseases have arisen, [one should act] according to their respective doshas.
And one should offer eight thousand oblations with each of the eight substances.
Then, it may be twice this amount, or even four times this amount.
It shall thoroughly destroy possession by spirits, possession by malevolent grahas, sorcery, and the like. || 331 ||

But he who performs recitation, worship, and so forth, having abandoned the sequence prescribed by the scriptures—whether on the Vāma path or the Kaulika path—is devoured by Bhairava and the other [deities]. || 332 ||
And for whomsoever there occurs a loss of memory, [it should be remedied] with the eight substances for the fire-oblation (homa).
By performing a homa of one thousand oblations, a dream occurs at that very moment.
If one performs two thousand oblations for each [deity] with the eight substances, |||
He shall destroy epilepsy, loss of memory, and the affliction of wasting away.

One should offer eight substances smeared with the three sweets as an oblation for his enjoyment; because of that, Mahālakṣmī was greatly ashamed before the Fortune of that Lord of the Gods. || 335 ||
If one should offer a hundred thousand or even fifty thousand oblations, anointed with the three sweets;
The eight substances [are effective] for up to three years; by them, the three worlds are brought under one's control.
The accomplishment of subjugation and other rites is proclaimed here by means of the eight substances.
One should understand that the fire-oblation (homa) for prosperity and other purposes is to be performed according to the gravity of the task.
If one performs a hundred thousand oblations with pure sesame seeds according to the prescribed rite, his great sins will swiftly go to destruction; it is not otherwise. || 338 ||
By offering one hundred thousand lotuses into the fire, great fortune (Mahālakṣmī) arises;
an oblation of sacrificial food bestows nourishment, and an oblation of clarified butter brings glory. || 339 ||
An oblation of *mālatī* flowers also bestows complete subjugation over all. || 340 ||
Having offered sea salt as an oblation, one should likewise accomplish subjugation. Then, one should properly grind the rice grains produced from paddy. (341)
The practitioner should fashion an image of the person to be acted upon using that very powder mixed with the three sweets;
having properly worshipped it, he should touch it. || 342 ||

Then, the practitioner of mantras should recite the *prāṇasthāpana* mantra one hundred and eight times; having divided that [offering], he should perform the oblation at night according to the sequence of ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
One who performs this for seven nights brings under control either a man or a woman; it is likewise effective for her—there is no need for doubt in this matter. (344)
Such is the fruit even of a doll made of sea salt. Then, once that fire of the banyan tree has appeared, one should offer clarified butter as an oblation.
The practitioner of mantra should recite one hundred and eight times over whatever has been spoken or fallen.
Filled with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) that has been boiled with full-grown medicinal herbs.
Having placed it upon the hearth, one should cause fire to be applied to the pot from below.
Having recited it that many times, one should grasp [the mantra], which bestows all accomplishments.
Through its characteristic marks, by smearing it on the body, by making a tilaka mark, and likewise by wearing it upon the head, all calamities are instantly destroyed. || 348 ||
It destroys the afflictions caused by spirits, ghosts, piśācas, poisons, diseases, and the like; it brings everything under control for men and bestows prosperity, good fortune, and victory. (349)
At that time, upon the completion of a thousand-fold oblation, the wise one should give to the preceptor a pala or even half a pala of excellent gold.
Just as the gods obtain their desired fruit from the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), so indeed do they attain success through the mantra of Gaṇeśa known as Prapañca. || 351 ||
In his presence, the great men of the royal court assembled;
he alone was the teacher of the world and the expounder of all the scriptures. (352)
Except for the Brahmins, all other people are proclaimed to follow the path of Tantra.
Everywhere, worship is performed by means of the five [syllables] beginning with *ma*. || 353 ||
Gradually, such a state of affairs came to prevail here and there upon the earth.
Due to the greatness of the five-syllable mantra, even the king’s mind became deluded. || 354 ||
People devoted to petty deities perceive Dharma through books composed under the names of men; indeed, they do not see Dharma through the service of the five elements (pañcaka). || 355 ||
They quickly attained perfection through the power of Gaṇeśa. "Aha!
This is the Supreme Brahman manifest; aha! This is the Lord of Gurus; aha!
This is the Lord of the eightfold perfections, proficient in all branches of knowledge. || 356 ||
Having churned the four Vedas through our good fortune, the compassionate one has revealed the Kaulika path, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 357 ||
Having heard these words of the men, the brahmins went toward him;
and having properly offered them hospitality, he praised the scripture.

"Alas, O Brahmins, this sacrificial rite is primarily characterized by violence toward living beings! This sacrifice and ritual, though proclaimed by my Guru, is a mere proliferation of worldly elaboration; it should not be performed. (359)
Furthermore, austerity (tapas) should not be practiced, for it causes the self to become miserable. One should perform Tantric rites, and never those of the Vedic tradition. 360.
Those who follow the Vedas are said to be like sacrificial animals, whereas those who follow the Tantras are liberated while living.
They perform internal action; let this reality be reflected upon. || 361 ||
That which is given is obtained; this is in accordance with the Vedas and the Shastras. How can happiness be attained by giving pain to oneself? (362)
O best of the twice-born, great happiness is to be accomplished by means of the seed-syllable of bliss.
Therefore, having resorted to the Kaula path which bestows happiness in both worlds, O Brahmins, may you be liberated;
let that Vedic ritualism be abandoned.
Many years have passed as they have been performing [these rites] day and night; has any accomplishment (siddhi) been seen there? Let this be seen directly. || 364 ||
Having abandoned that Agnihotra rite described in the Tantras as the Prāṇāgnihotra—which is illuminated by the sixfold [system]—let this [true] practice be performed and observed. 365.
Having heard those words and being utterly deluded by Sarasvatī, they abandoned the entire path of the Vedas and entered into the left-hand Kaula traditions. || 366 ||

I shall now describe the Prāṇāgnihotra as revealed by Gaṇeśa. For the wise, success is swift; for others, downfall comes quickly. Seated with a tranquil mind, facing the east, and with a steady mind, one should assume a very soft posture.
One should be upright in the lotus posture. || 367 ||

One should contemplate the triangular region at the mūlādhāra as being of the nature of power (śakti); in its center, one should contemplate the seed-syllable of Māyā, which consists of the qualities (guṇas). || 368 ||
