From the eastern corner, one should contemplate three triangles within the [larger] triangles; and in their center, one should meditate upon the letter *ha*, whose nature is the quality of *sattva*. || 369 ||
One should contemplate that light within the letter *ha*, which is like the sun and is encircled by the *sāttvika* *ha*. (370)

That letter *ha* is joined with the letter *ī*, which belongs to the quality of passion (*rājasa*); and that pair is further pervaded by the letter *ra*, which belongs to the quality of darkness (*tāmasa*). || 371 ||
Having meditated upon the Mūlādhāra, one should [visualize] five sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) there: in the center, in the east, in the west, in the north, and likewise in the south.
One should visualize those sacrificial pits as being perpetually ablaze with fire.
In that place, these five fires should be known as being situated starting from the center and proceeding to the east.
The Āvasathya fire, the Satya fire, the Gārhapatya fire, the Hutāśana fire, as well as the Āhavanīya fire, and the Anvāhārya fire as the fifth. || 374 ||
One should contemplate those twelve suns of the kalpa, who are the cause of the web of light, whose nature is knowledge, and who are stainless, abiding within the dvādaśānta. || 375 ||

There, one should perform the oblation by offering the letters of the Mātṛkā in the form of clarified butter in reverse order; the five letters to be known are: traṃ, kṣaṃ, haṃ, saṃ, and ṣam. || 376 ||

Those which cause the knowledge of the scriptures and other sciences are to be meditated upon as resembling emeralds. The five syllables Śaṃ, Vaṃ, Laṃ, Raṃ, and Yaṃ are to be meditated upon as resembling gomeda gems;
these five bestow victory in battle upon Rāhu (Saiṃhikeya). || 377 ||
And the syllables maṃ, bhaṃ, baṃ, phaṃ, and paṃ are considered the [seed-syllables] of Śani.
They should be meditated upon as equal to Nīlendra, bestowing the accomplishment of mantras. || 378 ||
Naṃ, dhaṃ, daṃ, thaṃ, and taṃ—these should be meditated upon as resembling coral.
These [mantras] grant success for Mars at the gambling hall, the place of strife, and the royal gate. || 379 ||
The syllables ṇaṃ, ḍhaṃ, ḍaṃ, ṭhaṃ, and ṭaṃ are proclaimed to belong to Śukra.
Those who resemble a diamond should be contemplated; they bring about auspiciousness in the affairs of one's journey. || 380 ||
Ñaṃ, jhaṃ, jaṃ, chaṃ, and cam—these, possessing a luster equal to that of topaz, are highly auspicious for the Guru during rites such as marriages and other ceremonies. (381)
Ṅaṃ, ghaṃ, gaṃ, khaṃ, and kaṃ—these should be meditated upon as resembling lapis lazuli. These [syllables] of Ketu, which destroy enemies, should be meditated upon by the wise. (382)
AḤ, AṂ, AUṂ, OṂ, CA, AIṂ, E, ḶṂ, and ḶṂ are like pearls;
ṚṂ, ṜṂ, ŪṂ, UṂ, ĪṂ, ĀṂ, and AṂ are like topazes; these syllables, resembling diamonds, are the performers of royal duties. || 383 ||

Having meditated thus, one should then perform the fire sacrifice (homa) for those who possess excrement and urine: *kṣaṃ śaṃ maṃ naṃ ṇaṃ ca ñaṃ ṅaṃ aḥ eṃ ūṃ* in the domestic fire (*āvasathyaka*). || 384 ||
Then one should offer *laṃ*, *vaṃ*, *bhaṃ*, *dhaṃ*, *ḍhaṃ*, *ca*, *jhaṃ*, *ghaṃ*, *aṃ*, *ḷṃ*, and *uṃ* into the *satyakuṇḍaka*.
Then, into the fire known as the *āhavanīya*, one should offer *haṃ*, *laṃ*, *baṃ*, *daṃ*, *ḍaṃ*, *ca*, *jaṃ*, *gaṃ*, *auṃ*, *ḷṃ*, and *īṃ*;
and then *saṃ*, *raṃ*, *phaṃ*, *thaṃ*, and *ṭhaṃ*, and *chaṃ*.
The wise one should offer oblations into the Anvāhārya fire with the syllables Khaṃ, Oṃ, Ṛṃ, Ca, and Iṃ. || 386 ||
Paṃ yaṃ paṃ taṃ ṭaṃ ca caṃ kaṃ aiṃ ṛṃ āṃ [are placed] in the Gārhapatya fire.
One should sequentially remove the letters beginning with *kṣa* and ending with *na* as they appear in their order.
Then [one adds] *tāra* (oṃ), *māyā* (hrīṃ), that letter, and thereafter *haṃsaḥ so 'ham*.
Having uttered "svāhā," one should offer each individual syllable into the previously described sacrificial fire-pit.

The letter *a*, which is the form of the Supreme Brahman, should be meditated upon; from that, one should perform the oblation. Having thus offered the entire collection of sounds, one should then offer all the scriptures and so forth. (389)
In the sacrificial pit called the *āvasathya*, one should [place it] with the seed-syllable *haṃ* according to the instructions of the Guru.
Or one should place the qualities of air, such as touch and the rest, into the Indra-pit with the seed-syllable.
One should offer all forms with the seed-syllable *raṃ* in the western [direction],
and likewise offer all tastes with the seed-syllable *vaṃ* into the fire-pit in the north.
With the *lambī* seed-syllable, one should offer all fragrances into the southern sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
Day and night, amidst blazing fires resembling the fire of universal dissolution. || 392 ||
One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) in the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), conjoined with the phonemes of the Mātṛkā.
This one, whose nature is eternal purity, supreme bliss, and consciousness, shines forth resplendent. || 393 ||
The oblation (homa) beginning with the Dhruva-sacrifice and ending with the recitation (japa) is to be performed as previously described.
Having performed [the rite] with the number fifty, one should deposit [the mantras] accordingly according to the rule.
The practitioner becomes liberated while living and becomes long-lived;
in splendor he is like the sun, and like Śambhu, he is both the creator and the destroyer. || 395 ||
If one takes food every day according to this rule, [the following occurs].
One should offer morsels of food into the sacrificial pits, such as the Gārhapatya and others, in their proper sequence.
By means of these five mantras spoken in the Atharvaparīśiṣṭa.
O golden-hued, pure, and purifying ones, come hither with the Gārhapatya fire;
having distributed the fire and honored the Self, may you go upward, svāhā! || 397 ||
In the Anvāhārya fire, the fires possessing the luster of the sky, having distributed the fire and attended upon the Self, may they move upwards, downwards, and across—svāhā! || 398 ||
In the Āhavanīya fire, within the Vyāna breath, may those who are red-hued, pure, and purifying go—having distributed the fire and honored the Self—obliquely, upwards, and downwards; Svāhā! || 399 ||
In the domestic fire, being equal, possessing excellent luster and color, pure and purifying—having distributed the fire and honored the self—may they go equally across, upward, and downward; svāhā!
Having thus performed the fire-oblation (homa), one should then recite this mantra. With such a contemplation, one should eat everything; thus says Manu. || 401 ||
Becoming Vaiśvānara, I offer the four kinds of food; by this fifth method, may it go upward, downward, and across.

This mantra, consisting of thirty-four syllables and ending with "svāhā," has been declared. Then, having performed a silent oblation (tūṣṇīṃ homa), the knower of mantras [should proceed] with consecrated food. || 403 ||
Having drunk a handful of water with the mantra beginning with "amṛte," and having performed the ritual sipping (ācamana) according to the rules,
one should thereafter perform the purification sipping (śuddhācamana).
Beginning from the *mūlādhāra* and extending as far as the *dvādaśānta*, one should meditate upon the individual soul (*jīvātman*) as pervading the universe, eternal, one, and non-dual. 405.
It abides in its own nature, auspicious, and supreme, devoid of beginning, middle, or end.
One should offer oblations with pure *havanīya* [fire]; by that, [the deity] is satiated. || 406 ||

Having thus consumed the oblation—which takes the form of flowing nectar, is sprinkled with the fifty letters, and is offered into the fire—the practitioner of mantra blazes with the five fires. || 407 ||
Performing the Prāṇāgnihotra rite morning and evening, the practitioner of mantra [attains his goal].
He never experiences the affliction of remaining in the womb. || 408 ||
In this regard, I shall proclaim the reality which is the cause for the extraction of the Kaulika [teaching]: whatever deity is accomplished by means of the left-hand path, that indeed is it. 409.
Satiated by the fivefold ritual (mapañcaka), she bestows the desired objects upon the practitioner; however, Brahmins have no authority for the practice of the fivefold ritual. || 410 ||
If attachment to the world of manifestation arises through ignorance, delusion, or even from association with those in difficult circumstances, one experiences hell. || 411 ||
To effect its removal, I shall explain the method of the Prāṇāgnihotra;
one should offer the object of thought regarding the consumption of meat into the western sacrificial pit.

"One should think: 'That which is offered into the fire by the deity Agnimukhī is what is being consumed'; and during sexual union, one should contemplate one's own semen as being in the form of clarified butter. || 413 ||
One should contemplate the Dakṣiṇa fire as kindled by that [breath]; from that, it comes into being.
In this manner, one should engage in sexual union with the young woman until she reaches a state of complete satiation. || 414 ||
Having brought the mind to the principle of Pūrṇa, the falling of the banner occurs; there, no sin born of the night remains if the deity is pleased. || 415 ||
The practitioner should offer the mudrā into the eastern fire-pit with the root mantra; by that, the deity becomes pleased and he is not overcome by sins. || 416 ||
One should offer liquor into the mouth of the deity within the northern sacrificial pit; by its mere scent, one incurs no sin, for that is indeed dharma. || 417 ||

In the middle [fire], however, one should offer oblations of fish while meditating on the submarine fire (vaḍavānala); if the practitioner has renounced worldly pleasures, that [fire] bestows both enjoyment and liberation. || 418 ||
Thus have you been instructed, O Brahmins, regarding those proclaimed in the path of the left (vāmamārga).
Disciples were initiated with various mantras that bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon those who possess knowledge.
The mantra of Vāgvādinī is proclaimed to consist of three powers (śaktis). One should utter the Praṇava, the pair of "vada" syllables, and the word "vāgvādini. (420)

"Hrīṃ klīṃ klīnne kledini, utter 'mahākṣobhaṃ kuru' (perform the great agitation). Having spoken 'sauḥ', having uttered 'mokṣam', one should say 'praṇavaṃ kuruṣva' (perform the primordial sound). || 421 ||
The mantra of Vāgvādinī is said to consist of twenty-nine syllables; by means of nine, seven, and five [syllables], its three constituent parts are produced. || 422 ||
The presiding deities there are the goddesses of speech belonging to the triad beginning with Brahmā.
Those verses are proclaimed as the [summary] stanzas on arising, persistence, and destruction. || 423 ||
For her, there is no ritual worship, no meditation, no desire, and nothing at all;
[this is attained] swiftly by means of the grace of Gaṇeśa through the recitation of one hundred thousand syllables. (424)
One attains mastery over speech;
one attains the accomplishment of effects, such as their production, by contemplating it in the heart and likewise reciting the mantra-section.
One should say this once.
Then that truthful Bhāratī, who speaks of both curses and favors, declared: "His perfection shall remain firm through silence;
for one who is incapable of much, measured speech leads to success. (426)
Then the thirty-fold Bhairavī exposition was proclaimed by Gaṇeśa: "Vada vada vāgvādini aiṃ"—this is the single nine-syllable mantra. (427)
Having said "klinne kledini," O highly fortunate one, he should say "kuru. Bhairavī is the deity here, and there should be a recitation of one hundred thousand syllables. || 428 ||

Neither worship and the like, nor the ritual placement (nyāsa), nor the practice of the fivefold expansion (pañcaka) have been taught in all the tantras as being sufficient for success alone; rather, this [method] has been kept secret. 429.
Those by whom [this] has been known through the path of the Guru have attained perfection; of this there is no doubt.
By these very two mantras, many Kaulikas were created. || 430 ||
Now I shall describe the goddess Tripurabhairavī, who is to be kept secret from brahmins, and who bestows swift accomplishment in the Kaula, Vāma, and Siddhānta paths. (431)
The letter *ha*, the letter *sa*, and the letter *ra* joined with the vowel *ai*.
The Vāgbhava peak-syllable is said to be conjoined with Nāda and Bindu. || 432 ||

Then, one should join the letter *ha*, the letter *sa*, and likewise the letter *ka* with the sound *ra*, combined with the *nāda* and *bindu*, to the letter *ī*. This pentad of syllables is considered the *kūṭa* known as Kāmarāja. (433)
The letter *ha*, the letter *sa*, and the letter *ra* joined with the vowel *ai*, enriched by the *visarga*—this is the third *kūṭa*, consisting of three syllables. || 434 ||
The third seed-syllable, enriched with a bindu and not joined with the visarga, is declared for women. (435)
First the letter *sa*, followed by the three consonants *ha*, *ta*, and *bha*, and likewise the three consonants *ka*, *ṭa*, and *ta*.
Likewise, the mantra should be recited and given to them for the sake of its successful accomplishment.
The metre is Paṅkti, the sage is said to be Muni, and the deity is named Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
The goddess Tripurabhairavī, whose lotus feet are worshipped by the gods.
From the feet up to the navel, and from the heart upward, the channels flow like a flood.
One should likewise place these three seed-syllables at the heart, the head, and the end [of the body].

One should place the first [syllable] on the left, the next on the right, and the third on both. *Aiṃ* is declared for the heart, *klīṃ* for the head; with *sauḥ* at the end, the tuft (*śikhā*) is intended. 439.
Aiṃ is the armor (varma), klīṃ is the eye (netra), and saurāstra is proclaimed [as the weapon].
Furthermore, one should place the mind upon the three peaks at the crown, the foundation, and the heart.
One should perform the armor-rite for the body with three seed-syllables; that is now described. One should place them in sequence upon the wrist, the palm, and the fingertips. 441.

First on the right, then on the left, [he should place them] on the armpits, elbows, and hands; again on the right and the left, and likewise on the two feet. At the end of the feet, on the heart, and on the *liṅga*, he should perform the placement according to the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*).
p. 396) Now, one should place the seed-syllables upon the limbs according to the sequence of emanation: first on the left, then on the right, then on the two ears, and then on the chin. (443)
One should likewise place [the syllables] on the two temples, on the mouth, on the two eyes, on the two arms, on the heart, on the two elbows, and on the waist. 444.
Also on the marks of the knees, on the feet where the skin is worn away, on both sides, on the heart, on the pair of breasts, and likewise on the throat. (445)

The placement (nyāsa) consisting of the nine wombs is said to be performed with the three seed-syllables. One should perform the placement on the linga with the first seed-syllable, saying "Obeisance to Rati. || 446 ||
One should place "Prītyai namaḥ" in the heart with the middle seed-syllable;
the third [syllable], "Manobhavāyai," should be placed in the heart between the eyebrows. || 447 ||

One should again perform the placement (nyāsa) upon those very locations using the seed-syllables *sauḥ*, *klīṃ*, and *aim*. Having performed the placement of these— Amṛteśī, Yogeśī, and Viśvayoni— in their proper sequence, one should then perform the placement of the forms (*mūrtinyāsa*) using the seed-syllables in reverse order.
Then, having uttered "Obeisance" at the end of the mantra "To the one whose form is Śrīmitīśāna, and to the mind," the wise practitioner should install Dhareśāna.
Having uttered "Śreṃ, obeisance to the one whose form is Tatpuruṣa, who has the nature of Makaradhvaja," he should place it on the face; then he should place it on the heart. (450)
Hsrūṃ, salutation to the one of non-terrible form, the self of Kandarpa. Hsrīṃ, salutation to the one of Vāmadeva form, the self of Manmatha. 451.
Having placed this in the secret place, one should likewise place it on the two feet with the mantra: "HsKaṃ, obeisance to Kāmadeva, whose self is Sadyojāta. || 452 ||
Respectively by means of the faces directed upwards, eastward, southward, northward, and westward.
Then, having properly arranged [the five arrows], one should place them upon the limbs.
Hrāṃ, hrīṃ, klīṃ, and hūṃ are proclaimed as the five arrows.
One should place [the syllables] in sequence upon the fingers, beginning with the thumb and ending with the little finger.
By name, they are agitation, liquefaction, attraction, subjugation, and intoxication; [they are located] on the forehead, between the eyebrows, in the mouth, the ears, the eyes, and the throat. (455)
Having placed these eight Śaktis in the heart, navel, and genitals—namely Śubhagā and the others—the fourth is Bhagā and the third is Bhagasarpiṇī. || 456 ||
The fourth is Parājeyā, the fifth is Bhagamālinī; Anaṅgā, Anaṅgakusumā, and Anaṅgamekhalā are thus proclaimed. || 457 ||

All of them, whose limbs are the very essence of passion and who move slowly with the intoxication of amorous play, should be meditated upon as auspicious goddesses wearing safflower-dyed garments and green lower cloths. 458.

Then, one should perform the placement known as "Ornamentation" (bhūṣaṇanyāsa), which consists of these five [syllables] beginning with *vā-kā-ma-vūṃ* and *strīṃ*, along with the *sastārāḥ*. This is what is now being declared. || 459 ||
One should place [the syllables] on the head, between the eyebrows, on the pair of ears and eyes, and on the nose.
One should place the vowels on the two cheeks, the two lips, the two rows of teeth, and the mouth.
On the chin, the neck, the throat, the two sides, the pair of breasts, the two armpits, the two elbows, the hands, and the region of their backs. || 461 ||
With the syllable *haṃ* once on both hands, and likewise the *nityaka* on their backs; then at the navel, the secret place, and again on the two thighs, the two knees, and the two shanks. (462)
On the two buttocks, behind the two ankles, on the two big toes of the feet, on the neck-ornament,
as well as on the waist, the heart, the leaf-shaped earrings, the left earring, on the head, the bracelet,
and likewise on the drinking vessel. (463)
She is situated in the center of the pericarp of a red lotus located within the heart.
Resembling a hibiscus flower, she is adorned with garments and ornaments of a crimson hue.
She whose great delusion is the mansion of her smile, who has three eyes, and who bears the moon upon her crest.
She who embodies the ocean from which the entire essence of the beauty of the universe is born. || 465 ||
By means of the syllables designated as maṇḍa—namely Brahmā (oṃ), abja (a), netra (i), rudra (u), īśa (e), śiva (m), and akṣa (ya)—||
The Great Goddess, whose limbs are adorned and who wears a rosary of pearls.

One should meditate upon Tripurabhairavī, whose hands are adorned with books, who bestows boons and fearlessness, who is sweet with bliss, whose eyes roll from intoxication, and who is beautiful with red unguents on her limbs. (467)
Now I shall describe the worship diagram for Bhairavī and Bālā. One should construct a mandala consisting of nine triangles according to the path of the Guru. (468)
One should place the letter *ha*, the letter *sa*, and the letter *ra* joined with the vowel *au*, followed by two dots (*bindu*), in the center of the middle triangle. || 469 ||

Within the eight-petaled womb [diagram], one should draw the seed-syllable of Kāma outside upon an eight-petaled lotus; the vowels are to be written in the filaments, and pairs [of consonants] on the formidable petals.
One should write the letters ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, and śakṣa in sequence.
Then one should proceed with the knots of the petals in sequence, using two *praṇavas*.
One should draw tridents on the tips of the petals and a surrounding enclosure of walls (bhūpura) outside;
then, one should inscribe the syllables in order starting from the three [tridents] in the east.
And likewise, kha, ga, gha, ṅa, cha, ja, jha, ña, ṭa, ṭha, ṇa, ḍa, ḍha, and ṇa.
And likewise, he [slew] the Thadadhānna, the Phava, the Bhasara, and the Lavaṣas.
And outside that, there are two squares, and on the pathway are the Mātṛkās.
One should construct three squares, and outside of that, perform the worship of the deities.
One should worship the deities facing the back of the yantra, proceeding in a clockwise direction.
These twelve are in the first street; however, there are three in one direction.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and likewise Raudrī; after that, Ambikā and Icchā.
Jñānotkriyā, Kubjikā, Bimbā, and the goddess Viṣaghnikā. || 476 ||
Likewise, Dhyāna is described as being present in Dustarā and Nandā; O Brahmins, you are knowers of the Vedas, so listen to that with concentrated minds. || 477 ||
A parasol shining with pearls and pure gems, possessing the luster of the moon.
O Daughter of the Mountain (Pārvatī), the two chowries are as white as the waves of the Gaṅgā.
A casket for betel-leaf, shimmering with the brilliance of the nine gems.
With garlands rich with jasmine, Arabian jasmine, jasmine, and the śatapatra flower; || 479 ||
A full vessel made of jewels, likewise filled with ornaments;
a cloth and a pair of fans, variegated with the nine gems. (480)
And it was likewise adorned with the tails of peacocks and graced by ushira roots.
Abundant with camphor and musk, and mixed with powdered camphor. || 481 ||
A drinking cup fashioned of gold, a hair-comb adorned with diamonds, a rod for applying collyrium, and a casket filled with moonstones.
The supreme sovereign Śaktis, established in the sacred seats (pīṭhas), bestow [their gifts].
All of them, adorned with every ornament, are arranged in order starting from the east.
Having worshipped the Mistress of the Gods in the center, one should worship the Pretasiṃhāsana (the throne of the ghost-lion).
Having the appearance of a red lotus, shining like gold, beautiful, and imperishable; it has five corpses as its seat and directly bestows liberation—of this there is no doubt. || 484 ||
"Hskauḥ! To Sadāśiva, the Great Preta, seated upon a lotus throne"—this sixteen-syllable mantra ending with "hṛt" (namaḥ) shall be for the worship of the sacred seat (pīṭha). || 485 ||

Having worshipped the lion-throne, which is beautiful and crowded with wheels, and having displayed the mudrās beginning with invocation (āvāhana), one should show the Varada-mudrā and the one called Abhaya, and meditate upon Tripurabhairavī. 486.
[She] is situated in the center of the pericarp of the heart’s red lotus.
Red like a hibiscus flower, adorned with golden ornaments. || 487 ||

She whose great delusion is a palace of smiles, who possesses three eyes and has the moon as her crest-jewel; she who is the embodiment of the ocean from which the entirety of the world’s beauty is born.
By those known as Brahmā, Arka, Viṣṇu, Rudreśa, and Śiva, who are designated as the "pedestals" (mañca).
The great goddess with adorned limbs, wearing a rosary of pearls.
Her hands adorned with books, she grants boons and fearlessness; the goddess is sweet with bliss, her eyes rolling with intoxication. || 490 ||
One should meditate directly upon Tripurabhairavī, whose limbs are red and who is most beautiful.
Then one should display the twenty mudrās to the Goddess. || 491 ||
One should likewise hold as weapons the gestures of boon and fearlessness, a book and a rosary, a goad and a noose, a bow and an arrow, a skull, and a lotus;
the palm of the left hand, known as the "skull," should be fashioned like a skull. || 492 ||
At the beginning, there should be four [mudrās] starting with the invocation (āvāhana), and five at the end;
these are the Yoni-mudrās to be observed, and their characteristics are now described. || 493 ||
When the yonimudrā is cast upon the heart, she becomes the one who paralyzes the three worlds.
And between his eyebrows is the power that intoxicates the three worlds and attracts the three worlds.

One should worship the one who brings the three worlds under control on the forehead and the one who bestows bliss at the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra); thereafter, one should worship the enclosure of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) around the pedestal.
In the center and in the cardinal directions—namely, the southeast, northeast, southwest, and northwest—one should [place them] in sequence;
thereafter, one places Rati in the southeast corner and Prīti in the northeast corner.
Then one should worship Manobhava in the southeast corner, and thereafter worship the Bāṇas.
Two by two on each side toward the west and north, and one at the front; and the sense-objects like arrows. (497)
There, the wise one should worship these [goddesses] in order, beginning from the east: Anaṅgakusumā is the first, and Anaṅgamekhalā is the second. || 498 ||
The third goddess is Anaṅgamadanāgrā, afflicted by the passion of the bodiless god; the fifth goddess is Śubhagā, who glides toward the *bhaga* at the front of the *bhaga*. (499)
The Bhagamālā is everywhere here, and the back of the deity faces the east. Within the eight yonis are Brahmā and the others, and on the outside are two sets of eight petals. 500.
Asitāṅga is joined with Brāhmī, Ruru with Māheśvarī, Caṇḍa with Kaumārikā, and Krodha is joined with Vaiṣṇavī. || 501 ||
Likewise, Unmatta [is born] from Vārāhī, and Kapālabhṛt from Māhendrī.
Cāmuṇḍā and Bhīṣaṇā, along with Mahālakṣmī, are joined with Saṃhārā. || 502 ||
The eight long vowels, joined with the nasal drop (bindu) and accompanied by the heart-mantra (namah).
In due order, there are eight supreme mantras for the worship of the eight Śaktis.
In the Hṛdbhairava mantras, the vowels are short and accompanied by the bindu. Then Kāmarūpa, Malaya, and thereafter Kollagiri are recorded. 504.
Kulmāṇṭaka and Vaca are indeed Hāra; beyond that is Jālandhara. Uḍḍīyāna and Devakoṭa are declared to be the eight sacred seats (pīṭhas). || 505 ||
Having performed worship at the locations of the knots in the sequence beginning from the west, one should worship Hetuka Bhairava as the first and Tripurāntaka as the second. || 506 ||
Vetāla, Agnijihva, Kāla, Antaka, Kapālin, Ekapāda, and Bhīmarūpa;
then, outside in the *bhūpura* (the outer enclosure), [these are to be placed]. 507.

One should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) and perform sacrifice to them in order from above to below; one should likewise worship Brahmā and Viṣṇu starting from the west. [The mantras] ending in "vaṃ" and "vaṭukaḥ" are used, as well as those ending in "hṛdaya". (508)

First, one should draw a triangle, and outside of that, a circle and a square; having worshipped Vaṭuka and the others with the previously mentioned mantras, and thereafter offering oblations with the bali-mantras, I shall now describe the yantras. 509.
Come, come, O Devīputra! O Vaṭukānta! O Nātha! O Kapila! O Jaṭābhārabhāsvara! O Trinetra! O Jvālāmukha! At the end of all [these names], [say]: "Destroy, destroy the obstacles! (510)
One should say twice: "Accept the bali offering together with all ritual services."
This mantra of Vaṭuka consists of fifteen syllables ending with "svāhā."
One should take water from the vessel previously set aside using another vessel; having taken the water, one should indeed release the bali offering with the left thumb.
Oṃ yāṃ yoginībhyaḥ svāhā; the word *yoginī* is in the same case-ending [as *yāṃ*]. Huṃ phaṭ svāhā—this mantra, consisting of ten syllables, is for the offering of the yoginīs' bali. || 513 ||
One should cause the bali offering to fall in the center using the left thumb and ring finger.
Having declared "kṣam" endowed with true vigor, [one attains] a place for drinking water in a suitable field.
The bride should offer the two-fold bali-oblation accompanied by incense, lamps, and other offerings.
This mantra of Agni consists of eighteen syllables; it is the mantra for the strength of Kṣetrapāla.
With the thumb and forefinger, or even with the forefinger alone, [one should recite]:
*gāṃ gīṃ gūṃ gaṇapataye vara varada śarva*. (516)
"Bring the people under my control; accept the offering"—thus he should say these two [phrases]. It is proclaimed that there are thirty-one syllables in this mantra, ending with "svāhā. (517)
Having sprinkled [the offering] with the left thumb and middle finger, one should cast the bali offering in front.
And his goddess is Tripuracaṇḍikā, who feeds upon the remains of offerings.
The practitioner should never recite fewer than thirty [times].
Having received the mantra from a guru whose self is purified by that tradition, the wise one [should proceed]. (519)
For the sake of attaining success in the recitation, one who is firm in his vows should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
he should then perform a fire-oblation of one thousand oblations with fresh palāśa flowers.
Or one should offer oblations with *aśvakarṇa* flowers prepared with the three sweets. || 520 ||
Clad in red garments, with a joyful mind, he was adorned with ornaments of pearls.
His body was anointed with an ointment made of sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor. || 521 ||
Delighting in the holy life, peaceful, and abstaining from the six external objects of the senses.
He should be a friend to all beings, observe silence, and be a worshiper of the Virgin Goddess. || 522 ||
Now, the practice of the "Single Seed" (ekabīja) for this [deity] shall be described: one should visualize the Goddess, who resembles a fresh kunda flower and is adorned with nets of pearls.
Whose four arms shine with a string of pearls, a book, and a rosary. || 523 ||
Restrained, one should recite the first seed-syllable of this [mantra] one hundred thousand times; for him, poetry arises, beautiful with various meters and meanings. (524)

Now, this meditation and so forth on the second seed-syllable is taught: [one should visualize her] as red, seated upon a jeweled throne shimmering at the base of a celestial tree (suratara). || 525 ||
I worship her who holds a noose, a citron, arrows, a goad, a skull-cup, and a bow in her six arms.
Adorned with red flowers, her eyes rolling from intoxication.
Endowed with playful charm and graced by the beauty of fresh youth. || 527 ||
Having meditated upon the Goddess, the self-controlled practitioner should recite the seed-syllable one hundred thousand times in the middle period.
He shall quickly agitate the three worlds and, as before, become a partaker of supernatural powers.
Now, I shall indeed explain the meditation and other aspects of the third seed-syllable.
Holding a rosary, a jar of nectar, a mudrā, and a book.
O King, having meditated upon the Śakti who resembles a fresh jasmine flower or the moon and is adorned with pearls,
and being self-controlled, the master who recites the Sārasvata seed-syllable (bīja) consisting of pure consciousness,
becomes possessed of poetic genius esteemed on earth. || 530 ||
One should perform twenty thousand oblations with *palāśa* flowers mixed with the three sweets.
One should do this for the satisfaction of Sarasvatī, for such a person indeed becomes an abode of good fortunes.
With excellent sacrificial fuel-sticks produced from the Jātī, Karañjaka, Śamī, and Vaṭa trees.
One should perform the fire-oblation with bilva flowers accompanied by the three sweets.
And it certainly brings delight to other men's wives and to kings. || 532 ||
With leaves produced from the *mālatī* and *vakula* trees, and with sandalwood water.
By offering oblations with these sprinkled [substances] in sequence, his capacity for poetic composition arises. || 533 ||

Having recited the mantra— situated in the middle, joined with the rite to be accomplished, and following the sequence both forward and backward (the form *amabhāva* is an archaic Vedic usage)— one should then offer oblations of salt and black mustard seeds.
One shall bring men, women, and kings under one's control; of this there is no doubt.
An oblation (homa) performed with bilva fruits that possess the three sweets and have pairs of cavities brings delight to mortals;
it shall also bring about the prosperity of the practitioner and of Kamalā. || 535 ||
An oblation performed with the three sweets, *yava*, and *guḍūcī* destroys diseases and enemies. Thus resides Tripurabhairavī in Kāśī in a hidden form. (536)
Now I shall describe the goddess Tripurabhairavī, the bestower of prosperity, who was invoked by Gaṇanātha and worshipped according to the Kaulika tradition. (537)
The letter ha, the letter sa, the letter kha, and likewise the letters pha and ra.
Joined with the vowel *ṛ*, adorned with the *bindu* and *nāda*, this peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) consisting of five letters is proclaimed as the first. || 538 ||

The second seed-syllable is formed with *ṛ*, *ja*, *ma*, and *i*; the third should be *kā* followed by *t* and *kau*. Thus the mantra is fully declared; by repeating it twice, the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) is accomplished.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) for this [goddess] as before; now her meditation (dhyāna) is described.
She possesses the splendor of a thousand rising suns, has the moon as her crest-jewel, and is three-eyed.
Adorned with various ornaments, she is the destroyer of all enemies.
She was adorned with a garland of skulls dripping with blood and wore garments of red silk.
A hand-drum and a trident, a sword and a shield, as well as a Pināka bow, arrows, nooses, a goad, and likewise a book. || 542 ||
And holding a rosary, seated upon a throne of corpses and lions—having meditated thus, one should first worship the seat with the seat-mantra. || 543 ||

One should utter the word *aghore* with *aiṃ oṃ caṃ*, followed by *ghore* and *māyāṃ* (hrīṃ), and between the two *ghora*s, one should say *śrīṃ sarvataḥ sarvasarvebhyo namaste*. Then follows *rudrarūpebhyo hrīṃ śrīṃ*; this is the seat-mantra (*pīṭhamantra*) consisting of divine syllables. || 544 ||
Then, the powers (śaktis) of the seat (pīṭha) are to be worshipped from the rear region: Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, and Varalocanā. || 545 ||
Then one should indeed worship Kalāḍhyā, Balāḍhyā, and Hiṃkāriṇī.
And likewise Balapramathinī, as well as Sarvabhūtadāmā. || 546 ||
These twelve goddesses, ending with Madanī and Manonmanī, having been raised up in sequence as the seat of worship (pūjāpīṭha), one should worship the limbs (aṅgas) as previously described. 547.

Having worshipped the triad beginning with Rati, one should likewise worship the deities beginning with Anaṅga. Having fully honored the pair beginning with Brāhmī, one should worship the Mātṛkās upon the eight petals, O Supreme Goddess, and the world-protectors (Lokapālas) together with their weapons within the outer enclosure (Bhūpura).
Every other ritual application of this kind is equal to that of Tripurābhairavī.
Now the three-syllabled mantra of Catanyabhairavī is being described.
The first seed-syllable is said to be conjoined with the vowel *a*. (549)
The second seed-syllable is said to be joined with all [the vowels] together with Īśa (H).
The third is joined with Saharaudrī (KṢ) and ends with the Visarga (Ḥ). || 550 ||
She possesses the splendor of a thousand rising suns, is adorned with various ornaments, has a crescent moon shining upon her crown, and is clothed in red garments. (551)
She is the eternal one, holding a noose and a goad, with a skull-cup in her left hand.
Abounding in the splendor of the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, she possesses full, elevated, and firm breasts.
Having meditated thus, one should worship the Goddess seated upon the eastern lion-throne.
By repeating [the mantra] twice, one should perform the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) according to the characteristics of all the limbs.
One should draw the mandala in this manner: a triangle, then a hexagon, then an eight-petaled [lotus], and finally a square with four gates. || 554 ||
And here, one should conceive of the first enclosure as consisting of the six limbs.
Then, Rati and the others are to be worshipped at the front of the triangle; one should worship Vasantaka on the left, Kāma on the left, and Candra on the right, and the arrows as before.
Then likewise the Ḍākinī, the Śākinī, the Lākinī, and the Kākinī.
One should also worship Śākinī and Hākinī, starting from the western direction in sequence.
And Anaṅgakusumā and the others [are placed] on the eight petals of wealth as before. || 556 ||
And there were those known as cuckoos and cranes, as well as parrots and clouds.
One should fully cultivate the play of the outer corners of the eyes and the eyebrows, as well as the *hāva* and *bhāva* gestures. || 557 ||

One should accomplish the preliminary rites (puraścaryā) and other applications as before; likewise, the worship is the same, as are the remaining rites such as the ritual placement (nyāsa). || 558 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the Bhuvaneśvarī-Bhairavī.
The first seed-syllable is said to be joined with the vowel *ha* (o) and the consonant *sa* (kṣa). || 559 ||
The syllable *haṃsa* joined with the digit (*kalā*) and *hrīṃ* is said to be the second seed-syllable.
The first two are joined with the syllable *au*, and the third ends in the *visarga*.
The six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅgaka) is said to be performed with the seed-syllable whose middle is endowed with the six long vowels. || 560 ||
Resembling a hibiscus flower, with the luster of a pomegranate blossom, she has a crescent moon in her mass of matted hair, possesses three eyes, and wears red garments. || 561 ||
Adorned with various ornaments, she possessed full and high, firm breasts.
I take refuge in Śivā, who holds a noose, a goad, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Whatever has not been stated here regarding Caitanyabhairavī and so forth, that should be understood; furthermore, one should worship the six-limbed enclosure here all around as before. (563)
O Goddess, one should then worship Rati and the others within the triangle.
Furthermore, the worship of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others takes place there outside.
The Ḍākinīs and others are on the eight petals, while those headed by Hākinī are on the six petals.
And Anaṅgakusumā and the others, as well as Brāhmī and the others, [are situated] on all sides.
One should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) and the Baṭukas and others upon the mandala of the earth.
This ten-syllable mantra, ending with the word *hṛdayāya*, is for the sixty-four Yoginīs. || 566 ||
One should worship [the deities] on the eight petals and within the earth-mandala with a single utterance.
One should pay homage to the eleven great koṭis of yoginīs. || 567 ||
The recitations (japa) and ritual applications (prayoga) are indeed to be understood as exactly as before. Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim Bhairavī Kamaleśvarī. (568)
Having said "saha" (together) in place of "hasa," she performed all the mantras and other rites as before. Then, cursed by the king, she became a river in Tuhiṇāga.
Out of fear of the king, she abandoned the left-hand path for my sake;
however, the suffering she has thereby incurred will become famous in the Kali age. (570)
Furthermore, she will become manifest before those gods;
and those who are without caste as well as those with caste shall become bestowers of boons.
Having abandoned the fivefold manifold world and performed worship, those who are devoted to me alone—
On the bank of this sovereign city-river, he does not take pleasure in them.
Bhuvaneśī and Bhairavī, having assumed other forms for my sake,
have made many disciples— both Kaulikas and Vāmanas— for the sake of their spiritual work.
Therefore, meditation, worship, and so forth, are performed as before via the southern path. || 573 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain Bhairavī, who begins with the syllable *hasara*.
One should recite "ha-sa-ra" at the beginning of the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśvarī-Bhairavī.
Of the three seeds as well, the first consists of the consonants.
One should know that the Hasara and other mantras are likewise as before; the worship and other rites are considered to be performed in the same manner.
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the perfected Kauleśabhairavī.
The syllables beginning with *ha*, *sa*, and *ra* are devoid of the letter *ra* in both their initial and final seed-syllables. || 576 ||
The Vidyā Kauleśvarī bestows purification upon the Kaulikas; like Bhairavī, she grants prosperity. All matters, such as meditation and the rest, are considered to be as [taught] for her. 577.
Even while performing such deeds, they were unable to remain there due to the splendor of Divodāsa and by the divine power of Lord Ḍhuṇḍhi.
Jayadurgā has been invoked; she bestows victory upon those who worship her. I shall now describe, in brief, those deities who belong to the Ūrdhvāmnāya.
The two mantras belonging to him consist of nine syllables beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *durgedurgehi durghaṭe ca*, and eleven syllables ending with *svāhā*. || 580 ||
The sage is declared to be Nārada, the metre is said to be Virāj, and its deity is Jayadurgā, who bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 581 ||
The intellect of the Lord of All is considered to consist of the five mantra-words beginning with Tārā.
The arrangement of the six limbs is formed by those six-footed verses joined with their respective birth-verses (jāti). || 582 ||
A pair of eight-petaled lotuses surrounded by three squares.
One should draw [the mandala] provided with four gates using saffron and other such substances. || 583 ||
In the worship of one's own seat (pīṭha), one should perform the adoration of the nine Śaktis: Prabhā, Māyā, Jayā, Suprabhā, and Viśuddhikā. || 584 ||
Nādinī is also of great power, as is Vijayā, which likewise bestows accomplishment.
One should worship with the [remaining] syllables, excluding those that are single, fire (r), arrows (s), and neuter (k), and with the waters (vowels). || 585 ||
*Tāraḥ* (Oṃ), *vajranakhadaṃṣṭrāyudhāya mahāsiṃhāya* (to the Great Lion whose weapons are adamantine claws and fangs) *huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*.
With this perfected mantra, one should worship the *pīṭha*. || 586 ||

One should offer a seat with that mantra and prepare it with the root-mantra (mūla). Having invoked the form (mūrti) within it, one should worship it with sandalwood paste and other offerings. || 587 ||
In sequence, with the limbs of the enclosure, such as Jayā and Suprabhā.
Meditation is said to consist of the weapons of the gods, the lords of the directions, and their various implements.
Having the luster of a cloud, wearing a moon as a crown, lion-faced, and possessing three eyes; with her hands—
I worship her who holds, in sequence, the discus, the sword, the shield, and the conch.
Jayā, Vijayā, Kīrti, Prīti, and Prabhā are also considered [deities].
Faith, intelligence, and sacred learning—these are preceded by the syllable Om and other [sacred] syllables.
The sword, mace, scimitar, noose, goad, arrow, and bow—these are declared to be the weapons; one should recite [the mantra] five hundred thousand times. || 591 ||
One should offer oblations with clarified butter ten times [the number of recitations], and then perform the libations and other rites.
Thereafter, the wise practitioner, having mastered the mantra, should carry out the ritual applications.
One should mutter this mantra repeatedly and then enter the battle of the kṣatriyas; one shall slay the enemy without exception—no doubt should be entertained in this matter. || 593 ||
Recited during a dispute, a legal proceeding, or similar matters, it shall grant victory. By means of this vidyā, even very many missiles and weapons [are neutralized]. (594)

When consecrated with mantras, these [weapons] indeed grant complete victory in battle. By propitiating them, Divodāsa became a god in an instant. Having observed the destruction of his army in battle, he was bewildered. (595)
Listen to the mantra of that Gaṅgā who, for the purpose of being invoked, was brought from the other side of the Gaṅgā and established in Vanadurgā by King Divodāsa. || 596 ||
Having said, "Arise, O man," one should say, "Why do you sleep? Speak of fear! and having uttered, "Pacify my [fear]," one should afterwards speak as it stands [in the ritual manual]. || 597 ||
"Whether it be possible or impossible, tell me that, O Blessed One."
The mantra "śamayāgnivadhūḥ" consists of eighteen syllables. || 598 ||
Having thus accomplished her own task, she was pinned down by Gaṇanātha.
One should recite this mantra which is free from obstacles; then success is produced. || 600 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ duṃ duṃ and again duṃ—this is the first group of five seed-syllables.
The knower of mantras should join "duṃ hīṃ oṃ" at the beginning and at the end of the mantra. || 601 ||
This lore, free from obstacles, bestows excellent accomplishment upon its practitioners. It is declared that the sage is Āraṇyaka and the meter is said to be Anuṣṭubh. (602)
Vanadurgā is its presiding deity, the destroyer of all enemies.
The six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅgaka) should be performed with the mantra-syllables consisting of [the numbers] Ṛtu (6), Aṣṭa (8), Bhū (1), and Bāṇa (5). || 603 ||
At the base of the toes of the right foot, at the ankle, the knee, and the thigh; likewise at the anus, the genitals, the *mūlādhāra*, and the abdomen. || 604 ||
On both sides, at the heart, on the pair of breasts, at the throat, and at the joints; on the two hands, the face, the nose, the cheeks, and the pair of ears—605.

The syllables of the mantra should be deposited according to the ritual rule between the eyebrows and at the crown of the head. [One should meditate on her] resembling lightning, possessing three eyes, and seated upon a reddish lotus.
The auspicious one, holding in her hands a discus, a conch, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness.
[He saw] the moon-crested Lord dwelling in the forest, clothed in a garment of shimmering golden luster. || 607 ||
Having thus meditated upon the Goddess— serene, richly adorned with flowers, with a young doe rising at her side—
one should then worship Her on the previously mentioned pedestal.

First, the limbs [of the deity] are to be worshipped; thereafter, one should worship the noble ones and so forth, as well as the weapons beginning with the discus, the Mothers, and the weapons of the world-protectors.
The noble Durgā, Bhadrā, Bhadrakālī, and likewise Ambikā.
The eighth is considered to be Kṣemyā, Vedagarbhā, and Śāṅkarī. || 610 ||
Upon the conch, discus, sword, shield, bow, trident, and mace,
one should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times and perform oblations with sesame seeds amounting to a tenth of that number.
Having meditated upon Durgā in the fire with offerings of rice, clarified butter, sesame seeds, milk, and cooked food, one should perform the libation,
the ritual purification, and likewise the honoring of Brāhmaṇas.
Having properly gratified his own guru with wealth, grain, and other offerings, the practitioner who has thus mastered the mantra shall accomplish all desired goals. || 613 ||

One should meditate upon Durgā, the forest-dweller, through various ritual applications; one should contemplate Śrī, whose limbs are dark-complexioned, seated upon the head of the enemy of the horse (Viṣṇu). || 614 ||
I worship her whose face is most gracious, who holds in her hands a conch, a discus, a sword, arrows, a threatening gesture, a shield, and a bow.

The practitioner of mantras should always recite [the mantra] one hundred times every day for the sake of self-protection; and at the conclusion of that, he should perform the ritual applications (prayogas) one thousand times. || 616 ||
Whatever object one has in mind, if one recites the mantra a thousand or ten thousand times, the practitioner will attain that very thing before long, even if it be otherwise unattainable.

Bathing in the morning, preceded by the ritual placement (nyāsa), the best of practitioners, with one-pointed mind, should daily recite the mantra a thousand times while remembering the Goddess. || 618 ||
The wise man should pacify such afflictions as cruel serpents, malevolent planets, and other evils.
Or one should offer oblations with wild sesame seeds and black mustard seeds.
Or one may destroy all the bodily afflictions by means of *apāmārga* fuel-sticks.
The mantra-practitioner [should employ this] for epilepsy and other ailments; no further deliberation is required here. || 620 ||
The wise one should offer oblations with fuel-sticks of *nyagrodha* wood together with its shoots; within ten days, the desired goal will be accomplished, and not otherwise.
For three days or for seven nights, the practitioner of mantras should offer oblations of each individual whole plant derived from *rāsnā* for the sake of attaining his desired success.
Having prepared thirty arrows with sharp white tips, the wise one should offer them as oblations.
Or one may perform it a thousand times with *kuṭu* oil, or thereafter ten thousand times.
Having duly worshipped those whose tongues are dripping with the oil of their own falling [bodies], according to the prescribed ritual.
The king should recite the mantra as before, and likewise those arrows.
Pure in conduct, steadfast, an archer whose mind is set on battle, he should enter the midst of the enemy army fearlessly; then his weapons will become effective in all directions on every side.
Having returned, he once again [honored] his teacher with grains and even with wealth.
And one should also satisfy the bestower of victory with garments and ornaments.
Then, by reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times over the ashes of a corpse and casting them upon someone's head,
that person shall become hated by the people; he shall wander constantly from country to country like a crow.
One should offer a thousand oblations with leaves fallen from the *kāraskara* tree, blown down by the wind,
together with the dust from the feet of the enemy.

(406) Then, by means of oblations made with flowers from poisonous trees, there shall be immediate eradication [1— this refers to the "enemy" mentioned in the preceding verse; 2— the sense is that immediately thereafter, immobilization occurs through the homa of poisonous tree blossoms].
The wise man should offer a thousand oblations with flowers and thus paralyze an army.
With that many leaves, the practitioner of mantra should cause the army to retreat.
One should fashion an auspicious image of the enemy, produced from the wood of a poisonous tree. || 630 ||
Having established her vital breaths within it, she was cut into pieces at night.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, [one should perform the rite] with the fat of a crow and an owl combined.
Indeed, through such an oblation with the wood of the *unmatta* plant, the enemy goes to destruction;
yet, from a thousand such oblations, the enemy surely becomes intoxicated.
Having fashioned an image of an enemy, one should properly install it upon a steady base.
One should properly cast [the powder] smeared with poison and the three pungents into warm water.
And by immediately reciting the mantra, the enemy shall be overcome by fever.
Through the consecration with milk, his peace is attained; of this there is no doubt.
One should cast an image made from a poisonous tree into hot water; insanity will immediately afflict the enemy, and the previously mentioned method of pacification should be employed. || 635 ||

Having meditated upon her as being as red as the orb of the sun, holding a trident and a threatening gesture (tarjanī) in her lower hands, one should then recite the mantra ten thousand times and thus destroy the multitude of enemies. || 636 ||
Holding a sword and a shield, standing upon the sun, and wrathful—that forest-dwelling goddess, when remembered through the recitation of the mantra, shall pacify the multitude of enemies. (637)
[The remainder is: Having meditated [upon her] as holding a bow and arrows, seated upon a lion, and resembling fire;
the wise one should indeed offer ten thousand oblations with fuel-sticks of the *kāraskara* tree. || 638 ||
Then, all those who are sick or hostile—
[the word "of enemies" being understood as the remainder]— will soon perish; they go to their destruction by means of leaves arising from a poison-tree,
and by the flowers of that tree, the certain eradication of elephants is achieved.
From oblations made with fuel-sticks of the *rājavṛkṣa* tree, diseases of elephants are destroyed.

Likewise, a herd of elephants will quickly come under one's control by means of the flowers of a poison-tree smeared with the three sweets, or by means of the leaves arising from the sun-plant (ādityakoti).
Elephants possessing the three sweets become endowed with noble birth; anointing with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is remembered as a means of protecting the world.

For elephants and for humans as well, the best among those who know the tantras have previously prescribed [the following]: ghee, sesame seeds, constant pungent mustard, and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
And with grains of sacrificial rice, each [offering] by the thousands.
One should offer oblations to the assemblies of spirits; in this way, prosperity occurs, and not otherwise. || 644 ||
Having cut down the great tree of Brahmā and split it into five parts.
Then, one should arrange the five weapons according to their respective directions.
The five weapons are stated in their respective order as follows: the mace (gadā), the conch (śaṅkha), the sword Nandaka, the discus (cakra), and the bow Śārṅga; and the mace Kaumodakī. || 646 ||

Having cast [the substance] into the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should recite the mantra five thousand times; for that long, one should offer oblations with clarified butter (ājya) and pour the residue (sampāta) therein. || 647 ||
Furthermore, the wise practitioner should perform the recitation again for the previously stated number.
One should place five deities in [five vessels] filled with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
In the center of those [spaces], one should place weapons upon level ground; then, one should perform propitiation with auspicious mantras, offerings, and oblations appropriate to oneself.
One should cause such security to be established for cities, villages, and countries; wherever this protection is maintained, there the Goddess of Fortune (Kamalā) increases. || 650 ||
There shall be an abundance of wealth and grain, and no fear from enemies or thieves. One may bring a king under one's influence with lotuses, and likewise his queen with blue lotuses. 651.
Having offered kumuda lilies to the Brāhmaṇas, and kahlāra lilies to the Vaiśyas;
By an oblation of salt, one [attains] a Śūdra; by jasmine flowers, a village. || 652 ||

One should meditate upon the auspicious Mukunda, holding a conch, discus, mace, and lotus in his hands, within the solar orb, possessing the desired characteristics as proclaimed by the mantra. || 653 ||
Or else, a person should recite [the mantra] at the feet of the Blessed One; this method, which brings about all accomplishments, has been proclaimed by the excellent mantrins. (654)

One should write the mantra properly interlaced with the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished; and having taken clay from the hand of a potter, [one should apply it] upon the yantra. || 655 ||
And one should place [the deity] within the heart of that image which has been fashioned by her.

Having established [the deity] with direct visualization, one should recite the mantra for seven days; at the three junctions of the day (sandhyā), by reciting it one hundred and eight times, that person shall become submissive.
One should offer one hundred and eight grains of rice every day; by doing so for a year, the result will be attained.
And by means of rice, māṣa beans, and milk, one certainly becomes possessed of cattle. || 657 ||
From oblations of clarified butter, the practitioner shall obtain great gold;
from curd, all perfections (siddhis) shall arise; and with offerings of food, there shall be an abundance of food.
Through the oblation of honey, one becomes a treasure-store of jewels; it is not otherwise. Through the oblation of dūrvā grass, the practitioner of mantra certainly attains long life. (659)
Having gathered auspicious white *guñjā* seeds measuring one *kuḍava*, one should recite this mantra and scatter them upon the enemy army. || 660 ||
That supreme mantra, well-recited by him, [overcame] the armies of his enemies.
She was afflicted for a long time by men with great diseases such as fever and others.
Due to mutual conflict among the chief commanders of the army, it indeed goes to destruction through various kinds of calamities such as these. || 662 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the seed-form of the great mantra. The single-syllable mantra "Duḥ" is considered the most excellent of all mantras. (663)

The sage is declared to be Kāśyapa, the meter is said to be Gāyatrī, and the deity is Durgā; such is the procedure for the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) by means of the seed-syllable (bīja) joined with the six long vowels and accompanied by the visarga. || 664 ||
Dark-green like durvā grass, with three eyes, and seated upon an eight-petalled lotus;
she holds a trident, an arrow, a sword, a discus, a conch, a shield, and a bow.
And one should meditate upon her holding skull-bowls in sequence below the right [hand].
One should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times and perform a fire sacrifice with sesame seeds ten times that number.
The worship and other ritual applications are remembered as being equal to those of Navadurgā.
Those mantras of Lakṣmī which were well-learned by Gaṇeśa for the benefit of kings in Kāśī are indeed bestowers of wealth; I shall describe them to you. (667)
"Obeisance to the dweller in the lotus, Svāhā"—this is the ten-syllable mantra. The seer and other [limbs] of Goddess Kamalā are declared to be the same as those of Dakṣa. || 668 ||

One should likewise install the goddess Padminī, the consort of Viṣṇu, who is considered the bestower of boons, as well as her form as Kamalā, ending with the word "Namaḥ. These [mantras] beginning with Tārā are to be placed upon the five limbs; now her meditation (dhyāna) is described. || 669 ||

She possessed the luster of lightning, her beautiful hands displaying the lotus pair, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness; illuminating the world with the radiance of her body, she sat upon a lotus.
I take refuge in her who is radiant with girdles, crowns, anklets, and bracelets;
first the limbs, and outside of those, the eight Śaktis beginning with Kamalā (in the nominative case used for the locative). || 671 ||
Outside of that, one should place the world-protectors (lokapālas) and their weapons; and outside of those as well.
One should worship Lakṣmī in this manner; one will immediately become a lord of wealth.
One who has conquered the senses and subsists on sacrificial food (haviṣya) should recite the mantra five hundred thousand times.
The wise one should offer a tenth part of that [number] with lotuses possessing three sweets and three faces.
Standing in knee-deep water in a river flowing toward the ocean.
By reciting the mantra three hundred thousand times, the practitioner shall become a man endowed with wealth.
In the northern rite, one should offer oblations with *nandyāvarta* flowers; having worshipped Ramā, one should likewise offer a thousand bilva fruits soaked in honey.
One should offer oblations with fruits on the full moon day, or with white lotuses on the fifth lunar day.
The wise person who offers oblations with lotus flowers on Fridays for one month [attains the desired result].
Within a year, one obtains full wealth; there is no doubt in this matter.
What need is there for much speaking? He who, having conquered his senses, worships this mantra, obtains his desired objects and becomes endowed with wealth, grain, and prosperity.

Now I shall describe how, for the sake of my obtaining the kingdom of Kāśī by means of Gaṇeśa, Lakṣmī was worshipped in the western direction of Sāṃbāditya; there, that elephant-faced one is renowned as Lakṣmī-Vināyaka. (678)
Her accomplishment is attained only through the right path, not from the left. The syllables *sa*, *ha*, *ka*, *la*, and *ra* constitute the five letters. (679)
The first peak-syllable (kūṭa) is said to be joined with the vowel *ī*; the second shall be the seed-syllable *haṃ*. This mantra is declared to consist of three syllables.
The seer is Hari, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is said to be Lakṣmī Mohinī, the bestower of sovereignty;
the seed-syllable (bīja) is proclaimed to be the "kūṭa. || 681 ||

One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the *śakti* syllable *śrīṃ* and the six long vowels. [She is] resembling the flax flower (*atasīpuṣpa*) and adorned with jewel ornaments. (682)
With her six hands she holds the conch, discus, mace, lotus, bow, and arrow;
with two hands the Goddess of Gods is graced by the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.

The worship diagram (pūjāyantra) should be a triangle with eight petals and an excellent outer enclosure. One should worship the Goddess in the center and then worship the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga). || 684 ||
In the corners of the triangle, [one should place] Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, and Sarasvatī.
Starting from the northeast corner, Brāhmī and the others [should be placed] in sequence upon the eight petals.
In the past, the enclosure of the earth was [drawn] by means of the mantra, following the sequence of a single recitation.
Homage to the eighteen mahākoṭi yoginīs! || 686 ||
Afterwards, one should worship the weapons of Indra and the other gods with mantras; then, having again worshipped the Goddess with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and so forth.

One should offer the bali-oblation to the Baṭukas, the Kṣetrapālas, and the Yoginīs. Having thus meditated upon her eight-armed form, the wise practitioner should perform three hundred thousand recitations.

One should offer oblations with lotuses numbering one-tenth of that amount for the sake of attaining universal sovereignty. For one who worships in this manner, prosperity and universal sovereignty shall undoubtedly come to pass. (689)
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the supreme mantra of Nityaklinnā: at the beginning of the ocean of existence (bhava) is Māyā (Hrīṃ), followed by "Nityaklinne Madadrave. (690)
Its ending is *svāhā*; its sage is Brahmā, its meter is *triṣṭubh*, and its deity is Nityaklinnā.
*Hrīṃ* is declared to be the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and likewise, *svā* is said to be the power (*śakti*). (691)
It is declared that "klinneti" is the *kīlaka*, and it is said to be applied to the heart and other [limbs].
The practitioner should place the remaining syllables two by two on the heart, the two eyes, the two ears, the two nostrils, the penis, the secret organ,
and the two feet, in their proper sequence.
She is ruddy, resembling Aruṇa, wearing ruddy garments, adorned with ruddy garlands and unguents, and possessing a beautiful lotus-face like that of Smara. || 694 ||
Her face shines with three eyes, and upon her forehead are the pearls of the water of dharma.
She was resplendent, with the crescent moon shining as an ornament upon her crown.
She sits upon a lotus, languid with intoxication, holding in her four arms a noose, a goad, a drinking vessel, and the gesture of fearlessness.
Having meditated thus, one should worship daily upon the previously mentioned Śaktipīṭha.
First, one should draw a triangle, and inside it, one should draw a hexagon on the exterior.
Outside, there is an eight-petalled lotus surrounded by a city of earth (bhūpura). There, in the center, one should worship the Goddess with the finest substances such as sandalwood paste. (698)
In the center of the womb of the pericarp, one should worship the six limbs in sequence in the directions of wind, Īśāna, fire, nairṛtya, the front, and the [remaining] directions. || 699 ||
One should worship Kṣobhiṇī, Mohinī, and Lokā in the three corners; and Nityā, Nirañjanā, Klinnā, Kledinī, Madanāturā, Madadravā, Drāviṇī, and Drāvitā upon the eight petals. (700)
410) Madāvilā, Maṅgalā, Manmathārtā, and Manasvinī.
She who possesses great delight, who consists of pride, who is illusory, who is slow, and who is white.
One should worship twelve [deities] at the sides of the doors, in the corners, and in the cardinal directions. || 701 ||
One should worship starting from the left side of the foremost door of the Goddess; likewise, one should worship the world-protectors outside of that, and their weapons further outside.
Having meditated thus, one should mutter this mantra one hundred thousand times, with the subsidiary rites performed in the tenth part of that number.
One should offer oblations with Bandhūka flowers that have sweet-smelling mouths, or else with clarified butter.
Having prepared a tenth part of that [quantity], one should [offer it] with waters scented with camphor.
Then, having consecrated himself, he should thereafter feed the Brāhmaṇas.

One should satisfy one's own guru with wealth, ornaments, garments, and other such things; once the mantra has been mastered, the best of mantra-knowers should perform the ritual applications (prayogas). || 705 ||

Then, one who is fit for the application of the vidyā, constantly devoted to daily worship, reciting it a thousand times, and dedicated to it, should perform what has been prescribed and not otherwise. || 706 ||
By performing oblations with red lotuses smeared with the three sweets, one shall obtain Lakṣmī; likewise, by means of red night-lotuses, a ruler shall lead his own lineage [to prosperity].
With the milk of a white cow that has a calf of similar appearance, [mixed] with water.
If one performs the oblation with jasmine, *mālatī*, jasmine, and *śatapatra* flowers, there shall be the attainment of gold,
as well as the immobilization of enemies, kings, and others, and even the quelling of their wrath.
By offering oblations of karavīra flowers smeared with clarified butter, [the desired result] is certainly attained.
Red garments bring profit from trade; one shall bring spirits and mortals under control.
Successes in ornaments, vehicles, and trade shall be attained according to one's own desires. || 709 ||
Or by means of oblations of salt, white mustard seeds, or other [mustard seeds].
Anointed with that oil, one shall bring the desired woman in the middle of the night.
One should offer oblations at night with black datura flowers smeared with oil.
For a month, he is tormented by an extremely intense fever of agony.
By performing oblations at night with the seeds of *aruṣka* smeared with excellent clarified butter, even those sores on the body that are difficult for physicians to cure shall be destroyed.
An enemy whose body is crushed by oil goes to the abode of Yama;
likewise, even with *aṅkola* seeds sprinkled with that same oil [the same result occurs]. || 713 ||
By performing a fire sacrifice at night with camphor and mustard seeds mixed with clarified butter while focused on the mind,
one will certainly bring back the desired woman who is afflicted by the fever of passion.
If one performs oblations at night for seven nights with *marīca* mixed with mustard seeds, [the desired result is attained].
One should bring home a bride who is always difficult for those with wealth, honor, and noble lineage to obtain. || 715 ||

One should offer oblations daily with various kinds of food, either one hundred and eight times or simply one hundred; by that, one will certainly become an eater in a house filled with food. Furthermore, through oblations of rice grains mixed with clarified butter, one shall obtain fine śāli rice.
[She] was made [to wear] the dust from the soles of the feet of Viṣṇu, which arose from the trees of the world-protectors.
At night, one should offer a doll into the fire with turmeric, black pepper, and salt, [starting] from the forefeet, the shanks, the knees, and the pair of thighs. (717)

Having cut [the portions] from below the navel, from the heart, from the throat, and likewise from the neck, and having severed the head with a sharp weapon, one should offer them into the fire in sequence. By performing the oblation in this manner twelve times, men, women, and kings [attain their goals]. (718)

Indeed, by his mere will, all shall become submissive; and by his will alone, those afflicted by fever go to their death, and not through any other means. [One should prepare a mixture] with flour mixed with molasses, along with black pepper and cumin. (719)
Then, having fashioned a doll from the mantra of the sādhya, one should place it in the heart.
Having cooked it again in ghee obtained from the *sanāma* oblation, one should [proceed].
Touching it with the tip of his own finger, he should recite the mantra a thousand times.
Having worshipped it, one should consume it while anointed with that ghee, reciting [the mantra] with focused intent.
Men, women, and kings shall remain under his control until their death.
Having likewise made a ball from those very same ground ingredients, [one should place it] in the middle of that.
Having made the name of the person to be accomplished clearly manifest and having performed the consecration as before, [the result follows] from consuming it. || 722 ||
They shall be under one's control for another year; furthermore,
having performed the rite with mantras associated with one's own name and purpose, and having cooked and eaten it, one should bring that person under one's power for the sake of that objective.
By satiating [the deity] with coconut water, a woman becomes submissive.
One may bring under control those people who remain present by means of waters scented with camphor. || 724 ||
By offering libations with salt water, all shall become his servants;
likewise, by means of water mixed with salt, a woman is brought under control. || 725 ||
If one offers libations with pure water for a month, or for half that time using heated water,
while uttering the name of another, that person shall remain perpetually under one's control.
By offering libations with water scented with *ketakī*, mixed with *jambū* and the juice of *rambhā* fruits, women become submissive;
they will even give up their dear lives. || 727 ||
By offering libations with salt water mixed with sesame seeds, Kinnaras become submissive;
by offering libations with pure water for a month, one's own wealth shall be restored.
By offering libations with water scented with *nameru* flowers, kings become submissive.
By offering libations with water scented with musk, kings become submissive.
Offering libations with water scented by campaka flowers brings delight to all. || 729 ||
With water libations scented by *pāṭalī* and *śatapatra* flowers.
He will certainly and perpetually become a source of wonder to the entire world. || 730 ||
Offering libations with water scented with musk brings about all accomplishments.
By means of satiating offerings consisting of water perfumed with the fragrance of Indra’s sandalwood; || 731 ||
The perfect accomplishment of one's desired object shall bring about the death of the enemy. [This connects with what precedes.]
For him, a severe fever arises from mere warm water alone. || 732 ||
By satiating [the fire] with water mixed with the juice of nimba leaves, [one destroys] enemies.
A mutual antagonism arises by which they would meet their destruction. || 733 ||
In the same way, by satiating an enemy with excessively hot water, one causes great suffering.
Through defects such as diarrhea and other ailments, they may incur abdominal diseases. Among all branches of knowledge, this [Vidyā] is preeminent; it is equal to the Śrīvidyā. (734)

(p. 412) Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the supreme mantra of Nityaklinnā: Oṃ Hrīṃ Maiṃ—these are the seed-syllables; [the mantra is] "O Nityaklinnā, you who flow with intoxicating fluid! (735)

"Oṃ hrīṃ svāhā"—this mantra, consisting of five syllables, bestows all desired objects. Sammohana is the seer (ṛṣi), Virāṭ is said to be the meter (chandas), and the deity is the goddess named Nityaklinnā, who grants the fruits of the four aims of life. || 736 ||
But without the Vāgbhava seed-syllable, [the mantra is formed] with two, two, two, five, and five [syllables].
One should meditate on Nityaklinnā with the entire group of six limbs. || 737 ||
In the midst of the ocean of wine, the wise man should contemplate Pṛthudvīpa; there is a forest consisting of light, filled with various wish-fulfilling trees. || 738 ||
It was attended by a gentle breeze and the sweet humming of swarms of bees.
In a pavilion of rubies, furnished with pleasing grass, flowers, and other such things.
One should visualize his jeweled lion-throne shining in the center of that triangle; and in the middle of that, one should contemplate the Goddess seated upon an eight-petaled lotus. (740)
She bears with her hands the radiance of the moon-crested Lord and the glow of the reddish lotus.
I meditate upon the eternal, three-eyed Goddess, who with her pair of arms holds a noose, a goad, a wish-fulfilling creeper, and a skull-cup, and who plays the lute of the arts (kalā-vīṇā). || 741 ||
Having meditated thus, the wise one should worship the pedestal endowed with the four powers.
A lotus with eight petals, shining and having its pericarp facing downward.
One should worship Āṃ Drāviṇī and Vāmā in the heart and in the northeast;
Īṃ shall be for Āhlādakāriṇī and Jyeṣṭhā in the heart and at the seat of the anus.

"Ūṃ, obeisance to Kṣobhiṇī and Radrī in the western corner. Aiṃ, obeisance to Guhyaśakti; this is declared for the heart; one should worship in the central triangle. Hrīṃ, [obeisance] ending with the word 'heart' to the Lotus-Throne of All Powers (Sarvaśaktikamalāsana). || 744 ||
One should worship the supreme seat of the Goddess with a thirteen-syllable mantra, and there one should worship Nityaklinnā according to the method that will be described.
The worship of the limbs (aṅgapūjā) should take place upon the filaments; one should worship these goddesses upon the petals: Īṃ Nityā, Mīṃ Subhadrā, Maṅgalā, and Vanacarī. || 746 ||

One should worship with the name-mantra ending in the dative case and the heart-mantra (namaḥ), preceded by *u*, *ūṃ*, "the auspicious one for me," "the inauspicious one for me," *manonmanī*, *oṃ*, *mauṃ*, and "she whose form is Rudra. (747)
Indeed, she was intent on playing the lute, glowing, red-complexioned, and captivating.
Moving slowly with intoxication, they were well-adorned with beautiful ornaments. || 748 ||
Having uttered the seed-syllable of Kāma, which is rich in sacrificial offerings and accompanied by two dots (bindus),
one should worship Anaṅga and the others in sequence, ending with the heart-mantra preceded by *ṅe*.
On the five petals, starting from the foremost [petal] and proceeding clockwise, they are likewise: Anaṅga, Smara, he named Manmatha, Kāma, and Māraka.
He holds the five flowers, the arrow, the noose, the goad, and the small bow.
On the back part is the Śakti joined with Bhrūṇa, situated at its side.
One should remember them as adorned with ornaments and having lotus-like faces, and one should worship them well. || 751 ||
Then, on the outside, on the ten petals, starting from the front of the Goddess and proceeding clockwise:
The letter *ka*, devoid of the vowels at the end of the neuter (*ṣaṇḍha*) and adorned with a bindu. 752.
Having first uttered each [name] individually, ending with "ṅe" and "hṛdaya," this shall be the worship mantra for all of them in their proper sequence. (753)
Rati, Virati, Prīti, Viprīti, and Mati likewise.
Durbhati, Nidhṛti, Vidhṛti, Tuṣṭi, and Vituṣṭikā. || 754 ||
Adorned with reddish ornaments, holding lutes in their hands, and with smiling faces, the world-protectors (Lokapālas) are then outside,
and beyond them are their weapons.

One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and then perform oblations ten times that amount; having performed the libation with clarified butter and other rites, one should satisfy the preceptor.

Then, one should practice the correct applications with wealth, grain, and so forth—[this connects to what precedes; the meaning is that he is requested for pleasure]. Then, one should perform the proper applications.
The wise one should [perform] those previously mentioned mantras correctly, according to the procedure stated before. (757)

Thus, whoever worships Nityaklinnā Manoharā with devotion attains great fortune (mahatīṃ lakṣmīm), being entreated for it by women. (758) [In this instance, the verb is used in the sense of the indirect object (gauṇe karmaṇi).]
Having investigated the lineage, it should be served for a long time through the six traditions (ṣaḍāmnāya).
Now, therefore, I shall proclaim for her the great mantra consisting of twelve syllables. (759)
Having uttered the seed-syllables *aiṃ* and *klīṃ*, followed by *nityaklinne madadrave svāhā*, this mantra is proclaimed;
its sage is considered to be Sammohana. || 760 ||
The meter is declared to be Nivṛt and the deity is Nityaklinnā; having performed the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) with the Vāgbhava syllable, one should meditate upon the Goddess. || 761 ||
She wears red garments, is red in complexion, and is anointed with red perfumes; she holds in her hands a lotus, a goad, a noose, and a skull-cup.

One should worship the Goddess, whose every limb is agitated with intoxication, who has three eyes and the moon as her crest-jewel, upon the Śāktapīṭha; one should first worship the previously mentioned limbs.
Then, outside of that, one should worship the previously mentioned Śaktis, beginning with Nityā; she is ruddy, her lotus-like hands enriched with blue lotuses and skull-cups. (764)
Then, one should [place] Śatakratu and the others externally, and after that, the vajra and so forth. Now I shall describe Mahākālī, who deludes all people. (765)
She was brought by Śrī Gaṇeśa, a practitioner of the Left-hand Path (vāmamārga); indeed, her success is swiftly produced through the Left-hand Path. || 766 ||

One should recite the mantra for the expulsion of Divodāsa, situated to the north of Durgā: "Oṃ kṣre& kṣre& kre& kreñca, seize the victim! I declare the armor (Kavaca). Astra svāhā! This mantra, consisting of the color of Indra, was proclaimed by Kālī. (767)
There is no ritual depositing (nyāsa), nor mudrās and the like; herein there is no deliberation whatsoever.
He is gratified by whatever food and drink one desires, and by sexual union. || 768 ||
And then, [one should place] Kālikā in a jar completely filled with warm water.
One should worship with devotion, endowed with the powers (śaktis) such as Brāhmī and the others. || 769 ||
Five-faced, most fierce, with three eyes in each face.
[He holds] a spear, a trident, a bow, arrows, a shield, a sword, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
The goddess, adorned with ornaments, holds the clever one with her skillful arms.
Having meditated thus, the perfected practitioner should accomplish the goal residing within the mind.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, as well as Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Caṇḍikā as the eighth. || 772 ||
