These have been described as situated within the belly of the pitcher (kumbha) up to Īśāna: Kārtikeyā, Tamodevī, Mahākālī, and Bhayāpahā. || 773 ||
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times according to its syllable count and offer oblations of fish smeared with ghee.
Then, having performed the libations and other rites, the mantra becomes perfected for him (this is the ellipsis). || 774 ||
While reciting the mantra of the Goddess, one who is enraged should offer oblations of the enemies into a blazing fire using a rope that has been empowered by the utterance of their names. || 775 ||
By offering fuel-sticks of *picumanda* upon the embers of *bibhītaka*, one kills an enemy within seven days through the application of the *kālikā* mantra. || 776 ||

Uccāṭana (driving away) should be performed in the afternoon, and likewise, māraṇa (killing) at twilight. Standing in the southern direction and facing south toward the village or other location, the homa should be performed with these very [mantras]; thus each respective rite is successfully accomplished. || 777 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the Great Kṛtyā, who is served by the great Gaṇas, and how women fall away from their vow of devotion to their husbands. || 778 ||
And various kinds of wonders were displayed by the women.
Because they fell away from their devotion to their husbands, a great heap of sin arose. (779)
When women have become like malevolent spells (kṛtyā) and domestic life has become fragile, it is by resorting to her that householders become happy. (780)
I shall now fully describe that Kṛtyā, the ornament of the householder’s stage of life: having uttered "Hrīṃ Mahāyoginī," and then saying "Gaurī" and "Bhuva. (781)
"Na bhayaṅkari huṃ" is this sixteen-syllable mantra; Aṅgiras is the sage (ṛṣi), and the goddess Gāyatrī is declared to be the meter (chandas). || 782 ||
Thus, ending with *phaṭ*, it is considered the head-mantra (*śiras*) for the one who causes terror to the world.
Furthermore, one should perform the six limbs by repeating this three times. || 783 ||
Seated upon a lion-throne, with a dark face and pendulous breasts.
With a face made terrifying by fangs, possessing three eyes, and blazing forth on all sides.
Clad in a black tunic, she possessed a radiance like that of a smokeless fire.
[She holds] a trident, a wheel, a cup, a khaṭvāṅga, and a lotus of boons. || 785 ||
Having meditated upon the Kṛtyā with her large tongue constantly lolling and terrifying with her lightning-like gaze,
the best of mantra-knowers should worship her according to the prescribed rite.
One should worship the formidable and glorious [goddess], beginning from the front of the deity.
And likewise, one should place the *Pratiṣṭhā* and the *Vidyā* on the four petals outside of that.
In the east is the one named Śāṅkarī, clothed in garments of white color.
The auspicious goddess Śivā has two arms, is gentle, bestows boons, and holds a noose and a goad.
Having worshipped the one named Mālikā on the right— she who has a long tongue and is terrifying—
one should daily recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.

Now, the external application beginning with the worship of Lokeśa is being described. Having determined the [appropriate] time, one should fashion an image facing downwards for the purpose of killing. (790)
Below that, in the southeast corner, is a triangle provided with a lower girdle (the sandhi is archaic).
Having made the fire white as the moon and having strewn it with reeds and grass, || 791 ||
And for his killing, one should prepare it with a fuel-stick made of *bibhītaka* wood.
One should perform oblations with the excrement of crows and owls smeared with neem oil. || 792 ||
"Split him, dry him up, kill him"—having thus commanded, [he acted].
And with this mantra, the wise one should perform one hundred and eight oblations.
Having performed the concluding oblation according to the rules in the presence of the fire of slaying:
"Whether he be at my throat, or even far away, or even nearby."
Having spoken thus regarding his poison, flesh, and blood, he should make this offering. || 794 ||
Having protected it according to the rules for the sacred fire, one should complete the nine-night rite; by that, the enemy’s thought regarding him remains dead for that duration. (795)

Having ground black pepper and white mustard seeds with the milk of the *arka* plant, and having stirred them in water while reciting the mantra, one should meditate on the enemy with a fixed gaze. (796)

Having stepped upon the enemy with a fierce foot while wearing a black upper garment, and having visualized [the foot] as a thunderbolt or a trident, one should sprinkle water over him; within nine nights the enemy dies—of this there is no doubt. (797)
If one offers *bibhītaka* fruits soaked in oil into a fire on a funeral pyre prepared by a master of sorcery, the enemy shall die;
this is the truth spoken by Uśanas. || 798 ||

Having meditated upon the enemy's image on a board made from the wood of the *sādhya* tree, one should grind black pepper with the milky sap of the *arka* plant and smear it upon that very image. (799)
Having placed the syllable *phaṭ* at the heart and having fashioned Śiva within the pit;
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should cast [the offering] after reciting the mantra a thousand times.

Having performed an immediate immersion in that very [water] and having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times according to the prescribed rule, one should pierce [the enemy] with the Śivamudrā; within six months, the enemy shall die during both twilights.
Then, having taken a dry leaf of the *vibhītaka* tree that has been thoroughly dried by the wind,
the practitioner of mantras should scratch [the diagram] with the blood from the mouth of a black cobra.
One should append the seed-syllable of Vāyu to the end of the enemy's name; by writing it in his house, he will certainly wander about like a crow. || 803 ||
With dry leaves and wood blown up by the wind, and with trees struck down by lightning.
By means of camel bones and the charcoal of a corpse, the eradication of an enemy shall occur.
Having ground dūrvā and guḍūcī together with ghee, [one should mix them] with sesame seeds and rice.
A wise person should perform the rite of pacification with oblations of rice and fuel-sticks made of Palāśa wood. || 805 ||
One obtains Lakṣmī with bilva fruits and leaves, and likewise Śrī with nandyāvarta flowers.
With red flowers, apāmārga plants, and charcoal from sea-shells.
One should perform the rite for subjugation using these [substances] mixed with the three sweets. || 806 ||
Having performed the rite of pacification according to the prescribed rule, one should recite this mantra for the *kṛtyā*.
This [mantra] constantly pacifies great diseases; it consists of one hundred and eight [syllables]. || 807 ||
With a one-pointed mind, he should mutter this supreme mantra which brings the world under control; in his mind, he should visualize the Kṛtyā mounted upon an elephant and moving through the air.

One should quickly worship her as mounted upon a horse; by doing so, she will surely come under one's control. Furthermore, she removes the fear of thieves, tigers, wild beasts, water, and other such dangers. (809)

Having drunk water consecrated seven times while concentrated on the mantra, one becomes intelligent and eloquent; by reciting it that many times and performing the ritual ablution, even poison becomes nectar once it has been consecrated seven times.
Whether for a fortnight, a month, two months, six months, or even a year—any mortal who acts in this manner shall attain a meritorious state. || 811 ||
Now I shall describe the Great Peace (Mahāśānti), which destroys all calamities, protects the practitioner of the left-hand path (vāmācāra), and grants satisfaction to all the gods. || 812 ||
It removes the sin arising from the left-hand path and increases merit.
She is the destroyer of untimely death and the constant increaser of victory.
It protects longevity, and it brings about nourishment, prosperity, good fortune, and subjugation.
She bestows sons and grandsons, and she is the destroyer of the stain of misfortune.
For she is the pacifier of great diseases and the destroyer of epilepsy. || 815 ||
Yoginīs, bhūtas, vetālas, pretas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and pannagas—especially the ḍākinīs and others—do not remain in that place. || 816 ||
One should worship Kṛtyā upon a cloth according to the prescribed ritual. One should draw a sixteen-petalled lotus, joined with a yoni and marked with a bindu. || 817 ||
In the center of that, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus and place the letters beginning with 'A' in sequence;
in its center, while recollecting the root mantra, one should draw a hexagon.
One should draw a lotus upon the lunar disc, and above that, one should draw a preta.
One should place that pitcher in the center, adorned with cloth and jewels.
One should place within the pitcher the Kṛtyā, endowed with all characteristics; one should worship her according to the rule and offer her the pāyasa.
One should worship the goddess Śāntā in the world and perform the fire oblation (homa) before her.
One should perform the oblation with Apāmārga and sesame seeds soaked in clarified butter.

One should perform the fire-offering (homa) rite in either a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or on a leveled altar (sthaṇḍila), using eight hundred sticks each of dūrvā grass, mango, khadira, and aśvattha wood. || 822 ||
On his right side, one should meditate upon Lakṣmī according to the prescribed rite.
One should install the Goddess in the center of the jar, and one should contemplate Śrī on the right.
On the left side, one should worship the goddess Hṛllekhā, the Supreme Sovereign;
indeed, on her left side, one should worship Gaṇanāyaka. || 824 ||
One should recite the root mantra ten thousand times to destroy death;
for the killing of a fetus, one hundred thousand times; and for the drinking of liquor, one thousand times. (825)

For treachery against one's guru, one should recite it ten million times, and likewise one hundred and eight times for treachery against a Brahmin; for violating the teacher’s bed, one million times; and for excessive intoxication, unrighteousness, and the like, one should recite it five hundred thousand times.
Whether one desires to proceed on the left-hand Kaulika path or the Kāpālika path,
one should first accomplish this mantra called Parimala.
Because it destroys evil and wards off the fear of enemies, all the faults of the preceptor,
the faults of the disciple, and those arising from unrighteous limbs— all these go to destruction when the recitation of this mantra is performed. || 828 ||
Even one devoted to the practice of the right-hand path (dakṣiṇācāra) should partake of these for the destruction of suffering:
fried cakes, *pheṇikās*, mung beans, meat, *vaṭakas*, and *eṇḍiras*. || 829 ||
Sauvīra, kāñjika, and wine—these are proclaimed as one's own wife, the śakti.
Or a dish of eggplant cooked with fish is even more effective for granting success. || 830 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the obstacle that deludes the three worlds, which is manifested even within the phenomenal world in many ways by means of its powers (śaktis). || 831 ||
Through the ascetic power of Divodāsa, they did not enter the path of Śakti; at that time, there was a place named Sammohana to the west of Kedāra. || 832 ||
At that time, he became Gaṇeśa, and by him the entire city was enchanted. I shall proclaim his mantra, which grants success through the Ūrdhvāmnāya tradition. (833)
Then one should utter: "To Vakratuṇḍa-Ekadaṃṣṭra, Klīṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Gaṃ."
One should address Gaṇapati as "the one with a pair of testicles," "the self-controlled," and "belonging to all people. || 834 ||
"Bring [him] under my control, svāhā!"—this is the mantra of thirty-three syllables. The sage is declared to be Gaṇeśa, and the meter is said to be Gāyatrī. || 835 ||
The deity proclaimed is the obstacle-remover Trailokyamohana.
[The syllables] of the mantra are, in sequence, the number of Rudras (eleven), the Vedas (four), the limbs of the Vedas (sixty-four), the eyes (two), and the colors (five). || 836 ||
The procedure for the six limbs has been indicated; now I shall describe the meditation, worship, and so forth.
One should perform all the ritual applications and so forth, just as in the case of Mahāgaṇeśa. || 837 ||

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Mantra of Gaṇapati according to the Ūrdhvāmnāya," in the Merutantra composed by Śiva with the approval of the illustrious Mahāmāyā and Mahākāla. || 17 ||
The illustrious Śiva said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the lords of the Gaṇas belonging to the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya): Hṛllekhā, Viri twice, Gaṇapati, and Varada twice. (1)
The syllable *da*, "bring all the world under my control," and the two *ṭha*s—this twenty-five-syllable mantra is proclaimed as the bestower of sons and grandsons. (2)
The sage is declared to be Gaṇaka; the meter is said to be Gāyatrī; the deity is Viriñci-Vighneśa, who bestows both seen and unseen fruits. || 3 ||
In the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, by means of five-syllable [mantras] numbering fifty-five.
One should perform the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) using the syllables of the root mantra, each divided [and assigned to its respective part]. || 4 ||
He has the luster of vermilion, possesses three eyes, and holds a noose in his upper left hand; in his upper right hand he holds a goad, while in the middle of his right palm he holds a skull-cup.
He bears the source of nourishment with the palm of his left hand, and with his right hand he holds the moon-crested elephant-faced one.
With her left hand, she touches him whose every limb is embraced by nourishment.
The tip of Gaṇeśa’s liṅga is held in his two upraised hands.
One should worship Gaṇapati, who thus holds a pair of lotuses, upon the previously mentioned pedestal endowed with the nine Śaktis. || 8 ||
Having invoked [the deity] into the form fashioned with the root mantra, one should worship it;
first, one should worship the couples, Āmoda and the others, who are naked.
Afterwards, the wise one should worship the limbs and likewise the Mothers.
One should worship the world-protectors and their weapons outside of that.
One should worship Viri-Vighneśvara, joined with the six enclosures. Now I shall state another mantra for Viri-Vighneśvara.
Then one should utter the word "loka," preceded by the two boons and the syllable "da."
This [meter], consisting of nineteen syllables, is declared to be the Nivṛt-chaṃdas.

The ritual placement (nyāsa) consists of thirty-six syllables, each preceded by a seed-syllable (bīja). Now I shall describe the meditation (dhyāna): [visualize the deities] in hands held one above the other. || 13 ||
In his right hands, he holds a citron, a mace, a bow, a discus, and a garland; in his left hands, a lotus, a noose, arrows, an elephant-goad, and a jar rich with jewels.
She has two lotuses in her hands, is nourishing, holds [a child] on her lap, and possesses a reddish radiance.
Embracing Aruṇa, whose cheeks were trickling with rut.
One should meditate upon the elephant-faced god, who has three eyes, wears yellow garments, firmly raises his banner, and is adorned with a crown and earrings. || 16 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe Viriñcigaṇanāyaka, who is worshipped by Brahmā and resides in the northern region outside of Kāśī. || 17 ||
Having uttered "hrīṃ" and the word for Brahmā (viriñcipada), one should again utter Gaṇapati ending in the suffix -ṅe.
One should recite the [names of the] lords and so forth as before; this is the mantra consisting of twenty-six syllables.
The six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅgaka) are stated by [the syllables] numbering four, five, five, and two from the Vedas.
The practitioner of this [mantra] should perform meditation, worship, and so forth as previously described, with this specific distinction. || 19 ||
Having heard the Saṅgas and Arthas but once, the performer of sacrifices recites the Vedas;
he himself becomes a progenitor, an agent, and a remover according to the prescribed rule.
419) It is taught that for all of them, the honor is one hundred thousand-fold.
One should offer oblations with the previously mentioned eight [substances], combined with the three sweets.
Having thus accomplished the mantra, one may perform the ritual applications: by means of an oblation of full-blown blue lotuses, one may bring the entire world under one's control.
By means of an oblation of sesame seeds and rice, one obtains irreproachable prosperity.
By offering modakas mixed with clarified butter as an oblation, one shall attain victory. || 23 ||
By means of an oblation of the three sweets, one may bring a king under one's control; an oblation performed with various kinds of food, both solid and soft, accomplishes all desired goals. || 24 ||
Now, the three-syllabled mantra of Śaktigaṇeśa is declared: Hrīṃ Grīṃ Hrīṃ. Its meter is said to be Virāj, and its seer is Bhārgava. (25)
The sage is Muni, the deity is Deva, and Śaktigaṇeśa is proclaimed as the lord of this mantra.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) using the seed-syllable associated with the six long vowels. || 26 ||
The Lord himself, with the face of a lordly elephant, four arms, and beautiful whisks; golden-hued, three-eyed, and holding a noose and a goad.
One should meditate upon him holding a sweetmeat in his right hand, a citron in his left, and lotuses in his [other] hands, while bearing sweetmeats in his palms. (28)
One should worship the Lord upon the previously mentioned pedestal, which possesses the nine powers beginning with Tīvrā, within an eight-petaled lotus surrounded by three squares.

The first enclosure is declared [to consist of the guardians of the quarters], the second is remembered as being formed by the Mothers; the third should consist of the World-Protectors (Lokapālas), and the fourth by the Vajra and other [divine weapons]. || 30 ||
One who has conquered the senses and subsists on sacrificial food (haviṣya) should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
One should offer oblations with cakes soaked in ghee, numbering one-tenth of that [total].
Thus, the practitioner who has mastered the mantra should accomplish the rites for specific desires; having worshipped Vināyaka on the fourth day of the bright fortnight, he should proceed. || 32 ||
With cakes mixed with molasses and cooked foods drenched in ghee.
With long pepper, cumin, and rock salt, well-mixed together. || 33 ||
In the presence of the deity, the practitioner of mantras should perform three thousand oblations; within seven days, his speech will certainly become composed of both prose and verse.

One desiring subjugation should bring a king under control by means of an oblation of honey; one desiring a maiden should offer parched grain (lāja) ten thousand times while reciting the mantra containing her name. || 35 ||
Furthermore, by feeding one girl or seven girls, one obtains a bride; when an eclipse of the moon or sun occurs, one should consume a *pala* of tawny cow's ghee.
Having mixed one karṣa of powdered vacā, one should consecrate it with mantras; then, becoming self-restrained and intent on meditation upon the deity, one should drink it. || 37 ||
As long as he lives, he shall not eat anything at all here.
Within seven days, he quickly becomes another master of speech.
But a barren woman, having worshipped Vināyaka on the day of her ritual bath, [attains her desire].
One should take turmeric, rock salt, and vacha in the measure of half a niṣka and one pāda respectively.

Having ground [the ingredients] in a kuḍava measure of cow urine, one should empower it a thousand times with mantras; then, having fed young maidens with various foods, delicacies, and meals. || 40 ||
Having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor, the woman should drink that medicine. Thereupon, she obtains a son endowed with all auspicious marks. || 41 ||
Now I shall describe its division: beginning with Tāra (Om), it consists of four syllables. Śukra is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi), and Gāyatrī is said to be the meter (chandas). || 42 ||
The deity is Śaktigaṇapa, the supreme bestower of all siddhis. As before, the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) are assigned, and his meditation (dhyāna) is now described. || 43 ||
Golden-hued, clad in golden garments, three-eyed, pot-bellied, and endowed with many arms.
Holding a noose, a rosary, and a tooth-stick, as well as a goad.
And holding a sweetmeat and a golden ornament in his lotus-like hand.
Resembling the midday sun and endowed with a beautiful spear.
Then, having invoked the deity upon the seat previously mentioned, one should worship him.
The first circuit should be with the ancillaries (aṅgas), and after that, on the six petals.

In an eight-petaled lotus, one should worship Vakratuṇḍa and the others at the tips of the petals; outside, in the outer enclosure (bhūpura), one should worship the Mātṛkās and the world-protectors (lokapālas). || 47 ||

And outside of that, one should arrange the weapons as previously described and complete the remainder; with a concentrated mind, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, or its tenth part. || 48 ||

One who is most proficient in mantras should perform oblations with sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter; thereafter, one should perform the libations (tarpaṇa) and other rites, whereby the mantra becomes perfected. || 49 ||
Then the preceptor, with a restrained mind, should perform the rites for the fulfillment of desires.
One who offers oblations with clarified butter and cooked rice daily shall become possessed of food within a year.
A person who worships this [deity] with milk-rice and clarified butter attains great prosperity; the man who worships him obtains a daughter equal to Rambhā.

Now, therefore, I shall fully explain its division according to the solar color (arkavarṇaka): having uttered "hrīṃ gaṃ hrīṃ ca mahaḥ," one should again [utter] Gaṇapati ending in the suffix -ṅ. || 52 ||
Its ending should be "svāhā," its meter is Nivṛt preceded by Gāyatrī;
the seer is declared to be Gaṇaka, and the deity is Śaktivināyaka. || 53 ||

The arrangement of the limbs (aṅga) here is declared by means of each individual syllable [of the mantra], by the first [syllable], by the seventh, by the second, and by the entire collection of the mantra's syllables. || 54 ||

He holds a pearl necklace and the moon in his right hands, and a serpent and an eye in his left; he holds a lotus and a stylus in his upper and lower right hands, and [a lotus and a stylus] in his upper and lower left hands.
One should propitiate the beloved Yoni situated at the base with ten jars; [one should meditate on] the Lord wearing a jewel-encrusted crown with a serpent's face. 56.

Having reflected thus, the practitioner, for the sake of all accomplishments, should perform worship according to the rules on the previously mentioned seat (pīṭha) by way of Brahmā and Gaṇeśa. || 57 ||
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, and thereafter perform ten thousand oblations.
When the fire has been duly worshipped with cakes mixed with clarified butter, [the rite is accomplished].
Having performed the libation (tarpaṇa) and the ritual sprinkling (mārjana), he should then feed the Brāhmaṇas;
thus, the practitioner who has mastered the mantra should perform the ritual applications according to the prescribed rules. || 59 ||
An oblation made with stalks of sugarcane bestows royal fortune;
an oblation made with plantains and coconuts brings about subjugation of the world.
An oblation of sesame seeds and *pṛthuka* grains brings a king under one's control;
an oblation made with roasted barley flour (*saktu*) brings Brahmins under one's control. (61)

One should offer oblations with clarified butter for the attainment of wealth, grain, and other riches; furthermore, the previously mentioned ritual applications should also be performed here by the practitioners.
Now I shall proclaim another mantra of the Lord of the Śaktis and Gaṇas: Oṃ hrīṃ gaṃ hrīṃ, bring [him] under control, svāhā; its deity is Bhavānī and the Sun. || 63 ||
The previously mentioned [deities] beginning with the Munis have their limbs fashioned from the syllables of the mantra—
one, two, three, a pair, or an equal number of mantra-syllables. [He is] bandhūka-red in hue, three-eyed, serpent-faced, moon-crested, wearing a garland of serpents, and holding a triple-corded goad.
[He] took choice sugarcanes with his lotus-like hands. || 64 ||
Holding his penis with his trunk, he likewise embraced her.
One should meditate upon her in the heart as having a dark-complexioned body, holding a liṅga and a lotus in her hands.

The wise practitioner should perform the aforementioned worship upon the aforementioned seat. One should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times and offer oblations with cakes soaked in ghee amounting to one-tenth of that number;
thereafter, one should perform the libations (tarpaṇa) and other rites.

Then, having meditated upon one's own guru, one should gratify him with wealth and grain; thereafter, one should accomplish the optional rites (kāmyaprayoga) as prescribed in that specific ritual manual (kalpa). || 67 ||
An oblation of cakes soaked in the three sweets brings one under the power of a beloved woman.
Without Śakti there is no Gaṇeśa, and without him there is no Śakti. (68)
Therefore, the wise should by all means accomplish union with Śakti. For that reason, I shall first describe Śakti, the illustrious Bhuvaneśvarī. 69.
The single-syllable seed-mantra (bīja) proclaimed for her is "Hrīṃ. Her seer (ṛṣi) is Śakti Vaśiṣṭha, and Sūta is said to be her meter (chandas). || 70 ||

The deity is Gāyatrī, who is expressed as the consciousness of awakening; she is the supreme digit (kalā). The letter *ha* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), while the letter *ī* is said to be the power (*śakti*). (71)
The letter *ra* is declared to be the *kīlaka* (stake) for the accomplishment of all applications.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) using the seed-syllables joined with the six long vowels. || 72 ||
Then, one should perform the placement of the Saṃhāramātṛkā and the Sṛṣṭimātṛkā.
Now, the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) for the purpose of achieving oneness with the Goddess shall be described.
On the forehead, *hoṃ* for Hṛllekhā; on the face, *hraṃ* and the name Bhaga; *hraṃ* for Raktā is to be placed on the heart; and *hrīṃ* for Karālikā on the anus. (74)
One should place *Huṃ* at the two feet and Mahocchuṣmā within the five faces.
And [they are] situated respectively in the directions of the zenith, the north, the south, and the east. || 75 ||
One should assign Gāyatrī to the throat and Sāvitrī to the left breast;
Sarasvatī to the right breast and Brahmāṇī to the left shoulder.
The wise practitioner should place Viṣṇu in the heart and Maheśa on the right shoulder; he should place Brahmā together with Gāyatrī upon the forehead.
One should place Viṣṇu together with Sāvitrī on the region of the cheek; and one should place Maheśa together with Vāgīśvarī on the left cheek. (78)
One should place Dhanapati, joined with Śrī, on the left ear-tip.
The practitioner of mantra should place Smara joined with Rati on the face, and Gaṇa joined with Puṣṭi;
he should place the two Treasuries (Nidhis) joined with their Śaktis at the tip of the right ear. (80)

Then one should place [the syllables] on the two inner corners of the ears, at the base of the face, at the root of the neck, on the pair of breasts, on the left shoulder, and on the right side of the heart. || 81 ||
The practitioner, composed in mind, should place these on the two shoulders and the pair of sides.
One should assign [the syllables] to the foreheads of the eight Mothers, as well as to their shoulders, sides, and bellies.
The knower of mantras [should apply them] likewise on the sides, the mouth, the feet, the throat, and the heart.
One should pervade [the body] with the root mantra and then meditate upon the goddess's form.

Resplendent with the luster of the rising sun, adorned with the cool-rayed moon as her crest-jewel, seated upon a lotus throne, and possessing three eyes; her four arms are graced with the noose, the goad, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, while her face shines with a gentle smile. (84)
One should meditate upon the Goddess in one's heart, her creeper-like body bent by the weight of her breasts; having first drawn a hexagon, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus outside of it.
Outside of that is a sixteen-petaled lotus, and outside of that are three squares.
The supreme maṇḍala is said to be provided with four gates. || 86 ||
There, one should first worship the Pīṭha, endowed with the nine Śaktis: Jayā, Vijayā, the one called Ajitā, and Aparājitā; || 87 ||
Nityā, Vilāsinī, Dogdhrī, Aghorā, and Maṅgalā—these Śaktis are to be worshipped in the filaments and in the center. || 88 ||
One should not offer a seat at the root; rather, one should conceive of the image by means of that very [root].
One should invoke the Goddess upon her [the yantra], together with her limbs and attendants. || 89 ||

Holding nooses, goads, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and resembling elemental spirits (bhūtas), they—beginning with Hṛllekhā and the others—are radiant with various ornaments; having worshipped them thus, [one should proceed]. || 90 ||
Likewise, in the positions of the center, the tip, the south, the north, and the west, in due order.
In the corners of Agni, Īśa, Asura, and Vāyu, [one should worship] the weapons, the heart-mantra, and the others.
One should likewise worship the weapons in the cardinal directions and the pairs at the tips of the corners.
Gāyatrī, possessing a reddish luster and adorned with ornaments appropriate for the Aruṇa stage.
One should likewise worship Brahmā in front [of her], who has four faces and holds a staff, a water-pot, and a rosary in her hands, as well as the gesture of fearlessness.
Sāvitrī, holding a discus, conch, mace, and lotus with her lotus-like hands, wearing yellow garments, and adorned with armlets and bracelets; || 94 ||
One should worship Viṣṇu, who possesses such a form and is adorned with a crown, necklaces, a girdle, and anklets, at the tip of the southeast corner of the sacrificial site.
She is radiant white, possesses three eyes, and is adorned within with bright white garments.
She has four arms, holding a ṭaṅka, an akṣasūtra, and displaying the gestures of granting fearlessness (abhaya) and supreme boon (vara). || 96 ||
One should worship Sarasvatī in the north-western corner (the direction of Vāyu), and Īśa in the same manner;
and one should worship Lakṣmī, seated on his lap, embraced by his right arm.
[This refers to the preceding context: through desire for her husband, she [offered] a lotus and a wealth-bestowing *pṛṣodara* [vessel].
One should worship her as she holds a yellow jewel-pitcher and a jewel-branch.

In the southeast, one should meditate on Rati, seated upon the lap of her lover, embracing the lover with her left hand while holding a lotus in the other; she has the luster of the bandhūka flower and holds in her hands arrows, a bowstring, a goad, and a bow. (99)
One should properly worship Vighnarāja, accompanied by his beloved, in the northeast.
Holding a spear and a noose, with his fingers touching the beautiful limbs of his beloved.
[He saw] Vighnarāja, naked and rich with skull-cups filled with honey-wine, holding in his lotus-like hand a shimmering goblet from which jewels were dripping. || 101 ||
Her form was like vermilion, and she was overwhelmed by intense intoxication.
With his other hand, he touched that banner which bore a red lotus.
[One should meditate on her] as embracing her beloved, ruddy, nourishing, and naked, yet adorned with flowers. || 102 ||
Having worshipped the treasure (nidhi) in the pericarp, one should then [worship] on both sides of the hexagon the first [goddesses]:
Anaṅgakusumā and Anaṅgakusumāturā. 103.
Another is Anaṅgamadanā, while another is Bhuvanapālinī; the sixth is Gaganavegā, and the seventh is Śaśiśīrṣā. || 104 ||
They were stationed all around on leaves that reached up to the very edge of the sky.
Holding a noose, a goad, a boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness, they are red in color and beautifully adorned. || 105 ||
Then, upon the sixteen petals are Karālī, Vikasalikā, Sarasvatī, Śrī, Durgā, Ūṣā, Lakṣmī, the two Śrutis, Smṛti, and Dhṛti. (106)
Faith, intelligence, wisdom, and splendor—these are the sixteen noble powers.
The dark-complexioned goddesses holding swords and shields are to be worshipped by circumambulation.
Brāhmī and the others are to be worshipped outside that [lotus] at the joints of the petals in the order of the directions. Outside the lotus, the Śaktis who are attendants are to be duly honored.
Anaṅgarūpā, Anaṅgādi, Madanā, and Madanāturā; likewise Bhuvanavegā and Bhuvanapālikā shall be in front. || 109 ||
The sixth is Sarvaśiśirā, and at its front is Anaṅgavedanā; and outside of that is Anaṅgamekhalā, where one should [place] the lords of the directions.
Red in color, adorned with brilliant red ornaments, and possessing large, reddish-cornered eyes.
Holding a red lotus in her left hand, she holds these [other implements] in her right hands in succession. || 111 ||
Holding in her right hands a wine-cup, a palm-leaf fan, betel, an umbrella, a chowrie, a mirror, fine cloth, and flowers. (112)

One should worship the vajra and other implements outside of that in the "most excellent of the excellent" [mandala]; in the "excellent" [mandala], one should worship them with all four [elements] within the mind, which is surrounded by the divine [deities]. 113.
With the Hṛllekhā-mantras and so forth, with their limbs (aṅgas), with the world-protectors (lokapālas), and with their weapons.
The worship is performed with the intermediate weapons, the enclosures, the lords of the world who are part of the worship, and their respective weapons. || 114 ||
With the two youngest fingers as the world-protectors, that [mudrā] is for one who is away from home.
For worship that has no other destination is indeed proclaimed to be complete with even a single limb. || 115 ||
One should never neglect the worship of Bhuvaneśī; as there is sin in the omission of the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), so it shall be in the omission of her worship. || 116 ||

If the seven-day worship is omitted, a terrible curse falls [upon one]. During the period of Venus, one should give dakṣiṇā to the right; during the period of the Sun, one must not omit the worship. (117)
The man who disregards these seven pure [substances] becomes one who is devoid of honor in this world.
With a concentrated mind, one should recite the mantra thirty-two hundred thousand times.

One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with eight substances combined with the three sweets, using one-tenth of that [number of mantras]. Then the practitioner of mantra should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) and other rites according to the path prescribed in the scriptures. || 119 ||
Now, another preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for the mantra is also described: Taking refuge in Dakṣiṇāmūrti in a temple of Śiva containing a single liṅga, || 120 ||
He sits in the bound lotus posture, reclines upon ashes, and uses a mat of kusha grass.
Beginning from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
Having worshipped Śiva and Śakti daily, one should recite the mantra one thousand times.
One should offer oblations of *vyāghāta* wood fuel smeared with curd, honey, and ghee. || 122 ||

Then, one should meditate upon the face of the Sovereign of All for one thousand plus one [recitations]; thereafter the mantra becomes perfected—no doubt should be entertained in this matter. || 123 ||
Likewise, sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) of the Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, and Nyagrodha trees.
And the substances—sesame, mustard, milk, and clarified butter—are eightfold. || 124 ||
For each substance, there should indeed be forty thousand oblations;
thus, having perfected the mantra, the practitioner of mantras shall accomplish all desires. || 125 ||

By performing an ablution after reciting the twenty-fifth [mantra] twenty-five times, one gains constant good fortune; and by drinking water that has been consecrated with that same number of recitations, one becomes wise and eloquent.
Having placed [the mantra] on the tip of the tongue and recited it, one attains mastery over speech and becomes a poet.
Collyrium consecrated with that [mantra] and mixed with camphor and agallochum brings others under one's control. || 127 ||

For the purpose of subjugation (vaśyāya), one should apply a forehead mark (tilaka) with a paste of blood and reddish ashes. Standing in water reaching the knees, motionless and with eyes closed, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times during that night; thus, one shall attract the desired woman. 128.
With parched grain one obtains a daughter; with sesame seeds one enjoys good health.
Nourishment is attained through oblations of curd and likewise with rice grains;
[the meaning is that it brings about subjugation]. || 129 ||
Popped rice mixed with the juice of *brāhmī* and combined with *vacā*.
Having consecrated it three thousand times, one should consume it for one month.
One who possesses mantras equal to Bṛhaspati shall become the sovereign of all vidyās. || 130 ||
Having offered fuel-sticks of the aśvattha tree, which are endowed with sweetness, that twice-born man [honored] the brahmins.
One may bring under control kings as well as their ministers by means of a lotus-homa. || 131 ||
With white water-lilies, blue lotuses, and flowers from the sacred field of Brahmā, one should fashion an image made of rice-flour paste, combined with delicious flavors. || 132 ||
Having performed the consecration of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) upon it and having consecrated it with this mantra, [one should proceed].
One should eat it on a Sunday; thereafter, one shall bring under control any man, whether a king or a woman, or whomever else one desires, however excellent they may be. || 133 ||

A wise person should well-inscribe the Śakti mantra together with the name of the person to be protected using ashes upon a wooden board; if he shows it to a pregnant woman, she will quickly experience an easy delivery. || 134 ||

Now the procedure for consecration (abhiṣeka), which grants all desired aims, will be described. (p. 425) One should construct an auspicious mandala within the pavilion, provided with the seat of the Goddess. 135.
Having worshipped the pedestal (pīṭha) as prescribed, the wise one should arrange the jars upon the pericarp and the tips of the petals,
made of gold, silver, or fine copper.

Having placed there either five or one earthen [liṅgas], the wise knower of the tantras, with the loud sound of musical instruments, should install them while reciting the mantra; and the knower of mantras should perform worship for his own desired deity using the previously mentioned services (upacāras). || 137 ||
And within these jars, the Mothers should be worshipped by the wise according to the sequence of the directions;
if there are five jars, one should worship them in order starting from the center. || 138 ||
Thereafter, one should consecrate [the disciple] with the five nectars beginning with Hṛllekhā; first with a jar of clarified butter, and after that with a decoction. 139.
Then, after that, the wise man should consecrate it with oil, a decoction, honey, and subsequently with the boiled extracts of the barks of the two types of *dvija* trees. || 140 ||
Thereafter, one should perform [the rite] within the intermediate space using the petals of the door-pitchers.
The knower of mantras should also perform the washing of the mouth, hands, and feet, as well as the sipping of water (ācamana).
Indeed, after each individual jar-bath, one should have him bathe again with that very water;
by doing so, a man shall become empowered.
One should feed the Brahmins and satisfy them with various kinds of foods;
one shall attain great fortune and be victorious at all times. || 143 ||
The fruit of the palāśa, aśvattha, and bilva trees should be taken in the measure of half a pala.
The best among those who know the ritual performed the rites for Agnimantha and Lakṣasevya. || 144 ||
Half of that [quantity] is for prasāriṇī, kāśmarikā, and rohiṇī.
The udumbara, pāṭalī, indu, and kubhāga are thus proclaimed. || 145 ||
Then, one should fill the pitcher with water from a large decoction; by sprinkling [it] every year, one obtains excellent longevity. || 146 ||
He is indeed like the sun combined with the splendor of the beautiful ones; Kamalā is his servant, and upon seeing him, various fears perish. His wealth increases, abounding in grain. || 147 ||
All the gods indeed pay homage upon seeing him, and even the serpents do not bite that practitioner who sleeps on the path; nor do his sons bite him. 148.
And now, moreover, I shall proclaim here the supreme three-syllabled mantra.
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ—thus the previously mentioned [mantras] beginning with the sages (muni) are proclaimed here.
And by the first of the firsts, by the middle, and by that which is endowed with the six long vowels.
The six limbs, beginning with the fingers, and the remaining ritual placements (nyāsa) are as before. || 149 ||
Having the luster of the bandhūka flower, three-eyed, and adorned with the crescent moon as her crest-ornament.
A jewel-bowl in the left hand, a lotus in the right, and then the mantra.
One should recite the mantra twelve lakhs of times and perform oblations with a tenth part of that amount.
Then one should perform the satiation (tarpaṇa) and other rites with an oblation (havis) endowed with the three sweets.
Then the practitioner of mantras should perform the ritual applications for the attainment of his desired fruits.
An oblation performed with the flowers of the Brahmavṛkṣa is considered to bestow prosperity. || 152 ||

By reciting [the mantra] for a year, one becomes a poet through drinking *brāhmī* ghee. By performing a fire-oblation (*homa*) with pairs of white mustard seeds and salt, one shall bring a woman under control; one shall likewise bring a man, a king, or anyone else under control—of this there is no doubt. (153)
By means of *āragvadha* flowers sprinkled with sandalwood water, and by heaps of jewels accompanied by fine silk garments, one attains the fortune of sovereignty. || 154 ||
Through oblations mixed with sesame seeds and rice, the aforementioned fruit is obtained.
The practitioner should also perform the previously mentioned applications here as well. || 155 ||
Now I shall speak of another three-syllable [mantra] that swiftly bestows the power of speech.
Aiṃ, Hrīṃ, and Aimiti are to be known as the [mantras] of the sages and others, as previously described. || 156 ||

The best of those who know mantras should perform the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), which possess their respective meters, by enclosing [the seed-syllables] at the beginning and end with the long vowels and the pair of middle [vowels]. || 157 ||

The supreme knower of mantras should perform the placement (nyāsa) as taught in the Ekākṣara [Tantra], [visualizing the goddess] with the luster of the rising sun, three eyes, and breasts that are full and immeasurable. 158.
A lotus, a jewel-bowl, the gesture of fearlessness, and likewise the gesture of granting boons.
Holding [these] with her hands, she is seated upon a red lotus and bears the moon as her crest-ornament.
One should meditate upon Bhuvaneśvarī as being adorned with a necklace of pearls.

One should worship Bhuvaneśvarī on the seat (pīṭha) denoted by the single syllable; the previously mentioned [deities] beginning with Hṛllekhā should also be worshipped by the practitioner as before. (160)
One should worship the six pairs in the six corners as before;

one should worship the six limbs upon the filaments, and those [goddesses] upon the petals—Brāhmī and the others, seated upon the laps of their respective lords, with smiling faces and languid grace. (161)
Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, Unmatta, Kapālī, Vibhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra—these are said to be their lords. || 162 ||
The trident, the skull-bowl, the corpse, and the small drum. || 163 ||
Wearing elephant skins as garments upon their hands, possessing terrifying forms, and having curly hair—these should be remembered at the time of worship by a wise counselor. 164.

The Mothers beginning with Dīrghā are to be worshipped, as are the Bhairavas beginning with Hrasva; outside of that, on the petals of the vowels, are those beginning with Karālā who were previously mentioned. (165)
The World-Protectors (Lokeśas), beginning with Anaṅgarūpa, together with their weapons, are to be worshipped.
One should mutter the mantra one hundred thousand times according to the principle (tattva) using flowers from the Brahma-tree.
Or else, with flowers of the *rājavṛkṣa* tree smeared with the three sweets, [one should offer] a tenth part of that [number].
One should perform oblations, libations, and other rites for the sake of attaining mastery over the mantra. || 167 ||
Thus, the wise man who worships Bhuvaneśvarī according to this prescribed method of hymns shall bring under his control women intoxicated with passion as well as kings.
One should likewise perform all the ritual applications taught in the Ekākṣara [Upaniṣad]. || 168 ||

Now I shall explain another [mantra], which bestows the accomplishment of the three-syllable yantra and other rites: *Oṃ hrīṃ kroṃ*. This is the single-syllable mantra beginning with the sage (the syllable *hrīṃ*) and so forth, consisting of the letters of fire (*ra*). || 169 ||

One should mentally construct the limbs through creative imagination; now the meditation on the mantra is described: one should visualize [the goddess] seated upon a lotus, possessing the brilliance of the rising sun, holding in her hands a goad, a rosary, a noose, and a boon-granting gesture, within the heart. (170)
One should worship on the previously mentioned pedestal the goddesses beginning with Hṛllekhā as before;
the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) are on the filaments, and Brāhmī and the others are in the middle of the petals.
Then Śakra and the others should be worshipped outside the two weapons, and beyond them; he who worships in this manner with devotion shall become like Kubera. || 172 ||
All the people in the world shall become devoted to that minister. He should mutter the mantra one hundred thousand times according to the true principle (tattva) and perform one thousand oblations.
With sacrificial fuel-sticks from trees that yield three-fold sweet milk, offered according to the prescribed number.
Then one should perform the libations and other rites with pure sesame seeds mixed with milk.
The aśvattha, udumbara, plakṣa, and vaṭa— these four trees alone are prescribed for the fire-oblation (homa),
each [to be offered] six thousand times.
This sacrificial offering (homa) should be performed according to the scripture in a number of twenty-four; by that, the palace is suddenly presided over by one who resembles the sun. (176) [Couplet]
Even at night, that which is without lamps appears to all people as if crowded with hundreds of lamps; this is through the grace of this mantra. || 177 ||
One should offer oblations of white mustard seeds mixed with salt and turmeric, saturated with ghee;
thus one shall bring even a king or a queen under one's control. || 178 ||
By means of an oblation of food, the knower of mantras shall become possessed of a prosperous household; by means of an oblation of blooming blue lotuses, Fortune shall never abandon him. 179.
An oblation with *caturaṅgula* flowers bestows poetic talent; indeed, for the practitioner, an oblation of sesame seeds brings about the destruction of sins. (180)
One who desires long life and is most skilled in mantras should offer oblations with ghee as if pouring it into the fire.
One should also perform the previously mentioned applications here with the mantra; when this mantra is mastered, the practitioner of mantra attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 181 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare: "Vakratuṇḍāya huṃ. This six-syllabled mantra is declared to be the bestower of all accomplishments. || 182 ||

The short armor-mantra (kavaca) should be recited by women; it bestows all perfections (siddhis). Bhārgava is declared to be the sage (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is cited as the meter (chandas), and Vakra-toḍa, who is saluted by gods and demons, is its deity (devatā). 183.
Having performed the purification of the hands with the root mantra, one who has conquered the senses [should proceed].
One should assign the six limbs by means of the six syllables contained within the mantra. || 184 ||
In the middle of the eyebrows, the throat, the heart, the navel, and likewise in the foundation (ādhāra).
Then, having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the six syllables, one likewise performs the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) with the entire mantra.

One should meditate in the heart upon the red-colored one, whose face is smiling, who possesses the luster of the rising sun, and who holds in his hands the noose, the goad, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness. 186.
One should worship Vakratuṇḍa Gaṇeśvara on the previously mentioned pedestal.
It has eight petals and two lotuses, provided with four gates.
Then, one should draw it surrounded by three squares in successive order. || 187 ||
Having worshipped the deity in the center with the honored offerings,
the one of vast intelligence should first worship the limbs according to their respective locations.
One should worship the eight Śaktis in sequence at the bases of the eastern petals.
Vidyākhyā, Viśvadhātrī, Bhogadā, Vighnanāśinī, Nidhipradā, Pāpaghnī, as well as Puṇyā and Śaśiprabhā. || 189 ||
And there, on the petals, one should worship Aṇimā and the others previously mentioned; likewise, on the second eight-petaled [lotus], one should worship Vakratuṇḍa and the others. || 190 ||
In the square, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) and their weapons; likewise, as before, one should perform the proper worship of Vakra-tuṇḍa in the two aisles. || 191 ||
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times according to its syllables and perform oblations with a tenth part of that number.
With the eight substances previously mentioned, anointed with honey, according to the prescribed rule.
When the mantra has been thus perfected, the practitioner of mantras should accomplish the rites for specific desires.
One should first satisfy Gaṇeśvara Vakratuṇḍa according to the previously mentioned procedure.
One should construct a square sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit in front of that;
having churned the fire, one should establish it and fetch it from the house of a learned Vedic scholar. || 194 ||
The practitioner of mantra should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) and then carry out the ritual action;
thereafter, having performed the six-limbed mantra-deposition (mantranyāsa) as previously described. || 195 ||

Then, having worshipped the fire with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should establish it; there, in the midst of the fire, [one should place] the one who has a serpent as his sacred thread.
Him who has a protruding belly, who is the sun, who has a single tusk, and three eyes.
Seated upon the lotus posture, with four arms and three eyes. || 197 ||
Adorned with a crown, necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and various ornaments—having thus meditated in his mind and invoked Gaṇeśvara, [he should worship him]. || 198 ||

Having worshipped thoroughly with perfumes and other offerings, and having sprinkled water upon the fire, one should offer oblations of clarified butter with the six-syllable mantra ending in *svāhā* (dviṭha) one thousand and eight times; thereafter, the mantra becomes perfected. || 199 ||
On the fourth days of each of the eight thousand fortnights, one should offer a hundred oblations of cakes;
after a year, one obtains wealth.

At midday, the wise man should always recite the mantra before that [image], either one thousand, three hundred, or one hundred and eight times; thus, without effort, he quickly attains great prosperity. (201)

Clarity of mind, praise from others, and likewise the attainment of other desired objects; aversion to sleep and the sight of an elephant in a dream—these are indeed said by practitioners of mantra to be the signs of mantra-siddhi. || 202 ||
One should offer three hundred oblations for three months with the aforementioned *siddhaudana*; one will then become like Vaiśravaṇa, and the abode of great treasures shall be his. || 203 ||

In the presence of Gaṇeśa, one who possesses the mantra should offer a thousand oblations into the fire using flattened rice (pṛthuka) smeared with jaggery, coconuts mixed with black pepper, and cakes combined with milk;
such a person shall become wealthy. || 204 ||
With powders made from śubhaśālī rice, along with black pepper and other spices, together with rock salt.
With auspicious items containing cumin and abundant jaggery, thoroughly saturated with clarified butter. || 205 ||
The mantra-practitioner should offer oblations of cakes in the presence of Gaṇeśa;
he obtains great prosperity in abundance and without delay. || 206 ||
The wise practitioner should perform the oblation with the mantra encased by the letters of the name of the person for whom the rite is intended.
Or with fuel-sticks of Apāmārga, or with ripe fruits produced from the Panasa tree. || 207 ||
Or else, with a thousand plantains, one may bring a man or a woman under one's control.
One should offer a thousand parched grain oblations into the fire for the sake of obtaining a maiden.

One who is proficient in the science of mantras should offer a thousand oblations of clarified butter and also a thousand oblations of milk for the sake of pacifying disease. By offering a hundred thousand oblations of all [substances], one shall become a conqueror of death.
The practitioner of mantra should offer a thousand oblations of fuel-sticks from the Brahma-tree, soaked in the three sweets; within a month, he will certainly conquer his enemies. || 210 ||
At night, one should offer one thousand and eight fuel-sticks of the Vibhītaka tree, smeared with red lac, into the fire of a cremation ground; thus one shall kill the enemy. 211.

Having drawn the form of the enemy upon the ground, the wise practitioner should kindle a fire within his belly with the best of white mustard seeds and offer a thousand oblations; he shall cause that person's death within seven days— of this there is no doubt.
Having seized the enemy with his own trunk, Gaṇeśa— who possesses a luster equal to a crimson cloud—
cast him into the fiercely blazing fire of the submarine mare's mouth (Vaḍavāmukha).
Having meditated upon Gaṇapati as throwing [the enemy], one should mutter the mantra; by doing so for three days a thousand times, one will certainly cause the enemy to be eradicated. || 214 ||
Having reached a river flowing to the ocean, he took water in his cupped palms.
Having consecrated it a thousand times, one should sprinkle it upon one's own head; by this rite, the practitioner of mantra will certainly destroy the flood of sins. || 215 ||
On a Saturday, having taken refuge under an Āśvattha tree, one should recite the mantra three thousand times;
by meditating on Gaṇeśa, one shall remove the afflictions born of the planets.

By offering oblations of fuel-sticks made from reeds (vetasa), one shall obtain a thousandfold rain. One desiring wealth should offer grains, and one desiring food should certainly offer food as oblations. || 217 ||
A wise person who desires land should offer oblations of lotuses or blue water-lilies, or even garments; one who desires a field should offer oblations of meat mixed with molasses. || 218 ||
Having worshipped that Lord of the Gaṇas, [one should take] turmeric, rock salt, and vacā.
One should constantly grind these together with a measure of half a half-kārṣa.

One should consecrate with a thousand recitations cow's urine measured by handfuls; then, on the day of her ritual bath after menstruation, one should cause that pure woman, dressed in red garments, to drink it. Thus, even a barren woman shall give birth to a son within a year.
Having observed a fast during a lunar eclipse or a solar eclipse, one should take one pala of powdered *kapilājya* and half a pala of *vacā*.
Having recited this one thousand times, the wise person should drink it one thousand times; having attained great intelligence, he certainly obtains the gift of poetic composition. || 222 ||
Having smeared an area the size of a cow's hide with earth and covered it with fine cloth,
one should place there a consecrated jar worshipped with sandalwood and other offerings.
And having placed either a boy or a girl at the front of the lamp.
One should recite that most excellent mantra one thousand and eight times.
Touched by that [mantra], a girl or a boy speaks all that is in the mind—whether concerning the future, the past, or the present—by the grace of this mantra;
of this there is no doubt. (225)
Now I shall declare another mantra of the Lord Gaṇeśa Vakratuṇḍa:
"To Megholkā, Svāhā! This six-syllabled mantra has been proclaimed; Bhārgava is its sage, and Anuṣṭubh is said to be its meter. (226)

Vakratuṇḍa Gaṇeśa, who is worshipped by the gods, is his presiding deity. The practitioner of the mantra should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) with the syllables of the mantra as before; the mantra-practitioner should perform all rites, such as meditation and worship, as previously described. || 227 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the mantra consisting of thirty-two syllables.
He is considered the beloved bestower of the increase of wealth, a treasure-chest, and a granter of jewels. || 228 ||
The six-syllable mantra is "rakṣohaṇo balagahano 'thādyo" (rakṣohaṇo balagahano 'thādyo). The seer and other details were previously mentioned;
meditation, worship, and so forth are as before. One should recite it one thousand times for each syllable of the sun (twelve thousand times) and perform oblations with a tenth part of that number.

At the conclusion of that, one should satisfy the Guru with an oblation sprinkled with clarified butter. When the mantra has been thus perfected, the practitioner of the mantra should accomplish his own desired goal. (230)
One should perform all desired rites with the mantra proclaimed as having six syllables. Now, I shall describe another similar mantra for this [deity]. (231)
The beloved of the increase of wealth, the giver of treasures, the bestower of jewels, and the granter of manly vigor.
"O slayer of Rakṣas, O devourer of strength, svāhā to the one with the curved trunk, hūm! || 232 ||
With three arrows, eight, four, and five, [and] six.

The six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) are formed with the syllables of the mantra; the sages and other [components] are considered as before. Its application is as previously described, and this mantra is especially a bestower of treasures. Now I shall declare the Gāyatrī of Vakratuṇḍa, which is dear to Gaṇeśa.
We know that Tatpuruṣa; we meditate upon Vakratuṇḍa; may that Dantī inspire us. 235.
A person performing the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) should daily recite this one hundred and eight times at the beginning and the end for the sake of the success of all mantras. || 236 ||
One should recite the names of the twenty-eight Gaṇeśas every day.
At the beginning and end of the recitation, one who recites other mantras should likewise perform it eight times for the sake of perfect accomplishment.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, the Illumination of the Mantra of Gaṇapati according to the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya), in the Merutantra composed by Śiva with the approval of the illustrious Mahāmāyā and Mahākāla. 18.
The illustrious Śiva said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain those [deities] who bestow the accomplishments of the Western Tradition (paścimāmnāya).
[He saw] the leaders of the Gaṇas stationed in Kāśī, who perform various wonders. || 1 ||
The sixty-four Vināyakas, who are portions of Mahāgaṇapati, each took a Yoginī and even a servant girl into their respective solitude. || 2 ||
Having reached the heavenly realm, as far as the end of my own abode.
The eight [deities] are established within the eight enclosures, bestowing the attainment of supernatural powers (siddhi).
There, eight [peaks] are situated on the heavenly ground outside Kāśī; that perimeter extending one yojana beyond Kāśī is thus described.
The six-syllable mantra "gaṃ vighnāya namaḥ" is declared [to be the one for Gaṇeśa].
The accomplishment of these eight is remembered as being equal to the swift production of serene faith.
One should recite the mantra ten thousand times, and perform oblations with ghee and milk-rice;
the ritual applications are as before, and success is attained very quickly.
The Yoginī Gajānanā, indeed, assumes the form of a Yoginī.
The mantra consisting of that name preceded by the syllable *nāndya* (namo) and followed by the *arṇa* (svāhā) and the *sabindu* (bindu) is thus declared. || 7 ||
His beloved has also been mentioned; I shall now describe the means for its accomplishment: "Oṃ, O Śivā, wife of Śiva! Peace, O Śivā, in your own hand! (8)
One should say with a mind as swift as thought, "Give me the lotus-fruit. Being thus addressed with "Give, give at my feet;
salutations to you," this thirty-six-syllable mantra is proclaimed; now its meditation (dhyāna) is described.
I worship Śivā, who possesses the splendor of a thousand rising suns, who is worshipped by the one seated upon the lotus, and who holds in her hand the noose consisting of delusion.
One should recite [the mantra] thirty thousand times within a forest of lotuses.

Then one should perform the fire-oblation with safflower blossoms, as well as the libations and other rites. Having thus perfected the mantra, the practitioner of mantras should also propitiate the servant-maid (ceṭikā). || 11 ||
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Śrāvaṇa, during the middle of the night.
Having performed worship, one should recite the mantra; then one hears the internal sounds (nādas). || 12 ||
And if he is firm of mind, even when spirits cause him fear at that time.
Then, joined by many gods, Śivā shall become manifest to perception.
Being pleased, she grants the fruit unilaterally to that best of practitioners; he travels far in an instant, possessing a speed even greater than that of the mind. || 14 ||
Invisible even to all the people within Rājagṛha, many individuals were thus deluded by the lord of the host of Brahmins. 15.
The heart-mantra of Vināyaka consists of eight syllables beginning with the seed-syllable Gaṃ.
The preliminary rite for the Ganeshas is proclaimed to consist of one hundred thousand recitations of their names. || 16 ||
For all the Yoginīs, however, [the mantras] begin with their own seed-syllables and end with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
Name-mantras are traditionally said to consist of one hundred thousand syllables as their preliminary ritual service (puraścaraṇa).
By the power of Gaṇeśa, success in the world beyond shall be attained.
By serving the Yoginīs here, one is not overcome by obstacles. || 18 ||
The maidservant bestows the aforementioned fruit; this is the certainty in every case. Here, the Yoginī Siṃhāsyā is matted-haired and bears poison. || 19 ||
Now I shall declare the twenty-syllable mantra of Kāmyā the maidservant, which,
from its two syllables, brings one to dwell in the depths of Pātāla.
One should contemplate: "O Śyāmalā, grant me the attainment of prosperity, svāhā! [She is] situated within the palm-forest, beautiful with the clapping of her hands. (21)
I worship Śyāmalā, who, accompanied by her female companions, performs songs.
With a tranquil mind, he should recite it ten thousand times in the Tāla forest.

One should perform oblations with pieces of palm fruit (*tālīphala*) mixed with camphor and agallochum (*aguru*), numbering one-tenth of that [total], and then perform three circumambulations to the right.

One should perform that [rite] in a grove of *tālī* trees, or else in another forest in the midst of them; on the full moon day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should recite the mantra two thousand times during the night.
At midnight, one should perform a complete homa with palm fruit; then a gale-force wind arises and an intense light is produced. || 25 ||
In the midst of that, however, is the Great Goddess, dark-complexioned and sixteen years of age.
She is clothed in blue garments and is fond of musk and sandalwood.
"Having paid homage to them, O lady of beautiful countenance, be pleased as the Sovereign of the Universe. Having spoken thus to the minister, she, being gratified, gives him three fruits. (27)
He attained the supreme knowledge of the mental consciousness, which is beyond birth and death, and his own form became like that of Kandarpa,
capable of enchanting the entire world.
"Gaṃ vīrāya namaḥ"—this is declared to be the six-syllabled mantra. And the Yoginī Gṛddhā, that ascetic woman, became his [consort] through her disguise. (29)
Her maidservant, however, was called Bālā; she consisted of twenty-nine syllables. Having uttered "Oṃ Pañcavārṣikī," she [possessed] the sweetness of speech like a child. (30)
At the end of "mama dehi," there are two *hurū*s, followed by a pair of *hurū*s, and then two *Bhuvaneśīs*;
thus her meditation (*dhyāna*) is described. || 31 ||
Her limbs were anointed with gorocanā, she was as fair as gold, and she was worshipped by the gods.
She who has the moon as her crest-jewel, whose speech is charming, and who is beautiful of eye.
Having smeared the floor of an empty house with cow dung, one should then smear it with sandalwood paste and subsequently with saffron.
There, Bālā should be worshipped with blades of dūrvā grass, and then one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
One should perform one thousand oblations with dhattūra flowers.
Worship should be performed with their seeds; one clad in silk should sacrifice. One wearing saffron robes, or even naked, may perform the rite once the mantra has been mastered.
On the night of the full moon at the rising of the moon, one should perform an anointing with dhattūra oil; having gone to that girl's house naked, one should mutter the mantra for her flower.
Then, at the end of the night, she was seen from a distance as a five-year-old girl;
having climbed a tree, she ran toward his presence.
She too, filled with joy and great delight, quickly kisses his face; from that kissing, his tongue becomes a repository of manifold flavors. || 38 ||
Upon hearing news of that, the king and all the people in the kingdom fall into a state of delusion.
That speech would be a delusion for species of animals such as tigers and the like. || 39 ||
Beholding his face, all living beings become bewildered. "Oṃ, salutation to Gaṇeśvara"—this is declared to be the six-syllabled mantra. || 40 ||
One should say: "Yoginī Kākatuṇḍā, Asphuṭākṣī, and she who is called Ceṭikā; O Viśālākṣī, Gajāntā—give, give a pair of sesame seeds. (41)
Having uttered "dāridryaṃ dāhaya," followed by *hrīṃ* clearly and *huṃ kalatrakam*, this mantra of the Fire-god is fully declared; it consists of twenty-eight syllables. (42)
Or in a grove of jambīra and coconut trees, or on the bank of a river; or else in a secluded and delightful place adorned with such a forest. || 43 ||

Alternatively, on the bank of a beautiful river adorned with the fragrance of lotuses, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and then perform a fire sacrifice (homa) consisting of one-tenth that number. || 44 ||

Then, having perfected the mantra, the practitioner of mantra should perform [the rite] with coconuts on the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Māgha, under the lunar mansion Viśākhā at night. (45)
If one recites the mantra a thousand times, Vetālas with swords in their hands will terrify the practitioner; at that time, one must not be afraid under any circumstances.
He sprinkles them with blood from his left hand, and they flee far away. When the recitation is begun once more, then Kātyāyanī herself [appears]. || 47 ||
Then a most terrifying woman appears, chewing upon human skulls; she sprinkles herself with blood from her left shank and then departs.
When the recitation is commenced again, the terrifying Bhairavī departs.
Chewing on an elephant's head, she vomits blood upon the ground.
Then terrifying Bhairavas arrive along with her; one should indeed sprinkle those Bhairavas with blood arising from the forehead. 50.

Furthermore, at the conclusion of a thousand recitations, one should offer three coconuts; then the Goddess, having arrived, bestows a coconut. When that is established, the entire world becomes submissive, as does the Fortune of the City.
Having uttered "Gamu" and then speaking "Pravaden Ngenta Varadakṣavināyaka," this mantra ending with "Hṛdanta" consists of Rudra-syllables; it is proclaimed as the Yoginī-mantra for him. 52.
She is called Uṣṭragrīvā, assuming the form of a Sairandhrī; her face is like the Vedas, her eyes are like yellow orpiment, and her mantra consists of seventeen syllables. || 53 ||
One should utter "Tāraṃ hrīṃ haritālākṣi," followed by "ratikalāṃ," then a pair of "dah" syllables and the wife of fire (svāhā). Her meditation is now described. || 54 ||

One should meditate upon that Great Goddess, who shines like a multitude of thousands of hibiscus flowers, whose eyes are like yellow orpiment, who bestows success, and who spreads forth auspiciousness. || 55 ||

When entering the second step of the deer [this word is in the nominative and locative case endings], it is certain; having gone to a solitary forest on the first day of the night, one should indeed proceed. (56)
And on that day, having brought yellow orpiment and having first smeared it upon his own face,
he should recite the mantra ten thousand times.
One should perform the oblation with ghee, camphor, saffron, and safflower; one should complete it with a *kuliṅga* bird that has been touched by the juice of yellow orpiment.
Then the goddess Lalitā Haritālikā arrives, tempting with various words;
the practitioner should not trust her. || 59 ||
Then, at the time of dawn, by the power of the root mantra, she bestows her own sister Ratikalā upon the practitioner.
Having brought the practitioner under her control, Ratikalā certainly takes hold of the mantra-practitioner.
Making one a sky-walker (khecara), she immediately leads [the practitioner] to the contemplated region.
She brings under the control of the mantra-practitioner, with respect and in an instant, yakṣiṇīs, bhūtas, vetālas, bhairavas, and even those more terrifying than bhairavas.
One may lead [the deceased] to the cities of the gods, kinnaras, gandharvas, and vidyādharas, and one may bring them back again to earth and show them various objects. || 63 ||
Having uttered "Gam" for the elephant-faced one (Gaṇeśa), this heart-mantra consists of eight syllables.
For this [mantra], Hayagrīva becomes the Yoginī who fasts for a month.
Her handmaid is Kuṇḍalī, and her mantra consists of eleven syllables: Oṃ kuṇḍini nāgavāhane phurphurvahnigehinī. || 65 ||
Mounted upon a great elephant, with eyes wide and downcast, she blazes even in the darkness,
felling trees with her hissing breath.

Where there may be a single-liṅga Mahādeva in a grove of bilva trees, one should recite this mantra there and perform one hundred thousand oblations; then, through the root of the bilva tree, the perfection of the mantra is attained. (67)
On the night of the fourteenth day of Śiva, in a secluded temple of Śiva, one should mutter [the mantra] three thousand times and perform oblations with a tenth part of that amount. || 68 ||
At the conclusion of the oblation with the root of a bilva tree, a great serpent named Kuṇḍa appeared, with a wide-spreading mouth and a long body, measuring twenty yugas in length. || 69 ||
Having extended its hood, that serpent remains before the practitioner once again.
That minister must stand before him without fear.
He certainly emits thousands of hisses with his hoods;
from his mouth, hundreds of flames issue forth again and again. (71)
Likewise, there were various kinds of poisons with blue and yellow hues, as well as raw flesh,
and trees with smoke-patterned leaves.
If, upon seeing such a great portent, one does not feel fear at all,
then that Goddess is seen seated upon the hood of that serpent.
One should praise that goddess with hymns of praise; being satisfied, she bestows [the fruits].
By that [mercury] weighing one *tolaka*, one becomes free from old age and death; he beholds treasures situated in the earth, and his speech becomes truthful. || 74 ||

The letter *ga* with one *daṃta* (d) and the suffix *ṅe* (ṅ), ending in *hṛdaya*, is the elephant-letter (*gajākṣara*). Vārāhī was born as a Yoginī, moving about in the form of a boar. Her maidservant for this deity is said here to be Madhuvāsinī. || 75 ||
The thirteen-syllable mantra is remembered as follows: having uttered "Praṇava," "Madhuvāsinī," and "Kāmadevī," the mantra is "klīṃ svāhā. || 76 ||
And being praised by Kāma, she bore a golden lotus.
One should meditate upon the goddess who possesses the nine rasas, who has the eyes of a deer, and who bestows the bliss of Brahman.
Standing at the foot of a Madhūka tree, one should mutter the mantra one hundred thousand times;
then, a fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed with Vāsantī flowers or else with Madhūka blossoms.

One should perform [the recitation] ten thousand times with incense mixed with camphor and agallochum. On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Madhu, one should recite it in a solitary, secluded place. (79)

At the foot of a Madhūka tree, and especially in the waters of the Godāvarī, one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) a thousand times as previously described, and recite [the mantra] nine thousand times. || 80 ||
Then the Yakṣa Jvālāmālin, terrifyingly formidable,
drank with his right hand from the horn of the buffalo as if it were honey.
The terrifying Yakṣa drinks blood and liquor with his left hand, and indeed, he consumes creepers, trees, and shrubs with his very tongue.
"Having torn off my limbs, O terrible one, eat me!"—thus he speaks. At that time, one should not experience fear from such false terrors and the like. 83.
The minister should then offer blood drawn from his own hand to him. After that Yakṣa has departed, the goddess [should be worshipped] at the foot of the tree at that time.
When she becomes visible to him, he should give her a flowery bow.
With that [mantra], even at the distance of a span (vitasti), one becomes the cause of universal delusion. || 85 ||
Possessing the bloom of fresh youth and bodies reddened with saffron, they, infatuated by desire, bestow their wealth and their very bodies upon him. || 86 ||

And he who has a protruding belly, with the eight syllables from the heart [mantra], is the Yoginī whose face is like that of a Śarabha and who bears a body garlanded with flames. Her servant is called Mantharā, and her mantra consists of twenty-four syllables. || 87 ||
Oṃ, one should then say to Mantharā: "O you who dwell in the quarters and on the earth, grant me my pair of desired boons—Tuṃ, Ghaṃ, Maṃ, and the consort of Fire. (88)
The tremulous-eyed woman held a sugarcane bow in her hand.
Her limbs are as red as the hibiscus flower, and she is the one who agitates my heart. (89)
And likewise in a place for sugarcane fields and a place for boiling molasses, having prepared an auspicious spot near the five juices (rasa-pañca). || 90 ||
One should perform the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) consisting of one hundred thousand repetitions and offer oblations with pieces of sugarcane.
On the night of the sixth lunar day dedicated to Mallāri, one should recite [the mantra] two hundred times under the Somavāra asterism.
One should offer oblations with pieces of sugarcane ten times that number; then Mantharā arrives and indeed gives a vessel of honey mixed with divine mead.
One should indeed worship that [deity] at the three junctions of the day; from its mouth, Mantharā shall speak with clear speech whatever is in her mind, after the worship has been completed. (93)
By the power of his mind, he knows the past, the present, and the future in their true essence; of this there is no doubt. || 94 ||
Whenever extreme distress certainly arises for the practitioner of mantras, at each such instance he should worship that Goddess with offerings of honeyed drinks. || 95 ||
One should worship [the deity] at the beginning of a conflict and so forth; it swiftly removes all distress.
But near the five juices, one should perform the worship of the ground. || 96 ||
With saffron, vermilion from the eastern mountains, red sandalwood, and aloe-wood paste. || 97 ||
One should worship with Madhyandinīja, pāpuṣpa, and karavīra flowers, as many as there are red objects [to be worshipped]. || 98 ||

One should recite the eight Vināyakas proclaimed by the Kaulikas as they are established: first, one should utter "Obeisance to the Blessed One" (namo bhagavate), followed by their respective names ending in the feminine suffix -ī. (99)
This mantra of the eight [deities] is Siddhivināyaka in the east;
there, the Yoginī Ulūkī assumes the form of a barber-woman.
The procedure there is declared to be the eightfold supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇimā*; whatever power the practitioner desires, one should utter that word joined with it. || 101 ||
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times within its midst and perform the fire offering (homa).
Then, having become like Mahāgaṇapati himself, one shall thereafter attain that perfection. || 102 ||
In Kāśī, in the south-eastern quarter, Arkavināyaka is to be known; and this Śivā is indeed a Yoginī who assumes the form of an image. || 103 ||

Haṃsā would be his female attendant (ceṭī), and the mantra would consist of twelve syllables: "Oṃ haṃsa geṃ bodha. This [mantra] consists of the Speech-seed (vāk-bīja), the Śrī-bīja, and the beloved of Agni (the Fire-seed). || 104 ||
She possesses a luster like the combined moonlight of a hundred moons, and she has the half-moon as her crest-ornament.
I serve her who moves with the gait of a swan, whose hands grant boons and bestow fearlessness.

The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for this consists of fifty thousand repetitions; thereafter, one should perform half of ten thousand (five thousand) fire-oblations with lotus seeds mixed with clarified butter.
Likewise, one should perform the fire-oblation with barley on the bank of a river adorned with lotuses.
Certainly on the lunar day that marked the time of the destruction of Hiraṇyakaśipu’s life.
Beginning at twilight, one should recite [the mantra] until three watches have passed;
one should offer oblations with birch-bark leaves and lotus seeds, numbering eighty thousand (khakhakhāṣṭaka).
Then that goddess, mounted upon a swan and possessing a radiance equal to a hundred moons, presented a garland of lotuses to that minister. || 109 ||
By reciting that garland of mantras, the practitioner becomes one who has mastered the scriptures.
