If, however, he becomes arrogant due to ignorance, his very being shall be destroyed. Durgavināyaka was established by Durgā to the south of Kāśī. || 110 ||
There, the Yoginī Māyūrī bestows medicine upon the worlds. Having uttered "Oṃ Hrīṃ Indu," followed by "Durgāyai" ending with the word "Hṛdaya," this consists of eight syllables. (111)
The sage is said to be named Nārada, and Gāyatrī is declared to be the meter; it is Goddess Durgā, by whom Gaṇeśa was worshipped for the purpose of slaying the demon Durga. || 112 ||
Having first uttered the Praṇava, accompanied by the six long vowels.
In sequence, one should place the *māyā* (the syllable Hrīṃ) at the beginning and the end, and the words "to Durgā" (*durgāyai*) in the middle.
The six limbs beginning with the sprout (pallava) are thus proclaimed as the mantras. || 114 ||
Seated upon a lion-throne, possessing the luster of emerald, with the crescent moon as her crest-ornament.
I worship her who holds a conch, a discus, a bow, and arrows, and who possesses three eyes.

In a pair of eight-petaled lotuses surrounded by three squares, provided with four gates and drawn with saffron and other pigments, one should perform the worship of the Śakti there during the worship of one's own seat. || 116 ||
Prabhā, Samā, Jayā, Sūkṣmā, Viśuddhā, and likewise Nandinī, Suprabhā, and Vijayā—granting the accomplishment of all goals, they are located starting from the eastern petal. || 117 ||

In this manner, one should worship with water, omitting the [syllables] *vahni* (ra), *sara* (sa), *klība* (ha), and *hīna* (the vowel *i*). Having uttered the great word: *oṃ vajranakhadaṃṣṭrāyudhāya*, [one should offer]. 118.
"Siṃhāya huṃ phaṭ"—this heart-mantra consists of nineteen syllables;
it is declared to be the lion-mantra, and with it one should worship the lion. || 119 ||
Having invoked the form [of the deity] into that [image], one should worship it with sandalwood paste and other offerings.
The first rotation should be with the [eight] limbs, while the second is with the [eight] splendors and so forth. || 120 ||
With the first letter of each name accompanied by a bindu, one should perform the rites of victory and so forth.
The third enclosure is proclaimed to consist of the Ṅenta and the Namonta [mantras]. || 121 ||
Jayā, Vijayā, Kīrti, Prīti, and Prabhā are considered [the deities]; Śraddhā, Medhā, and Śruti likewise constitute the fourth enclosure in sequence. || 122 ||
The conch, the discus, the mace, the sword, the noose, the goad, the arrow, and the bow.
And on the two outer processional paths, the weapons of the world-protectors [are placed] in sequence. || 123 ||

Having conquered the senses and subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya), one should mutter the mantra one hundred thousand times; or [one may do so] a thousand times with sesame seeds soaked in sweet liquids or with milk-rice. 124.

One should offer oblations into the kindled fire and then perform the libations (tarpaṇa) and other rites; when the mantra has been thus mastered, the wise practitioner of mantras should undertake its ritual applications. 125.
According to the prescribed method, [he should prepare] nine beautiful jars.
One should place those endowed with the five jewels in the nine positions. || 126 ||
The mantra-knower, having worshipped Durgā in the center and Jayā and the others elsewhere with sandalwood paste and the like, as well as incense and lamps, should perform the sacrifice. || 127 ||
A wise person should consecrate a beloved person to be accomplished, or a king, or a child.
Endowed with the glory of victory, he becomes a king; it is not otherwise. || 128 ||
One is liberated from afflictions by spirits, epilepsy, vetālas, piśācas, and the like; and even a barren woman shall obtain a virtuous and auspicious son. || 129 ||

A mortal is freed from disease and attains long life; of this there is no doubt. By this very procedure, one wins the favor of people, and for those who worship the mantra of Durgā, there is great longevity and the destruction of sin. 130.
To the southwest of Kāśī, Caṇḍavināyaka is to be known;
his Yoginī is Vṛttakarī, whose face is like a discus. His female servant is named Haṃsī;
her sādhana is now described. || 131 ||
Her moon-like luster is like the light of nectar, her beautiful hands are adorned with parrots, she holds a swan in her left hand, and her breasts are full and elevated. || 132 ||
And in a secluded spot on the bank of a river, one should mutter the mantra thirty million times;
one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) ten thousand times with mustaka roots and uśīra grass.
Thus, having perfected the practice, the wise one should perform it on a riverbank, in a forest, in a thicket of bilva trees, or in a secluded place.

On the bank of the Tuṅgabhadrā river, where Śiva resides as Lakṣmīśvara, one should bathe on its shore and worship Aṅgā and the others on that day. On a Sunday, one should offer oblations at night as before and likewise worship the Goddess.
Having bowed, praised, and made his request, he fearlessly gives to the practitioner, in a place devoid of people, the beautiful object called crystal. (136)
In that state, he perceives the past, the future, and the present; likewise, regarding both himself and others, that man becomes all-knowing. || 137 ||
In the western direction of Kāśī is that Dehalīvināyaka; there the Yoginī Aṣṭavaktrā performs the work of a merchant woman. || 138 ||

The twenty-third description is that of the maidservant named Vicitrā. One should utter the mantra: "Hrīṃ, O Vicitrā, O wearer of variegated garments, give me a garment," followed by the pair "pūraya" (fill) for the wind, and then "huṃ svāhā. Thus is the mantra declared. || 139 ||
One should recite the mantra ten thousand times on the bank of a river, and perform the subsidiary rites (daśāṃśa) one-tenth of that amount.
The oblation should be performed with lotus-seeds; one should carry out whatever specific desire one has.
In the month of Caitra and in the month of Āśvina, on the fourteenth day, one should recite the mantra throughout the entire night on the bank of a lake until the end. || 141 ||

Then the Goddess arrives, bringing a variegated hem of her garment; having worshipped it, one should place it in the house at night. That house becomes filled with garments, even those belonging to the royal palace. 142.
In the northwestern corner of Kāśī is the Vināyaka named Uddaṇḍa;
the Yoginī Koṭarākṣī is his servant, who bestows curds and milk. || 143 ||
Having uttered "Keśa," then the word "āvarttana-khara," followed by the mantra "hrīṃ śrīṃ svāhā"; now its meditation (dhyāna) is described here. || 144 ||
And in his left hand, he holds a water-pot filled with pure water.
The area around his temples was enriched by the placement of golden earrings, performed according to the prescribed rites.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times on a delightful riverbank and perform the fire oblation with the three sweets; thereafter, one should carry out the ritual application.
At the great holy ford on the bank of the Kṛṣṇā, or else at the auspicious Pañcanada, on the second day of the dark fortnight in the month of Māgha, during the middle of the night. || 147 ||
Having fashioned a sheaf of grass, one should deposit it in another spot;
then, having performed the evening rites, one should worship that sheaf.
There, the practitioner of mantra, recollecting the Goddess, shall certainly enter into the interior of the granary;
having assumed the bound posture (baddhāsana) there, the yogi indeed disregards the affliction of cold. 149.
One should mutter [the mantra] five thousand times according to the prescribed rite for the deity; then one shall behold the auspicious Śivā, who has five faces, three eyes, and eight arms. || 150 ||
Then that deity gives him a water-pot filled with water;
he should then sprinkle his son with that water. || 151 ||
At that very moment, that man declares his birth arising from seven previous lives, and at that time he performs those respective karmas. || 152 ||
To the north of Kāśī, however, is Vināyaka Pāśapāṇi; his Yoginī is Kubjā, who by her very nature is a snake-catcher. || 153 ||
When the Goddess dwelling in the Vindhya mountains was unable to slay Mahiṣa (the elision of the causative suffix *ṇic* is archaic), Vajra then acted as one by whom Mahiṣa was slain;
therefore, I shall briefly declare the mantra of Mahiṣamardinī. (154)

Having uttered "Mahiṣamardinī," the eight-syllabled mantra ends with "svāhā. Mārkaṇḍeya is the sage, Gāyatrī is the meter, and the deity of this mantra is the Goddess Mahiṣamardinī, who is praised by gods and demons. (155)

"O crusher of Mahiṣa, huṃ phaṭ"—this is proclaimed as the heart mantra. "O consort of the enemy of Mahiṣa, huṃ phaṭ"—this is declared to reside in the head. With these mantras joined with the [seed] syllables (jāti), one should fashion the five limbs. || 156 ||
I bow to her who possesses the luster of a garuḍa-stone, adorned with jewels, pearls, and earrings, standing upon the head of a buffalo, and having an eye in her forehead. || 257 ||
The discus, the conch, the sword, the arrow, the trident, and the threatening gesture.
She bore a bow and a shield in her hands, and wore the moon upon her crest.
Abounding in the splendor of a crown of matted locks, she is adorned with all ornaments.
The goddess, wearing yellow garments, with her two breasts full and elevated. || 159 ||
Then, one should worship Mahiṣamardinī on the seat previously mentioned.
The first rotation should be performed with the deities beginning with Durgā, as impelled by the others. (160)
Starting from the southeast and proceeding clockwise, there are Durgā, Varavarṇinī, Āryā, she named Kanakā, and Kṛttikā, the bestower of fearlessness. (161)
The forms of the virgins are preceded by the two vowels [ā and ī], namely: ā, īṃ, ūṃ, diṃ, and ghoṃ.
And here, the eight long vowels should be taken, excluding the neuter ones. || 162 ||
First, one should utter the letter beginning with *pa* together with the nasal dot (*bindu*); then, having pronounced the weapon of the Goddess, one should worship it in the third enclosure.
The fourth [offering] should be for the world-protectors (lokapālas), and the fifth for their weapons.
One should mutter the mantra eight hundred thousand times and perform a fire oblation with sesame seeds one thousand times.
When the mantra has been thus accomplished, the practitioner of mantras should then perform the ritual applications.
Through an oblation of sesame seeds, the subjugation of men and women will certainly come to pass. || 165 ||
A mortal is instantly freed from disease by the oblation of mustard seeds; likewise, through the oblation of lotuses, one shall achieve victory over a king in battle. || 166 ||
Through the oblation of dūrvā grass, the pacification of diseases for mortals will certainly occur.
With flowers arising from the Brahma-tree, one obtains supreme nourishment. || 167 ||

Through an oblation of grain, one obtains grains; and by offering the feathers of a crow, enmity arises in the world even between those who are most intimate friends. By an oblation of black pepper, it is true that the enemy goes to his death. 168.
Thus, whoever worships the goddess Durgā, the slayer of Mahiṣa,
shall destroy base spirits, thieves, and the like, even by their mere sight.
When worshipped again and again in close proximity, she bestows swift accomplishment.

In the north-eastern direction of Kāśī, Kharvavināyaka is to be known; there stands the Yoginī Jayadurgā, who has assumed the form of a maidservant and possesses fierce eyes, bestowing spiritual accomplishments upon those who dwell there. || 170 ||
Having uttered "Tāra" (Oṃ), "Durge," and the pair [of syllables], [one says] "Rakṣiṇī," O wife of Agni.
This ten-syllable mantra is proclaimed as the bestower of desired accomplishments for those who worship it.

The seer is the sage Nārada, the metre is Virāj, and the deity is Jayadurgā; this mantra is accepted by all as consisting of five words beginning with "Tārā," with the elision of case-endings being an archaic Vedic usage.
Now, the arrangement of the limbs associated with the [specific] caste is declared as the rite for desired results (kāmyakarman). || 172 ||
"Durge" is declared to be the heart, and "Durgā" is said to be the head. "Durgāyai" is the tuft (śikhā), and the armor (varma) is proclaimed as "Bhūtarakṣākṣi. (173)

The pair beginning with Tārā and Durgā is proclaimed as the two protectresses; the pair beginning with Tārā and Durgā is declared to be the weapon of the protectresses. [She is] dark as a cloud, adorned with a garland of skulls, three-eyed, and riding upon a lion. (174)
I worship her who bears a discus, a conch, a sword, and two spears in her arms.

The knower of mantras should worship the Goddess on the Durga-pīṭha according to the stated method; he should recite the mantra five hundred thousand times and perform oblations with clarified butter ten times that amount.
Then one should perform the satiation (tarpaṇa) and other rites; thereafter, the mantra becomes perfected.
Once the mantra is perfected, the practitioner of mantras should then carry out the ritual applications (prayoga). || 176 ||
One should mutter this mantra repeatedly and enter the battlefield against the enemy; one shall slay the foe entirely—of this there is no doubt to be made. || 177 ||
In disputes, legal proceedings, and the like, one shall become victorious through this knowledge (vidyā) when recited;
it is as if banners, flags, and kettledrums have been sounded. || 178 ||
Horns, conch shells, and so forth; all vehicles, as well as the army and the commander of the forces.
He may indeed become bewildered in battle, yet he surely attains victory. || 179 ||
Now, its distinction is declared: when [the syllable] falls upon a harsh place, or when a debt arises from the star, one should utter the name as before. (180)
The twelve-syllable mantra bestows victory in battle. The [assignment of] sages and so forth is declared as before, and likewise for meditation, worship, and other rites. || 181 ||
And with the mantra, both individually and collectively, one should assign the six limbs in due order.
These Gaṇanāyakas residing in the vicinity of Kāśī have been thus described. || 182 ||
Near Gaṇapati, known as Dehalī, there are sixteen others;
these Vināyakas in Kāśī are indeed the initiators of Vedic rites. || 183 ||
For Tantrikas there is no accomplishment here, and especially not for Vāmas.
The Veda, however, is beginningless; in this regard, its accomplishment arises swiftly. || 184 ||
He is the creator of obstacles for those who are not devotees, yet the bestower of victory upon his devotees;
he is the remover of the sins of sinners and the one who perfects the path of the Vāmamārga. || 185 ||
The protector of the penance grove, likewise the guardian of Sītā; the bestower of long life, the remover of disease, the giver of treasures, and the lord of the twice-born. (186)
Tundila, Viśvarakṣākṛt, Gaṇanātha, Gaṇādhipa, and Dugdhada—these names grant all accomplishments. || 187 ||
When the syllables of the mantra have been recited ten thousand times ending with the heart-mantra, accomplishment will necessarily follow according to one's name; of this there is no doubt. (188)
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare those who abide within the state of liberation.
The eight mantras that govern the boundaries are now being described. || 189 ||
Having uttered the seed-syllable *dharā* (la), one should then utter that same seed-syllable;
having pronounced the name ending in the letter *ṅ*, the mantra is said to conclude with the word *hṛdaya*. || 190 ||
In the eastern direction of Avimukta is Lambodara-Vināyaka; and the Yoginī Śuṣkodarī has taken recourse to the form of Dhātrī. || 191 ||
In that very context, the propitiation of Śūlinī Durgā is taught. One should say "Śūlinī" twice with the word "jvalat" (blazing) when there is an evil planetary influence. 192.
"Oṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā"—this mantra is proclaimed to have as many syllables as there are lunar days (tithis).
The sage is Dīrghatamas, the metre is Kakubh, and the deity is stated [as follows]. || 193 ||
Śūlinī, Mahādurgā, and Sarvāriṣṭavināśinī are her names; "Durge" is the heart-mantra, while "Varade Vindhyavāsinī" is the head-mantra. || 194 ||
After the *śikhā*, *varma*, and at the end of the *asura* [mantras], one should utter *damanyante*; thereafter, one should speak "pure" (*śuddham*) and "dear" (*priyam*).
Following that, the form of "terrifying" (*trāsaya*) is declared. 195.

And the mantrin should utter the Astra-mantra in the Devasiddhānta when it has been well-worshipped; within the Nandinī [section], the pair of Rakṣās, and "Samastayogeśvarī," as well as those beginning with the word "Śūlinī" and ending with Varma and Astra, are proclaimed. (196)
Thus has the five-limbed mantra been indicated and placed by the practitioner.

This shall certainly provide protection for the performer and destroy the afflictions caused by malevolent spirits; having thus performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the body and other parts, one should meditate on Durgā, who is praised by the gods. (197)
She holds a mace, a sword, a shield, arrows, a trident, and a buckler; she also carries Karālikā, a noose, and a bow with her hands directed toward the cardinal points.
She has the luster of a cloud, wears a moon as a crown, is mounted upon a lion, and possesses four [arms].
She was surrounded by young maidens, possessed of three eyes, and adorned with ornaments.
Having meditated thus and performed the ritual placements once more, the practitioner should proceed.
Having meditated upon the Goddess at the Durgā-pīṭha previously described, one should worship her. || 200 ||

The second [case-ending] should be used with Durgā and others, while the locative case is used everywhere with weapons and the like. Durgā, Varadā, Vindhyavāsinī, and Suramardinī—[these are the names]. (201)
They are declared to be fond of battle, worshipped by gods, siddhas, and others; they are also called Nandini and Sumahāyogeśvarī. || 202 ||
The discus, the conch, the sword, the mace, the arrows, the bow, and the trident.
And one should worship these, beginning with the noose in front of the Goddess, while performing a circumambulation.

Worshipped by the lords of the directions and others, such as Vajra and the rest, in fivefold enclosures, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with a tenth part of that amount.

Then one should perform the satiation (tarpaṇa) and other rites with clarified butter and oblations accompanied by ghee; having worshipped the Brahmins according to the rules, one should then honor the Guru with devotion. (205)
Thus, having accomplished the mantra, the practitioner of mantras should perform his own desired applications according to the prescribed rule, preceded by the command of the Guru. || 206 ||
Likewise, one should visualize Śūlinī, who possesses a fierce face and is equipped with weapons such as the trident.
Having reflected thus, one who has touched that [object] according to the prescribed rule should mutter the mantra.
Having entered that [person], one should speak everything for a moment; afterwards, [the spirit] perishes. By the repetition of the mantra at that time, the host of spirits flees. || 208 ||
And by remembering Śūlinī, accompanied by her own weapons, in the midst of the sick, the grahas, upagrahas, and others quickly flee from one who recites [her mantra]. || 209 ||

Having worshipped Kṣemaṅkarī, the wise one should mutter this mantra. The enemy army seizes their own weapons and likewise becomes motionless. [According to the Vārtika rule "senā apratyaye," or by the power of the word's connection, there is an elision of the word *para*; thus, the meaning here is "one's own army" (*svasenā*).]
It would be so. || 210 ||
One should offer a hundred thousand oblations with sesame seeds mixed with mustard seeds while uttering the names of the enemies; the enemy shall then become a guest of Yama.
One should offer eight thousand oblations every day using the method of the three sweets.
His power shall become sufficient and unimpeded before the end of a year. || 212 ||
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter while reciting the mantra, the practitioner shall obtain his desired object.
And before a year has passed, [one should worship] with dūrvā grass combined with the three sweets (madhuratraya).
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations correctly, he should approach the consecrated fire.
The practitioner of mantra should [prepare] one hundred and eight pills made of cow dung.
One should perform oblations for seven days with desired offerings; then, through devotion, a meeting will occur—this is the remainder of the sense.
Having taken auspicious cow-dung in a place untouched by the earth or the atmosphere, one should proceed.
If one desires to go forth, one should recite [the mantra] three thousand times at the gateway of the Śaṅkha [temple].
There is no doubt that it brings about the immobilization of him within that dwelling; moreover, when driven into the front of an army, it effectively causes the army to be paralyzed. || 216 ||
Whether going to a village or a city, the wise person should call Ambikā to mind.
And one should recite the mantra over water and food with a serene mind. (217)
Having gratified [them] and entered that [place], he shall obtain delicious food.
Accompanied by a retinue of a thousand servants; of this there is no doubt. || 218 ||
And with fuel-sticks of the *arka* tree, smeared with the three sweets, as previously described.

The practitioner should offer one thousand oblations for the sake of those whom he intends; indeed, they will surely become submissive, as will others through the use of excellent *aśvattha* fuel-sticks. (219)
And with a serene mind, one should offer oblations with sesame seeds for the sake of past karma.
The wise man should accomplish all the ritual applications (prayogas) prescribed in the Durgā-kalpa.

Now I shall describe Kūṭadanta Gaṇeśa, the bestower of secret perfections (kūṭasiddhi). His Yoginī is Jvalajjihvā, who assumes the form of a dancer; she resides near Gṛddhadurgā and grants the desires of the practitioner. || 221 ||
*Tāraḥ* (Oṃ), *namo bhagavati jvālāmālinī*, [and] *saṃvadet*. In the *vṛtta* meter, it consists of twenty-two syllables and ends with *svāhā*. || 222 ||
A wise person should sequentially fashion the five limbs of this mantra, joined with the [five] seed-syllables, using three, four, five, two, and one syllables respectively.
Another [protection] for Vatsa-varmā, who is like Durgā holding a trident, has been proclaimed. || 223 ||
(p. 443) Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the god Śālaṅkaṭaṅkaṭa.
His own fang is a Yoginī, skilled in various forms of musical performance.

And her maidservant is Vidhātrī; her sādhana is now described. One should utter the word "Oṃ Vidhātri," followed by "O you who separate water from milk," and then the word "pada. This mantra, ending with "svāhā," is considered to consist of this number of syllables; it is prescribed that one should recite it one hundred thousand times (lakṣa). || 225 ||
She was seated upon a lotus throne near a dhātrī tree, acting as the creator.
I bow to the large-eyed one, who distinguishes between water and milk. || 226 ||
But where there stands on the riverbank a delightful dhātrī tree bearing fruit, on its ground, on the full-moon day of the month of Kārttika—[this refers back to the preceding]. 227.

Then, on a Monday at night, the practitioner should recite the mantra three hundred times. A fire-oblation (homa) must then be performed with dhātrī fruits from that very tree; indeed, a magnificent and auspicious sound will surely arise, saying, "I am pleased. || 228 ||
By reciting that mantra, the practitioner of mantras shall here distinguish between water and milk.
Having extracted the kila as described above—[the word "by me" being understood as the ellipsis]—one should recite the supreme mantra.
Then, from that water, milk is produced with great care.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the Vināyaka known as Kuṣmāṇḍa.
Her lord is Bālagrahapati, and her Yoginī is Cāruṇānanā;
she is always devoted to playing the flute in Kāśī. || 230 ||
The mantra for her, whose eyes are like those of Vainateya (Garuḍa), is now declared:

"Tāraṃ ca vainateyākṣi sarpasevita" (Oṃ, O you with eyes like Vainateya, served by serpents); followed by "Nāgadevī" in the feminine vocative case, ending with "Svāhā"—this is the eighteen-syllable mantra. (231)

I meditate upon the auspicious Vindhyavāsinī, who is entwined by various lotuses, serpents, and other beings; she has eyes like those of Garuḍa and removes the affliction of poison. Her *puraścaraṇa* consists of sixty-four thousand [recitations]. 232.
On the fifth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, which is proclaimed as belonging to the Nāgas,
a practitioner of great mantras should recite them at night upon the ground of an anthill.
Recalling Vainateyākṣī (the remaining word),
one should perform ten thousand oblations (*homa*) with *mātuluṅga* fruits. Then, being pleased, she bestows the Gāruḍī lore and the power to summon serpents.
[She is] the destroyer of all poisons. || 234 ||

I shall describe the shaven-headed Vināyaka accompanied by the Yoginī Ṛkṣākṣī; she shines in Kāśikā, intent upon playing the lute. His female servant is named Kiṅkarī; I shall now declare her sādhana. 235.
"O servant, O water-goddess, fill, fill the water!"—one should mutter this seventeen-syllable mantra one thousand times. (236)
Indeed, during a time of drought, a man should recite [the mantra] at night while in the water of a river.
And with a concentrated mind, one should meditate upon the Goddess as being joined with the throat-mantra (Kaṇṭhamātṛkā). || 237 ||
She was Kiṅkarī, bearing the noose of Varuṇa, whose form was that of water.
Resembling the appearance of one wounded by poison and terrifying with its fierce roaring,
such rain that comes at dawn lasts for five days.

Now I shall describe Gaṇeśāna, known as Vikaṭadvija. The Yoginī of this [deity] is Kekarākṣī; she plays the mṛdaṅga drum, which is excellent. His Śakti is Vāgvādinī, and his mantra and so forth are now set forth. (239)
The mantra "vadayugmaṃ vāgvādini svāhā" consists of ten syllables; Kaṇva is the seer (ṛṣi), Virāṭ is the meter (chandas), and Sarasvatī is the deity (devatā). || 240 ||

Following the procedure taught by his mother, the practitioner of mantra should perform the six-limbed rite (ṣaḍaṅgaka) upon the head [ke], the two ears, the nose, the two eyes, the cheeks, the mouth, and likewise upon the sense organs. 241.
One should place the syllables in the anus and then worship Vāgīśvarī— the Goddess of Speech— who rests upon a white lotus,
is white in complexion, holds a pen and a book, bows under the weight of her breasts,
and has the moon as her crest-jewel. (242)

Having uttered "Oṃ hrīṃ varṇajāya" and "to the seat of Sarasvatī," this fifteen-syllable mantra is considered the mantra for the seat: "Namaḥ. One should first worship the limbs (aṅgas) and thereafter worship the pair of vowels. || 243 ||
Then, having worshipped that group of eight, these eight Śaktis [should be worshipped] thereafter.
And Yogasandhyā, Vimalā, Jñānavṛddhi, and likewise Smṛti. || 244 ||
Then Medhā and Prajñā are to be worshipped, as well as the Mātṛkās and the lords of the directions.
Then those weapons are to be worshipped in due order within the Bhūpura and other areas. || 245 ||
One should recite the mantra one million times, and at the conclusion, [offer] white water-lilies smeared with honey.
One should perform oblations with those [substances] in their tenth part, and then one should offer pure sesame seeds.

Having performed the libation and the ritual sprinkling, he should then feed the Brāhmaṇas; thus, when the mantra has been mastered, the practitioner of the mantra, remaining firm in the vow of celibacy, [should proceed]. || 247 ||
Devoted to recitation and fire-offerings, he should contemplate the woman with the thought that she is a deity; before long, he will certainly become the foremost among poets. || 248 ||

One should recite this mantra, accompanied by the ritual placement (nyāsa), every day at the beginning of the day; there is no doubt that such a person attains incomparable perfection of speech (vāksiddhi). || 249 ||
With the flowers of the Brahma-tree, the Rāma-tree, and the Sumanā, and with the best of sacrificial fuel-sticks.
The practitioner himself should perform oblations with substances mixed with the three sweets; before long, through the play of speech, he shall become the foremost among poets. || 250 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the prince Gaṇeśvara;
his Yoginī is Bṛhattuṇḍā, who is intent upon playing the cymbals.
This bestows the accomplishment of the Mātṛkās; therefore, its mantra is now being declared.
Within which are contained thirty-three crores of mantras.
Or even if the Gāyatrī Mātṛkā has been mastered, that man shall become [perfected].
There is no doubt that he is the giver of all the mantras of all the Āgamas. || 253 ||
The letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa', as well as the wind, are the deity; they declare the Goddess Mātṛkā, by whom all this is pervaded. (254)

Brahmā is the sage, Gāyatrī the metre, and the goddess Mātṛkā; the consonants are declared to be the seed-syllables (bījas), the vowels are the powers (śaktis), and the kīlaka is [the combination of both]. (255)
The unmanifest is that which cannot be defined as existent; it is the union of consonants with vowels.
Furthermore, all the previously mentioned nyāsas of the Mātṛkās are indeed primary.
Holding a jar of nectar, a rosary, a medicinal pill, and a sacred book.
Her limbs were pervaded by the fifty letters, and her crest was marked with the crescent moon.
She has three eyes, is as radiant as the jasmine and the moon, stands upon a lotus, and her breasts are full and swelling.
I worship Mother Sarasvatī, whose ornaments gleam, being both concealed and revealed by pearls. || 258 ||
One should draw an auspicious eight-petaled lotus on a leaf made of gold or other materials, using yellow pigment, saffron, and so forth, surrounded by three enclosures of squares. || 259 ||
In the pericarp, however, is the seed-syllable *spheṃ*; on the filaments, there are two [syllables] each.
And one should write the consonant groups beginning with ka, ṭa, and ḍa upon the eight petals.
In the cardinal directions at the tip of that lotus is the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, and in the intermediate directions is *ṭhaṃ*.
This is declared to be the seat of worship; first, one should perform the worship of the limbs.
Then one should worship these pairs of vowels and the consonant groups in the filaments. || 262 ||
Medhā, Prajñā, Prabhā, Vidyā, Dhī, Dhṛti, Smṛti, and Buddhi.
The Vidyeshvaris are to be worshipped at the end of the middle [line], and thereafter on the pedestal (pitha).
In the group of eight, however, these are to be worshipped: Vyāpinī, Pālanī, as well as Pāvanī, Kleśinī, Dhāriṇī, and likewise Mālinī. || 264 ||
Haṃsinī, Śāntinī, and the Mothers who are worthy of worship at the tips of the petals are supreme. One should worship the Lokeshvaras in front of the path and the weapons along the path.

One should perform oblations with pure sesame seeds mixed with the three sweets (honey, ghee, and sugar) in a tenth part of that [number]; having performed the libations and other rites, the mantra becomes perfected. || 266 ||

Having properly fashioned a triple-braided cluster (*triveṇī-stabaka*) using threads of different colors— representing the principles (*tattvas*), the kings, the directions, and the shoulders of gold, silver, and copper— one should then recite the mantra and offer oblations of cow’s ghee.

And one should sprinkle that Goddess with clarified butter from the ladles of the Vasus, having offered well-prepared oblations; having worshipped her, this yantra (as understood from the context) should be worn to pacify the afflictions of the planets and for victory in battle.
One should drink this water after first reciting [the mantra] over it twice; within a year, even a fool becomes fully endowed with the gift of poetry. 268.
One should cook ghee with the juice of *brāhmī*, *vacā*, and milk; when recited ten thousand times over and consumed according to this method, it bestows the gift of poetic composition. || 269 ||
One should sprinkle a person with golden jars filled with the decoction of *varṇa* herbs while reciting [the mantra] a thousand times;
thereby fame, fortune, poetic talent, and long life shall arise, and even a barren woman obtains an excellent son. (270)
Now I shall proclaim the preeminent Gaṇeśa, who is beloved by the gods and skilled in all rites;
his Yoginī is Śubhaṃkarī, and his servant is the river on the southern bank where his abode is located. || 271 ||
The syllable *ā* is the form, *ṛṇa* is the mantra, *tāra* is the auspicious-maker, and *parā* is the deity.
O beloved of the fire (*śikhivallabhā*), grant me my desired object; you are the one who bends even the difficult to bend (*durbhugnī*). 272.
They protect the entire collection of arts and discern manifold objects of the senses.
May that Śrī, who deludes even women and kings, be the bringer of auspiciousness in my mind;

having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times, one whose mantra is perfected should perform a fire-oblation with red *pārijāta* flowers. (Note: The absence of the vowel *i* in "japtvā" is a Vedic archaism.)
On the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, when the moon is in the constellation of Aśvinī, and also at the confluence of the Śiprā and the Sindhu rivers.

On the southern bank of the river at night, one should perform ten thousand recitations (japa) and offer oblations (homa) with a tenth part of that amount; then, having gone there at dawn, that best of practitioners conquers from the water those [obstacles] that cause suffering.
That goddess freely bestows whatever one prays for—be it excellent women, wealth, garments, and so forth—acting as the provider of manifold enjoyments. (275)
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe those who reside in Vārāṇasī: Āvṛta, Vakratuṇḍa, and the others, accompanied by their female attendants and Śaktis. || 276 ||
The mantra for them is proclaimed as "ṅenta tannāma hṛcca."
The ritual for Vakratuṇḍa has already been stated previously; it is indeed the same for the eight [forms].
The Yoginī of the constellations is prescribed for those holding skull-bowls in their hands; she is called "Yoginī of the Hundred Nādas," and thereafter one should say, "Give! Give! (278).
This mantra is "hrīṃ hrūṃ svāhā"; now its meditation (dhyāna) is described.
Her hands were shimmering over the strings of the lute, and her earrings swayed to its sound.

One should recite the mantra ten thousand times on the bank of a river in a mango grove, facing a yoginī who is dressed in saffron garments and bowed by the weight of her breasts; one should perform oblations with mango leaves and their roots, and the mantra will become perfected. || 280 ||
On the new moon day in the month of Śrāvaṇa, at night on the distant bank of a river,
one should there recite the mantra of the Goddess eight thousand times during that night.
Shaking it as before one hundred and eight times, he then hears sounds.
Of lutes, flutes, and drums, and of many kinnarīs; || 282 ||
Thus, a hundred sounds, terrifying to the ears, arise;
thereafter, she, in the form of a Yoginī, becomes manifest before the practitioner. || 283 ||
She bestows the *yogamudrā* and reveals the path of the *kuṇḍalinī*.
Thereupon, the practitioner becomes a master of mantra, a yogi, and a possessor of knowledge. He attains perfection of speech and is fit for becoming one with Brahman. (284)
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe Caikadantura, the dispeller of obstacles; his Yoginī is Raktākṣī, who is devoted to singing and playing musical instruments. || 285 ||
The mantra for him is "netraramyā ceṭikā," consisting of four, three, and five syllables, beginning with "om.
One should say "netraramye añjanaṃ ca dehi" twice and then utter "nidhiḥ. (286)

Having uttered the two "darśaya" [mantras] and the word "paṭalam," one should pronounce the word "padam. Then, uttering "dūrīkuru" five times along with "svāhā"—this is declared to be the mantra. (287)
One should perform the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for this [mantra] three times ten thousand times.
Then, one should accomplish the deity by means of an oblation of guggulu resin smeared with clarified butter.
In the month of Vaiśākha, at night in a grove of oleanders (karavīra), indeed.
On the fourteenth day, one should recite the mantra three hundred times while meditating on the Goddess who is beautiful to behold. (289)
It is said that either Tuesday or Friday is the appropriate day.
Then one should perform three hundred oblations with guggulu resin smeared with clarified butter. || 290 ||

He gives to that minister his own collyrium which awakens the eyes; [it reveals] treasures hidden in the earth as well as objects situated in distant lands. That minister beholds them, and immediately becomes a sovereign ruler. || 291 ||

Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the lion-faced and elephant-faced [deities]. Thus, for him who has three faces, the Yoginī is considered to be Śukī; and his Rasajñā is proclaimed as the maidservant Paṅkajākṣī. || 292 ||
"Oṃ, O lotus-eyed one, grant me the fruit of immortality—thus [the mantra] in pairs; likewise, Śrīṃ Svāhā.

This is the Meghavarṇa recitation, consisting of sixty thousand [repetitions]. The fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed with Palāśa flowers, or in their absence, with the best of sacrificial wood (samidh). || 293 ||
Like one reviving intoxication, the lotus-eyed and beautiful woman, adorned with various ornaments, brings about the desired effect with her tremulous eyes. (294)
And the two Vasatarṇas were on the bank of the Gaṅgā, in the forest of Brahmaruha trees.
And on the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Caitra, on a Tuesday or a Friday, at night.
Having recited [the mantra] three thousand times, one should perform a fire-oblation with palāśa wood; then the Goddess arrives and bestows the supreme fruit. || 296 ||
When that fruit has been consumed at that time, freedom from old age and death is attained;
then the true Guru is requested once again. || 297 ||

Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the five-faced Elephant-faced one (Gaṇeśa). Śyenī is said to be his Yoginī, intent upon the melodic recitation (ālāpana) of passion (rāga). His mantra consists of thirty-one syllables, beginning with "payodinī" and followed by the word "ceṭikā. (298)
Having uttered "Tārampayodinī," one should likewise say to the cloud: "Quench the fire, quench the Vāḍava fire; quench both. (299)
One should mutter "Śrīṃ Svāhā Namaḥ" one thousand times at the end; on the bank of a lake, milk should be used, and one should offer oblations of milk-porridge mixed with ghee.
And a beautiful garland of clouds rained down droplets of water.
Clad in dark blue garments, she is like a cloud-filled sky in my mind.

On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, when the moon is in conjunction with the Rohiṇī asterism, on that day, whether it falls on a Tuesday, a Thursday, or a Friday— || 302 ||
Having performed the ritual of bathing at night on the delightful shore of the lake,
One should recite the mantra ten thousand times and perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with milk-rice porridge.
This [is connected to what precedes]; she, however, is the Goddess herself, the one who bestows the milk of nectar.
And having attained satisfaction, she granted a single boon to the minister.
For him, there shall be no burning by fire, and he shall be endowed with the power to create water;
even in a time of drought, water shall arise through meditation upon the Goddess. || 305 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe Heramba, the leader of the Gaṇas. (p.
448) For one desiring success at crossroads and other such places, there is the Yoginī Kapotikā.
The power of Haṃsavāgīśvarī is now described as the beginning of the mantra and so forth. || 306 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ oṃ hrīṃ oṃ; having spoken thus, [one says] "Salutation to Sarasvatī. The seer is Śakti, the deity is the Goddess (Sarasvatī), and Gāyatrī is declared to be the meter. || 307 ||
The goddess Haṃsavāgīśvarī is proclaimed to be the deity.
The wise one should perform the six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) using the third seed-syllable. || 308 ||
At the tip of the Suṣumṇā, in the middle of the eyebrows, and likewise in the ninth aperture.
Having performed the placement of the mantra-syllables, one should meditate upon the chosen deity.
Seated upon a lotus placed on the back of a swan, she resembles lovely camphor.
She has a moon-like face, a gentle smile, and wears the crescent moon as her crest-ornament.
Having meditated thus upon her holding a book, a lute, a rosary, and a jar of nectar in her hands,
one should worship the Mātṛkās previously mentioned upon the pedestal.

One should offer food with the [mantra of] the syllables beginning with the letters (varṇa) and fashion the image with the root mantra (mūla). Having invoked that Goddess into it, one should worship her with perfumes and flowers. || 312 ||

Having worshipped both the Vācas—Sanskrit and Prākṛt—on the two sides, he should then worship the limbs (aṅgas), their powers (śaktis), the Mothers, the Lords of the World (lokeśvaras), and their weapons; thereafter, on the outside, he should worship the Goddess in this manner. || 313 ||

Wisdom (prajñā), intelligence (medhā), sacred learning (śruti), power (śakti), and the fifth is said to be memory (smṛti); Vāgīśī, Sumatī, and Svasti—these eight are considered her powers (śaktis). || 314 ||

With a concentrated mind, one should recite the mantra one hundred and twenty-five thousand times; one should then perform a fire sacrifice (homa) of one thousand oblations with white-smeared *nāgacampaka* flowers. Thereafter, the practitioner, firm in his vows, should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and other rites. || 315 ||
Whoever resorts to this mantra is liberated from sins after a long time.
Endowed with fortune, fame, and beauty, he shall become an abode of poetic talent. || 316 ||
The knower of mantras should perform here the ritual applications previously described. Now I shall declare another mantra of hers, which consists of sixteen syllables. (317)
Having first uttered the syllable *aiṃ*, and then "namo bhagavati," followed by the pair of Vedas (the Gāyatrī), and "vāgdevī svāhā"—this is declared to be the mantra. || 318 ||
And here, the sages and others previously mentioned in the mantra are fully proclaimed.
And by means of the six parts of the mantra, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) together with the seed-syllables (jāti).

She is clothed in garments as white as jasmine and the moon, adorned with white garlands and unguents; she likewise holds a forest garland, the gesture of exposition (vyākhyā), the ritual hand-gesture (mudrā), and a book. || 320 ||
Holding a jar of nectar with her lotus-like hands, she stands upon a white lotus; she has three eyes, the crescent moon upon her forehead, and full, elevated breasts. || 321 ||

The specific application of worship and so forth is here declared as before: one who has conquered the senses and subsists on sacrificial food (haviṣya) should recite the mantra eight hundred thousand times.
And at the conclusion of the recitation according to the prescribed rule, one should offer oblations of sesame seeds with such a mantra.
One should perform everything, beginning with the palāśa wood and so forth, soaked in clarified butter, as previously described. || 323 ||
Whoever should drink water after reciting this every day at the beginning of the day;
Within one year he becomes a learned scholar; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. || 324 ||
At the time of bathing, one should sprinkle water over one's own head with water consecrated by the recitation of mantras.
The wise person should satisfy her with all kinds of water; by reciting this mantra and offering flowers, perfumes, and other such items, a ram will certainly be born in his lineage. (325)
By wearing it upon his head, he becomes worthy of honor in the assembly; there is no doubt that he shall always achieve victory in debate. || 326 ||
Another mantra of this [deity], characterized by the form of Rudra, will now be declared: "Aiṃ! O Lord of Speech, O Immortal One, Pluva! Plu!"—thus it is proclaimed.
The other five limbs of this mantra, consisting of ten syllables, are performed by others as before.

I worship her who is seated upon a lotus, holding a lotus, a pair of rosaries, and a book in her hands; she wears a crown of the crescent moon, has three eyes, is white in complexion, is praised by various sages, and bows slightly under the weight of her breasts. 328.

And one should worship in the Mātṛkā-pīṭha according to the path described for the ten-syllable mantra; one should perform the ritual applications and so forth as before, just like the ten-syllable mantra. || 329 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe Vināyaka, the King of Obstacles. A Yoginī with a noose in her hand ascends his lineage-pole. Sarasvatī is his Śakti;
she consists of three syllables and is accompanied by a triad of maidservants.
"Cārusvāmī" is proclaimed as the mantra for Brāhmaṇas; "Vāktusvāmī" is to be recited by Kṣatriyas who afflict their enemies. || 331 ||
The Vaiśyas have "gvāruṃ svāmī" as their mantra, and those born from his feet have "aiṃruṃ svāmī."
The seer and other details are as stated for the ten-syllable mantra; the Goddess Sarasvatī consists of three syllables.
Having performed the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) together with the seed-syllable (mūla) recited twice, and having performed the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa),
one should then meditate upon the goddess Sarasvatī.
Adorned with a pearl necklace and having the crescent moon as her crest-ornament, she holds the gesture of exposition (vyākhyāmudrā),
a jewel-pitcher, a rosary, and a book.
One should meditate on Sarasvatī, who stands upon a white lotus, bent low by her full and elevated breasts. || 335 ||
One who daily worships the Goddess at the previously mentioned seat of Mātṛkā according to the former method shall certainly become a lord of speech. || 336 ||
One who has conquered the senses and subsists on sacrificial food (haviṣya) should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
Then, one should offer oblations into the fire with clarified butter and sacrificial offerings, using a tenth part [of the total].

Then one should perform the libations (tarpaṇa) and other rites according to the previously mentioned procedure; thus, once the mantra has been mastered, the practitioner of mantras is fit to perform the ritual applications (prayoga). || 338 ||
He who offers oblations with *sumana* flowers grown on four-finger stems will certainly attain, before long, the peerless perfection of speech. || 339 ||
With jasmine flowers and white lotuses sprinkled with water infused with fine sandalwood.
One should offer oblations with flowers produced from the naṃdyāvarta plant combined with kunda blossoms.
Before long, he undoubtedly attains incomparable perfection in speech; thus, by reciting the mantra, the practitioner of mantra shall achieve victory in the assembly. || 341 ||
He who, at the beginning of the day, should consume white vacā as well as brāhmī after they have been consecrated with this mantra,
shall obtain the desired power of intellect.
Pāṇḍavī, Pṛthumadhyā, and Pārthivā are the maidservants. Oṃ Pāṇḍavī, [addressed] to Bagalā; and then, O Bagalāmukhi! (343)
One should say "śatroḥ pādaṃ stambhaya dviḥ klīṃ hrīṃ bhuvaṃcare."
The thirty-syllable mantra is *sphrīṃ svāhā*; now its visualization is described.

I worship the daughter of Pāṇḍu, who is clothed in yellow garments, whose complexion is yellow, who is anointed with yellow perfumes, who sits upon a corpse-seat, who is yellow-hued, and who is most wonderful. || 345 ||

Having recited [the mantra] thirty thousand times, one should perform oblations with safflower blossoms. Having thus completed the preliminary rite (puraścaryā), one should subsequently perform the practice for attainment (sādhana).

At the beginning of the year, on the first lunar day (pratipad) falling on a Friday, one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times at night; then, with safflower blossoms, one should perform an oblation (homa) consisting of one-tenth of that number.
The goddess becomes pleased and bestows a garment; moreover, from the agitation caused by an enemy, a paralysis of movement occurs.
On the sixth day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika, he was staying at the foot of a banyan tree.
Having recited [the mantra] ten thousand times with mango leaves mixed with fragrant aloe-wood incense.
When the oblation is performed with substances mixed with oil, Pṛthumadhyā becomes pleased.
Standing upon that seat, one bestows [grace] through the gaze and may enchant women;
the five elements carry that seat, and by means of it, there is movement through the sky. (350)
The goddess who dwells among madmen, whose limbs are stout, and who is fond of quarreling.
I worship Kārtikeyaguhākhelā, who has a slender waist. || 351 ||
Oṃ pārthive ca pṛthivītalacāriṇi vāyumā | tato lini ca tāruṇyaṃ kuruyugmaṃ ca dhaṃ ca dham || 352 ||

The mantra of the Earth goddess (Pārthivī) is remembered as consisting of twenty-nine syllables, ending with *svāhā*. On the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight at night, by the riverbank during the time of rain— || 353 ||

Having dug into the bank, a cavity should be made seven yugas deep; likewise, ten thousand and five hundred oblations (homa) should be performed with pieces of plantain for half the number of recitations (japa). || 354 ||
I worship the auspicious Goddess Pārthivī, who wanders upon the surface of the earth, who is garlanded by the winds, and who bestows the embrace of youth. || 355 ||
When satisfied, she bestows the power to move within the earth.
And being all-pervading, he shall indeed be free from old age and death. || 356 ||
Vināyaka is the most excellent; his Yoginī has a staff in her hand. She is Rajjurohā by nature, and that servant is considered to be Kaṅkālikā.
One should utter "Aiṃ," followed by Kaṅkālī and Mahākālī, and then the two digits of the Kali age.
This syllable, ending with "svāhā" and containing the [seed] syllable, is considered to require one hundred thousand recitations. || 358 ||
By reciting [the mantra] one thousand times, Kaṅkālī shall become a granter of boons;
she bestows that single desired object upon the practitioner. || 359 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe Gaṇeśa, who is fond of sweetmeats (modaka). His fierce Yoginī is the maidservant Paṅkavāsinī.

Oṃ paṅkavāsinī paṅkajāvatī vanadevate | kedāraṃ dehi siddhiṃ ca | [The mantra consists of] the seed-syllable of desire (klīm) repeated twice, the seed-syllable of Ramā (śrīṃ), and the wife of Fire (svāhā); this is the thirty-one syllable mantra. || 361 ||

In the month of Vaiśākha, at a lotus pond that has very little water and is devoid of rain, one should recite the mantra for seven nights at a count of one hundred thousand per day. An oblation with its leaves and flowers is performed, and the meditation upon the Goddess is prescribed. (362)
O lotus-eyed messenger of Śiva, I remember you at night, with the playful grace of the lotuses that are your face and eyes.
O Goddess Smarā, who dwell daily in the forest of lotuses, do not take up residence in my mind. || 363 ||
The Goddess, always arriving there, grants a single kesara flower, which possesses a fragrance superior even to the flowers of the celestial kalpa-tree. || 364 ||
Having rubbed [this] and applied it as a tilaka, the entire world—kings, women, rulers, scholars, and even the gods—shall become submissive. || 365 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the Vināyakas situated in the eastern direction.
Having surrounded the great cremation ground, [he beheld] those who bestow fearlessness upon the deceased. || 366 ||
First, the human [seed-syllables] of these [deities], such as their own seed-syllables and heart-mantras, should have names ending in the dative case; the Yoginī is Vasuvikramā. (367)
Pārijātasarasvatī performs her movements like one who is mad;
her power (śakti) is said to be her eleven-syllable mantra. || 368 ||

Oṃ hrīṃ; the syllables "haṃsa" followed by "varṇā," accompanied by the letter "e" and joined with the nasal bindu; then again "hrīṃ māṃ sarasvatyai"; this is considered the mantra ending with the word "hṛdaya. || 269 ||
The meditation, ritual placement, and recitation of the Ṛṣis, as well as the system of Haṃsavāgīśvarī—all the previously mentioned applications indeed attain accomplishment. (370)
The practice for her, the maid with the beautiful face, is now described. Having uttered the word "O fair-faced one" (varānane), one should also say "O lovely-eyed one" (vāmalocane). || 371 ||
Having uttered "māriṇī" for the sake of another, followed by two "mālinīs," then "dhūṃ dhūṃ dhīṃ" ending with the wife of fire (svāhā), this mantra consists of thirty-six syllables. || 372 ||
I worship that goddess of beautiful countenance, who is the supreme essence of the mass of the nectar of beauty, who has been increased, and who is steadfast. (373)
On the seventh day of the dark fortnight, one who is pure should worship Kuja at the gate of the street.
The oblation consists of three thousand [offerings] made with conch shells and cowrie shells as well. || 374 ||
Then, assuming the form of a woman with a beautiful face, she should give a single cowrie shell;
one should place that cowrie in a small granary containing grains such as sesame seeds.
That grain, having been sold, does not suffer any loss for a period of three days; thereafter, other grain should be deposited, and interest accrues upon that as well. (376)
Siṃhatuṇḍa is the leader of the Gaṇas, and Veṇuprācā is his Yoginī.
She who envelops the earth is considered to be Saptakoṭeśvarī. || 377 ||
Śakti is the maidservant, and Vidhuśreṣṭhā is the means of accomplishment (sādhana) that follows; having uttered "Kaḥ saḥ," one says "Caṇḍikā," and "Saḥ kaḥ" is the seven-syllabled mantra. || 378 ||
The seer is Brahmā, the meter is declared to be Gāyatrī, and the deity is the Goddess Saptakoṭeśvarī, who is considered the bestower of mastery over speech. (379)

The six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) is proclaimed as follows: with the letter *ca* joined with the six long vowels—[cāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ, cīṃ śirase svāhā, cūṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ, caiṃ kavacāya huṃ, cauṃ netratrayāya vauṣaṭ, caḥ astrāya phaṭ]. Of this [goddess]:
All [rites] such as worship and so forth are proclaimed to be performed in the same manner as for Tripurā. || 380 ||
I shall now declare the mantra for Vidhuśreṣṭhā: Oṃ Vidhuśreṣṭhe, O you who have gone beyond misfortune, fulfill my honor; grant me, grant me earrings for the ears, Thaṃ Śrīṃ Svāhā!
O you who have gone beyond misfortune, fulfill my honor; grant me earrings at the ends of the ears.
The mantra of twenty-seven syllables is "thaṃ lakṣmīḥ svāhā.
When there is a lunar eclipse on a Monday coinciding with the Citrā nakṣatra, one should recite this mantra while in water for as long as the moon remains eclipsed. || 382 ||
Then the Goddess should place the earring upon her left ear.
And it makes that tranquility full, shining with the luster of the full moon. || 383 ||
The practitioner becomes honored by the world, and his meditation is now described.
Residing within the lunar disc, O best of moons, she was situated in the sky.
I meditate upon the beloved of Śiva, who wears a beautiful earring from Kāśmīra.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe Kupitākṣaṅgajānanā; she is the Yoginī who destroys evil, yet assumes the form of a son and a wife. || 385 ||
The power of Kupitākṣa is Bālā Vāmalocanā;
she is declared to be his servant, and her sādhana is now described. || 386 ||
The three-syllable mantra known as Bālā is said to be "aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ.

Regarding this Śrī Bālā mantra: Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the seer (ṛṣi), Paṅkti is the meter (chandaḥ), Bālā is the deity (devatā), aiṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), sauḥ is the power (śakti), and klīṃ is the bolt (kīlaka).
The application (viniyoga) is for the propitiation of the deity Bāla and for the accomplishment of desired ends. Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the deity and Paṅkti is its meter. || 387 ||

The seed-syllable of the Child (Bālā) consists of the Vāgbhava; the third is said to be Śakti. The Kīlaka is the Kāmarāja. By repeating these twice—[Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ]—one should perform the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with these six seed-syllables, as follows: *Aiṃ* to the heart...

*Namaḥ* *klīṃ* to the head, *svāhā*; *sauḥ* to the crest-lock, *vaṣaṭ*; *aiṃ* to the armor, *huṃ*; *klīṃ* to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*; *sauḥ* to the weapon, *phaṭ*. Thus is the six-limbed rite (*ṣaḍaṅgaka*). As for the three-syllable placements (*tryarṇanyāsa*) of Tripurabhairavī, they have been previously taught. With this seed-syllable (*bīja*), [perform them] for you.
All these should be performed for the attainment of their fruit. || 389 ||
Holding in her hands the gesture of fearlessness, a book, a garland, and the boon-granting mudrā.

[O Goddess whose husband is the Lord of the twice-born (Brahmā): She is reddish-brown in color, seated upon a red lotus, and clad in red garments. (390) [The analysis of the compound *dvijeśakām* is: "she whose husband (*kā*) is the Lord of the twice-born (*dvijeśa*").]

One should perform the extraction of the yantra and likewise worship everything in the ritual of worship; this is to be known as pertaining to Tripurabhairavī, and it is equal to that of the three-syllabled [mantra]. || 391 ||

The recitation [of mantras] is three hundred thousand times; for the fire-oblation, the materials and so forth are exactly the same. The worship of the maiden is prescribed as a daily rite for the sake of attaining desired results. (392)

One should offer oblations of *mālatī*, jasmine, and *mallikā* flowers mixed with honey, along with ghee and powdered parched grain; thus the state of Vāgīśvara (Lord of Speech) arises—even for one who is mute, dull-witted, or like a stone, there is no other way. (393)
With japā flowers combined with clarified butter and red milk, according to the prescribed ritual.
By means of the oblation, the mantra-practitioner shall delude the inhabitants of the three worlds. || 394 ||
Through oblation with musk, saffron, and camphor, one becomes like the God of Love; through oblation with *campaka* and *pāṭala* flowers, one shall attain great prosperity. (395)
And by means of the burnt offering (homa) of guggulu, agallochum, camphor, and sandalwood.
She brings under her control the wives of kings, lordly serpents, and gods. || 396 ||
One shall obtain a kingdom through the oblation of lac, and [prosperity] through the oblation of cooked food and honey.
There shall be the cessation of calamities—[the pacification of the great pestilence]—and wealth from an offering of white lotuses.
Through milk one gains longevity and wealth; through curd, intelligence and health; and through ghee, indeed, [the same].
From the fuel-sticks milk is produced, and with honey comes the destruction of death. || 398 ||
By means of an oblation of curd and honey, one shall obtain good fortune and wealth.
Fortune arises from the offering of white water-lilies, joined with honey, sugar, and molasses.
Goat meat (the flesh of a goat); however, this is forbidden for Brahmins and others, and even a Śūdra who possesses a pure mind is not entitled to consume it.
Why? Because non-violence is the supreme dharma, and non-violence is the supreme austerity.
By speaking thus, one should destroy the entire enemy kingdom and bring it under one's control.
The paralysis of enemies results from white oblations of lac, milk, water, and curd.
That oblation destroys premature death as well as diseases. || 400 ||
An oblation with red lotuses bestows complete prosperity when performed correctly.
The world is brought under control by red lotuses; prosperity and good fortune are attained through white lotuses. (401)

One should offer pomegranate, citron [a variety of *bījapūraka*], and whole orange in sequence; likewise, one should offer pumpkin—O Brahmins, there is no doubt that [the target] will be brought under control. || 402 ||
By offering one hundred thousand dates (*kharjūrī-phala*) into the fire, all kings become submissive;
likewise, by offering grapes, lac, *siddha-yaṣṭī*, and plantain fruits. (403)
Twenty thousand kings shall be under the control of that lord of the earth. If a hundred thousand oblations are offered with coconut, he shall become like a king of fire.
By performing one hundred thousand oblations of ripe mangoes, the entire earth is brought under control;
by performing one hundred thousand oblations of jackfruit, a hundred kings are brought under subjection. (405)
By means of an oblation of guggulu resin, one shall destroy all miseries;
by means of sesame seeds and clarified butter, all [beings] are brought under control, and by means of sandalwood, enemies are subdued.
By means of a homa with red sandalwood, men and women become submissive; by means of a homa with dates (kharjūra), the power to control the speech of men arises. || 407 ||
From the homa sacrifice with musk, kings, ministers, and attendants [are attained].
Through the oblation of blue rice grains, peace is established within the temple.
One shall accomplish all undertakings by means of an oblation of sugar and ghee; by an oblation of ghee and milk-rice, the attainment of grain is certain. 409.
Through the oblation of each respective food, the corresponding accomplishment arises. (p. 454) And with *vaṭaka* cakes together with their accessories, one should destroy the *upasargas*. || 410 ||
By performing oblations with *bandhūka* flowers, one brings all sentient beings under one's control.
With hibiscus flowers, the world is brought under control; with bāṇa flowers, there is enchantment.
One should offer oblations with *bahula* flowers; great good fortune will arise.
And from the offering of ten-fold incense oblations, incomparable good fortune shall arise.
By means of jambū fruits, women are brought under control; by means of pumpkin gourds, the daughters of the Daityas.
Through bilva fruits, incomparable prosperity is attained; through stalks of sugarcane, happiness shall arise. || 413 ||
The princess Rasādi, or Nālikera-phala, as well as all the Śaktis who grant boons, are pleased by an oblation of clarified butter alone. || 414 ||
Prior to union with a beautiful woman, one should mutter [the mantra] one hundred times while gazing at her left eye;
likewise on the full moon day, at the conjunction of the Viśākhā constellation and the Sun.
The Goddess becomes instantly pleased and grants him the power to paralyze virility;
even upon union with a hundred women, that man does not fail. || 416 ||

I immediately enjoyed the company of that beautiful-eyed woman, the goddess of delight, who is fond of pleasure, whose fame is desire, who is enchanting, and who instantly grants my every wish. || 417 ||
O fair-eyed one, having uttered "īṃ līṃ bhīṃ raṃ," and then saying "vam," say "paralyze the semen" twice; then it is said, "do not act within the resonance. || 418 ||

This mantra, consisting of twenty-five syllables and ending with "svāhā," has been proclaimed; through one hundred thousand recitations, either Madanāndha or a beautiful-eyed woman shall be accomplished. || 419 ||

The Lord of Obstacles previously mentioned, who is named Kṣipraprasādana, has as his power (śakti) the Yoginī Kālī, also known as Vāgīśabhairavī; and the Yoginī Citrākṣī dwells in his city as his handmaid.

The mantra is: *sthaiṃ [sthaiṃ hrīṃ nityaklinne madadrave śrīm]*. Having uttered *hrīṃ*, one should speak the word *nityaklinne*; and *madadrave* along with *saharā* (the letter *ha*) is conjoined with the vowel *au*. || 421 ||
The mantra consists of eleven syllables, and the ritual placement (nyāsa), meditation (dhyāna), and so forth are likewise performed.
This is the specific distinction regarding worship: it is equal to Caitanyabhairavī.
And in the front corner [is] Caitanya-nityaklinnā, flowing with intoxication; thereafter follows the six-limbed enclosure (ṣaḍaṅgāvaraṇa), and everything else as previously described.

The ritual application and other procedures for Caitanyabhairavī are proclaimed to be identical. I shall now describe the means of accomplishment for Citrākṣī—[O Citrākṣī, you who possess variegated forms, residing among Rudras and spirits; Śrīṃ Śrīṃ Svāhā!]. This should be performed in solitude on a riverbank. || 424 ||
Having fashioned a hexagonal mandala, one should place jars filled with water.
There, in the six corners, one should worship the gods beginning with Śakra:
Indra, Brahmā, Yama, Kāla, Viṣṇu, and Īśa, in due order. || 425 ||

This which has been proclaimed as the "Inexhaustible" (Akṣayya) covering of the undertaking—having performed that, one should sit and recite the mantra at midday. One should daily perform three hundred oblations with the fruits of the trilatā plant. || 426 ||

One should perform this every day; however, when the third lunar day (tṛtīyā) is conjoined with the asterism of Tvaṣṭṛ (Citrā), or when it is joined with either the Moon or the Sun, then [it is especially auspicious]. || 427 ||

From the time of dawn, the recitation (japa) should be performed; then the Goddess will speak clearly from the jar: "In whichever jars whatever substance is to be placed, that shall indeed become inexhaustible. Now her meditation (dhyāna) is described. 428.
I worship that Supreme Goddess, Citrākṣī, who wears diverse attire, who stands upon the head of a corpse belonging to Rudra and others, and who is garlanded with water-pots and sprouts. 429.

One should address the Rudras and other spirits with the mantra "O you of variegated eyes, O you of variegated form! followed by the pair "be gracious" (sthe prasīda), then "Śrīṃ Svāhā"; this consists of three and two syllables respectively. (430)
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe Cintāmaṇi Vināyaka; the Yoginī who knows his characteristics is named Rudhiravāhinī. || 431 ||
Ṣaṭkūṭabhairavī is the Śakti, and Citrakaṇṭhī is his servant-maid.
And [the letters] ha, sa, ka, la, ra, and kārā, conjoined with the letter ḍa and the vowel e.

The mantra of this [goddess] is proclaimed to be in the form of a *kūṭa* (peak-syllable) joined with the *bindu*. Bestowing prosperity like Bhairavī, all [rites] such as the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) are considered to be the same. || 433 ||
She bestows everything that is desired and destroys the burden of enemies; in ancient times, Senāvināyaka was established here in Kāśī by her.
Now, therefore, I shall explain in brief the means for attaining the Citrakanyā.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, during the spring season, one should perform the recitation at night.
An oblation of three thousand offerings made with Madhūka flowers should be performed; then that Goddess will grant thirty thousand [boons] to the practitioner.
Her voice was like that of the cuckoo, exceedingly enchanting even to the worlds;
it was a source of fascination even for birds, beasts, and serpents. || 437 ||
Adorned with a mango-sprout as an ear-ornament, resounding with the music of the lute, clad in white garments, seated upon the lap of Śiva, and wearing a red bodice. (438)
"O you with the variegated throat, grant me a pair of voices with variegated sounds! This mantra, "bhariṃ svīṃ he," is proclaimed to consist of fourteen syllables. (439)
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe Vināyaka, who has an elephant for his hand. || 440 ||
She is Vasādhā, the Yoginī, and the very embodiment of Citrarekhā; she is the power (Śakti) of Pañcabāṇeśvarī, perceivable through her symbols, and the handmaid (Ceṭikā). || 441 ||
"Drāṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Klūṃ Saḥ"—this is considered the mantra of Bāṇeśvarī.
The seer is Kāma, the metre is Gāyatrī, and the goddess is Bāṇeśvarī. || 442 ||
One should perform the six-limbed rite with the single-syllable mantra and with all the syllables of the heart-mantra.
I worship Bāṇeśī, the beautiful one, who wears red garments, who holds a bow of sugarcane and flowers, who is adorned with ornaments, and who possesses the splendor of the sun. || 444 ||
Having fully worshipped Tripureśī, one may delude the entire world; it is taught that one should perform a homa with Bandhūka flowers after reciting the mantra five hundred thousand times.
On the fourth lunar day of the dark fortnight, under the asterism Citrā, on a Monday.
Having meditated thus, one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times at night; then she will become a granter of boons.
All the ritual applications (*prayoga*) for her are proclaimed to be like those of Tripurā. (446)
There, at night in the house, he certainly bestows divine food as much as desired, and likewise divine enjoyments, O King of Mantras. || 447 ||

The mantra is "Śrīṃ Svāhā," consisting of as many syllables as there are lunar days (tithis); one should meditate upon this, born from the lotus-stalk at the throat, upon a divine lotus marked with signs. 448.
Holding a jar of nectar in his hand, adorned and captivating;
now, therefore, I shall fully describe Piciṇḍila Vināyaka. || 449 ||
The Yoginī Garbhahastā bestows success upon the Rākṣasas; Manoharā is his servant who performs his tasks, and Trilocanā is his maidservant. (450)

The mantra named Ramyā consists of twenty-three syllables. At the beginning is [the mantra: oṃ nāri ramye kamalavāsini tvaṃ nārīṃ mohaya-mohaya klīṃ svāhā]; then follows the Tāra (oṃ), then "nārīṃ ramyāṃ kamalavāsinīm. || 451 ||

"O you who delude the couple, *klīṃ svāhā*—this is said to be the meditation (*dhyāna*). [She is] clinging [to him], of auspicious form, yet standing in the forest in a form that deludes; she is sought after by the lotuses and by the gods, beginning with Śambhu, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā. (452)

On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, during the night of Mars, one should recite the mantra three thousand times on the bank of a lake; thereafter, one should perform a fire sacrifice with oranges.
A woman marked [with this] shall become submissive even at the cost of her life or her wealth. Whenever there is a desire for women, one should then recite [this mantra] for a beautiful woman. 454.

Now I shall briefly describe Uddaṇḍamuṇḍa Heramba. A Yoginī with a noose in her hand is his form, and she is the bringer of subjugation. His servant-maid ends with "Nidhi," and his mantra consists of as many syllables as there are lunar days (tithis). || 455 ||

One should say to the speaker: [Oṃ nidhiprānte nidhiṃ dehidehi śrīṃ sphrīṃ svāhā]. This mantra is: *nidhiprānte nidhiṃ dehi* twice, followed by *ramā*, *sphrīṃ*, and *svāhā*. One should meditate upon the Goddess Trimālinī. || 456 ||
She who is pleased by the treasure of elixirs (rasāyana), the bestower of the treasure of worldly prosperity (bhava-lakṣmī).
On the seventh or the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, being composed in mind, || 457 ||
One should recite the mantra seven hundred times in the presence of a Palāśa tree.
One should perform the fire-oblation with the extremely tender roots of the palāśa tree. || 458 ||
Then the Goddess, having reached the end of her treasure-store, became pleased with the minister; she indeed gave him one treasure that is very difficult to obtain even in the three worlds. || 459 ||

The recitation (japa) of these eight maidservants, numbering thirty-two thousand, should be performed in a secluded place beneath a banyan tree or in the presence of Gaṇeśa; then, after having worshipped the Lord of Gaṇas, success (siddhi) is attained. 460.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain those who reside within the enclosure of the city.
[One should worship] the eight Gaṇeśas, beginning with Sthūladanta, together with the Yoginīs.
[He should worship] those [deities] joined with their Śaktis and female attendants (ceṭikās), preceded by the seed-syllables (bīja).
One should recite that seed-syllable followed by the name ending in the suffix -Ṅ, and then the word "Bhagavate."
Thus, this mantra is proclaimed as being within the heart of the eight.
Pañcakāmeśvarī is his Śakti, and her mantra is stated as follows: having uttered "hrīṃ klīṃ aiṃ brūm," the five-syllabled mantra is "śrīṃ. (463)
The seer is Sammohana, the meter is Gāyatrī, and Kāmeśī is considered the deity.
The six limbs are formed by the individual syllables and all of them together: *hrīṃ* to the two thumbs, *klīṃ* to the two index fingers, *aiṃ* to the two middle fingers, *brūṃ*...

*Śrīṃ*, salutation to the two ring fingers (*anāmikābhyāṃ namaḥ*). *Hrīṃ klīṃ aiṃ brūṃ śrīṃ*, salutation to the two little fingers (*kaniṣṭhikābhyāṃ namaḥ*). *Hrīṃ klīṃ aiṃ brūṃ śrīṃ*, salutation to the palms and backs of the hands (*karatalakarapṛṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*). In this same manner, one should also perform the placement of the heart and other limbs (*hṛdayādinyāsa*). || 464 ||
She is red, with limbs smeared with red silk garments and adorned with red ornaments.
A noose, a goad, arrows, a rosary, an axe, and a bow. || 465 ||
And she holds a supreme book in her hands, the one who brings all under control.
Surrounded by the five objects of desire, her worship and so forth shall take place; [this is connected to what follows]. || 466 ||
One should likewise worship Kāma and Umā on the left, equal to Bāṇeśvarī.
In the three locations of the Goddess to the north and south, there are Yoginīs:
Añjanā, Siddhikarī, and Naṣṭaveṣā, who is her maidservant. || 467 ||

*Tāram* [Oṃ naṣṭaveṣe bhrāmiṇi hrīṃ hrīṃ strīṃ strīṃ svāhā]. This is the fourteen-syllable mantra. The six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) is performed with these six seed-syllables repeated twice: *klīṃ aiṃ sauḥ*, *kliṃ aiṃ sauḥ*. As follows:
*klīṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *aiṃ* to the head, *svāhā*; *sauḥ* to the crest-lock, *vaṣaṭ*; *klīṃ* to the armor, *huṃ*; *aiṃ* to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*; *sauḥ* to the weapon, *phaṭ*.
And in the case of a lost appearance, one should utter *bhrāmiṇī* and the two *hrīṃ*s; [then] *strīṃ*.
"Strīṃ Svāhā"—this is the mantra of Viśvavarṇa; now his meditation is described.
And she was most terrifying, instantly chewing upon flesh and blood.
I worship Mahādevī, who is seated upon a corpse and whose appearance has vanished. || 469 ||

One should recite [the mantra] three thousand times during the dead of night on the eighth day of the dark fortnight; and by performing a fire-oblation with an elephant’s tusk, one-tenth of that number, she becomes pleased.
And he gives a moist bone to the mantra-practitioner; by that means, the adept [attains his goal].
One may even subjugate spirits, ghosts, piśācas, and the like while playing with them.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the Elephant-faced One (Gaṇeśa) who is dear to the Kali age.
His Yoginī is Bṛhatkakṣī, and his pill (guṭī) is considered to bestow success (siddhi). His Śakti is Trivarṇeśī; and *klīṃ aiṃ sauḥ* is considered his mantra. || 472 ||

By repeating [the mantra] twice, one should install the six limbs and the five arrows [the names of the five arrows and the five desires have been written previously]. Having installed the five desires, one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) with the root mantra. || 473 ||
She possesses the splendor of a thousand rising suns and is adorned with excellent ornaments of rubies.
She was richly adorned with shimmering jeweled silk garments and decorated with various ornaments.
One should worship her as she holds a sugarcane bow, arrows, a rosary, and a book;
thereafter, one should worship the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga). || 475 ||
Then the five arrows are to be worshipped, followed by the triad beginning with Rati; then the eight Kāmas, the eight Bhairavas, and also the Mothers. || 476 ||

One should worship the eight seats (pīṭhas) and the deities, beginning with Lokeśa, in the center. [Then follows] the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa), and likewise all rites performed for specific desires (kāmyakarman). (477) p. 458)
Her mistress is Tripureśī, and her maidservant is Aninādinī. The mantra is: "O Ninādinī, give, give the pill!
O woman, svāhā! And [the mantra for] the pill is: "Give the woman who dwells in the fire-habitation. 478.
I worship that twelve-syllable mantra, that Khecarī with upward-pointing hair, three eyes, flickering eyes, and a great resonance. (479)
And on the new moon day, a man should especially bathe in a river in the evening.
On the night of the dark fortnight, one should perform ten thousand recitations on its bank.

An oblation of musk and lotuses should be performed there in ten parts; the deity therein utters a great sound that causes terror for one intent on meditation. When the practitioner of the mantra no longer fears, then the Goddess becomes pleased. 481.
He gives a single pill, which bestows perfection and is enchanting; by taking it, one becomes a minister capable of traveling through the three worlds. || 482 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the four-tusked elephant-faced one; his Yoginī is Sarpāsyā, who performs the practice of alchemy.
The single Śakti, Kāmeśvarī, is considered the mantra, the seed-syllable of desire (Klīm). The extraction (kraṣi) is Sammohana, the metre is Gāyatrī, and she is regarded as the deity. || 484 ||
The seed-syllable of Ekakāmeśvarī is *kaḥ*; *śakti* is said to be the bindu (*m*). *Laḥ* is the *kīlaka*.
The six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) are formed from the root mantra conjoined with the six long vowels. || 485 ||
One should also install the five previously mentioned arrows and perform the visualization (dhyāna). || 486 ||
One should meditate upon her who resembles a hibiscus flower, holding a bow and arrows in her hands.
Adorned with various beautiful ornaments, she captivated the three worlds. || 487 ||
One should then draw a triangle, an eight-petaled lotus, and the form of the earth; as well as Mohinī, Kṣobhiṇī, Śaśinī, and likewise Stambhinī.

One should worship Ākarṣiṇī, Drāviṇī, and likewise the one considered to be Āhlādinī, as well as Klinnā and Kledinī; thereafter, one should worship the Lion Throne (Siṃhāsana). Then, having invoked the Goddess, one should worship her and display the mudrās. 489.
The worship of the limbs is performed in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Asura, Vāyu, and the center.
Then, one should worship the limbs (aṅgas) of Tripurā upon the eight petals.

Having uttered the word *anaṅga*, one should join the word *pura* with the names such as *rūpiṇī* mentioned in the verse; for example, *anaṅgarūpiṇī*, *anaṅgamadanā*, and so forth, as well as *madanā*. (490)
Manmathā, Kusumā, and Madanāturā before them; likewise Śirā, Meṣabalā, and Dvipikā—these eight are proclaimed. (491)
Then the lords of the directions are to be worshipped, and one should recite the mantra one thousand times for the Sun.

Then one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) and other rites with the flowers of the *huned* and *bandhūka*. The ritual applications (*kāmyaprayoga*) for Tripureśī are to be understood in the same manner as those previously described. || 492 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain those numbering twenty-one.
