[He saw] those connected with Gaṇeśa, Antrajā, and Mātaṅgī, together with the Yoginīs. || 493 ||
One should utter the six seed-syllables of Gaṇeśa ending in the letter Ṅ, followed by his name.
Bowing down to those sages, I shall now state their names in sequence.
Vināyaka has two tusks and two eyes at the front and the back; likewise, there are Jyeṣṭha Vināyaka and Gajavināyaka. || 495 ||
The Vināyaka known as Kāla, and the Vināyaka named Nāgeśa.
Now, listen to the Vināyakas who stand having entered within the house. (496)
Likewise, there is Sṛṣṭigaṇeśa and Yakṣavighneśa as well.
Gajakarṇa, Citraghaṇṭa, and Maṅgalavināyaka are [names of the deity]. || 497 ||
Vināyaka, Mitra, and the others, or those Gaṇeśas who are stationed in Ānandakānana, shall now be described by me. (498)
Moda, Pramoda, Sumukha, Durmukha, Gaṇanāyaka, Vināyaka, Jñānapūrva, and Dvāravighneśa. || 499 ||
Near Avimukteśa is Avimuktavināyaka; and the Yoginīs, who ride upon corpses, are proclaimed as belonging to these [deities] in sequence. [This belongs to the lineage of Parā. 500.
Dandaśūkakarā, Raudrī, Mṛgaśīrṣā, Vṛṣānanā, Vyālāsyā, Dhūrttaviśvāsā, Vyomaikacaraṇā, and Ardhadṛk. || 501 ||
Tāpinī, Tuṣṭipūrvā, Śoṣiṇī, and likewise Koṭarī; Vidyutprabhā, Sthūlanāsā, Mārjārī, and Kaṇṭhapūraṇā. || 502 ||
Kāmākṣī, Aṭṭāṭṭahāsā, Balākā, Gatipuṇyadā, and Mūkāsyā—these are the Yoginīs; their names end in the letter Ṅ and conclude with the word "namaḥ. (503)
A mantra arises from its own seed-syllable and so forth, effecting its purpose according to its name. Now, therefore, I shall fully explain their Śaktis, which bestow excellent accomplishment. (504)

One should utter the celebrated mantra of Rājamātaṅgī, which produces immediate conviction: "Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ"—these are declared to be the seed-syllables (manavas); one should then say "Bhagavatīpradam" (the bestower of the Goddess). || 505 ||
In the Śrīmātaṅga, one should say "śūri," "sarvajaneti," "manohari," "sarvamukharāji," and "sarvamukha. || 506 ||
Then one should say, "O Queen of all kings, O Vaśaṅkarī! during the night.
Having uttered "sarvastrīpuruṣa," one should then say the word "vaśaṃkari."

Then [one should say] "O subduer of all wicked beasts," followed by the word "sarva"; then "O subduer of beings" (sattvavaśaṃkari), and having uttered "all worlds" (sarvaloka), one should state the specific name [of the person]. || 508 ||
"Bring [him] under my control, svāhā"—this mantra consists of eighty-eight syllables.
With twenty-one [verses] by Viśvadhṛti, Dhṛti, and Viśvakara, [the hymn] of Manu.
Oṃ, salutations with the syllables of the face-mantra, preceded by the seed-syllables Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ.
The six-limbed assignment (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) has been declared; now I shall describe the assignment of the words (padanyāsa).
In the head, forehead, space between the eyebrows, palate, throat, mind, and neck; in the heart, the anāhata center, the arms, the abdomen, and the region of the navel. || 511 ||
Having placed [the syllables] in sequence upon the Svādhiṣṭhāna, the consonants, the right and left feet, the Mūlādhāra, and the anus, one assigns the eighteen words in order. || 512 ||
The mantra-words consist of syllables numbering three, one, two, four, six, seven, eight, ten, eight, four, three, one, two, and three eyes (three). (513)
Having uttered "Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to Rājamātaṅgī," one should then perform the placement (nyāsa).
One should utter the three previous seed-syllables at the mūlādhāra and the word for "pleasure. (514)
Having said "Salutation to Mātaṅgī," one should again place [the mantra] upon the heart; then, one should utter the three seed-syllables followed by "Salutation to Manobhavā. (515)
Afterwards, one should place [the seed-syllables] between the eyebrows and then perform the nyāsa of the goddesses.
One should place [the mantras] in sequence upon the head, face, heart, private parts, and feet. || 516 ||
Hṛllekhā, Gaganā, and Raktā, and then also Kapālikā.
[One should worship] Mahocchuṣmā, preceded by the seed-syllable consisting of the initial letter of her own name. || 517 ||
Having duly assigned Mātaṅgī as the end, one should likewise assign Bāṇa and Śakti.
One should [place] Drāviṇī in sequence upon the head, feet, mouth, secret place, and heart. || 518 ||
Śoṣiṇī, Bandhinī, Mohinī, and likewise Ākarṣiṇī.
Then one should place Mātaṅgī, preceded by her own seed-syllable, and thereafter the eight objects of desire.
One should place the three seed-syllables at the beginning of Mātaṅgī and the god of love (Kāma) at the end of the word.
One should place Makaradhvaja on the left shoulder, Madana on the left side, Puṣpacāpa on the left hip, and Kusumāyudha at the navel; then Kandarpa on the right hip,
and Manobhava on the right side.
And Ratipriyā on the right shoulder; this is called the placement of their Śaktis. One should place Mātaṅgī and the others, beginning with Anaṅga, in these very locations. || 521 ||
Kusumā, Mekhalā, Madanā, and Madanāturā have been declared; then Madanodvegitā, Agra-sambhavā, and Bhuvanapālinī. || 522 ||
Then Śaśirekhā should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of Lakṣmī and the others according to the prescribed method.
He [worships] Ṅemā, Taṃgī, Naumtā, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī,
as well as Rati, Prīti, Kīrti, Śānti, Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi, in due order.

One should thus perform the placement (nyāsa) at the root-support (mūlādhāra), likewise at the base, at the maṇipūra, in the heart, in the throat, in the mouth, between the eyebrows, and in the head. || 524 ||
Those beginning with Brāhmī and ending with the word Mātaṅgī were previously indicated.
In the mūlādhāra, the adhiṣṭhāna, the navel, the heart, the throat, and the mouth; || 525 ||
Likewise, one should [place] the Bhairavas, beginning with Asitāṅga, between the eyebrows and on the crown of the head.
One should subsequently place these [mantras] beginning with Mātaṅgī and ending with Mātaṅgī.
One should place Dvāmā on the base and Jyeṣṭhā at the root of the liṅga;
likewise, one should place Raudrī at the navel, Śānti at the heart, and Siddhidā at the throat.
One should place Vāgīśvarī in the middle of the eyebrows, Kriyāśakti at the bindu, Lakṣmī at the location of Kalā, and likewise Sṛṣṭi in Rodhikā.

Having placed Mohinī upon the half-moon, one should place the first [syllable] upon the Nāda; likewise, Bhāvinī at the end of the Nāda, and then Mānyā, who is like a flash of lightning. One should place Viṣṇu upon the thunderbolt (vajra) and the power of Viṣṇu (viṣṇu-śakti) upon the Dhruva-maṇḍala.
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ—these [syllables] preceded by "pūrvi" and ending with "ṅe mātaṅgyai namaḥ."
The four powers should be installed; one should install Mātaṅgī on the head.
On the forehead, one should [worship] Mahāmātaṅgī, and likewise Mahālakṣmī on the heart.
Likewise, one should place Siddhalakṣmī at the root, in the mūlādhāra. || 531 ||
Having fully recited the root mantra, one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) over all limbs;
thus, with the body thus consecrated, one should meditate upon the deity of the mantra.
In the midst of the ocean of nectar, upon a charming island of jewels, within a pavilion constructed of gems and surrounded by a golden wall. || 533 ||
Adorned with kadamba, bilva, kahlāra, and kalpavṛkṣa trees, upon an auspicious jeweled lion-throne comfortably spread with cushions in the center of the altar. || 533 ||
There should be a great eight-petalled lotus, rich with filaments and possessing a pericarp; in its center there should be a triangle, and outside of that, an eight-padded area.
Furthermore, there should be a sixteen-petaled [lotus], and outside of that, a four-petaled one;
this mandala, possessing four corners and four gates, is declared to be the most excellent. (536)
In its center sat one of dark complexion with a pure smile, seated upon his face.
Adorned with garlands of Kadamba flowers, she is worshipped by both gods and demons.
She is adorned with long, hanging locks of hair, with a crescent moon as her ear-ornament;
her forehead is marked with a tilaka, and her face bears a slight smile.
Her forehead-slab was radiant, made sweet by a few drops of perspiration.
She possessed the luster of the space between the waves of her folds and was adorned by a line of body hair.
Adorned with all kinds of ornaments and decorated with pearl necklaces.
Adorned with waist-bands bound with various clusters of jewels. || 540 ||
Adorned with armlets set with jewels and encrusted with gems, the young girl had two arms and her eyes were rolling with intoxication. || 541 ||
Her breasts were elevated with the full expansion of a rounded orb; she was adorned with long pendants for her ears and shone with a golden crest-ornament. || 542 ||
The young Mataṅginī, dark as the tamāla tree and intoxicated with honey.
She embodies the sixty-four arts, with parrots and mainas perched at her side.
One should meditate upon the supreme Mātaṅginī as resembling ten million rising suns, or like a hibiscus flower, or likewise as being yellow in color. || 544 ||
In the previously described seats (pīṭha) beginning with Dharma, nine Śaktis are to be worshipped.
Preceded by the seed-syllables Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, they end with "ṅe mātaṅgine" and "namaḥ. || 545 ||
Prosperity, exaltation, splendor, fame, creation, and consensus.
Nourishment, excellence, and supernatural power—these are the nine powers of Mātaṅgī. || 546 ||

[Vāṅmāyā: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ sarvaśaktikamalāsanāya namaḥ*—this is the mantra. Having uttered the word *kamalām* at the end of *sarvaśakti*, followed by the words *sanāya namaḥ*, one should worship the seat (*pīṭha*) of Mātaṅgī. || 547 ||
Having fashioned the form of the Goddess from the root mantra according to the prescribed rite,
Immediately after that, one should worship the goddess Āvāhadevī.

One should display the noose, the goad, the boon-granting gesture, the fear-dispelling gesture, the sword, the shield, the bow, and the arrow; as well as the *mausalī*, the one called *durgabāṇā*, and the *yonimudrā* [the characteristics of the *yonimudrā* have been written by me in many places]. || 549 ||

In the triangle, one should worship Rati and the others in the eastern corner and the other corners. The first [deity] is white in complexion, holding a noose and a goad, and has her hands joined in the añjali gesture. || 550 ||
She whose hands shine with the final dawn, the sugarcane bow, and the five arrows—
[the meaning is that one should worship her whose hands shine with the sugarcane bow and so forth].
One should worship in the space between the triangle and the eight-petaled lotus. || 551 ||

In the center and in the directions, one should worship, in order, the five Śaktis beginning with Hṛllekhā (the remaining words are to be supplied). Carrying a goad, a noose, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and resembling living beings, one should worship the limbs in the corners of Agni, Īśa, Rakṣas, and Pavana, as well as in the directions of Agni.
Then the knower of mantras should worship the five arrows. || 553 ||
In the directions, from the front onwards, [he placed] pearls, gold, coral, and diamonds in sequence.
Likewise, [he saw] those endowed with a pure, reddish luster, bearing bows and arrows as their weapons.
On the petals at the front, Anaṅgakusumā and the others are to be worshipped.
Possessing a ruddy luster, they bear the qualities, the plow, fearlessness, and what is desired. || 555 ||
At the tips of the petals, Lakṣmī and the others, adorned with beautiful ornaments, are to be worshipped:
Lakṣmī, the bestower of gold, the source of lotuses, clad in saffron-colored garments. || 556 ||

Sarasvatī resembles a conch shell; she holds the gesture of consciousness (cinmudrā) and delights in books. She is white in luster, holds flowers, arrows, and sugarcane in her hands, and possesses pure eyes. || 557 ||
Prīti holds a bow and arrows in her hands, has a dark-blue luster, and wears white garments;
Kīrti is shaped like a water-pot (kuṇḍa) and is adorned with hands bearing the lotus and the *cinmudrā* gestures. || 558 ||

Cinmudrā is endowed with the gesture of fearlessness and possesses tranquility; her eyes are motionless in meditation. Bālābhayaṃkarā (or Varābhayā according to another reading) is Puṣṭi, whose limbs are yellow and who is adorned with beautiful ornaments. || 459 ||

Tuṣṭi, who grants boons and fearlessness and whose lotus-like face is serene, is to be worshipped on the second eight-petaled [lotus]; likewise Manmatha and the others, who are exultant with passion. || 560 ||
With their bows drawn forward and their quivers at their backs.
The Mothers are situated upon the vessels, and in front of them are the eight Bhairavas.

Their hands are occupied with a skull, a trident, and a *ḍamaru* drum, and they are accompanied by *vetālas*; these include the goddesses beginning with Brāhmī and those beginning with long vowels, as well as the Bhairavas beginning with short vowels. || 562 ||
Then, those beginning with Vāmā, possessing dark-complexioned forms, are situated upon the sixteen petals.
And then, after that, the mirror, the jewel, the lamp, and the fan. || 563 ||
As well as betel leaves, a fly-whisk, and a treasury of knowledge.
With garments, garlands, parasols, ornaments, fine silks, and dwellings. || 564 ||
Holding in their left hands a chowrie, a jeweled pitcher, a palm-leaf fan, and a lamp, these lords of gods carry swords in their right hands.
One should visualize and worship these [deities] as being red in color and perfectly pure; then, one should worship them upon the four petals as they are constantly playing the lute (vīṇā). || 566 ||
Mātaṅgī and the others are to be worshipped there with the gestures of the noose, goad, boon, and fearlessness;
their arms are adorned, they are red in color, and the second [of these] resembles the moon. (567)
Likewise, another [goddess] holds in her hands a sword, a shield, a trident, and a skull.
She holds a noose, a goad, and lotuses, and displays the yoni-mudrā.
The final [deity], Aruṇā, dark-complexioned and holding a golden jewel-leaf as well as the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness, should be meditated upon by the best of practitioners. || 569 ||
One should perform the sacrifice in the corners of Agni, Nairṛti, Vāyu, and Rudra.
One should worship Gaṇeśa, Durgā, Vaṭuka, and Kṣetrapāla outside.
In the square [of the mandala], one should place the world-protectors (lokapālas) and their weapons outside of that.
The practitioner of mantra should then recite the mantra ten thousand times, followed by one-tenth of that amount for each of the two subsequent words. (571)

One who desires to bring others under control should offer oblations with *bandhūka* flowers prepared with the three sweets (*trisvādu*). Having performed the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*), one should likewise honor the Brahmins.
Thus, the practitioner who has mastered the mantra shall accomplish his own desire. One seeking good fortune should perform oblations with jasmine, mallikā, and nāgakeśara flowers. (573)
By performing oblations with bilva fruits and their leaves, one shall attain the glory of sovereignty;
a prince, by means of lotuses, attains his own unsurpassed prosperity.
With *lakṣmī* flowers and blue lotuses, one may bring the entire world under one's control.
With hibiscus, bandhūka, and bakula flowers produced from the vajra-tree; || 475 ||
The knower of mantras should indeed offer oblations with *sumanaḥ* flowers for the sake of subjugation; by offering honey, all success comes to him in abundance. (576)
With the finest fuel-sticks made from vetasa wood, properly prepared and endowed with the three sweets.
One who desires rain should offer oblations; with *guḍūcī* plants, one may remove fever.

By offering oblations of Kadamba flowers, one shall bring women under one's control. One desiring long life should offer oblations of Dūrvā grass; of this there is no doubt. By offering oblations of food, the practitioner of mantras will soon become possessed of abundant food.
By an oblation of rice grains, one shall become a householder filled with wealth. As for the substance prescribed for the oblation, it should consist of the "three sweets" (trisvādu). || 579 ||
An oblation performed with Nandyāvarta flowers bestows supreme accomplishment of speech.
And by offering oblations of nimba blossoms, one shall obtain the desired Kamalā.
He who performs oblations with *huna* and *kiṃśuka* flowers shall become a treasury of splendors.
Also with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, gorocana, and saffron. || 581 ||
Through this oblation, one shall bring the entire universe under control; of this there is no doubt.
By reciting these eight times, one may apply a tilaka that fascinates all people.

One should offer oblations of the roots of *sindhuvāra* for release from bondage. One should sacrifice with salt drenched in the oil of *ugragandha*; he shall destroy the host of enemies before long—of this there is no doubt. (583)
One should paralyze the enemy with salts mixed with powdered black salt (niśā).
With fruits that were fully ripened and exceedingly flavorful, and with fragrant flowers.
Through the fire sacrifice, one obtains what is desired; there is no need for deliberation on this point. || 584 ||
(p. 464) Now I shall declare another mantra of Mātaṅgī, which bestows supreme accomplishment.
Having uttered "Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ Aiṃ," one should then utter "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ" and the Tāra (Om).
One should utter the twenty-four syllables beginning with "Namo bhagavati," followed by the serpent-mantra, and then say "Klīṃ," which is the enchanting [syllable]. || 586 ||

Likewise, having uttered the seed-syllable of Śrī, one should then recite all [the names] beginning with "Rāja" and so forth; thereafter, one should recite the forty syllables of the preceding mantra in their proper sequence.
Having uttered the word "vaśaṃkari," one should then state the name of the person, beginning with "amuka" and so forth, at the end of the mantra.
One should utter eleven syllables: *śrīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ sauḥ*, and then say *klīṃ ava*. Thus, one hundred minus two syllables are proclaimed in this mantra. (588)
This mantra is supreme for bringing the three worlds under one's control.
It is to be attained through the grace of the teacher by people who possess the greatest merit.
It is difficult to attain for those who have not performed meritorious deeds, yet it is served by the lords of sages and others.
It is proclaimed as a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpapādapa) in the granting of desires; indeed, the sages and others previously mentioned become [the components] of this mantra. (590)
Then, for the sake of accomplishing the state of being a deity, one should perform the placement of the *mātṛkās*.
The five arrows upon the fingers and the dolphin-bannered god (Kāmadeva) upon the two palms. || 591 ||
One should place the ten-syllable mantra, preceded by the Vagbhava syllable and ending with the feminine suffix -ṅi.
This [mantra] "makaradhvaja," ending with "klīṃ" and "namaḥ," is thus proclaimed. || 592 ||
Upon the crest-lock, the head, the forehead, the space between the eyebrows, and the pair of eyes;
In the ears, the two nostrils, the mouth, the cheeks, and the crown of the head, respectively. || 593 ||
Having placed [the hands] upon their two breasts, upon the lotus of the heart, upon the navel-circle, the secret place, the mūlādhāra, and also upon the feet. || 594 ||
They number twenty-three, distributed as three, three, one, and four.
By means of six, eight, one, moon (one), eight, nine, eighteen, and feathers (five). || 595 ||
One should place [the syllables] in sequence as eight, six, three, one, two, three, and two.
The mantra-syllables, numbering nineteen, are [to be placed] from the beginning in successive order. || 596 ||
One should perform the six limbs with six words preceded by Aiṃ, Hrīṃ, and Śrīṃ.
The seed-syllables of Kāma, Śakti, and Indirā are said to constitute the crest (śikhā) of the mantra.
One should arrange the six limbs by means of the six long vowels;
furthermore, the five [mantras] beginning with Drāviṇī should be placed in the belly, on the two sides, and in the heart. || 598 ||
One should place [the seed-syllables] here in Maṇipūra, and one should install Brāhmī and the others here as well.
At the base of the toes of the right foot, at the ankle joint, and at the knee; || 599 ||
One should then install Lakṣmī and the others at the base of the right thigh, the base of the left thigh, the knees, the ankles, and the base of the toes of the left foot. || 600 ||
At the base of the left arm, in the middle joint, and at the wrist.
At the base of the fingers of the left hand, against the surface of the fingers of the right hand.
At the wrist, at the middle joint, at the roots of the armpits, and successively on the head, between the eyebrows, in the eyes, in the ears, and in the anus. (602)
In the pair of nostrils, in the mouth, in the pair of cheeks, and in the region of the tip of the tongue.
One should place the [powers] beginning with Vāmā in the mūlādhāra, the adhiṣṭhāna, and the palate.
In the locations of Lakṣmī and the others, one should assign the Bhairavas, beginning with Asitāṅga.
And the tetrad beginning with Mātaṅgī [should be placed] in the heart, the navel, the head, and the anus.

Then one should install Gaṇeśa, Durgā, Baṭuka, and Kṣetrapāla; with the mantra, one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) upon the head, the two eyebrows, the throat, the root [the navel], and the feet. 605.
One should duly install Sarasvatī, Mahālakṣmī, and the pair of treasures (the Śaṅkha and Padma) in the mouth, between the eyebrows, on the right foot, and likewise on the left. || 606 ||

Having thus performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the mantra, the practitioner, with one-pointed mind, should meditate upon the Goddess in a great forest on a jewel-island within an ocean of nectar. || 607 ||
In a pavilion made of five wish-fulfilling trees, adorned with jewels.
One should contemplate her seated upon a lion-throne made of jewels. || 608 ||
She was delighted by the drinking of honey-wine, her face full as she gazed upon him.
Her face was like the moon, and her braid of hair was entwined with *nīpa* flowers.
Her hands were graceful with a lute, she wore red garments, and her beautiful lips were like the bimba fruit.
She who has a musk tilaka, a moon for a crown, and elevated breasts. || 610 ||
Her ears were shaped like conch petals, her waist was slender, and she possessed the luster of a dark blue lotus.
Adorned with bracelets, armlets, necklaces, and so forth, as well as anklets and a girdle.
She was pleasing her devotees with her laughter, while the silken garment on her side remained hanging down.
And upon the auspicious pedestal mentioned previously, one should fashion this yantra.
A triangle, a pentagon, or an eight-petaled lotus with sixteen petals; an eight-petaled lotus, a four-cornered square base, or a beautiful quadrangle. 613.
Equipped with four doors and enchanting to all who behold it, the practitioner of mantra, adorned in elegant attire, should invoke and worship the Goddess therein. (614)
Having conceived the form with the root mantra and performed the placement of the arghya vessel and other rites,
Having worshipped the Mātāṅgī-pīṭha and performed the fundamental ritual arrangement (mūlaprakalpana), [one should proceed]. || 615 ||

Then, at the conclusion of the worship with flowers, one should properly worship the limbs of dissolution (layāṅga). Within the triangles, as before, one should worship the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga). || 616 ||
Mātaṅgī and the others are in the four-petalled [lotus], the square, and from the triangle.
And one should worship the group of four beginning with Gaṇeśa at the four gates.

One should first recite the mantras of the presiding deities of the directions, such as Sarasvatī and the others, along with their weapons, as proclaimed by the Kanyās; and outside of that, one should mutter the mantra preceded by the ritual placement (nyāsa). || 618 ||
Furthermore, one should worship the six limbs with well-prepared foods and various kinds of eatables.
Then, having offered [the oblation] with milk and having bowed to the Goddess, one should thereafter present the bali.

The knower of mantras should offer [the oblation] with devotion; by that, one obtains the desired goal after no long time. Having uttered "Salutation to the Blessed One," followed by "O Mistress of Mātaṅga" (mātaṅgeśvari), [he should proceed]. (620)

"Accept this offering, O Pair! Svāhā!"—this is the mantra consisting of perfected syllables. Then, to the north of the Goddess, in the corner beginning with the northwest (vāyavya), [he should offer]. 521.
In the order of the line, one should utter: "Aiṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ, salutation to the Gurus. [Then] to the Parameṣṭhi-gurus and to the Paramācārya-gurus. (622) p. 466)
One should utter "Salutation to the primordial perfected gurus, the true gurus. Thus, one should worship the gurus in all five locations. || 623 ||
One should first recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for the sake of accomplishing the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa).
At the end, one should offer ten thousand oblations of *palāśa* flowers combined with the three sweets.
One should perform the libation and the ritual sprinkling, and also feed the Brahmins.
One should also feed young maidens; thus one shall bring them under control, cause agitation, and be victorious.
Having become a benefactor to the Mātaṅgas, one should accomplish all rites;
whether in a fire-pit or on a sacrificial mound, the rite for desired results should be performed. || 626 ||
His limbs were enveloped in red garments, and he was adorned with red garlands and unguents.
By offering oblations of guggulu resin smeared with clarified butter, the wise man shall bring even a king under his control.
One who offers oblations with Mallikā, Jāti, and Punnāga flowers shall become fortunate; one seeking a kingdom should offer Bilva leaves, and especially lotuses. || 628 ||
Furthermore, one who desires prosperity should offer oblations with white or red lotuses.
One desiring wealth, however, should perform the fire-oblation with blue lotuses (*utpala*) and *lakṣmī* flowers; [in certain regions, this is known by the local name *chītūra*]. || 629 ||
One seeking wealth and grain should offer oblations with *bandhuka* (or *bandhujīvaka*) and *kiṃśuka* flowers, as well as *bakula* (or *kesara*).

For the purpose of attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), one should offer salt and sesame seeds mixed with sweet substances. By offering *vañjula* flowers, one obtains rain; by offering *guḍūcī*, one removes fever. One who seeks food... [630] ...should offer oblations with *annārthī*.
One who desires grain should offer oblations with food, specifically with rice grains.
An oblation with fragrant substances, moreover, bestows all prosperity.
For one desiring subjugation, a fire offering with saffron and yellow pigment (rocanā) from Kashmir is prescribed.
Then, one seeking speech and meaning should offer oblations with *nandyāvarta* flowers.
One who desires splendor should offer oblations with *palāśa* flowers or with the clarified butter of a tawny cow.
A fire sacrifice performed even with flowers from madmen causes insanity in an enemy.

With *viṣameghāhva*, nimba, akṣa, śleṣmāntaka, and vibhītaka; with water-bearing trees, *picumanda*, pomegranates, and *bibhītaka*; and with the feathers of owls, crows, and vultures, all saturated with oil. || 634 ||
And in a triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) during the night for the destruction of enemies.
With milk-rice mixed with jaggery, as well as with sugar-candies and pieces of sugarcane; || 635 ||
A fire sacrifice (homa) with milk-rice (pāyasa) soaked in ghee destroys insanity;
black pepper treated with sesame oil removes cough, asthma, and fever.
By means of an oblation of the root of nirguṇḍī, there is liberation from fetters.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme method for attracting the life-force (jīva).

The one most skilled in mantras should fashion four effigies of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*). One should be made from the wood of the tree corresponding to the natal asterism of the *sādhya*;
the second image should be fashioned from the fuel-wood (*samidh*) of that same tree, using honey. (638)
And another [image] made from clay like that of a potter, and another from rice flour.
One should write upon their heart: "O [Name], bring such-and-such a person under my control."
One should place the name of the person to be accomplished in the appropriate location, and there, the vital breaths as well.
Having established them there and touched them, he should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times.
One should recite at the root and in the mouth, and one should join the name of the person to be accomplished [therein]. || 641 ||
If a certain word-form is seen among the mantras of the yantra, one should place that form— the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya)— in that location.
One should bury a wooden effigy two finger-breadths below the center of the pit.
Then one should dig up that which is turned face upwards, or that which has arisen from being ground, or likewise that which is beneath one's own seat.
At the spot where the footprint was placed, one should fill it with clay on the ground; thereafter, these three [footprints] should be filled with salt as well. || 644 ||
Then [he should fashion] an image made of beeswax with its feet upward and its face downward.
One should suspend her with her feet bound by a cord made of *arka*-cotton (*ādityaphala-kārpāsa*). Furthermore, by means of smoke over the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), she shall become distressed.

Then, one *kuḍava* of salt—[one *kuḍava* being four *palas* on a scale]—along with ghee, honey, and jaggery, should be ground; with that, one should fashion a hundred thousand small figurines (*puttalī*). || 647 ||
With clearly defined limbs, equal in form to the one to be accomplished (sādhya), smooth, and captivating.

Adorned with red garlands, garments, and unguents, and having himself performed the ritual of placement (nyāsa), he should perform the placement upon the image by means of the dissolution portion (saṃhāra-bhāga). || 649 ||

One should divide the vital breaths of those to be accomplished (sādhya), which are established upon the name, into seven parts [the meaning is that one should effect the division]. The first part is said to extend from the root of the right thigh to the end of the foot. || 650 ||
The second [portion] is the right side up to the neck;
the third would be the right arm; and the fourth is considered to be the head. || 651 ||
The left arm shall be the fifth, and the sixth [limb] begins with the left abdomen.
Likewise, the seventh [syllable] should be from the left side of the body, ending at the foot of the thigh and so forth.
The classification of women has been indicated; now that which is difficult to accomplish will be described.
Likewise, the two ankles, the two knees, and the two shanks. || 653 ||
One should likewise worship the two middle [fingers], the two arms, and the crown.
Indeed, the body is of eleven types; now, those that are incurable shall be described.
Of the seven ordinary [mantras], for each one there are seven [parts]; one should offer each part as an oblation at the onset of night, while remembering the enemy. (655)
From his right foot men were produced, and likewise from his left foot women; thus, within seven days, the women became agitated and afflicted by passion.
With limbs perspiring and trembling, they said to the practitioner, whose mind was satisfied: "Save us! Save us!
Forgive us! Look upon me; do not abandon me! (657)

Thus, all of them, speaking with minds filled with compassion and tormented by the fire of passion, fall before the practitioner; and the women, as his mantra-practitioners, always remain at his service like slaves. || 658 ||
One should offer oblations of salt and sesame seeds soaked in oil to destroy enemies.
Salt mixed with turmeric powder is considered effective for immobilization. (659)
Mātaṅgī is eternally pleased; one should worship her on Tuesdays. One should offer one, three, five, or even seven maidens. || 660 ||
And the maidens should always be honored by those who know the mantras with delicious foods and drinks, both solid and soft, that are pleasing to the taste and captivating to the mind. || 661 ||
In this rite, the practitioner should meditate upon all women as being dark-complexioned;
likewise, on a Tuesday, he should prepare lamps made of flour.
A wise person should kindle these [fires] with ghee for the propitiation of Mātaṅgī.
For the propitiation of Mātaṅgī, the practitioner of mantra should worship the group of eight Yoginīs.
And [he saw] the divine, great, perfected Gaṇeśī, the devourer of corpses.
[One should worship] Ḍākinī, Kālikā, and Kālarātri, who have Īśāna as their domain. || 664 ||
[He saw] Niśācarī, Ūrdhvakeśī, Śuṣkāṅgī, and likewise Bhojinī.
Vīrabhadrā, Virūpākṣī, Dhūmrā, and Jaṭādharā in the east;
Kalahā, Ghoraraktākṣī, Viśvarūpā, and Bhayaṃkarī; and Priyā, Rākṣasī, and Vīrakumārī in the southeast corner. || 665–666 ||
She had shaven heads, was engaged in the work of Rudra, and was terrifying and overcome with fear.
To Yama, [he gave] Tripurantā, Krodhinī, Durmadā, and Dhvaṃsinī.
Dīrghā, Lamboṣṭhikā, Haṃsī, Tāpinī, and Mantrayoginī.
And one should also worship Ādityā and Khaṭvāṅgī in the southwest, and Kālāgni in the south.
Then [he worships] Grāhiṇī, Cakriṇī, Kaṅkālī, and Bhuvaneśvarī.
Haṃkālī, Yamadūtī, Kaumārī, and Kapālinī. || 669 ||
Keśinī, Madirā, Ādyā, Cāriṇī, Lomajaṅghikā, Nāmakī, Kāmukī, Vāyu, Lomakā, and likewise Adhomukhī. || 670 ||
Vyāghrajaṭī, Sarpajaṭī, and Kuṇḍāmarivināśinī.
And in the northern direction, [he saw] Kapālinī, who is terrible, fierce in form, and formidable.
One should recite the mantra more than one hundred thousand times; it will agitate all women.
One shall bring even lords of the earth under control with half that amount; of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, by half of that [number], sentient beings come under one's control; all women, even those situated at a distance, come [under control] through ten thousand recitations. 673.
Those from one's own country certainly arrive with half of that amount.
From three thousand repetitions, the attainment of all desired objects will certainly occur. || 674 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the classification of mantras, which yields great fruit.
O mantra of eighty-eight syllables, you who bring all sentient beings under your control! || 675 ||
In front of this [image], one should likewise recite the seven syllables beginning with "sauśca rājalakṣmīprade," and then again recite the mantra beginning with "sarvaloka. (673)
This mantra is said to consist of one hundred and five syllables.
The rite beginning with the consumption of raw flesh has been previously described, as well as the six-limbed ritual performed with the six seed-syllables.
All [practices] such as meditation and worship are intended for the eighty-eight mantras.
And the applications here are those very same ones, as well as the preliminary rites (*puraścaryā*) and so forth.
Now I shall further proclaim another [mantra] consisting of fifty-four syllables.
Oṃ hrīṃ, salutations to Padmā; śrīṃ, O Rājite, O you who are worshipped by kings! One should utter the words "Jaye Vijaye Gauri" and likewise the word "Gāndhārī. || 680 ||
O subduer of the three worlds, O [you who are] all women and men; O subduer, O giver of happiness, Gheṃ Gheṃ Vā Vā Agnigehinī. || 681 ||
The sage is Aja, the meter is said to be Nivṛt-Gāyatrī, the deity is Rājamātaṅgī, and the six limbs are formed by means of Māyā. || 682 ||
Everything previously mentioned here, such as meditation, worship, and so forth, applies likewise. Now, its specific division consisting of sixty-one syllables is being declared. (683)
At the end of this, one should further say: "O Subduer of the Three Worlds."
This mantra may be devoid of the Praṇava in all cases, as previously described.
This mantra of Pārvatī has been declared with a slight variation in its phonemes; it is known as the one with the stars (tārā).
Now I shall state the verse of Vijaya.
One should conclude again as before with "Gaurī Gāndhārī. This mantra consists of sixty-one syllables; its meter is Nivṛt, and Aja is the sage (Ṛṣi). || 686 ||
The goddess Gaurī and her six limbs are formed by those originating from Indra, the horse, the elephant, and the directions— [namely, fourteen,
ten, eight, eight, ten, and eleven].
The six limbs [of her body] are formed by the syllables of the mantra; thus her visualization is described.

I worship her who holds a noose and a goad in her hands, whose braided hair is adorned with jewel-encrusted ornaments, who has the hue of the bandhūka flower, who possesses three eyes, and who bears golden streaks. || 688 ||
As before, one should worship these six limbs upon the seat of Bhuvaneśī.
First, the six limbs are in the hexagon, and Brāhmī and the others are on the eight petals.

One should worship the lords of the directions and their weapons within the outer enclosure (bhūpura) and so forth; one should recite the mantra ten thousand times and perform oblations with milk-rice and clarified butter.
Then one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa); thus the mantra becomes perfected.
And one should perform the ritual applications (prayoga) of either Annapūrṇā or Mātaṅgī. || 691 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the *Vaśyamātaṅgikā-mantra*: *Oṃ rājamukhī rājābhimukhī vaśyamukhī*. (692)
One should utter "māyāṃ hrīṃ [śrīṃ] klīṃ devadevi mahādevi" thereafter.
"O Goddess of the Gods, O All!"—thus one should utter the words from the mouth of every person. || 693 ||
"Make the pair of women subject to me, svāhā"—this is the mantra ending with *svāhā*, formed from the syllables.
The arrangement of the limbs [of the mantra] is performed with the letters of the Veda, Mitra, and the syllables, using the seven directions and the sacrifices as arrows. || 694 ||

One should understand that worship, recitation, and so forth are equal to the *Rājamataṅgī*; one should also know its ritual applications (*prayoga*), for this [tantra] is especially effective for subjugation (*vaśya*).
"Māyā, namaḥ, hili hili, Caṇḍamātaṅginī, and svāhā"—this mantra consists of fifteen syllables;
its ritual application, worship, and so forth should be performed accordingly. (696)

The recitation should be equal to that of the Rājamātaṅgika mantra, numbering ten thousand; there should be an oblation of ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa), and the ritual application and so forth are as before. || 697 ||
(p. 470) Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the Karṇamātaṅgikā-vidyā.
Then one should know the Vāgbhava, the Heart, and the word Śrīmātaṅgī. (698)
O infallible one, O speaker of truth, place your foot upon my ear; then, O Truth, tell me the pair of words concerning the two-fold descent. (699)
"Come, come! Obeisance to Śrīmātaṅgī!"—this mantra consists of three oceans (thirty-six syllables).
Here, the limbs [of the deity] are worshipped with the Vāgbhava [bīja], whether the worship and other rites have been performed or not. (700)

By reciting the mantra one hundred thousand times and performing a fire-oblation with milk-rice and clarified butter, the mantra becomes perfected; then the Goddess shall whisper the auspicious and inauspicious fate of the questioner into his ear.
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the most excellent of all mantras.
Having uttered "aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ māṃ," one should then recite "hrīṃ kroṃ klīṃ" as the final part.
O Śrīmātaṅgeśvarī, O subduer of all, O consort of Agni! This twenty-three-syllable mantra is the accomplisher of all undertakings. (703)
The metre is Nivṛdgāyatrī, the sage is Dakṣiṇāmūrti, and its presiding deity is proclaimed to be Karṇamātaṅgikā. || 704 ||
Having uttered "Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Āṃ," it should likewise be performed with the seed-syllables "Hrīṃ" and "Kroṃ."
And by repeating [the mantras] twice, there is the procedure for the six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga), such as worship, recitation, and so forth. || 705 ||
One should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times with [offerings] mixed with the three sweets.
The oblation should consist of bandhūka flowers, along with sugar and milk-rice (pāyasa). || 706 ||
And through the fruits of the *hunetkadalī* plant, the accomplishment of mantras (*mantrasiddhi*) arises.
Through the bestowal of all mantras and other rites, the supreme practitioner shall become accomplished. || 707 ||
Now I shall proclaim another, the supreme mantra of Mātaṅgī: "Kāminī rañjinī svāhā"; this is declared to be the eight-syllabled [mantra]. (708)
The seer is Sammohana, the meter is Nivṛt, and its deity is proclaimed to be Sarvasammohanī;
the limbs [of the mantra] consist of words repeated twice. (709)
A dark-limbed woman, beautifully adorned, playing the lute with her two arms.
She who has the moon as her crest-ornament, who deludes the universe with her various songs.

In the Mātaṅginī-pīṭha, Rati and the others are to be worshipped within the triangle; they are to be worshipped according to the five enclosures (pañcāvaraṇa), while the worship of the limbs (aṅga-pūjana) takes place upon the filaments (keśara). || 711 ||
Anaṅgakusumā and the others are the Mothers on the petals and tips; this [mandala] is considered to have seven enclosures by the World-Protectors and those beginning with Vajra. || 712 ||
One should recite the mantra twenty thousand times and then perform the fire oblation (homa) with one-tenth of that amount.
With [flowers] produced from the Madhūka tree, smeared with the three sweets (trimadhu), one may delude the entire world. || 713 ||
Now I shall describe Ucchiṣṭā Mātaṅgī, who has the color of a cow.
The mantra beginning with the words "Nama ucchiṣṭacāṇḍāli mātaṅgi" and ending with "sarvavaśaṃkari svāhā" would delude the entire world. 715.
The meters are Nivṛt and Gāyatrī; the sages are Nārada and Tumburu; the deities here are Māgaṅgī and Ucchiṣṭā, who are of the color of a cow. || 716 ||
The limbs [of the mantra] should consist of its syllables, measured respectively by the numbers two, three, one, and three;
thereafter, one should meditate upon it in the heart-lotus. (717)
She was clad in black garments, her feet moist with lac-dye, and possessed high, swelling breasts.
Adorned with garlands of pearls and coral, she wears earrings made of conch shells.
In the triangle, Rati and the others are to be worshipped; outside of that, however, they are on the pericarp.
Likewise, the five arrows are the limbs, and the eight deities beginning with Brāhmī are on the eight petals. (719)
In the second eight-petaled [lotus], Anaṅgakusumā and the others are to be worshipped;
in the square are the world-protectors (lokapālas), and outside of that, their weapons.
Now its variations will be described: one should recite preceded by *klīṃ*, *hrīṃ*, and *śrīṃ*; or one may recite the mantras preceded by *klīṃ*. For these two, Madana is the sage (*muni*). (721)
The worship, recitation, and so forth are as before; now hear from me its other divisions.
One should recite the mantra beginning with *āṃ klīṃ hrīṃ* and ending with *klīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ*.
It bestows eloquence, the power of poetry, and the ability for song. || 723 ||
The Sage shall be Dakṣiṇāmūrti; everything else is as previously stated.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) by repeating the syllables ĀṂ HRĪṂ KROṂ twice.
On her shoulder was a garland of jasmine flowers; her head was elevated and slender, adorned with pearl ornaments and a dark-blue crest-lock, as she played upon a lute.
Intoxicated by honey-wine, under the influence of the sweet nectar, she was dark-limbed and very delicate.
A triangle and a pentagon, and outside, two eight-petaled lotuses. || 726 ||
One should draw a sixteen-spoked wheel, an eight-petalled lotus, and three enclosures of earth; then one should utter the name of the deity to be worshipped along with the Ucchiṣṭapādukā mantra.
Having uttered "I worship," the worship of the deities is thus considered complete. Within the triangles are Rati and the others, while at the ends of the corners are the three Śaktis.
And those known as Will, Knowledge, and Action, along with the limbs [of the mantra], are to be worshipped on the outside.
The five Kāma-śaktis, beginning with Drāviṇī, are to be worshipped in the pentagon. || 729 ||
On the eight petals outside of that, they should be worshipped together with the eight long vowels.
Likewise, on the second desired petal, [the goddesses] beginning with Brāhmī, whose names end in "kanyā," [should be placed].
One should worship Anaṅgakusumā and the others, who are known as Kanyās; one should worship Urvaśī and the others, known as Kanyās, in the sixteen-spoked [cakra]. || 731 ||
Urvaśī, Menakā, Rambhā, Ghṛtācī, Mañjukeśikā, Kāśyapī, Sukeśī, Mañjughoṣā, and a Nāga maiden. || 732 ||
And a yakṣa maiden, a gandharva maiden, and indeed a siddha maiden.
[One obtains] a maiden capable of entering the bodies of others and possessing the power of far-sight. || 733 ||
[He should worship] the Guṭikā-siddhakanyā and the Pādukā-siddhakanyā; then he should worship the deities of the gates at the four gates.
The stringed instrument, the percussion instrument, the wind instrument, and likewise the hollow instrument;
and Baṭuka, Gaṇeśa, Kṣetrapāla, and the Yoginī. || 735 ||
Then, preceded by the word "ucchiṣṭa," I worship the sandals.
Having made the first syllable of one's own name the seed-syllable (bīja), one should worship [the deities] starting from the southeast (āgneya).

Furthermore, one should worship the Blessed Lady in the center with all ritual offerings. Then, following that, all the vowels joined with the *śrutis* [quarter-tones] are on the left side. (p. 472) 737)
And Rati, accompanied by Rāga, is to be worshipped at the right side.
One should worship the two parrots and the two mainas of the Supreme Goddess.
Then one should worship the lineage of gurus and one's own guru in front; the three seed-syllables of Bālā will bring auspiciousness to the practitioner. || 739 ||
Whether it be anything at all, or desire, speech, or even Lakṣmī;
Having first given the remnants of his meal to a female attendant (mātaṅgī) who is pleasing to him, he should worship the mantra.
Therefore, there are numerous varieties of mantras and rites such as worship, according to one's desire.
Whether out of respect or out of consideration for one's own capacity, one should act as is appropriate. || 741 ||
Pure, wearing garlands and fine garments, one should recite the mantra a hundred thousand times without sloth.
One should constantly offer the bali-oblation at night with the remains of the meal.
One should perform both the obligatory and the optional recitation while still impure from food remnants.
Furthermore, one should perform a fire-oblation here with palāśa flowers mixed with sweet substances.

If success is not achieved by this much, one should recite the mantra a hundred thousand times according to the number of its syllables; the practitioner should also perform the worship of a maiden as prescribed. (744)
The practitioner of mantra should also perform the worship of the sixty-four Yoginīs here.
At night, he should offer her an oblation (bali) with the remainder of the leftover food.
By means of this mantra, which has been previously declared by Manu, one attains success.
One should recite the mantra fourteen times after the worship; it is to be worshipped by kings and especially by women. (746)
A woman who desires the enjoyment of love should eat betel-leaf consecrated by reciting this mantra one thousand and eight times, having first requested it.
And he shall remain under the control of the minister for as long as his life lasts; of this there is no doubt. Likewise, *sahadevī*, *dūrvā*, *musalī*, and *madhuyaṣṭikā* [are used]. (748)
Bhadrā, Viṣṇudayitā, Lakṣmīvallī, Indravalī, and Añjalī are also mentioned; one should perform the recitation while touching these individually. || 749 ||
The practitioner of mantra should then place one hundred and eight [beads] upon its head; whether a man, a woman, or a king, whoever wears it shall experience a multitude of joys.

Indra, Agni, Viṣṇu, the pair (Umā-Maheśvara), Aṅka (Gaṇeśa), Manu, the eight Vasus, and the directions—these, when recited separately one hundred times each, should be combined and ground together. || 751 ||
Moreover, dried pills, over which the mantra has been recited a thousand times, when properly applied to the forehead, are enchanting to all women. (752)
They become experts in the art of pleasing the entire world. || 753 ||
And the best of those who know mantras should prepare a pill the size of a grain of pollen;
and collyrium should be held [in the eye] using a cotton wick saturated with black clarified butter.
Chanted a thousand times with the *manu*, this consecrated [substance] is auspicious for the eyes; daily it brings the world under control and causes the agitation of women. (755)
And one shall destroy the hosts of *preta*-grahas and others even before long.
With the ten substances previously mentioned, and with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the ashes of a tawny bull (kāpila).
If one applies ashes consecrated by reciting this mantra a thousand times upon the forehead, one shall bring the world under control; it cannot be otherwise. (757)
Having placed it upon a linen cloth, beautiful with lines drawn by a brush.
It was thoroughly infused with the lotus pollen that is dark like a blue water-lily and invoked by Viṣṇu.
It is kindled with black cow’s ghee, and the soot produced therefrom is used.
Chanted with the Mātaṅgī mantra and applied as collyrium to the eyes, it enchants men.
In the same way, the Namaskāriṇī has been proclaimed here; of this there is no doubt.
The pollen produced from the *bhṛṅgarāja* flower is like Lakṣmī, the beloved of Viṣṇu.

With its wick thus prepared and ignited by the clarified butter of Kapila, that lamp—even if produced from such [ordinary] materials—will undoubtedly yield its fruit, preceded by the removal of all impurities. || 761 ||
Camphor, sandalwood, a pair of lotuses, *bakula* flowers, and *rocanā*—the ink produced from these substances powerfully brings the three worlds under one's control. (762)
One should remove the fruit produced from the *kramuka* tree along with its victory over the senses by means of roots and water,
and then wrap the fruit with threads.
Then, one should place that fruit on the ground for the son of the Earth (the planet Mars).
Camphor consecrated on a non-earthday yields that same fruit as the aforementioned practice. || 764 ||
Having ground it with water and recited the mantra over it, the wise one should fashion it into pills.
These women, when eaten after being offered with a *sūryaka*, grant supreme subjugation. || 765 ||
And a golden five-limbed [ornament], joined with the five impurities of the self.
One should consume it, consecrated with a thousand recitations, along with drinks; to whichever king it is given, he will become submissive—of this there is no doubt. (766)
One who possesses the mantra should perform all the ritual applications (prayoga) previously declared in the mantra-texts. Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the thirty-two-syllable mantra.
*Tāra* [Oṃ Hrīṃ Aiṃ Śrīṃ Namo Bhagavati Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍāli Śrīmātaṅgīśvari Sarvajanavaśaṅkari Svāhā— this is the mantra].
*Māyā*, *Vāgramā*, and "Namo Bhagavatī," as well as the word "Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍāli."
O Śrīmātangi, likewise O Īśvarī! || 768 ||
"O you who bring all people under control, svāhā!"—this is remembered as the mantra. Mātaṅga is said to be its sage, the Anuṣṭubh its meter, and the deity [is the same]. (769)
The six limbs of Mātaṅgī should consist of the mantra-syllables [numbering] four, six, and six: *oṃ hrīṃ aiṃ śrīṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ bhagavati* to the head (*svāhā*),
*ucchiṣṭacāṇḍāli* to the crest-lock (*vaṣaṭ*), and *śrīmātaṅgīśvari* to the armor.
"Hūṃ! O you who bring all people under control! To the three eyes, vauṣaṭ svāhā! To the weapon, phaṭ!
Thus one should meditate upon her as having six or eight arms, dark-complexioned, and with beautiful eyes. 770.
And she was seated upon a jeweled throne, listening to what Śuka had spoken.
One should meditate upon that Mātaṅgī in the heart, wearing red garments, intoxicated by the drinking of wine, seated upon a lotus with excellent feet, and playing the lute.
One should perform ten million recitations (japa) and a fire sacrifice (homa) with madhūka flowers smeared with honey,
worshipping on the pedestal according to the procedure to be described hereafter.
Having constructed a pedestal consisting of a triangle, two sets of eight petals, a pericarp, and a square,
one should worship therein the nine pedestal-energies (pīṭhaśaktis) who bestow desired boons.
Vibhūti, Unnati, Kānti, Sṛṣṭi, Kīrti, and Sannati.
Vyūḍhi, utkṛṣṭi, ṛddhi, and ending with mātaṅgī—these are remembered [as the mudrās].
At the end of the mantra for all powers (*sarvaśaktika*), [one recites]: *oṃ hrīṃ aiṃ śrīṃ sarvaśaktikamalāsanāya namaḥ*; and for the seat (*āsana*), it ends with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*).
The first seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra) consists of the letters *tā-ra-mā-yā-vā-gra-mā*, and its syllables are the digits (*kalā*). || 775 ||
With this [mantra], one should offer a seat, a grass mat, and so forth;
at the conclusion of the worship of the pedestal (pīṭha), one should perform the worship of the surrounding deities (āvaraṇa) using the root mantra.
In the three triangles, one should worship the triad of Rati, Prīti, and Manobhava; in the filaments, the six limbs (of the mantra); and in the middle of the petals, the Mothers.
In the second [circle], on the eight petals, the Bhairavas beginning with Asitāṅga are to be worshipped; but in the sixteen-spoked [circle] are Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and Praśāntikā.
Śraddhā, Māheśvarī, and Kriyāśakti as the seventh; Sulakṣmī, Sṛṣṭimohinī, and likewise Prathamācāriṇī. || 779 ||
Vidyullatā, Cicchakti, Surāpā, along with Nandā, Nandabuddhi, and Ṣoḍaśī—these should be worshipped with great effort. || 780 ||
In the four directions of the square is that Mātaṅgī of great splendor; likewise, Lakṣmī and Mahālakṣmī are in the corners starting from the southeast.
One should first worship Dhruva and the others, and then Mātaṅgī and Parama.
The name of all the powers of obscuration, ending in the letter *ṅ*, is placed at the end of the heart-mantra.

Likewise, Vighneśa, Durgā, Baṭuka, Kṣetreśa, and the other deities, as well as Vajra and the others, should be worshipped; in this way, the fulfillment of one's heart's desire shall come to pass. || 783 ||
Through auspicious oblations with plantain stalks, one attains enjoyment; through bilva fruits, a kingdom;
and through the leaves or fruits of the Brahma-tree (palāśa), the people become submissive.
One should know that diseases are destroyed by pieces of *amṛtā*, prosperity by *nimba* and even by rice grains; drought by salt, and water by *tagara* and reeds.
By consuming salt smeared with neem oil, there is the destruction of enemies and superior eating.
By performing oblations with Kāśa grass mixed with the powder of Niśā, there shall be the immobilization of enemies. || 786 ||
Red sandalwood, camphor, spikenard, saffron, and yellow pigment; sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor—these are declared to be the eight fragrances.
From this oblation, the practitioner certainly brings the world under his control.
Having ground this and recited the mantra ten thousand times, one becomes beloved by the world through the use of this tilaka.
By the oblation of plantain fruit, one shall obtain all desired things. What need is there for much speaking?
When Mātaṅgī is worshipped, she grants the desires of men. || 789 ||
A doll fashioned from honey and flour, placed on the southern side.
A person should offer one hundred and eight oblations at night into a fire of khadira wood.
A woman who has been brought under control should eat that [image] made of rice flour.
Having cast the auspicious radiance into the belly of a crow on a dark night of the new moon.

Having wrapped it with a blue thread, one should mutter this mantra over it in the funeral fire; once it has been recited over a thousand times, to whomever one gives that fire, he becomes like a servant.
Thus have been described the lords of the Gaṇas established in the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya).
There is no counting the number of those served by sages, goddesses, and others in Kāśī. (793)
Accompanied by the syllable Om at the beginning, ending with the dative case, and also joined with the word "namaḥ."
The recitation of one hundred thousand syllables for each of these, known as their own seed-syllables, has been prescribed. || 794 ||
A fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed for them using pieces of sugarcane, sesame seeds, lotuses and other such items, along with sweetmeats,
all combined with the three sweets (madhuratra).
Those Vināyakas, beginning with Bindu, grant fruits; and those deities, the Baṭukas such as Ākarṣa and others, bestow rewards. || 796 ||

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Discourse on the Mantra of Gaṇapati," in the *Merutantra* composed by Śiva with the approval of the illustrious Mahāmāyā and Mahākāla, belonging to the Western Tradition (*paścimāmnāya*).
The illustrious Śiva said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the [mantra] perfected through the Northern Tradition (Uttarāmnāya).
"Vadeddhastipiśācī liḥ liḥ svāhā"—this is the nine-syllable mantra. || 1 ||
Kaṅkāla is his sage (ṛṣi), Virāḍ is his meter (chandas), and the deity is said to be Gaṇeśa, the bestower of all prosperity. || 2 ||
The procedure for the five ancillaries (pañcāṅga) is said to consist of two, three, two, one, and two [units];
meditation, worship, the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa), and so forth, shall be like those of Vakratuṇḍa. Nine hundred thousand recitations are prescribed;
now I shall describe the rites for specific desires. || 3 ||
A wise person should have an auspicious image fashioned from the wood of the nimba tree.
And [the image] of the great-souled Gaṇeśa should be the size of the worshiper's thumb. || 4 ||
Having touched it, one should recite the mantra; from that, the accomplishment of one's desired aim shall arise.
And on the sixth and the fourteenth days of the dark fortnight, the knower of mantras [should perform the rite].
If one recites this auspicious mantra while remaining impure (ucchiṣṭa) in the middle of the night, whatever is desired will come under the control of the practitioner; of this there is no doubt.

Having written the name of the person to be controlled (*sādhya*) upon a birch leaf according to the prescribed rite, and having encircled it with the mantra, one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind. Treading upon that leaf with the foot while drawing it toward oneself with the hand—this is considered "hand-drawing" (*hastakṛṣṭi*). || 7 ||
Having written the document as before and worshipped it according to the prescribed rite, one should recollect the target and mutter the mantra; thus, one shall bring the entire world under control.
Wearing the yantra on his head and reciting the mantra with one-pointed mind,
the wise practitioner may instantly attract a king or a queen.
Betel leaves, flowers, garments, and ornaments.
Having taken fruits, roots, and other such substances, one should mutter the mantra twenty-one times;
one should indeed give them to the desired deity, and not otherwise.
This application is proclaimed as that which brings all worlds under one's control.
By offering incense made of śrīkhaṇḍa, one shall bring the king under one's control. || 11 ||
The sacrificial fuel-sticks are made of nimba wood and combined with pungent oil.

Having offered oblations according to the ritual procedure using [fuel] joined with a raven’s wing, the mantra-practitioner, by means of a funeral pyre fire, utterly eradicates the enemy; it is not otherwise.
One should offer the feathers of an owl and a crow, combined with their fat and blood, into the fire of a cremation ground; by this, enmity shall arise between two who were once close.
The wise man [should avoid] earth from the hand of one who holds a discus, which is joined with the dust from the feet of an enemy.
One should fashion an effigy of the enemy, adorned with all its limbs, mixed with cremation-ground ashes and combined with unguents. || 14 ||

One should write her name on its heart and encircle it with the root mantra; having performed the rite of consecrating the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), [one should place it] in a vessel enriched with poison and blood.

Having established [the deity], one should recite the mantra with a mind that is perfectly one-pointed. One will not die by violence; of this there is no doubt, for one is well protected by the deities. || 16 ||
Having taken the ashes of the husband and wife who were cremated on the funeral pyre according to the prescribed ritual,
And one should write the name on birch bark, having the appearance of yellow pigment and saffron.

Having encircled [the object] with the root mantra, one should perform the rite of infusing life-force (prāṇapratiṣṭhā). Recalling the person to be acted upon, one should properly recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Instantly, a perfect affection arises between the two people who were previously hostile.

Now I shall declare another mantra of Ucchiṣṭa Gaṇeśvara: having uttered *oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ hrīṃ*, then *hrīṃ hrīṃ gheṃ gheṃ* and *phaṭ*, this mantra consists of sixteen syllables ending in *svāhā*. The visualization and other rites are considered to be as before. [The sages and others...]
The preliminary practice consists of a recitation measured by one hundred thousand syllables. || 20 ||
Now I shall further proclaim here the great mantra of Ucchiṣṭa: having uttered *oṃ hrīṃ krīṃ*, as well as *hrīṃ huṃ gheṃ gheṃ* and *phaṭ*. (21)
"To Ekadaṃṣṭra—[to Ekadaṃṣṭra, the elephant-faced one with a hanging belly, whose self is the remnants;

*krāṃ krūṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ gheṃ gheṃ svāhā*]—and to the elephant-faced one with a hanging belly," having spoken thus, [the mantra for] the one whose self is the remnants is: *krāṃ krūṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ ghe ghe gnigehinī*.
This mantra consists of twenty-seven syllables, like the six-syllable Vakratuṇḍa mantra.

By appending "Hastimukhāya" after the previously mentioned word "Ucchiṣṭātmane" ending in the dative case, it becomes the three-eyed, immeasurable mantra. Whenever one should utter even just this much, "Hastimukha": || 23 ||
Its mantra is proclaimed to consist of twenty-three syllables.
The Lord of the Gaṇas (Gaṇanātha) is proclaimed as the one who partakes of the remnants of the Munis and other deities. || 24 ||
The preliminary practices and so forth should be understood as before; however, accomplishment is attained swiftly in the Kali Yuga.
Now I shall further proclaim another mantra consisting of twenty-six syllables.

The Tāra: [Oṃ namo bhagavate ekadaṃṣṭrāya hastimukhalambodarāya ucchiṣṭamahātmane krauṃ kḷṃ hrauṃ hraṃ ghe ghe svāhā] Homage to the Blessed One, the Single-Tusked One, the Elephant-Faced One with a Hanging Belly. Homage to the Blessed One, the Single-Tusked One, the Elephant-Faced One with a Hanging Belly.
Likewise, [he gave] the leavings to the Great-Souled One. || 26 ||
Krauṃ klauṃ hrauṃ hruṃ, then gheṃ gheṃ svāhā—this is considered the mantra.
The seer and other details were previously stated: *Krauṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *Klūṃ* to the head, *svāhā*; *Hrūṃ* to the crest-lock, *vaṣaṭ*; *Gheṃ* to the armor, *huṃ*;
*Gheṃ* to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*; *Krauklūṃ Hrīṃ Hrūṃ Ghe Ghe* to the weapon.
And "phaṭ" and "ghe"—with these two, one should perform the six-limbed rite (ṣaḍaṅga), as well as the meditation and worship as before. || 27 ||
Now I shall declare another great mantra of his, consisting of twelve syllables: "Hrīṃ Gaṃ Hastipiśāci Svāhā" is the mantra. (28)
It is held that all [practices], such as meditation and worship, are to be performed just like those for the nine-syllable mantra.
The preliminary rite (puraścaryā) shall consist of one hundred and twenty thousand recitations; the ritual applications (prayoga) and so forth are as before. || 29 ||

*Tāra* [Oṃ namaḥ ucchiṣṭagaṇeśāya]. *Namaḥ ucchiṣṭagaṇeśāya* is the ten-syllable mantra (*daśākṣaro manuḥ*). Its visualization, worship, ritual application, and so forth, are all like those of the ten-syllable [mantra of Gaṇeśa]. (30)
If this nine-syllable [mantra] is stated at the end of this ten-syllable one;
When the mantra consists of nineteen syllables, it brings about excellent accomplishment. || 31 ||
All practices, such as meditation and worship, should be understood through the nine-syllable mantra.
And with two, six, three, two, and two syllables [of the mantra: oṃ hastimukhāya lambodarāya ucchiṣṭamahātmane āṃ kroṃ hrīṃ klīṃ hrīṃ huṃ ghe ghe ucchiṣṭāya svāhā].
It may consist of six limbs. || 32 ||
Now I shall proclaim another mantra consisting of thirty-two syllables: one should utter the *tāra* (om), then "hastimukha" ending in the letter *ṅa*, followed by "lambodara. (33)
One should recite "ucchiṣṭe" and "mahātmani," followed by "naṃ āṃ krīṃ hrīṃ. Then "klīṃ hrīṃ haṃ ghe" twice; this is Ucchiṣṭā, the consort of Agni. || 34 ||
The arrangement of the limbs is performed with syllables numbering six, seven, six, six, and two.
In these mantras of Ucchiṣṭagaṇanātha, there is no requirement for purification.

These mantras, which bestow success upon the Guru when the wheel of accomplishment and the like are attained within the Māyā-cakra and other spheres, must always be kept secret; they are not to be revealed here or there.
Indeed, without this propitiation of the left-hand path (vāmamārga), success is not attained;
otherwise, there would be loss of caste, poverty, and the extinction of one's lineage. || 37 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the powers joined with the Kṛta [age]; they must always be kept secret from Brāhmaṇas, especially regarding Vedic rites. || 38 ||
Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍalinī, Sumukhī, and Mahāpiśācī; [the seed-syllable] *Cini Hrīṃ* joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*) and the visarga. (39)

The mantra consisting of twenty syllables—[ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālini sumukhi mahāpiśācini hrīṃ vaṃ vaṃ vaḥ]—is declared to grant the desired success to those who worship it. He in whom this mantra resides is not afflicted by obstacles. (40)
Seated upon a corpse, she was clothed in garments of red silk.
Adorned with red ornaments and radiant with a necklace of virtues. || 41 ||

[One should meditate on her] as red in color, sixteen years of age, with full, high, and firm breasts; having offered the oblation with the remnants, one should recite [the mantra] with the mind fixed upon her. || 42 ||

One who desires success in this [mantra] should perform the recitation while remaining impure (ucchiṣṭa). For all supernatural powers (siddhis) arise for one who recites while in a state of impurity. 43.
Having prepared a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) as a mandala, being composed in mind;
The knower of mantras should worship the mandala of the Goddess with the root mantra.

Having established the fire there and meditated upon the Goddess stationed in the form of fire, one should perform the fire-oblation with curd, white mustard seeds, and rice according to the prescribed rule; by performing it one thousand times,
the king becomes subject to one's will.
He who performs a fire-oblation for the Goddess with the flesh of a cat attains the supreme knowledge that brings mastery over both weapons and scriptures. || 46 ||
One should perform a fire-oblation (homa) with the meat of a goat mixed with honey, one thousand times according to the prescribed rite;
thereby, the accomplishments of wealth (dhanasiddhi) come to pass. || 47 ||
One who desires knowledge should perform oblations with sugar, clarified butter, and milk-rice.
Within a month, his fourteen vidyās indeed become perfected.
O Great Goddess, by performing a fire-oblation with the garment of a menstruating woman, honey, and milk-rice, one may bring the three worlds under one's control. || 49 ||
One should perform the fire-oblation with honey and ghee using the *nāgavalī* plant ten thousand times according to the prescribed rite;
then the eight supernatural powers (*siddhis*) are attained.
With human and cat meat, together with ghee and honey, and combined with the hair of a *caṇḍāla*, the summoning of [the deity] Bhava is certain. || 51 ||
Likewise, by performing a fire-offering with the flesh of a crane mixed with honey, one obtains knowledge, wealth, and excellent women. || 52 ||
The knower of mantras, by means of an oblation of Madhurārka in the fire of the funeral pyre, [achieves his purpose].
And by means of an oblation of cuckoo feathers and crow wings, one shall destroy enemies. || 53 ||
And the knower of mantras should perform a fire sacrifice for the eradication of enemies in a fire made of funeral pyre wood, according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Having used the feathers of an owl and a crow, one should perform the fire-oblation continuously.
It shall cause enemies to hate one another and make them agitated by mutual strife.
By performing one thousand oblations with owl feathers according to the prescribed rite, a woman shall suffer a miscarriage;
[the practitioner] should perform the homa with a concentrated mind.
By offering bilva leaves with honey and clarified butter continuously for one month, even a barren woman obtains an excellent son who lives a long life. || 57 ||
Whoever, having risen early in the morning, should perform the fire-oblation day after day.
O beloved, by offering one hundred and eight japā flowers mixed with clarified butter for a period of six months, the power of attraction will certainly be achieved. (58)
Daughters of the gods and gandharvas, as well as daughters of the nāgas and others, afflicted by desire, forcibly embraced him with their power. || 59 ||

If an oblation is performed for the sake of knowledge with sesame seeds mixed with milk-rice, he attains the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā), which is illustrious through its mastery of the multitude of scriptures. || 60 ||
One should diligently perform the fire-oblation with honey and the flesh of the ruru deer.
Whether possessed of learning or wealth, he brings all the scriptures under his control.
And after every meal, having offered her a bali-oblation day after day, one should always recite the mantra one hundred and eight times with the remnants of the food.
Whether in a formidable cremation ground or in an empty house at a crossroads, by offering oblations,
the Goddess will certainly become manifest.
This must be guarded with great effort and should not be told to anyone; devotion to the Guru must be practiced through both body and wealth. 64.
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the determination of the left and the right [paths],
which was concealed in all the Tantras by the prayer of Viṣṇu during the Kali age.
Humans are to be known as animals, and even animals are gods in human form.
Even animals and even Asuras [engage in] food, drink, and sexual intercourse.

The six waves, such as cold, heat, and the rest, are known to be equal in their capacity to cause distinction; for they all indeed afflict everyone, including me, who dwell in this forest of bliss. (67)
"The destiny of both is said to be equal due to their desire for passion, anger, and the like. Therefore, how is it that humans are superior? This is what I ask you. (68)
Nothing other than the body of an animal can serve as a means for attaining another world.
Since that [state] arises from the human body, therefore human beings are considered superior. || 69 ||
Whoever proceeds according to the dharma prescribed for him, for him alone there is the next world,
as long as he dwells in heaven by virtue of his merit.
Furthermore, O gods, in this Kali age, birth occurs in wealthy households and association with the virtuous arises;
when one becomes attentive therein through listening to the scriptures, then, O Brahmins, he is born as a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya). 71.
If, even there, he remains vigilant and is devoted to the duties of a Brāhmaṇa, then he shall be initiated within my Forest of Bliss in the midst of the assembly.

Furthermore, someone established in their own duty may, due to a lack of knowledge, be born among the lower species; yet, through the assistance of dharma, he shall be liberated by me in Kāśī. There, he shall chant for a portion of time greater than that [of others] and live for a long duration. (73)
Worship is said to be of two kinds: with desire and free from desire. That which is free from desire is the seed of liberation, while that with desire is the seed of worldly existence.
The right path is considered good, while the left is regarded as even better;
he who truly understands the left is indeed the supreme teacher. || 75 ||
I know it in its entirety; Sanaka and the others know three-quarters of it; Vasiṣṭha and the others know half; and Śakra and the others know one quarter. || 76 ||
The Lords know a sixth part, while other people know but a ten-millionth part.
And millions of them are born here in the wombs of worms.
He who drinks wine becomes liberated while living; he who engages in sexual union becomes capable of creating the three worlds. (78)
He who eats fish is Śiva; there is no doubt about this. He who eats the *mudrā* shall become the lord of the *siddhis*. || 79 ||
For that mortal who eats meat, whence can there be fear of death? Furthermore, this [topic] has three aspects: the sāttvika, the rājasa, and likewise [the tāmasa]. (80)
And it is also tamasic; among these, the first, the Vāmamārga, is now described. Those who truly understand that path are liberated—of this there is no doubt. (81)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa taught the left-hand path (vāmamārga) to Phālguna;
while reflecting on this, I saw it and the sage was clearly discerned by me. || 82 ||

Whether he be a Cāṇḍāla, a Turuṣka, a slayer of a Brahmin, or envious; whether he be a learned Vedic scholar or a follower of the left-hand path—he is a fit vessel for both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 83 ||
This was known by the wise Śukadeva through the stabilization of his embryo; that sinner who censures him is born as a worm in excrement. || 84 ||
Furthermore, three Tantras were composed by me for the Vāmamārga; one was given to Dattātreya, and another likewise to Śrī Kṛṣṇa. || 85 ||
The third [revelation] was given to the Goddess by Datta during two yugas;
through the left-hand path (vāmamārga), many, beginning with Vṛṣṇika, were liberated. || 86 ||
That which was given to Śrī Kṛṣṇa in the Dvāpara age was distributed here among the worlds and caused to enter the world of the gods. (87)
But because that Tantra was given by me to the Goddess, even the learned are deluded by it within this cycle of existence; what then can be said of others? 88.

O gods, having raised the Kuṇḍalinī power by means of Haṭhayoga, one should make her hungry and then show the individual soul (jīva) to her; I shall now fully proclaim that essence which is hidden in all tantras. (89)
But when she opens her mouth for the purpose of devouring living beings, [it is the time of death].
It is said that the nectar of the moon from his head enters her mouth. (90)
O gods, let those who drink liquor drink that which removes old age and death for the sake of the Vāmins; by drinking it again and again, their bodies become like wood. 91.
Due to the momentum of past karma, various karmas manifest within the body;

yet, once the individual soul attains equality with the Self, it becomes composed of eternal bliss. When the identification with the body has dissolved, the practitioner becomes the Great Lord (Maheśvara).
Just as a wheel, set in motion by a potter, revolves with great speed, so too does this body move due to the activity of egoism. || 93 ||
Just as there is no pain when hair, nails, and the like are cut off once they have grown out, so too there is no suffering for the wise when their bodies are struck. 94.
The soul is omnipresent, just as it exists within the hair, nails, and so forth.
In this way, the growth and the functional activity of this body proceed. || 95 ||
Just as a tree, even though it possesses life, does not experience suffering, so too one intoxicated by the wine of the moon is not affected by desire and the like. || 96 ||

One should cause the vital breaths (prāṇas) from the iḍā and piṅgalā to flow into the suṣumṇā. The suṣumṇā is declared to be Śakti, and the individual soul (jīva) is the supreme Śiva. O gods, the union of these two is celebrated by the name "surata. || 97 ||
At the time of the descent of vigor (vīryapāta), when the vital wind has reached the suṣumṇā, the bliss that arises from that is indeed ten million times greater than the former. || 98 ||
But the lords of yogis, established in meditative concentration, are blissfully at peace through that very happiness.
They consider a period of a thousand yugas to be like the blink of an eye; this alone is declared to be true love (rata), while any other would be the love of a donkey (rāsabha-rata). 99.
The five afflictions are like fish; one should consume them only through discernment.
"Eating fish" has been declared by those who show the path to liberation. (100)
Indeed, there is a lack of connection with afflictions, karma, its maturation, and mental dispositions;
at that time, one attains the state of the Self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*).
Joy arises from the Self, and those are proclaimed as the *mudrās*. They are to be known.
But those known as dhāraṇā, dhyāna, and samādhi are the bestowers of liberation. || 102 ||
That which causes the binding of the body is proclaimed to be flesh; for by means of that, through ignorance, the living being is bound by the snare of the body. || 103 ||
The consumption of ignorance is said to be the consumption of its very flesh.
From the destruction of ignorance and the arising of knowledge, liberation is born. || 104 ||
That which was proclaimed to Dattātreya has been described as being characterized by purity (sāttvika). By this left-hand path (vāmamārga), liberation is attained in every way. (105)
Let the essential meaning of the *Tantrarāja*, which is dedicated to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, be accepted; for it is the settled conclusion in the scriptures that "whatever one gives, that one receives. (106)
There is no fault in eating meat, nor in wine, nor in sexual intercourse; for these are the natural inclinations of living beings, while abstention yields great fruit. (107)
Intoxicating liquor, which causes delusion and leads to hell, is forbidden; a Brāhmaṇa established on the Vedic path must not touch it. || 108 ||

As long as the Vedas and the sacrificial altar exist upon the earth in the Kali age, so long shall a Brāhmaṇa never consume intoxicants. Wine consumed at the proper time is declared to be like nectar. || 109 ||
In one place, liquor produced together with nectar becomes like nectar; yet in another, liquor produced even from poison becomes like poison. (110)
And that which is called Agni is the Gāyatrī; if it has been received from the mouth of a guru, [it bestows its fruit].
By the very Vedic path, purified by both families. || 111 ||
If one who is ignorant should immediately drink the drop from the fire of his mouth,
or if he deceives others with words out of a desire for wealth, he shall suffer misery in this world and,
