after death, go to the state of a rākṣasa. || 112 ||
If one is purified by a guru through the practice of Tantra, then, having attained some degree of happiness, one will become a lord of a hundred thousand after death. || 113 ||

One may also perform the worship of Viṣṇu and again offer libations with *surā*; such a person, even if not a Brāhmaṇa, attains happiness and, after death, merges into Brahman. *Surā* is designated as being of three kinds: *gauḍī*, *paiṣṭī*, and *mādhvī*. (114)

The Neṣṭṛ priest is not for the Kṣatriya or the Vaiśya; what then need be said of the Brāhmaṇa? Having consecrated it with mantras, that man who drinks the remnant of the Śakti liquor again and again shall never drink mother's milk nor any other milk. 115.
Sometimes even a Brahmin, deceived by the spells of rogues through fate, becomes a drinker of liquor by the power of destiny;
his deliverance from that state is now described by me. (116)

He should abandon Vedic ritual and never touch the *tulasī* plant. Whether he be an outcaste (*cāṇḍāla*) or a Turk (*turuṣka*), whoever has taken refuge in the Kaula path—association with him alone should be maintained, and never with any other Brahmin. 117.
One should worship the Goddess every day, as well as associate daily with those devoted to Śakti.
A man should indeed contemplate that power as the deity himself.
One who is thus engaged in meditation should cultivate association with those possessed of power (śakti).
Or else, [it may be restored] by the restraining of the vital breath (prāṇa), or likewise by means of medicines and mantras. || 119 ||
Having steadied the semen, one should recite the mantra until it falters; that faltering within the fire of the Śakti by a tenth part [of the recitation] is indeed the oblation (homa). 120.

Again, beginning from the moment of union, one should perform libation with the two faltering breaths; again, from the moment of union, one should perform purification—one should practice this for eight days.
Likewise, on the ninth day, the five powers (śaktis) are to be fed together. When this ritual procedure is performed in this manner, the deity will become a bestower of boons. (122)
From rauhitaka one obtains satisfaction for a year, and from mādguri for a month.
Satisfaction is obtained for three nights by means of antima fish, or even for two days by means of śṛṅgī fish.
Eight parts of powdered black gram (māṣa), six parts of liquorice (yavaphala), and four parts of well-ripened *surā* wine should be taken. || 124 ||
Two parts of rice, along with methikā, asafoetida, cumin, and an appropriate amount of salt, should be thoroughly ground together with wine. || 125 ||
Formed into a circle and wrapped with betel leaves, it is cooked in a water-mechanism;
this is declared to be the Śaktimudrā. || 126 ||
A black portion of karkara and chavya, processed by means of a mechanical device.
And it was accompanied by mung beans, adzukis, lentils, and dishes made from chickpeas.
With this powder in equal proportions, combined with hingu and the other ingredients, pills (vaṭakas) should be prepared and cooked in mustard oil; this is another excellent mudrikā.
The performance of all mudrās may take place either in water or on land; furthermore, wine, liquor, or spirituous liquor should be offered, and nothing else.
One should thoroughly mix wheat flour with cooked meat and place it in water for three days,
until it becomes sour.
A small fish, bean flour, and the powder of lentils.
Having placed it inside a wheat cake, one should cook it in clarified butter; this is indeed the supreme *mudrā*, which bestows extreme satisfaction upon the *śaktis*. || 131 ||
Dhārikā, Pūrikā, Veṣṭanī, and Pūrṇapūrikā.
The mudrās of the Śaktis situated on the path of Dakṣa have been fully described. || 132 ||
One should mix well-cooked meat, as well as the flesh derived from fish, with steamed harimantha and split pulses (dvidala). || 133 ||
Having ground it thoroughly, one should cook it in a cauldron with ghee; adding equal parts of ginger, black pepper, and cinnamon leaves. || 134 ||
And also cloves, small cardamom, nutmeg, kamkola, and camphor.
Having given there as is appropriate, one should have firm sweetmeats (modakas) prepared.
This mudrā brings supreme satisfaction to the Gaṇeśas of the left-hand path. || 135 ||
One should consume equal parts of black gram, lentils, chickpeas, mung beans, and pigeon peas.
Having ground it thoroughly and bound it together, one should add curd and stir it well. || 136 ||
Furthermore, his subtle pill is bound together with black mud.
The *mudrikā* known as *uddhūlikā* is considered to consist of fragrant substances such as cardamom (*elā*) and others. || 137 ||
Of meat that has been properly cut, seasoned with black mustard, dried by the rays of the sun, and cooked in ghee six times its weight. || 138 ||
Having added milk, one should cook it properly until it becomes a solid mass;
then, having added an equal amount of sugar, along with camphor and other ingredients according to taste—this is the seal (mudrā) of Gaṇanātha, which is always pleasing and gratifying. 139.
One should cook the meat of a partridge with a water-wheel [stove]; one should take chickpea flour equal in measure to that which has been fried in ghee. || 140 ||
Having combined and roasted them, one should cook them thoroughly in ghee.
This "White Mudrā" is dear to the lords of the Gaṇas. || 141 ||
Laddukas made from the flour of harimatsya,
fish, and beans, as well as wheat flour and mung bean flour,
are considered auspicious rings that bring delight to Gaṇeśa. || 142 ||

The meat of non-Brāhmaṇa men is considered the very best; likewise, the meat of deer and birds such as the partridge is said to provide satisfaction for three days, while that of the kālīyaka bird provides it for one day. 143.
For eight days, according to the prescribed rule, whatever [rites] should take place in whichever region.
One should properly offer that edible meat to the deity. || 144 ||

The worship-diagram (pūjāyantra) is said to be on the right-hand path; it should be drawn with the eight perfumes (gandhāṣṭaka), or one should draw it with saffron, camphor, and yellow pigment (rocanā). 145.
If one following the left-hand path should draw the yantra with the first flower, [it will be ineffective].
By worshipping him for six months, one shall swiftly attain success.
In the absence of a young woman who has given birth, the menstrual blood of one is taken;
in her absence, the blood of a healthy young woman is considered suitable. || 147 ||
And in its absence, the Aparājita flower should be taken; having placed red sandalwood that has been ground upon its upper part, [one should proceed]. || 148 ||
Then, one should draw the yantra with that [substance] from the root path of the Gaṇa; in its absence, however, with liquor, ghee, and red sandalwood. || 149 ||
As it has been said: "If one draws the yantra, the deity becomes pleased. O best of gods, this alone is revealed in the Vāmamārga. 150.

If one engaged in the left-hand path (vāmamārga) should neglect the worship or fail to perform it daily, the deity becomes exceedingly hungry; there is no doubt that she will consume his progeny and his prosperity. || 151 ||
The annual worship, however, should be performed according to the method prescribed for the materials of the yantra.

The left-hand path (vāmamārga), which brings about the satisfaction of the deities within half of half of half a month, should be practiced only by one who is destitute; [otherwise], it leads to ruin. 152.
Or rather, O beloved, one should maintain this understanding here: the linga is Śiva, the bhaga is Śakti, and the water from the Ganges is considered to be the water. 153.
Thus, by cultivating this meditation while engaging in sexual pleasure, one is liberated; otherwise, by approaching women [without such practice], one is cooked in hell. 154.
By the killing of a living being, no sin accrues to those who vomit [the truth]; if their intellect is such, then it is so, otherwise they would fall into hell. || 155 ||
This must certainly be performed by one who has encountered death or disease; therefore, it is for the sake of destroying this animal's sins and for its liberation. 156.
I cause [them] to be slain in the heavenly world for the sake of attaining even that happiness; by means of obtaining the supreme state of the deities, I destroy, I utterly annihilate, darkness. 157.

The deity is pleased with one who kills [the victim] after having reflected in this manner. Whatever worship was performed by those lovers in a previous birth— (p. 484) —[that is what is attained]. 158.
Those sacrificial animals indeed attain perfection and become worthy of the offering;
having cast off their lives in the presence of the deity, they go to the abode of the gods. || 159 ||
A man should treat all women with the same regard as he does his own wife; regarding them as goddesses, he should never speak harshly or anything unpleasant.
Likewise, one's own daughters, women, and others headed by Yakṣiṇīs should be enjoyed by the Vāmin; this is the eternal dharma. || 161 ||
In the Uttarā [nakṣatras], no one at all should cause the discharge of semen.
One should not consider the touch of even Cāṇḍāla women to be a fault. || 162 ||
Upon seeing a woman in her menses, one should perform a single preparatory rite;
one should then personally carry out the oblation with liquor alone. || 163 ||
Then, from the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), a deity appearing as half the body of a goddess shall arise;
she shall say, "Choose a boon," to whichever worshiper one may have in mind. || 164 ||

In a cremation ground, in an empty house, beneath a shrine, or upon a corpse; or upon a skull, in a place of purification, or in an empty temple; or in a liquor-distilling shed—one should perform [the rite] there, for the deities reside in those places. 165.
One should not worship a Śālagrāma stone, nor should one ever touch Tulasī.
One should not undertake a pilgrimage to sacred sites, nor should one perform a ritual bath in the Gaṅgā.

In the absence of bathing, one should perform the recitation (japa) during the first menstrual period; having placed a cloth beneath the seat while reciting, one shall attain success (siddhi). || 167 ||
Generally, when the Guru has mastered the mantra through the left-hand path (vāmamārga), success is attained at that very moment;
otherwise, one becomes like a ghost. || 168 ||
I shall explain to you that subtle and wonderful means by which success is swiftly attained through the practice of the left-hand path (vāmamārga). || 169 ||
On the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, or on a Tuesday, one should take a human skull and fill it with liquor, meat, and boiled rice mixed with fermented beans;
having prepared this, one should go to a site beneath an Aśvattha tree. (170)
Having smeared the ground at its base in a solitary, secluded place.
The staff-measures in the eight directions [and the characteristics of the staff have been stated by the venerable Bhāskarācārya].
"A finger-breadth (aṅgula) consists of eight barley-corns;
four fingers multiplied by six make a cubit (hasta). Four cubits make a staff (daṇḍa), and two thousand of those [staffs] make a krośa. One should fill the stakes with the root-mantra. 171.
With one thousand and eight [threads], he should tie a cord made of seven strands; there, he should perform the worship of the deity. || 172 ||
Having established the Goddess in his heart, he should place a lamp in that location.
And one should perform it with castor oil; in its absence, with the sacrificial offerings of Kapila.
In its absence, however, one should prepare a lamp with a *kuḍava* measure of oil;
a wick made of eight hundred threads is prescribed. || 174 ||
One should place a skull upon it for the sake of its soot; having gazed at the lamp, one should recite the mantra and not look at anything else. (175)
When half the oil has been consumed by the flame, bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas—assuming various forms and uttering diverse cries—terrify the practitioner. || 176 ||
One should not be afraid; one should cast that food with the left hand. One should not look at anything else in their presence, but should indeed gaze only at the lamp. || 177 ||
When a small amount of the lamp oil remains, that goddess shall become the bestower of boons;
having offered her that bali-oblation and praised her, one should request a boon. || 178 ||
If the deity does not come due to the ripening of past karma, one should take soot from the edge of a lamp after having worshipped the goddess there. (179)
One should bring that which has been perfected into one's house; by giving it to the eyes, the entire world shall come under one's control.
Having applied that collyrium to the eyes, one should then perform the ritual applications.
All these things succeed only when the Guru is free from greed; one should properly guard the ointment, otherwise Bhairava arises. (181)
Thus has this great work composed by Gaṇeśa been narrated to you; let all the gods speak, for what more is there to be said? 182.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Mantra of Gaṇapati according to the Northern Tradition," in the *Merutantra* composed by Śiva with the approval of the illustrious Mahāmāyā and Mahākāla.
The Illustrious Goddess said:

Now, therefore, I shall fully describe Vāmā Ghaṭasarasvatī.

And the syllables *hasakhaphara*—namely: *haṃ sphreṃ hsrauṃ hauṃ sphrauṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ drāṃ hrīṃ klīṃ blūṃ saḥ ghīṃ ghaṭasarasvati ghaṭe vada vada tura tura rudrājñayā mamābhilāṣaṃ kuru kuru svāhā*—this consists of forty-three syllables including fire (*va*) and the Vedas (*vedārṇa*). When this twelve-syllable mantra has been recited to the extent of one hundred thousand syllables;

The arrangement of the limbs is by means of five, five, eight, five, five, two, and four syllables.

In the third line of the house of the earth (Bhūmigṛha) are the Mothers: [Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Mahālakṣmī—these are the eight Mothers]. Again: 78.
Having thus performed the first enclosure, one should display the yonimudrā.

Kuleśī, Kulanandā, Vāgīśā, and likewise Bhairavī.
Umā, Śrī, Śānti, Caṇḍā, Dhūmrā, Kālī, and Karālinī. || 80 ||

Pratyaṅgirā, Siddhalakṣmī, Amṛteśī, and Caṇḍikā.

Homage! [Oṃ, homage to her who sits on the lotus, whose form is the lotus; Aiṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ, speak, speak, O Goddess of Speech, svāhā! This is the mantra. She who sits on the lotus, whose form is the lotus, is Vāgbhuvaneśvarī. 94.

"O eloquent speaker, may desire speak the two words; svāhā. If preceded by the *dhruva* (the syllable *oṃ*), that is, joined with the *praṇava* at the beginning, it becomes a twenty-four-syllable mantra.

The great poet [attains his goal] from the recitation of one hundred thousand syllables, and worship is performed in the east. || 95 ||

[Combined with *ha-sa-ka-la-ra-ā-yu*, having joined these four syllables—*ha-sa-ka-la-ra-ā-ni-ma*—one then says *hrīṃ*, followed by *vadavada*, then *citreśvari aiṃ svāhā*; through this arrangement of words, the twelve-syllable mantra is formed. The two instances of *vada* are [formed] by means of the syllable *īṃ*.

One should worship the woman born of the Kula with the eleven-syllable mantra.
Vāṅmāyā Śrīṃ [Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ vadavada Kīrtīśvari Svāhā]. The pair "vada" (speak, speak), Kīrtīśvarī, and the beloved of Agni (the letter Ra).
One should worship Kīrttināyikā in the southwest with the thirteen-syllable mantra. || 99 ||

Having accomplished the fifth cycle with [Aiṃ Heṃ Hīṃ Kiṇi Kiṇi Vicce Kiṇi Sarasvatyāṃ], this nine-syllable mantra [Aiṃ Heṃ Hīṃ Kiṇi Kiṇi Vicce Kiṇi] shall manifest the states of agitation and joy. 101.

With a pen made from a blade of dūrvā grass and smeared with the juice of gorocanā.
One should inscribe the mantra upon the tongue of a child whose umbilical cord has not yet been severed.

Vaca root, consecrated with ten thousand recitations of the mantra, [should be tied] around the neck of the child.
One should bind [the victim] after offering the oblation previously described according to the prescribed ritual.
When the twelfth year arrived, she, the author of the poem, was devoured.

Having abandoned shame and fear at a crossroads or in a cemetery, [one should practice].

Devoted to his recitation, he hears that sound at midnight.
Become one who has gone to the further shore of all branches of knowledge; attain every spiritual accomplishment.

Having constructed a beautiful altar in a secluded grove of plantain trees,

Knowledge, happiness, wealth, nourishment, longevity, fame, strength, and prosperity.

Two lotuses, a noose and a goad, and a hook and a sugarcane bow.
Holding fearlessness and flower-arrows with her sprout-like hands.
She was golden-hued and surrounded by seven youthful female messengers.
[He was attended] by those beautiful [attendants] holding chowries, mirrors, water-vessels, and betel-rolls in their hands. || 132 ||
Beholding the practitioner with a gracious gaze, she should think as follows:

Together with the bindus: [aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ klīṃ sauḥ]. The twelve vowels alone constitute the first seed-syllable.

One should perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) by joining "oṃ sāṃsīṃ" with the preceding mantras in the moments that serve as the locus for their prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). For example: *sām oṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *sīṃvāṃ* to the head, *svāhā*; *sūṃ śrīṃ* to the tuft of hair (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ*; *saiṃ hrīṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*), *hum*; *sauṃ sphreṃ* to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*; *saḥ sauṃ* to the weapon (*astra*), *phaṭ*. Thus, the arrangement of the limbs is performed with *saiṃ*, *sauṃ*, and *saḥ* preceded by the aforementioned syllables. (143)

O you who are garlanded with the blazing flames of the nectar-splendor of omniscience! O satisfied one, speak, speak! To the primordial awakened one, the wielder of the vajra, the holder of the vajra, who is independent, eternal, and whose innate form consists of undiminished power—to him, the infinite power, the sacrificial victim, the *paśu*, for the *pāśupatāstra* of the thousand-eyed one, *huṃ phaṭ*. After that:
Having said "I am satisfied," say "Speak, speak" to the Adamantine One of primordial awakening.
To the Vajra-holder, who is independent, eternal, and possesses unimpaired power.
And one should offer the bali of infinite power to the co-emergent formless one. || 145 ||
One should utter the words "paśuṃ huṃ phaṭ pāśupatāstrāya."
The mantra beginning with "sahasrākṣāya" is said to consist of seventy syllables.
Thus she is the granter of all desires; now her meditation is described.

Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the mantra of Viṣṇu and Vāgīśvarī.

Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the mantra of the supreme Mistress of Speech.
One should utter: *hrīṃ vācaspate amṛtaplūḥ plūṃhrīṃsauṃ*. (151)

The goddess Viṣṇuvāgīśvarī and the Virāṭ meter have been proclaimed. || 152 ||
The seed-syllable (bīja) should be *plūḥ* and *śakti*, and the heart-mantra (*hṛd*) is *vācaspate*.

"O Lord of Speech, [grant] immortality"—this is the eye-mantra; likewise, *plūḥ* and *plūṃ* are the weapon-mantra. (153)
The practice of meditation, worship, and so forth is now described as before.
Eating only sacrificial food for a year, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times every day. || 154 ||
At the end of the recitation, having recited it ten times, one should drink water with that [mantra].
By that, supramundane intelligence is born; of this there is no doubt. || 155 ||
One should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times during the lunar days while subsisting on food cooked in cow’s urine.
One should offer eight thousand oblations with fuel-sticks of kola wood smeared with clarified butter.
The practitioner knows all that has been, that is to be, and that which is present. || 156 ||
Whoever should drink the juice of *brāhmī* mixed with *kapilā* ghee in the morning;
One should recite the mantra ten times over a single handful of water for the purpose of purifying the three impurities.
One should retain in memory the Vedas, Shastras, and so forth, as they have been proclaimed, even if only once.
Whatever he hears but once, that is never forgotten by him at any time. || 158 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the auspicious mantra of Padmāvatī.

What is the use of much speaking? By the mere knowledge of this vidyā, [all is attained].
One will certainly obtain knowledge of the scriptures, the destruction of sins, and all happiness. || 673 ||
Having risen at dawn and sat upon his bed, he should recite [the mantra] one hundred times.
Within a month, the practitioner of mantra shall conquer the poet by means of his own poetic skill.
The Vidyā is fixed by Śiva; its extraction is now described.
One should recite the mantra over the Māyā-tāra cloth one hundred and eight times.
If it occurs at the beginning as well as at the end of the mantra, it shall indeed bestow accomplishment.
This rule must certainly be kept secret by a practitioner who desires spiritual accomplishment.
This Chinnamastā has arisen on this path, bestowing supreme siddhi.
Now I shall describe the supreme mantra consisting of sixteen syllables, which has four divisions.
*Śrīṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ aiṃ [śrīṃ hrīṃ eṃ aiṃ vajravairocanīye hrīṃ hrūṃ svāhā]. This mantra consists of fifteen syllables. *Vajravairocanīye hrīṃ ca hrūṃ* is the beloved [mantra].

The lunar day (tithi) of Fire, preceded by the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī (*śrīṃ*), is for wealth; that is to say, the previously mentioned mantra, having joined *śrīṃ* at the beginning, brings about the acquisition of wealth. || 678 ||

Beginning with the seed-syllable of modesty [Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hrūṃ Aiṃ Vajravairocanīye Hrīṃ Hrūṃ Svāhā], this is the mantra for subjugation. For the purpose of subjugation, one uses [the mantra] beginning with Hrūṃ; it destroys all sins.
Liberation occurs through that which begins with the seed-syllable Vāk; there are four [mantras] beginning with the Praṇava. || 679 ||
These sixteen syllables have been uttered by the mouth of the Four-faced One.
The sage Brahmā is proclaimed as the one to be worshipped by the four Vedas.
The ritual placement (nyāsa), worship, and so forth are as before; now, a certain optional rite (kāmya) is described here.
One should give a sacrificial fee to the teacher, as well as various kinds of garments.
The Guru alone is the refuge for dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
This great mantra has been accomplished; it bestows all spiritual attainments.
He bestows the eight great siddhis; how much more so his beloved minor ones?
One should prescribe the white flower for enjoyment, liberation, and peace.
In all rites performed for specific desires, the meditation should consist of the colors of the flowers.
Whether waking, sleeping, rising, eating, or even restraining himself.
One should recite the mantra at all times; for such a person, no transgression exists. || 684 ||
Having written the mantra on one's own hand, one should perform the fist-binding gesture.
One should paralyze the animal and the weapons as long as one does not release the fist.
Having written the mantra on his own hand, he should touch the patient and recite it.
One is indeed suddenly liberated from disease; freed from disease, one becomes happy. || 686 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the great mantra of universal color.
Vajravairocanīye hrūṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ svāhā, beginning with the eternal [mantra].
The meditation, worship, and so forth are as before; now some optional rites are being proclaimed. || 687 ||
And whoever recites this mantra with pure meditation alone, [attains success].
A man may raise up one who has been bitten by hundreds of mahoragas and is dead.
By means of blood, all those who dwell in the subterranean realms (bhūtalavāsinaḥ) are brought under control.
By means of the yellow [syllable], one should always paralyze boats, horses, elephants, and so forth.
Having written the mantra on one's own hand, as long as one does not release the fist.
By merely performing this meditation, a person shall cause his enemies to be eradicated.
One may even kill [the enemy] effortlessly through meditation on Kṛṣṇa; of this there is no doubt. || 690 ||
And one should perform the satiation rite with milk and milk-rice (pāyasa).
There, the practitioner [should offer oblations] with clarified butter, honey, or even liquor. || 691 ||
The Brahmin, the Kshatriya, the Vaishya, and the Shudra, respectively.
By means of the prescribed rite of satiation (tarpaṇa), one becomes spontaneously perfected. || 692 ||
Then one should perform the fire sacrifice with sacrificial fuel sticks and likewise with flowers.
And likewise by means of oblations of *śrīphala* fruits and of *udumbara* wood. || 693 ||
The fire sacrifice that bestows all accomplishments should be performed with diligent effort.
Having performed one hundred and eight repetitions [of the mantra—this is the understood sense], one should offer oblations after the libation (tarpaṇa). || 694 ||
I shall now describe the ritual procedure for the flower-oblation (puṣpahoma), which bestows the fulfillment of all desires.
One should perform this daily for one hundred and eight repetitions over a period of six months.
Alternatively, one should perform it for at least one hundred thousand times; then success will certainly be attained.
Every day, at the conclusion of the fire-oblation, there shall be an offering (bali) consisting of ghee and meat.
One may revive a person bitten by the Time-Snake using white horse-killer flowers.
By offering sesame flowers smeared with honey, there shall be supreme prosperity. || 697 ||
With a thousand karṇikāra flowers and sesame seeds, one shall obtain a beautiful woman.
By offering ten thousand bandhūka flowers accompanied by clarified butter, one shall become fortunate. || 698 ||
With bandhūka flowers mixed with sesame seeds and rice grains.
With red sandalwood and rakta-aśvamāra flowers, a king is brought under control. || 699 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the mantras of Tārā that bestow the gift of poetic inspiration.
[These mantras] were correctly received from the mouth of the Guru and accomplished through the Vāmācāra practice. || 700 ||
If, by the power of the unseen, the attainment of this mantra arises, [then success is achieved].
It should be given to the eldest son, and never to others.
All those mantras which are worshipped by way of the Left-hand path (vāmamārga), however—
A sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should never be given to one's own son or similar relatives.
That Brahmin who, abandoning his own family, bestows [his wealth] upon a stranger for the sake of a sacrificial fee.
But those two who practice the path of the left (vāmamārga) are fallen from both worlds. || 703 ||
Oṃ māyā trīṃ huṃ phaṭ; thus is considered the five-syllabled mantra.
The sage is named Akṣobhya, and the meter for this is said to be Bṛhatī. || 704 ||
The goddess Tārā is the deity; *hrīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *hūṃ* is proclaimed here as the power (*śakti*).

Here, by means of each one of these six long pairs of *jaya* syllables—[namely, hrāṃ, hrīṃ, hrūṃ, hraiṃ, hrauṃ, hraḥ]—one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs. Thus, the procedure for the six limbs has been declared. (705)
Then one should perform the sixfold placement (nyāsa) of Tārā, which bestows all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis).

In this regard, first is the primary assignment (*nyāsa*). [The assignment beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha has already been stated previously; therefore, it is not mentioned here. That which begins with Śrīkaṇṭha was explained earlier. (706)
Having uttered the letters of the alphabet, one should speak preceded by *hrīṃ*, *trīṃ*, and *huṃ*.
In the place of the Mātṛkās, [one should worship] Śrīkaṇṭha and the others, together with their consorts, ending with the word "namaḥ. (707)
Having thus assigned [the mantras] ending in the dative case, this is remembered as the first placement (nyāsa).
While performing this ritual placement (nyāsa), one should contemplate the Goddess in this manner: || 708 ||
Seated upon a corpse-throne, she is blue-hued and possesses three eyes.
She has the crescent moon as her crest-ornament, is enriched with various ornaments, and possesses four arms.

Secondly, one should perform the placement of the planets (*grahanyāsa*), recollecting them as follows: *Hrīṃ trīṃ huṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ*, salutation to the red-colored Sūrya in the heart; *hrīṃ trīṃ huṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ*, salutation to the white-colored Soma between the eyebrows; *hrīṃ trīṃ huṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ*, salutation to the red-colored Maṅgala at the three eyes; *hrīṃ trīṃ huṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ*, salutation to the dark-colored Budha on the chest. In this manner, the placement of the remaining planets should be performed.
One should place a red sun, preceded by the three seed-syllables and vowels, in the heart.
For likewise, one should place the white Soma preceded by the letter 'a' between the two eyebrows.
Thus, one who knows the ritual application of mantras should perform an auspicious rite beginning with the *ka*-group of consonants.
The three eyes are red, and the first letter of the *ca*-group is on the chest.
One should place Budha, who is dark-complexioned, and the yellow-colored Guru, the first of the Ṭa-group, on the throat.
The letter beginning with the *tavarga*, white in color, belongs to Bhārgava and is located in the uvula (*ghaṇṭikā*).
One should visualize Saturn, blue in color and beginning with the letter 'pa' (of the pavarga), in the region of the navel.
Having meditated upon Rāhu, who is smoke-colored and begins with the letter śa, one should place him in the mouth.
One should then place Ketu, who has the appearance of smoke-colored ash and begins with the letter *lakṣa*, upon the navel.
I shall now describe the third nyāsa, preceded by the triad of seed-syllables.

Having pronounced the corresponding vowels, [one should assign them as follows]: *hrīṃ trīṃ huṃ aṃ iṃ uṃ ṛṃ ḷṃ aiṃ oṃ aṃ mūrdhni pūrve indrāya namaḥ* (Hrīṃ trīṃ huṃ, aṃ iṃ uṃ ṛṃ ḷṃ aiṃ oṃ aṃ on the head, in the east, obeisance to Indra); *hrīṃ trīṃ huṃ āṃ īṃ ūṃ ṝṃ ḹṃ aiṃ auṃ aḥ mūrdhnyāgneyyām agnaye namaḥ* (Hrīṃ trīṃ huṃ, āṃ īṃ ūṃ ṝṃ ḹṃ aiṃ auṃ aḥ on the head, in the southeast, obeisance to Agni); *hrīṃ trīṃ huṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ dakṣiṇe yamāya namo mukhe* (Hrīṃ trīṃ huṃ, kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ in the south, obeisance to Yama at the mouth), and so forth. "Obeisance to Indra in the east," etc. (715).
Accompanied by a long vowel, [one should offer] "Salutation to Agni" in the southeast.
To the south, "Salutation to Yama"; on the forehead, the first letter of the ka-group.
The first letter of the *ca*-group is in the southwest; "Salutation to Nairṛti" is at the mouth.
Then, at the throat, [one should worship] the first letter of the ṭa-group, followed by "Salutation to Varuṇa. (717)
One should assign the first of the *tavarga* [the letter *ta*] to the heart, and "Salutation to Vāyu" to the northwest.
The first letter of the labial class (pa) is for Kubera; one should offer salutation on the right hand. || 718 ||
In the left hand, beginning with the *ya*-group, there is the heart-mantra for Rudra in the northeast.
One should place "namo" for the sake of the desire for that which is above the letter *śa* (the letter *ṣa*) at the navel.
One should perform the ritual placement (vinyāsa) with "huṃ lakṣādyaṃ pṛthivyai" at the heart and the feet.
Now the fourth assignment, known as Śiva-Śakti, is being described.
Preceded by *hrīṃ*, *trīṃ*, and *huṃ*, this supreme mantra should be employed to remove the sins of the senses.
Brahmā, joined with a Ḍākinī, preceded by the syllables beginning with *va* and ending with *sa*.

One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the four-petaled [lotus] as follows: at the *mūlādhāra*, "Hrīṃ Trīṃ Huṃ Vaṃ Śaṃ Ṣaṃ Saṃ, obeisance to Brahmā together with Ḍākinī"; at the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, "Hrīṃ Trīṃ Huṃ Baṃ Bhaṃ Maṃ Yaṃ Raṃ Laṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu together with Śākinī"; and at the *maṇipūraka*, "Ḍaṃ Ḍhaṃ Ṇaṃ Taṃ Thaṃ Daṃ Dhaṃ Naṃ Paṃ Phaṃ, obeisance to Rudra together with Lākinī. (721)
One should worship Śrī Viṣṇu, joined with Śakti and preceded by the letters beginning with 'va' and ending with 'la'.
One should place [the deities] upon the six-petalled wheel called Svādhiṣṭhāna, which is situated at the linga. || 722 ||
One should worship Rudra joined with Lākinī, preceded by the letters beginning with Ḍa and ending with Pha.
One should place [the mantra] upon the ten-petalled wheel located at the navel, known as Maṇipūraka.
The Lord, preceded by the letters from Ka to Tha and joined with Kākinī.
One should place [the syllables] upon the twelve-petaled [lotus] located in the heart, within the Anāhata [cakra].
[One should worship] Sadāśiva and Śākinī, conjoined with the sixteen vowels.
One should place [the syllables] in the sixteen-petaled lotus located at the throat, known as Viśuddha. || 725 ||
Likewise, one should meditate on Paraśiva, conjoined with Hākinī, at the Ājñā-cakra.
Preceded by the syllable *hakṣa*, it is situated between the eyebrows, O enchanting one. (726)
One should explain the fifth nyāsa, which destroys all misfortunes.

Aṃ Āṃ Ka-varga [hrīṃ trīṃ huṃ aṃ āṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ; salutation to Tārā at the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head); hrīṃḥ trīṃ huṃ iṃ īṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ; salutation to Ugrā on the forehead; hrīṃ trīṃ huṃ uṃ ūṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ; salutation to Mahogrā between the eyebrows—the same should be understood for the subsequent groups]. Hrīṃ trīṃ huṃ; salutation to Tārā is thus declared. || 727 ||
Then one should place the syllables *iṃ* and *īṃ*, as well as the *ca*-group, in the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
One should also place *hrīṃ trīṃ huṃ nama ugrāyai* on the forehead. || 728 ||
Uṃ ūṃ, the ṭa-group, hrīṃ trīṃ huṃ; salutation to Mahogrā.
And one should place the *tavarga* [consonants] along with *ṛṃ* and *ṝṃ* between the eyebrows and at the throat.
"Hrīṃ trīṃ huṃ" and "namo vajrāyai" at the end [of the mantra] for all [the goddesses]. (729)
One should place *ḷṃ*, *ḹṃ*, the labial class (*pavarga*), and *hrīṃ trīṃ huṃ namaḥ kālyai* upon the heart.
Eṃ Aiṃ, the *y*-group, Hrīṃ Trīṃ Huṃ, and to Sarasvatī at the navel.
Omauṃ savaraṃ hrīṃ trīṃ huṃ, [offer] to Kāmeśvarī upon the liṅga. || 730 ||
One should assign the syllables *aṃ*, *aḥ*, *lakṣau*, *ca*, *hrīṃ*, *trīṃ*, *huṃ*, and *cāmuṇḍāyai namaḥ*.
Afterwards, one should place [the mantras] at the *mūlādhāra* and perform the *pīṭhanyāsa*.
On the *ādhāra*: [Hrīṃ Trīṃ Huṃ Aṃ Iṃ Uṃ Ṛṃ Ḷṃ Eṃ Oṃ Aṃ; homage to the seat (*pīṭha*) of Kāmarūpa on the *ādhāra*. The one called Kāmarūpa is preceded by the seed-syllables and the short vowels.
One should place Jālandhara-pīṭha in the heart, preceded by the long vowels: [Hrīṃ Trīṃ Huṃ Āṃ Īṃ Ūṃ Ṛṃ Ḷṃ Aiṃ Auṃ Aḥ, obeisance to Jālandhara-pīṭha in the heart]. || 732 ||

On the forehead, the wise practitioner should perform the placement of the seat known as Pūrṇagiri, beginning with the *ka*-group: [Hrīṃ Trīṃ Huṃ Kaṃ Khaṃ Gaṃ Ghaṃ Ṅaṃ, salutation to the Pīṭha of Pūrṇagiri on the forehead].

[Uḍḍiyānaṃ (hrīṃ trīṃ huṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ), obeisance to the sacred seat of Uḍḍiyāna at the junction of the hair. One should place the second letter of the *ca*-group at the junction of the hair. (733)
The seat of Vārāṇasī, beginning with the *ṭa*-group [hrīṃ trīṃ huṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ; obeisance to the seat of Vārāṇasī on the eyebrows], is well-established on the eyebrows.

One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of Avantī upon the two eyes, preceded by the *tavarga* [consonants]: [Hrīṃ Trīṃ Huṃ Taṃ Thaṃ Daṃ Dhaṃ Naṃ; Namaḥ to the sacred seat (*pīṭha*) of Avantī on the two eyes, and so forth. 734.
One should place the sacred seat of Māyāpurī with the letter preceding the labial class (pa) at the mouth.
One should place the seat of Mathurā at the throat, beginning with the letter 'ya'.
One should not recite "nābhāvayodhyā"; rather, one should properly place the first letter of the *śa*-group [the letter *śa*].
One should install the tenth seat, Kāñcīpurī, on the hips.
The sixfold ritual placement (nyāsa) of Tārā, which bestows all desired boons, has thus been declared.
Seated upon a shimmering white lotus in the waters of the great dissolution.
Holding a scissor, a sword, a blue lotus, and a skull-cup in her hands.
She who has a serpent for a girdle, serpents for hands, and serpents for bracelets and earrings.
She was dark blue in luster, with red eyes, and adorned with bracelets, armlets, and anklets made of snakes.
She has tawny, fierce, single matted locks, three eyes, and is clothed in a tiger skin.
With a face made terrifying by fangs, a lolling tongue, and a smiling countenance.
She binds a band of human bone upon her forehead, bearing the Lord of Sages, Akṣobhya.
And one should meditate on her as she establishes that [corpse] beneath herself, seated upon the heart of the corpse.
Various kinds of worship for her have been revealed in each respective tantra. || 741 ||
Success will inevitably arise from recitation; that is what is here called worship.
For one who performs Vedic rituals, knowledge does not succeed.
If a follower of the Vedas should give or receive [a gift] out of greed or delusion, [he incurs sin].
There would be the destruction of both families, and poverty in birth after birth. (743)
But when Śakra was intoxicated by his own power, [the world was restored] by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
She was accomplished by means of the left-hand path for the sake of the victory of the gods. || 744 ||
Having produced the elephant and the others, and having honored the Lord of the Gods.
Having displayed his own prowess, Śakra was made the lord of the gods.
Therefore, when accomplished by means of the left-hand path, she brings about excellence.
Having performed the tantric ablution, one should fetch water for the purpose of worship.
*Tāraṃ* [Oṃ vajrodake hūṃ phaṭ]; *vajrodake hūṃ phaṭ* consists of seven syllables for the grasping of the joined palms (*añjali*).
Having set aside his sandals and shoes, the worshipper should fetch water.
And thereafter, one should perform the sipping of water (ācamana) three times with this mantra.
One should utter the *tāra* [Oṃ hrīṃ suviśuddhadharmasarvapāpāniśāmyāśeṣavikalpānayanāya svāhā] and then the *māyā*, which is the word for the utterly pure Dharma (*suviśuddhadharmasarvapada*). 748.
"May all evils be pacified without remainder," and "Bringing about the removal of conceptual constructions."
The mantra for sipping water (ācamana) consists of twenty-six syllables, beginning with "svāhā. || 749 ||
Then one should perform the binding of the topknot with this mantra: [Oṃ maṇidhari vajriṇi śikhariṇi sarvavaśaṅkariṇi huṃ phaṭ svāhā ||] Oṃ maṇi.
O you who hold the vajra upon the earth, O mountain-dweller, you who bring all under control! || 750 ||
The mantra consisting of twenty-three syllables ends with "ṇi huṃ phaṭ" and the wife of fire (svāhā).
Then the practitioner should perform the purification of the ground with the nine-syllable mantra.
Oṃ rakṣa rakṣa [oṃ rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ phaṭ svāhā] | Hūṃ cāstraṃ svāhā; this is the nine-syllable mantra.
Then, one should dispel obstacles with the thirteen-syllable mantra.
Oṃ, drive away all obstacles! [Oṃ, drive away all obstacles, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! Hūṃ phaṭ! Jvalanapriyā! || 753 ||
One should contemplate the seed-syllable of Māyā, *hrīṃ*, resembling a hibiscus flower, at the navel.
With the fire arising from that [meditation], one should burn the body together with one's own evil.
The knower of mantras should contemplate the three seed-syllables, golden in luster, within his heart.
One should scatter the ashes of that evil upon the ground with the wind arising therefrom. || 755 ||
One should meditatively contemplate with devotion the seed-syllable *hūṃ*, radiant as the moon or jasmine, upon the forehead.
By means of this purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one shall attain similarity with the Goddess. || 756 ||
Then, for the sake of worshipping the Goddess, one should consecrate the earth (Kāśyapī) with the syllable *dhruva* (the *oṃ*-syllable).
The mantra for the purifying vajra is: [Oṃ pavitravajrabhūme hūṃ phaṭ svāhā ||] Oṃ bhūme hūṃ svāhā; this is the imperishable syllable. || 757 ||
And one should draw a mandala on the ground with the twelve-syllable mantra.
[Oṃ āsurekhe vajrarekhe huṃ svāhā ||] Khe vajrarekhe huṃ svāhā, preceded by the Praṇava (Oṃ). || 758 ||
One should thoroughly purify the flowers with the fourteen-syllable mantra.
Regarding the "consecration as it was received": [Oṃ yathābhiṣeka-sāmagrī me hūṃ phaṭ svāhā ||] one should utter the words "sāmagrī me."
The mantra consisting of the letters of the king (nṛpa-varṇa), ending with *tārā* (om), *hūṃ*, *phaṭ*, and *svāhā*, is thus considered. || 759 ||
Then, the excellent practitioner should purify the mind by means of the five-syllable mantra.
Oṃ [Oṃ Oṃ Hrīṃ Svāhā]. Āṃ Hrīṃ Vahnigṛhiṇī; this five-syllable mantra is for the purification of the mind. (760)
Then, for the purpose of placing the *arghya*, one should say "Laṃ" and wipe [the vessel].
One should [purify] the ground and the mandala of the mandala with the previously mentioned mantra. (761)
One should draw a circle and a triangle, and outside of that, a square enclosure.
Therein, one should perform the worship of the foundational power (Ādhāraśakti), as well as Kūrma and Śeṣa.
One should place the support there with the mantra "Oṃ hrīṃ phaṭ."
There, one should worship the support with "vaṃ" for the fire-maṇḍala: [Oṃ vaṃ, obeisance to the fire-maṇḍala]. || 763 ||
Then, with the nine-syllable mantra beginning with *namaḥ*, [one should worship] the guardian of hell.
Having washed it with the mantra *huṃ phaṭ*, one should establish it with the seed-syllable *sthīṃ*.
Then one should worship the human skull and mutter those four mantras.
One should utter "namas" preceded by *hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ*, [namely: *hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ kālīkapālāya namaḥ*].
The mantra consists of eleven syllables; by means of it, worship and other rites are prescribed. || 765 ||
Having uttered "strāṃ strīṃ strūṃ tāriṇī," [strāṃ strīṃ strūṃ tāriṇī-kapālāya namaḥ], [strāṃ strīṃ strūṃ] ends with "namaḥ" for the skull (kapāla).
With the twelve-syllable mantra, the second worship of the skull should take place here. || 766 ||
Having uttered "hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ," one should say this: "Obeisance to Nīlakapāla."
The third worship of the skull is said to consist of eleven syllables.

*Māyāṃ strīṃ huṃ [hrīṃ strīṃ huṃ] svargakapālāya sarvādhārāya sarvāya sarvodbhavāya sarvaśuddhimayāya sarvāsurarudhirāruṇāya śubhrāya surābhājanāya devīkapālāya namaḥ.* One should utter "svargakapālāya" for every calamity (*sarvāpadam*).
Then [he offered it] to Dhārā, to Sarvā, and likewise to Sarvodbhavā. || 768 ||
"To that which consists of all purity" and "to the destroyer of all asuras."
And to Rāruṇa, to Śubhra, and to Itisurābhājana. || 769 ||
"Salutation to Devīkapāla"—thus the fourth mantra has been declared.
This [mantra] consisting of fifty-six syllables is for the worship of the skull-cup. (770)
Then, one should worship the solar mandala within that skull.
Oṃ sūryamaṇḍalāya namaḥ; this is the nine-syllable mantra. || 771 ||
In the worship of the solar orb, the mantra is considered to be within a human skull.
Reciting the root mantra [Oṃ hrīṃ trīṃ huṃ phaṭ], one should pour the liquor into it with the thought that it is nectar.
